stories.title: Gus, the world's oldest tortoise, wished a speedy recovery from surgery by N.S. politicians
stories.summary: Gus, 104, who has been a fixture at Halifax’s Museum of Natural History for decades, went into surgery Tuesday to remove a bladder stone.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A lowly 104-year-old tortoise that underwent surgery Tuesday to remove a bladder stone is getting encouragement from high places in his Nova Scotia home.

“Premier Tim Houston shared his well-wishes for Gus when it was announced that he would be undergoing surgery,” Houston’s press secretary, Catherine Klimek, said Tuesday in an email.

“It’s been very sweet seeing all the love Gus has received the last few weeks.”

Gus has been a fixture at Halifax’s Museum of Natural History for decades. He is believed to be the oldest gopher tortoise in the world, celebrating his 104th birthday on Aug. 10.

Halifax Mayor Andy Fillmore also had words of encouragement for the slow-moving museum attraction.

“For decades, Gus has welcomed countless visitors from all around the world,” Fillmore said in a written statement.

“Over these past few weeks, we’ve seen a remarkable display of appreciation and affection for him. I join the many residents who are wishing him well as he heads into surgery, and look forward to visiting him again very soon.”

Gus went into surgery early Tuesday to remove a bladder stone, said Rob Maguire, who speaks for Nova Scotia’s Department of Communities, Culture, Tourism and Heritage.

“The last I checked, he was still in surgery,” Maguire said mid-afternoon.

By 5 p.m., Gus was awake and doing well, according to Jeff Gray, the museum’s manager.

“They were able to remove the entire bladder stone,” Gray said. “It was a complete success … According to the vets, he’s doing great.”

Gus will stay at the animal hospital for 48 hours.

“When he does get back, we expect it will be eight to 10 weeks before he goes back on public view here at the museum,” Gray said.

Gus was initially diagnosed with the bladder stone in 2009. Bladder stones are common in reptiles and tortoises like Gus, Maguire said.

It wasn’t causing him any problems, and the veterinarian recommended leaving it alone.

“The alternative of removing it was a fairly invasive surgery,” Maguire said.

Fast forward to his most recent scans from this year. “It had grown, so the decision was made to go in and remove it now because if it grew any further, it might start to pose a problem for him,” Maguire said.

“Also, since 2009, there have been advances in veterinary care that have made this surgery a lot less invasive than it would have been back then.”

In 2009, surgeons would have had to cut through Gus’s shell to access his abdomen, Maguire said.

“Now they’re able to do it by creating a small incision in his leg and to access his bladder through his abdominal cavity through that leg,” he said.

“It’s much less invasive, it decreases the risk of surgery, and it makes recovery a lot easier and shorter.”

Generations of children have visited Gus for decades to feed him lettuce and bananas.

“My father (age 71) who was born and raised here — he remembers seeing Gus when he was a kid,” Maguire said.

“Now I’ve got a seven-year-old niece who also loves him, too.”

Gus is a Gopher Tortoise, otherwise know as gopherus polyphemus, which are native to the U.S. South and one of the oldest living species on the planet.

“But for Haligonians, we call him Gopher Gus the Lettuce King. Or just Gus, for short.” reads a history of Gus prepared by Halifax Public Libraries

One of the museum’s former curators acquired Gus in 1942 from a reptile institute in Silver Springs, Fla. He is believed to have been about 20 years old when he was purchased, according to the library’s Gus primer.

When he first took up residence in Halifax, he was given free rein of the museum. “He used to walk around the halls, in between the library stacks. Wherever you went, you were apt to fall over Gus.”

stories.title: Mark Carney to attend ‘Forever Canadian’ rallies ahead of Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney, who grew up in Alberta, focused his Thanksgiving Day message on the province's upcoming separation referendum, saying Canada is 'worth fighting for.'
stories.author: Catherine Morrison
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to attend two Forever Canadian rallies in Alberta this week, just ahead of the province’s referendum .

On Oct. 19, Albertans will vote on the whether to stay in Canada or hold a future separation referendum. There are also nine other questions involving constitutional and immigration issues.

The “Forever Canadian” campaign, launched by Alberta’s former deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk, seeks to encourage Albertans to vote to stay in Canada.

The organization’s website says Carney was invited to one rally in Calgary on Oct. 15 and another in Edmonton on Oct. 16. The Prime Minister’s Office confirmed Carney will attend both.

“We want the country’s leader to see what we see every day: Albertans from every walk of life standing up for a united Canada,” says the Forever Canadian website.

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, focused his Thanksgiving Day message on Alberta’s upcoming separation referendum , saying Canada is “worth fighting for.”

“This year, Thanksgiving is a bit different,” he said in a video message posted Monday and filmed at his old high school in Edmonton.

“A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future: whether to remain part of Canada or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada.”

Carney said the federal government is building “big things” in Alberta — including a planned new pipeline to the West Coast — but Canada can’t achieve those goals if the country is divided.

“You can’t build big things on fault lines,” he said.

Carney also said Canadians are “stronger together” as they face down threats to their economy, security and culture.

“Generations of Albertans helped build this country. It’s yours, it’s ours, and it’s worth fighting for,” he said.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is expected to deliver his own speech supporting Canadian unity in Calgary on Friday.

Poilievre is set to speak during the Canada Strong and Free Network conference on Oct. 16 in Calgary. His speech is expected to be followed by an address from Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

— With files from David Baxter and Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Saskatchewan politician says paid nearly $30K for private jets; NDP wants answers
stories.summary: Regina - A Saskatchewan Party backbencher says he paid close to $30,000 out of his own pocket for two trips on a private jet and that one of those flights was for government business.
stories.author: Jeremy Simes The Canadian Press
stories.content:
REGINA - A Saskatchewan Party backbencher says he paid close to $30,000 out of his own pocket for two trips on a private jet and that one of those flights was for government business.

By Jeremy Simes The Canadian Press

Kevin Weedmark released a letter Tuesday from Maurice Herauf, the province’s conflict of interest commissioner, who provided his opinion on the airfare expenses.

Herauf wrote in the Sept. 18 letter that Weedmark’s invoices indicate he paid for the flights with his own money and therefore did not violate a section of Conflict of Interest Act.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

“Since you paid for the flights from your personal funds there is absolutely no financial benefit that can be attributed to your decision to fly to functions on either date,” Herauf wrote.

The letter says Weedmark had asked Herauf to provide an opinion on his flights after the Opposition NDP had flagged it as a concern.

The trips took place over the course of a year.

On Aug. 21, 2025, Weedmark spent $8,271 on a private jet to fly the owners of the Moosomin Dairy Queen and two of their family members to the Jim Pattison Children’s Hospital in Saskatoon for a tour. The Dairy Queen had raised $42,000 for the hospital and Weedmark was one of their volunteers. Herauf wrote the trip was private in nature.

On Aug. 27 of this year, Weedmark spent $20,106 on another jet for two government functions in the province before making a stop in Regina and then flying back to Moosomin. One of the functions was an official opening of an addictions treatment facility in Lloydminster on the Alberta boundary, and the other was to celebrate the anniversary of a seniors complex in Saskatoon.

The letter says the health minister’s office had requested Weedmark attend both events, as Weedmark is also the minister’s legislative secretary. Weedmark has also said it would have been difficult for him to drive to Lloydminster in time, so he chose to fly.

However, the Opposition NDP says Weedmark still needs to show the receipts to prove he didn’t improperly benefit from his role as a legislature member.

Earlier Tuesday, the NDP sent a letter to Herauf asking for an opinion on whether Weedmark breached conflict of interest rules.

stories.title: U.S. court denies bail to alleged Tumbler Ridge shooting conspirator James Bryant
stories.summary: Seattle — A court in Seattle, Wash., has denied bail to James Bryant, who is accused of conspiring with Jesse Van Rootselaar, the shooter in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass killing in February.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
James Cody Bryant, centre, is seen in a court sketch drawn during the accused's appearance in U.S. district court in Seattle on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Lois Silver Lois Silver

By The Canadian Press

Posted October 13, 2026 6:03 pm.

Last Updated October 13, 2026 6:42 pm.

Seattle — A court in Seattle, Wash., has denied bail to James Bryant, who is accused of conspiring with Jesse Van Rootselaar, the shooter in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass killing in February.

Emilie Langlie with the Department of Justice says Bryant was ordered detained by the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington.

Federal prosecutors successfully argued to keep Bryant behind bars, alleging in a written submission that the Bellingham, Wash., resident “helped plan a mass murder over the course of several months” and would present a danger to the community if released.

Bryant’s public defender lawyer Dennis Carroll refers to her by female pronouns and says she goes by the name Melody.

Carroll had argued in a written submission that Bryant should be released because she has no criminal record, and has stable housing and employment and “strong community ties.”

The lawyer says his client voluntarily met with investigators and there’s no evidence she “initiated the planning or engaged in any violence” in relation to the attack that left eight victims dead, and instead “repeatedly tried to dissuade Van Rootselaar from committing mass murder.”

stories.title: Western PhD candidate advocates for hearing loss awareness in primary care
stories.summary: Western University PhD candidate Jana Bataineh is encouraging hearing loss screening in primary care to improve health, reduce dementia risk.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
When you put on eyeglasses for the very first time, you May be surprised at the wealth of new information that hits your senses. The individual leaves on a tree, road signs that become distinct or the particular way light spreads across a scene.

The same thing could happen when you put on a hearing aid for the first time, Jana Bataineh said.

“You don’t realize how much you’re missing.”

Bataineh is a PhD candidate in health and rehabilitation sciences, concurrently completing her master of clinical science in audiology in Western’s Faculty of Health Sciences.

Coming from a public health background, she’s seen time and time again how hearing loss is often minimized when it comes to people’s wellbeing.

She often encountered a common sentiment toward those with hearing loss: “Why can’t you just listen harder, pay more attention?” The misconception spurred her to bring hearing loss to light.

Inspired to make a change, Bataineh wanted to ensure people are tested for hearing loss before it’s too late, and get the resources they need to improve their health. The problem led her to develop a series of seminars designed specifically for primary care clinics, to bring hearing loss and screening to the forefront of the conversation.

Hearing loss is not isolated, she says. It can shape the way you interact with the world and completely change your quality of life. Importantly, it’s also one of the leading risk factors for dementia.

In the latest guidelinespublished by the World Health Organization, hearing loss is recognized as the leading, modifiable trait in cognitive decline. Not only does it often lead to social isolation, depression, and withdrawal from regular activities, but when hearing becomes challenging, the brain needs to work harder to make sense of sound, drawing from cognitive resources used in key mechanisms like attention and memory.

This is especially prevalent in adults over the age of 50; more than 60 per cent of older adults will develop hearing loss.

But despite the glaring statistics, the Canadian health-care system has no clear structure or program to catch or address this prevalent need. The Infant Hearing Program aims to screen all newborns at birth, but after that most Canadians aren’t regularly tested or prompted to be screened for hearing loss at any other moment in their health journey.

The responsibility often rests with individuals to identify hints of oncoming hearing loss and find a clinic where they can get tested; though because it develops slowly, it’s difficult for people to pinpoint and acknowledge.

“What really ends up happening is that they’ll spend many years with hearing difficulties, withdrawing from activities, dealing with the fallout, before they reach the point of taking action,” said Bataineh. Many cases are left untreated.

But hearing loss can be managed. Through interventions such as early screening, hearing aids and rehabilitation, people can maintain the communication they need to age well. It got Bataineh thinking: how could we better handle this condition, and how do we change the system to make it happen?

Bolstered by a student initiative grant from Speech-Language & Audiology Canada, Bataineh envisioned a future where patients are routinely screened by primary care providers like family doctors and nurses, connecting them directly with audiologists.

Not only could this catch hearing loss at its onset, it could lessen the load for busy physicians. This holistic model has been implemented with success in countries like the United Kingdom and Ireland, where integrating an audiologist directly into the primary care setting has relieved the caseload for family doctors.

In Canada, there largely remains a disconnect between the two health fields. Most physicians and patients aren’t discussing hearing in appointments. If it does come up, it could turn into a months long wait to see an Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) specialist or find a hearing test on their own. Beyond the challenge of getting to the right professional, audiology services are typically not covered by provincial health plans such as Ohip.

### “In order to stay on the world stage when it comes to health care, we want to make sure that our population is also getting access to these innovative models that streamline care.” – Jana Bataineh, PhD candidate in health and rehabilitation sciences

Seeing the gap, and the critical need for a new way forward, she took it upon herself to try and make this vision a reality.

Creating the Hearing Health Seminar Series, Bataineh reached out to primary care centres across the province, and set up lunchtime visits to present and discuss the importance of hearing well. Bringing along an audiologist to various sessions, Bataineh was able to spark direct conversations between hearing experts, physicians and clinic staff – from nurses to managers.

“There’s not a lot of education or training for physicians on the topic of hearing loss. At the same time, in audiology we don’t have a full understanding of what they’re facing in the primary care setting,” she said. “These seminars open a two-way discussion where we each get to learn about the challenges we’re confronting and identify opportunities for collaboration.”

The response was overwhelmingly positive. A slew of ideas for how to bridge the two fields quickly emerged.

“Once people get together, it’s great to see the simple ideas that arise,” she said, from adding hearing checks to the electronic medical system or including hearing health in case history forms, so doctors are prompted to ask about it at regular checkups.

The conversation didn’t end there. Through these sessions, audiologists and physicians had built a connection that turned into a referral pathway. Family doctors recognized the value in having a hearing expert they could connect patients to when necessary.

One physician who attended the discussion, Dr. Omar Elsalakawy from Thompson Medical Centre, took the information to heart.

“After the session, hearing loss started to become one of my regular questions, especially to older people who come in for a physical checkup,” Elsalakawy said.

Emma Van Lieshout from Beck Hearing Aid Centre. (Submitted)

One audiologist who was part of Bataineh’s sessions, Emma Van Lieshout from Beck Hearing Aid Center, recognizes the difficulties physicians face, attributing the friction to a systemic challenge.

“It’s an issue with how the health–care system is operating overall. There’s a gap in seeing health as holistic, in attempting to create an interdisciplinary team where everyone’s working together.”

Too often, health professions work in silos rather than partnering to provide coordinated care, as they don’t traditionally receive education on everybody else’s scope of practice, explained Danielle Glista, professor in Western’s School of Communication Sciences and Disorders. “Our goal is to create a patient-centred experience, where different providers are communicating and collaborating around health needs.”

Danielle Glista, professor of audiology. (Iulia Costache)

As Bataineh’s graduate supervisor, Glista has seen her student’s efforts to bring about this change from the ground up, describing the project as a grassroots initiative with great power to bring people together.

“Implementing change is hard,” Bataineh said. She knows scaling her initiative will require help from policymakers, clinicians and government to create systems that can support more accessible hearing screening and care.

The optimism that has sprouted from her growing initiative, from academics and healthcare professionals alike, has proven both the need and want for this change, and the capacity for a systemic shift, Bataineh said. She’s already heard evidence of audiologists and physicians working more collaboratively toward an interdisciplinary future.

“From a physician’s point of view,” Dr. Elsalakawy added, “lack of awareness is the biggest barrier.” And it’s a barrier that Bataineh is chipping away at.

Learn more about how Western is optimizing health for all.

One audiologist who was part of Bataineh’s sessions, Emma Van Lieshout from Beck Hearing Aid Center, recognizes the difficulties physicians face, attributing the friction to a systemic challenge.
“It’s an issue with how the health–care system is operating overall. There’s a gap in seeing health as holistic, in attempting to create an interdisciplinary team where everyone’s working together.”

Too often, health professions work in silos rather than partnering to provide coordinated care, as they don’t traditionally receive education on everybody else’s scope of practice, explained Danielle Glista, professor in Western’s School of Communication Sciences and Disorders. “Our goal is to create a patient-centred experience, where different providers are communicating and collaborating around health needs.”
Danielle Glista, professor of audiology. (Iulia Costache)

As Bataineh’s graduate supervisor, Glista has seen her student’s efforts to bring about this change from the ground up, describing the project as a grassroots initiative with great power to bring people together.

“Implementing change is hard,” Bataineh said. She knows scaling her initiative will require help from policymakers, clinicians and government to create systems that can support more accessible hearing screening and care.

The optimism that has sprouted from her growing initiative, from academics and healthcare professionals alike, has proven both the need and want for this change, and the capacity for a systemic shift, Bataineh said. She’s already heard evidence of audiologists and physicians working more collaboratively toward an interdisciplinary future.

content_blocks.text: When you put on eyeglasses for the very first time, you May be surprised at the wealth of new information that hits your senses. The individual leaves on a tree, road signs that become distinct or the particular way light spreads across a scene.
The same thing could happen when you put on a hearing aid for the first time, Jana Bataineh said.
“You don’t realize how much you’re missing.”
Bataineh is a PhD candidate in health and rehabilitation sciences, concurrently completing her master of clinical science in audiology in Western’s Faculty of Health Sciences.
Coming from a public health background, she’s seen time and time again how hearing loss is often minimized when it comes to people’s wellbeing.
She often encountered a common sentiment toward those with hearing loss: “Why can’t you just listen harder, pay more attention?” The misconception spurred her to bring hearing loss to light.

Inspired to make a change, Bataineh wanted to ensure people are tested for hearing loss before it’s too late, and get the resources they need to improve their health. The problem led her to develop a series of seminars designed specifically for primary care clinics, to bring hearing loss and screening to the forefront of the conversation.

Hearing loss is not isolated, she says. It can shape the way you interact with the world and completely change your quality of life. Importantly, it’s also one of the leading risk factors for dementia.
Why hearing health matters for cognitive decline and dementia

In the latest guidelinespublished by the World Health Organization, hearing loss is recognized as the leading, modifiable trait in cognitive decline. Not only does it often lead to social isolation, depression, and withdrawal from regular activities, but when hearing becomes challenging, the brain needs to work harder to make sense of sound, drawing from cognitive resources used in key mechanisms like attention and memory.
This is especially prevalent in adults over the age of 50; more than 60 per cent of older adults will develop hearing loss.

But despite the glaring statistics, the Canadian health-care system has no clear structure or program to catch or address this prevalent need. The Infant Hearing Program aims to screen all newborns at birth, but after that most Canadians aren’t regularly tested or prompted to be screened for hearing loss at any other moment in their health journey.

The responsibility often rests with individuals to identify hints of oncoming hearing loss and find a clinic where they can get tested; though because it develops slowly, it’s difficult for people to pinpoint and acknowledge.

“What really ends up happening is that they’ll spend many years with hearing difficulties, withdrawing from activities, dealing with the fallout, before they reach the point of taking action,” said Bataineh. Many cases are left untreated.

But hearing loss can be managed. Through interventions such as early screening, hearing aids and rehabilitation, people can maintain the communication they need to age well. It got Bataineh thinking: how could we better handle this condition, and how do we change the system to make it happen?

Bolstered by a student initiative grant from Speech-Language & Audiology Canada, Bataineh envisioned a future where patients are routinely screened by primary care providers like family doctors and nurses, connecting them directly with audiologists.

Not only could this catch hearing loss at its onset, it could lessen the load for busy physicians. This holistic model has been implemented with success in countries like the United Kingdom and Ireland, where integrating an audiologist directly into the primary care setting has relieved the caseload for family doctors.

In Canada, there largely remains a disconnect between the two health fields. Most physicians and patients aren’t discussing hearing in appointments. If it does come up, it could turn into a months long wait to see an Ear, Nose and Throat (ENT) specialist or find a hearing test on their own. Beyond the challenge of getting to the right professional, audiology services are typically not covered by provincial health plans such as Ohip.

### “In order to stay on the world stage when it comes to health care, we want to make sure that our population is also getting access to these innovative models that streamline care.” – Jana Bataineh, PhD candidate in health and rehabilitation sciences
Seeing the gap, and the critical need for a new way forward, she took it upon herself to try and make this vision a reality.

Creating the Hearing Health Seminar Series, Bataineh reached out to primary care centres across the province, and set up lunchtime visits to present and discuss the importance of hearing well. Bringing along an audiologist to various sessions, Bataineh was able to spark direct conversations between hearing experts, physicians and clinic staff – from nurses to managers.

“There’s not a lot of education or training for physicians on the topic of hearing loss. At the same time, in audiology we don’t have a full understanding of what they’re facing in the primary care setting,” she said. “These seminars open a two-way discussion where we each get to learn about the challenges we’re confronting and identify opportunities for collaboration.”
The response was overwhelmingly positive. A slew of ideas for how to bridge the two fields quickly emerged.

“Once people get together, it’s great to see the simple ideas that arise,” she said, from adding hearing checks to the electronic medical system or including hearing health in case history forms, so doctors are prompted to ask about it at regular checkups.
Connecting physicians and audiologists

The conversation didn’t end there. Through these sessions, audiologists and physicians had built a connection that turned into a referral pathway. Family doctors recognized the value in having a hearing expert they could connect patients to when necessary.
One physician who attended the discussion, Dr. Omar Elsalakawy from Thompson Medical Centre, took the information to heart.
“After the session, hearing loss started to become one of my regular questions, especially to older people who come in for a physical checkup,” Elsalakawy said.

stories.title: Woman who allegedly aided Tumbler Ridge shooter to remain in custody pending further court appearances
stories.summary: The American is accused of conspiring with the attacker to carry out one of the worst school shootings in Canadian history
stories.author: Jesse Winter
stories.content:
A Washington State woman accused of conspiring with the Tumbler Ridge shooter to carry out one of the worst school shooting attacks in Canadian history will remain in custody pending further court appearances.

James Cody Bryant, 30, of Bellingham, appeared in U.S. District Court in Seattle on Tuesday, wearing a beige button-down t-shirt over her slight frame with glasses and long hair that reaches to her waist. Ms. Bryant goes by Melody and uses she/her pronouns, according to her lawyers.

She faces charges of conspiring with and aiding Tumbler Ridge shooter Jesse Vanrootselaar, 18, in carrying out a mass shooting at a school in the northern B.C. mining town in February.

In issuing her ruling that Ms. Bryant should be detained, U.S. District Court Judge Mary Alice Theiler said she was not able to see any combination of release conditions that could satisfy the risks Ms. Bryant might post to herself or to the community, or the risk that she might fail to appear for future court dates.

Throughout the afternoon’s arguments, Ms. Bryant sat flanked by two U.S. Marshals. She remained still and made little visible reactions. At one point she appeared to use a tissue to wipe away tears.

More to come

stories.title: All charges dropped for lone female accused in Chesham Place firearms and explosives investigation
stories.summary: After months of court appearances and legal wrangling all charges against Feiyang (Astrid) Ji, 22, have been dropped by the Crown.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
After months of court appearances and legal wrangling all charges against Feiyang (Astrid) Ji, 22, have been dropped by the Crown.

Ji was released on bail in March after being arrested in January with three other former Western University students.

Her defence lawyer Nicola Circelli told CTV News, “She was facing a total of eleven charges and all of them have been dismissed.”

Ji had been charged along with three males after London Police raided a home on Chesham Place in January during a firearms and explosives investigation.

The house was searched for days by investigators following a break-in at Western University.

The three remaining accused, Jerry Tong, 27, Fei Han,26, and Zekun Wang, 27, are all expected in court later this month to possibly set a date for a preliminary hearing.

stories.title: Changes to prescribing safer supply drugs approved by Ontario medical regulator
stories.summary: The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario's board of directors will soon implement several changes to the practice of prescribing safer supply.
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
Ontario’s medical regulator approved significant changes Tuesday to the way doctors prescribe safer supply drugs, in an effort to reduce the amount of opioids making their way to the streets.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario’s board of directors will soon implement several changes to the practice of prescribing safer supply, which are medications given to people at high risk of overdose as an alternative to illicit opioids.

The board met Tuesday and passed a motion to enact the changes following a discussion on the proposals.

The college will make it mandatory for physicians to prescribe safer supply medications only in conjunction with opioid agonist therapy. The therapy uses medications such as Suboxone and methadone to treat opioid addiction.

“We are just here to protect the public and we’re here to ensure that the public is safe,” said Dr. Patrick Safieh, the board’s chair, near the end of the meeting.

“So we’re trying to prevent diversion as much as possible and at the same time, ensuring that those that do require safer supply are taking (opioid agonist therapy) so that eventually no one is on this and needs this, that’s the purpose.”

The most common form of safer supply is hydromorphone, a powerful opioid often prescribed for pain but significantly less potent than fentanyl and its derivatives that dominate the illicit drug supply chain.

Patients will now have to take the safer supply medications in front of health-care professionals, rather than take the pills home.

The college will not go ahead with an eight-week time limit for physicians to prescribe safer supply to patients it had previously considered.

Police forces in Ontario have said that diversion of patients’ prescription hydromorphone to the black market is occurring, Safieh said.

The board heard from Dr. Anil Chopra, the college’s associate registrar, who said they have also received information from governments, Addiction Medicine Canada, the addictions section of the Ontario Medical Association and from public health officers that diversion of hydromorphone to the streets is occurring.

Chopra, Safieh and others agreed there is no data available to properly quantify where the hydromorphone on the street is coming from, but said at least part of it is from safer supply prescriptions.

Board member Peter Wiesner said he was concerned that the policy will not work for everyone, citing information sent in by the Ontario Drug Policy Research Network that shows more than 87 per cent of patients on safer supply are also on opioid agonist therapy.

“But what about the 12 per cent that it doesn’t work for?” he asked.

“We need to find, I think, some exemptions for the 12 per cent.”

He said the new policy will have an outsized effect on those living in rural Ontario who are not close to a pharmacy. Another concern he raised are for those people who are employed who are using safer supply drugs. Those people May have difficulties getting to a pharmacy every day to take their medicine if they are not allowed to take some home with them.

Safieh said the college will monitor the changes and make adjustments down the road if necessary.

The office of Health Minister Sylvia Jones has previously said she supports the changes.

stories.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk shares first impressions from space
stories.summary: Kutryk and his crewmates aboard the International Space Station observed the Northern Lights over the weekend
stories.author: Ivan Semeniuk
stories.content:
Canada’s latest space traveller, Joshua Kutryk, may be far from home, but home is rarely out of sight, the astronaut said in his first conversation with reporters since arriving at the International Space Station.

“We’re actually over Canada right now,” he said during a live press briefing from space that was held on Tuesday. “We’re about to cross over Vancouver, and then we’ll be coming down over the top of Quebec and right over Sept-Îles about the time this interview is wrapping up. So, I do get to see the country a lot from here.”

Col. Kutryk, a native of Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., and three crewmates blasted off for the station on Oct. 1 . Following a crew switchover that was completed a few days later, he is one of seven astronauts on board the orbiting laboratory.

Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says he's having a blast on the International Space Station but the mission also shows how Canada can contribute to the leading edge of space flight. Kutryk is on a six-month mission to the ISS.

The Canadian Press

A former test pilot with the Royal Canadian Air Force, Col. Kutryk described the sensation of riding into space in a capsule atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as “exhilarating,” “spectacular,” “powerful” and “violent.”

“Your mind is alive, trying to bring in all these new experiences and feelings and sensations – things you’ve trained for, but never really felt for real.”

He added that once all the procedures and checks were completed after the launch, he was able to unclip his seatbelt and work his way to a window to look out at Earth spinning below. At that moment, he said, “your mind doesn’t know what to do.”

Col. Kutryk is the first Canadian to spend time on the ISS since Montreal businessman-philanthropist Mark Pathy made a self-funded visit in April, 2022, and the first to be on a long-duration mission at the space station since astronaut David Saint-Jacques returned from a six-month stint in June, 2019.

During the media briefing, which was conducted by video link, Col. Kutryk said he was just beginning to get down to the work of conducting the many science experiments on his to-do list, including several developed by Canadian researchers.

Among them are some that focus on mitigating the effects of microgravity on the human body, including bone and muscle loss.

Col. Kutryk noted that he had weighed himself after his first week in orbit and was down about five pounds.

He also showed that he was wearing a special sensor shirt associated with a Canadian-led experiment called AstroFit . The shirt is designed to provide 48 hours of continuous monitoring of heart rate, respiration and oxygen levels. It also features a built-in accelerometer that measures the wearer’s activity level, including when using an exercise device called a cycle ergometer.

Based on studies done with subjects under continuous bed rest on Earth, the experiment is designed to test the effectiveness of a fitness protocol that breaks up prolonged inactivity with exercise during three separate times in an astronaut’s day.

“We can track changes in his physical fitness by monitoring heart rate while he does the same session on the cycle ergometer early in flight, the mid-point of the flight and again in the final few weeks of the flight,” said Richard Hughson, a professor emeritus at the University of Waterloo and principal investigator for AstroFit.

Col. Kutryk said that, for him, the biggest challenges related to life in space involve having to figure out how to do basic things like eating and sleeping.

“You have to sort of learn to do everything again, almost like you’re a child,” he said.

The payoff, he added, was experiencing the novel environment of the ISS and seeing one amazing sight after another, including a brilliant display of Northern Lights, which the crew observed over the weekend.

“To see the whole Earth – the curvature of the Earth – just embraced by this blanket of dancing fluorescent oranges and yellows and pinks is magical,” he said.

The payoff, he added, was experiencing the novel environment of the ISS and seeing one amazing sight after another, including a brilliant display of Northern Lights, which the crew observed over the weekend.
“To see the whole Earth – the curvature of the Earth – just embraced by this blanket of dancing fluorescent oranges and yellows and pinks is magical,” he said.

content_blocks.text: Canada’s latest space traveller, Joshua Kutryk, may be far from home, but home is rarely out of sight, the astronaut said in his first conversation with reporters since arriving at the International Space Station.

“We’re actually over Canada right now,” he said during a live press briefing from space that was held on Tuesday. “We’re about to cross over Vancouver, and then we’ll be coming down over the top of Quebec and right over Sept-Îles about the time this interview is wrapping up. So, I do get to see the country a lot from here.”

Col. Kutryk, a native of Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., and three crewmates blasted off for the station on Oct. 1 . Following a crew switchover that was completed a few days later, he is one of seven astronauts on board the orbiting laboratory.

content_blocks.html: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk says he's having a blast on the International Space Station but the mission also shows how Canada can contribute to the leading edge of space flight. Kutryk is on a six-month mission to the ISS.

content_blocks.text: The Canadian Press

A former test pilot with the Royal Canadian Air Force, Col. Kutryk described the sensation of riding into space in a capsule atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket as “exhilarating,” “spectacular,” “powerful” and “violent.”
“Your mind is alive, trying to bring in all these new experiences and feelings and sensations – things you’ve trained for, but never really felt for real.”

He added that once all the procedures and checks were completed after the launch, he was able to unclip his seatbelt and work his way to a window to look out at Earth spinning below. At that moment, he said, “your mind doesn’t know what to do.”

Col. Kutryk is the first Canadian to spend time on the ISS since Montreal businessman-philanthropist Mark Pathy made a self-funded visit in April, 2022, and the first to be on a long-duration mission at the space station since astronaut David Saint-Jacques returned from a six-month stint in June, 2019.

During the media briefing, which was conducted by video link, Col. Kutryk said he was just beginning to get down to the work of conducting the many science experiments on his to-do list, including several developed by Canadian researchers.
Among them are some that focus on mitigating the effects of microgravity on the human body, including bone and muscle loss.
Col. Kutryk noted that he had weighed himself after his first week in orbit and was down about five pounds.

He also showed that he was wearing a special sensor shirt associated with a Canadian-led experiment called AstroFit . The shirt is designed to provide 48 hours of continuous monitoring of heart rate, respiration and oxygen levels. It also features a built-in accelerometer that measures the wearer’s activity level, including when using an exercise device called a cycle ergometer.

The shirt is designed to provide 48 hours of continuous monitoring of heart rate, respiration and oxygen levels. It also features a built-in accelerometer that measures the wearer’s activity level, including when using an exercise device called a cycle ergometer.

content_blocks.text: Based on studies done with subjects under continuous bed rest on Earth, the experiment is designed to test the effectiveness of a fitness protocol that breaks up prolonged inactivity with exercise during three separate times in an astronaut’s day.

“We can track changes in his physical fitness by monitoring heart rate while he does the same session on the cycle ergometer early in flight, the mid-point of the flight and again in the final few weeks of the flight,” said Richard Hughson, a professor emeritus at the University of Waterloo and principal investigator for AstroFit.

stories.title: Changes to prescribing safer supply drugs approved by Ontario’s medical regulator
stories.summary: Efforts are being made to reduce the amount of opioids making their way to the streets
stories.author: Liam Casey
stories.content:
Ontario’s medical regulator approved significant changes Tuesday to the way doctors prescribe safer supply drugs, in an effort to reduce the amount of opioids making their way to the streets.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario’s board of directors will soon implement several changes to the practice of prescribing safer supply, which are medications given to people at high risk of overdose as an alternative to illicit opioids.

The board met Tuesday and passed a motion to enact the changes following a discussion on the proposals.

The college will make it mandatory for physicians to prescribe safer supply medications only in conjunction with opioid agonist therapy. The therapy uses medications such as Suboxone and methadone to treat opioid addiction.

“We are just here to protect the public and we’re here to ensure that the public is safe,” said Dr. Patrick Safieh, the board’s chair, near the end of the meeting.

“So we’re trying to prevent diversion as much as possible and at the same time, ensuring that those that do require safer supply are taking (opioid agonist therapy) so that eventually no one is on this and needs this, that’s the purpose.”

The most common form of safer supply is hydromorphone, a powerful opioid often prescribed for pain but significantly less potent than fentanyl and its derivatives that dominate the illicit drug supply chain.

Patients will now have to take the safer supply medications in front of health-care professionals, rather than take the pills home.

The college will not go ahead with an eight-week time limit for physicians to prescribe safer supply to patients it had previously considered.

Police forces in Ontario have said that diversion of patients’ prescription hydromorphone to the black market is occurring, Safieh said.

The board heard from Dr. Anil Chopra, the college’s associate registrar, who said they have also received information from governments, Addiction Medicine Canada, the addictions section of the Ontario Medical Association and from public health officers that diversion of hydromorphone to the streets is occurring.

Chopra, Safieh and others agreed there is no data available to properly quantify where the hydromorphone on the street is coming from, but said at least part of it is from safer supply prescriptions.

Board member Peter Wiesner said he was concerned that the policy will not work for everyone, citing information sent in by the Ontario Drug Policy Research Network that shows more than 87 per cent of patients on safer supply are also on opioid agonist therapy.

“But what about the 12 per cent that it doesn’t work for?” he asked.

“We need to find, I think, some exemptions for the 12 per cent.”

He said the new policy will have an outsized effect on those living in rural Ontario who are not close to a pharmacy. Another concern he raised are for those people who are employed who are using safer supply drugs. Those people May have difficulties getting to a pharmacy every day to take their medicine if they are not allowed to take some home with them.

Safieh said the college will monitor the changes and make adjustments down the road if necessary.

The office of Health Minister Sylvia Jones has previously said she supports the changes.

stories.title: Fatal crash on Highway 401 near London
stories.summary: Highway 401 eastbound lanes are closed following a fatal multi-vehicle collision south of London.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Highway 401 eastbound and westbound lanes are closed following two collisions on the eastbound side, one being a fatal multi-vehicle collision south of London.

The first collision was at about 2:15 p.m. near Colonel Talbot Road and involved approximately three vehicles.

Just after 4 p.m. OPP responded to a second collision involving a transport truck and passenger vehicle, further down the highway near Union Road.

The transport truck collided with the rear of a passenger vehicle, that according to OPP was stopped in traffic. The vehicle burst into flames.

OPP says Highway 401 is closed between Colonel Talbot Road and Iona Road.

The number of deceased individuals is unknown at this time.

Motorists are being urged to plan alternate routes.

stories.title: Schulich students bring diverse stories, health education to young readers
stories.summary: Western medical students created Kids Health Shelf, producing diverse children’s books promoting representation, health literacy & inclusion.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
Stories can be a child’s first window to the world. But growing up, Nadith Ranasinghe, BSc’25, a second-year medical student at Western’s Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry, rarely saw children of colour or immigrant families in the books he read.

Today, Ranasinghe is helping create children’s books that reflect these diverse experiences and make health-related topics more accessible to young readers. During his undergraduate studies at Western, he founded the Kids Health Shelf initiative with his classmates to give students a creative outlet and produce stories that resonate with young readers.

“Our goal is to give students a space to be artistic while also giving books to children that reflect their diverse experiences and journeys in life,” said Ranasinghe.

To date, Kids Health Shelf has produced four stories and donated copies to the Children’s Health Foundation and Children’s Hospital at London Health Sciences Centre in London, Ont.

The club’s first story, published in 2024, was The Girl Under the Rambutan Tree. It drew on the childhood memories of Ranasinghe’s mother, Deepika, who grew up in Sri Lanka.

To date, Kids Health Shelf has produced four stories, including‘The Girl Under the Rambutan Tree.’(Megan Morris/Schulich Medicine & Dentistry)

Despite growing up in poverty, his mother was determined to build a better future for herself. She studied medicine and became an anaesthesiologist before immigrating to Canada in 2012, where she worked as an infection control nurse. At the time, Ranasinghe was eight years old.

“My mother left her medical career behind to give my little sister and me a better life. I wanted to write about that sacrifice,” he said. “In many ways, this book is a tribute to her. I made her the main character, and the story is based on her childhood in Sri Lanka.”

Other students in the club are focused on making complex health and science topics more accessible.

For Bahareh Rahimi Shahmirzadi, a medical sciences student specializing in microbiology and immunology, her experience as a picky eater inspired a book about the microbiome and healthy eating.

“I feel that having a book that explained the science in a way I could understand would have helped me overcome my picky eating,” said Rahimi Shahmirzadi.

She wrote and illustrated Microville: The Tiny Town Where Everyone Belongs over the summer of 2026. The book translates scientific concepts into memorable characters that children can understand. There’s Fiona Fibre, who helps digest the fibre we eat, and Vita Vitamin, who turns food into vitamins our bodies can use.

“I focused on turning science into little characters that might be easier for kids to understand,” she said.

This November, the team plans to donate copies of its fourth book, Arjun and The Championship Sigh, to children in Guyana. Team member Avin Sharma, a medical sciences student with Guyanese roots, hopes to give back to his community through the donation. The story follows a cheerful brain named Arjun who helps Leo, a young football player, manage pre-game anxiety by teaching him a simple breathing technique. It aims to help children understand anxiety and equip them with an easy tool for managing it.

They are also working with Dr. Jamaica Cass, a primary care physician at Tyendinaga Mohawk Territory, ON a book that brings more Indigenous representation into children’s stories.

“We are working on a story about Dr. Jamaica Cass who, despite all the adversity she faced, was able to earn her MD and PhD degrees and return to her community to help and give back,” said Ranasinghe.

For Ranasinghe and his peers, the hope is that young readers will see something of themselves in the stories they create. “When children see themselves in stories, it gives them the confidence to imagine themselves achieving things they May not have thought possible.”

Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

stories.title: Mack enjoying career season with Edmonton Elks
stories.summary: Reuniting with Cody Fajardo is paying huge dividends for Austin Mack.
stories.author: Dan Ralph
stories.content:
Reuniting with Cody Fajardo is paying huge dividends for Austin Mack.

Through 16 games in his first season with the Edmonton Elks, Mack has established career highs in catches (79), yards (1,229) and touchdowns (eight). Mack last had numbers like these in his first CFL campaign with the Montreal Alouettes in 2023 (78 receptions, 1,154 yards, four TDs).

The constant in both equations, though, is Fajardo. The veteran quarterback was with Montreal in 2023, leading the team to a Grey Cup championship that season.

This year, Edmonton (12-4) will return to the CFL playoffs for the first time since 2019. It will also host its first post-season contest since 2015.

If Edmonton can split its remaining two regular-season games (Friday versus Winnipeg, at Saskatchewan on Oct. 24), it will cement first in the West and host the division final Nov. 7. The Elks downed Calgary 45-31 in the 2015 West finale before beating Ottawa 26-20 in the Grey Cup, their last CFL title.

The six-foot-one, 208-pound Mack spent his first three CFL seasons with Montreal and finished his ’25 campaign playing in the club’s 25-17 Grey Cup loss to Saskatchewan. He was released by the Alouettes on Jan. 26 ahead of being due a reported $45,000 roster bonus.

But, with Fajardo’s persistence, the 29-year-old Mack signed a two-year deal with Edmonton three days later.

“It’s funny because Cody never calls anybody in the off-season because he’s with his family,” Mack said. “But he called me every single day until I signed.

“There was a lot that went into it … I wanted to make sure it was the right fit and was a decision me and my family made together even though I had my guy shooting me texts. I think had I gone anywhere else our friendship would’ve probably ended and it’s a good thing we didn’t have to go down that road.”

But, with Fajardo’s persistence, the 29-year-old Mack signed a two-year deal with Edmonton three days later.

“This locker room has a lot of great guys who want to win, who want to sacrifice,” Mack said. “It’s a lot of team guys and you need that in this league.”

“Everyone says Canada is cold, and it can be, but the best part about playing football in the cold is you’re playing in meaningful games,” Mack said. “One of the reasons why I wanted to come to this team was to contribute to helping this offence be more explosive and be in games and I believe that’s what I’ve done this year.

“We’ve still got to make sure we secure (a West final home berth) and that’s our biggest focus. If we could, that would be amazing and I’d hope we’d see 60,000 people in Commonwealth (for a division championship game).”

stories.title: Morgan defends homelessness strategy, proposes next steps, while warning against candidates using crisis ‘to score political points’
stories.summary: Incumbent mayoral candidate Josh Morgan unveiled the next phase of his homelessness strategy on Monday, urging Londoners not to let the crisis be used “to score political points or divide people” ahead of Election Day.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Incumbent mayoral candidate Josh Morgan unveiled the next phase of his homelessness strategy on Monday, urging Londoners not to let the crisis be used “to score political points or divide people” ahead of Election Day.

“Fewer people are dying. We have avoided preventable deaths on our street,” Morgan said, emphasizing progress made through the city’s current approach between 2022 and 2024.

The next phase of Morgan’s plan to address homelessness would include:

London will lead the ongoing emergency response by increasing spaces at the micro-modular shelter including a direct pathway to the provincial Hart (Homelessness and Addiction Recovery Treatment} Hub

London will open, with partners, 200 more highly supportive housing spaces (in addition to the 169 currently operating)

London will directly lobby Queens Park to fund residential treatment beds, expanding the Hart Hub, and doubling Ontario Works (plus increases to offset inflation)

“We need a new advocacy campaign with Queen’s Park and we need to push hard,” Morgan said. “We need more treatment beds in our city. We need more room in the Hart Hub, and we need Ontario Works and Odsp to pay a rate that allows people to stop falling into homelessness.”

Morgan argued London’s response to homelessness must remain focused on humanity, not politics, “Every person living outside is someone’s daughter, someone’s brother, someone’s son. It’s not something you score political points off-- it’s people who you need to help.”

While he avoided naming opponents directly, Morgan pushed back against statements made by other leading candidates for mayor, “The truth is, you need the province as a partner. You can’t solve homelessness in just one city. And anybody pretending to do that isn’t telling the truth.”

Contacted by CTV News, mayoral candidate Susan Stevenson responded that the current plan hasn’t accomplished enough to address deteriorating conditions on London streets, “Deaths were up in 2025. Homelessness is up. Open public drug use is up. Crime and safety concerns are up in terms of broken windows and theft from retail stores. All of these things are because we are focused on making it easier (and) safer to use illegal drugs in our city.”

Morgan directly addressed workers at shelters who have heard campaigning from some of his challengers, “I apologize that there are candidates in this race who villainize and degrade their work in the city. It’s important work, it’s meaningful, and I will always stand beside them. I will always stand beside the people who are homeless to find them a pathway.”

However, Stevenson argues the city’s strategy must better align with the provincial government’s support of treatment-based care, “We just brought forward a taxpayer-funded shelter policy that said illegal substances are to be allowed inside our taxpayer-funded shelters. I was able to have that removed, but the mayor said right after that, the shelters could still do whatever they want because we didn’t explicitly disallow it. Our highly supportive housing explicitly allows illegal drug use inside those $100,000 per apartment programs.”

Also speaking at the campaign event inside Motive Espresso on Pall Mall Street were incumbent candidates Skylar Franke in Ward 11, and David Ferreira in Ward 13, who both endorsed the mayor’s homelessness plan.

Franke said, “We are not policing our way out of a housing crisis, and we cannot expect people to get back on their feet if they cannot afford a house.”

Ferreira added, “I don’t think that politicking, fear mongering, or misinformation is really what this city, society, country and province needs right now.”

Morgan warned against calls to start over again, “We don’t need to stop, review, and start again. Starting over is a really nice promise to make during a campaign, but it is at a cost that our community will pay in the long run.”

“Any candidate can tell you what’s wrong in our city,” he concluded. “The question on Oct. 26 is who will actually have a plan to fix that? Who has proven that they can bring people together? Who has shown that they can access and advocate to the province and the feds?”

Ten other candidates are running to be Mayor of London, John Feher, Lawrence-Zachary Howe, Barry Douglas Jacklin, Tariq Khan, Kirsten Krose, Dan Lenart, Bronagh Joyce Morgan, Christine Rosehart, Jeff Yam, and Mustafa Zeboon.

Election Day is Oct. 26.

stories.title: What’s behind B.C.’s pink salmon boom? A fierce debate takes place as a salmon farm ban looms
stories.summary: Millions more of a species of salmon are returning to spawn up the Fraser River on Canada’s West Coast, but exactly why remains hotly disputed and solving that puzzle could have major implications for wild salmon stocks and coastal communities.
stories.author: Jon Woodward
stories.content:
Port Hardy, B.C. -- Millions more of a species of salmon are returning to spawn up the Fraser River on Canada’s West Coast, but exactly why remains hotly disputed, and the answer could have major implications for wild salmon stocks and coastal communities.

Some First Nations, in concert with environmental groups, have attributed this surge to the shutdown of dozens of salmon farms and are urging the federal government to enact a promised ban of the remainder of those farms by 2029.

But a W5 investigation has revealed that the federal government is not outwardly committing to that ban, as a confidential internal assessment recommended reopening 15 salmon farms, arguing that the operations pose “minimal risk” to wild stocks.

“Farm presence (or absence) is only one of many variables, and current evidence does not demonstrate a causal link,” the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) said in a statement to W5, as another scientist suggested that surging salmon species, the pink salmon, May simply be doing better in warming oceans.

A lot hinges on getting the science right: coastal communities are bracing for the impact of more salmon farm closures. The fallout could lead to hundreds more job losses in what was once a billion-dollar industry, affect a valued way of life for First Nations, and change what Canadian consumers put on their plates.

Meanwhile, Canadian consumers appear willing to consume farmed salmon whether it’s grown locally or increasingly imported from abroad.

The Discovery Islands: a pink salmon surge

Aboard his motorboat in the waters off the Discovery Islands, about 200 km northwest of Vancouver between Vancouver Island and the B.C. mainland, researcher Jody Erickson says he has noticed something incredible.

A seine net dropped from his motorboat can catch hundreds of young salmon smolts at a time, and Erickson draws up a few of them in a clear plastic case to see several different species: pink, chum and Chinook.

“What I would call very happy and healthy-looking fish right now,” he said. “No lice.”

It’s a far cry from what Erickson says he used to see in these waters a decade ago: juvenile salmon laden with parasites sticking to their skin, Erickson said. He still carries with him samples from those days that show small fish pockmarked with the parasites.

“They’re dying near fish farms. That’s what I see,” he said.

The Discovery Islands are a crucial thoroughfare for young salmon, who breed far up the freshwater rivers on B.C.’s coast, including the Fraser River, and then swim through these waters, around Vancouver Island, before making it out to sea.

Those islands, and the salmon farms that used to be there, were singled out by the Cohen Commission, a judicial inquiry that was called in 2009 after a salmon stock collapse.

Cohen pointed to many stressors that could affect the health of B.C. salmon, including warming waters, and recommended closing salmon farms in the Discovery Islands unless the federal fisheries minister is satisfied those farms pose at most a minimal risk to migrating sockeye salmon .

In 2019, the federal government followed through, refusing dozens of licences around the Discovery Islands, and then from the nearby Broughton Archipelago as a precaution. About half of all B.C. salmon farms are now gone.

A study by the Salmon Coast Field Station concluded that numbers of one species of lice dropped in the area once the salmon farms were removed, which could mean more salmon survive the long journey out to sea, said Research Crew Lead Kate Medcalf .

“As they out-migrate in these small sizes, they’re incredibly, incredibly vulnerable to parasitism and other stressors in the environment,” Medcalf said.

Erickson believes he is seeing the results of having fewer lice in the strait now.

“It’s very hopeful, because it shows that if we remove the fish farms, the fish can come back, really, really remarkably fast, faster than even I would have thought,” Erickson said.

Shuttered farms: the human cost

Nearby where Erickson cast his nets are what remains of several salmon farming operations. Some of them have been converted to other uses, while some have left no trace.

Those shutdowns meant lost jobs, and a narrowed future for the workers who hoped to launch long-term careers, said Kaitlin Guitard, a lab manager for one farm company, Mowi Canada West.

In an interview on the dock of one of the remaining farms, in the Queen Charlotte Strait near Port Hardy, she said she has lost hundreds of co-workers.

“It’s awful, it really is,” Guitard said. “I was relocated. But I think the hardest part for me was a lot of people that I worked with had either been laid off or could not wait around for certainty and had left.”

Guitard is among those fighting for the future of these farms, saying Canada needs the jobs and the food those farms produced.

Mowi Canada West’s production dropped from 40,000 tonnes a year, before the farms started to be removed in 2019, to 20,000 tonnes a year.

“The impact has been fairly devastating to the industry. We’ve lost 45 per cent of our production,” said Brian Kingzett, of the B.C. Salmon Farmers Association.

Kingzett says he’s aware that some farms have lice outbreaks, and that they do their best to manage them. But he doesn’t buy the connection drawn by researchers between his farms and the salmon collapse.

“We’ve had nine significant studies that have all identified that we can coexist with wild salmon, and we are continuing to innovate to further reduce any potential risks,” he said.

Rising numbers for salmon species; others are falling

Kingzett points to tracking by the Pacific Salmon Commission, a regulatory body run jointly by the Canadian and United States governments.

They use underwater sound waves and sonar to estimate the number of salmon passing the Mission hydroacoustic station in Mission, B.C., as they head up the Fraser River.

According to the commission figures, the number of one species of pink salmon, which has a two-year life cycle, has doubled since 2019, from about 8.5 million to 17.7 million in 2025.

But the picture for another species of salmon, which has a four-year life cycle, is much less clear.

The station counted promising returns of 8.1 million sockeye passing its station in 2025, which is an increase from 2021 and 2017.

That figure was lower than 2022, when the Discovery Islands farms had been removed, and lower than in 2018 and 2014, when all the salmon farms were operating.

The DFO also monitors salmon escapement numbers by region along the coast. In region 13, which includes the Discovery Islands, coho and pink salmon are increasing, but chinook and sockeye salmon are not.

The connection between salmon farms and the health of wild stocks was also doubted by the DFO, which advised the fisheries minister in 2023 that its preferred option was to re-licence all 15 salmon farms in the Discovery Islands.

“Current Departmental science advice includes nine risk assessments that were completed specifically to advise the Department on the issue of licencing in the Discovery Islands, found that pathogen transmission from Atlantic salmon farms in the Discovery Islands poses minimal risk to Fraser River sockeye salmon population abundance and diversity under existing fish health management practices,” the department wrote.

The licenses were not re-issued. In 2024, the federal government proposed a draft transition plan that would ban open net pen salmon farming by 2029 .

However, there has been no final transition plan released since.

In response to questions from CTV News about whether the federal government plans to follow through with the 2029 ban, a statement from Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson didn’t mention it.

“Pacific salmon are iconic to the West Coast and protecting and rebuilding wild salmon populations is a priority for our government,” the statement said, pointing to investments the government has made in three new salmon hatcheries, and consultation with stakeholders in B.C. this summer.

“There is no single solution to the challenges facing wild Pacific salmon, which is why we are taking a comprehensive approach to protecting and rebuilding these stocks,” she said.

Another school of thought

In his home in Nanaimo, B.C., retired fish scientist and winner of the Order of Canada Dick Beamish is convinced the answer to the mystery of the salmon returns lies farther out in the Pacific Ocean.

He points to studies that show pink salmon are surging not just in B.C. but worldwide, because they are better able to handle warming ocean temperatures.

“There will be populations in the north Pacific that are adapting to the ocean warming conditions better than others,” Beamish said in an interview.

Some species are coming back from their time in the ocean much smaller, ON average, than in previous years, he said.

“What is probably happening with the warming that we’re seeing in the ocean is that there’s less food being produced that’s allowing salmon to accumulate the energy that they need to survive ocean winters,” Beamish said.

Raising salmon on land?

Environmental groups are convinced that salmon farms are a threat and are pushing for alternatives to raise salmon on land.

In Port McNeill, in a cavernous warehouse only about a kilometre from where the Nimpkish River flows into the Queen Charlotte Strait, there are fish who will never see the ocean at all.

They’re grown in large circular tanks in a facility called Kuterra, built by the Namgis First Nation in 2013 for $10 million as a demonstration project to prove that a land-based aquaculture industry is possible in B.C.

“Those rates of return are far too low to attract the investment required to incentivize the development of a recirculating aquaculture system (RAS) salmon farming industry in British Columbia,” the report said.

“It’s different here in British Columbia, because we still have large, abundant populations of wild fish. We still have commercial fisheries. We still have recreational fisheries, we still have Indigenous fisheries,” she said.

Some First Nations, in concert with environmental groups, have attributed this surge to the shutdown of dozens of salmon farms and are urging the federal government to enact a promised ban of the remainder of those farms by 2029.

But a W5 investigation has revealed that the federal government is not outwardly committing to that ban, as a confidential internal assessment recommended reopening 15 salmon farms, arguing that the operations pose “minimal risk” to wild stocks.

“Farm presence (or absence) is only one of many variables, and current evidence does not demonstrate a causal link,” the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) said in a statement to W5, as another scientist suggested that surging salmon species, the pink salmon, May simply be doing better in warming oceans.

A lot hinges on getting the science right: coastal communities are bracing for the impact of more salmon farm closures. The fallout could lead to hundreds more job losses in what was once a billion-dollar industry, affect a valued way of life for First Nations, and change what Canadian consumers put on their plates.
Meanwhile, Canadian consumers appear willing to consume farmed salmon whether it’s grown locally or increasingly imported from abroad.
The Discovery Islands: a pink salmon surge

Aboard his motorboat in the waters off the Discovery Islands, about 200 km northwest of Vancouver between Vancouver Island and the B.C. mainland, researcher Jody Erickson says he has noticed something incredible.

A seine net dropped from his motorboat can catch hundreds of young salmon smolts at a time, and Erickson draws up a few of them in a clear plastic case to see several different species: pink, chum and Chinook.
“What I would call very happy and healthy-looking fish right now,” he said. “No lice.”

It’s a far cry from what Erickson says he used to see in these waters a decade ago: juvenile salmon laden with parasites sticking to their skin, Erickson said. He still carries with him samples from those days that show small fish pockmarked with the parasites.
“They’re dying near fish farms. That’s what I see,” he said.

The Discovery Islands are a crucial thoroughfare for young salmon, who breed far up the freshwater rivers on B.C.’s coast, including the Fraser River, and then swim through these waters, around Vancouver Island, before making it out to sea.
Those islands, and the salmon farms that used to be there, were singled out by the Cohen Commission, a judicial inquiry that was called in 2009 after a salmon stock collapse.

Cohen pointed to many stressors that could affect the health of B.C. salmon, including warming waters, and recommended closing salmon farms in the Discovery Islands unless the federal fisheries minister is satisfied those farms pose at most a minimal risk to migrating sockeye salmon .

In 2019, the federal government followed through, refusing dozens of licences around the Discovery Islands, and then from the nearby Broughton Archipelago as a precaution. About half of all B.C. salmon farms are now gone.

A study by the Salmon Coast Field Station concluded that numbers of one species of lice dropped in the area once the salmon farms were removed, which could mean more salmon survive the long journey out to sea, said Research Crew Lead Kate Medcalf .
“As they out-migrate in these small sizes, they’re incredibly, incredibly vulnerable to parasitism and other stressors in the environment,” Medcalf said.
Erickson believes he is seeing the results of having fewer lice in the strait now.
“It’s very hopeful, because it shows that if we remove the fish farms, the fish can come back, really, really remarkably fast, faster than even I would have thought,” Erickson said.
Shuttered farms: the human cost
Nearby where Erickson cast his nets are what remains of several salmon farming operations. Some of them have been converted to other uses, while some have left no trace.
Those shutdowns meant lost jobs, and a narrowed future for the workers who hoped to launch long-term careers, said Kaitlin Guitard, a lab manager for one farm company, Mowi Canada West.
In an interview on the dock of one of the remaining farms, in the Queen Charlotte Strait near Port Hardy, she said she has lost hundreds of co-workers.

“It’s awful, it really is,” Guitard said. “I was relocated. But I think the hardest part for me was a lot of people that I worked with had either been laid off or could not wait around for certainty and had left.”
Guitard is among those fighting for the future of these farms, saying Canada needs the jobs and the food those farms produced.
Mowi Canada West’s production dropped from 40,000 tonnes a year, before the farms started to be removed in 2019, to 20,000 tonnes a year.
“The impact has been fairly devastating to the industry. We’ve lost 45 per cent of our production,” said Brian Kingzett, of the B.C. Salmon Farmers Association.

Kingzett says he’s aware that some farms have lice outbreaks, and that they do their best to manage them. But he doesn’t buy the connection drawn by researchers between his farms and the salmon collapse.
“We’ve had nine significant studies that have all identified that we can coexist with wild salmon, and we are continuing to innovate to further reduce any potential risks,” he said.
Rising numbers for salmon species; others are falling
Kingzett points to tracking by the Pacific Salmon Commission, a regulatory body run jointly by the Canadian and United States governments.
They use underwater sound waves and sonar to estimate the number of salmon passing the Mission hydroacoustic station in Mission, B.C., as they head up the Fraser River.
According to the commission figures, the number of one species of pink salmon, which has a two-year life cycle, has doubled since 2019, from about 8.5 million to 17.7 million in 2025.
But the picture for another species of salmon, which has a four-year life cycle, is much less clear.
The station counted promising returns of 8.1 million sockeye passing its station in 2025, which is an increase from 2021 and 2017.
That figure was lower than 2022, when the Discovery Islands farms had been removed, and lower than in 2018 and 2014, when all the salmon farms were operating.

“There is no single solution to the challenges facing wild Pacific salmon, which is why we are taking a comprehensive approach to protecting and rebuilding these stocks,” she said.

“We are a fishing, logging, mining community. We’re resource based,” she said in an interview.
She said she is concerned about what would happen to the jobs, and by extension the community, if more farms are shut down.
“It would be very similar to when the mine closed here and there was a huge depression,” she said.
Over in the Queen Charlotte Strait, Guitard from Mowi takes a scoop of pellets and tosses it into an open pen. The fish respond by jumping.
She said she’s worried about what May be in store in 2029, when the ban is set to take effect, but is hopeful she can stay in her home in Campbell River.

“It’s awful, honestly. I’ve been here for six years. I have established a whole community, I have friends, it’s a lifestyle that I would love to live, but it really does rely solely on this industry continuing here.”

stories.title: Quebec flu vaccine appointments open amid warnings of early flu season
stories.summary: The Quebec health and social services department says vulnerable people should get their shots before the holiday season, adding only some vulnerable people will get free shots.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman
stories.content:
Appointments are now open for flu vaccines in Quebec as the province’s health department warns of an early flu season.

The Quebec health and social services department says vulnerable people should get their shots before the holiday season.

People will be able to get vaccinated for the flu, COVID-19 and Respiratory Syncytial Virus in the same appointment.

This year, only some vulnerable Quebecers will be eligible for free shots.

This includes people over 65, people who have chronic illnesses and pregnant women.

Others will need to pay for the shots in Quebec.

Most provinces in Canada will start providing the flu vaccine by the end of the month, and respiratory virus specialists say Canadians should get their flu shot as soon as it becomes available.

— With files from Nicole Ireland

stories.title: Rides closed at Canadian theme parks after deadly fall from Six Flags coaster in U.S.
stories.summary: Two rides at Canada's Wonderland in Toronto and another at La Ronde in Montreal were temporarily shuttered "out of an abundance of caution," the parks said.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Rides at two Canadian theme parks were closed after a man in the United States fell to this death from a Six Flags roller-coaster in Georgia.

Two rides at Canada’s Wonderland in Toronto and another at La Ronde in Montreal were temporarily shuttered “out of an abundance of caution,” the parks said. Six Flags owns Wonderland and recently sold La Ronde.

A 42-year-old man was killed while riding a roller-coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday, prompting the theme park operator to close nine similar rides across Canada and the United States. The man was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride, police said Tuesday.

The Leviathan and Behemoth roller-coasters at Canada’s Wonderland were closed, said a spokesperson for the park. There was no timeline for their reopening.

“The safety of our guests and team members remains on our highest priorities,” the spokesperson said in a written statement.

The Goliath roller-coaster at La Ronde was also closed and the park’s owner said it would carry out a safety review with the ride’s manufacturer.

“We are taking this additional time to carefully review the attraction. It will not reopen until this review is complete and we are fully satisfied that it can be operated safely,” read the statement.

The temporarily shuttered Canadian rides were manufactured by the same company as the coaster involved in the incident in Georgia.

Six Flags Entertainment did not immediately respond Tuesday to emailed questions about why specific rides were shut down and what would be done before they reopen.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct 13, 2026.

– With files from The Associated Press.
