stories.title: Advance polls open for Alberta’s separation referendum
stories.summary: Elections Alberta opened the doors at 310 polling stations for the first of five days of advanced voting
stories.author: Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Albertans across the province began lining up and casting their ballots Tuesday in the province’s historic vote on separation.

Elections Alberta opened the doors at 310 polling stations for the first of five days of advanced voting ahead of the official polling day on Oct. 19.

One downtown Edmonton polling station saw a lineup that stretched almost half a block after doors opened at 9 a.m., with voters spending anywhere between 30 minutes and an hour to cast their ballots.

Premier Danielle Smith has put 10 questions to a vote, including whether Alberta should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on quitting Confederation.

Some voters wore their vote on their sleeves by dawning hats or sweaters with the Canadian flag to go to the polls, including Christopher Hashmi.

“It is obviously a bad idea,” Hashmi said of separation, adding that he thought Alberta would only be more vulnerable to the interests of the United States and oil and gas corporations if the province went its own way.

Lizzy Somerville said it was patriotism that inspired her to vote to stay in Canada.

“Canada works better together,” she said.

For Samara O’Hagan, the issue of separation comes down to concerns over who has the rights to the land.

“I’m Indigenous, so it’s very important to me,” she said.

“It would just be totally wrong, essentially stealing land from Indigenous people. Alberta should not be able to do that.”

The other nine referendum questions have to do with immigration reform and Canada’s Constitution.

Somerville said she voted against all but one of the premier’s proposals. She voted yes to lobbying other provincial governments to garner support for abolishing the Senate.

She said the upper house was “useless” and that if abolishment wasn’t an option, she’d like to see the seats be subject to elections rather than the current appointment process handled by the prime minister.

Hashmi said he voted “no to the nine” – a slogan used by critics and third-party advertisers pushing against Smith’s referendum proposals. He said he would have considered voting for Senate abolition, but felt doing so would be a sign of support for Smith’s government.

“Is the unelected Senate bad? Yes, it sucks. It is an archaic and broken part of our Constitution,” he said.

“But Danielle Smith and her government are a broken and archaic part of my day-to-day life.”

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi was expected to cast his vote at an advanced poll in Calgary on Tuesday.

The start of advanced voting comes after Elections Alberta saw record interest in special ballots for the referendum, with roughly 658,000 Albertans requesting to vote by mail.

A spokesperson for the agency, Michelle Gurney, said that as of Monday evening about 391,000 mail-in ballots have been returned ahead of Friday’s 5 p.m. deadline.

Gurney also said about 46,000 workers have been hired to facilitate the vote and hand count the ballots. The agency has been aiming to hire 60,000 workers.

stories.title: ‘Every play I’ve worked on is about race in some way,’ director Jordan Laffrenier says
stories.summary: Associate artistic director at Canadian Stage in Toronto directs Alice Childress’s Wine in the Wilderness and American Buffalo this season
stories.author: Noel Ransome
stories.content:
Jordan Laffrenier was furious with Slave Play the first time he saw it on Broadway.

He was not the only one. The brew of spectacle and sexual role play by Jeremy O. Harris arrived in 2018 at a particularly noisy moment for Black representation, not long after cultural titleholders such as Moonlight and Black Panther . It complicated the celebration with uncomfortable questions. What, exactly, was Harris asking Black people to endure on a stage? Was Slave Play good for Black audiences? A petition demanding the production close attracted more than 6,000 signatures.

“I was just so angered by the idea that Black people who were being presented as enslaved were being presented as caricatures,” he recalls.

Laffrenier, an award-winning director, playwright and dramaturge – and associate artistic director at Canadian Stage in Toronto – has taste that carries weight. But to understand Laffrenier is to realize that his first reaction is rarely his last. And that was the case after he directed Slave Play last fall.

The first act asks whether a vision of historical Black trauma can take place in a bedroom. It opens on a plantation, with masters and servants experiencing a blend of submission, flirtation and degradation. Eventually the setting is stripped away, revealing that the plantation figures are actually three contemporary interracial couples engaged in therapeutic role play.

What Laffrenier found beneath the confrontation was an argument about intimacy. “To love somebody fully, you need to see them fully,” he says, “and to see somebody fully includes their race.”

That realization seems to have outgrown the play itself. A year after directing Slave Play , Laffrenier is arriving at a broader theory of his work. “Every play I’ve worked on is about race in some way,” he says, knowing that the productions May be American-set, but the conversations aren’t. “Some plays make it more explicit.”

Most recently, that theory was tested by Alice Childress’s Wine in the Wilderness , which Laffrenier directed at Canadian Stage earlier this month. That play confines the subject of Blackness to a single apartment and watches what happens when viewpoints clash. It looks at class and gender amid subtle whiffs of respectability politics.

Laffrenier’s life emerged from working-class Hamilton. His mother, who had him at 22, worked three jobs to keep their single-parent home afloat. He remembers his earliest household lessons being anchored by a familiar trifecta: Malcolm X, the Black Panthers and Martin Luther King Jr. It was a vast buffet of Black possibility.

Theatre, though, was never part of the household curriculum. “My first love is math. It’s still math,” Laffrenier says. For years, he assumed he would become an engineer, until a friend got into film school and introduced him to another path. “I didn’t even know that you could go to school for anything artistic.”

Once theatre entered the picture, it connected almost immediately to a need he had always carried.

“It just felt like this was the way to make change,” he says, “and this was the way to, frankly, at that time, tell Black stories.”

Laffrenier’s staging of Wine in the Wilderness platformed a sort of fuller, messier spectrum of Black life he had spent a good deal of time wanting to see given a stage. In 2015, he helped launch Then They Fight, an independent Toronto company founded by young artists who weren’t seeing themselves reflected in the city’s major institutions.

“A lot of the theatre companies in Toronto would never do our work,” Laffrenier says. “There were a few theatre companies that had all-white seasons.” Few people among the writers, directors, dramaturges and establishment leadership looked like him and his peers.

The issue Laffrenier often ran into – and which has long dogged pretty much every other Black theatre-maker – was one of imagination. Not his, but the lack of one caused by a centuries-long pileup of white institutional taste.

“When there’s only one work by a certain group of people, or when there’s no work by a certain group of people,” Laffrenier says, the challenge is how to “fill the imagination” of artistic directors so they can envision “more stories on the stage as part of their seasons.”

Now on the inside at Canadian Stage, Laffrenier treats that power as an obligation. “Power is something that needs to be distributed always. It’s given me a bigger responsibility to the community and all of its members.”

An all-Black room, however, isn’t a promise of a harmonious one. In rehearsals for Wine in the Wilderness , he kept returning to a fundamental question: “What is this thing we do to each other as Black people?”

The play taught Laffrenier how to ask the question, then handed him a harder answer: Black people can inherit “the language of the oppressor,” then turn around and use it to judge or police one another.

The conclusion it left him with is blunter still: “A revolution that leaves gender hierarchies and class hierarchies intact is no revolution at all,” he says. “A revolution needs to include everyone.”

For all that clarity, Laffrenier seems most interested in whatever disrupts it next – which in this case is directing American Buffalo for Toronto’s Coal Mine Theatre (opening Nov. 8). David Mamet’s play, about three working-class men circling a small-time theft in a Chicago junk shop, terrifies him in part because he reads it as deeply about whiteness.

“I would love to direct the play that people are like, ‘We don’t think Jordan could direct this play,’” he says.

The work he thinks he can’t direct, he has found, often leaves him with even more questions than answers. “I like plays that say things that I’ve never heard before. I like plays that feel like they reveal something about me that felt unknown.”

David Mamet’s play, about three working-class men circling a small-time theft in a Chicago junk shop, terrifies him in part because he reads it as deeply about whiteness.
“I would love to direct the play that people are like, ‘We don’t think Jordan could direct this play,’” he says.

The work he thinks he can’t direct, he has found, often leaves him with even more questions than answers. “I like plays that say things that I’ve never heard before. I like plays that feel like they reveal something about me that felt unknown.”

It complicated the celebration with uncomfortable questions. What, exactly, was Harris asking Black people to endure on a stage? Was Slave Play good for Black audiences? A petition demanding the production close attracted more than 6,000 signatures.

content_blocks.text: The first act asks whether a vision of historical Black trauma can take place in a bedroom. Theatre, though, was never part of the household curriculum. “My first love is math. It’s still math,” Laffrenier says. For years, he assumed he would become an engineer, until a friend got into film school and introduced him to another path. “I didn’t even know that you could go to school for anything artistic.”

stories.title: More than 300 advance polls open across Alberta in historic referendum on separation
stories.summary: Edmonton - Albertans across the province began lining up and casting their ballots Tuesday in the province's historic vote on separation.
stories.author: Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Elections Alberta opened the doors at 310 polling stations for the first of five days of advanced voting ahead of the official polling day on Oct. 19.

One downtown Edmonton polling station saw a lineup that stretched almost half a block after doors opened at 9 a.m., with voters spending anywhere between 30 minutes and an hour to cast their ballots.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Image 9Image 10

Premier Danielle Smith has put 10 questions to a vote, including whether Alberta should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on quitting Confederation.

Some voters wore their vote on their sleeves by dawning hats or sweaters with the Canadian flag to go to the polls, including Christopher Hashmi.

“It is obviously a bad idea,” Hashmi said of separation, adding that he thought Alberta would only be more vulnerable to the interests of the United States and oil and gas corporations if the province went its own way.

Lizzy Somerville said it was patriotism that inspired her to vote to stay in Canada.

“Canada works better together,” she said.

For Samara O’Hagan, the issue of separation comes down to concerns over who has the rights to the land.

“I’m Indigenous, so it’s very important to me,” she said.

“It would just be totally wrong, essentially stealing land from Indigenous people. Alberta should not be able to do that.”

The other nine referendum questions have to do with immigration reform and Canada’s Constitution.

Somerville said she voted against all but one of the premier’s proposals. She voted yes to lobbying other provincial governments to garner support for abolishing the Senate.

She said the upper house was “useless” and that if abolishment wasn’t an option, she’d like to see the seats be subject to elections rather than the current appointment process handled by the prime minister.

Hashmi said he voted “no to the nine” — a slogan used by critics and third-party advertisers pushing against Smith’s referendum proposals. He said he would have considered voting for Senate abolition, but felt doing so would be a sign of support for Smith’s government.

“Is the unelected Senate bad? Yes, it sucks. It is an archaic and broken part of our Constitution,” he said.

“But Danielle Smith and her government are a broken and archaic part of my day-to-day life.”

Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi was expected to cast his vote at an advanced poll in Calgary on Tuesday.

The start of advanced voting comes after Elections Alberta saw record interest in special ballots for the referendum, with roughly 658,000 Albertans requesting to vote by mail.

A spokesperson for the agency, Michelle Gurney, said that as of Monday evening about 391,000 mail-in ballots have been returned ahead of Friday’s 5 p.m. deadline.

Gurney also said about 46,000 workers have been hired to facilitate the vote and hand count the ballots. The agency has been aiming to hire 60,000 workers.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Federal government expands AI program with $500M boost
stories.summary: The federal government says it is making an additional $500 million available over five years to help Canadian businesses adopt artificial intelligence technologies and bring Canadian-developed AI products to market.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The federal government says it is making an additional $500 million available over five years to help Canadian businesses adopt artificial intelligence technologies and bring Canadian-developed AI products to market.

The announcement was made in London on Tuesday by Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon, who said the funding will expand the Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative, bringing total federal support for the program to $700 million.

The initiative is part of the federal government’s AI for All strategy, unveiled in June 2026, which is aimed at increasing the use of artificial intelligence across Canada while strengthening the country’s AI sector and technological sovereignty.

Federal officials said support will be focused primarily on sectors where Canada has established expertise and growth potential, including health and life sciences, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, manufacturing and robotics. Regional agencies will also have flexibility to support other local economic priorities.

The government said the expanded program will also help Canadian AI companies attract investment, secure customers and commercialize homegrown technologies. Funding will also be available to organizations that provide businesses with specialized expertise and support related to AI adoption and commercialization.

The federal government also said the investment is intended to encourage broader AI adoption across Canada, help domestic AI firms grow while remaining based in Canada, and support economic growth and productivity.

stories.title: B.C. photojournalist documents ICE operations in rural United States
stories.summary: B.C. photo journalist Greg Constantine has been documenting what is happening when ICE moves in on rural areas in the U.S.
stories.author: Emma Crawford
stories.content:
By Jack Rabb

Posted October 13, 2026 3:25 pm.

Following the latest shooting of an unarmed civilian by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers — this time with a child in the target’s car — protests erupted on the streets of New York.

Similar incidents have elicited widespread resistance in major cities across the country during President Donald Trump’s second term, but one B.C.-based photojournalist sensed that much more was going under-the-radar outside of city limits.

Dual citizen Greg Constantine was awarded a fellowship to investigate just that. He spent months in small towns in Republican strongholds like Indiana and Missouri, documenting how Trump’s immigration policies were playing out in the places where they are approved of.

“I think that, economically, it’s affecting people, but I think from my perspective, it’s really just this destruction, total destruction, of families,” Constantine said.

“That kind of violence that’s taking place may take on a different form, but it’s impacting communities just as much.”

Constantine’s work, published as a series of multimedia essays in Mother Jones, often captures absence: a family photo without a father, a car without a driver.

“What was left behind is this vaporized person, with a life still suspended.”

That’s the consequence of the quiet campaign of apprehension that’s happening in these rural Republican areas, where trusted local law enforcement has been contracted by ICE to whisk people away, most of whom have no criminal record, as they go about their daily lives.

“Routine traffic stops, profiling of people after they come out of a gas station,” are examples, Constantine said.

He also revealed the insidious economics of Trump’s deportation regime. Federal money pours into rural areas, funding sheriff’s offices and employing thousands of people at detention centres, becoming a lynchpin of municipal budgets.

“It’s much more of a mass-detention project than anything else, because of the money that is being made off of all this,” he said.

“And really, the raw materials of that profit are human beings. You know, human men, women, fathers, mothers, grandparents, aunts, uncles, brothers, and sisters. And that’s something that I think every American should be ashamed of.”

stories.title: Ontario woman once charged with witchcraft convicted in Buddha statue fraud
stories.summary: "The Buddha statues for which (the fraud victim) paid were never made and were never intended to be made," said the judge.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
An Ontario woman once charged with witchcraft has been convicted of defrauding a friend with a shared interest in spirituality, faith, healing and Buddhism out of $44,100, partly by promising that her fictitious brother Swamiraavi who lived in Montreal would make the victim Buddha statues.

The Crown argued that Vishwantee Persaud defrauded Carolina Gopaul, her neighbour, out of approximately $120,000 between 2017 and 2019 in Brampton, Ont. But prosecutors were only able to prove just over a third of that in the Ontario Court of Justice.

“The Crown alleges that Ms. Persaud exploited Ms. Gopaul’s age, naivety, and emotional vulnerability by inducing her to provide money for a variety of purported faith- and healing-related purposes that were, in fact, fraudulent,” Justice Robert Tomovski wrote in a recent decision finding Persaud guilty.

Gopaul testified that she gave Persaud between $4,000 and $5,000 in cash for several custom-made Buddha statues, but she only got one, which the judge determined was not made by Persaud’s brother. She also paid several expenses for the fictitious brother, totalling about $25,000.

The judge found that “Persaud did not have a brother in Montreal named Swamiraavi and, consequently, did not have a brother there who made Buddha statues.”

Persaud “deliberately misrepresented the purpose for which the money was requested and obtained the funds for her own benefit,” Tomovski said. “The Buddha statues for which Ms. Gopaul paid were never made and were never intended to be made.”

The court also heard Gopal gave Persaud $19,100 after being told that Persaud “was a lawyer who required money to pay a licence reinstatement fee,” said the Oct. 8 decision, which doesn’t grapple with whether or not Persaud was ever a lawyer.

The Crown argued that the money was never used for that purpose.

The judge agreed, ruling “the money received by Ms. Persaud was not applied toward the reinstatement of her law licence or expenses associated with employment at a law firm.”

Gopaul also provided Persaud with two credit cards and access to a chequing account “after being told that they would be used to cover expenses associated with the practice of law and the commencement of employment with a law firm in Quebec,” said the decision.

The transactions Persaud rang up on the credit cards included purchases of jewellery, lingerie, fitness memberships, flights to Greece and Jamaica, and veterinary services. “Ms. Gopaul testified that she was unaware Ms. Persaud owned a pet,” the judge said.

Tomovski said he was left with a reasonable doubt about the agreement regarding the use of the credit cards.

“There is credible and reliable evidence that Ms. Gopaul was aware, for nearly two years, that Ms. Persaud was making purchases of a personal nature that were unrelated to legal employment or licensing expenses. Despite that knowledge, she did not question the transactions, report them as unauthorized, cancel the credit cards, or close the account. This finding, however, does not detract from my overall conclusion that Ms. Persaud defrauded Ms. Gopaul. It affects only the quantum of the resulting loss.”

Gopaul, 69, has three adult children, “one of whom has significant physical and mental disabilities and remains dependent upon her for ongoing care and accommodation,” said the decision.

Gopaul testified that “she repeatedly sought repayment from” Persaud for racking up her credit cards and taking money from her chequing account, but she only got a tiny fraction of it back.

Gopaul maintained that Persaud still owed her $118,492.62.

The judge found that Gopaul’s “total loss attributable to the law-related component of the fraud was $19,100.”

Tomovski was left with reasonable doubt that Persaud’s use of Gopaul’s chequing account and credit cards was fraudulent.

Gopaul was receiving monthly statements and account records for them as early as October 2017, the judge said.

“I do not accept that Ms. Gopaul was so overwhelmed, vulnerable, or naive that she would not have appreciated what was plainly disclosed by the records,” Tomovski said.

He had similar doubts about Persaud’s car expenses. Gopaul testified that she paid approximately $700 per month for six months toward Persaud’s car payments, and $2,050 for her car insurance

But Tomovski was “satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that Ms. Persaud fraudulently deprived Ms. Gopaul of at least $44,100 through deceit and falsehood.”

This isn’t Persaud’s first fraud conviction. In 2009 Toronto police charged her with employing fake supernatural powers to defraud a lawyer out of $27,000.

She had claimed to be from a family of witches and said that she could embody the client’s deceased sister during a tarot reading.

The original witchcraft charges were later replaced by fraud charges, to which Persaud pleaded guilty in 2010.

stories.title: What could happen to home prices if the foreign buyers ban expires?
stories.summary: The foreign homebuyers ban is scheduled to expire on Jan 1, 2027, which means home prices are at risk of rising sharply if there is pent up demand from non-residents.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
The federal foreign homebuyers ban is scheduled to expire on Jan 1, 2027, which has real estate experts questioning whether home prices could be at risk of rising sharply if there is pent up demand from non-residents after being closed off for several years.

More buyers in the housing market creates more demand, which typically results in higher prices if new homes aren’t being built fast enough to meet that demand. But experts say Canada’s housing market is not as hot or attractive to buyers as a few years ago when the ban was put in place.

“It’s been an issue that was a hot topic several years ago, but has since died down quite a bit, and there was a lot of debate whether it was in fact an issue that really had an impact on housing affordability at the time,” says Robert Hogue, assistant chief economist at Royal Bank of Canada.

“Foreign buyers might have had a little bit of an impact in certain neighborhoods of Canada’s urban areas, like in Vancouver and Toronto in particular, but the evidence of the impact of foreign buyers was still very debatable at the time.”

The federal government has said it is looking into “options” for the foreign homebuyers ban as the expiration deadline approaches.

“That’s a measure … that has been in place for some time. The market is evolving,” Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne told reporters last week.

“We’re looking at all the options that we have in front of us, considering where the market is going, what has happened over the last few years, always keeping in mind that we want to make sure that we have a higher stock of housing opportunities for Canadians.”

Canada’s real estate market has been on a dramatic roller-coaster ride ever since the COVID-19 pandemic.

At the time, mortgages were more affordable because interest rates were at historic lows.

The Bank of Canada lowered its benchmark borrowing rate at the time to as low as 0.25 per cent, in order to help support struggling businesses and consumers while social distancing and other measures kept a lot of consumers at home and businesses shut down.

This ultimately led to a spike in demand for homes, which drove up sale prices dramatically. There were also many reports of bidding wars that drove up prices even faster.

Some of those placing bids were reportedly from foreign buyers looking to invest in Canada’ real estate market while demand was high, and more often in hotter urban areas like Toronto and Vancouver.

“When home prices were going up 10 per cent, 12 per cent, 14 per cent a year, it was a very attractive place for overseas investors to park their money,” says Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Missing Middle Initiative at the University of Ottawa.

To help cool the housing market, a multi-prong approach was needed.

The Bank of Canada began raising its borrowing rate quickly beginning in March 2022, increasing it from 0.25 per cent to a peak of five per cent by July 2023 — where it stayed until June 2024. This was comparable to putting the red-hot housing market on ice.

The federal government also initiated a ban on foreign buyers on Jan. 1, 2023, and after similar measures were put in place by individual provinces. The federal ban was in place for two years, and was extended for another two years until Jan. 1 2027.

Inflation in Canada was also spiking to multi-year highs as supply chains experienced intense bottlenecks from pent up consumer demand stemming from the pandemic years. Russia’s war with Ukraine, which began in 2022, also sent shockwaves through global economies and drove up energy costs for businesses and consumers.

“Once home prices started to fall, not only were they not wanting to buy in Canada, they were actually wanting to pull their money out of Canada — it just no longer made sense to be in this market,” says Moffatt.

The foreign homebuyers ban was launched at a time when the Bank of Canada was aggressively raising interest rates and as other global economic factors weighed on homebuyers. This means the effects of the ban May have been clouded, especially by the central bank’s monetary policy having arguably more of a cooling effect on the housing market.

“We saw a massive increase in interest rates and that absolutely not just cooled the housing market but sent in a very deep freeze in many parts of Canada, and in fact, some markets like Toronto and Vancouver are still struggling to recover from that big shock, and so that kind of triggered this cooling,” says Hogue.

According to Statistics Canada, non-residents made up a very small fraction of property owners in major markets like Ontario and British Columbia in recent years.

Prior to the ban, non-residents owned roughly 2.75 per cent of all properties in Ontario in 2021, 2022 and 2023. In 2024, that number dipped slightly to 2.62 per cent.

In B.C., non-residents owned about 4.5 per cent of all properties in 2021, just over four per cent in 2022 and 2023, and 3.8 per cent in 2024.

It isn’t clear if these dips in 2024 in particular were because of the foreign buyers ban, or because of other factors like higher interest rates and other economic factors at the time making it harder for many Canadians and non-residents to afford a mortgage.

Since it isn’t clear whether the ban had a meaningful impact on housing affordability or supply, Hogue says it’s no surprise the government is reviewing the ban’s viability.

“Government has to think real hard whether having this extra measure in place to address an issue that was a hot topic years ago, whether it’s worth maintaining,” says Hogue.

The federal government has launched other measures to tackle home affordability, including Build Canada Homes , which aims to build more housing units on federal lands, as well as eliminating the GST portion on some new home sales of up to $1 million for first-time buyers.

Hogue says it is unlikely that if the foreign homebuyers ban was abandoned, a wave of new buyers would result.

“I don’t think the conditions are there for it,” he says.

“Canada’s housing market will continue to recover very slowly, and it will likely to be a very bumpy journey.”

Moffatt says although letting the plan expire will have no short-term impacts on prices, there is also a case to keeping it, with modifications.

“It will have no noticeable impact on prices 12, 24 months from now, regardless if we keep it or don’t keep it — it’s basically a non-factor,” he says.

“I do think there is merit as well to keeping it, but making significant reforms to make sure that we can, builders and developers, can get oversee capital to help them build new projects.”

– with a file from Global News’ Alex Boutilier

content_blocks.text: Why was there a ban in the first place?
Canada’s real estate market has been on a dramatic roller-coaster ride ever since the COVID-19 pandemic.
content_blocks.html: Canada’s real estate market has been on a dramatic roller-coaster ride ever since the COVID-19 pandemic.

content_blocks.text: At the time, mortgages were more affordable because interest rates were at historic lows.

The Bank of Canada lowered its benchmark borrowing rate at the time to as low as 0.25 per cent, in order to help support struggling businesses and consumers while social distancing and other measures kept a lot of consumers at home and businesses shut down.
content_blocks.html: The Bank of Canada lowered its benchmark borrowing rate at the time to as low as 0.25 per cent, in order to help support struggling businesses and consumers while social distancing and other measures kept a lot of consumers at home and businesses shut down.

content_blocks.text: This ultimately led to a spike in demand for homes, which drove up sale prices dramatically. There were also many reports of bidding wars that drove up prices even faster.
Some of those placing bids were reportedly from foreign buyers looking to invest in Canada’ real estate market while demand was high, and more often in hotter urban areas like Toronto and Vancouver.

“When home prices were going up 10 per cent, 12 per cent, 14 per cent a year, it was a very attractive place for overseas investors to park their money,” says Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Missing Middle Initiative at the University of Ottawa.
To help cool the housing market, a multi-prong approach was needed.

The Bank of Canada began raising its borrowing rate quickly beginning in March 2022, increasing it from 0.25 per cent to a peak of five per cent by July 2023 — where it stayed until June 2024. This was comparable to putting the red-hot housing market on ice.

The federal government also initiated a ban on foreign buyers on Jan. 1, 2023, and after similar measures were put in place by individual provinces. The federal ban was in place for two years, and was extended for another two years until Jan. 1 2027.

Inflation in Canada was also spiking to multi-year highs as supply chains experienced intense bottlenecks from pent up consumer demand stemming from the pandemic years. Russia’s war with Ukraine, which began in 2022, also sent shockwaves through global economies and drove up energy costs for businesses and consumers.

“Once home prices started to fall, not only were they not wanting to buy in Canada, they were actually wanting to pull their money out of Canada — it just no longer made sense to be in this market,” says Moffatt.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Opportunities abound for 1st-time homebuyers as housing market softens'

content_blocks.text: Did the ban work to help cool the market?

The foreign homebuyers ban was launched at a time when the Bank of Canada was aggressively raising interest rates and as other global economic factors weighed on homebuyers. This means the effects of the ban May have been clouded, especially by the central bank’s monetary policy having arguably more of a cooling effect on the housing market.

“We saw a massive increase in interest rates and that absolutely not just cooled the housing market but sent in a very deep freeze in many parts of Canada, and in fact, some markets like Toronto and Vancouver are still struggling to recover from that big shock, and so that kind of triggered this cooling,” says Hogue.
According to Statistics Canada, non-residents made up a very small fraction of property owners in major markets like Ontario and British Columbia in recent years.
Prior to the ban, non-residents owned roughly 2.75 per cent of all properties in Ontario in 2021, 2022 and 2023. In 2024, that number dipped slightly to 2.62 per cent.
In B.C., non-residents owned about 4.5 per cent of all properties in 2021, just over four per cent in 2022 and 2023, and 3.8 per cent in 2024.

It isn’t clear if these dips in 2024 in particular were because of the foreign buyers ban, or because of other factors like higher interest rates and other economic factors at the time making it harder for many Canadians and non-residents to afford a mortgage.
Should the ban be renewed?
Since it isn’t clear whether the ban had a meaningful impact on housing affordability or supply, Hogue says it’s no surprise the government is reviewing the ban’s viability.
“Government has to think real hard whether having this extra measure in place to address an issue that was a hot topic years ago, whether it’s worth maintaining,” says Hogue.

The federal government has launched other measures to tackle home affordability, including Build Canada Homes , which aims to build more housing units on federal lands, as well as eliminating the GST portion on some new home sales of up to $1 million for first-time buyers.
content_blocks.html: The federal government has launched other measures to tackle home affordability, including Build Canada Homes, which aims to build more housing units on federal lands, as well as eliminating the GST portion on some new home sales of up to $1 million for first-time buyers.

content_blocks.text: Hogue says it is unlikely that if the foreign homebuyers ban was abandoned, a wave of new buyers would result.
“I don’t think the conditions are there for it,” he says.
“Canada’s housing market will continue to recover very slowly, and it will likely to be a very bumpy journey.”
Moffatt says although letting the plan expire will have no short-term impacts on prices, there is also a case to keeping it, with modifications.
“It will have no noticeable impact on prices 12, 24 months from now, regardless if we keep it or don’t keep it — it’s basically a non-factor,” he says.
“I do think there is merit as well to keeping it, but making significant reforms to make sure that we can, builders and developers, can get oversee capital to help them build new projects.”

stories.title: Ontario NDP urges Ford, Carney to buy Stelco as firm eyes layoffs
stories.summary: Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles told reporters Tuesday that public ownership of Stelco is emerging as the only option to save roughly 350 jobs.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello, Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
The Ontario NDP is calling on Premier Doug Ford and Prime Minister Mark Carney to use taxpayer funds to buy Stelco , the Hamilton steel giant whose owner has sided with U.S. President Donald Trump in his trade war with Canada.

Stelco, which is owned by U.S.-based Cleveland Cliffs, begins laying off hundreds of workers at its manufacturing plant in Ontario after claiming that the facility was producing more steel than the company could sell on Canadian soil.

Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles told reporters Tuesday that public ownership of Stelco is emerging as the only option to save roughly 350 jobs.

The party’s proposal is being echoed by Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis, who said “it’s time to nationalize Stelco.”

“Stelco’s American owners have broken their commitments. Their CEO supports Trump’s tariffs, which are designed to deindustrialize our economy and destroy our manufacturing base,” he said. Lewis said with more than 500 workers in Hamilton facing layoffs, nationalizing the firm is the path to saving those jobs.

Stiles said it could be an opportunity to use provincial power to fast-track new infrastructure projects that commit to using Canadian steel.

“This is a win-win-win, and it’s time for the premier to put his money where his mouth is,” she said.

Stiles was referring to comments Premier Ford made in Aug. 2025, when Cleveland Cliffs owner Lorenco Goncalves called Trump’s tariffs “bold action” that would “strengthen the American steel industry.”

Ford, at the time , said Golcalves “doesn’t give two hoots about his workers at Stelco and mused about potentially using taxpayer funds to take over the company.”

“Maybe they should find a new owner for Stelco, maybe we should just buy em,” Ford said.

Ford government insiders insist the comment was made in passing but acknowledged that the future of the steel industry is being challenged by the current US tariffs.

While a senior source said the government would take a “wait and see” approach, they suggested the country is facing the larger question of whether it wants to maintain a domestic steel industry.

The source said the federal government would have to take the lead on the issue, but would need to assess its options after the U.S. mid-term elections that could realign the political base of power in Washington D.C.

While the NDP wouldn’t offer a potential purchase price, Stilles acknowledged the Ndp’s proposal is “ambitious” and would require federal backing.

Members of United Steelworkers, a private-sector union that represents more than 225,000 workers in Canada, have been also vocal that public ownership is the best option, Stiles said.

In 2024, Canada gave U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs the go-ahead to purchase Stelco under the Investment Canada Act (ICA), which regulates foreign takeovers.

The obligations laid out in that agreement, the federal government said, could result in legal action against the American company.

In the letter to Stelco, Federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Canada’s approval of the deal was contingent on the new owner maintaining the number of union jobs and the majority of non-union positions.

Stelco pushed back on Joly’s accusations in its letter and said it “remains in compliance” with the undertakings in the agreement from 2024.

stories.title: Joly says it's 'unacceptable' that government offices continue to use banned Chinese cameras
stories.summary: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says it is "unacceptable" that some federal government organizations continue using Hikvision cameras.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says it is “unacceptable” that some federal government organizations continue using Hikvision cameras that she declared banned from Canada last year.

Last week, National Post reported that despite gear from Chinese surveillance camera giant Hikvision being banned from federal properties in June 2025 on national security grounds, at least two agencies — the National Research Council and the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority — continue to use them.

It also reported that the partly Chinese state-owned company operated “illegally” for nearly one decade in Canada despite growing security concerns within and outside of government about the security of Hikvision products.

The National Research Council told National Post last week that the organization removed all Hikvision gear from its security systems in 2025, but continues to use them to monitor “non-sensitive experiments and work areas.” A spokesperson confirmed that the remaining Hikvision cameras would be removed from operation by the end of the year.

“This is unacceptable,” Joly responded in a statement provided by her office. In addition, she said she had told her department — which oversees the National Research Council — “that these cameras need to be removed.”

Housing and Infrastructure Minister Gregor Robertson, who oversees the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority, was far less categorical.

The bridge authority, which oversees the crucial Gordie Howe International Bridge linking Canada and the U.S., confirmed to National Post that it still used Hikvision cameras in a community meeting space and would do so until November.

In a statement, Robertson’s spokesperson Jenna Ghassabeh touted “significant progress” in removing existing Hikvision equipment on government-owned and -leased properties.

“The office where legacy products exist and are being removed is one where only public non confidential information is managed,” Ghassabeh wrote. “To reduce risk exposure during replacement, interim mitigation measures, including the disconnection of internet connectivity and remote access capabilities have been explored at all sites.”

Following National Post’s reporting, Bloc Québécois leader Yves-François Blanchet accused Prime Minister Mark Carney of ignoring the plight of Chinese minorities (Hikvision is reportedly involved in mass surveillance of Uyghurs in China.)

“Meanwhile, as everyone tries to grasp the extent of China’s obvious intrusion into the affairs of Canada — and, to a lesser extent, Quebec —Prime Minister Carney is fixated solely on China’s financial clout and his desire to forge closer ties with the country,” Blanchet wrote on X .

In June 2025, Joly issued a federal ban on Hikvision Canada — a global leader in surveillance camera gear that is partly owned by the Chinese government — due to risks of espionage and mass surveillance on behalf of the People’s Republic of China.

She gave the company 120 days to pack its bags and shut down its Canadian operation. The order also demanded that the federal government — including agencies and Crown corporations — essentially strip all existing Hikvision cameras out of its offices.

Hikvision is currently contesting the order in Federal Court and has denied all the government’s allegations against its products.

Of the nearly 15 government bodies who declared using Hikvision gear in their offices in 2024, the majority told National Post that the gear had since been removed.

But five of those organizations refused to say if they had complied with the federal government’s diktat.

They are Canadian Space Agency, Employment and Social Development Canada (Esdc), Environment and Climate Change Canada, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada and Parks Canada.

That is unacceptable and raises serious questions about the Liberals’ handling of the file, according to Conservatives.

“After a year and a half, they cannot even confirm whether they have removed security cameras from government buildings. If they cannot give Canadians a straight answer on something this basic, why should anyone trust them to deliver on the rest of their promises?,” Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre’s spokesperson Sam Lilly said in a statement.

Michael Kovrig, CEO of Kovrig Group and a former Canadian diplomat infamously imprisoned by China from 2018 to 2021, said that Hikvision gear should be long gone from federal government buildings.

That’s even more the case when the Chinese government refuses to allow foreign camera manufacturers to bid on domestic contracts.

“Equipment made by a company that has to obey the Chinese Communist Party and its intelligence laws has no place in government facilities, and Canadians should think hard before putting it in their own private buildings,” Kovrig told National Post.

“A state that won’t tolerate foreign cameras and network gear in its own systems has no standing to demand that Canada tolerate Chinese surveillance tech.”

National Post cnardi@postmedia.com

stories.title: Flu vaccine appointments are now open in Quebec as early flu season looms
stories.summary: Montreal - Appointments are now open for flu vaccines in Quebec as the province's health department warns of an early flu season.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Quebec health and social services department says vulnerable people should get their shots before the holiday season.

People will be able to get vaccinated for the flu, COVID-19 and Respiratory Syncytial Virus in the same appointment.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Image 10Image 11

This year, only some vulnerable Quebecers will be eligible for free shots.

This includes people over 65, people who have chronic illnesses and pregnant women.

Others will need to pay for the shots in Quebec.

Most provinces in Canada will start providing the flu vaccine by the end of the month, and respiratory virus specialists say Canadians should get their flu shot as soon as it becomes available.

— With files from Nicole Ireland

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

TORONTO - Ontario’s medical regulator has approved significant changes to the way doctors prescribe safer supply drugs, in an effort to reduce the amount of opioids making their way to the streets.

Oct. 13, 2026

Chris Young/The Canadian Press[](http://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/ontario-s-medical-regulator-approves-changes-to-prescribing-safer-supply-drugs/article_6be35426-1b0e-517d-baf0-215c7eff8cde.html)

By Liam Casey The Canadian Press

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario’s board of directors will soon implement several changes to the practice of prescribing safer supply, which are medications given to people at high risk of overdose as an alternative to illicit opioids.

The college will make it mandatory for physicians to prescribe safer supply medications only in conjunction with opioid agonist therapy. The therapy uses medications such as Suboxone and methadone to treat opioid addiction.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

The most common form of safer supply is hydromorphone, a powerful opioid often prescribed for pain but significantly less potent than fentanyl and its derivatives that dominate the illicit drug supply chain.

Patients will now have to take the safer supply medications in front of health-care professionals, rather than take the pills home.

The college will not go ahead with an eight-week time limit for physicians to prescribe safer supply to patients it had previously considered.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Dominion Dynamics to build uncrewed ground vehicles for Ukraine through partnership
stories.summary: Ottawa-based company’s deal with Tencore aimed at moving production away from Ukrainian front lines
stories.author: Pippa Norman
stories.content:
Dominion Dynamics is aiming to manufacture uncrewed ground vehicles for use in the war in Ukraine , becoming the latest Canadian defence company to help Ukraine move production away from the front lines and bolstering an agreement recently signed by the two countries’ leaders.

On Tuesday, the defence-tech maker announced it has signed a memorandum of understanding with Tencore, a ground robotics company based in Ukraine, to manufacture its uncrewed ground vehicles in Ottawa and outfit them with Dominion’s own command-and-control software.

The partnership is a direct response to an agreement signed last month by Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to jointly produce uncrewed systems, counterdrone technologies and munitions. Mr. Carney has also committed to sending one-third of all drones manufactured in Canada to Ukraine.

“Canada has the work force and the suppliers to build at scale,” Eliot Pence, chief executive officer of the Ottawa-based company, said in a statement. “This agreement is how two companies start turning that commitment into vehicles, and we intend to move fast.”

Already, the two companies have moved quickly. Their relationship began about a month ago at an international defence industry exhibition in Poland, where Canada was highlighted. There, Mr. Pence said members of his team met employees of Tencore and struck up discussions about how they could collaborate.

“The rest is history. It happened in 30 days, which reflects the urgency of the moment.”

Dominion is the latest Canadian company to embark upon a defence agreement with Ukrainian industry. In May, Sentinel R&D Inc., a drone company based in Hamilton, announced a joint venture with Ukrainian drone company Airlogix to manufacture systems in Canada. Then, in September, Mr. Carney announced a partnership between General Dynamics Mission Systems-Canada, an Ottawa-based subsidiary of the U.S. defence giant, and Ukrainian company GreenTech Harvest to produce uncrewed systems in Canada for use in the war.

These partnerships come on the heels of Mr. Zelensky launching his “Build with Ukraine” initiative in June, 2025, to help diversify the country’s supply chain and give it access to more products made away from the front lines, where manufacturing faces a constant threat of attack. The move contrasts with the President’s approach during the first few years of Russia’s illegal invasion, when the country closely protected its IP and restricted the export of military technologies.

The deal between Dominion and Tencore is still in its early stages. Mr. Pence said he’s currently pursuing government funding in Canada and working with Tencore to ensure it’s authorized to export the Ukrainian technology. He’s also exploring whether Dominion could bring Canadian auto parts makers into its supply chain for the autonomous vehicles.

The platform Dominion plans to manufacture is a modular vehicle called TerMIT. Tencore has designed the drone to be adaptable to different use cases, including transporting supplies and people, deploying barbed wire and operating a machine gun.

A version of the Ukrainian platform is arriving at Dominion’s facility in Ottawa this week, Mr. Pence said, where his team’s job will be to take it apart and put it back together again.

“It will give us a better sense of ‘What are we thinking about? What do we need to prepare for? What should the production line look like? Do we have the testing facility necessary to test different types of contexts?’” he said.

If the partnership goes ahead as planned, Mr. Pence said Dominion will begin with five prototype builds. By 2027, it will kick off initial production. Tencore has delivered more than 5,000 of the uncrewed ground vehicles to Ukrainian military units since 2024, according to the company. Dominion’s goal is to produce between 500 and 1,000 units in its 30,000-square-foot facility over the next two years.

“Battlefield requirements change in weeks, so production, operational feedback and engineering have to run as a loop: build, deploy, learn, change, scale,” said Roman Tkachenko, co-founder of Tencore, in a statement.

“Canada gives us the manufacturing base, suppliers and reliable power to run that loop alongside allies who need these vehicles.”

The integration of Dominion’s AuraNet platform with the Ukrainian vehicles will also be a big step forward for the company, which has not yet tested the technology in Ukraine, Mr. Pence said. AuraNet is an array of sensor nodes that can be deployed together to collect and communicate data, such as video, images or voice notes, and detect threats.

Mr. Pence said his long-term goal is to “ruggedize” the Ukrainian vehicles for Arctic terrain and conditions, in order to sell to the Canadian Armed Forces. But for now, the focus remains on building for Ukraine.

stories.title: Activist calls on Carney to intervene after Palestinian president postpones elections
stories.summary: A Palestinian political activist has written a letter to Mark Carney urging him to help preserve the Nov. 28 Palestinian elections.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
A Palestinian political activist who campaigns for Palestinian-Israeli coexistence has written a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney urging him to help preserve the Nov. 28 Palestinian elections.

On Saturday, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas postponed legislative elections as well as the presidential elections until September 2027, citing “obstacles ⁠posed by Israeli measures” as the reason for the postponement of “free, fair and inclusive elections.”

Samer Sinijlaw, who is head of the Palestinian political movement New Path (Masar Jadid), said in his letter to the PM, which was written the same day the postponement was announced: “I recognize the legitimate concerns regarding Israeli cooperation, access to polling stations, and the integrity of the electoral process, particularly in Gaza. These are serious challenges, but they must be addressed rather than used to justify another indefinite postponement of Palestinian democracy.”

He also wrote: “I am therefore appealing to you to intervene personally and urgently with President Abbas, together with Canada’s international partners, to ensure that the Palestinian Authority honours its commitment to hold elections.”

Carney announced his government’s commitment to recognize a Palestinian state in July 2025 based on commitments made by the Palestinian Authority, including a promise to hold general elections in 2026.

In a statement at the time, the PM said: “Canada intends to recognize the State of Palestine at the 80th Session of the United Nations General Assembly in September 2025.

“This intention is predicated on the Palestinian Authority’s commitment to much-needed reforms, including the commitments by Palestinian Authority President Abbas to fundamentally reform its governance, to hold general elections in 2026 in which Hamas can play no part, and to demilitarize the Palestinian state.”

Global Affairs Canada released a joint statement with the Foreign Ministers of Australia, Canada, France and the U.K. on Tuesday, saying they “deeply regret” Abbas’ decision to postpone the elections.

“Credible elections are an important element of the commitment that President Abbas and the Palestinian Authority made to reform, including democratic renewal and accountable governance, and are in line with the July 2025 New York Declaration,” it read. “Strengthening Palestinian governance is essential to continue building the institutional foundations of a viable two-state solution, which is the only path to lasting peace and security for both Israel and Palestine.”

The statement added that the nations will “continue to support efforts to deliver on these elections.”

In his recent letter, Sinijlaw said “Canada has a particularly important role to play” in preserving the November elections. “It was a commitment made directly to Canada and the international community, and one upon which Canada relied when recognizing Palestinian statehood,” he wrote.

He added that an estimated 88 per cent of eligible Palestinian voters had already registered to participate, demonstrating how seriously Palestinians are taking the opportunity to choose their leadership.

“Postponing these elections would undermine precisely those Palestinians who are working to build a credible, peaceful political alternative,” he added.

The activist is asking Carney to take four steps to urge the Palestinian Authority to honour its commitment to 2026 elections: contact President Abbas; publicly reaffirm Canada’s expectation that the Palestinian Authority proceed with the elections; express Canada’s opposition to the decision to postpone; and review discretionary Canadian assistance linked to Palestinian Authority governance until a commitment to elections is restored.

“For the sake of our children, I ask Canada to stand firm. They deserve accountable leadership, a voice in their future, and a reason to believe that peaceful political change is possible,” he wrote.

Meanwhile, the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (Cija) is also calling on the Carney government to hold Palestinian leaders accountable for breaking its commitment to hold elections in 2026.

“Otherwise, the government risks a dangerous double standard that has implications for both the region and for the safety of Canadians as security experts warn that criticism of Israel has been exploited to fuel antisemitism, violence and even acts of terror.”

The November elections would have been the first Palestinian elections in more than 20 years.

“This intention is predicated on the Palestinian Authority’s commitment to much-needed reforms, including the commitments by Palestinian Authority President Abbas to fundamentally reform its governance, to hold general elections in 2026 in which Hamas can play no part, and to demilitarize the Palestinian state.”

Global Affairs Canada released a joint statement with the Foreign Ministers of Australia, Canada, France and the U.K. on Tuesday, saying they “deeply regret” Abbas’ decision to postpone the elections.

“Credible elections are an important element of the commitment that President Abbas and the Palestinian Authority made to reform, including democratic renewal and accountable governance, and are in line with the July 2025 New York Declaration,” it read. “Strengthening Palestinian governance is essential to continue building the institutional foundations of a viable two-state solution, which is the only path to lasting peace and security for both Israel and Palestine.”
The statement added that the nations will “continue to support efforts to deliver on these elections.”

In his recent letter, Sinijlaw said “Canada has a particularly important role to play” in preserving the November elections. “It was a commitment made directly to Canada and the international community, and one upon which Canada relied when recognizing Palestinian statehood,” he wrote.

He added that an estimated 88 per cent of eligible Palestinian voters had already registered to participate, demonstrating how seriously Palestinians are taking the opportunity to choose their leadership.
“Postponing these elections would undermine precisely those Palestinians who are working to build a credible, peaceful political alternative,” he added.

The activist is asking Carney to take four steps to urge the Palestinian Authority to honour its commitment to 2026 elections: contact President Abbas; publicly reaffirm Canada’s expectation that the Palestinian Authority proceed with the elections; express Canada’s opposition to the decision to postpone; and review discretionary Canadian assistance linked to Palestinian Authority governance until a commitment to elections is restored.
“For the sake of our children, I ask Canada to stand firm. They deserve accountable leadership, a voice in their future, and a reason to believe that peaceful political change is possible,” he wrote.
Meanwhile, the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (Cija) is also calling on the Carney government to hold Palestinian leaders accountable for breaking its commitment to hold elections in 2026.

“Otherwise, the government risks a dangerous double standard that has implications for both the region and for the safety of Canadians as security experts warn that criticism of Israel has been exploited to fuel antisemitism, violence and even acts of terror.”
The November elections would have been the first Palestinian elections in more than 20 years.

stories.title: Swath of Ontario boreal forest larger than Toronto to be protected from development
stories.summary: A chunk of Ontario's northern boreal forest bigger than Toronto is set to be protected from industrial development.
stories.author: Jordan Omstead
stories.content:
A chunk of Ontario’s northern boreal forest bigger than Toronto is set to be protected from industrial development.

The Nature Conservancy of Canada says it has acquired 814 square kilometres of boreal forest and peatlands south of Kapuskasing, previously owned by a company selling carbon offset credits.

The non-profit says where the landscape is healthy and free of vulnerable species, some day-use recreational activities such as hiking and paddling May continue, in line with provincial laws.

The federal government says it’s contributing $13 million to the project as part of a total $64-million investment from both public and private donors.

The announcement comes ahead of next week’s annual United Nations biodiversity summit, where the talks are expected to focus on global progress toward conservation goals.

Ottawa unveiled a new $3.8-billion nature protection strategy earlier this year intended to put Canada’s goals within reach, months after the federal environmental watchdog found it to be more than one-million square kilometres short of its 2025 goal to protect 25 per cent of its lands and inland water.

stories.title: Man arrested in connection with Israeli flags set alight in Toronto: police
stories.summary: Police have arrested a Toronto man in connection with an arson investigation after several Israeli flags were set on fire outside a church.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Canada

Syed Raza, 29, removed several Israeli flags from outside a church in North York and set them alight, according to police

The incident occurred on the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel.Ernest Doroszuk/Toronto Sun

Police have arrested a Toronto man in connection with an arson investigation after several Israeli flags were set on fire outside a church on Wednesday.

Toronto Police said in a news release on Tuesday that Syed Raza, 29, was arrested and charged with arson, mischief under $5,000, mischief interfering with the lawful enjoyment of property, and disobeying a lawful order of court.

It added that on Oct. 7, at approximately 1:02 a.m., Raza attended the area of Sunrise Avenue and O’Connor Drive and removed Israeli flags that were placed in front of the Word of Faith International Christian Centre and set them alight.

On Saturday, the accused was identified by investigators while at a demonstration in the area of Dundas Street East and Yonge Street at approximately 4:06 p.m.

He was scheduled to appear in court at the Toronto Regional Bail Centre on Oct. 11.

The incident came on the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas-led attack on Israel, which killed 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage.

A police spokesperson previously confirmed to National Post that the incident was being investigated by the TPS Hate Crime Unit.

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (Cija) and UJA Federation of Greater Toronto issued a joint statement on the day of the incident, calling it “disturbing.”

“Faith International Christian Centre has stood with the Jewish community and with Israel. To see that solidarity answered with fire is a disturbing reminder that hatred does not stop with Jews. Increasingly, those who stand beside us are being targeted too,” the statement read.

It went on to say that Cija and UJA are “deeply grateful” for the “friendship and solidarity” from the Faith International Christian Centre, and called on leaders at every level of government to condemn the attack and “confront the extremism that is making intimidation and violence increasingly commonplace.”

“When simply standing with the Jewish community carries a cost — when allies are intimidated, threatened, or attacked because they refuse to turn away — this is no longer only a Jewish problem,” the two organizations said. “It is a threat to the kind of country we all want Canada to be.”

Meanwhile, mayoral candidate and city councillor Brad Bradford commented on the incident in North York on social media, describing it in a post on X as “an act of intimidation.”

“I’m thinking today of Jewish families across Toronto who have spent 3 years watching this kind of thing move closer to their homes, their schools and their synagogues, and who are tired of being told it’s being taken seriously while it keeps happening,” he wrote.

By The Canadian Press

The 44-year-old is two weeks into a six-month mission which will see him conduct experiments and research and take part in critical maintenance work.

Kutryk floated inside the station and demonstrated one of the physiological experiments he’s taking part in during a news conference with journalists in Longueuil, Que., today.

Kutryk says he’s having a blast and it’s been life-changing to watch Earth from the station.

He launched to space on Oct. 1 as part of NASA Crew 13 in the fastest flight ever to reach the space station, taking just under eight hours.

By The Canadian Press

The city says 222,550 Torontonians went to advance polls over six days ahead of election day on Oct. 26.

That’s a big jump from the nearly 130,000 advance votes cast in the 2023 mayoral byelection, and nearly 116,000 votes cast in the 2022 municipal election.

City data shows advance voter turnouts in municipal elections dating back to 2010 also don’t come close to this year’s turnout.

The city also says residents who requested to vote by mail must return a completed mail-in voting package to Toronto Elections by noon on Wednesday.

More than 50 people are vying to lead Toronto for the next four years, but polls suggest it will be a tight race between incumbent Olivia Chow and councillor Brad Bradford.

stories.title: Federal government expands expands AI program with $500M boost
stories.summary: The federal government says it is making an additional $500 million available over five years to help Canadian businesses adopt artificial intelligence technologies and bring Canadian-developed AI products to market.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The federal government says it is making an additional $500 million available over five years to help Canadian businesses adopt artificial intelligence technologies and bring Canadian-developed AI products to market.

The announcement was made in London on Tuesday by Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon, who said the funding will expand the Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative, bringing total federal support for the program to $700 million.

The initiative is part of the federal government’s AI for All strategy, unveiled in June 2026, which is aimed at increasing the use of artificial intelligence across Canada while strengthening the country’s AI sector and technological sovereignty.

Federal officials said support will be focused primarily on sectors where Canada has established expertise and growth potential, including health and life sciences, energy and natural resources, transportation, agriculture, manufacturing and robotics. Regional agencies will also have flexibility to support other local economic priorities.

The government said the expanded program will also help Canadian AI companies attract investment, secure customers and commercialize homegrown technologies. Funding will also be available to organizations that provide businesses with specialized expertise and support related to AI adoption and commercialization.

The federal government also said the investment is intended to encourage broader AI adoption across Canada, help domestic AI firms grow while remaining based in Canada, and support economic growth and productivity.

stories.title: 'I did everything for nothing': Pearson Airport gold heist ringleader says fortune lost
stories.summary: Star witness at the trial of a former Air Canada employee takes the stand and says kidnappers took the gold and cash.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
The mastermind of the spectacular Toronto airport gold heist lost his share of the loot after fleeing to Pakistan, where he said he was kidnapped by police, blindfolded and tortured until he told them where he hid his gold and cash.

” Arsalan Chaudhary, 43, of Mississauga, Ont., testified Tuesday as a reluctant witness in court in Brampton, Ont.

Chaudhary said he was the man behind the gold heist, along with an inside man who worked with Air Canada, but after they split the stolen gold and cash, worth more than $22 million, he left Canada for Pakistan, where he was grabbed by men in police uniforms.

While he was in captivity and suffering torture and threatened with death, he was connected by FaceTime video calls to his kidnappers’ colleagues in Canada; he told them where to go to get his stash of gold hidden in a Toronto-area condo, and then to his family’s home to collect his cash.

“Before they could do anything further, I pretty much told them, ‘I’ll give you everything. You don’t need to do anything. You have me. My life is worth more than any money.’ They had their people go where the gold was, and they got the cash and the gold, everything.”

Once they had his loot, a hood was pulled over his head and driven from the small room where he had been held. When the car stopped, he said he was told to stay down and count to 30 before looking up or they would shoot him.

Chaudhary was asked by Crown prosecutor Jelena Vlacic how he felt at that point.

“I was just thankful to be alive,” he said, “and I wanted to get the F out of Pakistan Asap.

“All of this was not even worth it. I destroyed people’s lives. I did everything for nothing.”

Chaudhary is the star witness at the trial for an alleged co-accused in the gold heist, Parmpal Sidhu, a former Air Canada employee in the cargo warehouse where the crate of gold and cash was stolen in 2023 shortly after arriving on a flight from Zurich, Switzerland.

Although the trial is for Sidhu, who has pleaded not guilty to theft over $5,000 and conspiracy, Chaudhary said the Air Canada employee who was the key inside man at the cargo warehouse who he planned the heist with was Simran Preet Panesar, who is a wanted fugitive in the case, and believed to be living in India.

Chaudhary said that Panesar was in charge of getting the crate of gold and cash out of the cargo warehouse, and Chaudhary was in charge of handling it once it got out.

Chaudhary said he followed the truck that had collected the crate after Air Canada insiders redirected the cargo, as it headed north from the airport.

At a farm, which he said he couldn’t remember where, he, Panesar and the driver divided the loot with Chaudhary taking 30 per cent of the gold.

Chaudhary is in custody, serving his sentence at Maplehurst Correctional Complex, and was escorted into court by a police officer. He walked with casual confidence, almost a swagger.

His testimony was jagged, peppered frequently with him saying he didn’t recall key elements, such as most names and places, times and dates. He said he had post-traumatic stress disorder from his ordeal.

He said he was not testifying willingly, only after being served a subpoena by the Crown.

He pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 in March and in April was sentenced to four years.

Chaudhary’s testimony continues today, and Sidhu’s trial continues for several days.

stories.title: Ontario father runs nearly 8,000 kilometres across Canada to raise awareness about mental health
stories.summary: By the time Myles Dininio reached the Pacific coast, he had raised more than $50,000 for Camh on his journey.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Silvia Pontecorvi, Omni News

Posted October 13, 2026 1:45 pm.

Last Updated October 13, 2026 1:52 pm.

For 148 days, Myles Dininio ran across Canada, covering nearly 8,000 kilometres from Newfoundland to British Columbia. But for the 40-year-old Ontario father of two, reaching the finish line wasn’t necessarily the accomplishment he had imagined.

“It never felt like a sense of accomplishment or a great achievement,” Dininio said. “I’ve been trying to process the end of it all, and understand what it is I am feeling.”

Dininio, from Zephyr, Ont., set out from Newfoundland on April 1 and reached Vancouver on Aug. 22, completing a cross-country journey aimed at raising awareness about mental health and funds for Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (Camh).

The challenge was deeply personal.

“Mental health has affected me my whole life,” he said. “From a very young age, I had little issues that I didn’t realize were known as mental health issues.”

Running thousands of kilometres across the country meant facing physical exhaustion, isolation and a daily mental battle.

“I quit this run probably 50 times in my head, ON the side of the road, but never actually followed it through,” Dininio recalled.

But what began as a test of endurance gradually became something much bigger.

Along the way, strangers joined him for stretches of the journey, offering encouragement and companionship. Others stopped to share their own experiences with mental health, sometimes opening up about deeply personal and painful struggles.

Dininio said listening to those stories was both moving and emotionally overwhelming. At first, he struggled with the weight of what people were sharing with him.

Those encounters eventually changed how he viewed the purpose of his run.

By the time Dininio reached the Pacific coast, his journey had raised more than $50,000 for Camh, one of Canada’s leading mental health research and treatment institutions.

But he says the impact of the conversations he had along the way became more meaningful than the money raised.

“I lost interest in the actual fundraising part, not lost interest, but the fundraising didn’t matter once I realized how many people I was actually reaching,” he said. “And that was worth more than any dollar amount.”

For Dininio, the experience reinforced the importance of talking openly about mental health and creating spaces where people feel comfortable sharing their struggles.

Now back home in Ontario, Dininio is adjusting to everyday life after nearly five months on the road.

While he continues to process the experience, he hopes the message behind his journey will resonate long after the running has stopped.

“One of the primary things when we deal with mental health issues is that we feel so alone,” he said. “And I think we all need to know we are not alone. There is always someone willing to listen.”

For Dininio, the nearly 8,000 kilometres were never just about reaching the other side of Canada. They were about reminding people that, even in their most difficult moments, they don’t have to face their struggles alone.

stories.title: 'Did you do your job?': Poilievre says Liberal government should have protected Stelco workers
stories.summary: N/A
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is calling in to question whether the Liberal government did enough to secure job protections for steel workers at Stelco, after it approved its sale to American-based Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. in 2024.

“It was up to the Liberal government to negotiate job protections when it approved the takeover of Stelco a few years back,” said Poilievre, during a press conference in Windsor, Ont., ON Tuesday.

“So, the question really goes to the Liberals: Did you do your job and protect the steelworkers when the foreign takeover happened?” asked Poilievre.

Poilievre’s comments come after Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and Prime Minister Mark Carney have threatened legal action against Stelco’s Ohio-based parent company Cleveland Cliffs Inc., for laying off 500 workers at its plants in Hamilton and Lake Erie.

Stelco was acquired by Cleveland Cliffs in 2024, with the sale approved by Joly’s predecessor François-Philippe Champagne under the Investment Canada Act (ICA).

The approval was contingent on several binding commitments, including maintaining the same number of unionized employees and most non-unionized employees for a period of five years.

Stelco has cited the ongoing U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel, which remain at 50 per cent, as one of the main reasons for the cutbacks.

Earlier this month, Carney called the layoffs a “betrayal” to workers and said there was still federal money on the table for Stelco to retain its employees.

On Oct. 5, Joly sent a letter to Stelco president Paul Simon, in which she listed the remedies available to the government should the investor fail to comply under the ICA.

Those remedies include “an application to the superior court for orders that May include directing compliance, divestiture, or monetary penalties.”

On Sunday, in an interview with CBC News’ Rosemary Barton Live, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves disputed the government’s claims.

“There is no provision in the contract that I have to keep employment at a certain level every single day of the five years,” he said. “If that was an imposition of the Canadian government, I would not have accepted.”

Goncalves has called the layoffs “temporary” until Canada and the U.S. have reached a trade agreement. Goncalves is a supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump’s Section 232 tariffs and said he’s prepared to fight the Canadian government in court.

Joly has received a response to her letter from Stelco. On Saturday, she said a legal team is reviewing it and “all options are on the table.”

On Tuesday, NDP Leader Avi Lewis called on the federal government to nationalize Stelco.

“It’s a positive sign that the federal government is preparing to take legal action, but a court process will take years to resolve,” said Lewis, in a statement.

“If we’re serious about saving these jobs and the Canadian steel industry, we need immediate action,” he added. “That action must include nationalizing the plant.”

Poilevre said Conservatives are calling on the federal government to pursue legal action, but more importantly get back to the negotiating table with the U.S., to secure a tariff-free trade deal.
