stories.title: Cineplex reports record September box office revenue at $45.1 million
stories.summary: Toronto — Cineplex Inc. says its box office revenue totalled $45.1 million in September to set a record for the month, up from $37.7 million a year earlier.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — Cineplex Inc. says its box office revenue totalled $45.1 million in September to set a record for the month, up from $37.7 million a year earlier.

The movie theatre company says the result brought its third-quarter box office revenue to a record $215.7 million, up from $159.5 million in the same quarter last year.

The increase came as third quarter box office revenue per patron topped $14 for the first time as moviegoers increasingly chose premium formats.

Cineplex says Spider-Man: Brand New Day and the Odyssey helped drive the results as both movies generated exceptional attendance across its premium offerings.

It says September also benefited from the performance of Resident Evil.

Cineplex CEO Bill Walker says the consistency over the past several quarters, including a record-setting third quarter, reflect the appeal of the theatrical experience.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

Companies in this story: (TSX:CGX)

stories.title: Poilievre heads to Detroit to push for tariff-free trade
stories.summary: Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is scheduled to be in Detroit today where he says he will advocate for tariff-free trade, with a focus on the auto sector.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre will be in Detroit on Tuesday to make a case for tariff-free trade in the auto sector.

At a news conference in Windsor, Ont. before crossing into the United States, Poilievre said he planned to meet with representatives of a General Motors plant in Detroit and officials from a Ford plant in nearby Dearborn, Mich.

He is also planning to meet with members of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers while in Michigan.

Poilievre said he will be joined by members of the Conservative caucus from the Windsor area.

The Conservative leader blamed the trade war for declining auto production on both sides of the border.

“The story is not rosy there either and that is because of this ridiculous trade war that is only helping China and other overseas competitors. We should not be fighting with each other while our risks and rivals abroad get stronger,” Poilievre said.

The trade war has emerged as a major factor in the U.S. midterm election race in Michigan, the heart the of the U.S. auto industry.

Despite having previously supported U.S. President Donald Trump’s tariffs, Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers released a video last week saying “Canada is not our enemy” and calling for an end to the trade war.

In a debate last week with his Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed, Rogers said he wants a deal with Canada and the current tariffs are too high.

The U.S. currently has a 25 per cent tariff on Canadian autos. President Trump has threatened to increase that tariff to 50 per cent on Jan. 1 in response to Canada’s counter-tariffs.

When asked about Trump’s adviser Peter Navarro recently warning that Canada would pay a price for any interference in the midterm elections, Poilievre said he doesn’t see his visit ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm vote as meddling.

“I think we’re going there to fight for tariff-free trade on both sides of the border and Americans want lower prices and more jobs and we’re offering a plan for them to have both,” Poilievre said.

Trump ended trade talks with Canada last year after Ontario aired an ad during the World Series using clips of former president Ronald Reagan criticizing tariffs and supporting free trade.

In August, Prime Minister Mark Carney ordered the Canadian negotiating team to call off trade talks with the U.S. after accusing the Americans of making unreasonable demands.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Coroner’s inquest set to begin examining death of Toronto woman who fell from balcony
stories.summary: An inquest is set to begin to examine the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio
stories.content:
A coroner’s inquest is set to begin Monday to examine the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.

Korchinski-Paquet, a woman of Ukrainian, Black and Indigenous ancestry, died on May 27, 2020 after police responded to calls about a family dispute at the apartment. She was 29.

Her death came on the heels of the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, spurring further protests amid growing calls to defund the police.

It also cast a spotlight on how police interact with people experiencing mental health crises.

Ontario’s police watchdog investigated the case and eventually cleared Toronto police of wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death.

The Special Investigations Unit found it happened as she was trying to move from her apartment balcony to an adjacent one.

The inquest was announced earlier this year and is slated to last 14 days, with 15 witnesses expected to take the stand.

The inquest jury does not assign criminal responsibility but May make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future. The chief coroner’s office does not have the authority to impose the recommendations, however.

On the anniversary of her death this year, Korchinski-Paquet’s parents joined advocates in calling for the recommendations issued in coroner’s inquests to be binding and implemented within a reasonable timeframe.

Her mother, Claudette Beals, also said there should be a different system in place to investigate allegations of wrongdoing against police officers, adding she has no faith in “police investigating police.”

“My daughter’s been gone for six years and no one’s held responsible for that,” she said in a news conference at the provincial legislature.

stories.summary: Calgary - A group representing five First Nations says it has invested $65.3 million for an interest in the Coastal GasLink pipeline, which brings natural gas from northeastern B.C. to the LNG Canada plant in Kitimat — and is set for a big expansion.

CALGARY - A group representing five First Nations says it has invested $65.3 million for an interest in the Coastal GasLink pipeline, which brings natural gas from northeastern B.C. to the LNG Canada plant in Kitimat — and is set for a big expansion.

By Lauren Krugel The Canadian Press

FN CGL Pipeline Ltd. Partnership said in a news release Tuesday that members are putting up their own funds.

“Our Nations are making this investment with their own capital. No government loan guarantees, no borrowed money,” said Chief Harley Chingee of McLeod Lake Indian Band.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Image 9Image 10

“It was a deliberate choice, the best way to secure maximum benefits from what we believe to be a sound commercial investment. The returns will now belong entirely to the communities, as will decisions as to how they are used.”

Other members of the group are the Haisla Nation, Halfway River First Nation, Saulteau First Nations and West Moberly First Nations.

“This investment framework recognizes the importance of partnership, financial certainty and shared prosperity, while supporting our communities’ ability to make decisions about our own economic future,” Chief Roland Willson of West Moberly First Nations said.

TC Energy chief executive François Poirier congratulated the First Nations on completing the deal.

“This transaction reflects years of collaboration, leadership and determination by the Nations involved to create a long-term economic opportunity for their communities.”

Coastal GasLink runs 670 kilometres from northeastern B.C. to Kitimat, B.C., with a capacity of 2.1 billion cubic feet per day. It is operated by TC Energy Corp.

Under the deal, FN CGL and TC Energy collectively now hold an indirect 35 per cent interest in the pipeline through a TC subsidiary. The remaining 65 per cent is held by KKR Co. and Alberta Investment Management Corp. on behalf of certain clients.

“The structure provides stable cash flows without typical equity volatility, helping support long-term planning and managing of community priorities,” a spokesperson for TC Energy said in an emailed statement.

“It provides long-term predictable distributions, providing stable investment income while reducing risks associated with direct ownership.”

Tuesday’s deal is the first of two planned Indigenous investment transactions related to Coastal GasLink. TC Energy says a second transaction with another First Nations entity is expected to close in the fourth quarter of this year.

In 2022, TC Energy announced the signing of option agreements to sell a 10 per cent equity interest in the pipeline to Indigenous communities across the project corridor.

The company recently announced plans to double the existing capacity of the Coastal GasLink pipeline by adding new compressor stations and upgrading facilities.

For the second phase of the pipeline, LNG Canada — owned by Shell Canada and four Asian partners — is leading construction, limiting the Coastal GasLink owners’ spending and cost and schedule risk. The Coastal GasLink partners remain owners.

Construction is to begin in early 2027 and the expansion is set to come into service in the early 2030s.

The decision came after LNG Canada announced a final greenlight for the Phase 2 expansion of its facility, which enables natural gas chilled into a liquid state to be shipped across the Pacific. The first phase started up in the summer of 2025.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Toronto condo owners reject low offers, sell $100,000 below what they paid
stories.summary: The one-bedroom unit’s west-facing, walkout terrace was an attractive feature for buyers
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
150 Sudbury St., No. 104, Toronto

Asking price: $619,900 (July, 2026)

Previous asking price: $619,900 (May, 2026)

Selling price: $595,000 (August, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $695,000 (November, 2021); $521,000 (October, 2017); $248,547 (August, 2012)

Taxes: $2,548 (2025)

Days on the market: 12

Property days on market: 96

Listing agent: Christopher Bibby, Re/Max Hallmark Bibby Group Realty

The owners bought this one-bedroom unit with a den at Westside Gallery Lofts, near Queen and Dufferin streets in 2021, at the height of the market, for $695,000. This year, needing more space, they decided to sell. Agent Christopher Bibby warned them that the ground-floor unit would likely sell far below what they paid, but that spring was a good season to show off its best asset: a west-facing terrace.

“There were some units on higher floors that had no exterior space or maybe a smaller 20-foot balcony,” Mr. Bibby said.

“This unit has a big walkout terrace that almost felt like you had a backyard. The condo corporation also allowed these owners to put up an enclosure for a lot more privacy.”

For three months, the unit’s asking price stayed at $619,900, during which time the sellers rejected two offers. After negotiations, they signed off on a third and closed the deal at $595,000.

“In the last few years, if your unit is unique, you’re going to do better than most,” Mr. Bibby said.

“We sold for $595,000 for a 670-square-foot unit. Around the same time, there was a sale for a 640-square-foot unit that went for $500,000.”

This roughly 15-year-old unit has a loftlike design with exposed concrete finishes and floor-to-ceiling windows in the den and living room.

The kitchen is across from a dining area and next to a bedroom with a semi ensuite bathroom.

The unit has a storage locker and one parking spot. Monthly fees of $539 cover water, heating and use of a gym.

“Years ago, Vogue magazine rated Queen West one of the top neighbourhoods in the world,” Mr. Bibby said.

“The Ossington strip, maybe two-and-a-half blocks away, has a handful of highly acclaimed and ranked restaurants.”

stories.title: Anthony Scaramucci on Trump, Carney, and the trade war
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses the relationship between Canada and the U.S. and how Americans view the trade war.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
It’s hard to think of a time in the modern age when relations between the U.S. and Canada were at a lower point. Since U.S. President Donald Trump started the trade war, tensions have risen, while Canadians’ opinion of our neighbour to the south have fallen. While some politicians and commentators south of the border have taken aim at Canada and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s handling of the relationship, others are glad someone is finally standing up to Trump.

Host Caryn Ceolin is speaking with Anthony Scaramucci, host of The Rest is Politics: US , former White House communications director, and managing partner at Skybridge Capital, about the relationship between Canada and the U.S., how Americans view the trade war, and why he believes Carney now “leads the west.”

stories.title: Warm temperatures gives way to cooler, unsettled stretch in London forecast
stories.summary: Londoners can expect one more taste of summer-like weather Tuesday before a cooler and wetter pattern settles into the region for the rest of the week.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Londoners can expect one more taste of summer-like weather Tuesday before a cooler and wetter pattern settles into the region for the rest of the week.

Environment Canada is calling for a mix of sun and cloud Tuesday, with temperatures climbing to a high of 26 C and a humidex value of 33. There’s a 40 per cent chance of showers early in the day and a 30 per cent chance of showers late in the afternoon, along with the risk of a thunderstorm.

The chance of showers and thunderstorms will linger into the evening before skies become partly cloudy overnight. The temperature is forecast to fall to 13 C.

A cooler air mass will arrive Wednesday, bringing mainly cloudy skies and a 30 per cent chance of morning showers. The daytime high is expected to reach 16 C before dipping to 7 C overnight.

The unsettled weather pattern is expected to continue through the remainder of the week.

Thursday’s forecast calls for cloudy conditions and a 30 per cent chance of showers, with a high of 14 C. Shower chances increase to 70 per cent Thursday night.

Friday is expected to remain cloudy with a 70 per cent chance of showers and windy conditions. The temperature is forecast to top out at 14 C before dropping to about 4 C overnight.

By Saturday, temperatures will cool further, with cloudy skies and a forecast high of just 9 C.

stories.title: Roller-coasters at Canada’s Wonderland, La Ronde closed after deadly fall at Georgia park
stories.summary: Several people were injured and one man died on Monday after witnesses described watching him come out of his seat on a ride at Six Flags Over Georgia
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Rides at two Canadian theme parks were closed after a man in the United States fell to this death from a Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia.

Two rides at Canada’s Wonderland in Toronto and another at La Ronde in Montreal were temporarily shuttered “out of an abundance of caution,” the parks said. Six Flags owns Wonderland and recently sold La Ronde.

A 42-year-old man was killed while riding a roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia on Monday, prompting the theme park operator to close nine similar rides across Canada and the U.S. The man was thrown from his seat and struck other patrons before landing below the ride, police said Tuesday.

The Leviathan and Behemoth roller coasters at Canada’s Wonderland were closed, a spokesperson for the park said. There was no timeline for their reopening.

“The safety of our guests and team members remains on our highest priorities,” the spokesperson said in a written statement.

The Goliath roller coaster at La Ronde was also closed and the park’s owner said it would carry out a safety review with the ride’s manufacturer.

“We are taking this additional time to carefully review the attraction. It will not reopen until this review is complete and we are fully satisfied that it can be operated safely,” the statement read.

The temporarily shuttered Canadian rides were manufactured by the same company as the coaster involved in the incident in Georgia.

Six Flags Entertainment did not immediately respond Tuesday to e-mailed questions about why specific rides were shut down and what would be done before they reopen.

With files from The Associated Press.

stories.title: In B.C., a dose of judge-made drug policy
stories.summary: A B.C. Supreme Court ruling overreaches by striking down the federal law of possession for the purpose of trafficking
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
The death toll from toxic street drugs in British Columbia and much of the rest of the country is both astonishing and horrifying. But even in the context of a public health emergency, a judge’s ruling striking down the federal law of possession for the purpose of trafficking in hopes of reducing the death toll is misbegotten – the latest example of judges dressing up political decisions as legal or constitutional ones.

The case before Justice Catherine Murray of the B.C. Supreme Court focused on two people who bought street drugs such as methamphetamines, cocaine and heroin from the dark web, tested them for fentanyl and other impurities at university labs and sold them at cost to drug users.

In essence, Justice Murray found that drug users have a constitutional right, under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, to be exempted from federal possession and trafficking laws in B.C., so they May receive a “safer supply.”

It’s worth elaborating on what Justice Murray is asking Ottawa to do. People who use drugs must be permitted a source of drugs not overseen by the medical profession. Such is their need to avoid withdrawal, they need near-instant access, and medical supervision doesn’t work for them. They cannot be denied what she frames as a non-medicalized supplier.

This is an extreme ruling, by any measure. To Justice Murray, it is justified by the extreme times in which drug users find themselves – 2,585 deaths in British Columbia in 2025, or seven a day. She has given Ottawa six months to make legislative reforms, which would necessarily apply across Canada. For what, exactly? Is she demanding Ottawa also allow exemptions for people who promise to test drugs purchased from organized crime? If the federal government proves unwilling to accept the cartels’ involvement, should it instead create a public-private partnership of some kind that would provide pharmaceutical-quality drugs to so-called compassion clubs for distribution? Would the simplest answer be to decriminalize possession? Make methamphetamines available without regulation?

It’s not hard to see that each of these solutions would also bring serious problems. And that is what happens when judges take it upon themselves, as Justice Murray did, to make policy decisions better left to government – though to be fair, governments and health regulators have not done a good job on the drugs crisis. For instance, the widespread distribution of hydromorphone, a safer alternative to street drugs, led to large-scale diversion, with the cash used to buy even more fentanyl. It was a well-intentioned disaster.

In reaching her conclusions, Justice Murray held a mini-inquiry of the street drug-using environment, assessed facts and came to certain judgments. It is challenging terrain, and some of her factual assessments are shaky. For instance, more than half of users who purchased the drugs went on to divert them to others. Did they use any resulting cash to buy other drugs, perhaps because they sought the fentanyl high? To what extent did this program simply add to the street drug supply? The judge’s answer, that any diversion May have actually enhanced public safety, seems speculative at best.

And what of the fact that drug-testing kits, which allow anyone to test drugs within five minutes, are widely available for free? Justice Murray accepted the view that drug users don’t like showing up at medical-related institutions (not even the downtown pharmacies where the kits are placed conveniently on the counter) because of “stigma,” which she says federal law has helped create. Yet thousands of these kits are in circulation each year in Vancouver.

We’ve seen other rulings in which various groups accuse government of putting their lives at risk. In Toronto last year, a judge effectively declared a constitutional right to bike lanes – a right mercifully tossed aside by an appeal court. Three years ago, the then Chief Justice of the B.C. Supreme Court, Christopher Hinkson, blocked B.C.’s law keeping drug users away from playgrounds and child-care spaces, during a period when normally illegal use was exempted from federal drug laws; his thought was that using drugs in public could save lives. These are extreme rulings that turn judges into policy-makers, and ignore legislators’ role in addressing social problems. (More on that later in the week.)

Fentanyl and other impurities have made street drugs more potent and deadly. But inventing a constitutional right to the non-medicalized provision of dangerous drugs has its own dire risks.

stories.title: Lions fans gather for watch party in London, Ont. as Detroit blows out Arizona
stories.summary: In what has been a roller coaster season so far for Detroit Lions fans, they couldn’t have picked a better game to have a watch party with a few hundred supporters.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
In what has been a roller coaster season so far for Detroit Lions fans, they couldn’t have picked a better game to have a watch party with a few hundred supporters.

Members of the ‘One Pride’ community packed the Canadian Brewhouse in north London, Ont. for the third annual stop on the Detroit Lions’ Raise the Roar Canadian Bar tour.

“As a Lions fan I love this,” said Aaron Bayer from London.

“Pulling up and seeing all the blue and white all that Honolulu Blue, it’s as close to being at a tailgate in Detroit as we get here right now.”

The past two years, the party was held on Dundas Place and the watch party inside Canada Life Place. This time, the Lions switched to a bar tour.

“I’m from Windsor, and me and my dad were season ticket holders back home, so it is awesome to see stuff like this,” said Lions fan Ryan Walker.

“It still seems like a decent enough crowd here. Obviously when it was downtown they had a bigger venue, different experience and they were able to put more stuff on. But I mean, I think they’ve done a good job here with what they’ve had.”

Outside in the parking lot, they had games and photo opportunities with a giant helmet and signs. Inside they had a DJ, the Lions cheerleaders, more games and a photo booth.

After an up and down 2-2 start to the year, this date couldn’t have been better to watch a game. Detroit blew out Arizona 45-17.

The Lions were granted marketing rights in Canada in April 2024 and hosted its first Canadian watch party later that year. There are two more area stops to come in Kitchener on Nov. 15 for the US Thanksgiving game, and in Windsor on Nov. 26.

“It’s nice seeing that Canada is getting stuff like this now,” added Walker.

“It’s nice that they finally saw that there’s a lot of fans in Ontario and to put something like this together is awesome, especially for the city.”

stories.title: Inquest begins in death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet who fell from balcony while police were in her home
stories.summary: Toronto woman died in 2020 after police responded to calls about a family dispute at the apartment
stories.author: Paola Loriggio
stories.content:
A coroner’s inquest has begun to examine the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a Toronto woman who fell from a high-rise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.

Korchinski-Paquet, a woman of Ukrainian, Black and Indigenous ancestry, died on May 27, 2020 after police responded to calls about a family dispute at the apartment. She was 29.

Inquest counsel say Korchinski-Paquet had been diagnosed with epilepsy and experienced seizures earlier that day.

Roger Shallow says the inquest’s scope includes how police and first responders are informed about epilepsy and how to ensure safety when a person’s behaviour May be influenced by postictal delirium, a condition that May occur in the period after a seizure.

He says the inquest will not look into general mental health challenges or psychiatric care, however, or the investigations by various police watchdogs into the case.

Shallow says Korchinski-Paquet’s death was “sudden and profoundly tragic” and no matter what the jury concludes, her family has been left to grapple with a loss no one should experience.

Korchinski-Paquet’s death came on the heels of the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, spurring further protests amid growing calls to defund the police.

It also cast a spotlight on how police interact with people experiencing mental health crises.

Ontario’s police watchdog investigated the case and eventually cleared Toronto police of wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death. The Special Investigations Unit found it happened as she was trying to move from her apartment balcony to an adjacent one.

The inquest was announced earlier this year and is slated to last 14 days, with 13 witnesses expected to take the stand. Korchinski-Paquet’s mother, father and brother have been named as potential witnesses, as have five of the six police officers who attended the scene.

The inquest jury does not assign criminal responsibility but May make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future. The chief coroner’s office does not have the authority to impose the recommendations, however.

On the anniversary of her death this year, Korchinski-Paquet’s parents joined advocates in calling for the recommendations issued in coroner’s inquests to be binding and implemented within a reasonable timeframe.

Her mother, Claudette Beals, also said there should be a different system in place to investigate allegations of wrongdoing against police officers, adding she has no faith in “police investigating police.”

“My daughter’s been gone for six years and no one’s held responsible for that,” she said in a news conference at the provincial legislature.

stories.title: Senior theatre company prepares for the Matchmaker at the Grand Theatre
stories.summary: Silver Spotlight Theatre Inc. (Ssti) is rehearsing for its first production as its own charitable non-profit.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Silver Spotlight Theatre Inc. (Ssti) is rehearsing for its first production as its own charitable non-profit.

The group of senior actors is rehearing three times per week in preparation for a five-day run of The Matchmaker production later this month.

“If you know the story for Hello Dolly!, the Matchmaker is what it’s based on,” said Rick Smith, director of the Matchmaker for Ssti.

“Dolly Levi is hired by Horace van der Gelder to find himself a new wife. Little does he know, her plan is to marry him herself. Along the way, she’s brought in other members of his of his crew and people he knows to mess things up a little bit so that she has a better chance of winning the prize at the end.”

In 2025 Ssti separated from the umbrella of Musical Theatre Productions which got them started in 2023. After doing musicals including Babes in Arms, Grease, Into the Woods and Showtune this will be the first non-musical production.

“I’ve wanted to work with this group for quite some time,” said Sam Sabathy, who plays Dolly and is doing her first Ssti production.

“I’ve seen all their shows and when I found out that they were doing a play, that’s their inaugural production for Ssti, I thought, I’ve got to audition and Rick picked me, so here we are.”

Sabathy has a degree in drama from Western University and studied in New York. She moved back to Canada and got into local theatre around Southwestern Ontario.

Over the past four years, the senior actors have not only made great shows but great friends.

“We have people that we’ve known through every production, but then also we meet new people,” said Mitchell Zimmer, who plays Rudolph in the play.

“We meet behind the scenes at restaurants, breakfasts, get togethers. It’s become bigger than just theatre, it’s family.”

Sabathy describes the cast and crew as having an “absolute blast”.

“We’re laughing every single night, and it’s just so much fun and encourage everyone to try and do it,” she said.

For this production, half of the cast is new to Ssti and others have experience with the company.

“You can see the development over the past five productions,” said Smith.

“They continue getting that support from our other experienced cast members. So, it really is that community and they’re all supportive of each other as we’ve gone through the process.”

The five-day run on the Auburn Stage at the Grand Theatre takes place Oct. 28-Nov. 1, 2026.

stories.title: A military underfunded, undermanned and underprepared
stories.summary: Benchmark Canada: “The armed forces of Canada have basically been left to rot,” says ex-navy chief Mark Norman. “I’m not overstating it.”
stories.author: National Post
stories.content:
Countries don’t typically get report cards, but there are hard facts that can be collated, assessed and compared. Enter Benchmark Canada , a new project from the Macdonald-Laurier Institute that brings together more than 40 different metrics that measure this nation’s performance . This fall, the National Post is examining many of those findings.

The radars watching over Canada’s Arctic region were designed when the Soviet Union was a country. The Royal Canadian Navy’s frigates and the Royal Canadian Air Force’s fighter jets are nearing the end of their useful lives. As Canada looks to reinvigorate its defence sector with billions of dollars in new spending, years of neglect May have left Canadian Forces short of the equipment they need to fight alongside their allies.

Canada is expected to put 25 per cent of its 2026 defence budget toward major equipment, according to Nato data compiled by Benchmark Canada, a Macdonald-Laurier Institute project that ranks the country against its allies. That would exceed Nato’s 20 per cent guideline for a second consecutive year, but leave Canada ranked 28 among the 31 allies measured.

“It’s somewhat troubling but not surprising,” said retired vice-admiral Mark Norman, a former commander of the Royal Canadian Navy and vice-chief of the defence staff.

Canada’s spending pales in comparison to figures for its European allies such as Poland at 55.9 per cent, Lithuania at 46 per cent and Hungary at 45 per cent. Only Italy, at 24.5 per cent, Croatia and Norway rank below Canada.

Meanwhile, a recent report by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce puts the average equipment share for the United States, Britain, France, Germany and Italy at 31.2 per cent, 6.2 percentage points above Canada’s estimate. France has about 202,000 military personnel, Germany 182,000 and Britain 126,000, compared with Canada’s 71,000.

Canada devoted just 11 per cent of its defence budget to equipment in 2015. Norman said military training, maintenance, spare parts and equipment purchases are often cut when budgets tighten because spending on salaries and bases is harder to reduce.

“The Armed Forces of Canada have basically been left to rot,” Norman said. “I’m not overstating it.”

An attitude shift is happening, spurred on by the Trump administration’s demand that its Nato allies increase defence spending to five per cent of GDP to alleviate the burden on the U.S. shouldering much of the alliance’s military capabilities.

Canada’s defence budget grew by 138 per cent between 2014 and 2025, compared with 125 per cent in Germany and less than 30 per cent in France and Britain, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce report found. Canadian spending reached about $64 billion, or two per cent of GDP, in 2025, and the Carney government has pledged to reach the target of five per cent of GDP by 2035.

Retired lieutenant-general Christopher Coates, a former deputy commander of Norad and director of the Macdonald-Laurier Institute’s foreign policy, national defence and national security program, said the increase reflects how low Canada’s spending had been.

“We were digging a hole,” he said. “That two per cent (of GDP) starts to slow down the digging of the hole. But it doesn’t fill it up.”

Coates said much of the new defence spending had gone toward increasing pay for its existing soldiers rather than an increase in troop size. Canada ranks 29 among 30 Nato countries measured for military personnel as a share of population, ahead of only Luxembourg, which notably devotes more than half its defence budget to equipment, he said.

The Canadian Chamber of Commerce estimates that meeting Nato’s target of 3.5 per cent of GDP for core defence capabilities by 2035 would require about $160 billion in annual spending, roughly 2.5 times the 2025 level. Including a further 1.5 per cent of GDP for security-related spending would bring the total to at least $228 billion. Defence would account for nearly 30 per cent of federal spending, up from about 11 per cent, according to the report.

Poland has doubled defence spending as a share of GDP between 2021 and 2025, to 4.5 per cent, as it relies heavily on foreign suppliers, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce’s report said. In Canada, Canadian-controlled private firms account for just 18 per cent of the defence industry’s $17.3 billion in annual sales.

The Parliamentary Budget Officer has flagged years of unspent defence capital funds as equipment nears its end-of-life date. Fixing old equipment to return it to operations becomes an ongoing challenge as parts for 30-year-old jet planes “are not sitting on a shelf somewhere waiting to be purchased,” Norman said.

Meanwhile, Coates said Canada keeps too few fighter jets on alert and lacks airborne early-warning aircraft. “We’re just being lazy about it,” he said.

“I think Canadians might assume their military can operate shoulder-to-shoulder alongside our allies, and I think that’s questionable,” Coates added. He said Canada still has gaps in deploying long-range strike weapons, anti-armour and air-defence systems, and the ability to fly drones in large numbers.

“The people are trained and motivated and committed,” he said. “I just don’t think they’re equipped and resourced.”

Norman said Canada’s procurement system was built to “pace, regulate and control” spending and is not well suited to handling a rapid increase, while also criticizing how the Canadian Forces has sometimes over-engineered its equipment. The Canadian Navy’s River-class destroyer, which he described as a concept more than 20 years old whose design has still not been finalized, is “arguably the wrong platform for the wrong time,” he said.

Both Coates and Norman pointed to Poland, Germany and the Baltic states as examples Canada could follow to improve their civil defence, procurement and ties to their domestic defence industry.

Coates also wants Ottawa to be more transparent about what its defence spending delivers and explain which threats it is preparing to confront. “You don’t ever hear a discussion of the threats,” he said.

At a time when public support for defence spending is stronger than Norman has ever seen, further delays could cost Canada military capabilities, lives and the confidence of its allies, he said.

“You cannot surge trust,” he said. “You either have it, or you don’t.”

Meanwhile, Coates said Canada keeps too few fighter jets on alert and lacks airborne early-warning aircraft. “We’re just being lazy about it,” he said.

Norman said Canada’s procurement system was built to “pace, regulate and control” spending and is not well suited to handling a rapid increase, while also criticizing how the Canadian Forces has sometimes over-engineered its equipment. The Canadian Navy’s River-class destroyer, which he described as a concept more than 20 years old whose design has still not been finalized, is “arguably the wrong platform for the wrong time,” he said.

content_blocks.text: The radars watching over Canada’s Arctic region were designed when the Soviet Union was a country. The Royal Canadian Navy’s frigates and the Royal Canadian Air Force’s fighter jets are nearing the end of their useful lives. As Canada looks to reinvigorate its defence sector with billions of dollars in new spending, years of neglect May have left Canadian Forces short of the equipment they need to fight alongside their allies.

Canada is expected to put 25 per cent of its 2026 defence budget toward major equipment, according to Nato data compiled by Benchmark Canada, a Macdonald-Laurier Institute project that ranks the country against its allies. That would exceed Nato’s 20 per cent guideline for a second consecutive year, but leave Canada ranked 28 among the 31 allies measured.
“It’s somewhat troubling but not surprising,” said retired vice-admiral Mark Norman, a former commander of the Royal Canadian Navy and vice-chief of the defence staff.

Canada’s spending pales in comparison to figures for its European allies such as Poland at 55.9 per cent, Lithuania at 46 per cent and Hungary at 45 per cent. Only Italy, at 24.5 per cent, Croatia and Norway rank below Canada.

Meanwhile, a recent report by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce puts the average equipment share for the United States, Britain, France, Germany and Italy at 31.2 per cent, 6.2 percentage points above Canada’s estimate. France has about 202,000 military personnel, Germany 182,000 and Britain 126,000, compared with Canada’s 71,000.

stories.title: Canada's air force doesn't have enough people to run two fighter programs, says retired lieutenant general
stories.summary: The Carney government is considering supplementing its planned purchase of U.S.-made F-35 fighter jets with Swedish-made Gripen fighters.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
Alain Pelletier can still remember that new plane smell when he first climbed into the cockpit of a CF-18 more than three decades ago.

The retired Royal Canadian Air Force lieutenant general, who was deputy commander of North American Aerospace Defense Command (Norad) in Colorado Springs from July 2020 until June 2023, knows what it takes to get a new fleet of fighter aircraft up and running. He thinks the Royal Canadian Air Force (Rcaf) would be stretched thin for pilots, technicians and trainers if ordered to double that effort for a combined fleet of American-made Lockheed Martin F-35s and Saab Gripen-E fighters.

“Having two fleets of fighters is a challenge for any air force,” Pelletier said in a recent interview.

He is slated to speak Tuesday at The Mackenzie Institute’s Canadian Arctic Conference in Toronto to address Canada’s acquisition of new fighter aircraft, and the roles that they might play in northern defence.

Canada already has a shortage of men and women to fly and maintain its jet fighters, he said. “If they do go that route,” with a dual fleet, “the Rcaf will suffer in the short (term) because you need to be able to transition to that new fleet, but now you’re transitioning not to a single fleet, you’re transitioning to two new fleets at a time when you’re just short of people. You cannot duplicate people. You cannot clone people. So, it will be a growing pain.”

With the CF-18s heading for retirement in 2032-33, Prime Minister Mark Carney’s Liberal government, in the midst of a trade war with the United States, hasn’t revealed the outcome of a review of their planned replacement — 88 F-35 fighter jets, manufactured by U.S. defence giant Lockheed Martin.

While Ottawa has placed a firm order for 16 F-35s and has begun paying for critical equipment for 14 additional aircraft, there’s no word yet on how many of the stealth fighters this country will ultimately buy.

Meanwhile, the Carney government is talking about supplementing the fighter jet numbers with Swedish defence giant Saab’s Gripen.

Opting out of F-35 purchase would be 'three ways from Sunday stupid,' says retired major general

Canada's boutique military: 'Should we not be able to defend ourselves?'

Canada has evaluated its options twice and chosen the F-35 both times, Pelletier said.

“I’ve had a chance to look at all the contenders that are out there on at least two occasions,” he said. “I think that the F-35 was a good decision, a decision that is reflected by our Nato partners.”

The U.S., the United Kingdom, Australia, Denmark, Finland and Norway have all gone with the F-35, he said.

“I think it is the right choice. It’s the choice that will carry operational capability for the next 30 years or so.”

The F-35 stands out, Pelletier said, for technology that allows pilots to glean information from their own fighter’s sensors, as well as those of other aircraft, warships and satellites, all “fused into a single picture,” to get a better idea of what’s going on.

“Having been a pilot, that is crucial to mission effectiveness,” he said. “You’re able to sense a threat that is out there before it can sense you.”

Pelletier, who flew combat missions in the Balkans, said the unexpected can hurt a fighter jet pilot’s survivability.

“The more variables that you control, the better it is for any fighter pilot,” said Pelletier, who is slated to speak Tuesday at The Mackenzie Institute’s Canadian Arctic Conference in Toronto.

Russia and China both pose a military threat to Canada’s sovereignty in the Arctic, he said.

“They don’t come into Canadian air space because they are following rules, but they are coming close to Canadian air space,” Pelletier said.

Russian aircraft will fly close to North America’s air defence identification zone that covers the airspace surrounding the United States and Canada, then turn so their flight path parallels that line, he said.

“They have the ability to actually come much further south,” Pelletier said. “They will continue their flight until they see a reaction from Norad, whether it be the Canadian or U.S. air force assets responding to their presence.”

Chinese aircraft have also come close to Alaskan air space during exercises in recent years, he said.

Both Canada and the U.S. will often scramble fighter jets to intercept potential intruders, Pelletier said.

“The air threat is only one piece of the all-domain threat that Russia and China could actually exploit,” he said, noting Canada must also watch out for cyber- and sea-based threats.

“We’ve had the Canadian Navy monitoring transit of what China calls research vessels that have dual-use capabilities,” Pelletier said, noting they can be used for both civilian research and military intelligence gathering.

“We’ve had Russia positioning cruise missiles off of their coast, which is in proximity to Alaska, and those cruise missiles can actually reach into Alaska and the northern part of the Yukon.”

Russia also has intercontinental ballistic missiles that could reach both Canada and the U.S. through the Arctic, he said.

The development of hypersonic missiles “that have the ability to go five times the speed of sound,” and drones that can be launched off ships also pose a threat, Pelletier said.

“That’s why in Norad we had to prepare for all-domain awareness, scanning not only the traditional air corridors, but also the sea routes and having an understanding of what May be coming our way.”

“That’s why in Norad we had to prepare for all-domain awareness, scanning not only the traditional air corridors, but also the sea routes and having an understanding of what May be coming our way.”

stories.title: Letting Canadians 'know when to be upset': Introducing Benchmark Canada
stories.summary: A new project brings together more than 40 different metrics that amount to a kind of report card on how Canada is doing.
stories.author: National Post
stories.content:
How’s Canada doing?

Countries don’t typically get report cards, and it can be simplistic to rely on rankings that try to tell you which is the happiest or safest country in the world. But it’s not just a matter of opinion; there are hard facts to be collated, assessed and compared.

Enter Benchmark Canada , a new project from the Macdonald-Laurier Institute that brings together more than 40 different metrics that measure this nation’s performance across the economy, health care, immigration and others while comparing Canada with countries that face similar issues.

Over the coming weeks, the National Post will examine many of those findings, beginning with defence, and report on what they mean for Canadians and the government that they have entrusted to use their tax dollars wisely and pragmatically.

“Every incoming government, regardless of stripe, has an incentive to portray itself in the most positive light,” said Kevin Vuong, the former Toronto MP who leads the project as a senior fellow at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute. “Every government is going to be motivated to find the one metric, or multiple metrics, that tell the story they want to tell.”

A discussion about Canada’s debt-to-GDP standing inspired Vuong to think about how easily a national statistic could become a well-trodden political talking point. He wanted to assemble enough comparable data that readers could judge the country’s record for themselves through a global lens.

“Ultimately, it was intended to elevate the discourse so we can get past the political rhetoric,” he said.

Vuong spent about a year developing the project with specialists in Canada and abroad. Part of the idea came from his background as a tech entrepreneur, where a company’s growth can look impressive until it is compared with its peers.

“If you grow by 12 per cent, which sounds great, but the rest of the industry grew by 25 per cent, you didn’t actually do well,” he said.

He wanted the same scrutiny applied to Canada’s performance. For example, how much Canada spends on defence matters, but also, how is that money allocated among military equipment, personnel and the cost of running the Canadian Forces?

Other measures range across public and household finances, construction and business development, government services, security and living standards. There are also comparisons for infrastructure construction costs and how long it takes for Canadians to get timely service from their government when looking at Canada Revenue Agency wait times or the time it takes to process a new passport.

Across the Benchmark Canada website, Canada is usually measured against the countries belonging to the G7 or another relevant group of developed nations. Where international data cannot support a fair comparison, Vuong incorporated Canadian benchmarks, including the governments’ own service standards.

Vuong expected plenty of poor results, but he was surprised to find enough good ones to challenge some of his own assumptions. Gasoline taxes were one surprise, he said. Benchmark Canada found that Canada is ranked the second-lowest for the share of the pump price attributable to taxes among the major seven oil-producing democracies.

“It’s an important perspective for all the people who criticize how much tax we pay, which I, like most Canadians, do,” Vuong said.

But then some of the latest mortgage numbers raised some red flags for Vuong. Canada sits close to the bottom of a G7 comparison of mortgage arrears, albeit with a caveat that the definitions and reporting periods differ for each country. The Canadian Bankers Association’s latest figures put the national rate at 0.29 per cent in September, more than double its August 2022 low of 0.14 per cent.

“I knew it was getting worse. I just didn’t know to what extent,” Vuong said.

People will skip a meal before they miss their mortgage or rent payment.

During his time as MP for the Toronto riding of Spadina-Fort York from 2021 to 2025, he heard from constituents who were struggling to pay their bills. Now, the arrears numbers gave him ample evidence of the pressure they had described.

“Sometimes you chalk it up to someone exaggerating for dramatic effect, but this was a point of concern for me,” he said.

Vuong also thinks the website May be useful for Ottawa to have a better idea of the state of the country, without the need to navigate complex data and statistics that members of Parliament May not have the right background to fully understand or even know where to look.

Benchmark Canada was designed so its measures can be sorted by House of Commons committees, but the project should be useful well beyond Parliament Hill. Someone trying to understand the cost of a transit line, for example, can look at what other developed countries have built and what they paid and then understand if Canada’s on the right track or missing the mark entirely.

“It lets everyday Canadians know when to be upset,” he said.

stories.title: More damaging AI hacking incidents to come unless changes are made, scientists warn
stories.summary: Ottawa — Dozens of Canadian academics are among an international group of scientists calling for better containment measures for AI models.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Dozens of Canadian academics are among an international group of scientists calling for better containment measures for AI models.

“Multiple organizations have disclosed high-profile security failures: their AI models bypassed insufficiently sandboxed environments to compromise the systems of external organizations,” they say in an open letter.

The letter, released Tuesday, says that unless immediate changes are made to how AI is developed and deployed, “such incidents will continue to occur, and future incidents will be far more damaging to our exposed critical infrastructure.”

They say there is a need for more research on AI safety as well as emphasis on containment technologies and procedures. The scientists also want to see an international body that standardizes best practices.

“In the short term, strong sandboxing mechanisms including airgapping (disconnecting from the internet) should be used to provide high-assurance containment of cyber-capable AI models,” the letter says.

The Canadian signatories to the letter include AI pioneers Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton, as well as Nicolas Papernot and Catherine Régis, who co-lead the research program at the Canadian AI Safety Institute. Johns Hopkins University professor Gillian Hadfield, who was recently named to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s new AI advisory council, is also on the list.

Reports of rogue AI agents have helped fuel widespread public alarm about AI safety. OpenAI disclosed over the summer that its AI agents hacked AI startup Hugging Face without being instructed by any human to do so.

That was followed by other disclosures. Anthropic said its artificial intelligence models hacked into three other organizations during testing. Meta disclosed that one of its AI models accessed the internet on its own and hacked another company. And Google confirmed its Gemini AI model hacked three companies as part of a test of its cybersecurity capabilities.

A San Francisco-based lab that monitors AI activity said in a report on Sept. 30 that the website for Library and Archives Canada was one of the targets of a failed hacking attempt by an artificial intelligence agent.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon said in September he spoke with his international counterparts in the G7 about setting up a “technology stability board” that would evaluate AI models for testing.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Majority of Canadians support closer formal ties with European Union: poll
stories.summary: Approval ratings for the idea were highest in British Columbia and lowest in the Prairies
stories.author: Jesse Winter
stories.content:
Canadian support for more formal ties with the European Union appears to be growing, a new poll suggests.

Nearly eight in 10 respondents were supportive or somewhat supportive of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU so long as the agreement increased co-operation on trade and defence, but stopped short of full membership.

The poll, which surveyed 1,057 Canadians, was conducted for The Globe and Mail by Nanos Research in late September. It suggests a slight uptick from earlier figures released in April, which showed three in five Canadians supported the country gaining full membership in the EU.

The idea for associate membership was raised by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen who said in mid-September that Canada should become the EU’s first associate member.

That move came after Prime Minister Mark Carney spent months working to strengthen ties with European countries, in an attempt to diversify Canada’s trading partners amid the continuing tariff war with the U.S.

Various versions of an associate-type of membership have been floated by the bloc over the years, but there is no such legal category currently. The EU has 27 member countries.

While the poll’s numbers appear to show growing support for the idea, UBC political science professor Kurt Heubner said he believes the results speak more to Canada’s anger at U.S. President Donald Trump than to a real desire to join the European bloc in a formal capacity.

“I see it actually as a signal, a sign of ongoing deeper frustration with our neighbour in the south,” Prof. Heubner said. “It’s an expression of the frustration with what’s going on.”

Many Canadians do not fully appreciate the kind of sovereignty trade-offs that typically come with EU membership, Prof. Heubner said.

“You have a deliberate decision to give up political power and decision-making in key areas. That’s just the price ... to become a member,” Prof. Huebner said.

Pollster Nik Nanos agreed.

“My sense is that Canadians do not want to give up sovereignty to diversify the economy,” he told The Globe. “Hence the view of closer co-operation with Europe being more popular than full membership.”

Support for Canada gaining associate membership was highest in British Columbia, with more than 84 per cent of respondents saying they either supported or somewhat supported the move. It was lowest in the Prairie provinces where 70.4 per cent said they would support or somewhat support the idea.

In mid-September, Mr. Trump said that any move by Canada toward becoming an associate EU member could be seen as a “hostile act” that might trigger more tariffs.

The Nanos poll appears to show that, rather than discouraging Canadians from pursuing that course, it has emboldened some of them.

Half of Canadians who were surveyed said Mr. Trump’s comments would have no impact on their opinions, while one in three said the comments made them more likely or somewhat more likely to support EU membership.

Mr. Nanos said a key question remains: whether these shifts represent frustration with Mr. Trump alone, or a broader paradigm shift that will outlive the current U.S. administration.

What was clear from the survey is that Canadians don’t want the Prime Minister to unilaterally sign a deal on his own. Mr. Carney has said any new alliance with Europe would be debated and voted on in parliament.

Half of those polled said a House of Commons vote was enough to proceed, while 21 per cent said such a move should require a public referendum. Seven per cent said the potential of a new EU alliance would require calling a federal election. About 19 per cent said the government should be able to enter into such an agreement without doing any of the above and 4 per cent were unsure of what the government should have to do.

Regardless of Canada’s potential membership status, four in five Canadians told Nanos Research this country should pursue much closer (60 per cent of respondents), or somewhat closer (23 per cent) ties with the EU, including partnerships that go beyond trade.

Roland Paris, a University of Ottawa international affairs professor, said the specific name of a partnership matters less than how the relationship would function.

Nearly eight in 10 respondents were supportive or somewhat supportive of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU so long as the agreement increased co-operation on trade and defence, but stopped short of full membership.

The poll, which surveyed 1,057 Canadians, was conducted for The Globe and Mail by Nanos Research in late September. It suggests a slight uptick from earlier figures released in April, which showed three in five Canadians supported the country gaining full membership in the EU.
The idea for associate membership was raised by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen who said in mid-September that Canada should become the EU’s first associate member.

That move came after Prime Minister Mark Carney spent months working to strengthen ties with European countries, in an attempt to diversify Canada’s trading partners amid the continuing tariff war with the U.S.
Various versions of an associate-type of membership have been floated by the bloc over the years, but there is no such legal category currently. The EU has 27 member countries.

While the poll’s numbers appear to show growing support for the idea, UBC political science professor Kurt Heubner said he believes the results speak more to Canada’s anger at U.S. President Donald Trump than to a real desire to join the European bloc in a formal capacity.
“I see it actually as a signal, a sign of ongoing deeper frustration with our neighbour in the south,” Prof. Heubner said. “It’s an expression of the frustration with what’s going on.”
Many Canadians do not fully appreciate the kind of sovereignty trade-offs that typically come with EU membership, Prof. Heubner said.
“You have a deliberate decision to give up political power and decision-making in key areas. That’s just the price ... to become a member,” Prof. Huebner said.
Pollster Nik Nanos agreed.

“My sense is that Canadians do not want to give up sovereignty to diversify the economy,” he told The Globe. “Hence the view of closer co-operation with Europe being more popular than full membership.”

Support for Canada gaining associate membership was highest in British Columbia, with more than 84 per cent of respondents saying they either supported or somewhat supported the move. It was lowest in the Prairie provinces where 70.4 per cent said they would support or somewhat support the idea.
In mid-September, Mr. Trump said that any move by Canada toward becoming an associate EU member could be seen as a “hostile act” that might trigger more tariffs.
The Nanos poll appears to show that, rather than discouraging Canadians from pursuing that course, it has emboldened some of them.

Half of Canadians who were surveyed said Mr. Trump’s comments would have no impact on their opinions, while one in three said the comments made them more likely or somewhat more likely to support EU membership.

Half of those polled said a House of Commons vote was enough to proceed, while 21 per cent said such a move should require a public referendum. Seven per cent said the potential of a new EU alliance would require calling a federal election. About 19 per cent said the government should be able to enter into such an agreement without doing any of the above and 4 per cent were unsure of what the government should have to do.

stories.title: Manitoba’s ‘Wheat City’ wants to fix its derelict buildings. But how?
stories.summary: Abandoned properties in Brandon are an issue that crosses partisan lines in the coming municipal elections
stories.author: Temur Durrani, Photography by Shannon VanRaes
stories.content:
About this series

The Globe is reporting from cities and towns in Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia to hear from residents about the issues affecting their communities and their votes in the municipal elections.

Dozens of pigeons perch atop the abandoned McKenzie Seeds building on any given day. When the flock departs, this historic structure built more than a century ago in Manitoba’s second-largest city is virtually a lifeless void.

But the seven-storey, red-brick, ferroconcrete building and its signature clock tower continues to loom over downtown Brandon, as though it is a ghost from the city’s agricultural heyday.

Over the years, several housing projects and commercial ventures – including one touted as recently as this past summer – have tried to revitalize or redevelop the 120,000-square-foot former headquarters of the seed and grain powerhouse. None have been successful: The building – with its marble flooring, metal staircase, freight elevator, concrete seed bin, terrazzo hallways and mushroom-shaped columns – has been vacant since the 1980s.

Derelict buildings like this, dotting downtown cores across the country, create both an eyesore and a hazard.

Some communities have worked to deal with the problem through municipal bylaws, but the issue persists and has grown after the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Debates around ownership, municipal responsibility and a lack of funding have created roadblocks to solutions. And as cities and towns in multiple provinces hold elections this fall, the issue of vacant properties is becoming an increasingly important concern for both rural and urban voters.

At McKenzie Seeds, lewd graffiti is emblazoned on the walls outside, with holes smashed in the windows above, almost resembling gun shots but likely caused by thrown rocks.

“Because it’s still one of our tallest buildings and it’s located so centrally that you can see it from quite afar, it’s certainly a sad sight,” says Murray Fischer, the lead safety manager with Brandon’s planning and buildings department.

“I will admit it’s a blight on our city. It’s an issue we have to keep coming back to,” he says.

“And if we don’t find a way out of this, by next year, we’ll be forced to think of more drastic steps.”

Sections of the roof are in rough shape at this derelict building, once part of a mental-health facility in Brandon. Assiniboine College plans to restore it.

Unused buildings – residential and commercial – face a high risk of arson, structural collapse, and toxic contaminants such as asbestos or lead when left to the elements for far too long.

If they’re boarded up improperly, they tend to become makeshift shelters, especially during harsh winters, with the lack of affordable housing and encampment shutdowns displacing thousands of Canadians.

“So, if someone who is homeless comes in there and wants to keep warm, they’re not an arsonist, but that’s usually how fires there can start,” Brandon Fire and Emergency Services Chief Terry Parlow says.

As long as a property owner continues to pay taxes, most Canadian municipalities have little recourse to deal with vacant buildings.

In the Wheat City, as Brandon is colloquially called, the largest of these derelict structures are commonly owned by numbered companies, many with offices outside of Manitoba, Mr. Fischer says. Some vacant residential properties have similar ownership structures; but more often, they have been passed down from a deceased family member, with the new owner absent from Brandon.

“It’s made our job very difficult from a safety perspective,” Mr. Fischer says. “We’ve definitely had to put on our sleuth hat a lot of times to find out who the real owner is behind these numbered companies in order to get in touch with them.”

However, in late 2023, after a string of costly fires, Brandon made significant changes to its bylaws. Under the new rules, city staff are allowed to pro-actively identify and address the issues of vacant properties rather than relying on public complaints or emergencies such as fires.

Annual fees for unused properties were also raised by hundreds of dollars, motivating some owners to either demolish unsafe structures or restore and reoccupy them.

Chief Parlow says the amendments are working. The measures have led to a dramatic decrease in fires and lowered the number of “problem properties” from about 100 to around 10, the fire chief added.

But tending to these properties can be costly, says Jeff Fawcett, the incumbent mayor who is running for re-election. Last year, Mr. Fawcett helped pass a resolution with the Association of Manitoba Municipalities that called for the provincial government to establish its own penalties for neglected properties and to provide municipalities with financial assistance to remove or repair them.

“We need the province’s help on this,” Mr. Fawcett says, pointing to the buildings behind him, as he sipped coffee at Chez Angela Bakery and Café downtown. “But as of now, I haven’t heard from Premier Wab Kinew’s government on this yet.”

At an unrelated event late last month, Mr. Kinew was asked whether he would change provincial legislation to impose time limits on unused properties. “It’s a civic election question – I’m sorry,” he told reporters, declining to weigh in on the matter.

Len Isleifson, who is also running for mayor in Brandon, agrees with his opponent. “This isn’t exactly a partisan issue. And it’s not the first thing I hear as the biggest concern when I go speak with voters here,” he says from his office at Assiniboine College.

“But downtown Brandon is struggling with this cycle. We should definitely be doing more to attract businesses, to uplift the vibrancy and improve the quality of life for our residents. And yet, we can’t attract that sort of attention when these buildings are still a constant problem, so it’s just a cycle that’s continuing.”

A short drive around the small city – population 54,000 – will show many such properties sitting empty, such as a former bottling plant, boarded-up bungalows and a fenced-off bus depot. None are quite as glaring as McKenzie Seeds.

“I see that sad building every day on my way to work, and it’s like this reminder of the potential of our city,” says Janet Friesen, who works at a salon.

“You can see the Seeds building from here, across the train tracks,” says Brandon resident Honeybun Desmarais. “But even in my cul-de-sac, we also have another handful of abandoned houses. They’ve become sort of these local ghost stories. It’s a safety issue for everyone.”

This past May, Paul Souque, president of Blackbird Housing, a Brandon-based real estate development company, purportedly purchased the McKenzie Seeds building. He told multiple local media outlets that his proposed development would include 130 residential suites, medical and wellness spaces and a 10,000-square-foot rooftop deck.

Mr. Souque’s developers appear to have been exploring partnerships for senior housing, and he insisted that construction would begin this year for the ostensibly $20-million project.

But Mr. Fischer says the City of Brandon has not seen any plans from Blackbird yet – “nothing concrete on design, architecture, construction or anything like that.”

Property records suggest ownership of the building only changed from one numbered company to another in late September. “Blackbird’s media blitz appears to have been just another way of getting further investors on board,” Mr. Fischer says.

When reached for comment, the director of Blackbird’s parent company, Braden Bjornson from Alberta-based Fotonara Inc., responded via e-mail: “The project is 100% reliant on private investment. Capital formation has been the priority. City permits and design plans are secondary to that. No construction has started. We are not describing an approved, fully financed project.”

In the meantime, McKenzie Seeds has deteriorated to the point of structural collapse, Mr. Fischer says.

“We’re going to have to bring this to council next year. Whether we demolish it or come up with something else, it’s something that the city will have to inevitably decide on. It’s only getting worse – and it’s going to be costly.”

Vancouver: The population is shrinking in some neighbourhoods. What if we put more housing there?

stories.title: RCMP strengthens ties with FBI, but critics warn Mounties are too dependent on U.S.
stories.summary: Canada needs a radically reformed national police force better able to push its own complex cases through the courts, law professor says
stories.author: Colin Freeze
stories.content:
Canada’s national police force says it will continue to strengthen ties with the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation, even as experts warn against deepening the relationship at a time of growing divergence between the neighbouring countries.

This year, RCMP-FBI co-operation has been credited for dismantling gangs such as Ryan Wedding’s alleged drug-trafficking organization, with Mountie Commissioner Mike Duheme appearing alongside Trump administration officials to announce these takedowns.

“Given the shared border between Canada and the United States, the RCMP works closely with U.S. law enforcement partners,” RCMP spokeswoman Jessica Kingsbury said in an e-mail to The Globe and Mail, adding that “expanded operational collaboration with U.S. agencies has enhanced threat identification, information sharing, and contributed to high-profile arrests.”

However, in a new book, Kent Roach, a law professor at the University of Toronto who chaired the RCMP’s management advisory board in 2023, argues that the Mounties have grown too dependent on the FBI.

Prof. Roach writes that the Mounties have relied on the bureau’s tips to learn about impending terrorist attacks and other national-security threats to Canada, and they are also embracing FBI-led partnerships to put some of Canada’s most wanted criminals before U.S. courts. He argues, however, that this is not addressing the obstacles in the Canadian criminal-justice system against tackling complex crime and also exposes Canadian police to U.S. administrations who are being accused of politicizing policing.

“We have to imagine a world where the Americans, and specifically the FBI, May be less reliable partners,” Prof. Roach said in an interview. “We need to be able to do these complex national security, and also financial crime and organized crime prosecutions, as part of our sovereignty.”

In Prof. Roach’s book, Red Alert , he says U.S. law enforcement agencies are being politicized. He adds that Canada’s federal government has yet to address longstanding calls for structural RCMP reform, which has left the FBI filling gaps in Canadian law enforcement. A 2023 report from a committee of parliamentarians said the Canadian government might need to strike up a new national police force entirely, if it could not better enable the RCMP to tackle transnational crime.

Prof. Roach also criticizes the response of former prime minister Justin Trudeau to U.S. President Donald Trump, who imposed emergency tariffs on Canada in 2025 over concerns that fentanyl was flooding from this country into the U.S. (A Globe investigation found Mr. Trump was using misleading data about drug seizures at the border to justify the tariffs.)

Mr. Trudeau promised to be a better security partner to the United States, with his government pledging hundreds of millions in new funds to hire more Mounties and also leasing Blackhawk helicopters to patrol the border.

“I think Trudeau was panicking over Trump,” Prof. Roach said in an interview.

Over the past two years, the RCMP has unveiled operational partnerships with the California FBI that are now being credited for taking down transnational gangs.

Mr. Wedding, a former Canadian Olympic snowboarder, was among the Fbi’s most-wanted fugitives when he was arrested in Mexico in January on multiple charges of drug trafficking and murder conspiracy. He had spent more than a decade on the run and is now set to stand trial in Los Angeles, where he has pleaded not guilty.

About 30 individuals tied to his gang have been arrested under U.S. laws, according to indictments filed in California. At least 12 of those accused have been arrested by police in Canada and most are fighting extradition.

Canada’s top police official was in California as FBI Director Kash Patel escorted a shackled Mr. Wedding off a U.S. plane after he was apprehended in Mexico. “This is a great day for public safety in Canada,” Commissioner Duheme said in January, adding the RCMP supplied crucial information to the FBI to help dismantle the gang.

Court documents filed in California allege Mr. Wedding and his Canadian co-conspirators trafficked tonnes of cocaine by truck and hired gunmen to kill Canadian citizens.

In another operational partnership announced in July, the California FBI and RCMP highlighted U.S. charges against 37 people allegedly tied to gangs – including ones connected to India’s most notorious crime lord, Lawrence Bishnoi.

The U.S. Department of Justice now alleges Mr. Bishnoi personally directed political assassinations, murders and shootings, including the slaying of Hardeep Singh Nijjar, a Canadian citizen shot dead in Surrey in 2023.

Commissioner Duheme was quoted in the U.S. DOJ statement announcing the arrests, saying that “together, we disrupted the operations of organized criminals.”

The close ties have persisted despite an apparent threat from Mr. Patel on X in late August to withdraw from the Fbi’s relationship with Canada. The threat was over an internal CBC/Radio-Canada guideline about removing the word “terrorism” from coverage of the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11. It prompted the RCMP to make inquiries about whether the U.S. agency had halted intelligence sharing.

Three national-security sources with direct knowledge of the probe previously told The Globe and Mail that the RCMP had not found any indication that intelligence sharing from the FBI had been interrupted. The Globe did not name the sources because they were not authorized to speak publicly about the probe. (The public broadcaster subsequently reversed the policy .)

In late September, the FBI and the Mounties held a joint press conference in Los Angeles to announce a US$1-million reward for information leading to the arrest of an Indian gangster allegedly tied to the assassination of Mr. Nijjar. And on Oct. 6, representatives from the B.C. RCMP were present with FBI officials in Seattle to announce the arrest of a 30-year-old in Washington State who authorities allege provided advice, money and technical assistance to the teenager who perpetrated the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge, B.C., earlier this year.

Cases such as these show Canadian police are getting better at leveraging vital U.S. relationships, said Peter German, a retired former RCMP deputy commissioner.

“The United States is 10 times larger than us, it has a 10 times larger law enforcement footprint around the world,” Mr. German said. He added that U.S. laws make it easier for the FBI to obtain evidence and prosecute complex transnational crime cases. “The U.S. is much more agile at conducting a criminal investigation than we are in Canada.”

However, RCMP critics are wary of the close relationship.

“The FBI has bailed out the RCMP many times,” Mr. Roach writes in Red Alert , noting that FBI intelligence tips have kickstarted several of Canada’s most urgent national security investigations.

Ms. Kingsbury, the RCMP’s spokeswoman, said the Mounties maintain “full independence” while accepting tips about threats from foreign agencies.

Such exchanges, she said, have saved Canadian lives. “There is no doubt that the RCMP benefits from its international partnerships, including those in the United States,” she said. “The RCMP rejects the suggestion that it was ‘bailed out.’”

Other observers, however, say the Trump administration is changing U.S. law enforcement in ways which May make close Canadian partnerships fraught.

Wesley Wark, a Canadian security expert at the Centre for International Governance Innovation, agrees that the Mounties May need to be rapidly bolstered. “Acceptance of a significant degree of dependency and reliance by the RCMP on intelligence flows from the FBI now looks untenable,” he said.

Canadian police cannot be “subcontracting out our criminal prosecutions to a foreign jurisdiction,” said Paul Cavalluzzo, a Toronto lawyer. “If you become reliant on Big Brother, so to speak, you do not hone your own skills.”

After 9/11, Mr. Cavalluzzo served as commission counsel on the Arar commission, a judicial inquiry that unearthed how RCMP intelligence exchanges with more aggressive U.S. security agencies led to several innocent Arab Canadian citizens being secretly flown to Middle East jails where they were imprisoned and tortured by foreign agencies backed by the CIA.

Several strictures guide the RCMP’s security partnerships with international partners, said Ms. Kingsbury. The Mountie spokeswoman said the RCMP regularly runs risk assessments and also abides by the Avoiding Complicity in Mistreatment by Foreign Entities Act.

That federal law, she said, precludes Canadian officials from exchanging any information where “doing so would create a substantial risk of mistreatment abroad, including circumstances involving capital punishment.”

However, Prof. Roach, who has contributed research to most major Canadian judicial inquiries into policing failures over the past 25 years, says such guardrails May now be insufficient.

“The Trump administration loves the death penalty,” he said. He argued that Mr. Wedding’s apprehension circumvented international extradition norms, leaving the Canadian citizen exposed to potential capital punishment if convicted in California.

Mr. Roach says what Canada needs now is a radically reformed national police force better able to push its own complex cases through Canada’s courts. “We should be able to prosecute these cases,” he said.
