stories.title: How a Mexico-U.S. trade deal could set the terms for Canada
stories.summary: 2027’s Cusma review looms as U.S.-Mexico talks advance while negotiations with Canada stall.
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — Washington is gearing up for next year’s review of the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement, but signs of negotiating progress have come mainly from the U.S.-Mexico trade teams in recent weeks, while formal talks between the U.S. and Canada remain stalled.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says he speaks frequently with Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc, but there have been no formal meetings between the U.S. and Canadian sides since talks collapsed in August.

The Mexican and U.S. teams met for a round of formal talks in July and were supposed to meet again in September, but that has been postponed, likely until sometime this month.

Mexico’s Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard recently expressed optimism that new agreements are coming soon. “We are getting closer on many issues, resolving problems, and we are making progress,” he said at last week’s G-20 meeting in Milwaukee, Wisc., after meeting with Greer. “Every day we are closer to reaching new agreements.”

Washington has opened public consultations for next year’s Cusma review while maintaining bilateral engagement with Mexico — and not with Canada, which raises concerns about Ottawa’s ability to influence the process. Experts say there is no reason for Canada to panic, but they also warn that a Mexican agreement could set terms that Washington later expects Ottawa to accept.

Mexico was seemingly on the back burner while Canada made progress in late summer, said Diego Marroquín Bitar, a fellow with the Americas Program at Washington’s Csis.

“The Canadians made a lot of progress before negotiations collapsed,” he said. “So they could jump back … to the negotiation table at any moment and be very close to where the Mexicans are actually.”

The arrangement the U.S. and Mexico are working toward centres on tariff relief and policy concessions, rather than a comprehensive rewrite of Cusma.

Marroquín Bitar referred to it as a “skinny deal,” or a preliminary bilateral deal, that would give Mexico tariff relief in exchange for domestic-policy concessions and closer alignment with U.S. trade policy toward non-market economies.

This could help prepare the ground for the 2027 Cusma review, he said, but it’s not a final settlement or replacement for the trilateral agreement.

Carlo Dade, director of international policy and the New North America Initiative at the School of Public Policy at the University of Calgary, agrees.

“Mexico can sign an agreement on reciprocal trade with the U.S. to set a new tariff regime and to set a new economic security regime,” he said, noting that Ustr calls them agreements on reciprocal trade.

Dade also rejects the notion that Canada is being left out, noting that not every communication is shared with the public.

“I wouldn’t read this as necessarily being sidelined,” he said.

As for what Mexico and the U.S. could hash out bilaterally, there are a number of issues, but trade experts believe it will largely focus on immediate issues while laying a path for continued talks on tougher debates.

“I think there’s a lot that bilaterally can be addressed without Canada,” said Inu Manak, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, pointing to energy investments and reform in Mexico, labour reform and enforcement, including collective bargaining rights, Mexico’s external trade policies, and some agricultural disputes over seasonal produce.

Still, the bilateral bargains are closely tied to Cusma’s future, as Washington is using the prospect of renewal to press for settlements on other trade disputes, according to Christopher Sands, director of the Center for Canadian Studies at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies in Washington.

“The way that the Trump administration has taken this, the review, as you know from last year, is to hold the renewal of the agreement hostage until other trade issues are resolved,” he said.

One possible development that could really impact Canada, trade watchers say, is an agreement on sectoral tariffs. Any settlement by Mexico on the Section 232 tariffs, Marroquín Bitar warned, could become Canada’s benchmark.

“Whatever Mexico accepts in this interim deal will very likely become the floor rather than the ceiling for whatever Canada negotiates when it eventually returns to the table,” he said. “Every Mexican concession becomes the opening term of Canada’s negotiations.”

Manak largely agreed and pointed to the automotive industry.

“So let’s say Mexico can negotiate down … from the 25 per cent … auto or auto parts tariff, a tariff at 15 per cent or lower, for example … that would be something that would create … a baseline even for Canada,” she said.

Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute in Washington, also expressed concern over this, noting that the U.S. is unlikely to agree to a better deal for Canada later.

“If Mexico agrees to it, I find it difficult to believe that the Trump administration would … be open to being flexible when it comes to Canada specifically,” he said.

Even if Canada’s formal talks remain on hold, Sands says closer Canada–Mexico ties could help Ottawa stay informed about Washington’s demands.

“What we will have now that we didn’t have reliably before is … a Mexico-Canada dialogue where I’m sure they’ll pick up the phone and say, ‘Hey, this is what the Americans are asking us to … sign, and here’s where we’re trying to modify it,’” Sands said.

And while this approach May not stop Washington from using a “divide and conquer” approach, Sands said he thinks the “Mexicans are … trying anyway to be much better partners.”

“They May be forced to do a bilateral on security, or just a U.S.-Mexico agreement on some aspect, but I think they want to keep the band together.”

Changes to Cusma itself, however, require agreement among all three countries.

“Any changes to the agreement would need the concurrence of all three parties,” said Dade.

Marroquín Bitar said any deal the U.S. and Mexico might strike this autumn would leave broader trilateral issues — including rules of origin — for the next phase.

He referred to this as merely the beginning of a “15-round fight.”

“It’s going to be a very long and painful process, but I think Usmca will survive it,” he added.

“It’s not going to be the same agreement that we have now, but it’s still going to be a framework that’s going to give Mexico and Canada, I think, better market access compared to any other country or any other trading block in the world.”

Experts say there is no reason for Canada to panic, but they also warn that a Mexican agreement could set terms that Washington later expects Ottawa to accept.
Mexico was seemingly on the back burner while Canada made progress in late summer, said Diego Marroquín Bitar, a fellow with the Americas Program at Washington’s Csis.
“The Canadians made a lot of progress before negotiations collapsed,” he said. “So they could jump back … to the negotiation table at any moment and be very close to where the Mexicans are actually.”
The arrangement the U.S. and Mexico are working toward centres on tariff relief and policy concessions, rather than a comprehensive rewrite of Cusma.

Marroquín Bitar referred to it as a “skinny deal,” or a preliminary bilateral deal, that would give Mexico tariff relief in exchange for domestic-policy concessions and closer alignment with U.S. trade policy toward non-market economies.
This could help prepare the ground for the 2027 Cusma review, he said, but it’s not a final settlement or replacement for the trilateral agreement.
Carlo Dade, director of international policy and the New North America Initiative at the School of Public Policy at the University of Calgary, agrees.

“Mexico can sign an agreement on reciprocal trade with the U.S. to set a new tariff regime and to set a new economic security regime,” he said, noting that Ustr calls them agreements on reciprocal trade.
Dade also rejects the notion that Canada is being left out, noting that not every communication is shared with the public.
“I wouldn’t read this as necessarily being sidelined,” he said.

As for what Mexico and the U.S. could hash out bilaterally, there are a number of issues, but trade experts believe it will largely focus on immediate issues while laying a path for continued talks on tougher debates.

“I think there’s a lot that bilaterally can be addressed without Canada,” said Inu Manak, senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics, pointing to energy investments and reform in Mexico, labour reform and enforcement, including collective bargaining rights, Mexico’s external trade policies, and some agricultural disputes over seasonal produce.

Still, the bilateral bargains are closely tied to Cusma’s future, as Washington is using the prospect of renewal to press for settlements on other trade disputes, according to Christopher Sands, director of the Center for Canadian Studies at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies in Washington.
“The way that the Trump administration has taken this, the review, as you know from last year, is to hold the renewal of the agreement hostage until other trade issues are resolved,” he said.

One possible development that could really impact Canada, trade watchers say, is an agreement on sectoral tariffs. Any settlement by Mexico on the Section 232 tariffs, Marroquín Bitar warned, could become Canada’s benchmark.

“Whatever Mexico accepts in this interim deal will very likely become the floor rather than the ceiling for whatever Canada negotiates when it eventually returns to the table,” he said. “Every Mexican concession becomes the opening term of Canada’s negotiations.”
Manak largely agreed and pointed to the automotive industry.

“So let’s say Mexico can negotiate down … from the 25 per cent … auto or auto parts tariff, a tariff at 15 per cent or lower, for example … that would be something that would create … a baseline even for Canada,” she said.
Alfredo Carrillo Obregon, a trade policy analyst at the Cato Institute in Washington, also expressed concern over this, noting that the U.S. is unlikely to agree to a better deal for Canada later.
“If Mexico agrees to it, I find it difficult to believe that the Trump administration would … be open to being flexible when it comes to Canada specifically,” he said.
Even if Canada’s formal talks remain on hold, Sands says closer Canada–Mexico ties could help Ottawa stay informed about Washington’s demands.

“What we will have now that we didn’t have reliably before is … a Mexico-Canada dialogue where I’m sure they’ll pick up the phone and say, ‘Hey, this is what the Americans are asking us to … sign, and here’s where we’re trying to modify it,’” Sands said.
And while this approach May not stop Washington from using a “divide and conquer” approach, Sands said he thinks the “Mexicans are … trying anyway to be much better partners.”
“They May be forced to do a bilateral on security, or just a U.S.-Mexico agreement on some aspect, but I think they want to keep the band together.”
Changes to Cusma itself, however, require agreement among all three countries.
“Any changes to the agreement would need the concurrence of all three parties,” said Dade.
Marroquín Bitar said any deal the U.S. and Mexico might strike this autumn would leave broader trilateral issues — including rules of origin — for the next phase.
He referred to this as merely the beginning of a “15-round fight.”
“It’s going to be a very long and painful process, but I think Usmca will survive it,” he added.

“It’s not going to be the same agreement that we have now, but it’s still going to be a framework that’s going to give Mexico and Canada, I think, better market access compared to any other country or any other trading block in the world.”

stories.title: France open to defence deals with Canada despite its push for arms autonomy: envoy
stories.summary: France's new ambassador in Ottawa says her country is open to working closer with Canada on defence procurement, despite its push for Europe to develop a fully autonomous arms industry.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

Posted October 12, 2026 6:00 am.

Last Updated October 12, 2026 8:07 am.

Ottawa — France’s new ambassador in Ottawa says her country is open to working closer with Canada on defence procurement, despite its push for Europe to develop a fully autonomous arms industry.

“In the defence sector and in other equally strategic sectors, France advocates for a European preference in procurement,” French Ambassador Hélène Farnaud-Defromont said in a French-language interview.

“The ideal for us would be to achieve 100 per cent European content but, once again, we’re being realistic. We know we’re all going to need a bit of time to reach that goal.”

Farnaud-Defromont said France can help Canada build up its defence base by sharing best practices.

“France is the only member state of the European Union today to have retained a comprehensive defence industrial and technological base,” she said. “We have some really interesting ideas to put forward and develop together.”

In February, Canada became the first non-European partner in an EU loan program for joint defence projects called Security Action for Europe, or Safe. Only one contract for Canada has emerged from the program so far.

The program allows EU countries to access low-interest loans to buy military gear and weapons. It’s part of an initiative called ReArm Europe aimed at weaning the continent off its reliance on American weapons.

“The fact that Canada has joined Safe, I think that’s a very good thing,” she said. “We now need to see things come to fruition. We need this partnership to actually take shape.”

Much of Canada’s defence industrial base is made up of branches of American corporations. Farnaud-Defromont would not speculate on how that continental integration might affect Canada’s participation in Safe.

The ambassador said 65 per cent of the components in each piece of defence equipment France procures are of European origin — a threshold the EU is trying to apply to Safe projects.

Farnaud-Defromont said the people of France are “extremely concerned and worried” about the war in Ukraine and its implications for freedom across Europe.

Canada’s strong support for Ukraine is deeply appreciated across the continent, she said.

“We are in fact facing an all-out war on European soil following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine,” Farnaud-Defromont said.

“The front line is just a few hundred kilometres from Paris. It is not that far away.”

She said France is still trying to work toward peace through multilateralism, despite dozens of armed conflicts that — like those in the Middle East — have implications far beyond one region.

“The international order has been profoundly disrupted,” said Farnaud-Defromont, a career diplomat for 32 years.

“The environment in which I work today as a French diplomat bears no resemblance to the one I knew.”

While France is a founding member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, it has always maintained some autonomy.

France pulled out of Nato’s command structure for most of the Cold War and advocated for nuclear energy autonomy to avoid relying on others for electricity.

The country has for years advocated a vision of European collective security that runs at odds with American leadership. France ramped up its push for continental autonomy after U.S. President Donald Trump’s demands for control of Greenland.

“We have long been committed to developing, within the European Union and within Nato, a European pillar, and within the European Union a community that is also strategic,” Farnaud-Defromont said.

“We are by no means pleased with the situation within Nato, which is, to say the least, very confused.”

Kerry Buck, a former Canadian ambassador to Nato, has warned that Ottawa would be less safe if the alliance turned its focus more to the defence of Europe.

“Canada had long resisted the creation of a European pillar within Nato for fear of being sidelined, and because we didn’t want the EU exercising ‘strategic autonomy’ in decision-making, or otherwise competing with Nato,” she wrote in a June 2025 commentary in Policy Magazine.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 12, 2026.

— With files from Émilie Bergeron

The ex-soldier who tried to carry out a mass shooting at a synagogue in Belleville, Ont., last month did not have a firearms licence at the time of the attack, according to a police source with direct knowledge of the investigation.

Sean Ward, a former Canadian Armed Forces corporal, died after a shootout with police outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue on the evening of Sept. 20, in what investigators have called a hate-motivated attack against the Jewish community. While worshippers gathered inside for Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar, Mr. Ward ambushed a police officer who was parked outside to provide security, sparking a violent gun battle before he was shot and killed.

Since the attack, authorities have not released any details on the origins of the former soldier’s guns. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the police source because they were not authorized to discuss the case publicly.

The RCMP, which manages the Canadian Firearms Program, declined to answer questions about Mr. Ward’s status in the national database for gun owners, citing “operational and privacy reasons, including the integrity of the ongoing investigation.”

The Belleville Police Service, which is leading the investigation, also declined to comment on the shooter’s guns, or how the source of his firearms May have steered the focus of the criminal probe.

Despite being shot in the head at the scene, Belleville Police Constable Jeff Smith, the officer who was ambushed, called for backup and, with another officer, managed to thwart the attack and stop the shooter before he could breach the building’s doors.

Mr. Ward, who brought multiple firearms, including a shotgun, and significant amounts of ammunition and gasoline to the synagogue, died in hospital from gunshot wounds. Two dozen bullets pierced the building’s stained-glass windows, while about 25 members of the small congregation took cover on the floor. None were injured.

Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd has said Mr. Ward came prepared to inflict maximum casualties and was equipped “to carry on a gun battle for a long period of time.” The shootout marked a dramatic escalation of antisemitic attacks in Canada, and has fuelled calls for a national response and improved security at Jewish sites.

Firearms licensing can be useful to investigators after a shooting because it creates a paper trail for police to follow. When a gun is legally owned, police can often answer key questions much more quickly, including by tracing the firearm’s legal owners, origins and sale records. This helps investigators identify who acquired it and when.

Gun licences can also help investigators reconstruct how firearms move from the legal market into criminal hands, which May reveal straw purchases, thefts, unlawful transfers or smuggling networks. The vast majority of illegal guns that are smuggled into the country cross into Canada through U.S. land borders, according to federal and provincial authorities.

While Canadian soldiers are trained to use firearms as part of their jobs, they still need to be licensed to own guns in their private lives, including non-restricted weapons such as shotguns or hunting rifles.

The Globe previously reported Mr. Ward was involuntarily discharged from the military in 2022, after refusing to take the COVID-19 vaccine, according to sources. He later sued the Canadian Forces as part of a lawsuit filed by former soldiers who didn’t want to be vaccinated. Court records suggest the 29-year-old was struggling financially and held grievances against the army, and claimed he and other dismissed soldiers suffered “permanent psychological, physical and emotional trauma,” and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Most of the guns used in violent crimes and homicides in Canada are not legally registered, according to police and Statistics Canada data.

The gunman in Canada’s deadliest mass shooting, the rural Nova Scotia attack that killed 22 people in 2020, did not have a firearms licence. That became a significant part of the investigation because it raised questions about where his guns came from, who May have helped him obtain them and whether authorities had missed warning signs.

Since the gunman was not licensed to acquire firearms in Canada, investigators knew the weapons had not been purchased through normal legal channels. The investigation ultimately found that all of the firearms used in the attacks were illegally obtained, and three were traced to the United States.

Constable Smith remains in hospital and continues to recover from his injuries, according to Belleville Police Chief Rodd, who thanked the public for their messages of support.

“His treatment has included multiple surgeries, and he continues to receive ongoing medical care. Considering the extent of his injuries, he is doing remarkably well, and we remain encouraged by his resilience and recovery,” he said in a statement on Oct. 7.

A GoFundMe page started for the injured officer by members of Canada’s Jewish community had reached more than $940,000 in donations by Friday.

Ontario’s police watchdog, the Special Investigations Unit, is also completing its own investigation into the shooting – a standard procedure whenever the actions of officers have resulted in death, serious injury or the discharge of a firearm. The agency said it had assigned six investigators to the case.

stories.title: Room with a view: Glamping with Hyundai’s adventure-ready Palisade XRT Pro
stories.summary: Equipped with a 13-minute tent setup and cavernous cabin storage, Miranda Lightstone navigates the booming overland trend with her son and a clingy Sphynx cat
stories.author: Miranda Lightstone
stories.content:
There’s a specific kind of harmony that comes from packing up, leaving the concrete behind and finding tranquility beside the water. For three nights at a campsite in Long Sault, Ont., it was just me, my son, our Sphynx cat and the 2026 Hyundai Palisade. I wasn’t just looking for a family getaway; I wanted to know if Hyundai’s modified three-row SUV could genuinely bridge the gap between rugged outdoor living and on-the-road comfort.

Hyundai officially badges this rugged variant as the XRT Pro in Canada, though it firmly targets the overland and off-grid crowd. The Palisade has always been a reliable, spacious family hauler, but the XRT Pro trim changes the formula. It differentiates itself from the standard luxury-oriented models with a trail-ready stance. The design features dark-finish body cladding, functional underbody skid plates, elevated ground clearance and distinct 18-inch wheels wrapped in beefy all-terrain tires. Under the hood sits a 3.5-litre V6 engine, delivering 287 horsepower through a smooth automatic transmission and standard all-wheel drive.

Modifying a family SUV for the trails changes the financial equation. Before tax and freight, the entry-level Palisade Preferred Trend starts at $53,699. Stepping up to the XRT Pro costs $57,799. That $4,100 premium is the price of admission for genuine off-road hardware – including an electronic limited-slip differential – and a rugged aesthetic that looks far more at home in the wilderness than a school drop-off line.

Packing the Palisade for our getaway was remarkably easy. Because our sleeping quarters – a Thule Foothill 2 camp-in roof tent – were mounted outside the vehicle, the cavernous interior was entirely freed up. We didn’t use the available space on the Thule roof rack for bicycles, though the option was there.

Inside the cabin, the Palisade shines as a mobile basecamp. The upfront storage easily swallowed our road-trip essentials, snacks and the cat’s travel seat. In the second row, a 110-volt plug proved invaluable for keeping our electronic devices fully charged, ensuring we were never completely disconnected while resting by the St. Lawrence River.

But the true test of this rig was the rooftop tent itself. Here is where physical reality sets in: At five-foot-two, attempting to deploy a heavy canvas roof tent perched atop a lifted three-row SUV is a logistical comedy. Thankfully, I was lucky to have my son with me. At six feet, he managed the bulk of the heavy lifting. Even with his significant height advantage, we still had to bring a small step ladder to properly reach the heavy-duty zipper to open and close the shell.

The entire setup and teardown process took about 13 minutes. Once fully deployed, the structure is impressively solid, its thickly padded base exceptionally comfortable for a night’s rest. Space-wise, it is intimate. The tent offers just enough room for two people who are comfortable with one another or, in my case, one person and one clingy cat. Anticipating this tight squeeze, we packed a supplementary ground tent and took turns sleeping on the roof, allowing both of us to experience the elevated views.

The financial leap to a rooftop tent is significant. Depending on the exact model and size, a Thule rooftop camper will cost between $2,750 and $5,200. The Foothill 2 atop the Hyundai was the least expensive option at $2,750. Compare that to a traditional, high-quality, four-season ground tent from a premium outdoor brand, which typically retails between $600 and $900. It is a massive premium for the camp-in setup.

However, Hyundai and Thule aren’t the only ones leaning heavily into the overland lifestyle. Brands including Land Rover and Porsche offer their own highly specialized rooftop setups. Land Rover’s Defender pairs seamlessly with bespoke, hard-shell Autohome tents, while Porsche offers a beautifully engineered Tequipment roof tent for the 911 or Macan. They come with suitably astronomical price tags – upwards of $6,000 for the Autohome tents, and more than $8,700 for the Porsche tent.

Going overlanding these days can also be done in more mainstream vehicles. Brands such as Subaru (with its Wilderness trims), Ford (Bronco and Maverick), Toyota (Tacoma and Land Cruiser), Rivian and, of course, Hyundai (Palisade and Santa Fe XRT models) have completely re-engineered the roof structures. Instead of relying on aftermarket crossbars, these vehicles are leaving the factory with reinforced, heavy-duty roof rails designed specifically to handle the high static weight limits – often more than 318 kilograms – required to safely support a tent and a family of sleepers. Many dealerships even offer branded rooftop tents as official, warranty-backed accessories right at the parts counter.

Where the Palisade XRT Pro shines is in its sheer approachable utility. It offers massive passenger volume and daily drivability for a fraction of the cost. For those who camp frequently, investing in a camp-in vehicle setup May be worth the extra expenditure. By relocating the sleeping quarters to the roof, the cabin preserves vital interior volume for friends, family or extra supplies. Furthermore, a rooftop setup maintains a compact footprint and leaves the driver mobile, removing the need to be tethered to a massive, cumbersome trailer.

Our time in Long Sault proved that the right gear transforms a simple road trip into a memorable escape. The Palisade XRT Pro, paired with a functional rooftop tent, strikes the right balance between rugged capability and everyday practicality. Just remember to pack that ladder.

2026 Hyundai Palisade XRT Pro (AWD)

Price: $57,799, plus $2,400 for freight and pre-delivery inspection

Engine: 3.5-litre V6 GDI

Horsepower/torque (lb-ft): 287/260

Transmission/drive: Eight-speed automatic with Htrac all-wheel drive

Fuel consumption (litres per 100 kilometres): 13.4 (city); 10 (highway); 11.9 (combined)

Alternatives: Kia Telluride X-Pro, Honda Pilot TrailSport, Nissan Pathfinder Rock Creek, Ford Explorer Timberline

stories.title: A new centre asks: Why can’t seniors and toddlers be friends?
stories.summary: In Ottawa, kids in daycare are just down the hall from veterans in long-term care
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
Roly Lalonde sits in a walker while a toddler named Daa-Sha listens to his heart with a blue plastic stethoscope. Next, she checks his blood pressure.

The Second World War veteran boasts about his good health at 103, except for some challenges with his eyes. He’s also in good spirits, sporting a light-coloured suit and a smile, buoyed by his many new friends − who are about a century younger.

He often checks on his wee comrades here, at a daycare down the hall from his room in a long-term care wing for veterans at Ottawa’s Perley Health.

“I sometimes watch them eat and they wave their hands,” Mr. Lalonde said. “It’s beautiful.”

These are typical interactions at Canada’s first purpose-built intergenerational early learning centre. The aim of the project, which began welcoming children in July, is to foster community and combat loneliness among seniors through interactions between children and “grandfriends.” The model could serve as an example for other centres across the country as Canada experiences rapid growth in its aging population.

Two-year-old Daa-Sha is one of 49 children who attend daycare at Perley Health, which offers independent living and long-term care for seniors. Located near the gift shop, the learning centre is intentionally situated at the height of foot traffic. It is somewhat akin to a fish bowl, with large windows that allow for residents to greet children inside the centre.

The daycare space itself is about double the size of traditional child-care centres, in order to help seniors who use walkers or wheelchairs move with ease over non-slip tiles. It also features sound-absorbing materials to make it more comfortable for residents with dementia.

“We want to bring generations together and communities together,” said Katrin Spencer, vice-president of strategy and business development at Perley.

About 80 per cent of the children have parents who work for the health organization. “When you move into long-term care, you want to be part of a community still,” she added.

Many studies have shown the benefits of bringing generations together, including better mental health, improved well-being and increased sense of purpose. And similar centres exist elsewhere in the world, including in Australia and Britain.

But research on the effect of having child care situated inside a long-term care facility is still limited, says Annie Robitaille, named by Perley Health in 2020 as its Ottawa research chair of the Centre of Excellence in Frailty-Informed Care. She is also an assistant professor in the Interdisciplinary School of Health Sciences at the University of Ottawa.

Prof. Robitaille is leading a team studying the interactions at Perley and evaluating the program as it unfolds – but the work was already under way before opening day. They conducted interviews with residents, including veterans in independent living and those in long-term care.

In part, the research will look at whether the centre improves mental health for the seniors.

“Does it actually decrease loneliness? Also, what impact does it have on staff?” Prof. Robitaille said, referring to those who work on the campus and have kids in daycare there.

The centre is the product of a partnership between Perley Health and Andrew Fleck Children’s Services, a non-profit in the Ottawa region.

The project, which was about six years in the making, cost $4.8-million. It received $2-million from the Perley Health Foundation and $2-million from Ontario’s Ministry of Education.

Perley and Andrew Fleck collaborated throughout the process, and still do, said Ms. Spencer, adding that they work carefully to prevent the spread of infection, for example.

When the COVID-19 pandemic raised questions about bringing together young children and seniors – both vulnerable populations – the organizations worked through necessary regulations with support from Ottawa Public Health.

If an outbreak is declared in long-term care or in child care, interactions between the cohorts are paused.

As well, all of the furniture at the centre is wipeable and easy to clean, and handwashing stations are located at its entrance. When children arrive, workers conduct wellness checks.

The parents know the policies and ensure children stay home if they are ill, said Tina McLean, a program co-ordinator with Andrew Fleck who has worked in child care for three decades.

She described her work at the centre as deeply rewarding.

“The interactions that I see, let alone have myself, are so magical,” she said, adding that different generations are connecting like family.

And it’s not just the seniors who benefit.

The community draws valuable lessons from residents like Mr. Lalonde, who enthusiastically embraces life. A talented artist, he can frequently be found in Perley’s art studio when he isn’t visiting with his newfound friends.

“We have so much to learn from you,” Ms. McLean tells him.

With a grin, he replies: “I know it. Life is beautiful if you know how to live it.”

stories.title: Canada Disability Benefit payments go out this week. Here’s how it works
stories.summary: What to know about eligibility, payment amounts and how to apply.
stories.author: Matthew Daldalian
stories.content:
Eligible Canadians with disabilities are set to receive another Canada Disability Benefit payment this week.

The payment is scheduled for Oct. 15, according to the federal government’s benefits payment calendar . Payments are generally issued on the third Thursday of each month.

The benefit provides monthly financial support to Canadians with disabilities of age to work and is administered by Service Canada.

Here’s what you need to know about the extra money and how the regular benefit works:

The maximum payment for the July 2026 to June 2027 benefit period is $204.20 per month.

The amount depends on a recipient’s adjusted family net income and other factors, meaning not everyone receives the maximum.

The federal government has an online Canada Disability Benefit estimator that can provide an estimate of monthly payments.

Applicants generally must be between 18 and 64, be approved for the Disability Tax Credit, be a resident of Canada for tax purposes and have filed the required federal income tax return.

Once an application is approved, payments generally begin the following month and are issued on the third Thursday.

Some recipients May also qualify for retroactive payments for earlier months of eligibility.

Payments can be made by direct deposit or cheque and are not taxable.

The Canada Disability Benefit is a monthly benefit, not a one-time payment.

Payments began in July 2025 and continue each month for eligible recipients.

The federal government also introduced a separate $150 supplemental payment to help cover costs associated with obtaining the Disability Tax Credit, which is required to qualify for the benefit.

People who received a Canada Disability Benefit payment between July 2025 and June 2026 were scheduled to receive the $150 supplement on Sept. 17.

Those who received their first benefit payment after June 2026 can still qualify for the supplement, but it will be issued later. Recipients do not need to apply separately.

That means some Canadians May receive both their regular monthly benefit and the separate $150 payment.

Applications can be submitted online through Service Canada, by phone, in person or by mail.

Applicants generally need their Social Insurance Number and information about their status in Canada.

The next regular payment after Oct. 15 is scheduled for Nov. 19.

stories.title: Pigeon racing is ‘dying.’ Can these Ontarians save their sport from extinction?
stories.summary: They spend thousands of dollars on birds and fly them in races up to 1,000 kilometres in length. Now some say the sport is on its last legs.
stories.author: Mark Colley
stories.content:
Franco Bisceglia bought this pigeon, the one he is holding now with both hands in his Mississauga backyard, for several thousand dollars.

One of its aunts sold for 52,000 euros this year. The other sold for 48,000 euros. And this pigeon, with a shimmering turquoise neck, is Bisceglia’s prized possession. “No one,” he says, the pigeon bobbing its head back and forth, “has this bird in Canada.”

That is why, moments earlier, Bisceglia excused himself to shut the gate to his backyard, and why he keeps security cameras trained on his shed, and why he treats with suspicion phone calls asking about his champion birds. These racing pigeons, he says, are all valuable. He has been stolen from before. He does not want to be stolen from again .

But Bisceglia, who wears a shirt reading “Keep Calm and Race Pigeons,” is also deadly honest: Pigeon racing, he says, is a “dying sport.”

His observation is similar to that made by others who race pigeons. Sue Wiltshire, executive secretary with the Canadian Racing Pigeons Union (Crpu), said the sport is “slowing down” but will never die, citing a recent rebound in membership over the past decade. Bruce Bidon, president of the largest racing group in Canada, said the sport is “fighting a losing battle.”

A select few take it seriously all the same.

“You always want your bird to win,” Bisceglia said. “That’s just how it goes.”

They’re no park pigeons

Most weekends between May and September, some 1,500 pigeons from across the GTA fly in the Up North Combine, the largest racing competition in Canada. They are trucked somewhere north of Toronto — Burk’s Falls (about 220 km away) at the closest, Klotz Lake (some 840 km away) at the furthest — then released together.

Most of the time, they find their way home in a single day. The winner is the fastest pigeon. With no wind, they can fly up to 80 km in an hour.

How they do it, said Andrew Iwaniuk, who studies bird neuroscience as a professor at the University of Lethbridge, remains “one of the great mysteries in ornithology.”

The question has been studied intensely for some 70 years and has yielded intriguing results, but no fulsome answer. Research shows homing pigeons use visual landmarks to recognize home and use the sun as a compass. They also use their sense of smell.

There’s even evidence to suggest pigeons can detect differences in Earth’s magnetic field. (If you place a strong magnet on a pigeon’s head, it has more difficulty navigating.) Every few years, a new paper will suggest how a pigeon detects such subtle differences; the latest suggests it comes from the liver . But the ultimate answer of how pigeons navigate, Iwaniuk stresses, has yet to be determined.

Pigeon racers might not understand how, but they do select for homing skills. They breed and cherish the birds who are better than all the others at finding their way back home.

Bisceglia, a site supervisor for Toronto Water, caught the bug at age seven. His parents initially resisted, but his mom — who grew up on a farm — eventually caved. She told him he could start with two birds and see where it leads.

Now 50, it is Bisceglia’s obsession. (That and muscle cars; he has his eyes on a ‘68 Beaumont.) Inside his small loft — one of three in his backyard, separated by males, females and the white pigeons he rents out for weddings and funerals — pigeons flap and coo, pecking at each other’s necks and flying back and forth. The air smells of pigeon poop.

All of Bisceglia’s birds are vaccinated and dewormed, he says, and they are so well trained that they don’t land on his neighbours’ houses. He lets them out when they are slightly hungry, so they’re driven to come back when he shakes the food bucket.

His birds, he says, are in pristine condition. “Tight, tail, buoyancy, the muscles — you can feel the muscles are strong. The feather quality.” Even the eyes are important. Bisceglia tries to hold the beak of one pigeon to demonstrate, but it evades his fingers. A smile creeps across his face. A bit of feistiness, he says, demonstrates intelligence. “I love seeing this.”

How to train a racing pigeon

Months after a bird is born, Bisceglia begins training. He’ll drive his young pigeons several kilometres from his house, then release them. The next time, he’ll go further. Eventually, the pigeons are flying race distances.

But they don’t always come back.

Bidon, president of the Up North Combine, said he breeds about 40 baby pigeons each year. By the season’s end, he’ll have 32 to 35 left. Less experienced fanciers might lose 20 a year or more.

The problem, Bisceglia explained, is multi-faceted. Sometimes, hunters along the long route home will shoot at a flock, scattering the pigeons. Other times, a pigeon will latch on to the wrong flock and head the wrong way. And occasionally, a pigeon will run into a wire they couldn’t see.

Then there are predators. In his backyard, Bisceglia points to the sky as a hawk flies overhead. “Look at that,” Bisceglia says. “Right there’s the problem.”

It’s part of why pigeon racing is not viewed positively by everyone. An article published in 2023 by researchers at Newcastle University in the U.K. found there are significant benefits to the sport, but there are also significant disadvantages, including the use of performance-enhancing drugs — yes, even pigeons do steroids — and incentives to kill underperforming birds.

Wiltshire, the executive secretary of the Canadian Racing Pigeon Union, said every fancier takes the “utmost care” of their pigeons. They are dewormed, vaccinated and fed top-of-the-line food, she said, and the Crpu keeps tabs on fanciers around the country to ensure their lofts are in good shape and in compliance with local bylaws.

But the conflict remains. “It gets really contentious,” said Rosemary Mosco, an Ontario-based science writer and author of “A Pocket Guide to Pigeon Watching.” Once, while in Texas, Mosco came across a lost racing pigeon and took it to a rescue centre. There, the room was wall-to-wall with pigeons.

“It can be kind of heartbreaking from that perspective,” she explained, although she said, “our ethics around domestic animals are so complicated.”

Add it to the list of battles pigeon racers are currently fighting — a fight that, depending on who you ask, could lead to the extinction of the sport for good.

From working-class roots to million-dollar pigeons

Bidon’s father started racing pigeons when Bidon was four. He fell in love. He is now 67.

“Us kids were looking for something to do,” he said. “You catch a wild pigeon under a bridge or something, and you got fascinated.”

Today, the story is different. Bidon blames an infatuation with instant gratification, the internet and video games, the cost of living and everyday distractions, for the decline in his sport. Kids these days, he explained, simply aren’t racing pigeons. “There’s not a whole lot of positive things going on right now to grow the sport.”

Part of the reason is that pigeon racing was once a great bastion of the working class. Now, like horse racing, it is becoming a sport for the moneyed.

There is the cost of a loft, which runs $2,000 at the cheapest or more than $50,000 on the high end, Bidon said. Bisceglia’s loft is modest, but his friend’s is as big as a backyard. “He has heated floors,” Bisceglia said in hushed tones.

There is the cost of the birds, which at the low end can be no cost at all; many clubs will provide pigeons to new members for free, Bidon said. But when rookies inevitably don’t have success, they blame the birds and start spending money. Imported birds cost anywhere from $500 to $50,000. A Belgian bird once sold for 1.6 million euros .

Then there’s the electronic clocking system to measure race times ($1,000 to $2,000, Bidon said), the bird feed ($40 a bag, two bags a month for 25 birds) and the price of gas during training (drives of more than 50 km, three times a week).

Pigeon racing used to be known as the “poor man’s race horse,” Bidon said. That is no longer the case.

Regulation is making it harder to race pigeons, too. Fanciers feel cities are pushing them out with increasingly stringent bylaws , Bidon said; in Toronto, residents are limited to 30 domestic pigeons on a property and 50 during breeding season. A few years ago, the city wanted to ban domestic pigeons entirely, Wiltshire said; she and the Crpu helped talk them down.

Wiltshire, who is in charge of membership at the Crpu, remembers there being some 1,200 members in the 1970s, when she started racing pigeons with her husband. But many of those people have died. When she started at the Crpu in 2014, membership had fallen to about 430. At the time, she thought: “If we keep going down, it’ll be gone.”

Membership has rebounded to about 740, she said, and there are new members joining every year, many of whom are immigrants from countries where pigeon racing is more popular. Wiltshire disagrees with the premise that the sport is dying, though she acknowledges young people aren’t joining. “It’s slowing down,” she said, “but I don’t think it’ll ever die.”

The sport remains extremely niche. Of the millions who live in the GTA, only about 50 race pigeons, Wiltshire said.

Bisceglia worries the sport will die. He predicts that clubs and combines will shrink and merge, or cease to exist altogether.

He struggles to understand why the sport is where it is. He loves pigeon racing — the joy of caring for something, the pedigree and lineage that comes with elite birds, the rhythm of feeding and releasing and training and racing. Why someone wouldn’t be interested, he doesn’t know.

“I just love that feeling, to know that I could release them and they come home,” he said. “And it still hasn’t changed.”

stories.title: Ontario school reorganization is forcing students to switch classes. Parents ask if it could be avoided
stories.summary: Parents ask if schools’ scramble to balance classes can be avoided. Elsewhere in Canada, it often plays out differently.
stories.author: Isabel Teotonio
stories.content:
Lindsay Thompson’s daughter started the school year excited and eager to go to class each day because “she loved school so much.”

But when she learned her Grade 5 class was being dissolved, and she would be moved into a class with children she doesn’t get along with, she was “very upset.”

“She’s struggling with it,” said Thompson, whose daughter attends Williamson Road Junior Public School, calling the move a big change.

Similar scenes played out elsewhere as schools recently underwent reorganization, which can result in students and teachers switching classes and more split-grade classes. The Toronto District School Board says about 360 elementary schools were affected by reorganization in late September, compared with roughly 440 last year. Meanwhile, the city’s Catholic schools are still being reorganized, with students and teachers moving into new classes on Oct. 13.

Annual September reorganization stretches to October at Tcdsb, while Tdsb’s deadline is earlier than last year.

“This is a normal process that happens every year to make sure staffing reflects enrolment while meeting class size requirements and collective agreements,” said Emma Testani, press secretary for Education Minister Paul Calandra. “Boards are expected to manage these changes responsibly and minimize disruption for students and families.”

Yet as Ontario schools scramble to balance class sizes — a process that plays out differently, and often less disruptively, elsewhere in Canada — parents are left questioning whether the disturbance, weeks into the school year, could be avoided.

For Thompson’s daughter, it was the second consecutive year of upheaval.

“My daughter changed classes last year and was with a group of kids that she either didn’t really know or didn’t get along with — so it was really hard on her. ”

The girl was loving school this year. But then came the Friday afternoon email saying her Grade 5 French Immersion class of 18 was being eliminated, with students divided among three classes. The following Monday morning, she was among a group of kids moved to a new class of 28 students.

“There was one class that completely collapsed and then it rippled through every single class from Grade 1 to 5,” said Thompson, also co-chair of the school’s parent council.

“We talk about reorganization in terms of enrolment numbers, staffing allocations and class sizes, but for children it means losing the classroom they thought was theirs. Friend groups and learning partnerships are separated, teachers have to rebuild classroom communities, and children who have already settled in have to start over.”

Her experience echoed across the city. At Dewson Street Junior Public School, about 80 kids were shuffled to accommodate roughly five, said Nigel Barriffe, president of the Elementary Teachers of Toronto, the local union representing public school teachers.

Annual process seems more disruptive than usual, as staff work to bring class sizes in line with provincial requirements. And there are no trustees.

“Compliance with the regulation does not answer the question that parents and educators are asking: Is this actually the best decision for these children?” said Barriffe, at a press conference outside the school on Sept. 28, when Tdsb students who’d been affected began their new classes.

In a statement, the Tdsb said the timing of the Friday notification — parents say this leaves them with no time to process, prepare their children, or raise concerns before the Monday move occurs — “is intended to avoid a prolonged period of uncertainty, rather than having students spend days anticipating a potential move.” It also said that principals and staff “consider the individual learning styles, social skills and academic needs” when grouping students.

Elsewhere, reorganization resulted in three grades merged into a single class, with one teacher delivering lessons for three separate grades.

At The Grove Community School, a small alternative school, one of its five teachers was cut and students from grades 4, 5 and 6 were combined into one class of 27.

Ananya Ohri, co-chair of the parent council, says the new class spans different developmental stages, and many students have individual education plans, and complex social, emotional and educational needs, noting “This is a real blow in terms of the quality of education these kids are going to receive.”

Similarly, at Chine Drive Public School a Grade 4-5-6 class was also created, made up of 27 students.

“They’re speaking out of both sides of their mouth,” said mother Sara Wetmore, noting the province’s concerns about low math scores, but then allowing one teacher to cover three different math curricula.

The Tdsb said triple-grade splits occur when there are too few students for classes in successive grades.

Lindsay Thompson and her daughter outside Williamson Road Junior Public School. It was the girl’s second year of classroom upheaval.

In Ontario, reorganizations are complicated by the combination of hard caps on class sizes from kindergarten to Grade 3, and full-day kindergarten starting at age 4, explains Paris Semansky, co-executive director of the advocacy group People for Education. No other large Canadian province has that combination, she says, which leads to more classroom reshuffling and less predictability.

Because school isn’t compulsory until age six, families make different choices about when to start their kids in school, says Semansky. It can be tough to predict who will actually walk through a school’s doors in September.

Many parents say reorganizing in the first days of school would be far less disruptive. But enrolment can fluctuate in the opening weeks as families move, return from travel, or register their children. Boards typically take an official head count in mid-September to determine staffing needs and whether schools need to be reorganized, which can affect just a handful of students or dozens.

The ministry says school boards are responsible for staffing and reorganizing classes, but must follow provincial class-size rules and collective agreements governing class sizes and teacher assignments.

In a big city like Toronto, where families frequently relocate, just a handful of new students can push classes over their caps, triggering widespread reorganization, says Semansky. Yet while that can be chaotic, she’s not aware of “any lasting negative impact on kids. It’s disruptive for a bit, but it does settle out.”

Reorganization can also strain relationships and trust between parents and schools, she said.

“How that’s handled, both by principals and families, I think that’s what really matters,” said Semansky.

In Ontario, kindergarten classes must average no more than 26 students, with a cap of 29, though up to 10 per cent of a board’s classes can reach 32 under specific conditions. In grades 1-3, at least 90 per cent of classes must have 20 students or fewer, with the remainder capped at 23. For grades 4-8, there’s no cap on individual classes, but the board-wide average cannot exceed 24.5 students.

British Columbia also has hard caps in kindergarten through Grade 3, but unlike Ontario allows no exceptions to those limits. Quebec has class-size limits, but teachers are financially compensated when surpassed, with the amount increasing according to the number of extra students.

Meanwhile, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba have class-size guidelines, giving boards more flexibility to manage classes above target, says Shali Baziuk, president of the Canadian School Boards Association.

Whatever the model, Baziuk says adequate funding, resources and infrastructure are key to reducing disruption.

“If you have that, then you leave the school boards to manage that equitably, you’re not going to have to reshuffle kids,” she said. “These aren’t abstract numbers on the page — these are kids. Shifting kids around to achieve targets, you’re going to achieve a target. But we need to balance that against what’s best for kids.”

Friend groups and learning partnerships are separated, teachers have to rebuild classroom communities, and children who have already settled in have to start over.”

Her experience echoed across the city. At Dewson Street Junior Public School, about 80 kids were shuffled to accommodate roughly five, said Nigel Barriffe, president of the Elementary Teachers of Toronto, the local union representing public school teachers.
Annual process seems more disruptive than usual, as staff work to bring class sizes in line with provincial requirements. And there are no trustees.

“Compliance with the regulation does not answer the question that parents and educators are asking: Is this actually the best decision for these children?” said Barriffe, at a press conference outside the school on Sept. 28, when Tdsb students who’d been affected began their new classes.

In a statement, the Tdsb said the timing of the Friday notification — parents say this leaves them with no time to process, prepare their children, or raise concerns before the Monday move occurs — “is intended to avoid a prolonged period of uncertainty, rather than having students spend days anticipating a potential move.” It also said that principals and staff “consider the individual learning styles, social skills and academic needs” when grouping students.
Elsewhere, reorganization resulted in three grades merged into a single class, with one teacher delivering lessons for three separate grades.
At The Grove Community School, a small alternative school, one of its five teachers was cut and students from grades 4, 5 and 6 were combined into one class of 27.

Ananya Ohri, co-chair of the parent council, says the new class spans different developmental stages, and many students have individual education plans, and complex social, emotional and educational needs, noting “This is a real blow in terms of the quality of education these kids are going to receive.”
Similarly, at Chine Drive Public School a Grade 4-5-6 class was also created, made up of 27 students.

“They’re speaking out of both sides of their mouth,” said mother Sara Wetmore, noting the province’s concerns about low math scores, but then allowing one teacher to cover three different math curricula.
The Tdsb said triple-grade splits occur when there are too few students for classes in successive grades.
Lindsay Thompson and her daughter outside Williamson Road Junior Public School. It was the girl’s second year of classroom upheaval.

In Ontario, reorganizations are complicated by the combination of hard caps on class sizes from kindergarten to Grade 3, and full-day kindergarten starting at age 4, explains Paris Semansky, co-executive director of the advocacy group People for Education. No other large Canadian province has that combination, she says, which leads to more classroom reshuffling and less predictability.

Because school isn’t compulsory until age six, families make different choices about when to start their kids in school, says Semansky. It can be tough to predict who will actually walk through a school’s doors in September.

Many parents say reorganizing in the first days of school would be far less disruptive. But enrolment can fluctuate in the opening weeks as families move, return from travel, or register their children. Boards typically take an official head count in mid-September to determine staffing needs and whether schools need to be reorganized, which can affect just a handful of students or dozens.

The ministry says school boards are responsible for staffing and reorganizing classes, but must follow provincial class-size rules and collective agreements governing class sizes and teacher assignments.

In a big city like Toronto, where families frequently relocate, just a handful of new students can push classes over their caps, triggering widespread reorganization, says Semansky. Yet while that can be chaotic, she’s not aware of “any lasting negative impact on kids. It’s disruptive for a bit, but it does settle out.”
Reorganization can also strain relationships and trust between parents and schools, she said.
“How that’s handled, both by principals and families, I think that’s what really matters,” said Semansky.

In Ontario, kindergarten classes must average no more than 26 students, with a cap of 29, though up to 10 per cent of a board’s classes can reach 32 under specific conditions. In grades 1-3, at least 90 per cent of classes must have 20 students or fewer, with the remainder capped at 23. For grades 4-8, there’s no cap on individual classes, but the board-wide average cannot exceed 24.5 students.

British Columbia also has hard caps in kindergarten through Grade 3, but unlike Ontario allows no exceptions to those limits. Quebec has class-size limits, but teachers are financially compensated when surpassed, with the amount increasing according to the number of extra students.

Meanwhile, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba have class-size guidelines, giving boards more flexibility to manage classes above target, says Shali Baziuk, president of the Canadian School Boards Association.
Whatever the model, Baziuk says adequate funding, resources and infrastructure are key to reducing disruption.

“If you have that, then you leave the school boards to manage that equitably, you’re not going to have to reshuffle kids,” she said. “These aren’t abstract numbers on the page — these are kids. Shifting kids around to achieve targets, you’re going to achieve a target. But we need to balance that against what’s best for kids.”

stories.title: Carney says Canada is ‘worth fighting for’ one week from Alberta independence vote
stories.summary: The Prime Minister said 'you can't build big things on fault lines' in his Thanksgiving video.
stories.author: Stephanie Taylor
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is “worth fighting for,” exactly a week out from the referendum where Albertans will choose whether to set the province down a potential path of secession.

On Thanksgiving Monday, the Prime Minister’s Office released a short video of Carney delivering some remarks, saying that this year’s holiday “is a bit different.”

It comes as those campaigning for both the independence and federalist sides enter their final push, with numerous rallies and events planned across Alberta ahead of the Oct. 19 vote . Advance voting starts Tuesday.

“A week from today, Albertans will have the opportunity to make an important decision about their future,” he says in the video.

“Whether to remain part of Canada or begin a long and uncertain process through which Alberta could separate from Canada.”

Carney says he has some “perspectives” on the matter, pointing to the fact that he was raised in Edmonton and educated “right here” at St. Francis Xavier high school in the city, indicating the classroom he sits in.

Carney says lately, he has returned “home” often to the province, given the projects and announcements his federal Liberal government has made.

He specifically mentions “a new pipeline to the West Coast that will create lasting opportunity and prosperity for hundreds of thousands of people in this province and across the country.”

He goes on to say that “Canada is working,” but cautions that such progress can be undone should the country find itself split.

“The truth is, we can’t achieve any of this if we’re divided. You can’t build big things on fault lines,” Carney says. “And we should recognize that the world has changed. Canada is facing real threats to our economy, our security and our way of life.”

“Generations of Albertans helped build this country. It’s yours. It’s ours, and it’s worth fighting for.”

Monday’s video represents the latest comments Carney has made about the referendum.

He has previously characterized the vote as a “dangerous bluff,” and referred to his experience serving as Bank of England governor during Brexit, an event that Carney warned led to years of economic and political uncertainty.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has defended her decision to add an independence question to a set of existing referendum questions on constitutional and immigration reforms by saying thousands of Albertans signed their names to petitions on the issue over the past year.

Specifically, she added in the independence question after a court ruling quashed a petition that had been organized by separatist leaders in the province.

Albertans are now being asked to pick between two options: Either to remain a province of Canada, or to begin the legal process necessary to hold a future binding referendum on leaving.

Successive public opinion polls suggest support for separation is a minority opinion in the province. But independence leaders have been urging those frustrated by the province’s treatment from Ottawa as a way to cast a vote against the status quo.

Federalists have been urging those wanting to remain a part of Canada to turn out to the polls. Political heavyweights including former Conservative prime minister Stephen Harper and former Alberta premiers Jason Kenney and Rachel Notley have warned that a vote for independence will send a bad signal to investors.

Advance voting will run from Tuesday though Saturday. As of last week, Elections Alberta said it had verified more than 221,000 mail-in ballots, a record number reported by the provincial agency since Smith’s United Conservative Party government relaxed the rules around accessing them.

stories.title: Canadian cybersecurity executive arrested by FBI in hacking case
stories.summary: Kash Patel says FBI is working to ‘dismantle’ hacking group ShinyHunters, which breached the bureau’s internal database
stories.author: Stefanie Marotta, Jesse Winter
stories.content:
A Canadian cybersecurity executive whose career has focused on helping clients negotiate with ransomware attackers has been arrested in the United States in connection with a hacking group that the FBI says stole a huge trove of sensitive data about the bureau’s own employees, according to court records and Reuters.

FBI Director Kash Patel said on social media Friday that the agency had arrested what he described as another suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group, a collective of hackers who have conducted dozens of data breaches since 2019, including a hack of an FBI database earlier this year.

Reuters, citing a person familiar with the matter, reported that the person arrested was Edward Dubrovsky, a Canadian who has worked as an executive at numerous cybersecurity firms and has been credited by a former employer with helping thousands of clients recover from cyberattacks.

Court documents from the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania reveal that Mr. Dubrovsky has been charged and list two criminal complaints: conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money, and interference with commerce by threats.

The documents contain unproven allegations and attempts to reach Mr. Dubrovsky were unsuccessful.

The FBI declined to comment on Sunday, referring instead to Mr. Patel’s earlier social media post.

“This is the latest arrest this FBI has made in a matter of days involving this network, as we work non-stop to dismantle the group, pursue new leads and evidence, and act quickly,” the post said.

“We will continue to work closely with our partners to disrupt what’s left of the ShinyHunters group and their associates, no matter where they operate.”

In September, the ShinyHunters hacking group claimed responsibility for the FBI hack, which the bureau said May have compromised the private information of tens of thousands of its employees and applicants. The group said it had taken action over false allegations contained in an FBI public advisory from May that described the organization as a “cyber criminal group specializing in large-scale data breaches and extortion.”

U.S. federal prison and court records show that a 54-year-old man named Edward Dubrovsky was detained in Philadelphia and appeared in U.S. court last Thursday. The alleged connection between Mr. Dubrovsky and ShinyHunters is not detailed in publicly available documents.

The court records are partially sealed and include inconsistent spelling of his last name (including Dobrosky and Dobrovsky). The records also do not identify his profession or employer.

Reuters reported that electronic wallet records leaked in 2010 and preserved by dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs identify Dubrovsky as a resident of Richmond Hill, a suburb north of Toronto, and put his current age at 54.

RCMP spokesperson Ian Lordon said Friday “the RCMP is aware of the arrest of a Canadian in the U.S. in connection with the ShinyHunters hack,” but directed all further questions to the FBI.

Global Affairs Canada did not respond to a request for comment.

Over the past three decades, Mr. Dubrovsky held several senior positions in the cybersecurity field, according to his LinkedIn profile. In a LinkedIn post from last week , Mr. Dubrovsky is seen in photographs posing with colleagues and signing copies of his recently published book at the NetDiligence conference in Philadelphia. He wrote about his excitement at attending the conference with digital security company CyberSteward, which is also displayed in his profile photo.

CyberSteward did not return a request for comment.

His LinkedIn profile lists his most recent permanent post as at Cypfer, a global cybersecurity firm based in Miami, Fla., with offices in Toronto. The company provides services in cybersecurity breaches, cyberextortion, and ransomware recovery and negotiations.

In a 2022 press release announcing Mr. Dubrovsky’s appointment as managing director, Cypfer described him as a “30-year veteran of the cybersecurity and technology industries.” He “has helped thousands of organizations of all sizes and industries recover from devastating cyberattacks and consulted to management boards, executives, legal counsel and insurance carriers on resilience and risk mitigation methodologies.” He left the company almost a year ago, according to his LinkedIn page.

A representative for the company could not be reached for comment.

Mr. Dubrovsky’s book, published last month, is about cyberextortion and strategies for managing a ransomware crisis.

“I have negotiated with criminals who viewed themselves as martyrs ... even after deploying malware against critical infrastructure and causing billions of dollars in damage,” Mr. Dubrovsky wrote in his book.

“We must understand our opponents if we expect to survive on the digital battleground, and we must understand them better if we hope to reach common ground in negotiations.”

The Fbi’s advisory from May characterized ShinyHunters as “threat actors” who often “use their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims,” commonly harass or threaten people, and “May falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist.”

The ShinyHunters group has also attacked Canadian companies. In March, Vancouver-based telecom company Telus Corp. said it was investigating a cybersecurity incident at a recently reacquired technology business line. The matter involved unauthorized access by the hacking group.

According to technology news website BleepingComputer, ShinyHunters said it stole nearly one petabyte of data from Telus Digital, including customer data, in a multi-month breach. The group demanded a ransom in exchange for not leaking the data.

With files from Reuters and Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney condemns U.S.-Russia diesel deal, thanks Trump for ceasefire efforts
stories.summary: Deal calls for Russia to immediately supply 300,000 tonnes of diesel to U.S. and global markets, with more to be released in the weeks to come
stories.author: Unknown
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney condemned a U.S. deal for Russia to supply millions of barrels of diesel, which he said would fund the war with Ukraine and hurt efforts to end the conflict, even as he subsequently thanked Donald Trump for his work toward a proposed ceasefire.

Mr. Carney spoke with the U.S. President and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in separate conversations on Sunday, amid American efforts to broker a ceasefire aimed at protecting energy infrastructure.

The Prime Minister’s Office issued a statement summarizing his call with the Ukrainian leader, in which Mr. Carney attacked Mr. Trump’s diesel agreement. The deal calls for Russia to immediately supply 300,000 tonnes of diesel to U.S. and global markets, with more to be released in the weeks to come.

“The Prime Minister was clear: this agreement is in direct opposition to the efforts of Ukraine, Canada, and our allies to create peace and stability in Europe,” the statement said. “It will provide additional revenue for Russia and help finance its illegal, unjustifiable war against Ukraine.”

The United States, Canada and other allied countries placed harsh sanctions on the Russian energy industry after the country’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the White House agreement would involve a partial lifting of those.

The Pmo’s statement marked an unusually sharp public rebuke of White House policy on Ukraine by the Prime Minister, whose criticisms of Mr. Trump often don’t mention him or the U.S. by name.

Mr. Carney also broke with Mr. Trump in March, when Canada and other European countries pushed back against the U.S. for easing sanctions on Russian oil.

Later on Sunday, the PMO issued another statement that said Mr. Carney had spoken with Mr. Trump and thanked him for his efforts to broker what the President has described as an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia.

Mr. Trump made the surprise ceasefire announcement on his Truth Social platform but offered few details. Mr. Zelensky said he was still waiting to see further elements of the proposal but also said he supported it. There was no word from Moscow about the prospect of a ceasefire.

“Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Mr. Trump’s post said.

Mr. Trump has blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries, rather than his own war on Iran, for increased diesel prices in the U.S., which have become an issue ahead of the midterm elections in November.

Several U.S. lawmakers also criticized the diesel deal. U.S. Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, said the diesel supply deal with Russia May be illegal and will put American lives at risk.

During his call with Mr. Trump, Mr. Carney “expressed Canada’s strong support for this agreement and reiterated President Zelenskyy’s call for Russia to uphold it,” the statement said, referring to the ceasefire proposal.

“It is imperative that all attacks on energy infrastructure and civilians cease immediately,” it continued.

The Prime Minister’s Office did not say whether Mr. Carney raised his concerns about the diesel agreement during the call or if the two leaders spoke about stalled Canada-U.S. trade negotiations.

Meanwhile, Mr. Zelensky said he was looking for some sign that Russia was actually committed to the agreement.

“Ukraine supports this step, and we have stated so, but now we need a response from Russia – what Russia will say to the American President, and whether it will stop striking our energy infrastructure,” Mr. Zelensky wrote in a posting on X.

Mr. Trump also called for elections in Ukraine, suspended since the 2022 Russian invasion, to which Mr. Zelensky responded that he would call a vote if Mr. Putin agreed to a 60-day ceasefire.

Mr. Zelensky said it was “up to Ukrainians” to choose their leader but added that there needed to be an end to the fighting first. Ukrainian law prohibits elections under martial law for security reasons.

Ukraine’s government reported that attacks by Moscow on energy sites in Ukraine had continued after Mr. Trump’s statement. Still, in a televised evening address, Mr. Zelensky said Ukraine was “ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure – and we count on the same readiness from Russia.”

With reports from The Associated Press and Reuters
