stories.title: Environmentally conscious voters in NDP stronghold ridings dismayed by Eby’s track record
stories.summary: Some previous NDP voters are shifting towards the Green party this election
stories.author: Salmaan Farooqui
stories.content:
Joe Karthein steps over mossy logs and pushes thick bushes aside as he hikes up an untamed mountain slope high above the Nelson, B.C., area.

As he walks, he points out trees that are estimated to be more than 200-years-old, noting that local ecologists believe some could be more than 400-years-old. Massive fallen trunks as wide as sidewalks blend into the forest floor, a trait typical to old-growth forests.

This area is part of a contentious, 9.5-hectare parcel of land that is slated to be logged. Most of the slopes beside it already show signs of past clear-cutting.

Ecologists have estimated the forest is roughly 240 years old, just 10 years shy of being protected by an old-growth designation. Mr. Karthein said it would probably take less than a week for a five-person crew to harvest the plot, and the local mill could likely process the lumber in just two days.

The disappearance of forests like these are why Mr. Karthein, an activist in the area, has decided he can no longer vote for the provincial NDP, which is in a tough fight for reelection after nine years in power.

NDP Leader David Eby called a snap election last month in hopes of taking advantage of internal strife within the rival BC Conservative Party, but his party is now lagging in the polls. Election day is Oct. 24.

With the NDP promising to increase the province’s annual logging harvest from 30 million cubic metres to 45 million cubic metres, environmentally conscious voters are worried that more of these remaining slivers of forest that are just shy of old-growth status will disappear.

After decades of support for the BC NDP, including personally fundraising for the legal work Mr. Eby did in the Downtown Eastside in the 2000s prior to his political career, Mr. Karthein said he will vote for the BC Green Party this election.

“We were promised a paradigm shift,” said Mr. Karthein, referencing a pledge from Mr. Eby in 2022 to better protect old-growth forests by implementing recommendations from the Old Growth Strategic Review, a major independent review of forestry practices commissioned by the province.

“But in so many measurable ways, we’ve seen regression on forestry reform, and we’ve gone backwards instead.”

Several environmentally conscious voters in two NDP stronghold ridings in the West Kootenays region told The Globe and Mail they are coming to the same conclusion as Mr. Karthein. They feel abandoned by a party that is turning its focus toward resource extraction and away from climate change issues in light of Canada’s deteriorating relationship with the United States.

Mr. Eby himself has called the West Kootenays region a heartland for the environmental movement. Nelson has been home to hippie culture since the Vietnam War brought a wave of draft dodgers to the region, and is a place where residents are often scolded on Facebook pages for not clearing their fruit trees to keep bears away – not for the residents’ sake, but for the safety of the bears. Outdoor enthusiasts also worry about the effects of tourism and resource extraction on the mountains .

There are a pair of ridings in the region that have reliably voted NDP in recent decades. Kootenay-Monashee includes cities like Rossland, Trail and Castlegar, where environmentalists and the Ndp’s local candidate are opposing a proposed open-pit magnesium mine. The Kootenay Central riding has cities like Nelson and Creston, the latter of which skews conservative.

The NDP could hold onto these two ridings, especially Kootenay-Monashee, which is home to a large number of unionized jobs in Trail. But experts, and disgruntled NDP voters, believe there’s also a chance that the ridings could become a battleground, in which environmentally focused voters could shift to the Greens while other parts of the electorate vote Conservative in a bid for change after years of NDP rule.

Clare Kelly, a longtime resident in the Nelson area and lifelong NDP voter, said her whole family is considering voting Green this time around. That includes her son who has worked for the NDP in the past, but will be voting Green this month too.

Ms. Kelly says her local NDP candidate in Kootenay Central, Brittny Anderson, a two-term MLA who served as minister of state for local governments and rural communities before the election, presents as environmentally conscious in personal conversations, but her track record shows that she votes in line with the NDP on policies that are speeding up logging and limiting environmental oversight.

In the past, Ms. Kelly said she has voted strategically, choosing the NDP to ensure that a more conservative government wouldn’t be elected. Now, she feels like the party has left her no choice but to cast her vote elsewhere.

“I believe that we must have pluralism, it’s really important for Canadians to have more than a binary choice,” said Ms. Kelly.

“I would say the majority of our family feels like now is the time for action, we’re not interested in more studies or worrying about the economy, because there are economic benefits to conservation.”

The Globe made multiple requests to interview Ms. Anderson and Kootenay-Monashee NDP candidate Steve Morissette, but received unattributed written responses instead.

When asked about his government’s environmental track record during a meeting with The Globe’s editorial board last week, Mr. Eby said the West Kootenay region has always been concerned with the balance between forestry jobs and conservation, noting that increased forestry activity has led to more jobs at mills in the area.

He said liquid natural gas production in B.C. results in fewer emissions than some of the most efficient plants in the world, and said mines in the province are using electric power to lower their carbon footprint.

“These are hard conversations to have, they are nuanced, they are not easy, but they’re essential for the success of our province,” said Mr. Eby, adding that economic conditions are not what they were five years ago and his government’s priorities reflect new geopolitical realities for Canadians.

In some communities, even the most staunch activists have their reservations about not voting strategically for the NDP. Melanie Mercier has devoted years toward fighting a proposed open-pit magnesium mine just seven kilometres from the ski resort municipality of Rossland. Her candidacy for city council is based around opposing the project.

However, Ms. Mercier said she will vote NDP and is encouraging others to do so. Mr. Morissette, the NDP candidate in Ms. Mercier’s riding, has been an ally to her cause and has been on the record opposing the mine in local media. Ms. Mercier believes there’s no chance of the Greens being successful in a riding where there are so many unionized jobs, and said resuming the fight against the mine with a Conservative MLA in office would undo years of progress.

“For our riding, it feels like the only option,” said Ms. Mercier, who said she would vote Green elsewhere in the province.

Nicole Charlwood, the Green candidate for Kootenay Central, noted that she finished fewer than 2,000 votes shy of NDP candidate Ms. Anderson when she ran for the riding in 2020, receiving 32 per cent of the vote.

“There’s enough NDP dissatisfaction, whether it’s from inside the NDP or outside, that has folks from across party lines looking at my campaign,” said Ms. Charlwood when asked about people voting strategically for the incumbent government.

“People don’t like to be attached to parties here, and they know that I get an independent vote in the legislature and I’m not beholden to big union and big multinational corporations.”

Stewart Prest, a political science lecturer with the University of British Columbia, said the margins are tight enough that NDP losses in the West Kootenays are possible.

“The election call has tried the patience of voters everywhere, so even if you’re predisposed to align with the NDP on certain issues, there are frustrations here that will encourage every voter to think about whether they’re still committed to the project,” said Mr. Stewart.

“For anyone that’s looking to vote against the NDP, this election has given them reason to go in a different direction.”

However, Sanjay Jeram, a lecturer at Simon Fraser University, said that environmentalism is fading as a peak concern among the wider electorate, as people worry about Canada’s worsening relations with the U.S. That’s one reason why he suspects the status quo will prevail in the region.

For voters like Mr. Karthein, Mr. Eby’s lack of focus on the environment is why he has ultimately decided to stop voting strategically.

“I just know I couldn’t stomach voting for the NDP anymore,” said Mr. Karthein.

stories.title: Canadian housing policy wants you to live in shoebox condos in the middle of nowhere
stories.summary: Too often, governments measure the quality of housing by the number of units produced, rather than livability
stories.author: John Turley-Ewart
stories.content:
Jane Jacobs was wrong. So suggests the drift in government housing policy toward community-killing high-rises. The urbanist who fought for low-rise living in townhouses and apartment blocks didn’t believe livable communities existed high in the sky. Today’s decision-makers beg to differ.

Passé are eyes on the street, as is economically mixed and human-scaled density, defined by street-centric neighbourhoods where residents easily walk to local shops, entertainment, transit and civic spaces.

Tall sprawl is today’s preference, with vertical cities comprised of massive towers that house thousands and sit on podiums, circled by small patches of grass with a sprinkling of trees and the odd bench or two. Too often, governments measure the quality of housing by the number of units produced, rather than the livability of the communities being built.

The consequences, if governments are wrong and Ms. Jacobs proven right, will scar the Canadian housing landscape for generations.

For Ms. Jacobs, who passed in 2006, livable communities thrived on diversity: old buildings mixed with new ones; renters beside owners; singles, couples, families with children and seniors; and small builders alongside larger developers capable of more complex projects.

Her classic work, Death and Life of Great American Cities , is a community-building blueprint. Yet, the livable density it points to is too often ruled out by zoning restrictions, making towers the more viable option for developers tasked with building housing quickly and for many.

Ms. Jacob’s work didn’t suit the times when the economic reaction to the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 set off a housing boom.

Real interest rates reached historic lows, while condominium unit sizes continued to shrink in size, keeping booming prices per square foot in reach for first-time buyers and mom-and-pop investors.

That boom peaked in 2021 and began petering out in late 2022. In 2024, Toronto brought a record 25,572 condominium units to market, according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In Vancouver, that number was 12,442.

Developers chased profits and rushed completions to move on to their next towering project. Planning offices and the municipal officials behind them chased their version of profits, too – development charges.

In Toronto, those charges were more than $120,000 per condominium unit by 2025, according to a Cmhc report from last December.

No government took tall sprawl more to heart than Doug Ford’s in Ontario. It sees merit in extreme density. The Bridge Station project, located north of Toronto, is an example. It proposes 20,490 apartments, housing more than 43,000 people in towers as high as 80 storeys on just 63 acres of land.

Ontario has many more Bridge Stations in its housing plans.

Such projects are pitched as the future of communities, despite severing people from street-level sidewalks in skyscrapers jammed with small units unsuited to family life and community building.

They come with overcrowding, long waits for elevators, elevated amenity decks far from the street, and, if any, monoculture chain stores that are most capable of paying the high commercial rents demanded in new builds.

The boom in the condominium market burned itself out when interest rates rapidly rose in 2022 and sales slowed through 2023 and 2024.

Today, the consequences of the condominium bust are stark. Cancelled projects are common, new builds are almost non-existent, prices are materially lower for resales, and developers are converting tall-sprawl condominium plans to the new money-maker – purpose-built rentals.

In its Fall 2026 Housing Supply Report , the Cmhc notes that “purpose-built rental housing now accounts for two-thirds of all apartment starts in key markets.”

These projects are viable because of $55-billion in taxpayer-subsidized low-cost Cmhc loans with long amortization periods that make them profitable for developers. An Urbanation report from last October found that in the Greater Toronto Hamilton Area, 61 condominium projects had been converted to purpose-built rentals last year. More will follow.

Tall sprawl is finding a second coming in purpose-built rentals. It May be the housing that most Canadians turn to in the future. Cmhc says “the greater long-term risk” in the Canadian housing market is the “insufficient condominium and ground-oriented housing supply that leaves too few ownership options when demand strengthens again.”

Such construction has “weakened sharply in major cities, including Toronto, Vancouver, Ottawa and Montreal.” Using a 2.5 per cent annual inflation rate, the typical detached house in Toronto will cost about $1.6-million in 2036. In Vancouver, that price is likely to be roughly $2-million.

Squeeze supply, too, and the cost will be higher.

By favouring tall sprawl, purpose-built rentals over communities with a diverse mix of street-focused housing, planners and policy-makers are betting Ms. Jacobs’s warning about the dangers of vertical cities is bunk.

If they’re wrong, a decade from now, many Canadians will have few options beyond a unit in a tower they would rather leave than live in.

stories.title: Trump tariffs, trade war with Canada and Iran war driving up cost for U.S. manufacturers
stories.summary: Manufacturers in Ohio are becoming frustrated with Trump's tariffs, trade tensions with Canada and higher fuel costs due to the Iran war.
stories.author: AFP
stories.content:
For Doug Rende, who runs an aluminum product manufacturer in the state of Ohio, President Donald Trump’s tariffs have meant millions of dollars more in annual costs — and recently, the Iran war has made shipments even more expensive.

Rende is chief executive at Shapes Unlimited, one of many American producers smarting from Trump’s economic policies as midterm elections approach.

“Frustrating would be one word,” Rende told AFP.

“And I think that we’re sensing a lack of trust in not only the administration but the governmental process, the role of Congress to rein in executive power,” he added.

Since returning to the presidency in January 2025, Trump has wielded executive authority to slap tariffs on various products and countries.

Besides aluminum, the duties hit steel and autos too, while U.S. trading partners face additional tariffs that vary by country.

Even as some American manufacturers have benefited as their foreign competitors encounter higher barriers, others struggle with ballooning costs and persistent uncertainty.

Trump’s spiralling trade fight with Canada and war with Iran have only deepened worries.

Grievances over Trump’s trade policies are among fault lines that Democrats hope will work in their favour as they push to flip control of the Senate and House of Representatives in November’s vote.

Rende’s company in North Jackson, Ohio, makes and distributes aluminum building products used in fixtures like fences.

Trump’s tariffs on aluminum have steadily climbed, from 10 percent during his first presidency to 25 percent and then 50 percent last year, and Rende has felt the impact.

“This year alone, it’s upwards of US$4.5 million to $5 million in additional costs,” Rende said.

“There’s only so much that the end consumer is willing to eat,” he added. “So, we absorb a healthy portion.”

These added costs include steeper transportation fees, as fuel prices surged with the U.S.-Israel war on Iran. Surcharges are “upwards of $6,500 per container” of goods from suppliers, Rende said.

As a result, he has paused recruitment for new jobs while investing in more robotic assembly.

Sam Miller, another Ohio manufacturer who makes kitchen and bathroom products, has been hit on both fronts in Trump’s trade wars, paying tariffs on imported materials from Asia while finding it harder to expand into Canada because of trade tensions.

“It’s been difficult for businesses to manage,” Miller told AFP from his factory floor in Warren as a machine hummed nearby, cutting countertop material. “I do think that there will be a shift away from Republican views.”

Although Miller received refunds after the Supreme Court struck down many of Trump’s duties, the U.S. leader has since reinstated many of them.

Deteriorating U.S.-Canada ties add to his challenges, with Washington and Ottawa slapping tariffs on each other’s products after trade negotiations collapsed in August.

“We’re selling into Canada and it is particularly straining on both us and our customers,” Miller said.

He originally planned on opening a distribution facility in Canada this year, but progress has slowed.

Guy Coviello, president of the Youngstown Warren Regional Chamber, told AFP he is monitoring tariffs, the Iran war and immigration very closely.

These are a “mixed bag” for firms but negative overall, said Coviello, whose business group has some 3,000 members.

Some firms have lost customers or had to downsize, he said.

Canada is also Ohio’s biggest export market, with a third of Ohio’s exports going to the country.

“Where it gets even more complicated is that there are some goods that go back and forth across the border multiple times,” he said.

The Iran war adds to stresses, raising freight costs and hitting aluminum supplies due to drone attacks in the Middle East.

With a lack of new U.S.aluminum smelters, Coviello said: “We are all for tariffs for critical items such as defense and medical industry.”

But he added: “We have to be careful when you’re talking about products that are not crucial and are not available in the U.S.”

stories.title: Backstreet Boys extend Toronto residency to 11 nights
stories.summary: Toronto - Hit '90s boyband The Backstreet Boys are adding more tour dates to their Toronto residency.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
What was first announced as a four-night run at Rogers Centre has swelled to 11 shows, with the band’s recent announcement they’re adding concerts on March 5 and 6.

The band says on its website the new dates were added “due to overwhelming demand.”

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Dubbed “Into the Millennium – Homecoming: Live in Canada,” the residency will kick off on Feb. 12.

Apart from two shows scheduled at Las Vegas’ Sphere venue, the 11 performances in Toronto are the band’s only shows in 2027.

The concerts will draw on the group’s 1999 album “Millennium,” which included hits such as “I Want It That Way” and “Everybody (Backstreet’s Back).”

“You guys have blown through these tickets and we truly didn’t know the demand would be This BIG so we are adding TWO More Shows on March 5th & 6th so as many of you as possible can experience ‘Into the Millennium - Homecoming: Live in Canada’ with us!” a post on the band’s Facebook page said.

“Can’t wait to see you all there!!”

The Backstreet Boys and Canada have a history: the band had their first North American breakthrough in Canada — with 1995’s “We’ve Got It Goin’ On” — before conquering the United States.

Their music holds a nostalgic pull for Canadian millennials. Evidently even Drake, who joined the group onstage during their last concert in Toronto in 2022.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct 11, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Carney says U.S.-Russia diesel supply deal hurts Ukraine peace cause: PMO
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy today about U.S. President Donald Trump’s new diesel fuel supply agreement with Russia.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy today about U.S. President Donald Trump’s new diesel fuel supply agreement with Russia.

The Prime Minister’s Office says the two leaders discussed the new agreement for Russia to supply millions of tonnes of diesel fuel to the United States, which Trump announced on Friday.

The PMO says Carney made clear this agreement runs against the efforts of Canada and its allies to end the war in Europe by providing Russia with new revenue.

A readout from the office says the two leaders talked about increasing coordination with allies to help Ukraine with its air defence needs.

Trump posted on social media on Sunday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an “energy ceasefire,” which appeared to be news to Zelenskyy.

Zelenskyy said on social media that he supports Trump’s “energy ceasefire” but he is awaiting details from the White House, and that Russia must back it up by ending its strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 11, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: I planted vegetables, but my greatest crop was connection
stories.summary: Amid wars, climate disasters and rollbacks of human rights, a small community garden brought people together, turning a parking lot into so much more
stories.author: Jennifer Knoch
stories.content:
First Person is a daily personal piece submitted by readers. Have a story to tell? See our guidelines at tgam.CA/essayguide .

I despair often about the world. It’s tempting to give up and retreat into endless seasons of The Great British Baking Show . Instead, this spring, amidst the swirl of wars, climate disasters and rollbacks of human rights, I started a small community garden.

My grocery co-op agreed to host it and provide water; a soil company donated soil; I bought planters at a discount with a microcommunity grant. Seeds and seedlings flowed from local urban agriculture groups. The food would go to a community fridge, hosted by a church and maintained by volunteers.

When the day came to install the garden, I had a new sorrow: I had just said goodbye to my beloved cat of almost 15 years. My brain was like a radio stuck between stations. But my grief got quieter as Paul Simon and the Beatles played on my portable speaker, the spring sunlight poured into the parking lot and co-op volunteers assembled the beds and filled them with soil. A kid carefully pressed radish seeds into the soil, and even in my season of mourning, new life began.

The gardens, about 60 square feet of raised beds in a parking lot, sit by the store’s entrance, and I water, prune and harvest twice a week. Listening to a podcast while I do is tempting, but I deliberately avoid earbuds, staying open like a flower inviting pollination.

And so strangers have told me about plants from their childhoods, about their own garden successes and failures. (I could have hung a shingle like Lucy in Peanuts : “Horticultural Help, 5 cents. The doctor is in.”) Parents stopped by with children, and the garden became a living picture book: vegetables from amaranth to zucchini.

The zucchini grew into a monster, each leaf as big as a steering wheel. It would have stretched five feet tall if it hadn’t bent under the weight of its own fecundity.

Of course, there have been some setbacks. One bed was the victim of a hit and run, and now its side is crumpled like an aluminum can. (However, it still grew almost two pounds of beautiful fingerling potatoes.) Come August, aphids coated the kale and started to pepper the tumbling nasturtiums. I was spraying them off fiercely with a hose when a shopper said quietly, “The garden is so beautiful. Someone should paint it.” I saw the aphids. She saw the fuller picture.

One woman had just gotten a community plot after many years of not gardening. “It’s the most healing thing,” she said. “Plants are like children, you’re just tending, tending, tending. They’re so fragile and also so strong.” My grief had mostly receded by then, thanks in part to that tending.

The garden had other unexpected yields. One day, I was tying up the tomatoes when a woman stopped and asked about pruning. I explained the basics, but she still seemed perplexed. “Can I pay you to come prune mine?” she asked. “I live next door.”

“Oh, I’m sure you can do it!” I reassured her.

A few minutes later, the woman came back. “Really, I could pay cash. It would make me feel so much better. Maybe you could come take a look some time?”

“Okay,” I said, “I’ll come look now, and how about you put a couple things in the Community Fridges donation bin in the co-op some time.”

We went into her yard, and the tomatoes had vined wildly, limbs a tangled snarl and flopped over their cages. We chatted amicably as we tried to tame them. At the end she invited me to stop by any time and presented me with a jar of Indian chutney, which I gladly took home.

When I arrived at the co-op later that week, a staff member said, “Someone left a whole bin of stuff in the cooler for you.” I almost teared up seeing the crate of canned goods, organic fruits and veggies and bread. It was like we’d planted a zucchini of generosity.

The conversations continued away from the garden. I bike the harvest over to the community fridge, where one or two regulars are often waiting. In a world where food bank use climbs year over year, fresh food can be a luxury. “I left the basil in water and it made the whole kitchen smell good,” said one shopper. Another taught me how to know when the cherry bomb hot peppers were ripe: “It’s not the colour; it’s the smell.”

By the end of August I had harvested about $600 in organic, hyperlocal produce from our small veggie patch for our neighbours in need. We created, too, something for people to talk about, a point of connection in our often isolating world. As a fixture at the garden, I gained even more: solace in grief, hope under yellow wildfire skies and conversations I didn’t know I needed. The community came together to turn a parking lot into so much more.

The co-op, by the way, is called Karma, and garden was karma in action: We literally reaped what we sowed, yes, but so much of the harvest couldn’t be weighed on a scale. Farmers feed cities, as the bumper stickers say, but public gardens can provide a whole other form of nourishment.

Jennifer Knoch lives in Toronto.

(However, it still grew almost two pounds of beautiful fingerling potatoes.) Come August, aphids coated the kale and started to pepper the tumbling nasturtiums. I was spraying them off fiercely with a hose when a shopper said quietly, “The garden is so beautiful. Someone should paint it.” I saw the aphids. She saw the fuller picture.

One woman had just gotten a community plot after many years of not gardening. “It’s the most healing thing,” she said. “Plants are like children, you’re just tending, tending, tending. They’re so fragile and also so strong.” My grief had mostly receded by then, thanks in part to that tending.

The garden had other unexpected yields. One day, I was tying up the tomatoes when a woman stopped and asked about pruning. I explained the basics, but she still seemed perplexed. “Can I pay you to come prune mine?” she asked. “I live next door.”
“Oh, I’m sure you can do it!” I reassured her.
A few minutes later, the woman came back. “Really, I could pay cash. It would make me feel so much better. Maybe you could come take a look some time?”
“Okay,” I said, “I’ll come look now, and how about you put a couple things in the Community Fridges donation bin in the co-op some time.”

We went into her yard, and the tomatoes had vined wildly, limbs a tangled snarl and flopped over their cages. We chatted amicably as we tried to tame them. At the end she invited me to stop by any time and presented me with a jar of Indian chutney, which I gladly took home.

When I arrived at the co-op later that week, a staff member said, “Someone left a whole bin of stuff in the cooler for you.” I almost teared up seeing the crate of canned goods, organic fruits and veggies and bread. It was like we’d planted a zucchini of generosity.

The conversations continued away from the garden. I bike the harvest over to the community fridge, where one or two regulars are often waiting. In a world where food bank use climbs year over year, fresh food can be a luxury. “I left the basil in water and it made the whole kitchen smell good,” said one shopper. Another taught me how to know when the cherry bomb hot peppers were ripe: “It’s not the colour; it’s the smell.”

By the end of August I had harvested about $600 in organic, hyperlocal produce from our small veggie patch for our neighbours in need. We created, too, something for people to talk about, a point of connection in our often isolating world. As a fixture at the garden, I gained even more: solace in grief, hope under yellow wildfire skies and conversations I didn’t know I needed. The community came together to turn a parking lot into so much more.

The co-op, by the way, is called Karma, and garden was karma in action: We literally reaped what we sowed, yes, but so much of the harvest couldn’t be weighed on a scale. Farmers feed cities, as the bumper stickers say, but public gardens can provide a whole other form of nourishment.
Jennifer Knoch lives in Toronto.

stories.title: Ontario police warn public as repeat sex offender released again
stories.summary: A man convicted of sexually assault a seven-year-old boy, a blind woman and an epileptic woman has been released to live in the Durham region.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
For the third straight year, an Ontario police force is warning about the release of the same high-risk sex offender with several past convictions for sexual assaults against a child and women dating back almost 20 years.

The Durham Regional Police Service (Drps) has issued a safety alert that 48-year-old Keith Theodore Constantin, “who poses a significant risk to the community, especially children,” will be living at an undisclosed location in the region effective Sunday.

Constantin is “subject to electronic monitoring” 24-hours daily, but Drps said in a Saturday news release that its offender management unit will also keep tabs on his “whereabouts and activities.”

The Hamilton native was in custody after being arrested last March for breaching the conditions of his release in the Oshawa area after just two days of freedom, according to Drps .

The police service also warned of his release in May of 2024, as reported by the Toronto Sun .

It’s not immediately clear what Constantin had been imprisoned for at the time. National Post has contacted the Parole Board of Canada for more information about his release.

Drps warned that Constantin has a history of sexual assault with a weapon, robbery, possession of explosives and uttering threats, among other crimes.

His first serious convictions came in 2000 when he was sentenced for two armed robberies and two sexual assaults — one against a seven-year-old boy he’d lured to a park and another on a 45-year-old blind woman who lived in the same building as him.

It’s not clear how much time he served, but he was free in fall 2007, as he was later convicted of sexually assaulting an epileptic woman in the basement apartment of his parents’ home as she was recovering from a seizure that September, according to a 2014 story in The Hamilton Spectator .

He said “Shut up, or I will kill you,” when she screamed for help, CBC reported.

He never went to trial because the stress induced seizures and fears of suicide in his 27-year-old victim. Instead, he made a plea deal in 2009, was sentenced to eight years and received four years’ credit for time served. It also earned him a spot on the national sex-offender registry for life.

His 2014 release was met with considerable pushback in the Hamilton neighbourhoods where he was set to reside when York Regional Police (YRP) warned of it, National Post reported , leading him to break curfew and ask to be imprisoned again. YRP issued another warning in December 2015 when he was released again after serving 18 months for the curfew breach.

During a 2014 court hearing, Constantin said he’d begun taking a chemical castration drug, The Spectator reported, and that he is no longer a serious risk to the community.

“When I was younger I did mess up a lot, I did screw up, and I think I paid the price for it. But I do understand the seriousness of it, I do understand what I’ve done,” he said, adding that he would have his genitalia “surgically removed” to prove it if he could afford to do so.

“I know in my heart and my mind that I’d never do it again,” he said.

The Parole Board of Canada felt different at the time, according to a decision obtained by The Spectator, which highlighted Constantin’s own “urges of reoffending against children and young women and that (he) has thoughts of killing.”

The documents indicate diagnoses of alcohol and drug addiction, paranoid schizophrenia, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, depression, an “extremely low range of intellectual ability,” and “character features associated with psychopathy.”

He was also a problematic inmate who threw urine and feces at correctional officers, threatened suicide with a razor blade and ignored personal hygiene. His behaviour led him to spend time in maximum security facilities and in segregation, led to the suspension of mental health supports, and got him kicked out of prison programs.

Oshawa Mayor Dan Carter issued a press release thanking the Drps for “proactively informing the public and for its continued efforts to monitor high-risk offenders.”

Carter said residents are right to be concerned and that he supports provincial and federal work “to strengthen bail and sentencing laws, particularly for repeat and violent offenders and those convicted of serious crimes.

“These reforms are vital to enhancing public safety and ensuring that justice is served fairly and effectively.

Drps said Constantin is bound by multiple conditions as part of his high-risk release peace bond under the Criminal Code of Canada.

He must report to them weekly and abide by a 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. curfew, less lenient than the 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. curfew applied when added to the RCMP’s high-risk child sex offender database at age 45.

He’s not allowed to “associate or communicate” with kids under 16, nor “engage in any activities that involve contact with anyone under” that age. He’s also forbidden from being near daycares, swimming areas, school grounds, playgrounds or any community centre where children under 16 are present. He can go to public places where children under 16 May be, but only when accompanied by someone 21 or older.

He’s not allowed to possess, purchase or consume any alcohol, drugs, narcotics or controlled substances. Nor can he use “the internet or other digital networks” or possess a device that can go online.

He’s prohibited from associating with criminals or people with a record, can’t own or possess weapons and cannot be in a relationship with a parent of a child under 16.

“Police are asking the public to stay vigilant and remain aware of their surroundings,” Drps wrote. “Any suspicious or dangerous behaviour should be reported directly to the police.”

content_blocks.text: He never went to trial because the stress induced seizures and fears of suicide in his 27-year-old victim. Instead, he made a plea deal in 2009, was sentenced to eight years and received four years’ credit for time served. It also earned him a spot on the national sex-offender registry for life.

His 2014 release was met with considerable pushback in the Hamilton neighbourhoods where he was set to reside when York Regional Police (YRP) warned of it, National Post reported , leading him to break curfew and ask to be imprisoned again. YRP issued another warning in December 2015 when he was released again after serving 18 months for the curfew breach.

content_blocks.text: During a 2014 court hearing, Constantin said he’d begun taking a chemical castration drug, The Spectator reported, and that he is no longer a serious risk to the community.

“When I was younger I did mess up a lot, I did screw up, and I think I paid the price for it. But I do understand the seriousness of it, I do understand what I’ve done,” he said, adding that he would have his genitalia “surgically removed” to prove it if he could afford to do so.
“I know in my heart and my mind that I’d never do it again,” he said.

The Parole Board of Canada felt different at the time, according to a decision obtained by The Spectator, which highlighted Constantin’s own “urges of reoffending against children and young women and that (he) has thoughts of killing.”

He was also a problematic inmate who threw urine and feces at correctional officers, threatened suicide with a razor blade and ignored personal hygiene. His behaviour led him to spend time in maximum security facilities and in segregation, led to the suspension of mental health supports, and got him kicked out of prison programs.

“These reforms are vital to enhancing public safety and ensuring that justice is served fairly and effectively.
Drps said Constantin is bound by multiple conditions as part of his high-risk release peace bond under the Criminal Code of Canada.
He must report to them weekly and abide by a 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. curfew, less lenient than the 6 a.m. to 11 p.m. curfew applied when added to the RCMP’s high-risk child sex offender database at age 45.

He’s also forbidden from being near daycares, swimming areas, school grounds, playgrounds or any community centre where children under 16 are present. He can go to public places where children under 16 May be, but only when accompanied by someone 21 or older.

He’s not allowed to possess, purchase or consume any alcohol, drugs, narcotics or controlled substances. Nor can he use “the internet or other digital networks” or possess a device that can go online.
He’s prohibited from associating with criminals or people with a record, can’t own or possess weapons and cannot be in a relationship with a parent of a child under 16.
“Police are asking the public to stay vigilant and remain aware of their surroundings,” Drps wrote. “Any suspicious or dangerous behaviour should be reported directly to the police.”

stories.title: Could an indoor sports dome be coming to St. Thomas?
stories.summary: St. Thomas City Council is being asked to approve an application for provincial funding with the hopes of eventually bringing a massive sports dome to the city.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
St. Thomas City Council is being asked to approve an application for provincial funding with the hopes of eventually bringing a massive sports dome to the city.

There are two proposed concepts; but the preferred facility would include two small indoor turf fields, convertible court space which could be used for basketball, pickleball and volleyball, a walking track and a support building.

The projected cost is $14 million but is estimated to turn a profit as high as $160,000 per year.

On Tuesday’s agenda, city staff are asking for the endorsement of a submission of a Community Sport and Recreation Infrastructure Fund (Csrif) application.

Should council endorse the application, they would retain Baker Turner Inc. as Prime Consultant to undertake an Implementation Study for the proposed facility at a cost of approximately $91,000.

The site would require 2.5 to 3.0 hectares of land and the study would determine whether the preferred concept could fit on the land on the north side of Fire Station No. 2 on Silver Street next to the existing soccer complex at 1 Password Park.

In the report to council, Adrienne Lacey Griffin, director of Parks and Recreation details how “The City of St. Thomas is positioned to experience and capitalize on significant residential and economic growth over the coming decades and continues to invest in recreation infrastructure that supports a healthy, active and complete community.”

A feasibility report to council March 9, 2026 identified two priority recreation projects including a future community centre; an aquatic centre and an indoor sports dome.That study identified the city would require approximately 2.3 additional indoor turf fields by 2051 and identified an Indoor Sports Dome as a priority project to address the community’s need for year-round indoor field sport opportunities.

Applications for the Csrif are due December 22, 2026 and municipalities can apply for funding of up to 50 per cent of eligible project costs to a maximum provincial contribution of $10 million.

While they are asking for an endorsement of the Indoor Sports Dome, they are not currently applying for help with a Community and Aquatic Centre.

“Unlike the Indoor Sports Dome proposal, a preferred site has not been identified or secured, and the Council approved feasibility study noted that no municipally owned lands are currently available to accommodate the recommended program,” wrote Griffin.

“Given these constraints and the ongoing evaluation of alternative facility models, staff believe a Community and Aquatic Centre application is not sufficiently advanced to support a competitive Csrif submission during the current intake.”

stories.title: GM recalls more trucks over side curtain airbag risk
stories.summary: General Motors is recalling 126 Chevrolet and GMC trucks in Canada because defective side curtain airbag inflators could deploy without a crash. The recall follows a similar campaign earlier this year, while a related U.S. recall affects thousands of trucks.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
General Motors is recalling 126 Chevrolet and GMC trucks in Canada because defective side curtain airbag inflators could deploy without a crash, potentially sending metal fragments toward occupants.

An updated Transport Canada recall says the issue affects certain 2016 Chevrolet Silverado, Silverado HD, GMC Sierra and Sierra HD trucks.

The defect could cause the driver or passenger-side curtain airbags to deploy unexpectedly. If an inflator ruptures, its components could be propelled into the vehicle, creating a risk of injury.

GM will notify affected owners by mail and instruct them to take their trucks to a dealership to have both side curtain airbag modules replaced.

The latest campaign follows a similar recall issued in May which covered 357 trucks from the 2018 and 2019 model years and was identified as an expansion of an earlier recall in March. Both involved potentially defective side curtain airbag inflators that could deploy without a crash.

General Motors also issued an airbag-related recall in the United States in September. The U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration identified 1,559 potentially affected vehicles, including certain 2016 Chevrolet Silverado and GMC Sierra heavy-duty trucks, as well as 2016-2017 Silverado and Sierra 1500 models.

Owners can check whether their vehicles are affected by entering their vehicle identification (VIN) number.⁠

Customers south of the border can use the U.S. National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s VIN recall lookup tool ⁠.

stories.title: Canada advises no travel to Riyadh airport after Houthi attacks, embassy remains open
stories.summary: Canada’s ambassador to Saudi Arabia says the embassy in Riyadh remains open for Canadians who are in need of consular assistance, following deadly Houthi strikes against the international airport in Riyadh.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada’s ambassador to Saudi Arabia says the embassy in Riyadh remains open for Canadians who are in need of consular assistance, following deadly Houthi strikes against the international airport in Riyadh.

Ambassador Jean-Philippe Linteau says in a video posted on Sunday that anyone in Riyadh who encounters military debris should walk away and contact authorities, and not post about it on social media.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting Houthi rebels in Yemen says another projectile hit a passenger terminal at the Riyadh airport on Sunday, which comes a day after a missile attack on the same terminal killed 12 people and injured hundreds.

Canada has issued a travel advisory to avoid all non-essential travel to Saudi Arabia, and to avoid all travel to the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

Prime Minister Mark Carney condemned the violence late Saturday night, calling the Houthis’ attacks on civilian infrastructure “abhorrent” and unjustified.

Carney also expressed condolences to the families of those who were killed in the attack.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 11, 2026.

-- With files from The Associated Press

stories.title: Ottawa food bank holds donation drive to meet ‘never seen before’ demand
stories.summary: While many students were enjoying a sunny start to the long weekend in Ottawa, 14-year-old Liam MacInnis decided to spend his Saturday helping others.
stories.author: Michael Serapio
stories.content:
While many students were enjoying a sunny start to the long weekend in Ottawa, 14-year-old Liam MacInnis decided to spend his Saturday helping others.

He headed to a local grocery store with his mother to volunteer his time collecting donations for the Ottawa Food Bank.

“People struggle, so it’s important to have food banks out there,” he said.

Like food banks across the country, the Ottawa Food Bank held a food drive this weekend, hoping to stock its shelves and raise awareness about the growing need for food assistance.

At a Metro store in the Ottawa suburb of Orleans, MacInnis and other volunteers collected non-perishable food items as the organization grappled with unprecedented demand.

“Unfortunately for us, our growth right now is unprecedented. We haven’t seen this level of need in the city,” said Natalie Spooner, Chief Executive Officer of the Ottawa Food Bank.

“In the last year alone,” she said, “we’ve seen 588,000 visits. That’s something we’ve never seen before. And so, when we’re responding to that need, it is very challenging to be able to keep those donations high, to be able to meet that need.”

Food Banks Canada says in 2025 (the last year for which data is available), food banks across the country saw nearly 2.2 million visits each month.

That is double the monthly usage recorded six years ago.

A troubling trend for the organization, because it took decades for food banks to reach a million monthly visits, but little more than half a decade to double it.

But numbers only tell a part of the story. The people behind them also paint a fuller picture.

In 2025, Food Banks Canada said 40 per cent of their visitors were people on social assistance or disability supports. Thirty-three per cent were children, while 19 per cent of food bank clients were people who had jobs but still couldn’t make ends meet.

“The reality of the economy for some people is that affordability is a crisis,” said Michael Von Massow, Food Economist with the University of Guelph.

“And it’s not just food prices that have gone up. We know gasoline prices are up, and there aren’t very many gasoline banks or transit banks. So where people go is to food banks to try and bridge the gap.”

Spooner added that food insecurity doesn’t come out of nowhere. Oftentimes, it is the result of many other challenges a person is facing in their life.

“If you’re struggling to afford food, it’s because you have to make very tough choices already,” she said. “You choose medication, or choose to pay your rent, or choose to turn the lights on, or pay those bills. Unfortunately, food is the last thing that they would have to afford.”

The federal government has introduced measures in an effort to address the affordability challenge.

Those include a middle-class income tax cut, the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefits, and the temporary suspension of the federal fuel excise tax.

But Food Banks Canada wants more.

The organization’s call to action includes reforms to Employment Insurance (EI), increases to the Canada Workers Benefit and disability benefits, and more investments into affordable housing.

Priorities echoed by many in the fight against hunger in Canada, including Neil Heatherington, the Chief Executive Officer of Toronto’s Daily Bread Food Bank.

“We are hopeful that Canadians see the need, respond to the need, donate to their local food bank,” he said. “And at the same time, (that) all the elected officials this Thanksgiving reflect on what a Canada can be without food insecurity.”

Frontline workers also know things don’t look promising in the near future, with unemployment rising, and the price of diesel affecting the price of food and every aspect of the supply chain.

“Right now, we’re starting to get out of the Canadian harvest season and we’re getting into the time that we import,” said Von Massow. “So as freight prices go up and the distances that things are being shipped increases, we’re sort of confident that we’re going to see price increases over the course of this winter.”

A reality that will put more pressure on Canadians already struggling to get food onto their tables, and pressure on organizations like the Ottawa Food Bank, as it tries to stock its shelves to meet the demand of the next few months.

For now, food banks are counting on Canadians to remember their neighbours this Thanksgiving weekend, much like a 14-year-old boy who decided to do what he could to fight hunger in his community.

“In the last year alone,” she said, “we’ve seen 588,000 visits. That’s something we’ve never seen before. And so, when we’re responding to that need, it is very challenging to be able to keep those donations high, to be able to meet that need.”
Food Banks Canada says in 2025 (the last year for which data is available), food banks across the country saw nearly 2.2 million visits each month.
That is double the monthly usage recorded six years ago.
A troubling trend for the organization, because it took decades for food banks to reach a million monthly visits, but little more than half a decade to double it.

content_blocks.alt: Ottawa food drive
content_blocks.caption: Ottawa Food Bank. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: But numbers only tell a part of the story. The people behind them also paint a fuller picture.

In 2025, Food Banks Canada said 40 per cent of their visitors were people on social assistance or disability supports. Thirty-three per cent were children, while 19 per cent of food bank clients were people who had jobs but still couldn’t make ends meet.
“The reality of the economy for some people is that affordability is a crisis,” said Michael Von Massow, Food Economist with the University of Guelph.

“And it’s not just food prices that have gone up. We know gasoline prices are up, and there aren’t very many gasoline banks or transit banks. So where people go is to food banks to try and bridge the gap.”

content_blocks.alt: Ottawa food drive
content_blocks.caption: Ottawa Food Bank. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: Spooner added that food insecurity doesn’t come out of nowhere. Oftentimes, it is the result of many other challenges a person is facing in their life.

“If you’re struggling to afford food, it’s because you have to make very tough choices already,” she said. “You choose medication, or choose to pay your rent, or choose to turn the lights on, or pay those bills. Unfortunately, food is the last thing that they would have to afford.”
The federal government has introduced measures in an effort to address the affordability challenge.
Those include a middle-class income tax cut, the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefits, and the temporary suspension of the federal fuel excise tax.
But Food Banks Canada wants more.

content_blocks.alt: Ottawa food drive
content_blocks.caption: Ottawa Food Bank. (CTV News)

content_blocks.text: The organization’s call to action includes reforms to Employment Insurance (EI), increases to the Canada Workers Benefit and disability benefits, and more investments into affordable housing.
Priorities echoed by many in the fight against hunger in Canada, including Neil Heatherington, the Chief Executive Officer of Toronto’s Daily Bread Food Bank.

“We are hopeful that Canadians see the need, respond to the need, donate to their local food bank,” he said. “And at the same time, (that) all the elected officials this Thanksgiving reflect on what a Canada can be without food insecurity.”
Frontline workers also know things don’t look promising in the near future, with unemployment rising, and the price of diesel affecting the price of food and every aspect of the supply chain.

“Right now, we’re starting to get out of the Canadian harvest season and we’re getting into the time that we import,” said Von Massow. “So as freight prices go up and the distances that things are being shipped increases, we’re sort of confident that we’re going to see price increases over the course of this winter.”

A reality that will put more pressure on Canadians already struggling to get food onto their tables, and pressure on organizations like the Ottawa Food Bank, as it tries to stock its shelves to meet the demand of the next few months.
For now, food banks are counting on Canadians to remember their neighbours this Thanksgiving weekend, much like a 14-year-old boy who decided to do what he could to fight hunger in his community.

stories.title: Sunday sports notes: OUA football and hockey, U15 national soccer, OFC football
stories.summary: Quarterback Ben Casselman made the most of his first career OUA football start by throwing 3 touchdowns and 177 yards in a 49-7 Western Mustangs romp over Carleton.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Quarterback Ben Casselman made the most of his first career OUA football start by throwing 3 touchdowns and 177 yards in a 49-7 Western Mustangs romp over Carleton.

The Mustangs travelled to Ottawa and ran all over the Ravens to the tune of 384 yards and with a Queen’s Gaels loss to Windsor, they joined McMaster and Queen’s in a three-way tie for top spot in the league at 5-1.

Casselman got the start after Jerome Rancourt threw six interceptions in his previous two games and Faulds told media after the game that he’s going to stick with him next week against the Ottawa Gee Gees.

“Ben’s first start as a U Sports quarterback, it was good to see he was very efficient, didn’t show any signs of nerves, spread the ball around, we really leaned on our run game, especially when the score kind of dictated that, a lot of different guys getting carries, close to 400 yards of rushing,” said Faulds.

On the ground, running back Ethan Dolby had 140 yards and a touchdown on 12 carries. Western returned home, only to have to head right back to Ottawa next weekend.

Clarke singer wins 500th oua hockey game at Western

Western Mustangs head coach Clarke Singer has been behind the bench at Thompson Arena dating back to 1999.

That longevity and success was celebrated Saturday when he won his 500th career game in a 7-2 victory over Waterloo.

“Most importantly I was happy we got a win tonight and got a split of the opening weekend, I think our guys played hard in all areas and I was proud of them for that,” Singer told WesternMustangs.CA

After the win, he was doused with water and was drenched by the players emptying the water cooler on the legend.

“They say there are 10 things in life you always remember: the day you got married, the day your children were born are some of those for sure, but I think, based on the post-game reaction tonight, this will definitely be one of those occasions for sure.”

London alliance fc undefeated at u15 national soccer championships

Lafc has cruised through their first three games at the tournament in Surrey, BC with 3-0, 1-0 and 6-0 victories to reach the semi-finals.

Should Lafc win against Edmonton at 3:30 p.m. EDT they will advance to Monday’s final.

Lead by Elena Adamou – who has signed with AFC Toronto Academy- these girls have won five consecutive Ontario Cup titles including the most recent outdoor event which earned them the right to represent Ontario.

London beefeaters beat saints in overtime to advance to ofc final

The London Beefeaters have advanced to the OFC Football final after a dramatic win on the road over the Saint Clair Saints.

Trailing by seven on the final play of regulation, Jason Leonard caught a touchdown pass on third and goal to send the game to overtime tied at 19.

London had the ball first and Xavier Zatylny rolled out of the pocket and found Brandon Visouvath for the score to put the Beefeaters up 26-19.

When the Saints got the ball for their chance, defensive lineman Noah Williams came up with a huge sack to force one last long pass attempt for the tie.

The throw bounced off the hands of receiver Nate Carter and London came away with the victory.

The Beefeaters will now travel to Sault Ste. Marie to face the undefeated Sault College Cougars.

stories.title: Roblox side hustle helped this 25-year-old buy a five-bedroom home in Windsor
stories.summary: Starting with just $10, Aziz’s teenage hobby grew into a lucrative side business that sped up his path to homeownership
stories.author: Zahra Khozema
stories.content:
When Aziz was 15, he discovered he could make money reselling virtual hats, clothes and other collectibles on the online gaming platform Roblox.

Starting with just $10 and his mother’s PayPal account, his teenage hobby grew into a lucrative side business that sped up his path to homeownership.

Now 25, Aziz owns a five-bedroom detached house in the Southern Ontario city of Windsor. He bought the property on his own in July for $710,000, putting down $71,000.

Today, he earns around $100,000 annually working in public service. His salary, combined with his early Roblox earnings, investments and the money he’s saved while living with his parents, helped him become a homeowner well before most Canadians can afford to buy.

The journey began around 2016, when Aziz noticed that Roblox sold some virtual items, such as hats and other accessories for players’ avatars, in limited quantities. Players bought them using Robux, the platform’s virtual currency, but once an item sold out, the only way to get it was from another player. When he realized that some players were willing to pay real money for those digital collectibles through unofficial marketplaces, he began buying and reselling items.

Aziz estimates making roughly $1,000 during his first six months, but by 2017 and 2018, he was earning around $40,000 to $50,000 annually. He continued until 2022, when increased competition made the business less profitable.

“I think at the beginning I probably wasted a lot,” he said. “When you’re 16 and can’t open a TFSA or an investment account until you’re 18, and you have a bunch of money coming in suddenly, then you really don’t know what to do with it.”

In high school, he spent it on the latest iPhones and designer clothes. He also paid for his everyday expenses and a chunk of his tuition. It wasn’t until university that he began seriously considering saving for something like a home.

Aziz grew up in the Greater Toronto Area before the family moved to Windsor when he started university. The move to a less-expensive city allowed him to consider buying a home at a price he believes would have been out of reach in the GTA.

Although Aziz contributes to his family’s home expenses, he pays less than he would living independently and saves on groceries, utilities and car insurance. If he’d moved out, saving would have taken much longer, he said.

Still, it took Aziz almost two years to assemble his down payment. He maximized his RRSP contributions and added to his first home savings account for three years, investing mostly in index funds.

His RRSP grew from $55,000 to almost $64,000. He withdrew $60,000 through the Home Buyer’s Plan, along with $25,000 from his FHSA. Together, this covered the down payment and closing costs without having to touch his TFSA.

Although he initially planned to buy a less expensive property, Aziz believed his five-bedroom home was worth stretching his budget. He likes the possibility of accommodating a future family or renting out the place if things change.

For his mortgage, Aziz compared offers from a bank and mortgage broker. After receiving a competitive offer from a big bank, he asked his broker to keep looking for something better. The broker eventually found a credit union offering a variable rate of 3.45 per cent.

He chose a 30-year amortization, which keeps his monthly payments just under $3,000. He hopes to make additional payments and shorten that period.

The house still needs some updates and furnishings, including a new water heater, flooring, fresh paint and work on the deck, so Aziz is still living in his parents’ house. He plans to move in to his own home by the end of October and live there for at least five to 10 years.

Purchase price: $710,000

Down payment: $71,000 (10 per cent)

Home inspection: About $600

Legal fees: $2,000

Land transfer tax: around $2,700 after rebate

Repairs: $10,000 to $15,000 budgeted for renovations and furniture

Monthly costs

Mortgage: Under $3,000

Home insurance: $120

Utilities: No bills received yet

Property taxes: Around $500

Advice: Look beyond discouraging housing headlines and examine your own finances, savings potential and the programs available. “You just have to realistically check how much income [you] have. How much can [you] save per month?” he said.

stories.title: Armed robbery investigated at Oneida Nation of the Thames First Nation
stories.summary: Police officers are investigating reports of an armed robbery at a business in Oneida Nation of the Thames First Nation.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
Police officers are investigating reports of an armed robbery at a business in Oneida Nation of the Thames First Nation.

On Sunday at 3:06 a.m., members of the Oneida Nation Police and Middlesex County OPP were called to a business at 6201 Bodkin Road in Oneida Nation of the Thames First Nation for the report of a disturbance.

Investigation revealed four unknown individuals wearing dark clothing and masks entered the business demanding items. Police say a firearm was seen and reportedly discharged before the suspects left in a vehicle.

Members of the Middlesex County Crime Unit are assisting with the investigation.

There were no injuries reported.

The Middlesex County OPP and Oneida Nation Police can be reached, anytime, anywhere in the province of Ontario at 1-888-310-1122.

If you wish to remain anonymous you can contact Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477 (Tips) where you May be eligible for a cash reward of up to $2000.

stories.summary: It might be a good idea to bring an umbrella for London area residents doing anyth8ing outside today, according to the rainy Environment Canada forecast.
stories.author: Melanie Kentner
stories.content:
It might be a good idea to bring an umbrella for London area residents doing anyth8ing outside today, according to the rainy Environment Canada forecast.

Sunday is expected to bring periods of rain. Southeast winds will continue at 20 km/h gusting to 40 km/h, with a high temperature of 17C and a low UV index of 1. Sunday night will be cloudy with a 40 per cent chance of showers and a low of 13C.

Thanksgiving Monday is expected to be cloudy with a high of 22C. Monday night will remain cloudy with a 40 per cent chance of showers and a low of 11C.

On Tuesday, expect cloudy skies with a 40 per cent chance of showers and a high of 18C. Tuesday night will feature cloudy periods with a 30 per cent chance of showers and a low of 7C.

Thursday will be cloudy with a 40 per cent chance of showers and a high of 17C. Thursday night will also be cloudy with a 40 percent chance of showers and a low of 9C.

Friday will be cloudy with a high of 14C.

stories.title: Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week
stories.summary: Business
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week:

Shareholders of Roots Corp. will vote on Tuesday on a deal that will see the retailer taken private by Marquee Brands, the firm behind Martha Stewart, Laura Ashley and Roberto Cavalli. Marquee plans to partner with Joseph Mimran, the Canadian fashion visionary behind Joe Fresh, Club Monaco and Alfred Sung, to help grow the Roots brand.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford will give a speech to the Empire Club of Canada on Wednesday in Toronto. Ford has been one of the loudest voices in Canada’s trade fight with the United States.

Economic data

Statistics Canada will release its building permits data for August on Wednesday. It will also publish its monthly survey of manufacturing and figures for wholesale trade in August on Thursday.

Housing figures

There are a pair of key data points for the Canadian housing market coming this week. The Canadian Real Estate Association will release its September home sales figures on Friday, while Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. is expected to release September housing starts the same day.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly will be at the Canadian Club Toronto on Friday to talk about the pressures facing Canadian industry. Last week, she sent a letter demanding that Stelco outline a plan on how its U.S.-based parent company Cleveland-Cliffs will honour its legally binding commitments made at the time of its acquisition of Stelco in 2024. Stelco is laying off up to 500 workers, citing an ongoing trade crisis, among other factors.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 11, 2026.

stories.title: Danielle Smith's dream: A post-uncertainty Alberta
stories.summary: Analysis: The premier wants a strong 'remain' win, because that means Albertans think Canada is working for them. But work remains, she says
stories.author: Donna Kennedy-Glans
stories.content:
Premier Danielle Smith has taken plenty of flak for putting independence on Alberta’s Oct. 19 ballot. She has no regrets. She is betting the vote will show that support for a binding separation referendum is already losing steam.

“This is what citizens wanted,” she said in a telephone interview. “Four hundred thousand signed a petition saying they wanted a vote to remain; 300,000 signed a petition saying they wanted to vote on an option to leave. And we have legislation that obligates us, if you get the required signatures, to put it to the people. So I want to see what Albertans have to say about it on October 19th.”

The first nine questions on the referendum are the government’s. The 10th, the remain-or-proceed question, is there because of that citizen-initiated process. More than 650,000 Albertans ordered special ballots, more than 10 times the usual provincial election volume. Smith reads that as engagement, not alarm. “People want to tell us what’s on their mind.” Those who requested mail ballots, she adds, “had more time to digest it and have a thoughtful response.”

Current polling puts remain at about 72 per cent and the option to start a binding process to separate at 22 per cent. “I’m glad to see that number has come down,” she says. “After Carney got elected, it was as high as 45 per cent. The fact that it has come down is a demonstration that both myself and the prime minister are working on the things that matter to people.” She would like the leave number to be zero; that would mean people feel like the country’s working.

She points to Stephen Harper’s recent Postmedia column : He wrote that separatist sentiment sat near 25 per cent after the Chrétien years, and by 2015 it was at “a big fat zero,” because Ottawa had dealt with the irritants the West actually cared about. The other spike came in 1982, when Albertans elected Gordon Kesler, a Western Canada Concept MLA; the momentum faded after Brian Mulroney arrived and the National Energy Program was dismantled.

“We have had separatism go down to single digits, or imperceptible. That really should be the target,” Smith says. “If people are feeling confident that their country is working for them, and that they’re a valued part of the country, I think that’s possible again. We’ve got more work to do, but that’s what I’m hoping for.” Many grievances have been addressed in the last 18 months, she said, and she’s identified a few more that require attention.

Quebec’s election makes the timing sharper. Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s Parti Québécois won a minority on a promise of another independence referendum. Smith has not spoken to the premier-designate and expects the relationship to run formally, through the Council of the Federation and first ministers’ meetings. If she does get the call, one subject is ready: “I am greatly encouraged and enthusiastic to work with him on weaning Quebec off equalization payments. I’m very pleased to hear that he said that, because guess what, it’s a priority for Alberta.”

She is equally interested in another result: Éric Duhaime’s Conservatives took about 21 per cent of the vote and 19 seats, enough to matter in a minority legislature. “A party that got almost as much of the popular vote” as the winner, she says, “has some constructive things we can talk about together, and hopefully be able to focus on the economy.”

On Ottawa, she is more upbeat than her critics expect. Carney, she says, “is genuinely interested in bilateral agreements and finding out what the issues are in each province and working with each premier to address them. That is a refreshing change of pace. I think that’s the way our country was always intended to work.”

She is confident the Pacific Link pipeline, newly designated a project of national interest, will be built. From her perspective, Indigenous consultations are going well. “Part of our joint agreement to do the southern route was because we had fresh environmental reviews and fresh negotiations with First Nations.” She discounts advocacy groups “that are actually funded by American foundations.” The conversations that count, she says, are with “the real First Nations who are going to be getting real dividend cheques to address real priorities… I think that’s going quite well.”

She is also confident Alberta can now build a natural gas power industry that federal rules previously blocked. “The federal government heard our grievances, addressed them in a meaningful way and we’re beginning to see the outcome.”

But no one in Ottawa should relax; other irritants remain. The federal gun law, she warns, “is going to turn our citizens into criminals, unless they give an amnesty for those who currently own those firearms that they bought legally.”

Property rights are another. The Alberta Bill of Rights is the “highest law of the land in our province,” she asserts. “I know B.C. made a different choice about what the highest law of their land would be, but that’s part of the reason why you need these matters of property and civil rights to be determined by the provinces under the Constitution.”

Free speech is a third. Influencers are fielding calls from new federal agencies telling them they are being blocked. “I don’t think Albertans appreciate having a federal government leaning over their shoulder watching podcasts to see if they said something that’s going to hurt someone’s feelings.”

Immigration is next. Carney curtailed numbers, then began talking about raising them again. “He can’t do that without working with the provinces. We need to make sure that we’re getting economic migrants who have jobs in our economy, and the skills that we need. So I suspect there’s going to be some robust conversations after October 19th on that too.”

Smith intends to keep the pressure on long after the vote. Keeping the separation option alive as leverage is not the plan. She wants the referendum to deliver certainty: “I want businesses to have confidence when they invest in Alberta. I want when people move here to have confidence … they’re going to be able to put down roots and live here for decades and be able to have an excellent quality of life. That’s the kind of certainty that I’m looking for on October the 19th.”

A separatist party emerging from the result is a risk she acknowledges, then minimizes. “We’ve always had separatist parties.” More than one was on the ballot in the last provincial election. “There’s always been a place to put that vote, and it’s incumbent upon those of us in government to understand why.”

If the country has drained this sentiment before, she said, it can do it again. “If we’ve been there before, we can do it again.”

content_blocks.text: Premier Danielle Smith has taken plenty of flak for putting independence on Alberta’s Oct. 19 ballot. She has no regrets. She is betting the vote will show that support for a binding separation referendum is already losing steam.

“This is what citizens wanted,” she said in a telephone interview. “Four hundred thousand signed a petition saying they wanted a vote to remain; 300,000 signed a petition saying they wanted to vote on an option to leave. And we have legislation that obligates us, if you get the required signatures, to put it to the people. So I want to see what Albertans have to say about it on October 19th.”

The first nine questions on the referendum are the government’s. The 10th, the remain-or-proceed question, is there because of that citizen-initiated process. More than 650,000 Albertans ordered special ballots, more than 10 times the usual provincial election volume. Smith reads that as engagement, not alarm. “People want to tell us what’s on their mind.” Those who requested mail ballots, she adds, “had more time to digest it and have a thoughtful response.”

Current polling puts remain at about 72 per cent and the option to start a binding process to separate at 22 per cent. “I’m glad to see that number has come down,” she says. “After Carney got elected, it was as high as 45 per cent. The fact that it has come down is a demonstration that both myself and the prime minister are working on the things that matter to people.” She would like the leave number to be zero; that would mean people feel like the country’s working.

She points to Stephen Harper’s recent Postmedia column : He wrote that separatist sentiment sat near 25 per cent after the Chrétien years, and by 2015 it was at “a big fat zero,” because Ottawa had dealt with the irritants the West actually cared about. The other spike came in 1982, when Albertans elected Gordon Kesler, a Western Canada Concept MLA; the momentum faded after Brian Mulroney arrived and the National Energy Program was dismantled.

stories.title: Saskatoon woman transforming discarded saris, giving new purpose
stories.summary: Satya Muktinutalapati works from her house in Saskatoon turning discarded saris into beautiful new clothes. She says she's saved up to 6 thousand garments from the landfill.
stories.author: Ashley Beherns
stories.content:
A Saskatoon-based fashion business owner is giving new life to worn out traditional clothing, but American tariffs are threatening the viability of her craft.

Originally from India, Satya Muktinutalapati reuses traditional saris to make skirts, dresses and other fashion accessories.

She started her business Rangeelaa about 10 years ago when she was living in Yorkton.

After moving to Saskatoon in 2019, she decided she wanted to produce her clothing by reusing traditional garments.

“We make all our clothing with the repurposed sari fabrics,” she said. “Our mission is not to waste any fabric.”

She says this practice has allowed her to save about 6,000 saris from the landfill.

Muktinutalapati works in Saskatoon and has a team of 10 in India; the whole team takes pride in putting a lot of care into their work.

“This is slow fashion, nothing happens quickly,” Satya said, “They cannot make more than two in a day, so I am very strict about that because they have to personally take care of those fabrics.”

Recent American tariffs are putting a hit on Muktinutalapati’s business, with 80 per cent of her customer base living south of the border.

“We are paying tariffs up front and that is killing my margins, so this year I don’t think I made any money because of the tariffs,” Muktinutalapati said, noting she is paying an extra 30-35 per cent in customs fees.

Although Rangeelaa has had a tough year, she says her customers are supportive.

“I know we are creating great outfits, and my customers love love love and I have like loyal customers who have been buying since 2019, since I started this.”

And sometimes, she is able to teach people something new.

“They have become my friends after all these years. So initially they did not know much about saris, so I educated them.”
