stories.title: Sask. man among 6 identified in air ambulance crash off Massachusetts coast
stories.summary: Thomas (Tommy) Henry Farquhar was serving as the first officer on an air ambulance that crashed with six people on board while travelling from Bermuda to Boston.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
The family of a Saskatchewan plane crash victim has set up a scholarship to support future pilots.

Thomas (Tommy) Henry Farquhar was serving as the first officer on an air ambulance that crashed with six people on board while travelling from Bermuda to Boston, states a release from the U.S. Coast Guard.

Alberta-based Prairie College said Farquhar was a 2023 graduate of Prairie Aviation Training Centre (Patc).

Originally from Regina, Farquhar made the move to Alberta in 2021 to pursue flight school. It was there he met his wife, according to a fundraising page on Prairie College’s website.

“Tommy’s passion for life and the joy that he had was evident to everyone around him,” Patc director Dallas Derksen, said in a news release. “Flying with Latitude gave him the opportunity to use his skill and ability and to help those in need, living out his faith in a very real and practical way.”

According to the school, the scholarship will “support up-and-coming pilots who share Tommy’s passion for aviation and his commitment to using those skills to serve the needs of others.”

The plane, belonging to Hamilton-based Latitude Air Ambulance, lost contact with air traffic controllers on the morning of Oct. 3 on a flight from Bermuda to Boston.

Air traffic control audio suggests the plane was experiencing electrical issues before it went down off the coast of Nantucket, Mass.

Debris from the plane was found later that day and on Oct. 4, the Coast Guard suspended its search for those aboard the flight.

Authorities said six people were on board the plane at the time, including four Latitude staff and two Bermuda nationals.

Latitude confirmed all four flight staff were Canadian.

An investigation is underway by the Transportation Safety Board of Canada.

In an email to Global News, Latitude said it is co-operating in the investigation.

stories.title: Sask. trans rights supporters rally across province against Bill 137
stories.summary: Those attending the rallies in Saskatoon and Regina say the law has created unsafe spaces for many youth since it was passed three years ago.
stories.author: Ashley Beherns
stories.content:
People in Saskatoon and Regina gathered for several rallies Saturday, calling on the provincial government to repeal Bill 137.

The provincial law bars children under the age of 16 from going by a different name or pronoun at school unless their parents’ consent.

The province invoked the Notwithstanding Clause to override Charter rights to protect the law from constitutional scrutiny.

Those attending the rallies at Saskatoon’s city hall and the provincial legislature in Regina say the law has created unsafe spaces for many youth since it was passed three years ago.

“I’ve heard a lot of things from various trans youth that they don’t feel like it’s safe to try and be themselves at school, and then they’re just kind of running out of places to be themselves,” said Thios Mwunvaneza, who organized the Saskatoon rally with The Red Bear Party and Queer Momentum.

“I think it’s really important that we continue speaking out on the harms of Bill 137 and the way it’s affecting our youth as well as re-traumatizing trans adults who are living in this province and dealt with things similar to what the bill enforces while they were growing up,” said Blake Tait, Saskatoon Pride co-chair.

Bill 137 also allows parents to opt their child out of sexual health classes and prohibits third party sexual health organizations from teaching students.

“Kind of embarrassing for the province with the highest rates of syphilis and HIV to be letting kids have less access to sex ed,” said Mwunvaneza.

“The people who are now banned from schools are third-party sex educators, meaning the people who have really dedicated their lives and made it their entire job to be knowledgeable and up to date with sex ed.”

Opposition NDP Leader Carla Beck announced Friday that if voted into office after the next provincial election, an NDP government would repeal the bill within 100 days of forming government.

Nathaniel Teed, the first openly gay MLA in Saskatchewan says repealing the law is necessary.

“As we’ve heard here today, just the stories from kids and family members, we know that we need to build a better relationship with our kids and with our teachers and our parents in our province,” he said.

At the time the bill was introduced into legislature, a release from the government said the bill outlines a number of rights that parents have when it comes to being involved in their child’s education.

A challenge to the bill from UR Pride and other intervenors is awaiting a hearing at the Supreme Court of Canada, with the applicants questioning the province’s use of the Nothwithstanding Clause to enforce the law.

stories.title: High costs haunt Canadian ornamental pumpkin farm
stories.summary: "We're not impacted by tariffs but the trade issues are still ratcheting up costs for us across the board," said farm co-owner Patrick Butters.
stories.author: Brett Bundale
stories.content:
The Butters brothers know pumpkins.

The second-generation southwestern Ontario farmers have carved out a niche in ornamental pumpkins, gourds and corn, seasonal crops that decorate tables on Thanksgiving and porches on Halloween.

But the cost of getting a mini orange pumpkin or tiny green gourd from their farm in St. Thomas to stores across Canada and the United States ahead of the autumn holidays has surged.

“We’re not impacted by tariffs but the trade issues are still ratcheting up costs for us across the board,” said Patrick Butters, who owns and operates the roughly 2,200-hectare farm with his brother Christopher.

“We’ve been seeing incremental increases all season long.”

Butters Farms offers a window into how trade tensions and geopolitical issues can ripple through the economy.

Higher freight, packaging and diesel costs are putting added pressure on farmers’ thin margins, while limited room to raise prices means producers are often left absorbing some of the increase.

In addition to ornamental crops and pie pumpkins for eating, Butters Farms grows soybeans, wheat, butternut squash and sweet and field corn, which account for about 90 per cent of the farm’s acreage.

Ornamental crops — including decorative corn, star-shaped Crown of Thorns gourds and white, tennis ball-sized Baby Boo pumpkins — account for just 10 per cent of the farm’s acreage but generate about half its revenue.

Yet those sales depend on getting the seasonal produce from the family farm near Lake Erie to major grocery retailers across Canada and as far south as Texas.

“Our average trucking rate is up 30 per cent from last year,” Patrick Butters said.

He said his cardboard packaging costs have risen about 20 per cent after three price increases since the spring. Fertilizer, labour costs and other general farm inputs are also soaring, he added.

“At some point, it just becomes too expensive,” he said. “Somebody is not going to pay for that pumpkin if the price climbs too high.”

Butters Farms isn’t alone in grappling with higher costs.

Farmers across Canada are facing similar pressures, including higher energy, steel and aluminum prices, said Keith Currie, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.

“The cost of machinery has skyrocketed and along with that the cost of parts and fixing our equipment,” he said. “It’s also becoming very expensive just to operate machinery. The cost of diesel has gone through the roof.”

Currie, who grows crops like corn, soybeans and wheat on his farm outside of Collingwood, Ont., said the cost of operating a combine during harvest season has ballooned.

“It’s $2,500 to fill my combine, so if I’m going through a tank of fuel a day or every couple of days it starts getting expensive,” he said.

Even basic maintenance is pricey, Currie said.

The eighth-generation farmer said the cost of changing the hydraulic oil and filters in two tractors last weekend totalled nearly $2,000, a job that would have cost about $500 five years ago.

“That’s not anything special, that’s not a repair,” he said. “That’s just regular maintenance.”

The mounting costs come as farmers have little control over the prices they ultimately receive for their crops.

“Farmers are in a pinch this fall as they’re trying to harvest their crops,” said Brendan Gill, a relationship manager with TD Agriculture Services. “They’re at the mercy of the market.”

With diesel, fertilizer and commodity prices out of their hands, he said farmers are instead focusing on variables they can control: pre-buying inputs, locking in future crop prices through contracts, selectively diversifying crops and closely managing their balance sheets.

“It’s just taking back some control,” Gill said. “That’s how some of these farmers are combating this uncertainty.”

That uncertainty continues to loom over the Butters brothers as they plan their next season.

“As of today, I am not paying a tariff to have our product cross the border but that could change tomorrow with the political landscape, so it’s just an added level of unknown that we’re not used to,” Patrick Butters said.

“You’re buying your seed in the winter and planting your crop in the spring and spending money all along the way to keep it disease- and insect-free with the hope that these relationships we’ve developed with our customer base for decades can continue.”

He added: “You’re gambling every day.”

stories.title: Person dies after canopy collapses at Fairmont hotel construction site
stories.summary: A worker died after a canopy collapsed at the Fairmont Winnipeg hotel downtown construction site on Thursday. The worker was conducting asbestos abatement.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
A worker died after a canopy collapsed at the Fairmont Winnipeg hotel downtown construction site on Thursday.

The worker is employed at Kepsco Construction and was at the hotel doing asbestos abatement work, according to a provincial spokesperson.

“We extend our sincere condolences to the deceased’s family, friends, and colleagues during this difficult time,” said Barb Perreaux, James Richardson & Sons Ltd communications director, in an emailed statement.

The Fairmont Winnipeg building is owned by James Richardson & Sons Ltd.

Workers are more likely to be injured in Manitoba than anywhere else in Canada, said Kevin Rebeck, Manitoba Federation of Labour president.

“Something has to change, so I’m asking for government to conduct an external review,” he said.

“Let’s get to heart of the matter. Let’s shine a light on this issue.”

The hotel’s flags are at half-mast to honour the deceased.

Global News has reached out to Kepsco Construction for more information.

Watch the video above for the full story.

stories.title: Elections Alberta 'ready to deliver' as advanced referendum polls to open this week
stories.summary: Edmonton - Albertans can start trekking to the polls this week to have their say on whether it's time to look at quitting Confederation.
stories.author: Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Albertans can start trekking to the polls this week to have their say on whether it’s time to look at quitting Confederation.

Advanced polls for the Oct. 19 referendum are set to open Tuesday, and if requests for mail-in ballots are any indication, there could be a record turnout.

Officials at Elections Alberta say they’re ready.

“We’ve completed scenario planning, and our teams are prepared to handle any issue that May emerge,” Maia Hanrahan, a spokesperson for Elections Alberta, said this week.

“We are ready to deliver.”

The agency has said for months that Premier Danielle Smith’s Oct. 19 referendum, with a headlining question on whether Albertans want to stay in Canada, will be a herculean task.

About 45 million printed ballots are required, as are at least 60,000 workers to facilitate the process and hand count the votes — a requirement the agency says will mean results likely won’t be known until the early morning hours on Oct. 20.

As of Friday morning, Hanrahan said, about 44,000 people have been hired and that recruitment efforts will continue right up until voting day.

“We’ve had a strong response from Albertans; and we’re grateful to them,” Hanrahan said.

Elections Alberta has also said it’s preparing for a record voter turnout of about 85 per cent. That level of voter interest was made evident when roughly 658,000 mail-in ballots were requested last month, representing roughly 20 per cent of the province’s approximately three million registered voters.

Hanrahan said that as of Friday, the agency has received just over 300,000 completed mail-in ballots ahead of the Friday deadline for returning them.

The unprecedented demand for mail-in ballots wasn’t without hiccups.

About 300 voters who were among the first to receive their packages in the mail opened their envelope to some of the 10 questions missing, an issue Elections Alberta said was the fault of its service provider and was remedied by sending new ballots in the mail.

Other voters in the early weeks of the special ballot period reported concerns with a form that required people to declare they were voting by mail because they were unable to vote in-person. The form threatened hefty fines for misuse of the process.

Elections Alberta said the form was old, as the government had changed the rules to no longer require a reason for Albertans to vote by mail. It advised voters to simply cross out that form and complete the rest of the declaration process.

Earlier this week, the agency also reported that some 3,000 mail-in ballots had been mailed back with missing documentation, such as proof of ID, or issues with the declaration forms. It said it was contacting each voter to remedy their situation so that their ballots could be counted.

The premier told reporters this week that Elections Alberta’s ability to work with voters to fix their mistake is a sign the agency is managing the referendum process well.

Smith has faced criticism from the Opposition NDP for underfunding the electoral system, and setting Elections Alberta up to fail with her massive referendum.

She conceded Wednesday that there “May be issues” that need to be dealt with after the vote.

“I’m sure that Elections Alberta will have its own report on how things went and to see if there’s any modifications that need to be made to the process,” she said.

Tuesday is set to mark the first of five days of advanced in-person voting for the referendum.

There will be 310 advanced polling stations across the province, and voters must go to stations within their electoral divisions.

On referendum day, there will be just over 1,400 polling stations.

Hanrahan said the agency is encouraging voters to go to advanced polls if they’re concerned about long lines on Oct. 19.

It’s also encouraging Albertans to familiarize themselves with the questions before they go to vote.

There are five questions Smith has put forward on immigration reform, and whether temporary workers and residents should be charged fees to access social services such as health care and education.

There are also four questions related to Canada’s Constitution that Smith wants a mandate for to lobby her provincial counterparts across the country.

The 10th question is whether Albertans want to remain in Canada or hold a second, binding vote on quitting Confederation.

Elections Alberta modelling indicates that voters who show up knowing how they plan to mark their ballots could still spend about two minutes in the voting booth.

Those unfamiliar with the questions could spend up to four minutes, Hanrahan said, while others whose first language is not English, have lower literacy skills or are slower readers could spend nearly six minutes in the booth.

“Electors are all different in their voting approach,” she said.

“The length of time it will take an elector to mark their ballot May depend on different factors, and the above numbers are approximates based on our modelling.”

There is no time limit on how long a person can spend filling out their ballots.

Hanrahan also asked voters to remember election workers are their friends and neighbours.

“Please be kind,” she said, adding that election officials will be on hand to answer questions voters May have.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 11, 2026.

stories.title: B.C.’s debt trap is snapping shut
stories.summary: Whoever wins the October election will need to come to grips with province’s disastrously deteriorating finances
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
Mounting deficits, soaring debt loads and a string of credit downgrades: There can be no doubt that British Columbia’s fiscal position is abysmal now, and headed for much worse, soon.

In less than four years, David Eby’s B.C. NDP has erased not just years of painful fiscal restraint, but his own party’s carefully constructed reputation as prudent managers of the provincial budget.

The result is a mess that the next premier, after this month’s vote, will have to address if a debt spiral is to be avoided. We’ll have more to say on the fiscal plans of the two main parties, the NDP and the Conservatives, next week.

But first, a guided tour of how British Columbia, which until recently was one of the least indebted provinces, came to be on a clearly unsustainable fiscal path. Without aggressive action, a debt trap awaits B.C., in which interest costs will start eating up a bigger and bigger part of the provincial budget, inflating the deficit – and driving up interest costs even more, particularly as long-term rates rise.

British Columbia has faced this situation before, with a free-spending NDP driving up debt. In the 1990s, the left-leaning party turned in hefty deficits.

But that episode pales in comparison to the efforts of Mr. Eby – truly in a league of his own, as this first chart shows.

Under the first NDP government in the province, from 1972 through to 1975, the debt burden as a proportion of the economy was relatively stable, or even declining. It was the right-leaning Social Credit party that pushed up the province’s debt levels in the 1980s.

But the return of the NDP to power in 1991 saw debt surge. Taxpayer-funded debt as a percentage of the province’s gross domestic product rose as high as 20.8 per cent. A year later, the right-of-centre B.C. Liberals, under Gordon Campbell, swept to power, winning all but two ridings.

A period of consolidation followed, with debt as a proportion of the economy tumbling to 13.8 per cent by 2009. The financial crisis and Great Recession undid some of that progress, but by 2017, when the NDP returned to power, B.C.’s debt burden was shrinking.

That trend continued under then NDP Premier John Horgan, whose government balanced its spending program with fiscal prudence, a marked contrast to the free-spending ways of the 1990s. Even the pandemic didn’t degrade the province’s finances much. By fiscal 2023, the debt as a percentage of GDP had returned to 2020 levels.

That year was the last year of the Horgan government, with Mr. Eby becoming Premier midway through fiscal 2023. (Mr. Horgan stepped down because of an illness, and died in 2024.) And that fiscal year was the start of an alarming explosion of B.C.’s debt levels.

As this second chart shows, there is a stark difference in the fiscal track record of the Horgan and Eby governments. Mr. Horgan’s government ran surpluses outside the immediate pandemic years. Mr. Eby’s has dug the debt hole deeper and deeper, year after year.

The province’s first-quarter fiscal update from mid-September forecasts that taxpayer-funded debt as a proportion of GDP will hit 30.1 per cent in the current fiscal year, more than double the level in fiscal 2023. Even worse, that debt burden is projected to rise to 37.4 per cent in fiscal 2029.

At that rate, the province’s debt burden will surge past 40 per cent by the end of the decade, and then 50 per cent about three years later. That is a debt crisis in the making.

As bad as that picture is, it is likely to get worse. For one, any new government will have election promises to pay for. Beyond that, the Eby government has had a habit of shifting its projections, for worse, with each budget, as this third chart shows.

The 2024 budget, for instance, forecast a $6.3-billion deficit for the current 2026-27 fiscal year. But last month’s first-quarter update projected a deficit more than twice as large, at $13.8-billion.

That update projects a slight improvement over the next two years, with the deficit slated to contract to $12-billion. But other budgets have made similar forecasts, which have failed to materialize. In the Eby government’s 2023 budget, its first, the 2025-26 deficit was forecast to shrink to $3-billion. The actual figure was $7.7-billion, more than double.

What has led to this debt and deficit debacle? The Ndp’s spending proclivities are many, but one thing stands out: the size and cost of the public service.

The NDP government largely caved to the demands of the main public sector union last year, locking in wage hikes that have been estimated to cost $16-billion over four years.

Part of why the cost of the public service will surge so much is that the Eby government, and to a lesser extent its predecessor, has embarked on a hiring spree, putting to shame even Justin Trudeau’s bloat of the federal civil service.

As this final chart shows, the Horgan government did expand the size of government over five years, increasing the number of public servants by around 21 per cent. The Eby government nearly matched that rate in just three years (with the absolute number of people hired a little larger).

To be clear, that expansion has not happened because of a push to hire teachers, nurses or other front-line workers. The data in the chart don’t count those kinds of public sector workers.

True, the Eby government’s last budget did forecast a decline in the ranks of the public service in coming years. But that is a projection only. The most current figures show an uninterrupted hiring spree. And even if those projections came to fruition, they would only return employment levels to just under 2024 levels, far from what would be needed to return the size of the public service to the levels of the last decade, and woefully insufficient to make much of a dent in B.C.’s surging deficit and debt burden.

That underscores the reality that there is no easy, nor quick, escape from B.C.’s debt trap. It will take years of spending discipline, coupled with a restructuring of government, to keep that trap from closing.

stories.title: Book excerpt: When Canadians faced danger, defiance — and gruesome evidence we had to preserve
stories.summary: From the new book "Into the Breach: A Soldier's Journey" by retired Gen. Wayne Eyre, former Chief of Defence Staff.
stories.author: Wayne Eyre
stories.content:
Looking back at 1993, retired Gen. Wayne Eyre writes in his new memoir, “Force was the one thing and only thing the belligerents understood, and UNPROFOR could not provide it.” The Battle of Medak Pocket, as it became known, in Croatia is generally regarded as the most difficult action faced by Canadian troops during the period between the conflicts in Korea and Afghanistan.

On Sept. 14, hundreds of soldiers from the 2 Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry (2PPCLI) were sent, as part of the United Nations Protection Force (UNPROFOR) mission intervening in the wars in the former Yugoslavia, to the town of Medak, Croatia. They were to reinforce a Canadian platoon there, in a supposed neutral zone between Croat and Serb forces. However, when the newcomers got there the Croatian forces rained down heavy machine-gun and artillery fire. 2PPCLI soldiers held their ground and drove the Croatian forces back. The next day, an impromptu news conference by Canadian commander James Calvin pressured Croatians to relent, and the Canadians including then-captain Eyre’s Recce Platoon advanced into the pocket.

Finishing the sweep, we had much welcome momentary relief as our resupply arrived. Ed Larabie and our storesman, Cpl. Tony Orr, had been able to move forward with water, food and fuel. We compared notes over lunch and soon had to move out to another task.

As the FREBAT3 company explored an adjacent area, we were to search in the vicinity of a dominating hill. The next day I accompanied Calvin to the Croatian headquarters in Gospić to sign an agreement on the buffer zone boundary. By then I was quite familiar with its contours, having been to most locations in it. As the CO sat with Croatian senior officers, I went into a side room with some of their staff to plot the detailed boundary. Expecting a contentious negotiation, it was surprisingly straightforward, and they readily agreed to the line on the map I presented. Continually standing up to them and showing our resolve over the previous weeks had had an effect. Returning in short order, we presented the results, which were duly signed and became the official boundary.

That finished the Medak Pocket operation for Recce Platoon, and we soon returned to the protected villages for the rest of the tour. It had been a long one, and indeed it was a full and eventful tour even before we relocated to Sector South. The battalion was tired, and many had experienced horrors that would stay with them forever. The psychological impact for many was to prove crushing.

content_blocks.html: On Sept. 14, hundreds of soldiers from the 2 Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry (2PPCLI) were sent, as part of the United Nations Protection Force (UNPROFOR) mission intervening in the wars in the former Yugoslavia, to the town of Medak, Croatia. They were to reinforce a Canadian platoon there, in a supposed neutral zone between Croat and Serb forces. However, when the newcomers got there the Croatian forces rained down heavy machine-gun and artillery fire. 2PPCLI soldiers held their ground and drove the Croatian forces back. The next day, an impromptu news conference by Canadian commander James Calvin pressured Croatians to relent, and the Canadians including then-captain Eyre’s Recce Platoon advanced into the pocket.

content_blocks.text: For the next three hours we were the battalion’s forward element, held up at a roadblock. As the afternoon progressed, along with the smoke, we could hear gunfire and explosions coming from the area of Lički Čitluk two kilometres to our south. I continued to send situation reports to Battalion Headquarters describing the suspected ethnic cleansing but was instructed to continue to hold in location. I asked the Croatian officer commanding the roadblock what was happening. He just smiled at me. It took much to control my frustration.

content_blocks.text: Finally, 1800 hours arrived and we mounted, ready to proceed. The Croatian officer still refused us passage, and his soldiers started to make threatening gestures with their weapons. Unwilling to wait any longer, I gave the go-ahead and our lead vehicle pushed through the roadblock.

content_blocks.text: I did not know what to expect but knew being attacked was a distinct possibility. Getting on the radio, I issued anticipatory fire-control orders to the platoon, with every detachment covering arcs around our little convoy, allowing us to immediately return fire in any direction if attacked. The next two-kilometre drive was one of the longest in my life.

content_blocks.text: Earlier, I had placed an accompanying combat camera film crew in the back of my APC, and their footage, subsequently used in many media pieces, captured what we found. Despite everything that we had seen on the tour, nothing had prepared us for the carnage we were entering. Arriving in Lički Čitluk, we found every building in the village either razed to the ground or on fire. The smell of wood smoke and death was overpowering. Around the village were about 40 Croatian soldiers still there, laughing and smiling at us as they prepared to leave.

content_blocks.text: I got out of my APC and placed our detachments to secure the village as the Croatian soldiers were packing up. We were puzzled by the many surgical gloves on the ground, which we later learned were for removing bodies to dispose of the evidence of murder.

content_blocks.text: Typical of many military operations, radio communication with our higher headquarters was sporadic. Through the broken message relayed to me as I was dismounted, it appeared that the CO had continued heading west and was perhaps in some trouble. I left Lt. Al Trainor and two detachments in the village, and took the remaining four detachments with me to follow the CO. Two kilometres down the road we ran into a group of Croatian soldiers, who did not appear happy. I left three of the detachments there to watch them and act as a reserve if I needed them forward.

content_blocks.text: Carrying on, before long I found Jim Calvin, and contrary to the message, he was not in trouble but having some of the same radio challenges as us. He was with a French platoon whose company was working to occupy its Phase Three positions along the original Croatian front line. The Croatians were very upset that we had penetrated as far and as fast as we had. After giving him a brief update, I moved all of Recce Platoon back to Lički Čitluk.

content_blocks.text: Meanwhile, back in Lički Čitluk, three Serb soldiers who had been in hiding for several days came out of the woods and surrendered to Trainor and Pte. Tim McMeekin. They put the Serbs into the back of an APC to keep them out of sight of the multitude of Croatian soldiers still in the area. These three were lucky.

content_blocks.text: Night was coming fast as we returned to Lički Čitluk. After a quick update from Trainor and placing our returning detachments around the village’s perimeter, the CO gave me a new task. Our access to the pocket at that point was along Maple Route, which entailed having to cross Croatian lines to link up with the rest of the battalion. We needed to find another route that avoided being cut off if the Croatians decided to block our ­access.

content_blocks.text: Taking two of my detachments, a section from the battalion’s combat engineer troop and the troop’s reconnaissance sergeant, Sgt. Kennedy, we headed southeast. Our less-than-precise maps showed some dotted lines that might be useable trails. As we left the village, we stopped at our detachment securing its east side, where Warrant Officer Grant Treger warned me that he had recently seen Croatian soldiers and had heard firing from the direction we were heading.

content_blocks.text: This, along with the mine threat, was top of our minds as we headed down the dirt road. The engineer section commander donned a blast suit and drove his vehicle in the front. Sgt. Kennedy and I followed some 50 metres behind on foot so we could hear any incoming small-arms fire over the sound of the engines, provide warning, and return fire, and our two Recce detachments followed behind. We spent two hours trying to locate a route, following one until it turned into a dead end, and then finally finding one that was not on the map.

content_blocks.text: Following this route, we could see lights several hundred metres to our front, and arriving there, I found Lt. Alex Brennan, a D Company platoon commander. My feeling of relief was intense. I briefed Dan Drew on what we were doing and then returned along our new route to Lički Čitluk, arriving at approximately 2300 hours.

content_blocks.text: Another task awaited. We had important items to get back to Battalion Headquarters. Along with film footage clearly showing atrocities and the three Serb soldiers, the French Battalion 3 (FREBAT3) company had discovered several victims of ethnic cleansing. Two young women, obviously held for several days and subjected to untold horrors, were subsequently burnt beyond recognition as the Croatian forces withdrew. Gruesomely, their bodies had to be watered down to avoid melting the body bags. We needed to escort this evidence back without Croatian interference, and we were reluctant to radio the information back, due to a lack of encrypted ­communications.

content_blocks.text: Assembling a small convoy, we took the three Serb soldiers, the bodies of the two Serb girls, and the film footage back to the Serb side. We arrived at the battalion command post in Medak at half past midnight, where I filled in Brennan and his deputy, Capt. Ed Haverstock. Years later they would tell me my eyes were like saucers. UN Civilian Police interviewed the Serb soldiers before we turned them over to the local Serb brigade, to a joyous reunion.

content_blocks.text: We returned along the same route and arrived back in Lički Čitluk at 0200 hours, where Recce Platoon had moved into a tighter, all-round defence perimeter in an open clearing at the southern edge of the village. Shortly after moving in, Cpl. Dean Thompson was conducting a security patrol with night vision goggles when he came across what he thought was a brush pile, but on closer inspection found it to be the body of an elderly Serb woman who had been shot several times. Given the risk of another night move, we stayed in place, with a body metres away.

content_blocks.text: Knowing that we would likely encounter much evidence of war crimes, the battalion formed a team specifically for the operation to gather and document evidence. Commanded by Maj. Craig King, the Sweep Team consisted of medical personnel, UN Civilian Police, Mortar Platoon, and one of our two chaplains, Padre Mike Brown. None were experts in forensics, but through their efforts this became the best documented case of ethnic cleansing in the former Yugoslavia.

content_blocks.text: I awoke to the Sweep Team arriving to examine and collect the body. Along with being shot numerous times, she had also been mutilated. Exhausted and detached, I stood some 25 metres away, breakfasting over the hood of the Iltis on a pork with rice ration pack, heavily dosed with Tabasco sauce to cover the smell and taste. I had become numb to these scenes of atrocity.

content_blocks.text: We were soon on the move again, this time in support of the Sweep Team clearing the nearby villages of Rogići and Uzelci. Here we found no human remains, however, the entire area was razed to the ground, ruins were still smoking, and farm animal carcasses were strewn about.

content_blocks.text: Finishing the sweep, we had much welcome momentary relief as our resupply arrived. Ed Larabie and our storesman, Cpl. Tony Orr, had been able to move forward with water, food and fuel. We compared notes over lunch and soon had to move out to another task.

content_blocks.text: Moving five kilometres northwest to Strunići, the CO told of persistent reports of a Serb platoon cut off in the woods south of the village. As the FREBAT3 company explored an adjacent area, we were to search in the vicinity of a dominating hill. Calvin finished with a warning: “Either side may try to shoot a Canadian soldier to create an incident and blame it on the other side — be careful.”

content_blocks.text: Given the nature of the ground, we used two converging foot patrols that would meet at the top of the hill, while keeping a section in reserve, a classic area reconnaissance that we had exercised many times in Canada. Along with plenty of ammunition (of Argentine origin), fresh food and fresh footprints, the patrols again saw many rubber gloves and came across the body of an elderly Serb who had been shot several times. We found no Serb soldiers, although we had a disquieting sense throughout of being watched.

content_blocks.text: Finishing this task, we returned to an all-round defence closer to Lički Čitluk, and I headed to the CO’s orders group. This was the first time the battalion’s leadership had assembled since the beginning of the operation and gave us a good chance to compare notes. The exhaustion in the eyes of all was clear, but so was an overwhelming sense of camaraderie, of pride that we were operating at our peak, and an appreciation we were involved in something monumental. With the smell of death and smoke still hanging in the air, it was a good meeting to steady our nerves. Recce Platoon was again to be the battalion’s reserve to respond to the unforeseen.

content_blocks.text: The next morning, Brennan tasked us to find a route around a wooded area at the south part of the buffer zone and link up with the FREBAT3 company. Again, the maps showed what appeared to be a trail. With an engineer section attached, Recce Platoon moved west of Lički Čitluk. Before long we came across an abandoned roadblock. After checking it for booby traps, we dozed it out of the way and continued.

content_blocks.text: Still well within the buffer zone, a Croatian platoon blocking the road stopped us a kilometre later. Noting their MUP (Ministry of the Interior) badges and that they had the reputation as the ethnic cleansing police, we became immediately suspicious. My discussion with their commander began cordially enough but rapidly deteriorated when I made clear our intention of moving forward, and that his platoon needed to get out of the buffer zone.

content_blocks.text: He cocked his M-70, the Yugoslav version of the AK-47 assault rifle, and his platoon followed suit. Mine did likewise, with our seven .50-calibre heavy machine guns, seven C-9 light machine guns, and one C-6 medium machine gun from the engineers readied in unison. As I looked behind me, I saw Cpl. Bill Martina take up a firing position with his C-9. I counted one machine gun in the Croatian platoon — we had 15. They were seriously outgunned, but I knew if shooting started, my position right in the middle of it was not good.

content_blocks.text: The armed standoff continued as I walked back to my APC. Working to control surging adrenaline, I sent a radio update to Battalion Headquarters, who told me to remain in location until reinforcements arrived. Minutes later, the commander of one of the French companies, Senior Capt. Cot, the son of the UNPROFOR commander, arrived with part of his company. I told him my intent to push through. He tried to talk to the Croatian commander, also without result.

He tried to talk to the Croatian commander, also without result.

content_blocks.text: With the French element remaining in location, Recce Platoon pushed forward. For dramatic effect, the Croatian platoon re-cocked their weapons and then disappeared into the bush. Now anticipating an ambush, we continued with our original mission with weapons at the ready and great vigilance. There was to be no further sign of this platoon, and before long, the trail we were following disappeared into nothing.

content_blocks.text: Moving back into reserve near Lički Čitluk, devastating news arrived. There had been a vehicle accident, with Capt. Jim Decoste killed and Transport Officer Lt. Rick Turner and driver Cpl. Stacey Bouck both seriously injured. I knew Rick well from our time together in Cyprus, and later in Recce for a stint, and I had just been talking with Jim the night before. Jim was an incredibly well-respected and liked leader who had come from the ranks, and his death sent shock waves through the unit, and especially in Recce Platoon where many had served with him in Germany. We were bitterly aware of the paradox that despite all the close calls with the fighting, our two deaths on the tour came from vehicle accidents.

content_blocks.text: Recce Platoon remained on call in the pocket for the next two days. On Sept. 19 the chief of the defence staff, Admiral John Anderson, visited and once again we provided security as we escorted him around the devastation of the pocket. I could tell from his look that he was shocked by what he saw.

content_blocks.text: During this visit, the rest of the platoon, under Al Trainor, had another confrontation with a Croatian platoon. One of the battalion’s liaison officers found them in the buffer zone and called for backup. After a short standoff, our troops disarmed them, put them in a truck, and unceremoniously sent them out of the buffer zone. They loaded the captured weapons into the back of the CO’s Iltis, and after a debate about whether to destroy them, later that day the CO dropped them off on the front steps of the Croatian headquarters in Gospić, with a message to stay out of the buffer zone.

content_blocks.text: On the 21st, with the situation much more stable, Recce Platoon redeployed out of the pocket 15 kilometres east to the camp at Sveti Rok, where we were able to unwind for a short period and enjoy a good night’s rest. There we remained for several days to ensure the situation remained stable.

content_blocks.text: The next day I accompanied Calvin to the Croatian headquarters in Gospić to sign an agreement on the buffer zone boundary. By then I was quite familiar with its contours, having been to most locations in it. As the CO sat with Croatian senior officers, I went into a side room with some of their staff to plot the detailed boundary. Expecting a contentious negotiation, it was surprisingly straightforward, and they readily agreed to the line on the map I presented. Continually standing up to them and showing our resolve over the previous weeks had had an effect. Returning in short order, we presented the results, which were duly signed and became the official boundary.

content_blocks.text: That finished the Medak Pocket operation for Recce Platoon, and we soon returned to the protected villages for the rest of the tour. It had been a long one, and indeed it was a full and eventful tour even before we relocated to Sector South. The battalion was tired, and many had experienced horrors that would stay with them forever. The psychological impact for many was to prove crushing.

stories.title: Pothole the 480-kilogram pumpkin on track to outgrow Newfoundland's famed Gourdzilla
stories.summary: ST. John's - When Leslee Lake hops out of his car after work these days, he doesn't hurry up to the house to see his wife.
stories.author: Sarah Smellie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - When Leslee Lake hops out of his car after work these days, he doesn’t hurry up to the house to see his wife.

Instead, the 52-year-old heavy equipment operator in Newfoundland hustles to his greenhouse, which has been overtaken by a massive pumpkin weighing as much as a grand piano. He’s named it Pothole.

“He doesn’t even come in an say, ‘Hi, how was your day?’ He goes up to the pumpkin,” said his wife, Krista, laughing during a video chat from their greenhouse in Clarenville, N.L.

Leslee Lake has a peculiar hobby growing enormous pumpkins in Clarenville, N.L. This year, his prized gourd weighs as much as a grand piano. Lake explains why he named it Pothole. (Oct. 11, 2026)

“Of course!” said Lake, his hand never leaving the top of the bulbous orange gourd. “It’s been 12 or 13 hours since I’ve seen him!”

Growing enormous pumpkins is a serious hobby for Lake. For a time, he and his wife stopped taking vacations during prime growing season so he could be close to his crops. He sources his seeds carefully and tries to outdo himself each year.

In 2022, Lake grew a pumpkin he named Gourdzilla that ultimately weighed in at 469 kilograms or 1,034 pounds. There is no authority keeping tabs on large gourds in Newfoundland, but it was believed Gourdzilla was the largest pumpkin ever grown on the island, the Lakes said.

Pothole is expected to end Gourdzilla’s reign.

On Friday morning, Lake’s wife entered Pothole’s length, width and circumference into an online pumpkin calculator, which estimated the gourd’s weight at about 482 kilograms. An official weighing will take place later this month.

The towering squash sits on one side of the greenhouse, which is otherwise overrun with Pothole’s network of vines and nodes, all working to supply the fruit with energy.

The pumpkin gained nearly 23 kilograms a day in the warmest part of the summer, Lake said. He plays heavy metal music for the gourd and sprays its leaves with milk and molasses, which helps nourish it and keep pests away.

Pothole got its name from a wound inflicted by an overheating electric blanket, which Lake had laid over the gourd during a chilly night last month.

“It healed,” he said of the large burn in the pumpkin’s skin. “And everything grew around it, so now it’s a perfect pothole.”

For the past few years, the Lakes have hosted a festival in October where local growers could weigh their large gourds. A company in St. John’s would send out gear capable of weighing the fruit.

This year, after a bad growing season, the festival is cancelled. But Pothole will still be properly weighed, they said. After Halloween, the Lakes will chop it up and hand it out, without a piece wasted.

“Anybody can do this,” Lake said, “with unlimited time and money and patience from the wife.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 11, 2026.

stories.title: ‘Not good public policy’: Cannabis retailers concerned about minimum staffing requirements at stores
stories.summary: Manitoba is considering new cannabis-store safety measures that would allow retailers to remove window coverings and could require a minimum number of employees to work during higher-risk hours.
stories.author: Alex Karpa
stories.content:
Winnipeg – Manitoba is considering new cannabis-store safety measures that would allow retailers to remove window coverings and could require a minimum number of employees to work during higher-risk hours.

The proposed amendments to the Liquor, Gaming and Cannabis Control Act were introduced by the provincial government earlier this week as part of an effort to address safety concerns at cannabis stores.

Under the proposed legislation, the Liquor, Gaming and Cannabis Authority of Manitoba (Lgca) would have the power to establish mandatory minimum staffing levels during certain hours, ensuring workers are not alone when the risk of violence is higher.

The province is also proposing to remove the requirement for cannabis retailers to cover their storefront windows.

Justice Minister Matt Wiebe said the change would improve visibility from outside the store and help ensure workers are not hidden from public view.

“We’re still mandating that the cannabis product will not be visible, because we want to protect kids,” Wiebe said.

“We’re finding that balance where we don’t want cannabis displayed in window fronts. We don’t want kids riding by and seeing cannabis and being enticed into trying a product that’s not appropriate for them, but at the same time, we have to prioritize worker safety.”

The proposed changes come after a Winnipeg cannabis store employee was sexually assaulted during a robbery in May, prompting renewed calls from labour groups for stronger workplace safety measures.

This followed the release of a survey by the United Food and Commercial Workers (Ufcw) Local 832, which found that only eight per cent of cannabis store workers felt safe at work at all times.

The survey prompted the union to call on the province to legislate new safety measures, including a ban on working alone, controlled entries, removing window coverings and mandated closing times.

Other provinces, including Ontario, eliminated similar rules around window coverings to address safety concerns.

“Our union welcomes these first steps,” said Ufcw Local 832 secretary-treasurer Marie Buchan.

“Cannabis workers told us their top priority for safer workplaces was ensuring that no one is required to work alone, and we look forward to the Lgca’s implementation of the mandatory minimums and to being part of the consultation process.”

Advocates concerned about impact on small businesses

While labour advocates have welcomed the proposed changes, others in the industry say mandatory staffing requirements could put significant pressure on small, independent retailers.

“Many family-owned and independently operated stores simply cannot absorb the added labour costs the way large corporate chains can,” said Canadian cannabis advocate Steven Stairs.

“If passed, these changes risk creating an uneven playing field by placing a heavier financial burden on small businesses while giving larger retailers a competitive advantage. That is not good public policy.”

John Arbuthnot, vice-president of commercial growth at Fika Cannabis shares those same concerns.

He says he wants further consultation with industry stakeholders to understand the government’s intent.

“Our fear is the impact on small business, especially in the cannabis industry, could be drastic, when it comes to the difference between even one or two staff on,” Arbuthnot said.

“But obviously open to a robust round of government consultation in terms of next steps for that aspect of the bill.”

He believes many smaller shops in Manitoba will be impacted by the move.

“You look at the industry in Manitoba; you obviously have high volume shops. You also have a lot of smaller independent shops that realistically cannot take on a second staff member, and still be profitable,” Arbuthnot said.

Stairs hopes the province will consider staffing requirements on a case-by-case basis, taking the circumstances of individual retailers into account.

“We want to encourage small, independent retailers to be here in this province, and for local tax dollars to be going to local employees and retail owners,” Stairs said.

“We don’t necessarily want every store to be owned by a corporation from another country or another province. So I think this is a step towards diminishing the power of independent local retailers.”

stories.title: Canadians join international convoy bringing vehicles to Ukraine’s front lines
stories.summary: Islander Randy Garrett is back home after driving roughly 2,600 kilometres across Europe to deliver a four-wheel drive vehicle destined for Ukraine’s front lines.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Long River, P.E.I. - Islander Randy Garrett is back home after driving roughly 2,600 kilometres across Europe to deliver a four-wheel drive vehicle destined for Ukraine’s front lines.

Garrett was one of three Canadians who joined volunteers from around the world for a recent Jeeps for Peace mission. The group has delivered about 800 4x4s, pickup trucks and ambulances to Ukraine. The vehicles are modified for military units, then used to evacuate civilians in danger, retrieve wounded soldiers and transport food and medicine.

“It was tiring, but it was worth it,” Garrett said, sitting at the dining room table of his sunny home, nestled in the rolling hills of Long River. “You had such a sense of purpose.”

He took part in the organization’s 18th convoy, setting out from Edinburgh, Scotland, with about 55 others. Their route included an overnight ferry crossing of the North Sea, followed by a drive through the Netherlands, Germany and Poland to the Ukrainian border.

Locals helped the group navigate the crossing with 36 vehicles, packed with children’s books, clothing, food and other supplies.

When time allows, the missions also include visits to schools, hospitals, churches, cemeteries and memorials, as well as meetings with Ukrainian military personnel and orphanage staff. Garrett recalled the warmth of the welcome that waited for them.

“I was very proud to be a Canadian because when they found out you’re a Canadian, they just hug you twice,” he said.

More than four years after Russia’s full-scale invasion, the war of attrition grinds on.

In one of Moscow’s latest deadly barrages , Russian missiles and drones struck Kyiv and a dozen other Ukrainian regions overnight Oct. 7. The attacks killed at least 25 civilians, including five children, and wounded about 100 people, Ukrainian officials said.

“I think it’s very important that people don’t forget about Ukraine and do what they can,” Garrett said. “And this was my way of doing something that I could.”

Volunteers pay their own way, covering flights, fuel and hotels. But Garrett said his community stepped up to help, surprising him with $1,300 tucked inside a card full of well wishes after learning about his plans.

Jeeps for Peace and individual volunteers also organize crowdfunding campaigns to support the work. Some vehicles are donated, and their owners often join the convoys.

Garrett shared the story of a Ukrainian woman named Alla, who lost both her home and summer home to the war, and whose husband was killed in combat. She has driven more than 90 vehicles to Ukraine to support its troops.

The next mission is already underway as Jeeps for Peace works toward its goal of delivering 1,000 vehicles.

“Would I do it again? I would,” Garrett said.

“It was tiring, but it was worth it,” Garrett said, sitting at the dining room table of his sunny home, nestled in the rolling hills of Long River. “You had such a sense of purpose.”

He took part in the organization’s 18th convoy, setting out from Edinburgh, Scotland, with about 55 others. Their route included an overnight ferry crossing of the North Sea, followed by a drive through the Netherlands, Germany and Poland to the Ukrainian border.
Locals helped the group navigate the crossing with 36 vehicles, packed with children’s books, clothing, food and other supplies.

When time allows, the missions also include visits to schools, hospitals, churches, cemeteries and memorials, as well as meetings with Ukrainian military personnel and orphanage staff. Garrett recalled the warmth of the welcome that waited for them.
“I was very proud to be a Canadian because when they found out you’re a Canadian, they just hug you twice,” he said.
More than four years after Russia’s full-scale invasion, the war of attrition grinds on.

In one of Moscow’s latest deadly barrages , Russian missiles and drones struck Kyiv and a dozen other Ukrainian regions overnight Oct. 7. The attacks killed at least 25 civilians, including five children, and wounded about 100 people, Ukrainian officials said.
“I think it’s very important that people don’t forget about Ukraine and do what they can,” Garrett said. “And this was my way of doing something that I could.”

Volunteers pay their own way, covering flights, fuel and hotels. But Garrett said his community stepped up to help, surprising him with $1,300 tucked inside a card full of well wishes after learning about his plans.
Jeeps for Peace and individual volunteers also organize crowdfunding campaigns to support the work. Some vehicles are donated, and their owners often join the convoys.

Garrett shared the story of a Ukrainian woman named Alla, who lost both her home and summer home to the war, and whose husband was killed in combat. She has driven more than 90 vehicles to Ukraine to support its troops.
The next mission is already underway as Jeeps for Peace works toward its goal of delivering 1,000 vehicles.
“Would I do it again? I would,” Garrett said.

stories.title: Nova Scotia alcohol vending company expands to top American sports and entertainment venues
stories.summary: A small Nova Scotia business that installs high-tech robotic vending machines in sports and entertainment venues is making a major splash in the U.S. alcohol marketplace.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax - A small Nova Scotia business that installs high-tech robotic vending machines in sports and entertainment venues is making a major splash in the U.S. alcohol marketplace.

“We have a product that is always going to be in demand,” said Corey Yantha who is the founder and CEO of Dispension Industries Inc., a Dartmouth, N.S. vending company that has 25 employees.

“Currently, we are set up at maybe our most high-profile venue, which is Dodger Stadium where we have done more than $200,000 in sales with two machines, over the period of the year and that’s the highest revenue per square foot in that stadium,” said Yantha.“And we have just launched at Empire Field, the home of the Nfl’s Denver Broncos.”

Yantha has also begun negotiations with other NBA, NHL and Ncaa arenas and stadiums.

“Once we proved it in some of the biggest most iconic venues in the world, everyone else has started calling,” he said. “Our challenge now is not developing a product from scratch and testing it in the market, but our challenge is building enough of these machines to satisfy the demand.”

Before breaking into the American market, Yantha already had vending machines in place in several Canadian cities.

“We did some work with Scotiabank Centre in Halifax,” said Yantha. “And we have had units at Mary Brown’s Centre in Newfoundland, and they’ve been performing well for a few years.”

Each vending machine is equipped with high-tech and strict serving protocols.

“A customer walks up and they insert their ID and our technology uses ultraviolet, infrared, invisible light to scan all the security features on the ID,” said Yantha. “We check the age of the guest, and the expiry date of the ID and then a camera opens and compares their face to the photo on the ID.”

Canned alcohol is then served, pre-opened for customers to drink.

Alcohol historian Rod Phillips said the technology that ensures vending machine customers are legal drinking age could pave the way for these devices to grow in popularity across North America.

“I could see vending machines like this in stores, and I could see them in malls and other places where other people want convenience,” said Phillips, who is a professor at Carleton University in Ottawa. “And convenience is one of the things people are looking for, and if they could get alcohol through a machine, then I am sure a lot of people would like to.”

The success of Yantha’s company south of the border comes at time when trade tensions have strained the relationship between Canada and the U.S.

“We think we have developed a technology that transcends tariffs,” said Yantha, who added while both federal governments might not be getting along, his American-based corporate partners have given him a helping hand while setting up his beer and ready-made alcoholic drinks vending business for future success.

stories.title: Alberta separatists are expected to lose. They’re not preparing to quit
stories.summary: Eight days remain in the campaign in which Albertans will decide whether to set their province on the path to secession.
stories.author: Stephanie Taylor
stories.content:
Ottawa — If Mitch Sylvestre is worried about losing, he isn’t letting it show.

In fact, the avowed separatist offers a blunt prediction for his side should Alberta’s Oct. 19 referendum results confirm a loss.

“It will get stronger,” he told the Star.

Even with eight days left in the campaign, in which Albertans must decide whether to set their province on the path to secession — a push that successive public polls suggest is destined to fail — the battle lines over future fights are already being drawn.

The loudest independence organizers are setting their sights on Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and her United Conservative Party as the vehicle through which to push their agenda. Anticipating that May happen, some federalists in the province are preparing to adapt their fight.

So, while the majority of Albertans May choose to “stay” on Oct. 19, the push to leave will not end with the referendum.

“If you see what we see,” Sylvestre said of the independence movement, “you have two choices: either you capitulate or you accept it. I don’t think people are going to accept it.”

Calls for separation have ebbed and flowed throughout Alberta’s 121-year history, swelling at times like the province’s glacier-fed rivers. Always a minority opinion, the sentiment only ever saw one openly separatist MLA elected back in the 1980s during the height of anger over Ottawa’s long since dismantled National Energy Program.

With no clear leader, the campaign had the effect of cajoling otherwise “disparate voices,” largely speaking online, into something more organized. Morgan pointed to the emergence of numerous third-party advertisers, each of which now has its own membership list, volunteers and ground organization.

“I do believe it’s made it stronger,” Morgan told the Star. “It’s been kind of accidental, but interesting.”

Sylvestre’s group, the Alberta Prosperity Project, boasts in its handbook of having volunteers that range into the “thousands.” He told the Star they relied on 7,000 canvassers to collect 300,000 signatures that pushed the referendum issue.

Drew Barnes, a former UCP MLA who also served with the Wildrose Party, a predecessor to the UCP, agrees the movement will only become more entrenched after Oct. 19.

“Look at how it’s grown,” he said.

It was after a court decision quashed the independence petition drive that Smith announced in May she would put an independence question to Albertans in the form of two options.

The first, that Alberta should remain in Canada, or the second, that it should hold a binding vote on separation.

In the nearly 150 days since, federalist groups have scrambled to mobilize while separatist camps have tried to fill in the blanks about how leaving Canada could work — taking aim at a key criticism over how their unwieldy movement lacks any sort of plan or credibility.

‘We went really heavy on YouTube’

Enter Keith Wilson, the constitutional lawyer best known for representing key organizers of the 2022 “Freedom Convoy” and a co-founder of the Alberta Transition Council, which released a 214-page plan outlining timelines and potential costs associated with seceding from Canada.

His third-party advertising group, Let Alberta Decide, also raised more than $581,000, the most of any independence or federalist group.

Speaking to a recent town hall, Wilson described how writing economic reports was not their only strategy, but sought to drive more attention to their side by marketing in such a way that drew in eyeballs.

“YouTube is a really good way to reach a lot of demographics, a lot of seniors or people who are my age, whose parents are in their 80s and 90s. They say they’re able to do YouTube on their tablets, right? So, we really went heavy on YouTube,” he told the room, according to an online video.

Citing concerns about “voter integrity” in the upcoming vote, Wilson told the audience his group had been canvassing supporters for volunteers to act as scrutineers and had already submitted a list of 124 names, with another group to follow.

While separatist organizers have criss-crossed the province holding town halls and rallies that have drawn hundreds of supporters, their movement remains a very online one.

Chris Ross, a senior analyst at the Canadian Digital Media Research Network who has been tracking the online activities of separatist accounts since the petition drive began, says artificial intelligence has played a major role in their messaging.

“Their advertising strategy is this guerrilla marketing technique, where they really are leveraging technologies like AI in their campaign materials to kind of paint this idyllic post-Canada vision of what Alberta could look like.”

But the biggest shift separatists have undertaken is to say that the vote on Oct. 19 isn’t about separation at all.

“One question matters: who should decide Alberta’s future, Ottawa politicians or Albertans?” declares a radio ad taken out by Wilson’s group.

“Option 2 does not immediately separate Alberta. It begins the legal process toward a future binding referendum, with more debate and a final decision made by Albertans.”

Posting to X earlier in the week, Wilson also wrote, “You can want Alberta to stay in Canada and still vote Option 2” and “Not a separatist? You can still vote Option 2.”

Federalists, including Conservative heavyweights like former Alberta premier Jason Kenney and Stephen Harper — the country’s last Conservative prime minister who championed the “West wants in” message — have cautioned frustrated Albertans against giving in to the temptation of using their vote to voice whatever long-standing displeasure they have against Ottawa out of the risk of the separation debate taking hold for years to come.

They and others warn that the longer the province embroils itself in the issue, the larger the risk it leads to economic pain in the form of business and investment moving elsewhere.

What the data says

In terms of the breakdown of who wants to leave, different public opinion research suggests a majority of Albertans wanting to stay compared to a minority — a figure pegged at around 20 per cent — wishing to pursue the independence path.

New data from Leger this week suggests the margin of those wishing to stay had increased to 70 per cent, up slightly from several months earlier. Abacus Data findings from early September suggest support for remaining within Canada hovering around 64 per cent compared to the roughly 24 per cent who say they would vote to move further down the path of separation, with even fewer saying they would want to outright separate.

“I think the simplest way to describe how a lot of Albertans who are going to vote for Option 2 feel is that it can’t get much worse than it is in their mind,” said Abacus Data CEO David Coletto.

But even as separatist groups have grown more sophisticated in their efforts to drum up support, concerns remain within the province and on Parliament Hill about some leaders seeking backing from U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration.

Jeffrey Rath, a separatist leader and legal counsel for the Alberta Prosperity Project — the group headed by Sylvestre that travelled to Washington three times last year, including to meet with unnamed State Department officials — has spent the past week rejecting a Globe and Mail report which alleged another organizer offered access to Alberta’s resources, including oil and water, in exchange for support.

“These are traitors,” said Edmonton NDP MP Heather McPherson. “I do not expect they will go quiet into that good night.”

Speaking to the Star, Rath defended his decision to meet with U.S. officials and claimed such overtures were what led to U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wading into the matter back in January.

Rath said he was still in touch “from time to time” with his State Department contacts. “I think they enthusiastically would support Alberta independence, but they don’t have a dog in the fight.”

Sylvestre has spent the final months of his campaign pitching supporters on making their voice more loudly heard within Smith’s UCP.

“What we have to do is we have to go to these (annual general meetings), we have to get on boards, and we have to represent ourselves and our views inside the UCP,” he told a crowd gathered at Sylvan Lake, a town about 25 kilometres from Red Deer, Alta.

As chair of the party’s riding association in Bonnyville, a town located more than a two-and-a-half-hour drive from Edmonton, he told the Star that Smith’s government “basically lined up against our movement.”

“Most of the independence people supported Danielle. Most of the independence people were very, very disappointed in her.”

Much of the independence leaders’ anger toward Smith stems from the fact she has publicly stated that she wants Alberta to remain in Canada, including through the launch of an estimated $4 million advertising campaign.

Sylvestre, who backed Smith after Kenney stepped down following months of internal turmoil with his base over his handling of COVID-19, warns the current premier May be heading for the same fate with her core supporters, a sizable number of whom want independence.

“I think that it’s very hard for me to support a leader that doesn’t support us, or at least is not going to stay neutral,” he said.

Regardless of how the Oct. 19 vote goes, Rath, a UCP member, says the movement will be “redoubling our efforts to get rid of Danielle Smith.”

Sam Blackett, a spokesperson for Smith, said in a statement on Friday that she will “respect and honour the results” of the referendum.

The Star, simplified

“We expect all Albertans to do the same.”

Those warnings have prompted Stephen Carter, one of the founders of Alberta’s Voice, a third-party advertiser for the “stay” side, to consider turning it into a permanent political advertiser targeting candidates who support separation. He pointed to UCP MLA Jason Stephan as one example after Stephan told CBC News he plans to vote for Option 2 but does not want Alberta to separate.

“They’re not going to stop,” Carter said.

Evan Menzies, who worked as communications director for the UCP and Wildrose Party before that, suggests the average party voter will want to move on from the independence issue and begin thinking about the province’s slated 2027 election.

But those who lose will likely try to take more control through the party’s internal governance mechanisms in hopes to “bend” it toward their will, he says.

“I think there will be a real sense of responsibility and duty for those who are on the federalist side of the party, or those who just want to move on, to mobilize over the next few months.”

stories.title: TNT shortage has one company angling to get Canada back in the explosives business
stories.summary: TNT shortages have sent a panic all along the West's explosives supply chain as militaries and civilian mining and construction companies reliant on the explosive are confronted with delays and
stories.author: Allan Woods
stories.content:
It has taken the rubble and dust and fog of wars in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran to make one thing shockingly clear to explosives experts and entrepreneurs around the world.

“We’re vulnerable,” said Patrick Gagnon, a former Liberal member of Parliament now running Nalagx Corp., a company that hopes to bring the production of TNT back to Canada after a decades-long hiatus.

Vulnerable on the battlefields, which are increasingly dominated by the side that can launch the most drones with the most explosives packed into or carried beneath them.

Vulnerable economically too, in a world where cars, computers and other hi-tech goods rely on critical minerals that must be blasted and mined from the ground or the rock.

Vulnerable because one of the Western world’s most important suppliers — a Polish firm operating out of a factory founded by Nazi occupation forces during World War II — is no longer able to keep up with the booming demand for its main product, trinitrotoluene.

Gagnon first learned of the global shortage in 2024 from his son, who works in the defence industry in California.

Clark Mica started hearing similar issues in the fall of 2024 from civilian members of the Washington-based industry association he runs, the Institute of Makers of Explosives.

“Their main supplier … was no longer able to guarantee supply due to Nato allies needing that TNT as a resource,” Mica said.

Nato militaries needed TNT to feed the Ukrainian military with the shells and other munitions needed to fight off invading Russians.

Ukraine had its own TNT plant, located in the eastern region of Luhansk, that was capable of producing 10,000 metric tonnes annually. But it was lost shortly after the war began in 2022, when the territory was invaded and occupied by Russian forces.

The war has seen Ukrainian drones and missiles targeting Russian explosives and ammunition plants. One particularly daring 2023 attack involved a remotely piloted Ukrainian boat, loaded with 450 kilograms of TNT, striking a Russian tanker.

The TNT shortages have sent a panic all along the West’s explosives supply chain as militaries and civilian mining and construction companies reliant on the explosive are confronted with delays and skyrocketing costs, with price increases reaching as high as 400 per cent at one point, according to Mica.

Efforts to convince the White House to exempt imported explosives from the trade duties, at least until domestic production gets up and running, have been unsuccessful.

The situation is a far cry from the Second World War, when Canada’s economy went on a war footing that saw it become the world’s fourth largest producer of munitions and a major producer of TNT .

But the cloak-and-dagger tactics of the Cold War, which emphasized detente over detonations, resulted in a movement to wind down domestic TNT production, which had left an environmental legacy of tainted and toxic soil and water.

The advent of stronger industrial environmental regulations in the 1970s and 1980s, coupled with globalization, made it more attractive to outsource explosives production, Mica said.

The keeper of the world’s largest explosives arsenal, the United States, shuttered its last TNT plant in 1986.

But Mica said there has long been an awareness that the long supply chain for what is known as energetics was a vulnerability.

“It wasn’t until everything kind of came to a head between Russia and Ukraine, and Israel and Gaza, and now Iran, that everyone woke up to the fact that we can’t be reliant on even our allies for these really critical materials that are used both for national security and our domestic economy.”

Canada is facing a similar reckoning as Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government seeks both to build up Canada’s military strength and capabilities and to turbocharge the Canadian economy by fast-tracking infrastructure, energy and mining projects, all of which will require explosive charges in addition to massive financial investments.

The Polish TNT producer Nitro-Tech currently produces about 10,000 metric tonnes annually. In March, it announced plans for a new production line that would double output within four years.

The U.S. military is planning a TNT production facility in Kentucky that could be in operation by 2029, but it would reportedly only produce about 2,300 metric tonnes a year.

Similar projects have been launched in Sweden and Finland, and the British government has funded feasibility studies with an eye to building six new ammunition plants.

The Canadian proposal by Gagnon’s Nalagx Corp., which counts former Liberal cabinet minister Wayne Easter and retired general Maurice Baril as advisers, is to produce 10,000 metric tonnes of TNT annually with up to 40 per cent for civilian purposes and the remainder going to the militaries of Nato member states.

That still falls well short of Russia, which can produce about 50,000 metric tonnes of TNT a year, or China, which is also a major producer but restricts exports to the U.S. and Western countries.

Over the summer, Nalagx Corp. and the New Brunswick government agreed on a site for the proposed plant in the north of the province, near the Port of Belledune.

“This is going to be a Canadian project, built by Canadians, operated by Canadians and owned by Canadians,” Gagnon said, adding that the company plans to unveil more details about its financing and operations later this month.

“We’re answering the call and we are perfectly aligned with the vision that Prime Minister Carney has for Canada and Nato.”

If Gagnon sounds bullish, it’s because the competition is stiff.

Last month, PGZ, the state-owned Polish firm, told Reuters it was “in the discussion phase” about opening a Canadian production facility in Canada, although it had not found financing or a specific location.

In late 2025, Nalagx Corp. came to an understanding with a French firm, Eurenco, to operate its proposed TNT plant.

Gagnon said Eurenco later cast doubt on the feasibility of the project and backed away from it, only to later announce a partnership with PGZ.

It has the appearance of a cutthroat race just to get to the starting line.

“I think it’ll be interesting to see how many of these plants actually get built,” said Mica.

The other question is whether TNT plants should be built at all.

Certainly, there is a military and national-security case to support the scaling up of production among Nato allies, particularly as Europe increasingly braces for the possibility of direct war with Russia.

But activists have also challenged the use of explosives that have been produced in Europe and shipped through Canada for use in American shells, missiles and bombs that are provided to Israel for use in Gaza and across the Middle East.

It’s part of a “doubly destructive business” for which TNT production in Poland is responsible, Polish academic Ewa Górska, an assistant professor at Wroclaw University’s Digital Justice Centre, which studies the intersection of technology and criminal justice, wrote in a paper last month .

The Polish plant “not only facilitates explosive violence in war zones around the world but also precipitates ecological violence in Poland.”

The three-step chemical process for producing TNT results in wastewater “characterized by high toxicity, carcinogenicity, resistance to degradation and a tendency to accumulate in the natural environment,” Górska wrote.

A 2019 audit found that the presence of “explosive substances” in the Polish wastewater had been “significantly reduced.” But this was due to “natural processes, such as sunlight” rather than any technology implemented by the company.
