stories.title: Complaint filed to medical regulator over MP saying fentanyl 'readily available' in Maid report
stories.summary: Toronto - Remarks made by a member of Parliament, who is also a doctor, suggesting illicit drugs such as fentanyl are a “painless” and “readily available” option to end one’s life are now the subject of a complaint filed to the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario.
stories.author: Hannah Alberga The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Remarks made by a member of Parliament, who is also a doctor, suggesting illicit drugs such as fentanyl are a “painless” and “readily available” option to end one’s life are now the subject of a complaint filed to the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario.

The complainant, Claire Brosseau, a 49-year-old woman who has been trying to get access to medical assistance in dying for persistent mental disorders that began when she was a child, said she was triggered by Dr. Marcus Powlowski’s “irresponsible, thoughtless and dangerous” words.

She takes issue with his supplementary opinion, attached to a special joint committee report published in June on medical assistance in dying and mental disorders as a sole underlying medical condition. In it, he wrote:

“The option to end one’s life remains, irrespective of MAID, readily available in Canada. Furthermore, there are painless options readily available. One example being illicit narcotics like fentanyl. To my dismay it is arguably easier for my teenage sons to access fentanyl in my hometown of Thunder Bay than it is for me (a doctor) to renew my Lipitor prescription (a cholesterol medication).”

The quote is included in Powlowski’s written argument against expanding access to MAID for mental illness until fundamental concerns are addressed. He outlines his reasons, saying it is impossible to determine that a person’s mental illness is irremediable, as required by law. He also raises the issue of access to mental health services and social supports, and says testimony from practitioners suggests there is no consensus on how to distinguish suicidality from rational decision-making.

In a section titled “Why do we try to prevent suicide?,” Powlowski analyzes the role of authorities in intervening in suicide attempts in order to prevent harm, versus personal autonomy. It’s there that the lines Brosseau takes issue with are written.

From Brosseau’s perspective, “He gave us information on how to kill ourselves,” she said in an interview from bed in Toronto, where she says she spends most of her days, hair bundled in a bandana.

Her written complaint has been reviewed by The Canadian Press, along with her emails with an investigator from the regulatory college, who said in the correspondence that Powlowski has until Oct. 22 to file a response before it goes to a committee for review.

However, Powlowski’s chief of staff said that the Liberal MP for Thunder Bay-Rainy River, who was an emergency room doctor before he was elected in 2019, had not received notification of the complaint and did not want to answer questions about it.

“He prepared something, but in the end, he decided he doesn’t want to comment on it,” William Fassett, his chief of staff, said over a phone call.

The college said it could not confirm whether an investigation was underway because the complaints process is confidential.

On Wednesday, the federal government said it will introduce legislation this fall that would bar people suffering solely from a mental illness to access medical assistance in dying.

THE COMPLAINT

Brosseau acknowledges in the complaint that a member of Parliament is entitled to freedom of speech. And though she was personally pained by the findings of the parliamentary committee — which Powlowski was the co-chair of and which recommended the federal government “indefinitely pause” an expansion of MAID to people with mental disorders — she says her complaint is separate from all of that.

“In a public document dealing directly with suicide, mental illness and medical practice, he stated that ending one’s life is ‘readily available,’ characterized illicit fentanyl as a ‘painless’ option, and added that fentanyl is arguably easier for his teenage sons to obtain than it is for him to renew a prescription,” Brosseau wrote.

“Those statements identify and normalize a lethal means, present a medically misleading account of opioid poisoning, and create a foreseeable risk of harm to vulnerable readers.”

Brosseau argues that Powlowski positions suicide in an attractive manner, contrary to the college’s standards, which characterize unprofessional behaviour as “words, actions or inactions by a physician that interfere with (or may interfere with) the delivery of quality care, public trust in the profession, the safety or perceived safety of others.”

“It is therefore reasonable for the college to examine whether the statement was misleading and whether Dr. Powlowski adequately considered its foreseeable impact,” Brosseau states in the complaint.

“It triggered me and I’m not the only one,” she said.

Avery Teplitsky, who says he’s spent most of his life in the mental health system, said he was also outraged by the level of disregard coming from someone who is both a doctor and an elected official. “It’s just completely missing the entire point,” Teplitsky, 53, said of Powlowski’s remarks.

In a blog post for Dying with Dignity, Justin Dickie also wrote about the fentanyl comments from his perspective as someone who lives with depression. “Does this sound like an unbiased party to you?” he wrote in August.

Less than a week before Brosseau filed the complaint, a Toronto judge denied her motion for a constitutional exemption from a law that currently prevents people from applying for MAID on the basis of mental illness alone.

She is also the plaintiff in a constitutional challenge, arguing that excluding Canadians whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness from accessing MAID is a breach of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

“I’m clinging to life by my fingernails,” she said.

Brosseau said she does not care if the timing of her complaint looks strategic with her court battle – she just wants Powlowski to acknowledge the danger of his remarks.

The regulatory college says complaints can result in issuing advice to a doctor on how to improve their practice or conduct; requiring remedial self-study; ordering the doctor to take specific courses; issuing a verbal caution; or, where appropriate, referring the matter to the Ontario Physicians and Surgeons Discipline Tribunal.

Brosseau said she wants Powlowski to make a public statement taking back what he said, and informing people of what happens when you overdose on fentanyl, including how awful it is.

“But what I want and what’s going to happen are two very different things.”

If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 24-7 by calling or texting 988, Canada’s national suicide prevention helpline.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 10, 2026.

stories.title: Overlapping local, provincial elections in B.C. causing confusion: candidates
stories.summary: Cori Ramsay, a candidate for city council in Prince George, B.C., says a voter told her they can't wait to cast a ballot for her on Oct. 24. The voter would surely be disappointed, as Ramsay's election is a week earlier, ON Oct. 17.
stories.author: Marissa Birnie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Cori Ramsay, a candidate for city council in Prince George, B.C., says a voter told her they can’t wait to cast a ballot for her on Oct. 24. The voter would surely be disappointed, as Ramsay’s election is a week earlier, ON Oct. 17.

As British Columbians contend with local and provincial elections in October, some candidates say the overlap is confusing and overwhelming voters.

The local elections on Oct. 17 will see voters elect mayors, councillors, school board trustees and other local officials, while a provincial vote will be held Oct. 24 to elect 93 members of the legislature, which will determine B.C.‘s next premier.

NDP Leader David Eby’s decision to call a snap election came as the local election campaign period had already begun, and earned swift condemnation from the Union of BC Municipalities, which represents local governments in the province.

Ramsay, the union’s former president, said she thinks the decision has put an unfair strain on the electorate.

“I’m hearing candidates going door-to-door for the municipal election being told that ‘I can’t vote for you because I’m voting for our MLA,’” she said.

The union’s current president, Jenna Stoner, who is running for mayor in Squamish, B.C., said she’s seen voters confused about where and when to vote.

While the election dates are separate, the local election day overlaps with provincial advance voting.

“There’s just so much confusion in the community right now that we’re having to navigate, and it’s just so frustrating,” Ramsay said.

She said the dual elections are hurting voters’ ability to assess candidates in a crowded field, and that one frustrated and overwhelmed voter said she would base her vote on a “vibe check.”

Tanya Webking, who is running with the BC Green Party for Vancouver-Strathcona in the provincial election, said she’s had voters mistake her as running for the Green Party of Vancouver. A few said they forgot about the double elections.

She said she’s heard from multiple voters who are angry about the provincial election call and view it as costly and unnecessary.

Paul Thompson, a Vancouver voter, said it’s been difficult to get a handle on the multiple candidates running in the city’s municipal elections, where there are more than 100 people on the ballot.

“It’s pretty much impossible to sit down and read every single person’s point of view and what they’re campaigning for,” he said.

It was also hard to understand how the city and its various bodies, such as the park board, differ, he said.

Thompson has since cast his votes early in both elections, but said the provincial election call was a poor choice.

“They had the majority in the government and they still went ahead and wasted taxpayers’ money on something that nobody that I’ve spoken to actually wanted,” he said.

When asked about the overlapping elections at a campaign event on Wednesday, Eby said he had confidence in electors’ ability to vote in two elections.

“The local candidate elections, as far as I can tell, are running just fine,” he said, adding that a future report from Elections BC May address the issue.

Elections BC said it hasn’t weighed the outcomes or impacts of the dual elections because the provincial election campaign is not finished.

The independent agency, which administers the provincial election, added that it has received a “large number” of applications for election officials and other staff, more than the last provincial election. It previously said 17,000 election officials were needed for the 2026 election.

“However, in rural and remote communities, we are still hiring election officials and office staff up to final voting day,” Elections BC said in an email on Thursday.

Stoner, Ramsay and Webking each expressed concerns about the dual elections’ effect on campaign volunteers and election staffing.

Stoner said she’s seen volunteer burnout, and there is the potential of volunteers or polling staff being pulled to provincial campaigns at the expense of local efforts.

“There’s limited capacity in the system and we’ve doubled the requirement of that system without necessarily doubling the resources,” she said.

Ramsay said the local election has lost some campaign workers who went to work on the provincial election instead, since it offers a few extra days of employment at more pay.

Michael MacKenzie, a professor of political studies and the Jarislowsky chair in trust and political leadership at Vancouver Island University, said the overlapping campaigns are bad for democracy.

“We tend to think that our municipal governments are somehow less important. This is not true. They make important decisions that affect our lives,” he said.

He noted that both local and provincial candidates often rely on the same volunteer base to run their campaigns, and resources are stretched thin. Some of his own students are volunteering in multiple elections or have switched campaigns entirely.

He said he doesn’t think voter fatigue will be an issue because British Columbians are already used to having elections every four years.

“The problem really is just the work that needs to be done to cast an informed vote,” he said.

Municipal elections tend to have abysmal voter turnouts, and competing with the more visible provincial election could siphon the attention of voters, MacKenzie said.

In Prince George, where Ramsay is pursuing a third term on city council, voter turnout in the local elections has been among the lowest in the province in recent years.

“I’m hoping that we see some activity at the polls, but I do think that voters will favour one election over the other at the end of the day,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 10, 2026.

stories.title: 'Home' documentary from 'Degrassi' co-creator explores complexities of Ontario encampment
stories.summary: Toronto - When tents started popping up on the lawn in front of a sprawling provincial property in Cobourg, Ont., television producer Linda Schuyler wondered who the people living in the encampment were.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - When tents started popping up on the lawn in front of a sprawling provincial property in Cobourg, Ont., television producer Linda Schuyler wondered who the people living in the encampment were.

“I started to go in and get to know them,” said Schuyler, a filmmaker and producer who is best known as the co-creator of the “Degrassi” television series.

“As Torontonians, we have been very aware of the homeless crisis for a long period of time. And I always felt kind of helpless about it. It seemed like such a big problem. I didn’t know what I could do to help,” said Schuyler, who splits her time between Toronto and a community near the southern Ontario lakeside town.

Filmmakers Linda Schuyler and Will Bowes discuss getting to know the individuals who lived inside an encampment in Cobourg, Ont., and helping them feel comfortable to be interviewed for the TVO documentary, "Home." (Oct. 10, 2026)

She teamed up with filmmaker Will Bowes to explore the inner workings of the encampment and the complex individual circumstances of its residents.

The result is a new documentary, titled “Home,” set to premiere on TVO on Saturday, coinciding with World Homeless Day.

The film introduces audiences to several unhoused people who settled at Brookside, a vacant property owned by the province that had previously been home to Cobourg’s elite and later became a youth detention centre. It details the myriad reasons how someone can end up without a home, from executives and business owners losing their livelihoods, to those who faced abusive partners, the death of loved ones and the challenges of addiction and mental health.

The filmmakers said they first entered without filming equipment and simply listened to people’s stories. Once they formed relationships, the filmmakers asked if people were comfortable speaking on camera. If they did, they’d receive a Tim Hortons gift card to acknowledge their time.

Schuyler said they’d also ask people if they would give them a tour of their tents or structures.

“And without a doubt, they would all say, ‘Oh, just a minute. Let me tidy up a bit,” she said.

“They really took pride in building little gardens and little pathways to get to their homes,” Bowes added. “It was remarkable what they were able to accomplish.”

Along with highlighting the people inside the encampment, the film, which collected around 60 hours of footage over about a year, also shared the perspectives of people in the local community. That included the town’s mayor as well as social workers, community advocates and concerned citizens who had reservations about the proximity of the encampment to local schools.

“Even though we wanted to get to know the people in the encampment, we did want to be fair to the community and give some of the local people an opportunity to talk about it from their perspective,” Schuyler said.

The documentary does not, however, include any narration, a deliberate choice because “narration can be leading and it can be judgmental,” Schuyler said.

“It’s a principle that we had way back in ‘Degrassi.’ We really wanted to give our young people an authentic voice and we really wanted to look at whatever issue we were dealing with from multiple sides. And that approach spilled over into this documentary,” Schuyler said.

“Without getting too political about it, we wanted to just show that it’s a multi-faceted story,” she said.

Bowes said the experience of making the documentary forced him to acknowledge the biases he had formed around homeless people.

“I also felt like if you end up in an encampment, that is a result of years, if not decades of bad decisions (and) definite substance abuse,” Bowes said. “But that couldn’t be farther from the truth. Many people are there because they had a really terrible time during COVID.”

Making this film also showed him how the journey of homelessness is not linear. For example, at one point, the documentary follows a few people who moved into a motel after the encampment was dismantled following the sale of Brookside. However, their motel stay was temporary and soon after they arrived, they had to leave.

“Sometimes you’re getting ahead and then the rug gets pulled out from under you, and that was really frustrating for us obviously as filmmakers, who are trying to put together a narrative, and you want the narrative to progress and get better and see someone start thriving or at least start taking the steps to,” Bowes said.

“But unfortunately that just wasn’t possible,” he said.

The filmmakers said the goal isn’t for the documentary to provide a clearcut answer for how to solve the issue but rather for audiences to walk away having to mull it over for themselves.

“We are so rich with resources, both land and otherwise, I find it embarrassing as a Canadian that we cannot treat our unhoused better,” Schuyler said. “I hope that that sentiment somehow will arouse in people who watch the documentary.”

Bowes said he also hopes the film leads to more empathy for homeless people.

“A little bit more understanding for the human being that you might have otherwise walked past or put a label on,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 10, 2026.

stories.title: He challenged Canada's immigration decision over its ‘copied and pasted’ refusal. A judge ruled in his favour
stories.summary: Federal Court rules immigration officer’s analysis was “largely copied verbatim” from the first refusal by a colleague.
stories.author: Nicholas Keung
stories.content:
The Federal Court has quashed the refusal of an Afghan immigration applicant because the officer’s analysis was “largely copied verbatim” from the first refusal by another colleague against the same man.

In sending the case back to the Immigration Department for a new assessment, Judge Darren R. Thorne ruled that it was procedurally unfair for the officer to refuse the humanitarian and compassionate resettlement application of Atiqullah Lali, who lives without status in Turkey and faces deportation to Afghanistan.

“Much of the analysis is largely copied verbatim, with effectively identical wording, with some minimal cosmetic edits,” the judge wrote in the ruling released on Friday.

“I am not satisfied that a reasonable person apprised of the circumstances would conclude that the officer turned their mind to the evidence and the issues and rendered an impartial, independent decision.”

Lali, 30, said he fled from Afghanistan to Turkey in August 2021 to escape persecution by the Taliban, which threatened to forcibly recruit him as punishment for the women’s rights activism of his father and sister. He lived in Istanbul as an undocumented migrant while awaiting the processing of his resettlement to Canada.

His immigration application to Canada was first refused in May 2024 because he did not provide the “refugee status determination” document issued by the Turkish government or the United Nations Refugee Agency that certified him as a refugee.

Afghan refugee says similarities show he didn’t get a fresh look at his application as ordered by Federal Court.

He had requested an exemption from that requirement because Turkey doesn’t allow the UN agency to provide refugee certificates in the country and it would put him at risk of detention and deportation to Afghanistan if he came forward. The officer rejected his request.

A second refusal was issued April 2025 despite updates by Lali following his arrest and detention by Turkish police the year before. He is currently subject to an enforceable Turkish deportation order to send him back to Afghanistan. The court heard his appeal in August.

“Essentially all of the decision-making analysis in the decision has clearly been directly copied from the earlier decision,” wrote Thorne.

The court also rejected the government’s argument that any editing of the language of the first refusal by the second officer was an indication that there was a fresh assessment of the case.

“It is fair to say that the respondent struggled to provide examples of any such meaningful edits when asked, ultimately identifying only the addition of a date in one section of the decision, and elsewhere the addition of the word ‘indeed,’ prior to an otherwise verbatim replicated paragraph,” Thorne noted.

The judge agreed with the government that when an officer is faced with almost exactly the same submissions under the same legislative and policy constraints, the reasoning and decisions would look similar. However, he also pointed out that the second officer did not address any of the information and arguments updated in Lali’s file, indicating “a lack of engagement with those matters.”

The court ordered the Immigration Department assign Lali’s case to a new officer and make a new decision within 45 days, given the urgency of the matter.

Lali’s co-counsel Andrew Koltun said his client and his sponsors in Canada were grateful for the court ruling, which “vindicates” their views of the officer’s failure to reconsider the case by using mostly “copied-and-pasted material” from the reasons for the first refusal.

stories.title: Knights fall to Otters for second straight loss
stories.summary: The London Knights have now dropped two games after a loss on home ice at the hand of the Erie Otters.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The London Knights have now dropped two games after a loss on home ice at the hand of the Erie Otters.

London got out to an early 2-0 lead in the first period with goals from Eloan Le Gallic and Cohen Bidgood, before Erie came back with two goals of their own in under a minute midway through the second period.

Thomas Zocco would restore the lead for the Knights early in the third on the power play, before Broden McArthur evened it up for the Otters with four minutes left in regulation.

The Knights hope to get back in the win column on Tuesday when they head up to the 401 to take on the rival Kitchener Rangers.

stories.title: Supreme Court sets sentencing framework for Indigenous intimate partner violence cases
stories.summary: The court clarifies how judges should appropriately sentence offenders when both the accused and victim are Indigenous
stories.author: Willow Fiddler
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada has clarified how courts should appropriately sentence offenders in cases of intimate partner violence when both the accused and victim are Indigenous.

The 5-4 decision released Friday upholds the reduced three-year sentence of a Mi’kmaq man and provides new guidance on what the Supreme Court has called the “twin crises” of violence against Indigenous women and the overincarceration of Indigenous people.

The tight vote demonstrated how difficult it is for judges to rule on cases that have seemingly conflicting sentencing provisions for Indigenous offenders while protecting Indigenous victims.

The Supreme Court panel of nine judges, which included majority-voting Indigenous Justice Michelle O’Bonsawin, considered how sentencing provisions in the Criminal Code related to addressing the issues of the overrepresentation of Indigenous people in prisons and the vulnerabilities of Indigenous women to intimate partner violence. The court concluded they have to be considered together. The case was heard last December.

In its decision, the majority said courts have to take Indigenous perspectives and the voices of Indigenous victims seriously, particularly in sentencing circles.

“This means treating that circle as a bridge between the criminal justice system and Indigenous models of justice, not an exercise in performative tokenism, which will only erode trust, set back reconciliation and exacerbate the challenges Indigenous people face with the criminal justice system,” the decision states.

Courts aren’t bound by sentencing circle recommendations and rulings are at the discretion of each judge.

The court heard the notion that courts must choose between supporting Indigenous women victims of crime or addressing the mass incarceration of Indigenous people is a false dichotomy, a position argued in submissions by the accused and interveners, including Aboriginal Legal Services (ALS) from Toronto, where lawyer Christa Big Canoe is based.

It’s not an either-or, Ms. Big Canoe told the Globe.

“We think this is a clear instruction to all other courts that when you have an Indigenous offender, an Indigenous woman victim, that you have to balance and that you should be taking into consideration the Indigenous community justice processes that have occurred,” she said.

Ms. Big Canoe said the original trial judge failed to properly consider the sentencing circle that was held for the accused (the victim did not participate) and conducted by two Mi’kmaw lawyers who didn’t recommend further incarceration because of the accused’s history of mental health illness.

As one of 21 interveners, Ms. Big Canoe said the position of the ALS was that prison sentences don’t make communities safer.

“People come out worse off and much more violent. It hasn’t been working for decades and generations now,” she said.

Justice O’Bonsawin wrote in the majority decision that sentencing judges must follow three specific steps in such cases.

First, the judge must weigh the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender in the context of the Indigenous identities and backgrounds of the parties.

Second, the judge must sensitively identify the relevant criminal sentencing objectives, prioritizing denunciation and deterrence.

Lastly, the judge must choose the proportionate and just sentence within the context of the Indigenous parties, given that Parliament has expressly directed sentencing judges to consider all available sanctions other than imprisonment.

The top court added that the sentencing circle process can be relevant to understanding the availability of alternative sentencing options in the community, as well as the community’s perspective on the sentence that would best achieve the objectives.

The ruling comes in the case of Harry Arthur Cope, a Mi’kmaq man with severe mental health challenges who was sentenced to five years in prison after pleading guilty in 2022 to aggravated assault against his partner, a Mi’kmaq woman.

The Nova Scotia Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to three years.

The Supreme Court ruled Friday the three-year sentence should stand.

The top court found the sentencing judge did not recognize that the offender’s mental illness contributed to the commission of the aggravated assault and did not consider the effect of that illness on the relevant sentencing objectives.

The sentencing judge would have settled on a shorter prison term had she properly considered the offender’s significant mental health issues, particularly when viewed in light of a sentencing circle’s recommendations in the case, the Supreme Court said.

The four dissenting Supreme Court judges argued that the Crown’s appeal should be allowed and the original sentence imposed by the sentencing judge restored.

They said the majority’s sentencing framework fails to reflect Parliament’s direction to sentencing judges to prioritize denunciation and deterrence, and to generally impose harsher sentences for the abuse of vulnerable victims, including Indigenous women and girls.

The majority found the original trial judge made two errors in her sentencing, including failing to consider how a longer prison sentence could aggravate the accused’s severe mental health illness, ultimately decreasing chances of rehabilitation.

Gladue principles, derived from a case decided by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1999, require courts to consider an Indigenous offender’s life experience and history as they relate to systemic impacts stemming from colonization (such as residential schools) through presentencing written reports.

More recent provisions were added to the Criminal Code following the national inquiry report on missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls, recognizing those groups as vulnerable individuals facing disproportionate violence, and that such increased vulnerability can weigh in favour of a more severe sentence (whether the accused is Indigenous or not).

stories.title: Second crossing debate resurfaces in Central Okanagan during B.C. election campaign
stories.summary: The issue was highlighted earlier this month again when an accident forced the closure of all three southbound lanes for several hours, creating significant traffic backlogs.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
A second crossing connecting Kelowna and West Kelowna is once again emerging as an election issue, with local candidates offering different views on how to address growing traffic congestion on and around the W.A.C Bennett Bridge.

Calls for another bridge have persisted for years, as commuters regularly face delays on the existing crossing on Okanagan Lake.

“I think bridge traffic in the morning can be a bit much,” says Ryan Burley, who uses the bridge regularly.

The issue was highlighted earlier this month again when an accident forced the closure of all three southbound lanes for several hours, creating significant traffic backlogs.

BC NDP candidate for Kelowna Centre, Loyal Wooldridge, recently took a humorous approach to the issue, posting a social media video of himself attempting to cross the lake in a small dinghy.

But while Wooldridge is using humour to draw attention to the problem, he says building a second crossing is a long-term prospect and improving the existing bridge should be the immediate priority.

“There’s actually a plan on the books to improve traffic flow without the time and cost it would take, which would be billions of dollars to build a second crossing,” Wooldridge said.

Asked why improvements have not moved forward despite the BC NDP being in government for nearly a decade, Wooldridge pointed to the need for stronger advocacy locally.

“My commitment is that I’m going to advocate for Kelowna,” he said. “This is a province-approved plan that needs advocacy locally for both Kelowna, WFN (Westbank First Nation) and West Kelowna to improve traffic flow by increasing capacity at the bridge, also improving the intersections right when you get off the bridge into Kelowna and it’s done by adding another lane to the existing bridge itself.”

During the 2024 provincial election campaign, the BC Conservatives, then led by John Rustad, promised to build a second crossing by 2032 if elected.

That timeline is no longer being reaffirmed under the party’s new leadership.

BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson has not ruled out another crossing but says he wants to hear from British Columbians before making commitments.

“Right now I am all ears. I’m listening to British Columbians, visiting British Columbians, and I absolutely, of course, want to look at everything,” Doerkson said.

Locally, BC Conservative candidate for Kelowna Centre Kristina Loewen maintained the party has not abandoned the idea.

“I don’t feel like we’re backtracking on that promise exactly. I would say that we’re continuing to look at it,” Loewen said. “We haven’t really had the chance and the opportunity in the opposition to look at building a bridge, and we’d like to.”

Loewen added she wants planning for a second crossing to start.

“We need to start planning for it in a way that works together with the city, works with multiple levels of government and reopens the studies that have been done on it,” Loewen said. “We need to start building the infrastructure, at least in and around the bridge.”

BC Green Party candidate Saoirse MacKinnon was unavailable for comment on the issue Friday.

paragraphs: A second crossing connecting Kelowna and West Kelowna is once again emerging as an election issue, with local candidates offering different views on how to address growing traffic congestion on and around the W.A.C Bennett Bridge.
Calls for another bridge have persisted for years, as commuters regularly face delays on the existing crossing on Okanagan Lake.
“I think bridge traffic in the morning can be a bit much,” says Ryan Burley, who uses the bridge regularly.
The issue was highlighted earlier this month again when an accident forced the closure of all three southbound lanes for several hours, creating significant traffic backlogs.
BC NDP candidate for Kelowna Centre, Loyal Wooldridge, recently took a humorous approach to the issue, posting a social media video of himself attempting to cross the lake in a small dinghy.
But while Wooldridge is using humour to draw attention to the problem, he says building a second crossing is a long-term prospect and improving the existing bridge should be the immediate priority.
“There’s actually a plan on the books to improve traffic flow without the time and cost it would take, which would be billions of dollars to build a second crossing,” Wooldridge said.
Asked why improvements have not moved forward despite the BC NDP being in government for nearly a decade, Wooldridge pointed to the need for stronger advocacy locally.

“My commitment is that I’m going to advocate for Kelowna,” he said. “This is a province-approved plan that needs advocacy locally for both Kelowna, WFN (Westbank First Nation) and West Kelowna to improve traffic flow by increasing capacity at the bridge, also improving the intersections right when you get off the bridge into Kelowna and it’s done by adding another lane to the existing bridge itself.”
During the 2024 provincial election campaign, the BC Conservatives, then led by John Rustad, promised to build a second crossing by 2032 if elected.
That timeline is no longer being reaffirmed under the party’s new leadership.
BC Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson has not ruled out another crossing but says he wants to hear from British Columbians before making commitments.

stories.title: The high risk of seeing double in Toronto’s mayoral race
stories.summary: Braeden Chow and Olivia Chow share a surname but are running very different campaigns
stories.author: Patrick White
stories.content:
In his promotional photos, Braeden Chow dons mayoral chic: button-down shirt and loose tie. On this day, with a Globe photographer present, he opts for black Ray-Bans, a black leather jacket and black pants. He’s become the Toronto election’s man of mystery. Why not embrace the part?

With the Toronto mayoral race tightening in recent days, neither of the front-runners can afford miscast ballots. That scrutiny has wrenched Mr. Chow’s candidacy out of obscurity. He shares a last name with the incumbent, Mayor Olivia Chow, and appears immediately above her on the ballot, creating the real possibility of Ms. Chow losing voters to Mr. Chow, political scientists told The Globe.

“It’s a serious issue,” said York University politics professor Dennis Pilon. “If the numbers even up, then suddenly a candidate that surprisingly gets a few thousand votes could be decisive.”

But who is the unknown Chow?

His was a inconspicuous candidacy until Ms. Chow emerged from early voting on Tuesday to speak with reporters. They wanted to ask about Chris Alexander, the former federal candidate who had dropped out of the race that morning. She had something else on her mind.

“I just noticed there is two Chows on the ballot and there is one before me,” she said, admitting she’d nearly voted for the wrong person.

Her campaign followed up with a social media post and a statement reminding voters to mark the right Chow on their ballots. Reddit commenters soon labelled him a decoy candidate, a plant and a spoiler – someone whose last name alone could siphon enough votes away from Ms. Chow to allow her main challenger, Brad Bradford, to win an ever-tightening contest.

“I’d feel bad for sure if that happened,” said Mr. Chow, who insisted nobody recruited him to the race while sitting on a bench outside the Art Gallery of Ontario and sipping a double-double. “But I’d also say Olivia could join forces with me. If I win, she’s on my team for sure.”

That’s a stretch – for a few reasons. His support has failed to register in polling.

What’s more, they have incompatible political philosophies (he wants to fund city services through donations from the rich and train 100 police to be Navy Seals, “like GI Joe and GI Jane,” he said).

And then there’s the family matter.

He insists he’s the mayor’s second cousin.

But, according to the mayor’s campaign team, that’s simply not true.

“We can confirm that Braeden Chow is not related to Olivia Chow,” said campaign spokesman Zeus Eden in a statement to The Globe. “We have no idea where he comes from. Our campaign is encouraging all voters to look to Olivia Chow, who is number 9 on the ballot.”

No hard feelings. He says he endorses Ms. Chow all the same and hopes she wins. It’s an unconventional campaign.

She could use the support. Ms. Chow’s odds of winning appeared to narrow this week, with Mainstreet Research releasing a poll on Friday showing she leads Mr. Bradford by just 2.9 points among decided and leaning voters. The poll of 1,000 people carries a margin of error of 3.1 per cent 19 times out of 20 and was conducted Oct. 6 and 7, after Mr. Alexander had withdrawn.

Researchers have found that minor candidates can pick up as much as two-tenths of a per cent if they appear next to a major candidate, said Charles Tessier, expert in citizen behavior at Tact, a Quebec-based public affairs firm and a ballot-order researcher.

Fifty-three candidates are vying to be Toronto’s chief magistrate. That’s down considerably from the 102 who ran in 2023, but far greater than other Canadian cities. The upcoming Vancouver election has eight mayoral candidates while Winnipeg has 12.

“The decision in Toronto is more prone to that kind of mistake because there are so many candidates,” he said. “If the election is decided by a few votes, it could have an effect.”

Some jurisdictions put candidate names in random order to avoid side-by-side name duplication. Others place pictures next to the candidates. Still others place high fees and endorsement requirements on anyone applying to be a candidate. In Toronto, mayoral aspirants need endorsements from 25 people and a $200 filing fee to enter the race.

Mr. Chow said he got 25 names when he filed his candidacy in May, but some endorsers messed up the form. He had to ask strangers outside City Hall to complete the list.

Since then, he hasn’t done much campaigning. He says he was homeless for about a week last month, showering at GoodLife Fitness. He’s also been taking care of a friend’s cats and working on registering a charity, the Nora Foundation, which will provide free groceries, laundry, transportation to those in need, according to a website he registered in June. He isn’t certain yet how it will accomplish those lofty goals.

“Honestly, that’s a ChatGPT site,” he said. “But I had the homeless week, and the taking care of cats and I’m landscaping in the summer. I haven’t had time to open a location and all that. But soon.”

stories.title: Steven Galloway testifies his book sales ‘cratered’ because of sexual-assault allegations
stories.summary: Former UBC professor faces first day of cross-examination at defamation trial at B.C. Supreme Court
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Steven Galloway’s follow-up to The Cellist of Sarajevo sold a fraction of the copies that the 2008 international bestseller had, and he received much lower Canadian advances for his next planned endeavour.

But Mr. Galloway testified in British Columbia Supreme Court Friday that these metrics don’t prove his career as a writer was on the downslope before a former student’s accusation that he sexually assaulted her led to his suspension from teaching in 2015 and near-immediate exile from Canada’s literary world.

During the first day of his cross-examination at the defamation trial he has been pursuing for eight years, the former chair of University of British Columbia’s creative-writing program disputed the assertion by a defendant’s lawyer that 2014’s The Confabulist was a flop for selling 8,390 total copies in Canada compared with the 132,256 of his smash hit.

“Cellist was a zeitgeist book, and this was just a book,” he explained to Arden Beddoes, lead counsel for the woman who made the allegations, known only as A.B. because of a publication ban on her name.

Mr. Beddoes took the novelist through months of financial records and posited that sales had already fallen off before his client’s allegations ignited an online and industry firestorm over his suspension and eventual dismissal from UBC.

Mr. Galloway pushed back, saying The Confabulist had not enjoyed a run of success from paperback sales because these books were put on stands around the time of his fall from grace.

“It had a paperback life without an author,” he said.

Mr. Galloway maintained that his sales had “cratered” because of the allegations made by A.B., whom he is suing for defamation along with three other women who publicly repeated the allegations of sexual assault.

The trial will not hear testimony from A.B. Mr. Beddoes told the court that her defence no longer includes an assertion that she was assaulted, but rather that she reported the alleged assaults. Mr. Beddoes has said A.B. has twice tried to kill herself in recent months because of the stress of the ordeal.

A retired judge hired by the university to investigate her complaint found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established that he committed sexual assault or assault. Mr. Galloway was never charged with a crime, but he was fired without severance in 2016 due to breach of trust.

Earlier Friday, Mr. Galloway testified that there was no official prohibition on sexual relationships between students and faculty, and that he knows of “numerous instances” of similar relationships in the university’s faculty of arts.

He testified that it was normal for other professors to attend a regular night at a Vancouver legion to hang out and drink with students.

Mr. Beddoes questioned Mr. Galloway about a voicemail that he left for A.B. shortly before his suspension that offered an apology that said he was ashamed and was working to be a better person and “turn over a new leaf.”

He told the court that he is ashamed for having an affair with the student and cheating on his then-wife, but he didn’t think he would be fired for violating the university’s conflict-of-interest policy.

The court heard how in November, 2015, Mr. Galloway had repeatedly called both A.B. and fellow faculty member Keith Maillard, whom had received an e-mail where A.B. had described feeling at risk and “unsafe.”

Mr. Beddoes suggested that the numerous calls were Mr. Galloway “panicking,” but Mr. Galloway said that he wanted to disclose the pair’s past affair himself to Mr. Maillard, a mentor and “father figure.”

Mr. Galloway testified that no other faculty members had ever been terminated for similar conduct, though he says he should not have cheated on his wife, especially with a student.

But Mr. Galloway testified in British Columbia Supreme Court Friday that these metrics don’t prove his career as a writer was on the downslope before a former student’s accusation that he sexually assaulted her led to his suspension from teaching in 2015 and near-immediate exile from Canada’s literary world.

During the first day of his cross-examination at the defamation trial he has been pursuing for eight years, the former chair of University of British Columbia’s creative-writing program disputed the assertion by a defendant’s lawyer that 2014’s The Confabulist was a flop for selling 8,390 total copies in Canada compared with the 132,256 of his smash hit.

“Cellist was a zeitgeist book, and this was just a book,” he explained to Arden Beddoes, lead counsel for the woman who made the allegations, known only as A.B. because of a publication ban on her name.

Mr. Beddoes took the novelist through months of financial records and posited that sales had already fallen off before his client’s allegations ignited an online and industry firestorm over his suspension and eventual dismissal from UBC.
Mr. Galloway pushed back, saying The Confabulist had not enjoyed a run of success from paperback sales because these books were put on stands around the time of his fall from grace.
“It had a paperback life without an author,” he said.

Mr. Galloway maintained that his sales had “cratered” because of the allegations made by A.B., whom he is suing for defamation along with three other women who publicly repeated the allegations of sexual assault.

The trial will not hear testimony from A.B. Mr. Beddoes told the court that her defence no longer includes an assertion that she was assaulted, but rather that she reported the alleged assaults. Mr. Beddoes has said A.B. has twice tried to kill herself in recent months because of the stress of the ordeal.

Earlier Friday, Mr. Galloway testified that there was no official prohibition on sexual relationships between students and faculty, and that he knows of “numerous instances” of similar relationships in the university’s faculty of arts.

Mr. Beddoes questioned Mr. Galloway about a voicemail that he left for A.B. shortly before his suspension that offered an apology that said he was ashamed and was working to be a better person and “turn over a new leaf.”

He told the court that he is ashamed for having an affair with the student and cheating on his then-wife, but he didn’t think he would be fired for violating the university’s conflict-of-interest policy.

The court heard how in November, 2015, Mr. Galloway had repeatedly called both A.B. and fellow faculty member Keith Maillard, whom had received an e-mail where A.B. had described feeling at risk and “unsafe.”

stories.title: With Alberta referendum in sight, the nine other ballot questions are capturing attention
stories.summary: Some federalist leaders, claiming early victory on independence, have shifted their energy to persuading Albertans to vote against Smith’s proposals
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
With little more than a week until the Alberta referendum, campaigners on both sides of the separation question have turned an eye toward the nine other ballot proposals around immigration, voter ID and constitutional issues – but they are doing it for different reasons.

Some federalist leaders, claiming early victory on the question around independence, have shifted their energy to persuading Albertans to vote against the nine proposals and have pitched their campaign as a proxy war against Premier Danielle Smith. On the flipside, some separatist camps are suggesting voters boycott the nine questions, arguing their participation would be capitulating to federalism.

The nine questions propose new fees for non-permanent residents accessing health care and education, limiting non-permanent residents’ access to other social supports and working to reopen the Canadian Constitution with the aim of wresting more power from Ottawa.

“We are very likely to reject the premise that we should be a separate country, but the other nine questions remain very much in play,” said Stephen Carter, a political strategist who has organized a campaign around the slogan, “Stay in Canada, no to the nine.”

On Friday, the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project posted to social media: “Ignore THE 9, Vote Option 2,” referring to the choice on the 10th question for a binding independence referendum.

Alberta’s referendum campaign has been subsumed by the ballot question asking voters whether they wish to remain in Canada or begin working toward a second, binding secession referendum. Support for separation has held steady during the campaign, floating between 20 per cent and 25 per cent.

The nine other questions, meanwhile, have received less scrutiny and face greater odds of winning public support.

The provincial government has offered little detail how it would enact the proposals if approved by voters.

Ms. Smith says the nine questions will give her a mandate and is focused on successfully having them pass. The government has dedicated a $4-million advertising budget to the campaign – nearly seven times what third-party advertisers are legally allowed to receive or spend during the referendum period.

Ms. Smith has characterized the proposals as a tool for leverage over Ottawa, the same argument some separatist camps have made in their pitch for voters to endorse a binding secession referendum.

Mr. Carter, the political strategist, said he’s pivoting away from the separation question to campaign exclusively on the nine others for the final week. Unlike the separation question, there are still swaths of undecided voters on the remaining questions, he said.

His campaign is attempting to frame a rejection of the questions as a rebuke of Ms. Smith’s leadership.

“It’s up to us to make sure that people understand that they can oppose these questions and oppose Danielle Smith at the same time,” he said.

Ms. Smith has said she will vote for Alberta to remain in Canada and her government has vigorously campaigned on the nine other questions, with brochures and advertising deployed across the province. Asked on Thursday how she and her United Conservative Party will be working to get out the federalist vote, she said: “Well, I want people to vote for our nine questions.”

“We want to seek a mandate on that, and if people want to change the relationship with Ottawa, that’s the best way to do it.”

Ms. Smith has said the proposals would help boost Alberta’s autonomy within Canada.

Mitch Sylvestre, chief executive of the Alberta Prosperity Project, said in an interview that he’s “disgusted” by the nine questions, though he May vote for the proposals he believes are “pertinent.”

“I haven’t really taken a chance to inform myself on anything but the one directly related to us,” Mr. Sylvestre said.

Not all movement leaders agree, however. Keith Wilson, a lawyer and co-founder of separatist group Let Alberta Decide, called the nine proposals a “political gimmick” but said refusing to vote for them would be foolish.

“I still think they send a message,” Mr. Wilson told The Globe.

Despite bubbling interest in the nine questions, they appear likely to continue to take a back seat to the question of national unity.

Thomas Lukaszuk, leader of Forever Canadian, said he has planned rallies with “very interesting speakers” next Thursday and Friday in Calgary and Edmonton, and he’s planning a get-out-the-vote drive that will encourage his list of 1.5 million electors.

“Our campaign has always been about remaining in Canada, so that’s our primary focus,” he said.

The Alberta NDP will be hosting rallies on Tuesday and Wednesday, and it has bought advertising slots that will air during Edmonton Oilers and Calgary Flames games.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said on Friday that he’ll be campaigning in Alberta next week “to keep our country united.”

Ms. Smith’s office said she will be in southern Alberta next week, and will be urging Albertans to vote with new campaign literature.

Let Alberta Decide’s Mr. Wilson, meanwhile, is organizing a pro-independence rally next Saturday at the Alberta legislature, and Mr. Sylvestre is planning to activate the roughly 250,000 people in the Prosperity Project’s database ahead of referendum day. He said he’s unsure if he’ll attend Mr. Wilson’s rally.

stories.title: B.C. parties pitch contrasting income-tax proposals in the third week of election campaign
stories.summary: Tax hikes proposed by NDP, Greens could raise less revenue than projected, while Conservatives’ cuts could put province further in debt, economists say
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
British Columbia’s three largest political parties are proposing different approaches to how the province should raise and spend public money, pitching contrasting income-tax proposals in the third week of the election campaign .

The fiscally focused election promises tap into some of voters’ top concerns – affordability, health care and the province’s finances. But as B.C. faces a projected $13.8-billion deficit, the differing approaches from each of the three main parties come with their own risks. Economists say tax hikes proposed by the NDP and Greens could raise less revenue than projected and discourage economic activity, while the Conservatives’ tax cut could put B.C. further in the red.

NDP Leader David Eby said his government, if re-elected, would increase income taxes for the province’s highest earners to fund health care services, while Green Leader Emily Lowan said she would target the ultra-wealthy with a “fair share” tax to fund public services and drive down the provincial debt. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson has pledged to put cash back into the pockets of British Columbians by cutting income taxes.

An Angus Reid Institute Poll released Oct. 5 found 57 per cent of respondents said the cost of living was their top concern; 42 per cent, health care; and 24 per cent the provincial deficit.

At a campaign stop in Victoria on Oct. 4, Mr. Eby said his party would raise income taxes by 2 percentage points on the top two brackets; the portion of income between $190,405 and $265,545 would be taxed at 18.8 per cent, and the portion between $265,545 and $1-million at 22.5 per cent. A new bracket of 24.5 per cent would apply to income above $1-million.

The progressive taxation plan, which would start in the 2027 tax year, would generate $1-billion by 2028-29, Mr. Eby said. The changes would apply only to income earned over each tax bracket threshold and affect only the top 4 per cent of earners in B.C.

A person who makes $250,000 a year, for example, would pay an extra $2,169 per year, for a total of $28,649 in provincial income tax – which would still be $5,250 less than they would pay in Ontario. Those earning $190,000 or less would see no changes.

“We’re going to ask those who are the wealthiest to pay a little bit more so that we can deliver the care that you and your family deserve,” Mr. Eby said.

Trevor Tombe, a professor of economics at the University of Calgary, said the Ndp’s projected gains May be overly optimistic. Using a Statistics Canada tax-modelling tool, he estimated the proposed increases would raise about $700-million by 2027 and affect about 175,000 British Columbians.

The actual amount could be much lower because those high-income earners could change their consumption, production and investment decisions as a result.

“Economists call this the behavioural effect of a tax change, and it offsets some of the mechanical effect of a tax change,” Prof. Tombe said.

“It’s sometimes possible that the behavioural changes are so large that tax increases lower revenues.”

He cited a Fraser Institute 2022 paper that suggested a rate increase in B.C. would generate approximately one-quarter of what the mechanical effect suggests, which would shrink his $700-million estimate to less than $200-million and the Ndp’s $1-billion estimate to $250-million.

Mr. Eby’s proposed new tax bracket of 24.5 per cent on income over $1-million, combined with the federal income tax of 33 per cent, would put B.C.’s combined marginal rate at 57.5 per cent – the highest in the world, Prof. Tombe said. But over all, B.C. would still be one of the lowest-tax jurisdictions in Canada, the third-lowest on incomes of $400,000 and the second-lowest on incomes of $250,000.

Ms. Lowan, of the Green Party, said Mr. Eby’s plan fails to reflect that the ultra-wealthy grow their fortunes in stocks and real estate, and not paycheques. One day after the NDP announcement, Ms. Lowan announced that her party would introduce a one-time tax of 5 per cent on net wealth above $50-million, 10 per cent above $100-million and 20 per cent above $1-billion. This would raise an estimated $22.2-billion after accounting for administrative costs and behavioural responses, the party said.

An ongoing annual tax of 2 per cent on net wealth above $50-million, 3 per cent above $100-million, and 5 per cent above $1-billion would then generate about $5.4-billion each year, according to the Greens.

Jared Walker, executive director of the non-profit, non-partisan organization Canadians for Tax Fairness, said such progressive taxation plans are in line with successful policy pushes to tax the rich across North America.

In Massachusetts, for example, an additional tax of 4 per cent on income above US$1-million, introduced in 2022, generated US$3.4-billion in fiscal year 2026.

“Asking fewer people than it takes to sell out BC Place to pay a bit more tax so we can keep hospitals running for millions of British Columbians is both good policy and common sense,” Mr. Walker said in an Oct. 6 statement.

Conservative Leader Mr. Doerkson, meanwhile, announced on Oct. 8 that his party would raise the province’s personal income tax exemption level to $32,000, from $13,216, saving most workers $1,000 a year.

“With a $1,000 tax cut, British Columbia will be well on its way to becoming the most affordable, competitive province in Canada,” Mr. Doerkson said at a campaign stop at a Surrey grocery store on Thursday.

Mr. Doerkson did not answer a reporter’s question about how much his plan would cost and instead spoke generally of growing the economy. But Prof. Tombe said the plan would take $2.5-billion a year out of the province’s coffers – raising questions about how the Conservatives would offset the lost revenue while addressing the deficit and honouring Mr. Doerkson’s earlier campaign pledge to freeze taxes across the board for as long as he’s premier.

The NDP also raised the $2.5-billion price tag and added that Mr. Doerkson’s plan would give $190-million to B.C.’s top 4 per cent of earners.

Prof. Tombe said all policy has tradeoffs, and reasonable people will reach different conclusions based on the outcomes they give most weight to.

“I’d note that B.C. has a long-term fiscal challenge, so raising the basic personal amount by this much will make that challenge more difficult,” he said of the Conservative plan.

“I’d also note that B.C., like Canada, has a large economic and productivity growth challenge, so raising income tax rates – especially at the top – risks making that challenge more difficult, too.”

stories.title: Incoming Parti Québécois eyes friends and foes across the aisle
stories.summary: Minority government needs collaboration from across the political spectrum, but finding independence help is unlikely
stories.author: Eric Andrew-Gee, Maura Forrest
stories.content:
Two parties at opposite ends of Quebec’s ideological spectrum have been thrust into the national spotlight after an election that leaves the province’s political future – and possibly the unity of Canada – in their hands.

The left-wing Québec solidaire and right-wing Conservative Party both won enough seats in Monday’s vote to potentially decide whether the incoming minority Parti Québécois government stays in power long enough to launch an independence referendum.

With the PQ at 59 seats, five shy of a majority, premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has vowed to collaborate across the aisle, while his rival party leaders are starting to hint at what they will demand in return.

“It will be a context of rivalry and contention on many issues,” said André Lamoureux, a political-science lecturer at the University of Quebec at Montreal.

Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon has promised not to hold a referendum while U.S. President Donald Trump is in the White House, and throughout the campaign spoke little about sovereignty, which is currently unpopular in Quebec.

But during his victory speech Monday, he reaffirmed his commitment to fighting for independence.

The premier-designate suggested that opposition lawmakers could help realize his plan to hold a vote on secession, though he has also made clear that sovereignty will not be among his early priorities. In reality, partisan jockeying May well bring down his government long before he can hold an independence vote.

The Quebec Liberal Party will retain its position as Official Opposition with 40 seats, though it seems least inclined to collaborate with its old adversaries in the PQ. Although there are some areas that the two parties agree on, such as trimming bureaucracy and building housing, the animosity between the federalists and sovereigntists runs deep, noted Mr. Lamoureux.

The Liberals May have their first chance to clash with the government over its plans to abolish the role of lieutenant-governor, which Leader Charles Milliard said was “constitutionally an issue” and “not a priority for Quebeckers” in a postelection interview with Montreal radio station Cjad.

The government’s most likely partner in its goal of separating from Canada is Québec solidaire, with its nine seats concentrated in the cores of Montreal and Quebec City. The PQ needs a majority of votes in the National Assembly to adopt a referendum question.

But the two sovereigntist parties are not natural allies. QS was born in 2006, partly out of frustration with the PQ’s drift to the right on economic and identity issues, and they diverge sharply on everything from immigration to the question of how to bring about independence.

The left-wing party describes its vision of separation as “inclusive” and proposes a four-year process that would involve consulting minorities on a proposed constitution, which would then be put to a referendum, at a cost of $840-million. The PQ wants a more pared-back constitutional consultation at far less cost.

Despite these differences, party leaders have collaborated before, including on a “roadmap” to independence in 2017, when both were in opposition.

Their bases are deeply at odds, however, ON ideological grounds and have blocked attempted reconciliations in the past, including when QS members voted down a proposed alliance with the PQ ahead of the 2018 election.

Despite its iron-clad commitment to independence, QS draws major support from urban progressives who like its environmental and social policies but are not interested in separation. Polls show that only a minority of the party’s supporters would vote Yes in a referendum.

QS is also conscious of avoiding the fate that befell the NDP in last year’s federal election, when the New Democrats were decimated after propping up a minority Liberal government. The QS caucus will include Alexandre Boulerice, a former NDP MP now representing the Montreal riding of Gouin in the National Assembly.

“Politically, it wasn’t a winning choice for the NDP,” said Quentin Janel, QS director of communications. “And we have fundamental disagreements with the PQ on immigration and inclusivity, which makes it out of the question to strike a formal pact with the government on that level.”

The most likely dance partner for the PQ on many bread-and-butter issues is the provincial Conservative Party, founded in 2009, which had never won a seat in the National Assembly and now has 19, clustered in the Quebec City area. (An earlier iteration of the party dissolved in 1936).

The breakout star of the 2026 election was Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime, who campaigned on the cost of living and voters’ dissatisfaction with the Coalition Avenir Québec government’s management of public funds.

Mr. Duhaime promised to act as a watchdog on behalf of taxpayers if voters gave his party the balance of power, and during a press conference in Quebec City on Wednesday, he said his caucus members are united by their commitment to fiscal conservatism.

“These are people fighting for individual freedom, for civil liberties, for democracy, and also for more money in your pockets – a smaller government that’s tightening its belt,” he said. “That’s the Quebec version of conservatism today.”

Shortly before the campaign, Mr. Duhaime unveiled a plan to cut government spending by $47-billion over five years, in part by eliminating 20,000 public-service jobs.

The proposal was the cornerstone of his campaign, and it set the narrative for an election that saw most parties announce measures to shrink the size of the bureaucracy, said Rudy Husny, a political analyst and former federal Conservative adviser.

There is considerable common ground between the Conservatives and Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s PQ, the most “centre-right” version of the party that Quebec has seen, Mr. Husny said.

Both parties want to scrap the sales tax on used goods and to abolish Santé Québec, a Crown corporation created by the CAQ government to operate Quebec’s health care network, which critics have labelled as little more than a new layer of bureaucracy. On Wednesday, Mr. Duhaime said he also supports the PQ’s plan to freeze the salaries of elected officials.

But the Conservative Leader has been adamant that his party wants nothing to do with a vote on sovereignty. “Our position is non-negotiable,” said spokesperson Cédric Lapointe in a statement. “There will be no referendum.”

Mr. Husny said it’s very unlikely the PQ will launch the process to hold a referendum in this mandate, especially given Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon’s promise to wait until Mr. Trump leaves office in 2029. Quebec’s two previous minority governments survived less than two years.

This election campaign was primarily about change, he said.

“The next one will certainly be about the referendum.”

stories.title: Ex-UBC prof Steven Galloway cross-examined at defamation trial about repeated phone calls to accuser
stories.summary: Lawyer for A.B., former student of Steven Galloway, questioned him about why he repeatedly called her and a fellow faculty member.
stories.author: Susan Lazaruk
stories.content:
The former head of the University of B.C.’s creative writing department, who is suing a former student for defamation, testified that he was worried about the news of the affair coming out.

Steven Galloway was under cross-examination Friday by the lawyer for A.B., a former graduate student in his department with whom he had a relationship for two years, during the trial in B.C. Supreme Court.

In late 2015, two years after the affair had ended, A.B. sent an email to another UBC faculty member, Keith Maillard, to discuss a sexual assault allegation in a separate UBC faculty, A.B.’s lawyer, Arden Beddoes, told Justice Neena Sharma. In it, she asked Maillard not to forward the email to others because she felt “very unsafe for reasons of my own,” court heard.

A.B. had copied Galloway on the email and he said he called A.B. to ask her about it. He said she was short with him before ending the call.

Galloway had testified earlier that A.B. had been posting on social media about “power dynamics” and imbalances in relationships, and he worried that she was characterizing their consensual relationship to Maillard as one in which he had taken advantage of her.

Galloway then called both A.B. and Maillard a number of times — Beddoes said Maillard had 34 calls that day from an unknown number and A.B. during the same time had repeated calls from an unknown number.

After being unable to reach A.B. by phone that day, Nov. 11, 2015, Galloway left a voicemail for her, a transcript of which was read in court.

Galloway told her on the message that he wanted to apologize to her and “to take responsibility for our relationship” and to “turn myself in.” He told her he was “pretty ashamed of the way I acted,” that he had “turned over a new leaf” and was “trying to be a good person.”

“It does seem you’re in distress?” Beddoes asked him. “Your concern is she was talking about a consensual affair?” he asked.

He agreed and said he was worried that she felt there was a power imbalance in the relationship and was fearful how news of their consensual affair would affect Maillard, a good friend, and he wanted the chance to speak with him first.

“And that’s because you were panicking?” because of fear of losing his job, asked Beddoes.

But Galloway said a sexual relationship with a student wasn’t a firing offence and he was instead worried instead about how that news was going to be upsetting to Maillard, who was like a father figure to him.

In reference in his voice message to being ashamed about the affair, Beddoes asked: “That was the only thing you were ashamed of?”

“I should not have been cheating on my wife and I should not have been doing it with a student,” he said.

Beddoes also asked Galloway about regularly drinking with students at the Legion pub and questioned whether other faculty did the same, as Galloway maintained.

Much of the cross-examination Friday focused on the money Galloway made from his four novels and about a $100,000 advance he was offered by his publisher to write a series of three lighter books about Pepatone, a ventriloquist detective, around the time the allegations came out and that were never written.

The trial continues.

content_blocks.text: The former head of the University of B.C.’s creative writing department, who is suing a former student for defamation, testified that he was worried about the news of the affair coming out.

Steven Galloway was under cross-examination Friday by the lawyer for A.B., a former graduate student in his department with whom he had a relationship for two years, during the trial in B.C. Supreme Court.

In late 2015, two years after the affair had ended, A.B. sent an email to another UBC faculty member, Keith Maillard, to discuss a sexual assault allegation in a separate UBC faculty, A.B.’s lawyer, Arden Beddoes, told Justice Neena Sharma. In it, she asked Maillard not to forward the email to others because she felt “very unsafe for reasons of my own,” court heard.
A.B. had copied Galloway on the email and he said he called A.B. to ask her about it. He said she was short with him before ending the call.

Galloway had testified earlier that A.B. had been posting on social media about “power dynamics” and imbalances in relationships, and he worried that she was characterizing their consensual relationship to Maillard as one in which he had taken advantage of her.

Galloway then called both A.B. and Maillard a number of times — Beddoes said Maillard had 34 calls that day from an unknown number and A.B. during the same time had repeated calls from an unknown number.
After being unable to reach A.B. by phone that day, Nov. 11, 2015, Galloway left a voicemail for her, a transcript of which was read in court.

Galloway told her on the message that he wanted to apologize to her and “to take responsibility for our relationship” and to “turn myself in.” He told her he was “pretty ashamed of the way I acted,” that he had “turned over a new leaf” and was “trying to be a good person.”

content_blocks.alt: Steven Galloway (centre) walks out of B.C. Supreme Court in Vancouver on Oct. 5, 2026.

content_blocks.text: “It does seem you’re in distress?” Beddoes asked him. “Your concern is she was talking about a consensual affair?” he asked.

He agreed and said he was worried that she felt there was a power imbalance in the relationship and was fearful how news of their consensual affair would affect Maillard, a good friend, and he wanted the chance to speak with him first.
“And that’s because you were panicking?” because of fear of losing his job, asked Beddoes.

But Galloway said a sexual relationship with a student wasn’t a firing offence and he was instead worried instead about how that news was going to be upsetting to Maillard, who was like a father figure to him.
In reference in his voice message to being ashamed about the affair, Beddoes asked: “That was the only thing you were ashamed of?”
“I should not have been cheating on my wife and I should not have been doing it with a student,” he said.
Beddoes also asked Galloway about regularly drinking with students at the Legion pub and questioned whether other faculty did the same, as Galloway maintained.

Much of the cross-examination Friday focused on the money Galloway made from his four novels and about a $100,000 advance he was offered by his publisher to write a series of three lighter books about Pepatone, a ventriloquist detective, around the time the allegations came out and that were never written.
The trial continues.

stories.title: Nova Scotia shelter serves up 2,000 Thanksgiving dinners
stories.summary: A rescue mission in Nova Scotia served 2,000 Thanksgiving meals to visitors on Friday as the community celebrated the holiday weekend.
stories.author: Paul Hollingsworth
stories.content:
Halifax - Souls Harbour Rescue Mission provides food, shelter and other forms of assistance for Nova Scotians each day. But on Friday, the non-profit facility started the holiday weekend early.

“Today was Thanksgiving at Souls Harbour,” said CEO Michelle Porter, as everyone who visited received a midday, multi-course, free turkey dinner with all the fixings.

By noon, the dining room was jampacked with a lineup outside of people waiting to enter.

“The message is, we all belong and this is about gratitude and celebration,” Porter said. “And we all celebrate together.”

At a time when the need has increased to provide food for people who cannot afford groceries, the facility typically feeds hundreds each week. Provincewide, Porter said on Friday alone, they were providing more than 2,000 Thanksgiving meals for men, women and children.

“Big picture, Souls Harbour has 14 locations in Nova Scotia and nine of our drop-in centres are having a Thanksgiving dinner,” said Porter, who acknowledged the non-profit now provides food for more people than ever before.

“This year, we opened two new Nova Scotia-based drop-in centres in Yarmouth and Dartmouth, and this will be their first Thanksgiving,” she said. “It does warm my heart that we can do that, but it also means that there is a cost-of-living factor that is impacting our neighbours.”

Laurie Thibodeau comes to Souls Harbour for food, usually each day. She knows the volunteers and staff are there to serve, and she expressed her gratitude for the continued assistance.

“They make you feel welcome and feel at home,” said Thibodeau, who added the festive Thanksgiving vibe made the day feel even more special. “I am really happy, with honest and amazing appreciation and I am grateful for that.”

Porter said the pre-holiday weekend event captured what she believed to be the true meaning of Thanksgiving – showing generosity toward people who live in the community and often go hungry.

“The best part of my job is to be able to serve more than 2,000 people a Thanksgiving meal,” she said. “Never in my life did I think we would get numbers like that here in Nova Scotia, and it saddens me.

“But at the same time, it brings me joy to know we are helping that many people,” she added.
