stories.title: Alberta's employment rate increases despite national decline
stories.summary: While national employment rates are on the decline, Alberta saw an uptick in employment in September, according Statistics Canada.
stories.author: Devon Dekuyper
stories.content:
As Canada’s labour market flopped under the weight of expanding tariffs last month, Alberta reinforced its claim as the country’s leading job creator with the addition of 23,000 positions.

The strong September gains mean Alberta has now created 76,000 jobs in the past year; the province’s employment rate rising to 64.5 per cent, from 64 per cent a month earlier.

“It’s a story of both Alberta doing well, but also a story of the rest of the country not doing well because of the tariffs,” said Charles St‑Arnaud, chief economist at Servus Credit Union.

Across Canada, employment saw a September drop of 68,000 jobs, resulting in a decrease in the national employment rate by 0.2 percentage points, and an increase in unemployment by 0.1 percentage points, according to Statistics Canada.

September marks the second consecutive month that national employment has fallen amid the ongoing trade war with the United States. A further 42,000 jobs were lost nationally in August.

St‑Arnaud said Alberta, despite making up only 13 per cent of Canada’s labour market, has created about 80 per cent of new jobs across the country over the past year.

He attributes the relative strength of Alberta’s labour market to two factors: its strong population growth, and a lesser impact from the U.S. tariffs.

Alberta’s effective tariff rate is around one per cent, he said, compared to Quebec’s 12 per cent and Ontario’s 10 per cent.

“It’s clear that Alberta is a bit more insulated from all the negative impacts of the tariffs,” he said. The province’s population growth has also “outperformed” that of the rest of the country, he said, with a growth rate of 1.5 per cent compared to the national average of around 0.5 per cent.

Optimism in the oil and gas industry, with higher oil prices and pipeline conversations underway, has yet to generate any direct impact on employment.

“We can expect that, in the medium term, we’re going to start seeing that, but so far, higher oil prices have not translated into higher jobs in that sector,” he said.

Uncertainty around the upcoming referendum has also had minimal impacts on the job market so far.

“There might have been a marginal slowing since the start of the discussions . . . but I would say it’s pretty mild, if anything,” he said.

But if Albertans vote on Oct. 19 to hold a second referendum, “that’s going to be really different because then the level of uncertainty is going to jump up very quickly.”

Brad Parry, president and CEO of Calgary Economic Development (CED), said Calgary’s labour market “remains highly resilient” amid global uncertainty.

“This is the first full month of labour market data following the latest round of U.S. tariffs, and Calgary’s economy continues to compare favourably with major Canadian cities,” he said.

“Our diverse economy, lower direct exposure to tariff-affected industries, and continued population growth are providing a structural buffer.”

About 2,100 people entered Calgary’s labour force in September, and the city’s employment rate of 66.8 per cent remains the highest of Canada’s major cities, CED said in a Friday report.

The city’s unemployment rate fell by 0.4 percentage points to 6.3 per cent — lower than Toronto, Edmonton and Ottawa-Gatineau, and 0.2 percentage points lower than the national average.

Year-over-year, Calgary’s public administration, construction and health care and social assistance sectors saw the highest employment gains.

Some industries did see declines, however, including professional, scientific and technical services; finance, insurance, real estate, rental and leasing; and accommodation and food services.

Alberta’s unemployment rate fell to 6.4, its lowest rate since February and below the national average for the first time in six months following a summer slowdown, according to ATB.

Employment was 2.9 per cent higher in September than the same time last year — the third highest year-over-year increase among provinces behind only P.E.I. and Nova Scotia.

“In short, the labour market is rebalancing, as jobs are now keeping pace with population growth and entry into the labour force,” it said.

Joseph Schow, Alberta’s Minister of Jobs, Economy, Trade and Immigration, said in a Friday statement that the increase shows “the Alberta Advantage in action.”

“These are not accidental statistics — they are the result of deliberate, business-friendly policies brought in by this government that welcome investment and facilitate growth,” he said.

stories.title: ‘Sometimes I didn’t really have much food to eat at all’: Volunteer reflects on past need as Thanksgiving Food Drive enters final phase
stories.summary: A wave of economic pressure – and government relief – has resulted in a significant swing in the number of people using the London Food Bank (LFB).
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
A wave of economic pressure – and government relief – has resulted in a significant swing in the number of people using the London Food Bank (LFB). But officials contend the need remains as the Thanksgiving Food Drive enters its final stretch at grocery stores and drop-off sites across the city.

Some volunteers sorting through donations at LFB headquarters on Leathorne Street truly understand the need. Michelle Seah is among them. Today, she is a new volunteer, but a decade ago she was a client. “Sometimes I didn’t really have much food to eat at all, but the LFB would come with the essential food, so I never had to worry about going hungry if I didn’t have the money to go and buy groceries,” she said.

Running out of money for food is a reality for 5,700 London families that use the LFB every month. One in six are parents who work full-time jobs, said co-executive director Jane Roy. “And those folks might only come in once or twice a year.

They don’t come in all the time, but they’ve just had a bad patch, and here they are.” 2026 has been a rollercoaster of need. Roy said the year began with peak demand, then eased as summer approached. “There was the new grocery benefit, and then the increase in the grocery benefit by 25 per cent,” said Roy.

“So, we actually saw our numbers drop, which was great. Now, we are starting to see our number incline once again.” Which highlights the need for a big weekend of donations as many families prepare to celebrate. “Just pick up a few extra items, pop in the bin at the grocery store, and know that it makes a huge difference to the people that are coming to us for help,” said Roy.

The Thanksgiving Food Drive coincides with a milestone anniversary. “40 years ago, October 1986 was their first month of statistics, and we helped 360 families a month,” recalled Roy. They were the first of thousands who would benefit from the efforts of a community that always seems to find a way to give back.

Seah concedes she wouldn’t have it any other way. “Yes, definitely, because I’ve been through that. I wanted to get back later because I knew how much it meant to me when I needed help,” she said.

stories.title: Ontario's top court paves way to reopen challenge of Hamilton's anti-encampment law
stories.summary: Ontario’s top court has revived a constitutional challenge brought by a group of homeless people in Hamilton against the city’s anti-encampment bylaw.
stories.author: Jordan Omstead The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A challenge to Hamilton’s anti-encampment bylaw was revived on Friday by Ontario’s top court, after a panel of appeal judges found the lower court relied on stereotypes to discount the testimony of some homeless residents.

The Ontario Court of Appeal left the constitutionality of the bylaw and the city’s enforcement practices for a new trial judge to decide.

The challenge was brought by 14 encampment residents who argued their evictions and the city’s bylaw that blocks sleeping in parks were unconstitutional. It’s among a number of court cases in Canada to grapple with whether a city can clear an encampment when there’s no viable alternative place to shelter and city-run sites are filled up.

The Appeal Court’s unanimous ruling found the trial judge’s rejection leaned heavily on his finding that none of those evictions had taken place overnight, contrary to the testimony of several residents.

The trial judge treated the residents’ testimony as unreliable because all but one of the residents suffered from mental health and addictions issues, which he suggested impacted their memory or perception, the Appeal Court ruling said.

“The application judge’s apparent blanket assumption that the appellants’ evidence was unreliable because of those considerations perpetuates myths and stereotypes about some of the most vulnerable people in our society,” read Friday’s decision.

“It was incumbent on the application judge to analyze their evidence individually and, if he rejected it based on this individual assessment, to articulate why, without resorting to myths and stereotypes.”

The errors extended to other parts of the initial decision, the Appeal Court said. The panel found the trial judge improperly excluded evidence, including data about Hamilton’s homeless population, and failed to engage with the proper legal tests to determine whether a breach of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms had been made.

On key legal issues, the trial judge’s reasons “lacked the depth of analysis that is required” when dealing with homeless encampments, an issue of “great public importance”.

“The errors I identify in each ground of appeal can be traced back to the lack of analysis and the conclusory nature of the decision,” read the decision penned by Justice Lise Favreau.

The Appeal Court sent the case back to Superior Court to be decided by a different judge.

The City of Hamilton said it’s reviewing the implications of the Appeal Court decision, which does not affect enforcement of its bylaw.

“The city remains committed to supporting individuals experiencing homelessness with compassion and care while ensuring all residents can safely access and enjoy parks and other public spaces,” the city said in a statement, adding that it has invested more than $130 million in housing and homelessness supports this year.

Friday’s ruling follows a court decision earlier this year to block Waterloo Region from clearing an encampment after a judge found the region lacked adequate alternative shelter spaces for those residents. The ruling drew the ire of Premier Doug Ford who later called the decision “cockamamie” and mused about using the notwithstanding clause.

stories.title: Canada’s labour market stumbles again with loss of 68,000 jobs in September
stories.summary: Economy is facing serious headwinds, most notably U.S. tariffs, with the central bank less likely to raise interest rate this month
stories.author: Joy SpearChief-Morris
stories.content:
Canada’s labour market stumbled in September, posting a second consecutive monthly decline and reinforcing forecasts that the Bank of Canada will hold interest rates steady later this month.

Employment fell by 68,000 in September, adding to a loss of 42,000 jobs in August, Statistics Canada reported on Friday. The unemployment rate nudged up to 6.5 per cent from 6.4 per cent.

The economy has faced serious headwinds over the past couple years, most notably tariffs imposed by the United States. The trade war has intensified with the introduction of new tariffs in recent weeks and negotiations between Ottawa and Washington have been suspended since August.

“A second consecutive month of sizable job losses washes away the surprising strength reported in Canada’s job market through the early summer,” said Douglas Porter, Bank of Montreal’s chief economist, in a research note.

“On balance, we continue to believe that the appropriate stance by the Bank of Canada is watchful waiting, particularly so with employment suddenly clouding over.”

The Bank of Canada is widely anticipated to resume raising interest rates in the coming months, with several hikes expected by next summer.

The U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September for the first time this year. Central bankers are wary of how higher energy prices resulting from the Iran war could feed into more widespread inflation.

The Bank of Canada’s key interest rate is 2.25 per cent, and its next decision is on Oct. 28.

Friday’s jobs report showed that the biggest decline last month was in the public sector, where there was a loss of 70,000 positions, with half of those attributed to education services in Quebec. This is the fourth consecutive month showing a decline in the public sector, which is down 119,000 jobs year-over-year.

Health care and social assistance also saw their first monthly decrease since December, 2022, while September also saw a decline in manufacturing.

The loss in the manufacturing sector May be, according to Mr. Porter, “an early warning of the weight from the amped-up trade tussle.”

Regionally, Quebec saw the biggest drop in employment at 49,000 jobs, with British Columbia and Ontario following with a loss of 20,000 jobs apiece, and 4,400 job losses in Manitoba. In comparison, Alberta saw an increase of 23,000 last month. Newfoundland and Labrador and Prince Edward Island also saw job gains.

Andrew Hencic, a senior economist at Toronto-Dominion Bank, said in a note to clients that the unemployment rate is expected to “tread water in coming months, as trade frictions and higher [interest] rates weigh on activity.”

Mr. Hencic added that the one positive takeaway from Friday’s report was a steady employment rate in the private sector.

The jobless rate for women between the ages of 25 and 54 rose to 5.3 per cent from 5 per cent both because fewer women in this cohort were working, and more were actively searching for a job. The unemployment rate for men in the same age bracket fell slightly to 5.8 per cent.

Employment for youth aged 15 to 24 declined by 48,000 jobs in September for a second consecutive monthly loss, although the rate remained little changed at 13 per cent.

Royce Mendes, head of macro strategy at Desjardins, said in a research note that the slight increase in the unemployment rate “could have been worse, were it not for a drop in the participant rate to its lowest level in almost 30 years.”

The labour participation rate – the proportion of the population aged 15 and above that is working or actively looking for work – fell to 64.8 per cent, the lowest level since December, 1997, excluding the early parts of the pandemic. The agency attributed this trend to aging demographics, though more recently, the country’s population growth has been meagre after strong immigration from 2022 to 2024.

“Overall, the decline in employment and hours worked, combined with the increase in the unemployment rate, point to a shift in economic momentum. After a solid first half of the year, it looks like economic activity has cooled off,” Mr. Mendes added.
paragraphs: Canada’s labour market stumbled in September, posting a second consecutive monthly decline and reinforcing forecasts that the Bank of Canada will hold interest rates steady later this month.
Employment fell by 68,000 in September, adding to a loss of 42,000 jobs in August, Statistics Canada reported on Friday. The unemployment rate nudged up to 6.5 per cent from 6.4 per cent.

The economy has faced serious headwinds over the past couple years, most notably tariffs imposed by the United States. The trade war has intensified with the introduction of new tariffs in recent weeks and negotiations between Ottawa and Washington have been suspended since August.

“A second consecutive month of sizable job losses washes away the surprising strength reported in Canada’s job market through the early summer,” said Douglas Porter, Bank of Montreal’s chief economist, in a research note.
“On balance, we continue to believe that the appropriate stance by the Bank of Canada is watchful waiting, particularly so with employment suddenly clouding over.”
The Bank of Canada is widely anticipated to resume raising interest rates in the coming months, with several hikes expected by next summer.

The U.S. Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September for the first time this year. Central bankers are wary of how higher energy prices resulting from the Iran war could feed into more widespread inflation.
The Bank of Canada’s key interest rate is 2.25 per cent, and its next decision is on Oct. 28.

Friday’s jobs report showed that the biggest decline last month was in the public sector, where there was a loss of 70,000 positions, with half of those attributed to education services in Quebec. This is the fourth consecutive month showing a decline in the public sector, which is down 119,000 jobs year-over-year.
Health care and social assistance also saw their first monthly decrease since December, 2022, while September also saw a decline in manufacturing.
The loss in the manufacturing sector May be, according to Mr. Porter, “an early warning of the weight from the amped-up trade tussle.”

Regionally, Quebec saw the biggest drop in employment at 49,000 jobs, with British Columbia and Ontario following with a loss of 20,000 jobs apiece, and 4,400 job losses in Manitoba. In comparison, Alberta saw an increase of 23,000 last month. Newfoundland and Labrador and Prince Edward Island also saw job gains.

Andrew Hencic, a senior economist at Toronto-Dominion Bank, said in a note to clients that the unemployment rate is expected to “tread water in coming months, as trade frictions and higher [interest] rates weigh on activity.”
Mr. Hencic added that the one positive takeaway from Friday’s report was a steady employment rate in the private sector.

The jobless rate for women between the ages of 25 and 54 rose to 5.3 per cent from 5 per cent both because fewer women in this cohort were working, and more were actively searching for a job. The unemployment rate for men in the same age bracket fell slightly to 5.8 per cent.
Employment for youth aged 15 to 24 declined by 48,000 jobs in September for a second consecutive monthly loss, although the rate remained little changed at 13 per cent.

Royce Mendes, head of macro strategy at Desjardins, said in a research note that the slight increase in the unemployment rate “could have been worse, were it not for a drop in the participant rate to its lowest level in almost 30 years.”

The labour participation rate – the proportion of the population aged 15 and above that is working or actively looking for work – fell to 64.8 per cent, the lowest level since December, 1997, excluding the early parts of the pandemic. The agency attributed this trend to aging demographics, though more recently, the country’s population growth has been meagre after strong immigration from 2022 to 2024.

“Overall, the decline in employment and hours worked, combined with the increase in the unemployment rate, point to a shift in economic momentum. After a solid first half of the year, it looks like economic activity has cooled off,” Mr. Mendes added.

By Nicole Ireland The Canadian Press

Toronto - Respiratory virus specialists say Canadians should get their flu shot as soon as it becomes available in their area this fall.

Most provinces will start providing the flu vaccine to the general public by the end of October and it will be free of charge.

In Ontario, both the flu and COVID-19 shots became available on Sept. 28 for people age 65 and older, residents of long-term care or retirement homes and hospital patients and staff.

The flu vaccine is recommended for everyone six months of age and older, said Dr. Winnie SIU, a senior medical adviser for the National Advisory Committee on Immunization (Naci), during an online briefing for health-care professionals on Tuesday.

A higher-dose version of the flu shot is recommended for adults aged 65 and older because aging immune systems often need a bigger boost.

A nasal spray alternative to the flu shot, called FluMist, is approved in Canada but availability May vary between provinces and territories, SIU said.

Even though last year’s flu vaccine wasn’t an ideal match with the circulating strains, evidence still showed 40 per cent protection against requiring medical attention or hospitalization for flu infections, she said.

Dawn Bowdish, an immunologist at McMaster University and head of the Firestone Institute for Respiratory Health in Hamilton, said the flu vaccine works for about six months, but peak protection lasts for about three months.

“This year it looks like we’re heading towards an early season so the advice is pretty clear — get your flu shot as soon as you can because it looks like we’re about to tick up into the epidemic range fairly shortly,” she said in an interview on Friday.

It takes about two weeks for protection to kick in after vaccination.

Bowdish said rates of flu vaccination for children have been declining since the pandemic and urged parents to get their kids immunized.

“Flu is really, really bad for kids. Super bad for kids with asthma or any other sort of health conditions but even ... healthy children need to get a flu shot,” she said.

Bowdish also said people who are pregnant sometimes don’t realize they are a priority group for vaccination against flu and other respiratory viruses.

“Serious respiratory infections — be they COVID, be they flu, be they RSV — during pregnancy can be really problematic both for mom and for baby so pregnant people should absolutely get vaccinated as well to protect themselves and their baby.”

Early data from the Public Health Agency of Canada shows that the H1N1 influenza A type is circulating in parts of the country.

Last year, H3N2 was the dominant influenza A type in Canada.

Bowdish said in general, H3N2 tends to hit older adults and long-term care homes particularly hard, while H1N1 tends to be more serious in children.

But it’s too early to tell whether H1N1 will become the primary strain for this season, she said, noting that the Southern Hemisphere had another H3N2-dominated flu season this year.

RSV — respiratory syncytial virus — infects almost all children by the time they are two years old, said Dr. Elissa Abrams, a pediatrics specialist and another senior medical adviser for Naci, at the Tuesday online briefing.

Although the symptoms are typically cold-like, RSV can also be very serious as the most common cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in the lungs.

Naci recommends nirsevimab or clesrovimab — ready-made antibodies — be given to all infants during their first RSV season and to high-risk infants during their second respiratory virus season, Abrams said.

The exception is non-high risk infants who got protection from their mothers who were vaccinated against RSV during pregnancy, she said.

Infants who were born prematurely, have cardiorespiratory disease, are immunocompromised, have airway problems or Down syndrome are considered high-risk for serious RSV illness, Abrams said.

Adults age 75 and older are also at higher risk for RSV during respiratory virus season and should be vaccinated, she said.

Adults between 65-74 with the same high-risk health conditions affecting infants, as well as those with neurologic or neurodevelopment conditions, diabetes, chronic kidney or liver disease or high obesity — as well as long-term care residents, stem cell or lung transplant recipients, people on home oxygen and people on dialysis — should also be vaccinated against RSV, Abrams said.

Right now, high-risk adults just get one lifetime RSV vaccine, as the evidence is not yet clear on whether it should be given each year, she said.

Naci strongly recommends COVID-19 vaccination for anyone 65 years of age and older, residents of long-term care, retirement homes, or assisted living.

Because COVID has not established a seasonal pattern solely in the fall and winter, a second dose is recommended each year for people age 80 and older, long-term care residents, people who are immunocompromised and people 65 or older who have underlying medical conditions.

Nicole Forbes, technical lead on COVID-19 for Naci, said in Tuesday’s briefing that age — both old and very young — is the most significant risk factor for getting seriously ill with the virus.

Seniors account for the most COVID-19 hospitalizations and deaths, she said. The next-highest risk group — even though the rate is much lower — is children under five years of age.

Naci also strongly recommends COVID-19 vaccination for children and adults with complex health needs, people who are pregnant, health-care workers and people from Indigenous or racialized communities.

The immunization advisory committee recommends that anyone six months of age and older could be offered a COVID-19 vaccine – but it’s up to the provinces and territories to decide whether they will publicly fund them for the general public.

This year’s COVID-19 vaccine targets the XFG strain of the coronavirus, a subtype of the Omicron variant.

Bowdish said it is expected to be similar to the other Omicron subvariants in terms of the illness patients experience.

Pfizer’s and Moderna’s COVID-19 mRNA vaccines are available this year, as well as a non-mRNA protein-based vaccine called Nuvaxovid by Sanofi.

Nuvaxovid can be given to anyone 12 years of age and older.

Moderna’s vaccine, Spikevax, is approved starting at 6 months of age.

Pfizer’s vaccine, Cominarty, can be given starting at 5 years of age.

B.C., Ontario, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland and Labrador and Yukon Territory have all confirmed that they will be providing COVID-19 vaccines free of charge to anyone who wants it.

Alberta’s website says COVID vaccines will be funded for people at risk based on Naci’s strong recommendation, as well as teachers and people who are homeless.

According to Quebec’s website, the COVID-19 vaccine will be free for people at high risk for serious infection as well as people living in remote and isolated areas.

A spokesperson for Nova Scotia said in an email that the details of its respiratory virus immunization program would be announced soon.

The Canadian Press has not yet been able to confirm the COVID-19 vaccination plans in the Northwest Territories and Nunavut.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

stories.title: Toronto police had no choice but to shoot suspect in raid that killed officer, SIU says
stories.summary: SIU Director Joseph Martino says there’s no doubt that the officers believed their lives were in danger and cleared police of any wrongdoing in the June case
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto police had “no alternative” but to fire at a man accused of fatally shooting Const. Marc Pinizzotto during a raid in June, Ontario’s police watchdog said in a report Friday that offers new details about the case.

The Special Investigations Unit concluded that the suspect fired multiple times at police, and that Pinizzotto and another officer who fired back were defending themselves and other officers involved in the June 11 raid.

“There can be no doubt that the officers believed their lives to be in danger and that they acted to protect themselves from grievous bodily harm and death,” SIU Director Joseph Martino wrote in the report.

Toronto police have said the raid was part of an investigation into multiple shootings, including one at the U.S. consulate in March .

The suspect was the target of a search warrant obtained by the guns and gangs task force, and police had information that he was armed, the SIU report said.

Body-worn camera footage showed that police forced their way into an apartment in the area of Black Creek Drive and Trethewey Drive around 5:40 a.m., and Pinizzotto made his way down a hallway leading to the bedrooms, the SIU report said.

The suspect then emerged from one of the bedrooms, pointed a handgun at Pinizzotto and fired “at close range,” the SIU said. The 43-year-old officer fell backward into the hallway, it said.

“Within seconds,” another officer fired his rifle through a wall separating the hallway and the suspect’s bedroom. That officer then moved toward the bedroom doorway and fired additional rounds toward the suspect, the SIU said.

“Audible cries of pain were heard following the exchange,” the report said. “The entire gunfire event occurred within a matter of seconds.”

Pinizzotto was shot in the arm and chest, the SIU said, and he was pronounced dead in hospital. The suspect was seriously injured and taken to hospital with multiple gunshot wounds. Other people who were in the apartment at the time were not injured, the SIU said.

Toronto police have identified the suspect as 19-year-old Nicholas Bennett, who was charged with first-degree murder in Pinizzotto’s death. The allegation has not been proven in court.

The SIU director wrote in his report that police were “lawfully placed” in the apartment at the time of the gunfire exchange and that officers acted reasonably when they fired at the suspect.

“The complainant’s use of a gun against the officers left them with no alternative but to try to defend themselves with a resort to lethal force of their own,” Martino wrote.

“Put simply, nothing short of a firearm had the stopping power required of the moment. Retreat or withdrawal were not viable options given the speed at which events unfolded, and the use of less-lethal weaponry would have exposed the officers to a greater risk of harm.”

There’s no basis for criminal charges against the officer who fired multiple times at the suspect, Martino wrote.

stories.title: Third Toronto soldier charged in kidnapping investigation turns up Armed Forces ammunition
stories.summary: A third Toronto soldier is facing charges in a kidnapping where the alleged kidnappers had six different types of CAF ammunition.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A third Toronto soldier is facing charges in a July kidnapping where police discovered the alleged kidnappers had six different types of Canadian Armed Forces ammunition in their possession.

Jack David Miley of Etobicoke is a 24-year-old master bombardier in the 7th Toronto Regiment, a reserve artillery unit based at Moss Park Armoury in Toronto.

He is one of seven people facing charges for the July 25 kidnapping of Seyedkasra Hosseini “to hold him for ransom,” according to court documents. He is also accused of using a handgun during the kidnapping and pointing it at Hosseini.

“We can confirm that Jack Miley is a current member of the 7th Toronto Regiment,” the Defence Department’s Kened Sadiku said Friday in a written statement.

Miley, whose rank is equivalent to master corporal, has been a reservist since enrolling in the Canadian Army in August 2018, Sadiku said, noting he deployed last year on Operation Reassurance, the ongoing Nato mission in the Mediterranean, Black Sea and Baltics in response to Russian aggression.

After his arrest on Sept. 24, Miley was removed from duty and his access to the Forces’ equipment, facilities and bases was restricted, Sadiku said.

He remains in the CAF pending the outcome of an administrative review, Sadiku said.

Two other soldiers from the same regiment, Sachintha Fernando of North York and James Moreau of Markham, are also facing multiple charges in the kidnapping case. They have also been removed from their military duties and blocked from using their base or army equipment since they were arrested in August.

Fernando, 22, and Moreau, 29, have both been charged with kidnapping for ransom, forcible confinement and the use of a firearm during the commission of an indictable offence, according to a Toronto police spokesperson.

Fernando is also charged with multiple other counts of firearms-related offences, including unauthorized possession of a prohibited device, possession of property obtained by crime and careless storage of ammunition.

Fernando has been charged with storing five types of ammunition in a careless manner on Aug. 11, the day he was arrested. Those include .223 caliber ammunition, .223 caliber blanks, 9 mm bullets, .270 caliber ammunition and 12-gauge shotgun shells. All were property of the Canadian Armed Forces, according to court documents.

Miley was also in possession of one round of the military’s 25mm Bushmaster ammunition when he was arrested last month, according to court documents.

Police charged Fernando with possessing a nine millimetre handgun and a Churchill 12-gauge shotgun without a licence for either, as well as prohibited over-capacity magazines.

Police also seized a Beretta handgun, ammunition for the weapon, and at least one firearm silencer during their investigation.

All three soldiers were military instructors within the Greater Toronto Area, one source said Friday.

Another source who has served with the three soldiers said learning of the charges has hurt morale within the regiment.

“The Canadian Armed Forces is supposed to be a respectable organization, many have fought and died for the same colours we wear today,” said the source.

“The unit needs a major rework; there’s too much incompetence allowing these fraudulent and troublesome individuals to flourish.”

Four other men who are not in the military — Saiefeddine Aden, Raheem Bishop-Jackson, Christian Darbandi and Suhaib Alekozai — have also been charged with conspiring to kidnap Hosseini.

The commanding officer of the 7th Toronto Regiment sent a note to his subordinates recently telling them not to talk to reporters about the case.

“A reminder that this is an active investigation by TPS (primarily), the MPs, and we have our own related admin investigation,” Lt.-Col. Curtis Roach said in his email obtained by the National Post

“As such, we should not be providing comment or opinion on this incident.”

Two other soldiers from the same regiment, Sachintha Fernando of North York and James Moreau of Markham, are also facing multiple charges in the kidnapping case. They have also been removed from their military duties and blocked from using their base or army equipment since they were arrested in August.

Fernando, 22, and Moreau, 29, have both been charged with kidnapping for ransom, forcible confinement and the use of a firearm during the commission of an indictable offence, according to a Toronto police spokesperson.

Fernando is also charged with multiple other counts of firearms-related offences, including unauthorized possession of a prohibited device, possession of property obtained by crime and careless storage of ammunition.

Fernando has been charged with storing five types of ammunition in a careless manner on Aug. 11, the day he was arrested. Those include .223 caliber ammunition, .223 caliber blanks, 9 mm bullets, .270 caliber ammunition and 12-gauge shotgun shells. All were property of the Canadian Armed Forces, according to court documents.
Miley was also in possession of one round of the military’s 25mm Bushmaster ammunition when he was arrested last month, according to court documents.
Police charged Fernando with possessing a nine millimetre handgun and a Churchill 12-gauge shotgun without a licence for either, as well as prohibited over-capacity magazines.
Police also seized a Beretta handgun, ammunition for the weapon, and at least one firearm silencer during their investigation.
All three soldiers were military instructors within the Greater Toronto Area, one source said Friday.
Another source who has served with the three soldiers said learning of the charges has hurt morale within the regiment.
“The Canadian Armed Forces is supposed to be a respectable organization, many have fought and died for the same colours we wear today,” said the source.
“The unit needs a major rework; there’s too much incompetence allowing these fraudulent and troublesome individuals to flourish.”
Four other men who are not in the military — Saiefeddine Aden, Raheem Bishop-Jackson, Christian Darbandi and Suhaib Alekozai — have also been charged with conspiring to kidnap Hosseini.
The commanding officer of the 7th Toronto Regiment sent a note to his subordinates recently telling them not to talk to reporters about the case.
“A reminder that this is an active investigation by TPS (primarily), the MPs, and we have our own related admin investigation,” Lt.-Col. Curtis Roach said in his email obtained by the National Post
“As such, we should not be providing comment or opinion on this incident.”

stories.title: Prince Harry 'slipped into depression' after relocating to Canada
stories.summary: Harry was "emotionally numb" after the death of his mother Princess Diana because he felt "disloyal and guilty" for being happy without her.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
Prince Harry has revealed that he “slipped into depression” for about two weeks after relocating to Canada from the U.K. in 2019.

The Prince opened up about his mental health during an episode on the online educational platform, MasterClass. It’s part of a course designed to help people coping with grief.

Harry and his wife, Meghan, welcomed their son Archie in May 2019, spending the end of that year in Canada. They eventually moved to California, with Harry and Meghan giving up their royal duties. However, they announced last month they were returning to the UK with their children Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, after six years in the U.S., reports the BBC .

Harry described being in Canada, away from the stress of his life in Britain, when he experienced an adrenaline crash. “I actually slipped into depression for about two weeks. I felt like I couldn’t function without the adrenaline,” he revealed.

Harry also said that he felt “emotionally numb” after the death of his mother, Princess Diana, because he felt “disloyal and guilty for the possibility of being happy and joyful without her.”

During the MasterClass session, Harry said he struggled to process his grief in the years after the death of his mother when he was 12. He recounted that after crying at Diana’s funeral, he did not cry for nearly two decades, adding that a therapist suggested he spray Diana’s perfume to “unlock everything.”

The MasterClass also featured Mary-Frances O’Connor, a neuroscientist and University of Arizona professor who told Harry: “Your brain doesn’t register your loved one as gone. It registers them as lost. And it will keep searching until you teach it otherwise. We still expect that they’re going to walk through the door.”

MasterClass approached Harry about appearing in the program last year, reports reports People Magazinec . It was filmed in California over the summer.

The course is titled ‘Redefining Grief: Building Resilience Through Loss,’ It explores the effects of grief on the brain and body through Harry’s experience of losing his mother.

“Grief is physiological as well as emotional, and what we know from research is that there are very common responses to the loss of someone important in our life,” O’Connor says in the episode.

After returning from his second tour in Afghanistan in 2013, Harry said he began to see that his military experiences triggered earlier trauma.

“The things that I saw, the things I experienced, appeared to be a trigger for other traumas that had stored themselves within me,” he says. “I started to realize that I probably had become seriously depleted when just putting a simple dress shirt on — the tightening of the collar — literally felt like I was suffocating, and I would be experiencing panic attacks just in the car on the way to work,” he recalled. “And that’s when I realized, ‘Okay, there’s something bigger, there’s something else that you need to look into here.’”

O’Connor speaks in the session about how prolonged stress can affect the body. She compared the nervous system to parts of a car, and cortisol to its fuel injection system.

Harry also said he eventually came to the realization that his mother “just wanted me to be happy. And that was a huge mental shift for me. It freed me, and it gave me a whole different outlook on life.”

He said his charitable work gives him a meaningful way to carry Diana’s legacy.

It has been released ahead of World Mental Health Day on Oct. 10, and will benefit two bereavement charities, Comfort Zone Camp and Scotty’s Little Soldiers, a charity for which Harry is a global ambassador.

The Daily Mail reported Friday that Harry was paid US$100,000 for participating in the MasterClass.

stories.title: Parti Québécois leader asks caucus to stay ready for next election after minority win
stories.summary: Drummondville - Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is asking his team to stay mobilized as the party is set to form a minority government.
stories.author: Caroline Plante The Canadian Press
stories.content:
He told Parti Québécois members that they should be ready for another election campaign, even if it’s not in the short term.

St-Pierre Plamondon invited all his party’s 127 candidates to a postelection meeting at a hotel in Drummondville, Que.

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

The PQ leader said he wanted to take stock of the latest campaign and to hear from both the winning and defeated candidates.

On Monday, the party won a minority mandate by winning 59 seats, compared to 40 for the Quebec Liberal Party, 19 for the Quebec Conservative Party, and nine for Québec solidaire.

The Coalition Avenir Québec was completely wiped off the map after failing to elect a single member.

St-Pierre Plamondon said Friday that he planned to take a collaborative approach to governing.

“Will this olive branch be accepted by the other parties? That’s not within our control,” he said.

“It also gives us the obligation to remain mobilized for an election campaign — not in the short term, but eventually.”

There were questions about whether high-profile candidates Alex Boissonneault and Pascal Paradis could be assigned special tasks, after both were defeated in their ridings.

The party must also figure out the best way to represent the Quebec City region, where the party failed to win a seat.

François Gariépy, who was defeated in the Charlevoix—Côte-de-Beaupré riding northeast of the city, said he believed the party was punished for its refusal to commit to building a third road link between Quebec City and its south shore in its first term.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Toronto police had no choice but to shoot suspect in raid that killed officer: SIU
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario's police watchdog says Toronto police had no choice but to fire at a suspect who shot and killed an officer during a raid in June.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Toronto police had “no alternative” but to fire at a man accused of fatally shooting Const. Marc Pinizzotto during a raid in June, Ontario’s police watchdog said in a report Friday that offers new details about the case.

The Special Investigations Unit concluded that the suspect fired multiple times at police, and that Pinizzotto and another officer who fired back were defending themselves and other officers involved in the June 11 raid.

stories.title: Okanagan growers say crop insurance isn’t keeping up with a changing climate
stories.summary: The weather can bring extreme heat, cold, drought, hail or wildfire smoke, and any one of those can wipe out a crop or make grapes impossible to sell.
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
For Okanagan grape grower Karnail Singh Sidhu, farming has always meant accepting something he cannot control.

The weather can bring extreme heat, cold, drought, hail, or wildfire smoke, and any one of those can wipe out a crop or make grapes impossible to sell.

But Sidhu says what is becoming harder to accept is what happens after the damage: trying to recover with an insurance payout he says does not reflect the true cost of farming.

“Agriculture is relying lots on nature. There are lots of stuff we cannot control,” Sidhu said. “It can be too hot, too cold, too much rain, not enough rain, smoke, and we have hails. It’s all which is not in our control.” Pasted markdown

Sidhu has been in the wine industry since 1995 and has farmed his current vineyard for more than two decades.

He says he’s seen the impact firsthand when a cold spell severely damaged the crop. This year, he is dealing with another problem: wildfire smoke.

About 15 tonnes of grapes at one of his vineyards were affected by smoke from fires in the Summerland area, according to Sidhu.

The grapes can still look and taste fine on the vine, but the smoke taste compounds during fermentation, potentially making the crop commercially unusable.

Jeff Guignard, CEO of the BC Wine Growers Association, says that is happening across parts of the Okanagan.

“Because we’ve had a few climate events, the evaluation they’re doing right now is suggesting the wineries make less and in turn the pay-outs are below the actual operation costs” said Guignard.

“A crop can still be hanging on the vine, but I’ve lost its commercial value if it’s been impacted by smoke,” he added.

And that’s where growers say the insurance model is falling short.

Production insurance uses a grower’s production history to help determine how much they are covered for. But growers say that becomes a problem when several climate disasters happen in succession.

A bad year lowers production.

Then another bad year lowers it again.

And when the grower eventually makes a claim, those previous losses can be part of the historical record used to determine coverage.

Sidhu says that is exactly what worries him.

He says insurance payouts May account for the damaged plant, but not the years of production that are lost while a replacement vine grows.

“I get paid for one year; nobody count that we lose crop for next three years,” Sidhu said. “I get only paid for the plant. That plant come to the fruit takes time, that cost money. And I lose crop from three years from that plant too. Nobody compensate that.”

Sidhu says the difference between the payout and the actual cost can be substantial.

For a damaged plant, he says he May receive around $10 to $12, while bringing a replacement vine to fruit-bearing age can cost more than $50 or $60.

Growers also say smoke-tainted grapes can create another financial problem: contracts with wineries can be cancelled when fruit is no longer commercially viable.

And under the production-insurance rules described by growers, grapes that are claimed under the program must be harvested and destroyed rather than being sold for another use, creating additional labour and disposal costs.

Guignard says the issue is ultimately whether an insurance model based on historical losses can keep up with a climate where extreme events are becoming harder to treat as isolated incidents.

“The evaluation they’re doing right now is suggesting historical losses are less reliable at predicting those future claims,” he said.

He says the association wants a transparent review involving growers, with coverage based on current production capacity and risk modelling that reflects changing conditions.

“We need a financially sustainable programme that provides a meaningful protection for our growers so that they can recover from this loss and continue to farm again in the future,” Guignard said.

He says farmers learn to live with uncertainty, and find other ways to pay the bills when the crop doesn’t come through.

Sidhu says he keeps farming because he believes in what he does.

“As a farmer, I think I feel myself the food provider to the people. That gives me satisfaction. We grow something, we give to people.”

But he says if the insurance system does not account for the real cost of recovering from repeated climate disasters, farmers will continue to shoulder the difference.

Global News reached out to the provincial ministry of agriculture and food for comment, but was told that, due to the ongoing election campaign, the government is in a temporary caretaker mode and communications are limited to critical health and public safety information.

For Sidhu, the concern is not simply whether insurance will pay for this year’s damaged crop.

It’s whether the coverage will be enough to make sure there is still a farm here to produce a crop next year.

paragraphs: For Okanagan grape grower Karnail Singh Sidhu, farming has always meant accepting something he cannot control.
The weather can bring extreme heat, cold, drought, hail, or wildfire smoke, and any one of those can wipe out a crop or make grapes impossible to sell.
But Sidhu says what is becoming harder to accept is what happens after the damage: trying to recover with an insurance payout he says does not reflect the true cost of farming.

“Agriculture is relying lots on nature. There are lots of stuff we cannot control,” Sidhu said. “It can be too hot, too cold, too much rain, not enough rain, smoke, and we have hails. It’s all which is not in our control.” Pasted markdown
Sidhu has been in the wine industry since 1995 and has farmed his current vineyard for more than two decades.
He says he’s seen the impact firsthand when a cold spell severely damaged the crop. This year, he is dealing with another problem: wildfire smoke.
About 15 tonnes of grapes at one of his vineyards were affected by smoke from fires in the Summerland area, according to Sidhu.
The grapes can still look and taste fine on the vine, but the smoke taste compounds during fermentation, potentially making the crop commercially unusable.
Jeff Guignard, CEO of the BC Wine Growers Association, says that is happening across parts of the Okanagan.
“Because we’ve had a few climate events, the evaluation they’re doing right now is suggesting the wineries make less and in turn the pay-outs are below the actual operation costs” said Guignard.
“A crop can still be hanging on the vine, but I’ve lost its commercial value if it’s been impacted by smoke,” he added.
And that’s where growers say the insurance model is falling short.
Production insurance uses a grower’s production history to help determine how much they are covered for. But growers say that becomes a problem when several climate disasters happen in succession.
A bad year lowers production.
Then another bad year lowers it again.
And when the grower eventually makes a claim, those previous losses can be part of the historical record used to determine coverage.

He says insurance payouts May account for the damaged plant, but not the years of production that are lost while a replacement vine grows.

stories.title: Alberta Court of Appeal says Ottawa's impact assessment act is still unconstitutional
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Alberta Court of Appeal has ruled that the federal government's Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional.
stories.author: Nick Murray The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The Alberta Court of Appeal has ruled the federal government’s Impact Assessment Act is still unconstitutional, following a second court challenge of the federal legislation.

The act was first passed by the Liberals under former prime minister Justin Trudeau to set out a process to review the environmental, economic, health and social effects of proposed projects like ports, mines and pipelines.

In a 4-1 decision issued Friday, the court said even though Ottawa modified the law after the Supreme Court struck down much of it in 2023, the new version still infringes on provincial jurisdiction.

The Court of Appeal found that, among other things, the act still gives Ottawa the power to stop a project in provincial jurisdiction if it has even the smallest impact on federal jurisdiction.

“While Parliament May have the power to create an impact assessment scheme that complements existing regulation in environmental matters, the (Impact Assessment Act) creates great uncertainty due to the potential for previously unpronounced standards to apply to designated projects,” the court wrote.

“This merely exacerbates the concern that a federal assessment scheme might enable the federal government, ON the pretext of some narrow ground of federal jurisdiction, to conduct a far-ranging inquiry into matters that are exclusively within provincial jurisdiction.”

The court said while some of the changes Ottawa made to the previous version of the act weren’t constitutionally problematic, the law still gave Ottawa overly broad powers in areas of provincial jurisdiction.

“The decision maker May regulate the project causing the impacts through imposition of conditions and followup programs, or indefinite prohibitions on entire projects and matters within provincial jurisdiction rather than confining oversight to federal effects caused by the project,” the court wrote.

Ontario and Saskatchewan both backed Alberta’s legal challenge.

The Impact Assessment Act, otherwise known as C-69, has been staunchly opposed by oil and gas industry players and critics such as federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre. Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney dubbed it the “no more pipelines act.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said on social media Friday that the ruling was “yet another big win for Alberta.”

“I’m calling on the federal government to accept this ruling, refrain from yet another appeal, and immediately work with Alberta and the other provinces to clean up this flawed Trudeau-era legislation once and for all so it no longer inhibits economic development in our country,” she said.

Friday’s ruling comes as Ottawa and Alberta are partnering on a new oil pipeline to the West Coast.

Earlier this month, the Pacific Link pipeline project became the first to receive a national interest designation under Ottawa’s new Building Canada Act.

And while the Building Canada Act gives Ottawa the power to skirt a dozen federal laws to help move hand-picked projects forward, critics like Poilievre have long called for the Impact Assessment Act to be repealed.

Through the newly tabled Bill C-39, Ottawa is trying to transfer the assessment process for pipeline and energy transmission projects from the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada to the Canada Energy Regulator.

The federal government has said it has been told by industry that the level of expertise on energy projects that existed at the Canada Energy Regulator couldn’t be found at the Impact Assessment Agency.

Ottawa has said the Canada Energy Regulator will still be bound by the provisions of the Impact Assessment Act — which the Alberta Court of Appeal now says is unconstitutional — when carrying out its reviews.

In a statement, the office of federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said the government is reviewing the decision and considering next steps.

”To position Canada for long-term prosperity in a rapidly changing global economy, the Government of Canada is moving forward to build at a pace not seen in decades. The (Impact Assessment Act) is fundamental to the advancement of this work,” wrote press secretary Amy Falkner.

”The (Court of Appeal) opinion does not change our commitment to engage all provinces in the spirit of co-operative federalism.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

— With files from Lauren Krugel in Calgary.

stories.title: Paul Godfrey removed from Order of Ontario advisory council
stories.summary: Former Postmedia chairman waded into legal battle this week between the province and a technology company chaired by his son
stories.author: Laura Stone, Jeff Gray
stories.content:
Former Postmedia chairman Paul Godfrey has been removed from the advisory council to the Order of Ontario, days after accusing Premier Doug Ford’s office of trying to use the potential extension of a government contract with a company run by Mr. Godfrey’s son as “political leverage.”

The Ontario government said Friday that the 87-year-old Mr. Godfrey, a longtime Progressive Conservative, is no longer on the nine-member council that evaluates nominees and makes recommendations for the province’s highest civilian honour. Mr. Godfrey was appointed to the part-time position in October, 2024, and was set to serve until October, 2027.

“Mr. Godfrey has made false public claims and has put himself in a conflict of interest,” said Jaskarn Kailey, a spokesperson for Ontario’s Citizenship and Multiculturalism Minister Graham McGregor, ON Friday.

In a statement Friday, Mr. Godfrey said it was an honour to serve on the council and said he stood by his previous statement.

“I am grateful to the fine Ontarians who served on the advisory council with me. Many months ago, I signed a sworn statement under penalty of perjury that was made public this week. I stand by that statement,” he said.

“I am sure there will be more to say in the coming days and week.”

The decision to remove him was made on Thursday, according to a senior government source. The Globe and Mail is not identifying the source as they were not authorized to speak publicly about internal matters.

Mr. Godfrey, a longtime political powerbroker who is himself a member of both the Order of Ontario and the Order of Canada, served as chairman of Metro Toronto from 1973 to 1984 and later was chief executive of the Toronto Blue Jays. He waded into a tangled legal battle this week between the province and a technology company called Keel Digital Solutions Corp., chaired by his son, Rob Godfrey. The company, which faces an Ontario Provincial Police probe, was put into receivership this week over unpaid debts.

In an allegation that has been denied by both the Premier’s Office and Postmedia, the elder Mr. Godfrey says he felt pressed to ask his former newspaper chain to print an op-ed by the Premier before last year’s snap provincial election – in return for help from a senior official to hurry the approval of a new three-year government contract for Keel.

Keel Digital and its subsidiary Get A-Head Inc., which operated an online mental-health counselling portal, had received about $40-million in government payments over the past five years from the province’s Ministry of Colleges and Universities, the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Labour’s Skills Development Fund, which distributes cash for worker-training programs and was the subject of a political firestorm last year.

Last year, Ontario forwarded a forensic audit of Get A-Head to the OPP, prompting the force to open an investigation.

Early this year, the province took the companies and their executives to court, accusing them of “fraudulent misrepresentation” and demanding $25.7-million in repayments. The defendants have denied any wrongdoing and countersued, alleging $100-million in damages. Talks to settle the legal fight have not resulted in a deal. The allegations have not been tested in court.

In a sworn statement that was released this week, the elder Mr. Godfrey alleges that in January, 2025, his son told him that he had just spoken to Patrick Sackville, then Mr. Ford’s chief of staff. The statement says Mr. Sackville had agreed to help hurry up an approval for a proposal to switch Keel’s contract with the Ministry of Colleges and Universities to span a three-year term, instead of having to renew it each year.

But the statement alleges that Mr. Sackville then added that he needed a “favour”: the publication of a letter from the Premier in all of Postmedia’s Ontario newspapers justifying the province’s impending early election call. Mr. Godfrey’s time at the helm of Postmedia had ended in 2022, and while he said he was “uncomfortable” with the request, he still brought it to the media company’s brass.

“I have spent an entire career either in or around politics,” his statement reads. “I understood what this demand from the Premier’s office meant. This was using political leverage and power over a small company to extract a benefit that Keel had no ability to provide.”

Mr. Sackville told The Globe and Mail on Thursday that “the allegation is entirely false.”

In a statement provided Thursday by Mr. Ford’s spokesperson Hannah Jensen, the Premier’s Office said Mr. Godfrey’s “claims are categorically untrue and completely disconnected from reality.”

Mr. Godfrey repeated the allegations in a statement sent to media on Thursday, and called the response from the Premier’s Office “laughable.”

Postmedia said it was the Premier’s Office that approached the company’s current CEO about an op-ed, and that the request was passed for consideration to the editorial team, who chose to run it.

“No commercial consideration would ever be required for the Premier, or any political figure, to share their opinion in our editorial pages,” said the Postmedia statement, which had no name attached. “We have no knowledge of the background events described by Mr. Godfrey.”

stories.title: FBI describes arrest of Tumbler Ridge conspiracy suspect
stories.summary: The FBI has described the arrest of the alleged co-conspirator in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting, saying James Bryant was calm and "not particularly surprised" when agents turned up at their Bellingham, Wash., apartment on Tuesday.
stories.author: Chuck Chiang The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The FBI has described the arrest of the alleged co-conspirator in the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooting, saying James Bryant was calm and “not particularly surprised” when agents turned up at their Bellingham, Wash., apartment on Tuesday.

W. Mike Herrington, special agent in charge of the Seattle field office for the Federal Bureau of Investigation, said in an interview Friday that Bryant believed they were not criminally culpable because they were not directly involved in the Feb. 10 killings of eight victims by Jesse Van Rootselaar.

But Herrington said Bryant was “very cognizant” of the risks in having discussed plans for a shooting with the attacker, who killed herself at Tumbler Ridge Secondary School, where most of the victims died.

FBI Special Agent W. Mike Herrington says this week's arrest in Washington state of James Bryant for allegedly conspiring with the Tumbler Ridge, B.C., mass shooter went off calmly. Herrington says the Fbi's release of extensive details about the investigation reflects their confidence in the case. (Oct. 9, 2026)

“It was a very peaceful arrest,” Herrington said, noting agents detained Bryant after making sure the suspect would be home from work at a fast-food restaurant.

“Our agents actually contacted them and asked to meet after Bryant completed an overnight shift. And after that shift, they came by the apartment and were able to pretty peacefully put the subject under arrest.”

Bryant was charged in Washington state this week with conspiracy to murder in a foreign country, with an extensive FBI complaint citing months of online conversations with Van Rootselaar in which the pair allegedly discuss tactics, targets and attempts to livestream the attack.

The complaint also includes photos said to have been shared between Bryant and Van Rootselaar, as well as descriptions of the attacker’s guns and possible motivations that had not been released by the RCMP.

Herrington said Friday that the release of such a wide range of details is not typical, but its inclusion was justified by “intense” Canadian public interest.

He said it also reflected “our confidence in the strength of the case.”

“The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Western District of Washington is going to be the one who ultimately decides what they’re comfortable with putting in there,” he said.

“In some cases, we’re going to be a little more reticent to put out information because we feel sometimes it could cause people to prejudge the case or could in other ways endanger the integrity of the prosecution going forward.”

But he said in Bryant’s case, there was deemed to be no “significant risk” from releasing the information.

The complaint cites previous discussions between the FBI and Bryant, although Herrington said no interviews had been conducted with Bryant since the arrest.

The complaint alleges Bryant tried to livestream the mass shooting on the Twitch platform to “amplify” its impact, but the stream only lasted about 20 seconds, showing the armed shooter in a vehicle.

Conversations cited in the complaint say Bryant gave Van Rootselaar suggestions on target locations, and Bryant’s “misplaced loyalty” and willingness to operate the livestream May have encouraged the shooter to go through with the attack.

Herrington added that Canadian policy and legal regimes were more restrictive about the release of information, but U.S. authorities and the RCMP actively discussed what to release in “a difficult balance because there are very real privacy interests for everybody involved.”

“I think we’re very cognizant of our relationship with the RCMP and Canadian authorities, as well as the extreme level of importance in protecting the integrity not just of our case, (but also) of their case,” he said.

“So I would say if RCMP expressed discomfort with us releasing more information than they were comfortable with, we would take that very seriously and would … likely defer to that, because what we don’t want to do is release something that is going to cause trouble for their investigation, for any charges they May be contemplating, and for them as an organization.”

The RCMP has said its investigation into the attack is ongoing.

It has declined to provide details about the guns used in the attack citing “ongoing court processes in Canada.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

stories.title: Are you 55 years or older and looking for a job? Tell us your story
stories.summary: Canada’s employment rate rose to 6.5 per cent in September with a net total of 68,000 jobs shed, Statistics Canada reports.
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
Canada’s employment rate rose to 6.5 per cent in September with a net total of 68,000 jobs shed, Statistics Canada reported on Friday .

The largest job losses were felt in the public sector, particularly in health care, social assistance and education.

Canada has lost a net 41,000 jobs so far this year, compared with a gain of 211,300 in the same period of 2025.

Among Canadians aged 55 and older, the unemployment rate rose 0.2 percentage points to 5.3 per cent , as more people in the age group looked for work.

A report released earlier this year also found that Canadian seniors are staying longer in the workforce.

A Statistics Canada report released in April found that 15.2 per cent of Canadians, aged 65 and older, were either employed or looking for work, the highest participation rate recorded since the agency began recording the data in 1976.

Are you 55 years old or older and looking for a job? What kind of jobs have you been looking for and what has the search been like? Do you find age has played a part in your search? What parts of the application and interview process have you found most challenging? When do you think you’ll be able to retire?

CTVNews.CA wants to hear from you. Share your story by emailing us at dotcom@bellmedia.CA with your name, general location and phone number in case we want to follow up. Your comments May be used in a CTVNews.CA story.

stories.title: The 8 wars Trump claims to have 'settled' in his last-minute Nobel Peace Prize pitch
stories.summary: Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, despite a last-minute pitch from Donald Trump in which he claimed to have settled eight wars.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
South African lawyer Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday, despite a last-minute pitch from U.S. President Donald Trump.

“I don’t know what their decision is going to be. They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office on Wednesday when asked about the accolade. “I settled eight wars … I did things that nobody else has ever done. I’m not bragging, I’m just telling you the facts,” he added, claiming to have saved “millions of lives.”

It’s not the first time the U.S. president has touted his role in settling eight wars. In fact, he’s mentioned the figure several times before. But what are those wars? Did they really end? And, if they did, is it thanks to Trump? Here are the facts.

The two former Soviet republics and Trump signed a provisional peace agreement at the White House on Aug. 8, 2025. But movements towards implementing the deal have been halting.

On the anniversary of the signing of the joint declaration, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio released a press statement reaffirming Washington’s commitment to realizing the deal. Azerbaijan’s president, Ilham Aliyev, wrote an open letter to Trump praising the U.S. president’s role in bringing about “a turning point in the pursuit of lasting peace” in the region.

But, in July this year, Azerbaijan said it will not sign a final deal unless Armenia changes its constitution, specifically its reference to a Soviet-era document calling for the reunification of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh, a region Azerbaijan took control of in 2023.

Cambodia and Thailand agreed to a ceasefire in July 2025, following a five-day military conflict, after efforts by Malaysia, the U.S. and China to bring both sides to the table. Trump said he would not conclude trade deals with them until the conflict ended.

A few months later, in October, the leaders of Thailand and Cambodia signed an enhanced ceasefire deal in the presence of Trump. Then, in December, a new ceasefire deal that Trump wasn’t involved in was reached after widespread fighting resumed earlier that month.

Trump announced a peace agreement between the two African nations in June 2025, which was signed by the countries’ foreign ministers in Washington and required Rwandan troops to withdraw from eastern Congo within 90 days.

In December, the leaders of the DRC and Rwanda gathered in Washington to affirm commitments to the Trump-backed deal, but the deal hasn’t been implemented and the fighting has continued.

Since then, representatives of the U.S., the DRC and Rwanda have met in Washington in March and in Geneva, Switzerland, in July in attempts to further implement and reaffirm commitment to the peace agreement. But the conflict is far from over, with M23 rebels continuing to hold territory in Congo.

This conflict is one the Trump administration dealt with in his first term, though it’s not technically a war, just a period of heightened tensions.

The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam on the Blue Nile has caused friction between the two countries because of Egypt’s worries about its water supply, for which it relies on the Nile. Sudan is also affected.

The U.S. president facilitated talks between Ethiopia, Egypt, and Sudan in Washington in 2019 and 2020, but negotiations stalled and no agreement was signed — though Trump has claimed on several occasions that his intervention helped stabilize the situation.

Tensions have persisted between these two countries since Kosovo declared independence in 2008 until this day, and no official peace deal has been signed.

In his first term as president, Trump negotiated a wide-ranging deal in 2020 between the countries, but much of what was agreed on was never carried out.

Plus, it was never technically a war, so it also wasn’t technically a peace deal. Though Kosovo’s former president Vjosa Osmani did previously say that Donald Trump helped prevent further escalation in the Serbia-Kosovo region, the then Serbian president, Aleksandar Vucic, denied that any escalation had been looming.

Trump has claimed that a ceasefire brokered between India and Pakistan in May 2025 was down to the U.S., after several days of cross-border strikes marked the worst regional fighting between the two nuclear-armed nations in decades.

But while Pakistan’s government thanked Trump for his involvement, India downplayed the U.S. president’s claims, saying the two countries came to the agreement without external help.

Meanwhile, Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif nominated Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize for the second year in a row on Friday, writing in a social media post: “(Trump’s) timely intervention helped bring Pakistan and India back from the brink and secure a ceasefire, that is holding till today.”

On June 23, 2025, Trump announced a peace deal between Iran and Israel following 12 days of military conflict. Though shaky, the ceasefire ultimately held until a new war broke out following a joint US-Israeli attack on Iran in February.

In June, Washington and Iran signed a ceasefire agreement that quickly broke down over control of the Strait of Hormuz, and in September Trump rejected Iran’s seven-day ceasefire proposal.

More recently, the U.S. president said in a Truth Social post that his administration will not launch an attack on Iran before November’s mid-term elections.

At the White House on Wednesday, Trump claimed: “I’ve stopped maybe the total obliteration of the world because Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”

The U.S. administration did help to broker a ceasefire that came into effect in October last year, but while it ended large-scale hostilities, violence in the region has continued.

Elsewhere, Trump has made it clear that he hopes to play a part in ending the Russia-Ukraine war. While speaking to press at the White House in July, he said an end to the conflict is “getting ‌closer than people realize.”

He said he had held a “good call” with Putin ​on the Fourth of July holiday, “And President Zelenskiy actually wants it to end now. And we’re going to be going to Nato, and we’re going to be talking about it, and I think we’re going to ​get it,” he added. “I think we’re going to get it ended. It’s been a terrible situation.”

stories.title: Poilievre to deliver Canadian unity speech in Alberta ahead of referendum
stories.summary: Conservative Leader says he will campaign in the province next week as Albertans prepare to vote on Oct. 19
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Friday he will be in Alberta just days before the province’s referendum to deliver a speech on Canadian unity.

The House of Commons will be on a break next week after MPs head back to their ridings for the Thanksgiving weekend.

Poilievre is scheduled to deliver his speech during the Canada Strong and Free Network conference in Calgary on Oct. 16. His speech is expected to be followed by an address from Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

The schedule lists the title of Poilievre’s speech: “The Canadian Drift: Reclaiming Confidence, Abundance and Freedom for Alberta.”

Poilievre told a press conference in Burlington, Ont., ON Friday he will be doing “additional campaigning on the ground” in Alberta.

“We encourage all Canadians of all parties to join in uniting all Canadians to make ourselves safe, affordable, and fully independent here at home,” Poilievre said.

When asked about tech industrialist Elon Musk saying recently that Alberta, Saskatchewan and Quebec should separate , Poilievre said “Canadians control their own destiny.”

“Frankly, people can tweet whatever they want, but tweets and memes do not affect Canada. What affects Canada is the decisions made by the Canadian people,” he added.

The premiers of Alberta and Saskatchewan brushed off Musk’s comments, while Quebec’s new premier has said he won’t trigger a separation vote while U.S. President Donald Trump is in office.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said the future of Canada will be decided by Canadians when asked Thursday about Musk’s comments at a press conference in Sherbrooke, Que.

While Musk was born in South Africa, he holds Canadian citizenship because his mother was born in Saskatchewan. He has lived previously in Canada.

Alberta Conservative MP Dane Lloyd has been tasked with leading the federal Conservatives’ unity campaign in the province.

Responding to reports in The Globe and Mail about Alberta separatists allegedly seeking the help of the U.S. government in exchange for potential water rights and oil royalties, Lloyd said Monday “no one has the right to promise away Alberta’s birthright.”

Lloyd stopped short of describing that activity as foreign interference, saying more information needs to be gathered.

Mitch Sylvestre of the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project denied offering oil and water rights to the U.S. in his group’s three conversations with U.S. State Department officials in Washington. He also said he only attended one of those meetings.

Albertans will vote on the prospect of a future separation referendum, along with nine other questions involving constitutional and immigration issues, ON Oct. 19.
