stories.title: Canada weathered the first tariff shocks. But Deloitte sees trouble ahead
stories.summary: Deloitte Canada’s chief economist explains why the economy proved resilient in Q2 and why the forecast has changed for 2027.
stories.author: Tracy Moran
stories.content:
Washington, D.C. — The Canadian economy proved more resilient than feared earlier this year.

Now, while many hope domestic infrastructure and investment projects will help the economy grow and boost its export diversification, the country is likely facing a period of slower growth in the short term.

That’s why Deloitte Canada recently raised its forecast for this year but cut next year’s growth forecast from 2 to 1.6 per cent, a figure that accounts for Canada’s retaliatory tariffs but not the Sept. 15 expansion or the Sept. 29 import bans. To better understand where the economy has proven most resilient, and where future challenges lie, National Post reached out to Deloitte Canada’s Chief Economist Dawn Desjardins for some insights.

This Q&A has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Dawn Desjardins: In the second quarter, Canada’s economy really did grow very strongly, and it was pretty broad-based, which I thought was interesting. It wasn’t just the consumer, but it was also the housing market, and we saw business investment pick up. Exports also picked up. So it was really strong growth in that second quarter.

Now, as we are monitoring the third quarter, there is still growth, not nearly as rapid, but still seeing signs of growth.

That’s all to describe how we netted out to get a stronger growth rate for 2026. It really was that lift from the second quarter and the fact that the first quarter, which had initially been indicated to have contracted, actually was positive. So that kind of set the benchmark, and we did end up seeing our forecast being upgraded.

But for 2027, all the events of recent weeks and months certainly suggest that it’s having an impact on Canadian business confidence, Canadian consumer confidence, and we think very likely we will see slowing export activity as we go through the course of 2027. So those factors taken together, it does suggest that we’re in for a period of slower growth in 2027 compared to what we previously thought.

So still growth, but just 1.6 per cent. Previously, we thought 2 per cent.

I think what we’ve seen is that, especially in the most recent data we have, which was for the month of August, we saw actually some strong export activity as exporters tried to sell into the U.S. quicker than they otherwise would have. So they were kind of front-running those tariffs.

Now, as we go forward, of course, they are in place. And so we will see, we think, softer demand for some of Canadian goods sales into the United States, and that’s what’s going to weigh overall on our exports.

We don’t actually have them falling. We just have them going very, very, very slowly. They will be negative, we think, in the next few quarters, but then start to pick up again as supply chains are rearranged, as Canadian companies look for other markets to sell to.

So a lot of it is, in fact, reflecting weaker demand we expect from the U.S. market.

I think we have seen already in August a decline in jobs. It’s likely going to remain a rough outlook for people who are looking for jobs, especially until we get to a period of time where we’re starting to see more business investment pick up.

So right now, I think the fact that we are seeing such a weight on business confidence, businesses today are obviously very concerned about where demand is going to come from. And so right now, I feel like they’re in that kind of perhaps low-hire, low-fire type of environment.

By that, I mean not necessarily looking to expand, but given that we’re seeing such weak immigration growth, probably looking to maybe retain some of the workers. And so you don’t see a lot of movement, I don’t think, in the labour market in the medium term, immediate term. But as we move forward, we do think that we’re going to start to see hiring pick up pace.

And this is going to reflect changes that we’re anticipating to come, whether it’s from public infrastructure investments, so by the public sector, or starting to see some private-sector money move into accompanying some of the investments that we’re seeing put in place by the federal and provincial government.

Right now, what we’re seeing is that our inflation rate is being largely driven by energy prices. So, we have an inflation rate of three per cent right now, at the upper end of the Bank of Canada’s target band.

And when you look below that, prices are rising at a slower clip. If you exclude energy, I think it’s about 2.4 per cent. So just a little bit above the Bank of Canada’s target.

Now, as we move forward, it’s going to depend on how long tariffs stay in place, if companies are going to absorb some of it or … And this is more the retaliatory tariffs on Canadian goods coming into the country. And there, I have to say the overall amount of these retaliatory tariffs, the amount that they’re impacting is relatively contained. It will filter in and probably to other parts of the supply chain, but we don’t have a huge flow-through to consumer prices.

The big wildcard, I think, for the inflation outlook right now, there’s a few. One is, how long do energy prices remain elevated at these very high levels?

Also, how are Canadian consumers and Canadian businesses expecting inflation to evolve? Because that’s often, of course, the mechanism, right? They look to see whether or not they think prices are going to go up. Should they be demanding higher wages? And so we start to see even more upward pressure on prices.

So at this stage, we haven’t seen that evolve. We do think the inflation rate will likely start to move lower as we go through 2027. I think one of the factors there is that we are looking for this slower growth than we previously had been anticipating.

And when we look at the futures curve for oil prices, they are gradually coming down. Now, they’re not going back to the $60 level or $65 level of prior to the beginning of the war, but they’re still on a downward trajectory.

So that upward pressure from energy prices, when we look to where they were a year ago, starts to come out of the calculation. It doesn’t mean that prices are necessarily going to go down significantly, but at the same time, they’re going to stop rising. And when we’re there, we’re just using the futures market.

It’s manufacturing where we are seeing a hit, especially in the motor vehicle industry. When we look at things like forestry, lumber, that is getting pretty hard hit.

And then steel and aluminum, again, these are sectors that are being really hard hit by very high tariff levels. And so, to the extent that that’s impacting demand, those are the areas where we are seeing the biggest hit in terms of the economy and jobs.

And when you look across the country, the provincial economies, there it is more central Canada, so Ontario and Quebec, as well as British Columbia. So provinces where we have more of the manufacturing hubs, these are the types of areas where we anticipate we’re going to see a bigger impact.

I think one of the things we are anticipating is that when we look at a lot of the public spending that is going to go on, it is pretty widely dispersed across the whole country, so that could put some mitigants.

But I think when we think about if you are in a city that really is relying on one particular industry, that is going to be incredibly impactful. And so to that extent, yes, I think that there is a risk that certain areas will be. And they are being, I think, more dramatically impacted than the overall national numbers.

I think that’s one of the things that it’s hard. It’s hard to see — because you know that some of these areas are being very badly hit, and if one of their major industries is impacted, it just filters out into demand for services. So it does impact those areas very dramatically.

I think it’s a combination of both, to be honest. I don’t have the exact split, but it certainly is.

When we think about the impact of the uncertainty, of concerns about demand from our largest trading partner for some of our products, it certainly is impacting the way Canadian businesses are thinking about putting money to work, investing.

And so to the extent that they’re just sitting back right now, looking, trying to figure out, “How can I diversify where I’m sending my exports? What’s going to have to accompany that for me to be successful?” as well as, “How can I sell across the country?”

For Canada, of course, we have some barriers to trade across Canada: the provincial trade barriers. And those, when you look through the data and try and model it, do show a pretty substantive impact overall on the economy.

So to the extent that we’re seeing some of these barriers being either reduced or eliminated, if we can have some success on that front as we move forward, it will have a material impact on Canada’s economy.

We’ve run an analysis. It’s a longer-term analysis, but it suggests that Canada’s economy could be 2.4 per cent larger than if those interprovincial barriers remained in place.

So there are substantive gains. And so to the extent that we see some action on removing, just being able to have a more robust domestic market, I think that’ll be helpful over time.

It’s more downside risk to our view. It will continue to have negative impacts. As I said, we haven’t included them in this, but I would say there’s a downside risk there. Should we have additional tariffs apply to our exports, we would revisit our forecast, and it’s the most likely outcome that we would have even slower growth in 2027 than we have in the current forecast.

I think to the extent that we do see governments working to facilitate investment activity, help ease it a bit in terms of some of the constraints that are currently in place, that will be very helpful.

What we have seen from the government is support for businesses that are suffering under the tariffs, that are seeing a significant reduction in demand. We’re also seeing support for Canadian workers who either lose their position or work fewer hours. There are employment benefits they can get now to help them get through this period.

So if you’re working 40 hours one week and then you’re suddenly cut down to 30, there is a government program that can help you move through that transition. So that is definitely going to ease some of the burden, but not totally offset it.

So, yes, getting infrastructure spending in place — we know that building infrastructure takes a long time, so the immediate impact, it’ll build momentum over time. But starting, getting the permitting done, getting the workers in place, starting the whole project. So it does all take time. There’s a process involved in that.

So that’s one thing. I think, yes, we see government programs that are trying to help in the short term and then looking further to invest over the medium term and to get Canada’s competitiveness up. So those will reap benefits over time.

But one of the things they can’t do necessarily is definitely restore confidence among Canadian businesses. So Canadian businesses who are worried, and when you look at surveys, it seems that’s what they’re saying: “We’re worried about where we’re going to be selling our goods to. We’re worried about developing new supply chains. How can we do that?”

So there’s still this overhang, I think, of a softness in confidence by Canadian businesses that I think that is sort of the part that, although governments are doing things and the central bank has so far maintained the policy rate at two-and-a-quarter per cent, these are certainly positives, but it really is seeing some of the movement, getting this underway, that’s what I think is going to be the turnaround for Canadian businesses.

And Canadian businesses looking to put money to work, I think they want to really see things moving forward, and that in itself should help restore confidence.

I think it could certainly return. It’s such a volatile and uncertain backdrop. So yes, if there was relief in terms of having the Canada, U.S., Mexico free trade agreement completely in place, I think that would be a pretty good lift in terms of confidence measures as well as a lift in terms of export growth.

But I think it has been very volatile. And so when we think about over the past while, all of the tariff fight, that has really, I think, created such uncertainty for Canadian businesses that it is keeping them a bit on their back foot as they try to assess what are the real prospects of growth as we move forward.

I think to the extent we do see movement in terms of some of these big projects, and we do start to see hiring associated with that and a general sense that Canadian consumers and businesses are more optimistic, that certainly would be a reason to upgrade.

And of course, any changes in our relationship in a positive way with our largest trading partner, that would also see us upgrade that forecast.

I think the main concerns is, A, that we do see energy prices remain or continue to climb, because that does have a serious impact, of course, ON households and their balance sheets and what they have available to spend on other goods and services.

An escalation, of course, in terms of tariffs that damage other parts or continue to damage certain parts of our economy.

Of course, these are always things — they are downside risks to our view right now simply because there are external factors that we really can’t control.

So we’re trying to look inward and saying, “Okay, how can we make our economy more competitive? How can we draw in capital investment? How can we make our economy more self-sufficient by having a domestic economy across the whole country that is barrier-free?”

So there’s a few things happening, but again, a lot of them take time.

I think when we look as recently as the second quarter, the fact that we did see such strong resilience in the economy — it was much stronger than we had been anticipating, and I think others were anticipating.

And the fact that it was relatively broadly based: strong consumer spending, business investment picking up, and a housing market that looked like it was on the road to recovery.

Now it has slowed subsequently, but nonetheless, it does show that there is still some momentum in the economy. There is still some activity happening, and that very strong growth rate did show that even under conditions of great uncertainty, the Canadian economy was continuing to grow.

It’s very, very, very hard to say. I think one of the things when we think about diversifying, we do need the infrastructure for that to happen. That takes time.

So this sense that yes, we’re going to build or expand ports, pipelines, railways, things to get our goods to other areas of the world in a more expedient and cost-effective way. So those things are all positive movements, and I think it will support the idea that there are other markets that we May be trying to build relationships with.

But again, none of that happens very quickly. So I don’t know exactly when the pickup is going to occur. We do have conditions improving in the latter part of 2027.

Generally, it’s just this idea that we’re all kind of rowing in the same direction towards economic growth. I think once people believe that, then that’s when we’ll start to see this improvement.

We’ve run an analysis. It’s a longer-term analysis, but it suggests that Canada’s economy could be 2.4 per cent larger than if those interprovincial barriers remained in place.
So there are substantive gains. And so to the extent that we see some action on removing, just being able to have a more robust domestic market, I think that’ll be helpful over time.

It’s more downside risk to our view. It will continue to have negative impacts. As I said, we haven’t included them in this, but I would say there’s a downside risk there. Should we have additional tariffs apply to our exports, we would revisit our forecast, and it’s the most likely outcome that we would have even slower growth in 2027 than we have in the current forecast.

I think to the extent that we do see governments working to facilitate investment activity, help ease it a bit in terms of some of the constraints that are currently in place, that will be very helpful.

What we have seen from the government is support for businesses that are suffering under the tariffs, that are seeing a significant reduction in demand. We’re also seeing support for Canadian workers who either lose their position or work fewer hours. There are employment benefits they can get now to help them get through this period.

So if you’re working 40 hours one week and then you’re suddenly cut down to 30, there is a government program that can help you move through that transition. So that is definitely going to ease some of the burden, but not totally offset it.

So, yes, getting infrastructure spending in place — we know that building infrastructure takes a long time, so the immediate impact, it’ll build momentum over time. But starting, getting the permitting done, getting the workers in place, starting the whole project. So it does all take time. There’s a process involved in that.

So that’s one thing. I think, yes, we see government programs that are trying to help in the short term and then looking further to invest over the medium term and to get Canada’s competitiveness up. So those will reap benefits over time.

But one of the things they can’t do necessarily is definitely restore confidence among Canadian businesses. So Canadian businesses who are worried, and when you look at surveys, it seems that’s what they’re saying: “We’re worried about where we’re going to be selling our goods to. We’re worried about developing new supply chains. How can we do that?”

So there’s still this overhang, I think, of a softness in confidence by Canadian businesses that I think that is sort of the part that, although governments are doing things and the central bank has so far maintained the policy rate at two-and-a-quarter per cent, these are certainly positives, but it really is seeing some of the movement, getting this underway, that’s what I think is going to be the turnaround for Canadian businesses.
And Canadian businesses looking to put money to work, I think they want to really see things moving forward, and that in itself should help restore confidence.

I think it could certainly return. It’s such a volatile and uncertain backdrop. So yes, if there was relief in terms of having the Canada, U.S., Mexico free trade agreement completely in place, I think that would be a pretty good lift in terms of confidence measures as well as a lift in terms of export growth.

But I think it has been very volatile. And so when we think about over the past while, all of the tariff fight, that has really, I think, created such uncertainty for Canadian businesses that it is keeping them a bit on their back foot as they try to assess what are the real prospects of growth as we move forward.

I think to the extent we do see movement in terms of some of these big projects, and we do start to see hiring associated with that and a general sense that Canadian consumers and businesses are more optimistic, that certainly would be a reason to upgrade.
And of course, any changes in our relationship in a positive way with our largest trading partner, that would also see us upgrade that forecast.

I think the main concerns is, A, that we do see energy prices remain or continue to climb, because that does have a serious impact, of course, ON households and their balance sheets and what they have available to spend on other goods and services.
An escalation, of course, in terms of tariffs that damage other parts or continue to damage certain parts of our economy.
Of course, these are always things — they are downside risks to our view right now simply because there are external factors that we really can’t control.

So we’re trying to look inward and saying, “Okay, how can we make our economy more competitive? How can we draw in capital investment? How can we make our economy more self-sufficient by having a domestic economy across the whole country that is barrier-free?”
So there’s a few things happening, but again, a lot of them take time.

I think when we look as recently as the second quarter, the fact that we did see such strong resilience in the economy — it was much stronger than we had been anticipating, and I think others were anticipating.
And the fact that it was relatively broadly based: strong consumer spending, business investment picking up, and a housing market that looked like it was on the road to recovery.

Now it has slowed subsequently, but nonetheless, it does show that there is still some momentum in the economy. There is still some activity happening, and that very strong growth rate did show that even under conditions of great uncertainty, the Canadian economy was continuing to grow.
It’s very, very, very hard to say. I think one of the things when we think about diversifying, we do need the infrastructure for that to happen. That takes time.

So this sense that yes, we’re going to build or expand ports, pipelines, railways, things to get our goods to other areas of the world in a more expedient and cost-effective way. So those things are all positive movements, and I think it will support the idea that there are other markets that we May be trying to build relationships with.

Generally, it’s just this idea that we’re all kind of rowing in the same direction towards economic growth. I think once people believe that, then that’s when we’ll start to see this improvement.

content_blocks.text: Washington, D.C. — The Canadian economy proved more resilient than feared earlier this year.

Now, while many hope domestic infrastructure and investment projects will help the economy grow and boost its export diversification, the country is likely facing a period of slower growth in the short term.

That’s why Deloitte Canada recently raised its forecast for this year but cut next year’s growth forecast from 2 to 1.6 per cent, a figure that accounts for Canada’s retaliatory tariffs but not the Sept. 15 expansion or the Sept. 29 import bans. To better understand where the economy has proven most resilient, and where future challenges lie, National Post reached out to Deloitte Canada’s Chief Economist Dawn Desjardins for some insights.
This Q&A has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

content_blocks.text: Deloitte Canada raised its forecast for this year but cut next year’s. What has kept Canada’s economy afloat so far, and why do you expect that resilience to weaken?

Dawn Desjardins: In the second quarter, Canada’s economy really did grow very strongly, and it was pretty broad-based, which I thought was interesting. It wasn’t just the consumer, but it was also the housing market, and we saw business investment pick up. Exports also picked up. So it was really strong growth in that second quarter.

It wasn’t just the consumer, but it was also the housing market, and we saw business investment pick up. Exports also picked up. So it was really strong growth in that second quarter.

content_blocks.text: Now, as we are monitoring the third quarter, there is still growth, not nearly as rapid, but still seeing signs of growth.

That’s all to describe how we netted out to get a stronger growth rate for 2026. It really was that lift from the second quarter and the fact that the first quarter, which had initially been indicated to have contracted, actually was positive. So that kind of set the benchmark, and we did end up seeing our forecast being upgraded.

But for 2027, all the events of recent weeks and months certainly suggest that it’s having an impact on Canadian business confidence, Canadian consumer confidence, and we think very likely we will see slowing export activity as we go through the course of 2027. So those factors taken together, it does suggest that we’re in for a period of slower growth in 2027 compared to what we previously thought.
So still growth, but just 1.6 per cent. Previously, we thought 2 per cent.
Why hasn’t the full effect of the latest tariffs arrived yet? How does a tariff imposed today translate into weaker growth tomorrow?

I think what we’ve seen is that, especially in the most recent data we have, which was for the month of August, we saw actually some strong export activity as exporters tried to sell into the U.S. quicker than they otherwise would have. So they were kind of front-running those tariffs.

Now, as we go forward, of course, they are in place. And so we will see, we think, softer demand for some of Canadian goods sales into the United States, and that’s what’s going to weigh overall on our exports.
When you talk about exports slowing in 2027, are you referring specifically to the U.S. market?

We don’t actually have them falling. We just have them going very, very, very slowly. They will be negative, we think, in the next few quarters, but then start to pick up again as supply chains are rearranged, as Canadian companies look for other markets to sell to.
So a lot of it is, in fact, reflecting weaker demand we expect from the U.S. market.
What will the next phase feel like for Canadians? Will they see higher prices, fewer jobs, smaller pay increases, layoffs, or business closings?

I think we have seen already in August a decline in jobs. It’s likely going to remain a rough outlook for people who are looking for jobs, especially until we get to a period of time where we’re starting to see more business investment pick up.

So right now, I think the fact that we are seeing such a weight on business confidence, businesses today are obviously very concerned about where demand is going to come from. And so right now, I feel like they’re in that kind of perhaps low-hire, low-fire type of environment.

By that, I mean not necessarily looking to expand, but given that we’re seeing such weak immigration growth, probably looking to maybe retain some of the workers. And so you don’t see a lot of movement, I don’t think, in the labour market in the medium term, immediate term. But as we move forward, we do think that we’re going to start to see hiring pick up pace.

And this is going to reflect changes that we’re anticipating to come, whether it’s from public infrastructure investments, so by the public sector, or starting to see some private-sector money move into accompanying some of the investments that we’re seeing put in place by the federal and provincial government.
What about consumer prices?

Right now, what we’re seeing is that our inflation rate is being largely driven by energy prices. So, we have an inflation rate of three per cent right now, at the upper end of the Bank of Canada’s target band.
And when you look below that, prices are rising at a slower clip. If you exclude energy, I think it’s about 2.4 per cent. So just a little bit above the Bank of Canada’s target.

Now, as we move forward, it’s going to depend on how long tariffs stay in place, if companies are going to absorb some of it or … And this is more the retaliatory tariffs on Canadian goods coming into the country. And there, I have to say the overall amount of these retaliatory tariffs, the amount that they’re impacting is relatively contained. It will filter in and probably to other parts of the supply chain, but we don’t have a huge flow-through to consumer prices.
The big wildcard, I think, for the inflation outlook right now, there’s a few. One is, how long do energy prices remain elevated at these very high levels?

Also, how are Canadian consumers and Canadian businesses expecting inflation to evolve? Because that’s often, of course, the mechanism, right? They look to see whether or not they think prices are going to go up. Should they be demanding higher wages? And so we start to see even more upward pressure on prices.

So at this stage, we haven’t seen that evolve. We do think the inflation rate will likely start to move lower as we go through 2027. I think one of the factors there is that we are looking for this slower growth than we previously had been anticipating.

And when we look at the futures curve for oil prices, they are gradually coming down. Now, they’re not going back to the $60 level or $65 level of prior to the beginning of the war, but they’re still on a downward trajectory.

So that upward pressure from energy prices, when we look to where they were a year ago, starts to come out of the calculation. It doesn’t mean that prices are necessarily going to go down significantly, but at the same time, they’re going to stop rising. And when we’re there, we’re just using the futures market.

stories.title: How a Chinese surveillance camera giant operated 'illegally' in Canada for almost a decade before being banned
stories.summary: The Hikvision case raises serious questions about how the federal bureaucracy guards itself against technology it considers harmful.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — In July 2025, a senior federal official delivered a stark warning in a court affidavit. Every day that Chinese surveillance camera giant Hikvision continues to operate in Canada is another day China could spy further on Canadians.

“The continued operation of Hikvision Canada leads to an increase of the capabilities of the PRC (People’s Republic of China) to conduct surveillance of Canadians and others in Canada,” swore Robert McCarty, a senior investment officer in the Innovation, Science and Economic Development (Ised) branch responsible for reviewing foreign investments.

The potential espionage uses of the thousands upon thousands pieces of Hikvision surveillance equipment in Canada were numerous and unnerving, he warned.

The PRC could use it to monitor specific people, collect “pattern of life” information or use the company’s artificial-intelligence powered tools for facial recognition, license place monitoring or even record audio and video of people meeting in public or private spaces, McCarty wrote.

At the time McCarty swore his affidavit, Hikvision had operated “illegally” in Canada for nearly one decade. During that time, the Chinese giant catapulted from a relative newcomer to a “leader” in the Canadian security and surveillance gear market.

By 2024, over a dozen federal government departments and agencies offices had Hikvision equipment deployed on their properties. Today, there are over 28,700 of the company’s devices connected to public-facing Internet connections in Canada (and likely far more on private connections), according to device search engine Shodan.

Hikvision is the most valuable manufacturer of “Internet of Things” surveillance equipment in the world, but also one of the most controversial. It is partly state-owned by the Chinese government and benefits from PRC subsidies that allow it to sell its equipment cheaper than most competitors.

But over the last decade, the company has been linked to multiple major cybersecurity vulnerabilities , is allegedly used by the Chinese government for mass surveillance of Uyghurs and other minority groups , and has been blacklisted by governments around the world over concerns about espionage and cybersecurity.

And yet, it was only in 2025 that the Liberal government took what appeared to be decisive action against the company that Canada’s security apparatus had viewed as a potential threat to national security for years. In June 2025, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly issued a rare order demanding the company pack its bags and leave Canada.

In the confidential order obtained by National Post, the government laid out five broad reasons for the ban. Those include Chinese laws compelling companies to spy for the government, Hikvision’s proximity to the PRC and its ability to access end user data is some cases.

All issues security analysts, other Western governments and even Canada’s intelligence apparatus had been warning about for years.

The Hikvision case raises serious questions about how the federal bureaucracy guards itself against technology it considers harmful, and if it heeds the advice of its own security agencies.

Hikvision is one of only a handful of companies that the federal government has moved to outright ban from Canada due to national security concern. Details — including confidential and classified information — revealing the process behind-the-scenes are laid out in thousands of pages of Federal Court documents as part of Hikvision’s legal battle to remain in Canada.

In both the court documents and a statement, Hikvision denied all the government’s concerns regarding the safety of its equipment and said it could not use its gear to spy on Canadians on behalf of China.

“The existing court submissions accurately reflect the company’s stance that there is no evidence that our products or operations pose a national security risk in Canada. We continue to expect a fair and transparent environment for all businesses and investors in the country,” Hikvision told National Post.

Until Hikvision’s lawsuit, much of the government’s grave concerns about the Chinese company were locked away from the eyes of the public. Even the government’s 2025 order in council justifying the Hikvision ban is still marked as “privileged information and cannot be published” online .

The information reviewed by National Post invites scrutiny into how the federal government reviews foreign investments in Canada that could be injurious to national security.

That’s because, despite repeated warnings from its security and intelligence apparatus about Hikvision gear, copious public reporting detailing security vulnerabilities in Hikvision cameras and the risk of espionage posed by the Chinese tech giant, Ised only launched a review of the company’s Canadian presence in 2024.

That’s when the department discovered the company had been operating “illegally” in Canada for nearly one decade, according to government court filings.

Hikvision had never notified Ised when it incorporated in 2014 and began operating in Canada in 2015, a mandatory step that allows Ottawa to review the investment for national security concerns. In court, the company said it wasn’t aware of the obligation at the time, which a judge dismissed in September 2025 as “no excuse” while declaring Hikvision to have “unclean hands.”

Csis and other Canadian security agencies have long warned about the espionage risk of some Chinese tech. But those concerns spiked when the Chinese government adopted a National Intelligence Law in 2017 that requires local companies to “support, cooperate with and collaborate” with the China’s intelligence efforts if required.

Another key government concern was Hikvision’s participation as a “Tier One Technical Support Unit” in China’s cybersecurity vulnerability reporting program run by the government’s Ministry of State Security.

Not only did the company fail to disclose its voluntary participation in the program early in Ised’s review, the government charged, but the PRC is suspected of passing on reported cyber vulnerabilities to its “hacking teams” before disclosing them publicly.

In its lawsuit, Hikvision Canada said it complies with all Canadian privacy laws and regulations and is “not subject to PRC law”. It argued that it “cannot” be compelled by the PRC to provide end user data or any other information, nor had it ever received any such request from the Chinese government.

The company also fiercely opposed the government’s position that it could access users’ data, arguing that it had essentially no way to access such information. Furthermore, it said its participation in China’s cyber reporting program was aligned with industry norms.

Ottawa’s national security concerns about Hikvisions are simply “speculation,” the company charged.

Despite that, in early 2025, Hikvision offered a series of concessions to Ised in order to avoid a ban. Court records show the company proposed six undertakings, including adhering to Canadian privacy laws, appointing Canadian citizens to its board and issuing “transparency reports.”

But the offer did not sway Ottawa. China’s national security laws are a key reason why Canada declared Hikvision persona non grata in the federal government’s confidential 2025 order.

“Despite Hikvision Canada’s representations that it would attenuate the national security risks… it is likely that, even if those undertakings were given, Hikvision would act contrary to Canadian interests under the direction of the CCP (Chinese Communist Party) or the government of the PRC (and) would not adhere to any such undertakings,” reads the confidential document.

Samy Khoury, a former top Canadian cybersecurity official, told National Post that China’s National Intelligence Law applies to Chinese companies regardless of the intent of foreign staff. That’s particularly the case for state-owned companies like Hikvision.

“The National Intelligence Law compels companies to sometimes … act against the customers’ interests, regardless of the good faith of the local staff,” said Khoury, who headed the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and worked over three decades for the federal signals intelligence agency before retiring in July.

“The fact that the country has a law that compels a technology company, or presumably any company, to fork over data, that is something I would think twice about.”

Hikvision video surveillance gear should be given national security consideration and due diligence, particularly on Government of Canada facilities, Csis warned in the 2022 document.

In other words: don’t use it.

These cameras are worse than asbestos. They are super duper dangerous time bombs waiting to explode

Yet two years after the 2022 Csis alert, a dozen government departments and agencies still used Hikvision surveillance equipment on their property in 2024. Thursday, National Post reported that over one year after the government’s ban, at least two federal agencies still used Hikvision gear on their properties.

Now, Hikvision’s lawsuit against the federal government in a last-ditch attempt to quash the 2025 order requiring it to leave Canada May be reaping fruits.

In a September hearing, lawyers for both parties told the court that they were negotiating a settlement and hoped to find a “mutually acceptable outcome” by December. Presumably, the negotiations are about finding a way to allow Hikvision to continue operating in Canada, though both parties declined to comment.

In its submissions, Hikvision noted that being forced to cease its operations in Canada would effectively shut out its products and destroy its Canadian business.

“You don’t want to know when they’re going to start activating these backdoors they’ve put in place.

The potential espionage uses of the thousands upon thousands pieces of Hikvision surveillance equipment in Canada were numerous and unnerving, he warned.

The PRC could use it to monitor specific people, collect “pattern of life” information or use the company’s artificial-intelligence powered tools for facial recognition, license place monitoring or even record audio and video of people meeting in public or private spaces, McCarty wrote.

At the time McCarty swore his affidavit, Hikvision had operated “illegally” in Canada for nearly one decade. During that time, the Chinese giant catapulted from a relative newcomer to a “leader” in the Canadian security and surveillance gear market.

By 2024, over a dozen federal government departments and agencies offices had Hikvision equipment deployed on their properties. Today, there are over 28,700 of the company’s devices connected to public-facing Internet connections in Canada (and likely far more on private connections), according to device search engine Shodan.

Hikvision is the most valuable manufacturer of “Internet of Things” surveillance equipment in the world, but also one of the most controversial. It is partly state-owned by the Chinese government and benefits from PRC subsidies that allow it to sell its equipment cheaper than most competitors.

But over the last decade, the company has been linked to multiple major cybersecurity vulnerabilities , is allegedly used by the Chinese government for mass surveillance of Uyghurs and other minority groups , and has been blacklisted by governments around the world over concerns about espionage and cybersecurity.

And yet, it was only in 2025 that the Liberal government took what appeared to be decisive action against the company that Canada’s security apparatus had viewed as a potential threat to national security for years. In court, the company said it wasn’t aware of the obligation at the time, which a judge dismissed in September 2025 as “no excuse” while declaring Hikvision to have “unclean hands.”

stories.title: Taxes — hike them or hold them — become theme in B.C. election campaign
stories.summary: Taxes have become a central theme in the first half of British Columbia's election campaign with leaders promising to hold, hike or cut them.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
British Columbia economist Ross Hickey compares the tax policies of all three major parties in the provincial election campaign to candy — the kind that gives you a stomach ache.

“I think what all these politicians, and maybe the public, (are) forgetting is that we May not like taxes but there’s a difference between better and worse tax policy and the proposals that they’re making are leaning toward worse tax policy, all of them,” he said.

“They look like candy. It’s nice right now to have, but it’s gonna ruin our dinner.”

Taxes have become a central theme in the first half of the election campaign, with the B.C. Conservatives promising cuts in a bid to “supercharge” the economy, the NDP seeking to fund health care at the expense of top earners, and the Greens proposing a tax on wealth, not income.

But Hickey, an associate professor of economics in the faculty of management at the University of British Columbia’s Okanagan campus, labels all the options as “different kinds of bad” ideas that are “the most politically savvy pandering policies,” as they try to lure voters to the polls on Oct. 24.

“The BC NDP called a snap election because of the political convenience. They don’t have a new economic policy agenda that they’re putting forward. They’re just going because they think that the other side is weak,” he said of the decision to call the election two years early.

“The other sides, these other parties, the Greens and the Conservatives, weren’t prepared with the economic policy platform for this election, and so they’re trying their best to scrape something together, and what can you come up with on short notice?”

NDP Leader David Eby is proposing to suspend gasoline taxes, while bringing in a new tax bracket for people making more than $1 million and increasing taxes on the two highest existing income brackets starting at about $190,000.

“We’re asking (the highest earners) to pay a little bit more so we can deliver health care for British Columbians that they need,” he said earlier this week.

Eby has said the changes would generate $1 billion in 2028-29, while the Conservatives say increasing taxes will drive away much-needed doctors.

Hickey questions the NDP calculations, suggesting $1 billion in revenue is unlikely when you factor in people’s response to a new tax.

“When you increase marginal tax rates, that gives people an incentive to work less,” he said.

“So you have to account for that when you calculate how much revenue you’re going to get,” he said, suggesting independent economists estimated the increases would garner between $500 million and $700 million.

The Conservatives promise no new taxes, the elimination of the PST on some items and cuts to provincial taxes by $1,000 a year for nearly every working British Columbian.

The party platform says they would achieve the tax cut by raising the province’s basic personal exemption to $32,000 from $13,216.

Hickey said increasing the exemption level would put money in pockets but not motivate people to work in the same way a cut to marginal tax rates would.

He estimates the Conservative tax cut would cost about $2 billion.

“We already have a deficit of $13 billion in this province. So that’s saying, if we don’t change anything else, we’re going to go from $13 billion to $15 billion. Now who pays that … that’s the future generations of B.C.,” he said.

Interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson has not said how much his cuts would cost, but argued they were needed to “supercharge” the economy, which lost 20,000 jobs in September.

“The reality is we have to supercharge the economy first and get things going because that is our revenue. That is how we fund everything in this province,” he told reporters earlier this week.

The BC Greens’ election platform includes a promise to introduce a one-time “fair share tax” on extreme wealth, beginning at five per cent on net wealth above $50 million, 10 per cent above $100 million, and 20 per cent above $1 billion.

The party estimates the changes would raise approximately $22.2 billion.

Leader Emily Lowan has criticized Eby for co-opting “the language of the left” after she said he refused her proposal for an extreme wealth tax while he was in power.

Hickey said there are a lot of options for the extremely rich to move their wealth to more tax-friendly jurisdictions.

“Lots of studies have shown that people respond quite dramatically to these wealth taxes,” he said.

“They’ve tried them in a lot of European countries. They haven’t done a very good job of raising revenue because people move their wealth. So that’s actually kind of ugly. We want to encourage people to keep their investments in British Columbia.”

Hickey, who said he is not associated with any of the parties, said one of the best ways to raise revenue for the province is a harmonized sales tax, but acknowledged no political party would touch the idea.

Former premier Gordon Campbell introduced an HST in 2010 but the backlash was so severe that Campbell resigned and the idea was scrapped.

“We’re in this really bad spot because no one is strong enough as a leader to lead and give us the tax policy that we need, not just the tax policies that we want,” said Hickey.

“That’s the problem.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

stories.title: Outgoing Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette pushed off 'glass cliff' in election
stories.summary: Montreal - When former Ontario premier Kathleen Wynne watched the results of Quebec’s election come in, she says she couldn’t help but draw parallels between herself and Christine Fréchette.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - When former Ontario premier Kathleen Wynne watched the results of Quebec’s election come in, she says she couldn’t help but draw parallels between herself and Christine Fréchette.

The outgoing Quebec premier stepped down as leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec after her party failed to win any seats in Monday’s election.

The CAQ, founded in 2011, was in power for eight years in Quebec and held 79 seats in the provincial legislature before Fréchette triggered the election campaign in August. But the Parti Québécois capitalized on voters’ desire for change, winning enough seats in the election to form a minority government.

In a fractured political landscape, no party won more than 28 per cent of the overall vote. The CAQ received 13 per cent of all votes, down from the 40 per cent it received in 2022.

Fréchette had taken over as head of the party in April, replacing its founder, former premier François Legault, who resigned after tanking in the polls.

Wynne says she was also thrust in a position of leadership when the risk was high. Women in Canadian politics often face a “glass cliff” where they are given power with a high likelihood of failure, she adds.

“I wasn’t surprised,” said Wynne in a phone interview after the Quebec election. “There’s a definite pattern if we look at the situations that women have stepped into as leaders of parties both provincially and federally.”

Wynne succeeded Dalton McGuinty as Ontario premier in 2013, at a time when the provincial Liberals were unpopular due to a slew of scandals. She led the party to a majority victory in 2014 but lost the following election in 2018 to Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservatives.

Wynne had twice as much time as Fréchette to distance herself from her predecessor, which she believes made all the difference. Wynne was premier for a year and her government passed a provincial budget before going into the general election that she won.

She also draws comparisons between Fréchette and Kim Campbell, the only woman to serve as prime minister of Canada.

Campbell won the 1993 Progressive Conservative leadership race following Brian Mulroney’s retirement. She was in office for 132 days before the party lost to Jean Chrétien’s Liberals in what is considered the worst defeat for a federal governing party.

Much like Fréchette, Campbell inherited a deeply unpopular party with only a few months to rebrand. Mulroney and Legault both had strong political presence, and their successors struggled to make the parties their own.

Fréchette was first elected under the Caq’s banner in 2022. She served as immigration minister before taking over the energy and economy portfolio.

Wynne, also served as a minister under McGuinty, making it more difficult to distance herself from the track record of her predecessor.

“We both were part of a government that enacted those policies. So, there’s only so much you can do to disavow things that you’ve sat at the cabinet table to support,” she said.

But Université Laval political professor Thierry Giasson says gender is only one factor in the Caq’s defeat.

While Fréchette seemed to gain some momentum in the first half of the 40-day electoral campaign, due in part to the trade war with the United States, she quickly lost steam and struggled to make her mark in debates.

About a week before election day, she stumbled on the campaign trail by requesting an urgent meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney to discuss allegations of American interference in the election before she walked back her comments a few hours later. After she acknowledged there was no evidence of foreign interference, the CAQ sunk in the polls and faced a crushing defeat.

In her resignation speech on Tuesday, Fréchette denounced the lack of political opportunity for women and said she hopes her time as premier will open more doors for them. She was Quebec’s second female premier after Pauline Marois’ minority Parti Québécois government dissolved in 2014.

Despite her years of experience and having handled key portfolios in government such as finance, health and education, Marois held her minority government for less than two years. Fréchette held the role of premier for six months.

“Quebec was led by women for a total of 25 months in 159 years,” Fréchette said. “It’s too little.”

Political scientists have studied what University of Calgary professor Melanee Thomas calls the gendered structure of opportunity. She questioned whether men who would have otherwise vied for the CAQ leadership chose not to because of the party’s difficult position.

“Women come forward in that context because they’re like, ‘it’s my chance … if I don’t go now, will I be competitive when things are good?” she said.

Dominique Anglade May also come to mind, having taken over the Quebec Liberal party after the CAQ won its first majority government. She resigned after the following general election when her party lost 10 seats.

An expert in political marketing, Giasson says that while women face additional barriers in politics due to sexism, Fréchette was aware of the “colossal” task ahead when vying for the role of premier.

But he warns against putting all the blame on Fréchette. He believes that her opponent in the leadership race, Bernard Drainville, would have also come out of the general election empty-handed due to the sinking popularity of the Coalition Avenir Québec after its two consecutive mandates.

While Fréchette had hoped to have a “Mark Carney moment,” Giasson said she ended up paying the price for the political baggage left by her predecessor.

“In the end, she had a ‘Kim Campbell moment,’ which must be heartbreaking,” he said. “It’s incredible, 33 years later in another context … to try to reframe things and fail to do so because the (party) legacy is just too overwhelming.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.
paragraphs: Montreal - When former Ontario premier Kathleen Wynne watched the results of Quebec’s election come in, she says she couldn’t help but draw parallels between herself and Christine Fréchette.
The outgoing Quebec premier stepped down as leader of the Coalition Avenir Québec after her party failed to win any seats in Monday’s election.

The CAQ, founded in 2011, was in power for eight years in Quebec and held 79 seats in the provincial legislature before Fréchette triggered the election campaign in August. But the Parti Québécois capitalized on voters’ desire for change, winning enough seats in the election to form a minority government.
In a fractured political landscape, no party won more than 28 per cent of the overall vote. The CAQ received 13 per cent of all votes, down from the 40 per cent it received in 2022.
Fréchette had taken over as head of the party in April, replacing its founder, former premier François Legault, who resigned after tanking in the polls.

Wynne says she was also thrust in a position of leadership when the risk was high. Women in Canadian politics often face a “glass cliff” where they are given power with a high likelihood of failure, she adds.

“I wasn’t surprised,” said Wynne in a phone interview after the Quebec election. “There’s a definite pattern if we look at the situations that women have stepped into as leaders of parties both provincially and federally.”

Wynne succeeded Dalton McGuinty as Ontario premier in 2013, at a time when the provincial Liberals were unpopular due to a slew of scandals. She led the party to a majority victory in 2014 but lost the following election in 2018 to Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservatives.

Wynne had twice as much time as Fréchette to distance herself from her predecessor, which she believes made all the difference. Wynne was premier for a year and her government passed a provincial budget before going into the general election that she won.
She also draws comparisons between Fréchette and Kim Campbell, the only woman to serve as prime minister of Canada.

Campbell won the 1993 Progressive Conservative leadership race following Brian Mulroney’s retirement. She was in office for 132 days before the party lost to Jean Chrétien’s Liberals in what is considered the worst defeat for a federal governing party.

Much like Fréchette, Campbell inherited a deeply unpopular party with only a few months to rebrand. Mulroney and Legault both had strong political presence, and their successors struggled to make the parties their own.
Fréchette was first elected under the Caq’s banner in 2022. She served as immigration minister before taking over the energy and economy portfolio.
Wynne, also served as a minister under McGuinty, making it more difficult to distance herself from the track record of her predecessor.
“We both were part of a government that enacted those policies. So, there’s only so much you can do to disavow things that you’ve sat at the cabinet table to support,” she said.
But Université Laval political professor Thierry Giasson says gender is only one factor in the Caq’s defeat.

While Fréchette seemed to gain some momentum in the first half of the 40-day electoral campaign, due in part to the trade war with the United States, she quickly lost steam and struggled to make her mark in debates.

About a week before election day, she stumbled on the campaign trail by requesting an urgent meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney to discuss allegations of American interference in the election before she walked back her comments a few hours later. After she acknowledged there was no evidence of foreign interference, the CAQ sunk in the polls and faced a crushing defeat.

In her resignation speech on Tuesday, Fréchette denounced the lack of political opportunity for women and said she hopes her time as premier will open more doors for them. She was Quebec’s second female premier after Pauline Marois’ minority Parti Québécois government dissolved in 2014.

Despite her years of experience and having handled key portfolios in government such as finance, health and education, Marois held her minority government for less than two years. Fréchette held the role of premier for six months.
“Quebec was led by women for a total of 25 months in 159 years,” Fréchette said. “It’s too little.”

Political scientists have studied what University of Calgary professor Melanee Thomas calls the gendered structure of opportunity. She questioned whether men who would have otherwise vied for the CAQ leadership chose not to because of the party’s difficult position.
“Women come forward in that context because they’re like, ‘it’s my chance … if I don’t go now, will I be competitive when things are good?” she said.

Dominique Anglade May also come to mind, having taken over the Quebec Liberal party after the CAQ won its first majority government. She resigned after the following general election when her party lost 10 seats.

An expert in political marketing, Giasson says that while women face additional barriers in politics due to sexism, Fréchette was aware of the “colossal” task ahead when vying for the role of premier.

But he warns against putting all the blame on Fréchette. He believes that her opponent in the leadership race, Bernard Drainville, would have also come out of the general election empty-handed due to the sinking popularity of the Coalition Avenir Québec after its two consecutive mandates.
While Fréchette had hoped to have a “Mark Carney moment,” Giasson said she ended up paying the price for the political baggage left by her predecessor.

“In the end, she had a ‘Kim Campbell moment,’ which must be heartbreaking,” he said. “It’s incredible, 33 years later in another context … to try to reframe things and fail to do so because the (party) legacy is just too overwhelming.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

Public Service Announcement

[](http://london.ca/newsroom/public-service-announcement/temporary-closure-woodward-avenue)

Friday, October 9, 2026

Woodward Avenue will be closed between Tozer Avenue and Edinburgh Street from October 14 to October 16 while work is completed on a private water connection.

Above: A map of the road closure on Woodward Avenue between Tozer Avenue and Edinburgh Street.

A detour will be in place using Riverside Drive, Beaverbrook Avenue and Oxford Street West. The west sidewalk on Woodward Avenue will also be closed during this work.

Drivers should also be aware thatRichmond Street will be closed between Mill Street and Piccadilly Street during this time for railway crossing repairs. Drivers should plan ahead and use alternate routes.

Some LTC routes will be impacted. Please check theLondon Transit Commission websitefor the most up-to-date information on bus schedules and detours.

For more information about construction projects in London, visit theRenew London map.

Friday, October 9, 2026
Woodward Avenue will be closed between Tozer Avenue and Edinburgh Street from October 14 to October 16 while work is completed on a private water connection.
Above: A map of the road closure on Woodward Avenue between Tozer Avenue and Edinburgh Street.
A detour will be in place using Riverside Drive, Beaverbrook Avenue and Oxford Street West. The west sidewalk on Woodward Avenue will also be closed during this work.

Drivers should also be aware thatRichmond Street will be closed between Mill Street and Piccadilly Street during this time for railway crossing repairs. Drivers should plan ahead and use alternate routes.
Some LTC routes will be impacted. Please check theLondon Transit Commission websitefor the most up-to-date information on bus schedules and detours.

Friday, October 9, 2026

Huron Street at the intersections of both Highbury Avenue and McNay Street will experience lane restrictions beginning today until Tuesday, October 13. These temporary lane restrictions are to allow repairs to underground water valves in the area.

Drivers and pedestrians are encouraged to plan ahead and allow extra time when travelling through the area.

Nearby businesses remain accessible. Drivers should follow signs and directions from crews.

Please check the London Transit Commission website for the most up-to-date information on bus schedules and detours.

stories.title: Salah Bachir, former Cineplex president and philanthropist, dies at 71
stories.summary: Bashir passed away at home Oct. 8 following a prolonged illness, said his husband, artist Jacob Yerex.
stories.author: Morgan Sevareid-Bocknek
stories.content:
Salah Bachir, the Canadian philanthropist and film entrepreneur, has died at age 71.

He passed away at home Oct. 8 following a prolonged illness, said his husband, artist Jacob Yerex.

In a post written prior to his death and shared on his Facebook page , Bachir wrote that he spent the end of his life “surrounded by family and friends.”

“I have had an amazing life that I am lucky to have shared with my wonderful husband, Jacob Yerex, two brothers and two sisters, eight nieces and nephews, eight grandnieces and nephews, 15 godchildren and a fantastic daughter, all of whom have brought me immense joy,” he wrote.

Bachir was born in Lebanon, and moved to Toronto in 1965, where he grew up in the city’s Rexdale neighbourhood.

In his Facebook post, he said his greatest source of pride was his work in the arts, social justice and philanthropy worlds. He highlighted the wing named for him at the 519 community centre, as well as a space at the Art Gallery of Ontario and two St. Joseph’s Hospital dialysis centres named after him and his husband.

Yerex said it was important to him to highlight Bachir’s social activism and work supporting different causes.

“It’s an opportunity to kind of put that out there, advocating for people to get involved, show up, be present, and fight the good fight,” Yerex told the Star.

Bachir’s philanthropic activities were extensive: He was a founding member of the Canadian Film Centre and served as a board member for the Art Gallery of Ontario, the Luminato Festival, the Canadian Foundation for Aids Research, and the 519. He was twice the grand marshal of the Toronto Pride Parade. In 2012, he received the Canadian Centre for Diversity’s Human Relations Award for outstanding contributions to Canadian society.

Salah Bachir speaks after receiving the lifetime achievement award at the Pride Toronto Gala & Awards in 2009.

He was also appointed a member of the Order of Canada and the Order of Ontario.

Bachir was president of Cineplex Media from 2006 to 2021. He was the publisher of the cinema chain’s magazine (including a brief partnership with the Star in 2021, when the magazine was relaunched as Star Cineplex ), co-founded the company’s Scene Points loyalty program, and worked on its partnership with Scotiabank.

extensive art collection , 3,000 pieces of which were on display in his Toronto condo. His collection included pieces by Canadian artists Betty Goodwin, Stephen Andrews and Attila Richard Lukacs, as well as “more Warhols here than you can shake a tin of Campbell’s soup at,” Zekas wrote.

he published a memoir titled “First to Leave the Party: My Life with Ordinary People … Who Happen to be Famous,” and shared stories about his encounters with stars and celebrities, including Paul Newman and wife Joanne Woodward, Joan Rivers, Mary Tyler Moore, Keith Haring, Orson Welles, Aretha Franklin and Elizabeth Taylor, just to name a few.

profiled in the Star’s “Home of the Week” series in 2024 after he listed his Paris, Ont. home for sale — a 8,900-square-foot mansion where he hosted many of the celebrities he wrote about in his book.

stories.title: 15,000 attend unsanctioned Homecoming gatherings in London, 3 arrested
stories.summary: London police say about 15,000 people attended unsanctioned gatherings across the city on Homecoming weekend, resulting in 248 penalties and three arrests.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
London police say about 15,000 people attended unsanctioned gatherings across the city on Homecoming weekend, resulting in 248 penalties and three arrests.

About 5,000 people remained into Saturday evening, prompting traffic measures to support public safety, including closures on Broughdale Avenue and Huron Street and lane reductions on Richmond Street.

“Most young adults we encountered cooperated with emergency services and partner agencies,” said London police Supt. Bill Berg.

He said downtown bars reached capacity and sidewalks remained busy. At times, people moved onto roadways, disrupting traffic, and officers responded to maintain public safety.

They issued 248 administrative monetary penalties and provincial offence notices for public nuisance parties, liquor-related offences, excessive noise and parking violations.

Police also made three arrests for public intoxication.

Officers issued multiple verbal warnings while managing crowds and helping maintain public safety for attendees, community members and emergency personnel.

The Middlesex-London Paramedic Service reported 23 calls for service and 14 patient transports related to Saturday’s gatherings.

stories.title: Indigenous cultural burn near Osoyoos revives traditional fire stewardship
stories.summary: Smoke rising over the grasslands west of Osoyoos this week is part of a carefully planned burn aimed at doing more than reducing wildfire risk.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Smoke rising over the grasslands west of Osoyoos this week is part of a carefully planned burn aimed at doing more than reducing wildfire risk.

The multi-day burn in the Nighthawk Road area is also helping revive Indigenous cultural fire practices that were suppressed for generations.

The Lower Similkameen Indian Band is working with partners, including the B.C. Wildfire Service, ON the approximately 160-hectare burn.

Julia Peterson, a councillor with the Lower Similkameen Indian Band, says the project is about bringing traditional knowledge back together with modern wildfire management.

“It was abolished, you know, by previous law, and so we’re really trying to bring those practices back, and combine these together with Western science,” Peterson said.

For Peterson, the work is also deeply connected to ceremony and the relationship between the land and the community.

“Ceremony connects us to land, it connects us to the animals, to the water,” she said. “This is bringing this ceremonial practice back into our community.”

The controlled fire is also intended to improve the health of the grasslands by clearing overgrowth, encouraging native grasses and improving habitat for wildlife.

Daryl Gibb, who owns the Nighthawk RV Park near the burn area, has seen how quickly wildfire can threaten the region.

“At the bottom of the hill there was a lot of sagebrush that choked out the grass,” Gibb said. “Getting rid of that sagebrush will definitely bring the grass back again.”

4:52 Summerland prescribed burns were in planning stage before Bald Range wildfire

Gibb also hopes the work will help reduce the risk to nearby communities and properties.

“About six or eight years ago, there was a big fire burning in the Cascades just across the river from us,” he said. “And then there’s been little local ones close.”

The project is also an example of First Nations and government agencies working together on wildfire preparedness.

Justin Smith, with Lower Similkameen Indian Band Emergency Management, says wildfire does not respect the boundaries between jurisdictions.

“Everybody’s in the same boat,” Smith said. “The fire doesn’t recognize the boundary. The fire doesn’t even recognize the border. It just goes where it wants to go.”

That makes cooperation particularly important as communities across the region work to reduce wildfire fuels and prepare for increasingly severe fire seasons.

Peterson says the Nighthawk Road burn is only part of a larger need for treatment across the region.

“We still have many other areas that need this kind of treatment to bring safety to the communities, both on and off reserve,” she said.

stories.title: Steven Galloway accuser threatened to sue UBC for up to $3-million, defamation trial hears
stories.summary: School had already given former creative-writing student bursary worth $30,000, money that Galloway testified she wasn’t entitled to
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
The former creative-writing student who accused best-selling novelist and then-professor Steven Galloway of sexual assault threatened to sue the University of British Columbia for up to $3-million, claiming negligence by the school and other offences.

The B.C. Supreme Court heard Thursday that the university had already given the woman a bursary after graduating worth $30,000, money that Mr. Galloway testified Thursday the woman was not entitled to.

Mr. Galloway, who was the chair of the school’s creative-writing program, launched a defamation case against almost two dozen defendants. He claims that their allegations that he sexually assaulted and harassed the woman ruined his reputation, cost him his job and destroyed his personal life. Only the woman and three others are on trial. The rest have settled with Mr. Galloway.

The court heard about an April 7, 2016, e-mail from the woman’s then-lawyer, Joanna Birenbaum, to Ubc’s associate vice-president of equity & inclusion, Sara-Jane Finlay. In it, Ms. Birenbaum thanks the school for its “very quick transfer of funds,” which Mr. Galloway said he found out in 2017 amounted to $30,000. The payment was first revealed during his arbitration with the school over his firing.

Mr. Galloway told the court he believed that the woman, his former lover, was not eligible for the money because she had already graduated.

“There’s no academic reason to have given this,” he stated during questioning from his lawyer, Daniel Burnett.

Court also heard that later in 2016, sometime in the middle of December, Ubc’s general counsel Hubert Lai was involved in an e-mail discussion over the woman’s draft statement of claim to sue the school for up to $3-million for negligence, breach of contract and other reasons.

It was not revealed in court Thursday what happened with her lawsuit threat.

Arden Beddoes, lawyer for the woman who is known as A.B. because her identity is protected by a publication ban, objected to Mr. Galloway’s testimony about the internal UBC e-mails because he said it called for Mr. Galloway to speculate.

“The documents speak for themselves,” Mr. Beddoes said of the exhibits of internal UBC communications.

But Mr. Burnett was allowed by the judge to pursue the discussion of financial compensation for A.B. because – if his client is awarded damages − it could point toward her malicious actions.

“The communications by or on behalf of A.B. getting and seeking money out of UBC is arising from the very thing that is the defamation,” he said.

A.B. is not testifying and, at the start of the trial, Mr. Beddoes told the court that she was withdrawing her defences of truth and fair comment – but not admitting that she spread lies about her former romantic partner. Mr. Beddoes said she had tried to kill herself twice in recent months because of the stress of the ordeal.

After the woman’s allegations surfaced in 2015, Mr. Galloway was suspended and then fired as head of Ubc’s creative-writing program without severance due to breach of trust. News of the incident spurred an online firestorm over the CanLit luminary’s rights to due process versus the rights of his alleged victim.

A retired judge hired by the university to investigate the complaint found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established that he committed sexual assault or assault.

Mr. Galloway was never charged with a crime.

Earlier Thursday, Mr. Burnett asked his client about the up to $1.5-million in total royalties he made from his 2008 international bestseller The Cellist of Sarajevo . Court heard that the book had been optioned for a movie adaptation, which never materialized.

Mr. Galloway testified that he had signed a contract to produce three new books about a ventriloquist detective before the allegation surfaced and detonated his ability to continue as an author or be booked as a paid public speaker.

He said his income from book royalties had since “cratered” to about $5,000 to $10,000 a year “tops,” and that he hasn’t received any invitations for speaking engagements.

Mr. Galloway also testified that people who signed a letter criticizing the university’s handling of the misconduct case against him were subjected to “extremely hurtful” comments and suffered socially and professionally.

The letter, known as “UBC Accountable,” was published in November, 2016, with signatories from the literary community, including Margaret Atwood, but Mr. Galloway said many removed their names after a wave of vitriolic online criticism.

He said people lost jobs and friendships were ruined, and one signatory called him in tears, saying her daughter was never going to speak to her again.

A number of friends, even those who believed in his innocence, would not talk to him any more because being associated with him would be “career suicide,” he said.

Mr. Galloway said that after he’d won an arbitration award from the university, he “briefly had the hope” that the social-media storm would subside, but the posts continued.

He did not get his job back as part of the arbitration.

“I wouldn’t have gone back for a million dollars a year to that place,” Mr. Galloway said.

Mr. Galloway is due to be cross-examined by lawyers for the four defendants starting Friday.
