stories.title: Author Galloway says his defenders lost jobs, friends after letter opposed suspension
stories.summary: Vancouver - Author and former University of British Columbia professor Steven Galloway says people who signed a letter criticizing the university’s handling of a misconduct case against him were subjected to “extremely hurtful” comments, and suffered socially and professionally.
stories.author: Darryl Greer The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Author and former UBC creative writing professor Steven Galloway wept as he testified that he can no longer write since unproven allegations of sexual assault derailed his career.

“I just can’t do it anymore. I wish I could,” he said in court on Thursday in the defamation case he brought against his accuser and others.

Galloway told the B.C. Supreme Court judge that writing had been the “greatest part” of his life.

The lawsuit was launched by Galloway after a former student, known only as A.B., alleged he sexually assaulted her, while others spread the claim on social media.

A.B.‘s lawyer said Wednesday that his client’s defence no longer includes an assertion that Galloway sexually assaulted her, but only that she reported he had done so.

A.B. is not testifying in the case, and her identity is protected by a publication ban.

After Justice Neena Sharma allowed for a short break in testimony on Thursday, Galloway stood and briefly rested his head on a concrete wall behind the witness box.

Galloway’s lawyer, Dan Burnett, asked him about the “biggest changes” to his life since the allegations against him surfaced in November 2015.

“Whatever it holds, I’m not particularly excited by it. I don’t know what my life will be, but you know, probably scrape together a living till I’m old enough to retire. Or I’ll be one of those old guys bagging groceries, which is nothing against them, but I don’t think anyone wants to be that old guy bagging groceries,” he said.

“I don’t particularly like the person I have to be now. I don’t want to be me.”

He now sells boats for a living.

The court heard he’d been writing a comedy novel to be part of a three-book deal with a major publisher, and a paperback version of his novel “The Confabulist” was in the works, before the allegations.

He said his income from book royalties had since “cratered” to about $5,000 to $10,000 a year “tops,” and he hasn’t received any invitations for speaking engagements since the woman, with whom he had an affair, accused him of rape, and sexual and physical assault.

He estimated he’d made between $1.3 million and $1.5 million in royalties worldwide, and told the court that “The Cellist of Sarajevo” had been optioned for a movie adaptation that never materialized.

Galloway has long denied A.B.‘s allegations and did so again during his testimony on Wednesday.

On Thursday, his lawyer questioned him about the state of his career.

“I, like every writer, got plenty of bad reviews, and it ruins your lunch, but not your supper,” he said. “I’ve never had my humanity torn apart the way this process has done that.”

Galloway testified earlier Thursday that people who signed a letter criticizing the university’s handling of the misconduct case against him were subjected to “extremely hurtful” comments, and suffered socially and professionally.

The letter, known as “UBC Accountable,” was published in November 2016 with signatories from the literary community, including Margaret Atwood, but Galloway said many removed their names after a wave of vitriolic criticism online.

He said people lost jobs and friendships were ruined, and one signatory called him in tears, saying her daughter was never going to speak to her again.

A number of friends, even those who believed in his innocence, would not talk to him anymore because being associated with him would be “career suicide,” he said.

Galloway told the court that “UBC Accountable” became a hashtag that spread widely online, and became an “all encompassing” term referring to him, and that he reacted with disgust, dismay and horror to the thousands of vitriolic social media posts that were published.

He told the court that a reporter from The Canadian Press had phoned him “relentlessly” and came to his home and left messages in his mailbox, seemingly having access to confidential information.

Galloway said he had attended a hospitality suite during a writers festival in October 2016, against his “better judgment,” and said some people spoke to him and others saw him and walked out.

He said an article in the Walrus magazine reported that he was given a “standing ovation” at the festival, which he said didn’t happen and he contacted the publication’s editor about the inaccuracy.

Galloway said the article portrayed the Canadian literature scene as “a den of rapists and rape apologists” who applauded him after his public shaming and firing.

“I still don’t quite understand how the editors at the Walrus didn’t fact check that,” he said.

He said after he’d won an arbitration award from the university, he “briefly had the hope” the social media storm would subside, but the posts continued.

Galloway did not get his job back as part of the arbitration.

“I wouldn’t have gone back for a million dollars a year to that place,” Galloway said.

He said journalists had been pursuing him for interviews “since Day 1,” and he decided to grant one to Globe and Mail columnist Gary Mason, thinking it May cause people to leave him alone.

“The Gary Mason article didn’t do anything. If anything, it made it worse,” he said. “One thing I’ve learned through all this is that when a mob starts coming for you, it doesn’t matter what you do.”

He said he learned about an art show being held in New York in 2018 through defendant Mandi Gray’s Twitter account, a “rape narrative” exhibition that didn’t mention him by name but included the “UBC Accountable” hashtag.

Burnett later took the court through documents, including evidence that UBC had given A.B. a $30,000 bursary after her graduation.

Galloway said the sum “eclipses the entire bursary program for the entire creative writing program. There’s no academic reason to have given this. After having endured UBC accuse me of a whole manner of crime to see them do this was flabbergasting,” he said.

The documents, which came out in the earlier arbitration proceedings, also included the draft of a lawsuit from A.B. in relation to the alleged assaults. It was never filed.

Galloway said the claim was for millions of dollars.

He said learning that A.B. was still “perpetuating” the allegations — after both his firing and a report by a former judge had determined that the allegations against him were unsubstantiated — was “another kick in the teeth.”

He said near the end of his testimony on Thursday that now his “world is small,” with few friends and only his family, isolating himself from social life.

The court heard he got a job cleaning and fixing swimming pools, writing online marketing advertisements, and he currently works as a boat broker, working as a subcontractor and paid on sales commissions.

Galloway’s cross-examination is set to begin on Friday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Arrests, detentions of Canadians in U.S. up 60 per cent, Ottawa says
stories.summary: The department's annual report on consular cases, published Thursday, tracks an increase in arrests between April 2025 and March 2026.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
By Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press

Posted October 8, 2026 2:14 pm

The number of arrest and detention cases involving Canadians citizens has jumped 60 per cent, Global Affairs Canada says.

The department’s annual report on consular cases, published Thursday, tracks an increase in arrests between April 2025 and March 2026, despite a 25 per cent decline in visits by Canadians to the U.S.

The report does not explain what caused the increase, though U.S. President Donald Trump has expanded immigration raids and Canadians have reported facing uncomfortable questions from U.S. border officials.

3:14 ‘This is Trump’s America’: Protests erupt in Austin, Texas after ICE agent shoots man

Overall, the report tracks a one-fifth increase in the number of arrests of Canadians around the world, including a threefold increase in the number of arrests in Thailand.

Global Affairs Canada has warned in recent years that the growing frequency of wars and natural disasters is resulting in more consular cases that are more complex and expensive to manage.

The data also shows an increase in the number of Canadians voluntarily registering with the department when they go abroad, which helps Ottawa send safety advice and co-ordinate evacuations.

stories.title: Air Canada CEO Michael Rousseau rebuked over English-only message
stories.summary: The commissioner's annual report says the office received a large number of complaints after Michael Rousseau posted a four-minute video that only included two French words.
stories.author: Morgan Lowrie
stories.content:
The Commissioner of Official Languages of Canada is rebuking Air Canada’s outgoing CEO for a condolence message he delivered almost entirely in English after a deadly plane crash in New York earlier this year.

The commissioner’s annual report says the office received a large number of complaints after Michael Rousseau posted a four-minute video that only included two French words — “bonjour” and “merci.”

“The intensity of the reactions and the high volume of complaints received in response to this video show that both of our official languages genuinely matter to the Canadian public and that we must continue to protect them,” Burke told reporters in Ottawa, adding that the complaints are still under investigation.

2:17 Business Matters: Air Canada names new, French-speaking CEO

“This situation illustrates that bilingualism is an essential skill for any leader, whether in politics, federal public service, or even in the private sector.”

Rousseau’s video message came after an Air Canada regional jet that took off in Montreal, collided with a fire truck crossing the runway at LaGuardia Airport in New York on March 22, killing two pilots and sending more than 40 people to hospital.

Quebecer Antoine Forest and Mackenzie Gunther, from Ontario, were the two pilots killed in the collision .

Burke’s report says it’s important for Canadians to hear and see their leaders speaking equally in both official languages in times of crisis, “and not solely through an interpreter or subtitles.”

Seven days after Air Canada posted Rousseau’s video, the company’s board of directors announced that he would retire by the end of the third quarter of 2026 and that it was considering a number of criteria for his successor, including the ability to communicate in French.

The commissioner’s office said in an email that it received 2,425 complaints on the video, including 98 that arrived after the end of the current financial year on March 31.

Burke’s 31-page report also touched on a number of other issues, including concern over how federal budget cuts could impact the government’s language obligations and minority language communities.

“In the past, spending on official languages-related activities has often been targeted during periods of fiscal restraint,” the report read.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has promised to cut the size of the public service, relying mainly on attrition.

Burke said it’s still too soon to measure the impacts of the 2025 federal budget, which laid out a plan to save tens of billions of dollars over five years in budget cuts and government efficiency measures.

“We’re watching the government’s actions closely on this subject, and we’re waiting to see how the cutbacks will actually play out within the administration, so we can then assess how the government has addressed the concerns we raised at the beginning,” Burke said.

2:10 Air Canada CEO Rousseau to retire amid language controversy

The report also cited what it saw as positive developments, including $150 million in funding announced for CBC/Radio-Canada in the 2025—2026 fiscal year and a Supreme Court decision in June that ruled that New Brunswick’s lieutenant-governor must be bilingual.

This decision “represents a step forward for the province’s language rights and a major victory for official language minority communities,” the report read.

The report also dedicated several pages to the issued raised by the use of artificial intelligence.

It noted that AI has potential to be used as a tool for translation and interpretation, as well as promoting bilingualism and language learning.

But Burke noted that AI is prone to errors, and has a “language bias” towards English due to the predominance of English-language “content and perspectives” on the internet.

The commissioner recommended that the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat incorporate official languages to its artificial intelligence strategy and other documents by March 2027, “so that they are systematically taken into account during the development, implementation and use of any tools, training, programs, policies or guidelines aimed at deploying artificial intelligence across the public service.”

stories.title: Quebec Conservatives are celebrating wins for the party — and its ideas
stories.summary: Éric Duhaime's party won over 20 per cent of the votes and a whopping 19 seats on Monday, mostly in the Quebec City area.
stories.author: Catherine Lévesque
stories.content:
Plessisville, QC — “Plessisville is Conservative. He’s wasting his time here.”

Samuel Côté, a country music DJ, and his girlfriend Mélanie Lévesque, a social worker, were eating lunch on their porch, just steps away from where Parti Québécois Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon was trying to shore up support before the Quebec election.

Clearly, the PQ did not have their vote. Their lawn sign showed they instead supported their Conservative candidate, Tarek Henoud, who would end up winning the riding of Arthabaska—L’Érable, located between Montreal and Quebec City, ON Monday.

This is also one of the handful of seats that would end up costing the PQ its coveted majority, having underestimated the voter turnout for their Conservative opponents.

“To begin with, I’m not a huge separatist,” said Côté, who also goes by the alias DJ Sammy. “I used to vote for Québec Solidaire when I was much younger — like a lot of young people in the 18-to-25 age range. But I really lost interest in them during COVID.”

Côté said he was skeptical of the “medical conspiracies” during the pandemic and refused to get vaccinated. It was during that time that he subscribed to follow Conservative Leader Éric Duhaime who was not shy to address those questions.

“That’s what made me move from the far left to a less extreme right, I’d say.”

One example that spoke to them was the promise to abolish the provincial tax on used goods. Lévesque said it makes no sense to pay taxes on a used car, for instance, when those same taxes were already paid for when that same car was brand-new.

Côté also said Duhaime’s promise to abolish Quebec’s “carbon tax” appealed to him. The province remains the only jurisdiction in Canada to have maintained its carbon pricing system, which is adding to the already bloated price at the pump.

The PQ government has promised to abolish the provincial tax on used goods. It also intends to cut the provincial tax on gas by half for one year and reimburse it completely for individual Quebecers earning less than $40,000 per year with a cheque of $125.

Côté said he was happy to see the ideas promoted by the Quebec Conservatives be adopted by other parties — and in this case, make their way to government.

“The important thing is for the ideas to get through — not for the Conservative government to get elected. No. The goal is for the ideas to get through,” he said.

While lots of ink has been spilled on the referendum issue, many Quebecers have expressed they just want to get by. And Duhaime was able to pound that message.

As a result, the Quebec Conservatives are making a noticeable comeback in the National Assembly with over 20 per cent of the votes and a whopping 19 seats. They won 15 out of the 18 seats in Quebec City, spilling into central Quebec and the Eastern Townships. Their navy blue seats now form a large blot on a map of Quebec.

“It exceeded our expectations,” said director of communications Cédric Lapointe.

Duhaime has said he built on the lessons of the past campaign, where his party won no seats despite finishing with 13 per cent of the popular vote. So, he focused his efforts on the Quebec City area, campaigning in surrounding regions as his support grew.

Lapointe said the idea was to develop their brand as the “party of taxpayers” by focusing on people’s purchasing power. He said it was a clear contrast with the PQ and the Quebec Liberals, which were more focused on constitutional debates.

“We were considered by many people as an alternative to the old parties,” he said.

The Quebec Conservatives were not immune to criticism, however. Some of their candidates made headlines for recent comments on vaccines, abortion or Canada becoming the 51st state. Duhaime dismissed those comments as “distractions.”

His campaign was also overshadowed by revelations that 62 per cent of his most recent book, “Destination Autonomy: Expanding Quebec’s Powers within the Canadian Confederation,” was written with artificial intelligence.

Duhaime argued that AI is a tool like any other and those were still his ideas.

In the last stretch of the campaign, Duhaime called on voters who were disappointed by the incumbent Coalition Avenir Québec government to instead opt to vote for the Conservatives to block a PQ majority and a possible third referendum.

Duhaime made that ultimate appeal in front of a garage with two buses — one with a “Yes” sign and the other with a “No” sign.

“There is only one party that can stop them from leaving the garage,” he said.

The Quebec Conservatives were aiming for at least 12 seats and form a recognized party at the National Assembly. Poll aggregators were showing there would be close races with the PQ in many ridings which could reduce it to a minority government.

The race in Arthabaska—L’Érable was especially personal for both parties.

The PQ had won a byelection in the riding in 2025 with former journalist Alex Boissonneault against Duhaime, who had asked Henoud, who was also their candidate in 2022, to step aside in an attempt to finally win a seat at the National Assembly.

St-Pierre Plamondon had even promised, days before the vote, to name Boissonneault as one of his ministers in a PQ government. In the end, it wasn’t even close.

Henoud won 41 per cent of the vote against Boissonneault’s 33 per cent.

Duhaime mentioned this accomplishment in his speech the night of the election.

“Tonight, we made history. For the first time in (nearly) 100 years, Quebecers have decided to send a large caucus of Conservative members to the National Assembly.”

“And just think about this: we defeated six incumbent ministers, and we even defeated a Parti Québécois minister, believe it or not,” he added.

That comment prompted loud boos from the PQ supporters on their election night.

Duhaime said the rise of his party on Monday night is certainly no accident.

“It is about a political family — about values ​​deeply rooted in our identity, our history, and our regions,” he said.

“Individual freedom, entrepreneurship, the importance of family, regional autonomy, Quebec’s autonomy within the Confederation — in short, the pride of being Québécois,” he continued.

During an unrelated announcement in Sherbrooke on Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney would not comment on the rise of the Quebec Conservatives at the provincial level.

“For us, at the federal level, we take messages from byelections and federal elections,” he said.

In that sense, he said he was “very encouraged” that his own party won over 50 per cent of the votes in a Quebec byelection back in August.

stories.title: Covert U.S. effort led to Canada's acceptance of dubious postwar immigrants: study
stories.summary: Newly released passages of a landmark 1986 study say at least 35 people with apparently suspect backgrounds came to Canada after the Second World War through a covert program set up by U.S. intelligence agencies.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Newly released passages of a landmark 1986 study say at least 35 people with apparently suspect backgrounds came to Canada after the Second World War through a covert program set up by U.S. intelligence agencies.

The previously secret details appear in a recently released version of a study on the resettlement of alleged Nazi war criminals in Canada during the Cold War era.

B’nai Brith Canada fought for years to see more of the report by researcher Alti Rodal, which was conducted for Canada’s inquiry on war criminals led by Jules Deschenes in the 1980s.

The Federal Court last month ordered the release of some long-concealed portions of Rodal’s study.

The Canadian Heritage Department did not appeal the decision and Library and Archives of Canada provided B’nai Brith with the latest public version of the Rodal report.

Simon Wolle, B’nai Brith Canada’s chief executive officer, calls it a historic outcome, adding in a statement the organization is pleased the information has been made available to historians, survivors of the Holocaust and their descendants, and the public.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alberta government tells Edmonton to dump infill rules, cites parking, property value
stories.summary: Edmonton - Alberta's government says it's ordering the city of Edmonton to revert to its old rules for infill housing development.
stories.author: Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Premier Danielle Smith says the city’s policies, which have largely been in place since 2024, are too permissive and are harming homeowners by reducing property values and creating parking headaches.

The 2024 changes paved the way for housing redevelopment across much of Edmonton in an effort to increase density and manage population growth.

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

Smith says the goal can’t just be to build more housing, and that more attention needs to be paid on making sure new developments are properly integrated into the existing community.

She says Edmonton city council will have three months to comply, after which it will be required to review and consult on its land use rules.

The province is also ordering Calgary to maintain its current rules after that city’s council backtracked on its own zoning policies earlier this year.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: NewsAlert: Cold Lake First Nations seeks judicial review of pipeline designation
stories.summary: Ottawa - Cold Lake First Nations has filed an application for judicial review in Federal Court challenging Ottawa's decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline a project in the national interest.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Cold Lake First Nations filed an application for judicial review in Federal Court on Thursday challenging Ottawa’s decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline as a project in the national interest.

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced last week the pipeline from Alberta to British Columbia would be fast-tracked under the Building Canada Act.

The designation as a project of national interest does not eliminate the requirement for the government to consult with First Nations on the impact of the project itself. Rather, the goal is to complete the required reviews and consultations over the next year so construction can begin next September.

Cold Lake First Nations Chief Kelsey Jacko has told The Canadian Press his community was left out of consultations on the pipeline designation, despite the fact that his community is situated in the oilsands region.

In an interview Thursday, Jacko said his community was left with no choice but to turn to the courts because the federal government and Carney have ignored their concerns.

“I’m here to protect the best interests of my people and for the ones yet to come,” he said. “They’re going to use my backyard as a garbage dump.”

In the application for judicial review, Cold Lake First Nations’ lawyers said the designation breached Canadian law and is inconsistent with the honour of the Crown.

“Increasing oilsands production will have significant adverse effects on the ability of Clfn members to maintain their Luechogh Tue Denesuline way of life as promised by Treaty no. 6,” the application said.

“Canada has made no effort to understand or mitigate the massive cumulative effects of oilsands development on Clfn’s Luechogn Tue Denesuline treaty rights.”

The First Nation is asking the court to quash the national interest designation and to declare that Canada has a duty to consult with the community on the pipeline.

Indigenous communities along the route for the pipeline were given just two months for consultations on whether the pipeline should be designated a project of national interest — and that was still more than the government had planned.

At first, the consultations were to take place over one month. They were extended to two months after Indigenous leaders raised concerns about the tight timeline.

A summary of those consultations posted online by the federal government says Indigenous groups denounced what they called a lack of information about the project, which they said prevented them from fully assessing its impact.

The Assembly of First Nations told The Canadian Press last week it had identified “many red flags” in the pipeline’s national interest designation and said the federal government appeared to be predetermining outcomes and approving projects in advance of meaningful consultations.

“The government’s decision today is coming only 12 days after the consultation deadline. As we have said on many occasions, First Nations support economic development and prosperity for all, but not at the expense of our rights, the planet, and the government’s legal obligations to our people,” the statement from the Assembly of First Nations said.

Carney promised his major projects agenda would not interfere with Canada’s obligations under the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. Indigenous leaders have warned his government risks violating their rights with “national interest” designations through the Major Projects Office and the controversial Building Canada Act.

The United Nations declaration — which Canada adopted — outlines the need for free, prior and informed consent before decisions are made that could adversely affect the rights and lands of Indigenous communities and people. Indigenous communities also have recognized rights under Section 35 of the Constitution.

The UN declaration is cited in the pipeline consultation document, which says Ottawa’s engagement efforts were designed with those principles in mind.

Cold Lake First Nations is also concerned about the Pathways Project, a multibillion-dollar plan to transport and store oilsands greenhouse gas emissions. The carbon capture and storage project is linked to the pipeline; Ottawa and Alberta have said that one would not be able to proceed without the other.

The court filing says if the national interest designation for the pipeline stands, Ottawa will have granted pre-approval of Pathways without meaningfully consulting with Cold Lake.

“Since March 2023, Clfn has repeatedly written to Canada seeking engagement with the relevant federal ministers regarding the Pathways Project. Canada has not responded in any substantive or meaningful way,” the filing says.

It also says Cold Lake First Nations raised concerns about Pathways to the government’s major projects office, which responded by saying Canada would not consider the effects of that project or the doubling of oilsands production in its assessment of the pipeline designation.

In a statement, NDP MP Leah Gazan said Carney’s major projects plan is failing and the legal challenge from Cold Lake is only the start.

“The government clearly needs a legal reminder that free, prior and informed consent and the duty to consult and accommodate is not a constitutional option,” she said. “It’s unfortunate that in only a year and a half, this government has taken us back decades in our path to reconciliation.”

The court filing says Cold Lake First Nations has made multi-generational sacrifices for Canada’s “national interest” through the relocation of the community for military training, and through Canada’s failure to share resource revenue generated in their territory.

“We trusted them before and now we’re expected to trust them again?” Jacko said. “We’re trying to work with Canada. We keep trying, but nobody’s trying with us.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Hamilton to pilot bylaw to protect downtown renters from extreme indoor heat
stories.summary: Hamilton city council has voted to pilot a bylaw intended to protect downtown tenants from stifling indoor temperatures, the first of its kind in Ontario.
stories.author: Jordan Omstead The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Landlords in downtown Hamilton will soon face new requirements to protect renters from stifling indoor summer temperatures after local councillors backed a first-of-its-kind pilot in Ontario.

The pilot will require landlords in the city’s downtown Ward 2, where most residents are renters, to keep at least one room in each unit below 26 C, a threshold recognized by Health Canada.

The results will likely be watched closely by other cities, including Toronto, that are studying how to protect renters from rising temperatures driven by climate change.

The pilot is expected to inform staff recommendations, due in early 2029, ON how to expand the bylaw Hamilton-wide.

“We recognize the significance of addressing the impacts of extreme heat on Hamilton residents and want to take a thoughtful approach to implementing this groundbreaking bylaw,” Mike Zegarac, the interim city manager, said in a statement.

The pilot is the first time a city in Ontario has voted to make landlords responsible for keeping rental units cool in the summer. The city’s health committee first directed staff to come up with a maximum temperature bylaw in 2023.

Ontario’s tenant laws require landlords to heat an apartment, but not to keep it cool in summer, a distinction some advocates say is increasingly untenable as climate change increases the frequency and intensity of dangerous heat waves across the province. Hamilton is expected to see roughly an extra 25 days above 30 C by mid-century, according to models based on current climate policies.

Toronto has also directed its city staff to come up with a similar bylaw by next summer.

The Hamilton pilot will start next year and run through September 2028. Exemptions are available to landlords who show there are structural, electrical or physical barriers to compliance, or if the only way to comply would require constructions or demolition. Tenants can also choose to opt out.

One of the recognized risks is the pilot’s possible impact on above-guideline rent increases sought by landlords to cover associated air conditioning costs, a staff report says. The report also notes there’s an overall lack of consistent funding programs available to property owners to complete retrofits.

Recent changes to provincial law give tenants the right to install air conditioners and allow landlords to pass off extra utility costs in seasonal rent increases, but do not provide for access to cooling as a minimum standard.

Tenant and environmental groups argued the pilot did not go far enough. At a minimum, it should be expanded to the other downtown wards and applied citywide by summer 2028, said a written submission co-signed by Acorn Hamilton, Environment Hamilton and the Canadian Environmental Law Association.

A landlord group, meanwhile, said a decision should be deferred and the bylaw studied further. The Hamilton and District Apartment Association said in its submission there was “no need to rush this decision.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

Toronto has also directed its city staff to come up with a similar bylaw by next summer.

The Hamilton pilot will start next year and run through September 2028. Exemptions are available to landlords who show there are structural, electrical or physical barriers to compliance, or if the only way to comply would require constructions or demolition. Tenants can also choose to opt out.

One of the recognized risks is the pilot’s possible impact on above-guideline rent increases sought by landlords to cover associated air conditioning costs, a staff report says. The report also notes there’s an overall lack of consistent funding programs available to property owners to complete retrofits.

Recent changes to provincial law give tenants the right to install air conditioners and allow landlords to pass off extra utility costs in seasonal rent increases, but do not provide for access to cooling as a minimum standard.

Tenant and environmental groups argued the pilot did not go far enough. At a minimum, it should be expanded to the other downtown wards and applied citywide by summer 2028, said a written submission co-signed by Acorn Hamilton, Environment Hamilton and the Canadian Environmental Law Association.

A landlord group, meanwhile, said a decision should be deferred and the bylaw studied further. The Hamilton and District Apartment Association said in its submission there was “no need to rush this decision.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Three horses en route to Equestrian Canada event killed in B.C. highway crash
stories.summary: Revelstoke - Three horses being transported to an Equestrian Canada event in Langley, B.C., have been killed in a crash on Highway 1 in the British Columbia Interior.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Revelstoke - Three horses being transported to an Equestrian Canada event in Langley, B.C., have been killed in a crash on Highway 1 in the British Columbia Interior.

Equestrian Canada said in a statement that four horses were being towed to the National Dressage and Para Dressage Championships.

The national federation said the horses were from Alberta and Manitoba and that the surviving animal was injured and is being treated by a veterinarian.

“Our equestrian community functions as a close-knit family, and a sudden loss of this magnitude is felt deeply by every rider, coach, groom and owner across the country,” the organization said in the statement issued on Wednesday.

It said mental health support has been extended to athletes and owners of the horses.

RCMP said the crash happened Tuesday about 40 kilometres east of Revelstoke, B.C., when the driver lost control of the vehicle.

Police said in a news release on Thursday that the vehicle hit a rock wall, although the driver, a 73-year-old woman from Alberta, wasn’t seriously hurt.

The BC Highway Patrol says in a statement that the woman was issued a $109 fine for failing to maintain her lane position and driving off the road to the right.

James Hood, high performance director with Equestrian Canada, said in a statement that a horse named Fearless, whose rider is Mackenzie Abbott, was killed.

Rosario, ridden by Kate Wall of Manitoba, was also killed, the statement said.

Both horses were owned by Lisa Paterson of Solace Stables.

The names, riders and owners of the other two horses haven’t been made public.

In a post on social media, Abbott, a Manitoba-based equestrian coach and dressage school owner, commented on the crash.

“There are truly no words for what we are feeling right now. I don’t think I have even begun to comprehend that this is real,” Abbott wrote in the message posted on her Facebook account.

She said the horses were being taken to Langley for the Canadian National Dressage Championships by transport truck when the crash happened.

Abbott, based in Headingley, Man., said that she is asking for prayers for the horse that survived, as the animal “will require recovery mentally and physically.”

“I loved my horses more than I could ever explain,” Abbott wrote. “My heart is completely shattered.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: ‘Very large question mark’: Decision on Kingston Alto rail stop won’t come until 2027
stories.summary: Kingston remains “promising” as a potential stop on the Alto high-speed rail corridor, but an official decision May have to wait until spring, the crown corporation said.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
Kingston remains “promising” as a potential stop on the Alto high-speed rail corridor, but an official decision May have to wait until spring, the Crown corporation said.

During its annual meeting Wednesday, Robert Prichard, chair of the Alto board of directors, said the city has made a strong case for inclusion, but a feasibility assessment would still need to be completed.

“We think there is a presumptively strong case to go to Kingston, but we still have to do the work,” he said.

The company has only officially announced Peterborough as a stop on the Toronto to Ottawa corridor.

Prichard said with each additional stop there is a tradeoff between journey time and how many passengers will be added to the trip. An analysis will need to be undertaken to determine how much a stop in Kingston will increase ridership.

“Every additional stop extends the journey time,” Prichard said.

Other eastern Ontario communities like Smiths Falls and Perth will not be directly serviced by Alto, but Prichard said those communities will still have access through the high-speed rail’s intersection with VIA Rail.

“It’s the synergy between the two systems,” he said.

Martin Imbleau, the CEO of Alto, said the company’s first priority is the Ottawa to Montreal corridor, so the earliest a decision would be made about Kingston would be spring 2027.

Kingston was not a stop on the initial corridor, Prichard said, so consultations with that community have yet to happen.

But opponents of the rail system say those who could be directly affected by the rail line, deserve to have their questions answered.

“At some point, being told to wait for answers simply isn’t good enough,” Heather Levy, local lead of Stone Mills Against Alto and a member of United Against Alto, told Global News.

“We are being asked to live inside a very large question mark, with potentially life-changing consequences hanging over us, while the people making the decisions continue to tell us to be patient,” she added.

The concern is particularly great for farmers and the owners of rural properties in Lennox and Addington and South Frontenac townships.

“What seems to get lost in that conversation is the distinction between the potential benefits of a station in Kingston and the consequences of getting the railway there,” Levy said. “For communities like Stone Mills, that could mean losing homes, severing farmland and permanently altering rural communities. Those impacts deserve at least as much consideration as the potential benefits to Kingston.”

Stone Mills is located approximately 50 km northwest of Kingston.

Imbleau said Alto will continue to listen to the concerns of residents and has new consultations planned for next year.

“We don’t want to cut land,” he said. “We will find the route that has the least impact.”

David Bellerive, founder of the advocacy organization Go Alto, said he feels Alto is actively listening to the public and “refining its plans based on community feedback.”

“The project is still in development, and finding the right solutions takes time,” he said.

At an unrelated news conference Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the federal government will continue to work with the governments of Quebec and Ontario to advance the rail project.

Quebec’s premier designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon was adamant throughout his campaign that he would end the province’s co-operation with the project.

An Abacus poll released in the spring found 62 per cent of Canadians supported the rail project with 25 per cent strongly supporting it.

stories.title: Saskatoon encampment removal resumes to address ‘safety concerns,’ city says
stories.summary: After being paused in early-August, the cleanup of an encampment at 20th Street and Avenue K South in Saskatoon resumed Thursday morning, according to the city.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The process of removing an encampment in Saskatoon began Thursday morning after previously being paused by the city due to protests .

The clearing of the site, which sits on private property at 20th Street and Avenue K South, began Thursday. It has the city’s support, as well as that of community, Indigenous and provincial government organizations, Yvonne Raymer, deputy fire chief at the Saskatoon Fire Department, told reporters at a news conference Thursday after the work began.

Police officers and firefighters were witnessed at the site by Global News crews on the ground.

It comes after an injunction application was dismissed last week at Saskatoon Court of King’s Bench over a lack of standing from the applicants. A second injunction attempt was originally supposed to be heard in court on Thursday, but the interim application was denied with a court hearing still set for Oct. 27.

Global News has reached out to Lawyers with Community Legal Assistance Services for Saskatoon Inner City, the party involved in the second injunction request, for comment.

“Encampments are removed because they begin to become unsafe for both the residents living in them, the schools, services, businesses and neighbourhoods around them,” Raymer said.

Clean-up work at the encampment included representatives offering available supports to those who live there. Encampment residents who reject those offers are told they must move out, she said. The deputy fire chief was unsure if the residents are being given a deadline for when their belongings must be removed, as Saskatoon police officers are also at the scene to support fire department staff and ensure safety.

Encampments in general present significant fire, public safety and sanitation risks – and the site being removed Thursday is no exception, according to a City of Saskatoon news release.

“Safety concerns increase as encampments grow,” Raymer said, adding since Monday the city’s fire service has been called to four fires at various encampments.

Two of those fires spread to trees in Optimist Park, another destroyed a makeshift shelter in the backyard of a vacant property and the fourth was said to have become out of control in a park off Idylwyld Drive.

The city also alleged possible gang activity, domestic violence, assaults and open drug use have been observed or reported at the 20th Street encampment.

“While we recognize the challenges people face, we also have an obligation to address significant wider community safety risks and work towards safer, more sustainable alternatives,” Raymer said.

Saskatoon Tribal Council (STC) Tribal Chief Mark Arcand described the encampments as having “too much violence and gang activity, including drugs and sex trafficking,” in the city’s news release.

“In the last few weeks, we have seen an escalation of violence throughout that neighbourhood and seen that relatives who had been interested in supports are now refusing them,” he continued.

“The real solution is for people to access the supports they need, to get housing, addiction treatment, medical care, and connection to culture, in a safe environment. This won’t happen as long as they are at an encampment.”

He said help is available through the STC – including its housing outreach program and outdoor washroom project.

The exact cost of this removal project is not yet available, according to the fire chief.
paragraphs: The process of removing an encampment in Saskatoon began Thursday morning after previously being paused by the city due to protests .

The clearing of the site, which sits on private property at 20th Street and Avenue K South, began Thursday. It has the city’s support, as well as that of community, Indigenous and provincial government organizations, Yvonne Raymer, deputy fire chief at the Saskatoon Fire Department, told reporters at a news conference Thursday after the work began.
Police officers and firefighters were witnessed at the site by Global News crews on the ground.

It comes after an injunction application was dismissed last week at Saskatoon Court of King’s Bench over a lack of standing from the applicants. A second injunction attempt was originally supposed to be heard in court on Thursday, but the interim application was denied with a court hearing still set for Oct. 27.
Global News has reached out to Lawyers with Community Legal Assistance Services for Saskatoon Inner City, the party involved in the second injunction request, for comment.
“Encampments are removed because they begin to become unsafe for both the residents living in them, the schools, services, businesses and neighbourhoods around them,” Raymer said.

Clean-up work at the encampment included representatives offering available supports to those who live there. Encampment residents who reject those offers are told they must move out, she said. The deputy fire chief was unsure if the residents are being given a deadline for when their belongings must be removed, as Saskatoon police officers are also at the scene to support fire department staff and ensure safety.
Encampments in general present significant fire, public safety and sanitation risks – and the site being removed Thursday is no exception, according to a City of Saskatoon news release.
“Safety concerns increase as encampments grow,” Raymer said, adding since Monday the city’s fire service has been called to four fires at various encampments.

Two of those fires spread to trees in Optimist Park, another destroyed a makeshift shelter in the backyard of a vacant property and the fourth was said to have become out of control in a park off Idylwyld Drive.
The city also alleged possible gang activity, domestic violence, assaults and open drug use have been observed or reported at the 20th Street encampment.
“While we recognize the challenges people face, we also have an obligation to address significant wider community safety risks and work towards safer, more sustainable alternatives,” Raymer said.
Saskatoon Tribal Council (STC) Tribal Chief Mark Arcand described the encampments as having “too much violence and gang activity, including drugs and sex trafficking,” in the city’s news release.
“In the last few weeks, we have seen an escalation of violence throughout that neighbourhood and seen that relatives who had been interested in supports are now refusing them,” he continued.

“The real solution is for people to access the supports they need, to get housing, addiction treatment, medical care, and connection to culture, in a safe environment. This won’t happen as long as they are at an encampment.”
He said help is available through the STC – including its housing outreach program and outdoor washroom project.
The exact cost of this removal project is not yet available, according to the fire chief.

stories.title: Carney says Canada's future up to Canadians after Musk voices support for separatism
stories.summary: Sherbrooke - Prime Minister Mark Carney says the future of the country will be decided by Canadians — not by large U.S. tech firms.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Sherbrooke - Prime Minister Mark Carney responded Thursday to tech industrialist Elon Musk’s endorsement of provincial separation movements by saying Canada’s future will be decided by its citizens — not by large U.S. tech firms.

Speaking at a news conference in Sherbrooke, Que., Carney said Canadians can live their lives in Quebec and across the country “free from interference from foreign governments and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do.”

“The future of Canada will be decided by Canadians and the priorities of Canadians, the priorities of the people of Quebec,” he said in reply to questions from a reporter about Musk’s comments.

He added those priorities include affordability, social justice and building a strong Quebec within a more independent and prosperous Canada.

Musk argued on his X platform on Wednesday that Quebec should leave the federation, and that Alberta and Saskatchewan should follow suit.

“Quebec should separate,” Musk said. “They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too.”

On Wednesday, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe replied to Musk’s post with a terse rebuttal: “No.”

Carney recently announced a major $2.3-billion contract with Telesat for low-Earth orbit satellite connectivity for the military.

That service has aspirations to become a direct commercial challenger to Musk’s Starlink, which dominates the global market for low-Earth orbit satellite internet service.

Quebec voters elected a separatist government on Monday by granting the Parti Québécois a minority government.

PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon pledged during the election that his party would not hold a referendum on separation while U.S. President Donald Trump remains in office.

Carney has sought to use his ambitious economic agenda as an olive branch to the province and its new government, vowing Quebec will benefit from cooperative federalism.

The prime minister said in French on Thursday that he and St-Pierre Plamondon had a “cordial” first conversation this week that touched on “great investments here in Quebec,” immigration and other matters.

But the PQ has opposed the Carney government’s plans for the Alto project, a proposed high-speed rail link between Quebec and Ontario, raising questions about its viability.

Carney talked up the Alto project on Thursday when asked about its future prospects. He said in French it will create tens of thousands of jobs in the province and that he will work with the new provincial government to advance the project.

Alberta holds its own separation referendum in less than two weeks on Oct. 19.

Speaking in Edmonton on Thursday, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith argued that separatist sentiment in her province has weakened because she and Carney have addressed the “very real issues that were frustrating Albertans.”

“The federal government has changed. Their approach to us has changed and they’re willing to work together on addressing those issues,” she said.

stories.title: Saskatchewan MLAs racked up $10.9 million in expenses last year
stories.summary: Saskatchewan MLAs are opening up their books to share their expenses from the last fiscal year on everything from phone bills to travel.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
Saskatchewan MLAs collectively spent nearly $11 million in taxpayer dollars during the last fiscal year, with opposition members spending more on average than their government counterparts, according to newly released expense statements.

The report, released annually by the Legislative Assembly Service, details a range of expenses by each member across four spending categories, including phone bills, travel and office-related costs, between April 1, 2025, and March 31, 2026.

When combining totals across all four categories, the average Saskatchewan MLA spent around $179,000.

But spending was not consistent across the board, with Opposition MLAs spending more than government caucus members on average.

During the fiscal year, members of the Opposition NDP spent about $182,000 each, compared with roughly $176,000 among government MLAs.

Meanwhile, government ministers spent slightly less than the average MLA, coming in at about $2,500 below the overall average.

However, these figures do not include out-of-province travel by ministers, which is reported separately twice a year. The latest of these statements covers the period between Oct. 1, 2025, and March 31 of this year and includes a $63,000 trip to India taken by Premier Scott Moe in February.

Gage Haubrich, the Canadian Taxpayers Federation’s prairie director, said MLAs should look for ways to keep their expenses below the average.

“If they’re below the average, they should keep those expenses there. If they’re above the average, they should talk to their colleagues and figure out a way to get under that average to save taxpayers some money,” he told Global News in an interview.

Four of the five MLAs with the highest expenses last fiscal year were members of the opposition.

Cumberland MLA Jordan McPhail topped the list, with expenses totalling about $233,100.

Behind him was Athabasca MLA Leroy Laliberte at $212,700.

Jamie Martens, provincial secretary and MLA for Martensville-Blairmore, came in at third at $211,500. With Saskatoon Fairview’s Vicki Mowat and Saskatoon Meewasin’s Nathaniel Teed holding the fourth and fifth spots with $207,700 and $203,600, respectively.

In a statement to Global News, the opposition party said its MLAs work throughout the province.

Haubrich said the spending figures warrant some context, particularly when comparing government and opposition members.

Ministers typically travel throughout the province for government announcements and other duties, he said, making higher expenses expected in some cases.

“So it warrants a little more of an explanation to say, why are they in the top?” Haubrich said, referring to the top MLA spenders.

At the other end of the list, David Marit, the province’s agriculture minister, held the lowest spot, spending around $134,000 last fiscal year.

Behind him were White City-Qu’appelle’s Brad Crassweller at $139,500 and Moe at $144,600.

The fourth- and fifth-lowest spending spots are held by opposition MLAs Bhajan Brar at $145,300 and Nicole Sarauer at $148,000.

The amount an MLA spends can also depend on where they represent.

MLAs based in Saskatoon and Regina — where all but two city-centre constituencies are currently represented by the NDP — are likely to spend more on office-related costs, while rural MLAs tend to incur higher travel expenses.

Across the four categories, MLAs spent the most on constituency assistant costs, at around $4.3 million, and the least on telecommunications, at $358,000. Travel and living expenses totalled $2.4 million, while constituency services, which include rent and office supplies, totalled $3.8 million.

The Legislative Assembly Service publishes MLA expense statements annually, allowing the public to see how elected officials are spending public dollars.

stories.title: Bail granted for driver in Saskatchewan crash that killed mother and daughters
stories.summary: Kelly Knopf, a 40-year-old South Carolina resident, appeared in Yorkton court Thursday – almost a week after the fatal crash near Foam Lake, Sask.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A truck driver involved in a crash that killed three people, including two girls, in Saskatchewan last week has been granted bail.

Kelly Knopf, a 40-year-old South Carolina resident, appeared in Yorkton court Thursday – almost a week after the fatal crash near Foam Lake, Sask.

RCMP said Knopf was driving a truck when he allegedly smashed into an SUV while trying to pass a semi-truck on a rural road.

Three people in the SUV were killed, including 40-year-old Amber Olsen and her two daughters, eight-year-old Isla and five-year-old Everly. A man who was also in the SUV was taken to hospital in serious condition. The driver of the semi was not injured.

Knopf and two other truck passengers were also taken to hospital. He was charged with dangerous driving causing death and bodily harm.

Knopf’s lawyer, Brian Pfefferle, said the man was on a hunting trip in Saskatchewan when the crash occurred.

Knopf will be able to return to the United States on $20,000 bail, court heard Thursday. Several conditions were attached to his release, including not being to operate a vehicle in Saskatchewan and that he return to Canada to address the charges.

“He is returning to his home in South Carolina to receive treatment for the injuries he sustained in this accident,” Pfefferle said in a statement. “This is a terrible tragedy and Mr. Knopf intends to comply with the conditions and is grateful the Crown agreed to his release.”

stories.title: Big tech can’t ‘tell us what to do,’ Carney says on Musk’s separatism talk
stories.summary: The trillionaire tech businessman and former adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump said on X that Quebec would benefit from independence, as would Alberta and Saskatchewan.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canadians will decide the future of Canada, not “large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday, responding to Elon Musk’s comments that three Canadian provinces “should separate” from Canada.

“The future of Canada will be decided by Canadians, and the priorities of Canadians, the priorities of the people of Quebec,” Carney told reporters in Sherbrooke, Que., ON Thursday.

Musk, a former adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump, said on his social media platform X that Quebec should separate, as should Alberta and Saskatchewan.

Any discussion on the future of the provinces should be “free from interference from foreign governments and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do,” Carney said on Thursday.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe had a concise response to Musk on social media: “No.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, who states she’s voting to stay in Canada in an upcoming provincial referendum, says she also strongly disagrees with Musk’s opinion.

On Oct. 19, Albertans go to the polls to decide if the province should stay in Canada or whether there should be a second binding referendum to begin the process of separation.

–with files from Canadian Press

stories.title: Weston family to acquire U.K. pharmacy chain Boots in $8.9B deal
stories.summary: The Weston family holding company, Wittington Investments, said Wednesday it is purchasing Boots and its associated businesses for USD $8.9 billion (CAD $ 12.7 billion).
stories.author: Rachel Goodman
stories.content:
The Weston family, which owns Canada’s largest grocery chain, Loblaw , and Shoppers Drug Mart , has acquired Boots, the British high street pharmacy and beauty retailer.

The Weston family holding company, Wittington Investments, said Wednesday it is purchasing Boots and its associated businesses for USD $8.9 billion (CAD $ 12.7 billion).

Along with Boots’ retail operations in the U.K. and Ireland, Wittington will acquire the company’s franchised arm in Thailand as well as its optical division and beauty brand No7.

Wittington’s connection to the U.K. includes having previously owned Selfridges — the high-end department store —from 2003 to 2021. The famous retailer first opened on Oxford Street in London in 1909. Boots was founded in Nottingham 177 years ago by John Boot. Nottingham remains the home of its headquarters.

Wittington said in a press release that it plans to “continue to invest to build on Boots’ strengths and potential, including upgrading stores, optimizing the online experience and supporting the expansion of healthcare services available to customers.”

“Boots is one of Britain’s most enduring businesses, with a rich heritage, a trusted name and a vital role in everyday life across the UK and Ireland,” Weston said.

“We have great respect for Boots’ legacy and leading market position. We see a meaningful opportunity to make a great business even better through stable long-term ownership, further capital investment, and the renewed operating focus required to serve customers with excellence for generations to come,” he continued.

Boots operates 1,800 stores across the U.K. and has 50,000 employees.

The investment firm Fairfax, which owns The Sporting Life Group and Sleep Country, is backing the acquisition and said it is “very confident that Wittington will be an excellent steward of the Boots business and a terrific partner.”

The transaction marks the exit of Boots’ long-standing backer, Stefano Pessina and the private equity firm Sycamore Partners, which took control of Boots in August 2025 after acquiring its parent company, Walgreens Boots Alliance.

“One year ago, we re-established Boots as a standalone company, allowing its management team and more than 50,000 colleagues to focus solely on their business and customers,” Stefan Kaluzny, managing director of Sycamore Partners, said.

“This transaction is a testament to the work they have done and the incredibly bright future ahead.”

Pessina called the brand “a British institution,” and said it had been a privilege to be closely associated with the brand for the last two decades.

“We are delighted to be passing on a thriving Boots to strong and reliable owners who understand the value of its great heritage,” he said.

Boots is known for its innovation and enduring own-name brands. Its chemists, Stewart Adams and John Nicholson, invented ibuprofen in Nottingham in 1961, and its popular No7 beauty brand, which sells makeup, cosmetics and skin care products, has been operational for nine decades. It was also the first U.K. chemist chain to introduce self-service stores in 1951.

stories.title: Ottawa in talks with First Nations about airport privatization, Transport Minister says
stories.summary: MacKinnon notes no decisions have been made on which airport will go through the process first
stories.author: Bill Curry, Andrew Willis
stories.content:
Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said Thursday that Ottawa is in talks with First Nations about partnerships as it seeks new private investors for Canada’s four largest airports.

However, he said, no decisions have been made on which airport will go through the process first.

The Globe and Mail reported Wednesday, citing sources, that bankers and lawyers advising Ottawa have decided that Vancouver International Airport should be the first of the four airports to go through Ottawa’s privatization process. Further, Ottawa’s advisers are offering Indigenous groups in British Columbia an opportunity to be minority investors.

Advisers view Vancouver Airport, or YVR, as the priority because they expect it to draw First Nations investment.

The Globe report said the government’s airport plans are in their early stages, and the timing and structure of investments could change, according to four sources.

The Globe is not naming the sources because they are not permitted to speak for their employers.

Indigenous investors listening to pitches for stakes in the Vancouver Airport include the Musqueam First Nation, The Globe reported. The airport is on the Musqueam’s unceded territory.

In a speech to a gathering of the International Air Transport Association in Ottawa Thursday, Mr. MacKinnon told industry representatives that the government is seeking their ideas on the best way to proceed with the plan.

Speaking with reporters after the speech, Mr. MacKinnon did not dispute that talks have been held with the Musqueam First Nation as part of broader consultations.

“I certainly acknowledge that there have been fulsome discussions, as you can imagine, whether it be major projects, reconciliation writ large, or this initiative. We’re in constant communication with relevant First Nations,” he said.

Mr. MacKinnon said Ottawa is relying on advisers for technical expertise but cautioned that talk of which airport will go through the process first is speculative.

“These are large and complicated transactions. They require expertise,” he said. “So that creates a number of people who are involved in this, and a number of people who speculate, but I want to be clear that no decisions have been made.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney first announced the airport plan at an investment summit held last month in Toronto.

At the time, the government said the plan would see Ottawa retain ownership of the underlying land and assets but seek private investment through long-term agreements that will bring in new capital and expertise for airport operations and growth.

In his speech, Mr. MacKinnon described the plan as an effort at “unlocking” new investment in Canada’s airports.

The minister has previously said that some of the revenue raised through the process will be redirected to support improvements for Canada’s smaller, regional airports.

“We’re looking for ideas around innovation, ideas around taking risks and being entrepreneurial with many of our airport assets,” he said in his speech Thursday.

“So, beyond the four identified facilities, we’re looking to all of you – airlines, airports, and all the players in the system – for ideas about how we can make our system more affordable, work more fluidly, and take better care of the people who entrust their travel to us,” he said.

Speaking at the Ottawa conference on Thursday, executives who run some of Canada’s smaller airports urged the federal government to take its time on plans for the four largest hubs. They said they want to ensure Ottawa selects the right model and doesn’t merely create a more expensive toll collector for airports, travellers and airlines, as well as a poorly funded second tier of hubs.

All but three of Canada’s 26 largest airports have, since the 1990s, been operated by non-profit corporations that rely on user fees and pay rent to the federal government. The airports have long pushed Ottawa to reinvest the rent – which totalled more than $500-million in 2025 – in the airport system.

Joyce Carter, chief executive officer of the Halifax International Airport Authority, agreed that the model for all airports is due for a review and change. “But we have to do it slowly and we have to do it carefully,” Ms. Carter said.

The airport operator paid $12-million in federal rent in 2025 and made a profit of $19.4-million, according to its annual report.

“It really is prohibitive for an airport my size to have to pay the rent we do, and it really does restrict the development that we can do in our community,” Ms. Carter said.

“And so, revisiting that model to be able to have it more fair and equitable as part of this would be a good outcome.”

Monette Pasher, CEO of the Canadian Airports Council, which represents more than 100 airports, said there are many questions about the “massive change” in how the country’s biggest airports are run, including the government’s goal. Is the privatization about making profits or improving affordability for travellers, she asked.

At stake, she said, is the ability of the airport industry to grow to meet demand for air travel that is expected to double in the next 20 years.

“We really don’t know what concession model they’re going to choose, and there are many,” Ms. Pasher said.

“And in our experience, there’s some really good ones out there. We think we’re a good one, and there are also many others that are good, and there are many that are bad.”

stories.title: Ottawa to launch $2-billion heat pump rebate program early next year
stories.summary: Program will make up to $10,000 available to households that make the switch
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A new federal heat pump rebate program will launch early next year, even though the program’s full details have not yet been finalized, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday.

It also might not be cheaper for all Canadians to switch to heat pumps because natural gas is less expensive than electricity in some provinces.

The program, which will make up to $10,000 available to households that make the switch to heat pumps, is being geared toward homeowners whose heating systems are broken or getting close to replacement. The program, which is being launched in early 2027, will be made retroactive to this fall.

Carney made the announcement at a heating and cooling system manufacturer in Sherbrooke, Que., alongside Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin.

The government is budgeting $2 billion over eight years with a target of retrofitting one million homes.

“Over one million households in Canada still heat with oil, propane, or diesel. These fuel sources are more polluting, less efficient and at the mercy of global markets,” Carney said.

“Right now, those markets are hitting families hard. Heating a home with oil costs 70 per cent more than it did in 2024, at least $2,500 more per household every year.”

While Carney is pitching this announcement as an affordability measure, government officials acknowledged that it would be more expensive for some homeowners to switch from their natural gas furnaces.

At a technical briefing on background for journalists ahead of the announcement, officials said that in parts of the country with lower natural gas costs, switching to a heat pump would not save money.

All homes would be eligible for the program and adoption of heat pumps serves to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, the officials said. They also said the government will make clear to Canadians the cost implications of switching from natural gas to a heat pump.

Households below the median income level can get up to $10,000 back on a heat pump purchase, while other homeowners can get $2,000 by switching to a heat pump.

Ottawa is in the process of winding down an existing program to subsidize purchases of heat pumps for homes heated with oil. As of March, the Oil to Heat Pump Affordability program helped to install more than 30,000 heat pumps across the country. About two-thirds of those were in Atlantic Canada, where heating oil accounted for a greater proportion of home heating systems.

Leaders of Canada’s Hvac industry applauded Thursday’s announcement – particularly the decision to make the program retroactive to the fall.

“Our industry group has worked closely with Environment and Climate Change Canada to help shape a program that, above all, delivers real value for consumers while being practical and workable for the businesses and skilled tradespeople responsible for delivering it,” said Martin Luymes, vice president of government relations with the Heating, Refrigeration and Air Conditioning Institute of Canada.

In a document detailing some elements of the new program, the government said homeowners could apply for the rebate when their current heating system breaks down, or when it’s approaching the end of its life.

But government officials briefing reporters on background said having a heating system fail isn’t necessarily a requirement for eligibility in the new program.

The officials said government data shows 80 per cent of Hvac replacements in Canada happen when current systems break and the new program is trying to target that group – something officials say is a first for a federal rebate program.

The new program delivers on a promise Carney made while running for the Liberal leadership last year, although his exact promise then was to strengthen the existing oil-to-heat-pump program.

Carney also promised at the time to renew funding for the government’s Greener Homes Grant program for lower-income households and explore discounts for low- and medium-income homeowners who make energy-efficient retrofits.

He recommitted to that pledge when pressed by reporters at an announcement in April.

Government officials said Thursday the new heat pump program is a successor to the Greener Homes Grant program. They also pointed to the Canada Greener Homes Affordability program, which launched last year and was expanded to more provinces back in June.

Officials wouldn’t say whether more announcements are coming.

stories.title: Canada records 60 per cent spike in arrests, detentions of Canadians in United States
stories.summary: Global Affairs Canada says the number of arrest and detention cases involving Canadians citizens has jumped 60 per cent.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Global Affairs Canada says the number of arrest and detention cases involving Canadians citizens has jumped 60 per cent.

The department’s annual report on consular cases , published today, tracks an increase in arrests between April 2025 and March 2026, despite a 25 per cent decline in visits by Canadians to the U.S.

The report does not explain what caused the increase, though U.S. President Donald Trump has expanded immigration raids and Canadians have reported facing uncomfortable questions from U.S. border officials.

Overall, the report tracks a one-fifth increase in the number of arrests of Canadians around the world, including a threefold increase in the number of arrests in Thailand.

Global Affairs Canada has warned in recent years that the growing frequency of wars and natural disasters is resulting in more consular cases that are more complex and expensive to manage.

The data also shows an increase in the number of Canadians voluntarily registering with the department when they go abroad, which helps Ottawa send safety advice and co-ordinate evacuations.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: University of Guelph, police to join ‘homecoming working group’ after chaotic party
stories.summary: Police in Guelph say they're establishing a "homecoming working group" to manage large unsanctioned gatherings after a chaotic University of Guelph party made headlines last week.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Police in Guelph say they’re establishing a “homecoming working group” to manage large unsanctioned gatherings after a chaotic University of Guelph party made headlines last week.

Police say the working group is being jointly created with the city, the University of Guelph and Guelph General Hospital to support community safety and identify ways to hold offenders accountable.

The force says police, the hospital and municipal services already do extensive planning each year in the run-up to homecoming, but “this year demonstrated that the environment surrounding unsanctioned gatherings has changed.”

Videos from an off-campus homecoming party on Sept. 26 showed massive crowds of young people in the streets, with some throwing bottles and other objects as police officers tried to control the situation.

Guelph police said at the time the gathering was “significantly larger” than similar events in recent years and officers were dealing with people climbing buildings, as well as shoplifting and vandalism at nearby businesses.

University of Guelph president Rene Van Acker said last week the party risked the safety of students and neighbours and the university was reviewing the incident.

Police say social media and “individuals who encourage disorder” have played key roles in escalating the size and risks of unsanctioned gatherings.

They say the working group will meet regularly to consider recommendations on how to prevent and respond to gatherings of this kind.

Last week, police asked for the public’s help identifying people seen in social media videos of the Sept. 26 party.

The force said several people were charged with criminal and provincial offences over that weekend.
