stories.title: Allergic to gold jewelry? Western study shows earrings can dissolve under certain conditions
stories.summary: Buying high-quality jewelry is better for your skin because cheap jewelry often hides reactive nickel beneath a thin surface.
stories.author: Jeff Renaud
stories.content:
Gold has a reputation for being chemically untouchable. But according to Western University chemist Yolanda Hedberg, that reputation is a little misleading – gold is not unreactive so much as selective about what it reacts with.

“Every material has their own enemy. Its own kryptonite,” said Hedberg, Canada Research Chair in Corrosion Science. “For gold, one of those enemies is sulphur.”

That distinction helps explain what Hedberg and her collaborators at Surface Science Western and the University of Copenhagen found when they tested five pairs of 10K and 14K gold earrings purchased from a jeweller.

After a week in cysteine-modified artificial sweat, all five pairs released measurable amounts of gold. Cysteine is an amino acid, or protein building block, made naturally by the body that contains sulphur, which binds to gold.

The amounts were tiny, and the findings do not show that the released gold is enough to cause an allergic reaction. But the study, published by the journal Contact Dermatitis, demonstrates gold in jewelry can become chemically available under the right conditions – a finding that helps explain how exposure to gold can occur at the skin.

In the study, none of five earrings purchased from professional jewellers released detectable nickel, distinguishing them from the inexpensive gold-plated earrings bought from e-commerce sites like Temu that were examined in a previous study. (Christopher Kindratsky/Western Communications)

Gold, silver and platinum are known as noble metals because they do not readily react with oxygen. That resistance to oxidation is a big part of gold’s reputation for stability. But, Hedberg says, it does not mean the metal is universally unreactive.

“Gold reacts to different things,” said Hedberg, a chemistry professor in Western’s Faculty of Science. “Gold doesn’t react much with oxygen, but it can react with sulphur and some amino groups.”

And for some people, that reaction poses a problem.

“Gold allergy is real, although it is less common than nickel allergy. But for a metal to trigger an allergic response, some of that metal has to become chemically available to the body,” said Hedberg. “So we wanted to understand how that might happen when gold jewelry is in contact with skin.”

Sweat contains amino acids and other compounds that can interact with metals. The researchers added cysteine, an amino acid containing sulphur, to an artificial sweat solution and exposed the earrings to it for 168 hours at about 30 C. The team then measured the metals released into the solution using highly sensitive mass spectrometry, a scientific technique used to weigh molecules.

There is no standard artificial-sweat test specifically designed to capture how gold behaves in the presence of sulphur, so Hedberg added cysteine to the solution to create conditions that would reveal whether gold could become soluble.

“The experiment was designed around a simple chemical principle. For a metal to cause an allergic response, it first has to become chemically available,” said Hedberg.

Gold was detected in the release solution from all five pairs of earrings.

Only tiny amounts of gold were released over the week-long test, with a median of 0.057 micrograms per square centimetre. The amount varied among the earrings, ranging from 0.016 to 0.15 micrograms.

Copper was released in much greater amounts, exceeding gold in every sample. The median copper release was 0.53 micrograms per square centimetre per week. Copper is generally considered harmless for humans and has beneficial antibacterial properties. Its higher release was expected, since the earrings were alloys, meaning gold was combined with other metals. Surface analysis showed the materials consisted mainly of gold, copper, silver and zinc, with only small amounts of nickel detected at the surface.

But unlike the inexpensive gold-plated earrings purchased from businesses like e-commerce site Temu, which Hedberg and colleagues examined in an earlier study, none of the five jeweller-purchased earrings released detectable nickel under the conditions of the new experiment.

Gold-plated jewelry can have a thin gold coating over one or more underlying layers that May contain nickel. In the earlier study on inexpensive earrings, nickel was detected in the artificial sweat in which all 10 inexpensive gold-plated earrings were tested, often at levels that exceeded European regulatory limits for jewelry sold for pierced body parts.

Element-specific spectroscopy showed gold throughout the material, rather than just a thin surface coating for the jewelry-store earrings, while the Temu earrings, if they contained any gold, had only a thin-plated layer.

“The chemistry and composition can vary widely, and price alone doesn’t tell you whether a material will cause an allergic reaction. In this particular comparison, however, the distinction between thin-plated earrings and the more expensive gold-alloy earrings from the jewelry store helps explain why nickel behaved so differently,” said Hedberg.

The study measured how much gold became soluble (able to dissolve in a liquid) under specific laboratory conditions. It did not measure how much gold reaches or remains on a person’s skin during actual wear, nor does it establish a dose at which gold jewelry triggers dermatitis.

Hedberg says the very small amounts of gold detected in the study would probably not be enough to trigger an allergic reaction in most circumstances. But that does not make the result irrelevant to someone who already knows they are allergic to gold.

“If I had a gold allergy, I still wouldn’t take the chance,” said Hedberg. “Jewelry moves against your skin, sweat chemistry varies and friction can increase the release.”

For most people, however, nickel remains a more immediate concern with inexpensive jewelry, rather than gold. In the earlier study of cheap gold-plated earrings, nickel was detected in every release solution. In the new study of jeweller-purchased 10K and 14K gold earrings, nickel was below the detection limit in every sample.

“This study doesn’t show that gold jewelry is causing widespread allergic reactions. What it shows is something narrower, but chemically important. Gold can be released from jewelry under conditions that make the metal soluble, so there is a potential pathway for exposure,” said Hedberg.

Learn more about how Western is turning curiosity into solutions.

Surface analysis showed the materials consisted mainly of gold, copper, silver and zinc, with only small amounts of nickel detected at the surface.

But unlike the inexpensive gold-plated earrings purchased from businesses like e-commerce site Temu, which Hedberg and colleagues examined in an earlier study, none of the five jeweller-purchased earrings released detectable nickel under the conditions of the new experiment.

stories.title: Nobel Prize in Literature goes to Canadian poet and essayist
stories.summary: Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in literature Thursday “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canadian poet Anne Carson, whose work blends the ancient with the avant-garde, has won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary to the Swedish Academy, said she reached Carson Thursday in Iceland, where she was “listening to the wind.”

“She was taken by surprise, but very happy,” Carlberg said. “I could hear that in her voice.”

Carlberg said the academy rewarded Carson for her “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”

A poet, essayist, classical scholar and translator, Carson is renowned as a master of esoterica whose body of work constitutes a genre unto itself.

With a bibliography of more than 20 books of poetry, essays, plays, libretti and translations of ancient Greek texts, Carson has defied literary conventions.

She’s amassed a devoted readership and a raft of critical accolades, including two Griffin Poetry Prizes, a Governor General’s Literary Award, the T. S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur “genius grant” and a Guggenheim Fellowship.

But as her poetic profile has grown over more than three decades, the particulars of Carson’s personal life have remained notoriously elusive.

Her public reticence is encapsulated by her scant book-jacket biography: “Canadian poet, essayist and translator of Greek mythology.”

View this post on Instagram

Various accounts suggest that Carson was born in Toronto in 1950 and studied classics at the University of Toronto, and has held teaching positions at institutions including McGill University, Michigan University and Princeton University.

The Swedish Academy confirmed some of those details, but offered few others.

“In 1981, she published her doctoral thesis in Classics entitled Odi et Amo Ergo Sum , and has, throughout her entire career, combined poetry writing with translation work and teaching at various universities,” said Anders Olsson, chair of the Nobel committee for literature.

“Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning.”

After her thesis, Carson made her publishing debut in 1986 with her academic essays on love, “Eros the Bittersweet.”

She gained recognition with a series of genre-bending books in the 1990s establishing her style of culling from the literary canon to explore eternal themes. She invoked influences ranging from the Bronte sisters to the Greek poet Stesichorus in the early sixth century BC.

Carson cemented her reputation with her 1998 novel in verse, “Autobiography of Red,” which recasts the legend of Hercules as a modern-day love triangle.

Carson became the inaugural Canadian winner of the Griffin Poetry Prize for “Men in the Off Hour” in 2001, and was awarded England’s T. S. Eliot Prize for “The Beauty of the Husband” the same year.

In 2014, Carson took the Griffin again for “Red Doc,” a quasi-sequel to “Autobiography of Red.”

At the time, she told The Canadian Press she was surprised to win, partly because she doesn’t “really like the book” and partly because she’d already won the honour and “thought it wouldn’t be fair” to get it again.

“I don’t mean it’s a bad book,” she said. “I mean, I don’t know if it’s a good book or a bad book. I just have a vision when I start of what a thing is and sometimes it gets there and sometimes it doesn’t.”

She also prevailed in the poetry category at the 2020 Governor General’s Literary Awards for “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy,” which in trademark style blends the story of Helen of Troy with elements from Marilyn Monroe’s life. She was shortlisted again two years later for “H of H Playbook,” a retelling of Euripides’s Greek tragedy, Herakles.

Her more recent works include 2024’s “Wrong Norma,” her first original work since 2016. The collection of “poetic prose pieces” was published alongside her own illustrations.

Carson is the second Canadian woman to be named a Nobel laureate in the literature category, following short story master Alice Munro’s 2013 win. The prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or roughly $1.7 million.

One of the earliest congratulations to Carson came Thursday morning from her Canadian publisher, Penguin Random House Canada.

“It is a true honour for all of us at Penguin Random House Canada to bring her groundbreaking work to Canadians, and to congratulate her on this recognition for the way that work has changed the perspectives of readers the world over,” said CEO Kristin Cochrane in a press release.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

Nicole Thompson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Regulator publishes guidance on extended trading as it comes to Canada
stories.summary: Toronto - The Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization says extended trading hours can offer more flexibility by allowing investors to react to new developments outside of regular hours, but it also comes with risks.
stories.author: Daniel Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - The Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization says extended trading hours can offer more flexibility by allowing investors to react to new developments outside of regular hours, but it also comes with risks.

Ciro made the comments in new guidance on the risks and benefits of extended trading as a new alternative trading platform brings after-hours access to investors.

Stock markets typically hold trading hours between 9:30 a.m. and 4 p.m. ET. After-hours trading broadens the times when investors are permitted to buy and sell securities.

“It gives additional choice and flexibility to retail investors, but I think the retail investor really needs to just understand and make conscious decisions of whether this is right for them,” Kevin McCoy, senior vice-president of market regulation at Ciro, said in an interview.

“For a certain segment of investors, this is going to probably be perceived as something that’s really good, but it’s not a one-size-fits-all where every investor is going to benefit from it.”

In publishing the guidance, McCoy said Ciro is aiming to ensure transparency regarding the risks when trading outside typical hours, which could lead to “better decision making” among investors as to whether after-hours trading is appropriate for them.

“Dealer members should consider whether additional controls, disclosures, policies and procedures are appropriate when providing clients with access to extended hours trading,” the guidance reads.

Ciro said extended hours could involve lower trading volumes, greater price volatility and increased reactions to events like earnings, economic reports or other news. It also said trade prices could differ significantly from those during regular trading.

“There’s less trading, there’s less volume. That May result in the prices at which somebody is willing to buy, or the price at which somebody is willing to sell; the difference between those two prices May be significantly greater than you May see in the regular trading session,” McCoy said.

Ciro said investors should keep in mind that extended hours are not available through all investment dealers.

McCoy said the U.S. is furthest along on extended trading. The Nasdaq Stock Market is preparing to implement trading 23 hours a day, five days a week, in early December.

Meanwhile, CIX Trading Inc. is a new marketplace that recently launched in Canada with extended trading hours. CIX Trading currently offers market hours between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m. ET and plans to expand those hours to between 7 a.m. and 8 p.m. ET in the fourth quarter.

Ciro also reminded dealers that they are “equally obliged” to abide by all of the requirements and securities legislation as normal trading hours.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: List of Canadians who have won the Nobel Prize
stories.summary: Canada
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto-born writer Anne Carson is the latest Canadian to be awarded a Nobel Prize. The celebrated poet, essayist and translater earned the literature prize Thursday for “bold and inventive” works.

Here is a list of Canadians who have been recognized over the years with a Nobel.

1923: Frederick G. Banting, Nobel Prize in medicine for the “discovery of insulin.”

1949: William F. Giauque, Nobel Prize in chemistry for “contributions in the field of chemical thermodynamics, particularly concerning the behaviour of substances at extremely low temperatures.”

1957: Former prime minister Lester Bowles Pearson, Nobel Peace Prize for his role in defusing the 1956 Suez crisis.

1966: Charles B. Huggins, Nobel Prize in medicine for “his discoveries concerning hormonal treatment of prostatic cancer.”

1971: Gerhard Herzberg, Nobel Prize in chemistry for “his contributions to the knowledge of electronic structure and geometry of molecules, particularly free radicals.”

1976: Saul Bellow, Nobel Prize in literature for “the human understanding and subtle analysis of contemporary culture that are combined in his work.’’

1981: David H. Hubel, Nobel Prize in medicine for “discoveries concerning information processing in the visual system.”

1983: Henry Taube, Nobel Prize in chemistry for “his work on the mechanisms of electron transfer reactions, especially in metal complexes.”

1986: John Polanyi, Nobel Prize in chemistry for “contributions concerning the dynamics of chemical elementary processes.

1989: Sidney Altman, Nobel Prize in chemistry for discovery of catalytic properties of RNA.

1990: Richard E. Taylor, Nobel Prize in physics for “investigations concerning deep inelastic scattering of electrons on protons and bound neutrons, which have been of essential importance for the development of the quark model in particle physics.”

1992: Rudolph A. Marcus, Nobel Prize in chemistry for “his contributions to the theory of electron transfer reactions in chemical systems.”

1993: Michael Smith, Nobel Prize in chemistry for “his fundamental contributions to the establishment of oligonucleotide-based, site-directed mutagenesis and its development for protein studies.”

1994: Bertram N. Brockhouse, Nobel Prize in physics for “the development of neutron spectroscopy.”

1996: William Vickrey, Nobel Prize in economic sciences for “contributions to the economic theory of incentives under asymmetric information.”

1997: Myron S. Scholes, Nobel Prize in economic sciences for “a new method to determine the value of derivatives.”

1999: Robert A. Mundell, Nobel Prize in economic sciences for “his analysis of monetary and fiscal policy under different exchange rate regimes and his analysis of optimum currency areas.”

2009: Jack W. Szostak, Nobel Prize in medicine for “the discovery of how chromosomes are protected by telomeres and the enzyme telomerase.”

2009: Willard S. Boyle, Nobel Prize in physics for “the invention of an imaging semiconductor circuit _ the CCD sensor.

2011: Ralph M. Steinman, Nobel Prize in medicine for “his discovery of the dendritic cell and its role in adaptive immunity.”

2013: Alice Munro, Nobel Prize in literature for being the “master of the contemporary short story.”

2015: Arthur B. McDonald, Nobel Prize in physics for “the discovery of neutrino oscillations, which shows that neutrinos have mass.”

2018: Donna Strickland, Nobel Prize in physics for co-developing a “method of generating high-intensity, ultra-short optical pulses.”

2019: James Peebles, Nobel Prize in physics for physical cosmology, for laying out the chemical makeup of the universe at its beginning and later explaining the way that galaxies are formed.

2021: David Card shared the Nobel Prize in economic sciences for pioneering research on labour-market impacts of minimum wage, immigration and education.

2024: Geoffrey Hinton, known as the “godfather of AI,” shared the Nobel Prize in physics for work that laid the foundation for machine learning and neural networks.

2025: Peter Howitt, shared the Nobel Memorial Prize in economics for “having explained innovation-driven economic growth.”

2026: Anne Carson, Nobel Prize in literature, for her “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Fact File: Headlines falsely claim woman approved for Maid because she couldn't cook
stories.summary: This week, media headlines and social media posts claimed a Canadian woman was approved for medical assistance in dying because she lost her ability to cook.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
This week, media headlines and social media posts claimed a Canadian woman was approved for medical assistance in dying because she lost her ability to cook. The claim stems from an opinion article written by two Canadian psychiatrists who recount the woman’s story.

But the article’s co-author says the woman had an underlying condition that meant she qualified for Maid, and her story was meant to highlight how psychological factors influenced her decision to choose the procedure, a decision she eventually delayed.

The claim A headline this week in the British tabloid The Daily Mail reads, “Canada approved woman’s euthanasia request because she could no longer cook for her family, as country’s leading doctors warn the system is far too permissive.” The claim was shared several times on the X platform, as well as on Instagram, including a post that claimed the government “almost killed” the woman because she couldn’t cook for her family.

The Daily Mail article drew from an opinion piece published Monday by the New York Times, in which two University of Toronto professors of psychiatry argue that medical providers should “pause” in order to help patients who are considering medical assistance in dying.

The authors share anecdotes involving two patients, including a woman in her 70s who “sought and received approval for assisted dying after she lost the ability to cook,” as she felt she had lost value to her family. The other patient, a man in his 80s, said he chose a medically assisted death because the choice gave him agency as a Holocaust survivor.

However, the authors say both patients changed how they viewed the process after counselling and conversations that helped them understand alternatives to suffering or confront the psychological factors behind their decisions.

The woman ultimately chose to delay ending her life, while the man initially delayed and later chose the procedure, the authors say. The facts Medical assistance in dying, also known as Maid, lets adults end their life with the help of a medical practitioner if they meet specific requirements spelled out in federal law.

A key condition is that the person must have a grievous and irremediable medical condition that causes unbearable physical or mental suffering. There are separate tracks for people whose natural death is reasonably foreseeable, and those whose death is not reasonably foreseeable but who meet the other eligibility requirements.

The federal government said Wednesday it would not extend Maid to people seeking it on the basis of mental illness alone. Dr. Gary Rodin, a co-author of the New York Times article, said the claim that the woman was approved for medical assistance in dying because she lost the ability to cook is wrong.

“This patient had an underlying health condition that qualified her for Maid,” Rodin said in an email Tuesday. He did not elaborate on what her condition was, although in their article, he and co-author Madeline Li introduce themselves as psychiatrists who work with patients with advanced cancer.

The authors describe the woman as a matriarch who made Sunday dinners, and Rodin explained that her loss of function affected her sense of value as a person. Being unable to cook for her family “affected her will to live,” Rodin said.

“The patient clearly met criteria for Maid. The anecdote was meant to illustrate how psychological factors can affect patients’ decisions about the timing of proceeding with it,” he said. Some critics of Maid argue the procedure has been fast-tracked without adequate safeguards and that a focus on approval ignores that not everyone needs Maid; others believe the practice is unethical.

The authors of the New York Times opinion piece, who have counselled patients about medical assistance in dying, caution that too many patients are getting the procedure without the opportunity to think carefully about it with a health provider.

“A society that permits assisted dying should also ask whether it has done enough to help people sustain their sense of dignity and meaning in life,” they write. “Death must not become the only kind of relief people can imagine.” This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct.

7, 2026. Marissa Birnie, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Terror groups drawn to recruit in Canada because of multiculturalism, academic says
stories.summary: "There are some people always that feel left out, so they tend to engage in crass stereotypes," says professor Arne Kislenko.
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
The recent slew of hate-motivated incidents in Canada had myriad alleged motivations, from Islamism to white supremacy. The terror groups that promote such ideologies were likely drawn to recruit in Canada because of its multiculturalism, says one academic.

“Most Canadians are big fans of multiculturalism. We celebrate it. It’s part of our existence,” says Arne Kislenko, a professor of international relations at Trinity College, University of Toronto and in Toronto Metropolitan University’s history department.

But, he said, there’s also that friction that exists. “There are some people always that feel left out, so they tend to engage in crass stereotypes.”

Recent weeks have seen incidents across Canada: a shooting at a synagogue in Belleville motivated by antisemitism, the arrest of three people in Ontario in separate incidents related to antisemitic and anti-Muslim threats made online, the arrest of an Alberta teen in relation to the 764 network , which is classified as a terrorist group in Canada, the arrest of a man in Quebec for allegedly planning to attack Canadians with chemical weapons, and antisemitic flyers handed out in Belleville nearly two weeks after the shooting.

There are currently 89 terror groups listed in Canada, including Hamas, Isis, Al Qaeda, Proud Boys and the Bishnoi Gang.

Kislenko said it’s no different than Germans in the 1930s. Despite some of them being highly educated, they started to think that Jewish or Slavic people “were somehow not human or that they had evil designs.” Today, there’s a similar sentiment of placing blame on others, he said.

Another reason why terror groups might recruit in Canada? From the outside, at least, it appears to be an “easygoing” society. It’s “safe place” where they can operate.

One way recruiters acquire targets is to find someone who has made a comment on a mainstream platform, like Instagram or Twitter. Recruiters from terror groups with similar ideologies to whatever post the person commented on then bombard them with messages. Eventually, the person May be put in contact with like-minded people, who might recruit them.

“We saw that with Isis. It’s super sophisticated, targeted propaganda — high-tech recruitment videos with music and the promise of everything you could imagine,” said Kislenko.

Radical ideologies can also spread on encrypted and unmoderated forums and game sites, according to Dr. Valarie Findlay. She is an Ottawa-based expert in extremism and ideological violence. She founded non-profit resource network IVY , dedicated to supporting youth.

Forums like Discord, Gab, Telegram, 4chan, 8kun (formerly 8chan) and game sites like Roblox and Rimworld “all operate in a similar fashion” and are places where “anyone can create groups focused on hate movements, extremism and social violence,” Findlay told National Post.

Groups like the 764 network coerce youth and “psychologically manipulate them to do the most abhorrent, terrifying crimes towards themselves, their own family, to family pets,” she said.

“Once you’re out of that situation, you realize what you’ve done and how horrifying it is, and that now somebody knows about it, somebody has that evidence or proof, then you have a sort of responsibility to yourself to try and maintain that ‘friendship’ on an even keel, so they never use it against you,” said Findlay.

“But they’re going to use it against you. That was the plan all along. It’s a very slippery slope.”

She said it’s a red flag when someone online becomes increasingly interested in your personal life. “It’s the unfortunate thing about social media. It’s great for the friends that you already have, but it is the worst place to actually make enduring, trustful friendships,” she said.

“People blame Jewish people for everything. It’s a convenient scapegoat. Or you blame big government, or you blame women, right? Findlay said that although it May seem like there are more hate-motivated attacks now, it’s been going on “for a long time.”

“How it manifests and how it channels and how (terror groups) establish their reach obviously has changed because of the advent of technology from the 1970s roughly onward. It has really made everything look like it’s happening more often in a way,” she said.

“And (terror groups) really do attach to waves of prosperity and economic decline, as well as the rise of conspiracy theories. They follow trends. When things are not looking so great … these things kind of seem to flourish a little bit more.”

Kislenko said just because it’s hard to police against recruitment, it doesn’t mean that we shouldn’t. He recommends an educational approach and possibly putting some restrictions on social media.

“We should empower law enforcement and intelligence not with more authority, but with a better capacity and more funding and training to look for these (recruiters),” he said.

“We should be judicious in prosecution…because it is hate and it is terrorism, and they are closely connected, and that leads to (the shooting in) Belleville, amongst other places.”

stories.title: Therapy dog reaches 1,000 visits, first in southwestern Ontario
stories.summary: Made possible through the St. John Ambulance Therapy Dog Program, Mulligan offers comfort to families staying at Ronald McDonald house
stories.author: Lauren Stallone
stories.content:
A mulligan is a second-chance or fresh start and for Jenny Hauser it was the perfect name for her new pup.

“It was in my 40’s when I got my first dog,” said Hauser. “She was a therapy dog as well and then when she passed away, we got Mulligan.”

Years later, Mulligan celebrated a major accomplishment Wednesday night at the Ronald McDonald house in London Ont.

“This is Mulligan’s 1000th visit,” said Hauser. “A lot of the visits have been at the Ronald McDonald House so that’s why we chose here to do the celebration.”

Made possible through the St. John Ambulance Therapy Dog Program, Mulligan offers comfort to families staying at the home.

“You can just imagine after a stressful day or people who have had dogs in the past who can’t have them anymore how important it is to have that love and care,” said Lynn Loubert, dog coordinator with the program. “And that unconditional attention.”

Families say Mulligan is always a big hit with the children staying at the home.

“They’re so cute, they’re so much fun,” said Amelia, Ryan, and Rosalie Rouselle. “They’re so fluffy.”

Mulligan is the first dog in southwestern Ontario to achieve this milestone and has touched the lives of over 112,000 people.

“Mulligan is just that type of dog that wants to greet everybody, love everybody,” said Hauser. “He just has that demeanor and that personality trait that is just full of love.”

Volunteers said the program started 32 years ago and currently has 62 dogs like Mulligan, sharing their love with the community.

“We really reduce the stress of so many of our participants,” said Loubert. “Its just a fabulous experience, for us, for them, and for the dogs.”

stories.title: Cost of medicines from Canada set to soar for millions of Americans
stories.summary: The U.S. Customs and Border Protection rule targets the de minimis exemption, which previously allowed shipments valued under $800 to pass through customs more easily.
stories.author: Fatima Hussein
stories.content:
Millions of Americans who buy cheap drugs from Canada could soon lose access when a customs rule goes into effect later this month, a change that has sparked opposition from Democrats and some Republicans with the cost of living a top issue for voters ahead of midterm elections.

The rule applies to a swath of goods beyond drugs and is intended to collect tariffs and prevent illegal drugs from coming into the U.S. It comes as President Donald Trump has made lowering drug prices a top target in addressing soaring healthcare costs, and critics say the rule will hurt patients seeking affordable medicine.

“The issue is a matter of life and death for me,” said Susan Hooper, a 75-year-old Toledo, Ohio, resident who has been on oxygen for 14 years and takes two daily medications purchased through a Canadian pharmacy that are not available in the U.S.

The U.S. Customs and Border Protection rule targets the de minimis exemption, which previously allowed shipments valued under $800 to pass through customs more easily. As of Oct. 22, that exemption will be indefinitely suspended, and medications mailed from outside the U.S. will require additional data and a bond guarantee.

The rule puts added fees and registration requirements on low-value shipments that previously entered the U.S. duty-free — on everything from textiles to toys — but the people who could see the most significant impacts are those who buy their cheap drugs from across the border.

And while the rule doesn’t specifically target Canadian drugs — it applies to international mail generally — the practical consequence could be delays, refusals or substantially more difficulty getting their medications delivered.

Roughly 2.3 million Americans buy their drugs abroad, according to a 2020 study by Jama Network.

The Trump administration has made lowering drug prices a priority in its bid to show Americans that it is tackling soaring costs. Trump, a Republican, has struck multiple most-favoured-nation drug deals with pharmaceutical firms and has launched the discounted-drug website TrumpRx, among other steps.

Federal data from this summer showed that U.S. prescription drug prices were down 3.1% from a year ago, the steepest year-over-year drop since 1963. Trump has sought to take credit for the steep decline, but the real picture is more complicated, and experts say factors beyond the president’s policies likely contributed more to the drop.

Advocates say the rule will hurt patients seeking affordable medicine.

Ken Hunter, executive director of the Campaign for Personal Prescription Importation, which advocates on behalf of Americans who access the Canadian drugs, said those who have enjoyed the lower drug prices from across the northern border May not benefit from Trump’s drug pricing moves.

“There has been a lot of talk of lowering drug prices, but in many cases it doesn’t cover all drugs for all people for all conditions,” he said.

Hunter warned that costs will explode for some medications after his organization conducted a study in August looking at 10 of the most commonly prescribed medications imported from Canada.

He cited Eliquis, a prescription blood thinner used to prevent and treat dangerous blood clots. A three-month supply of 180 5-mg pills would cost $565 from a mail-order Canadian pharmacy. The same medication would cost roughly $1,017 from Amazon’s pharmacy arm or $1,029 from GoodRx.

“I’ve had so many of our members calling me and telling me, ‘I don’t know what I’m going to do,’” Hunter said. “We really need someone to step forward and say, ‘We really need this to stop.’”

Allison Schuster, a White House spokesperson, said in a statement that Trump “remains dedicated to lowering the cost of prescription drugs,” citing the most-favoured-nation deals.

“The Trump administration continues working to ensure Americans have access to low-cost pharmaceuticals across the board,” Schuster said.

The Trump administration could drop the rule, alter it or decide not to enforce it. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have demanded answers to how the administration will protect access to affordable care for people who get their drugs from over the border.

Three Florida Republican members of Congress wrote to the administration last month expressing concern about how the rule would impact their constituents, who, unlike residents of border states, are unable to easily travel to Canada to buy the drugs.

Florida has separately crafted a Canadian prescription drug importation program with authorization from the federal government, but that initiative has stalled.

Customs and Border Protection and the Food and Drug Administration “must ensure that Floridians simply seeking relief from high drug prices will not be inadvertently impacted by the rule,” said the letter signed by Florida Reps. Aaron Bean, Gus M. Bilirakis and C. Scott Franklin.

A group of more than 70 Democrats last week sent a letter to health and immigration enforcement officials, asking them to pause the new rule unless they could provide assurances that prescription medicines meant for personal use would be able to enter the U.S.

“Americans should not lose access to affordable medicines simply because the government has better information about packages entering the country,” the letter said.

Representatives from CBP did not respond to requests for comment.

Hooper, who has serious drug allergies, said her medications have already increased in price since the Trump administration imposed additional tariffs on Canada in August.

She says Theophylline, a medication that relaxes her airways and is bought in Canada, used to cost $85 with shipping. It now costs $141 because of tariffs. And her Foradil bronchodilator for asthma, which used to cost $151, now costs $273. Hooper said she will find a way to manage through the change. Until then, she said, she’s been in a rush to stockpile.

“The Trump administration continues working to ensure Americans have access to low-cost pharmaceuticals across the board,” Schuster said.

stories.title: Voters’ ability to fix errors in mail-in ballot packages show system works, Smith says
stories.summary: Elections Alberta had said those ballot packages were returned with either declaration forms missing or with other errors
stories.author: Lisa Johnson
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says the fact the provincial election authority is helping voters correct errors in about 3,000 mail-in ballot packages shows the system is working.

It comes after Elections Alberta announced those ballot packages were returned with either declaration forms missing or with other errors, like missing the required copies of identification.

At an unrelated news conference Wednesday, Smith said the ability for electors to correct the necessary documents in time for their vote to be counted shows Elections Alberta is managing the situation as expected.

“I think that’s a sign the system works,” she said.

She and Elections Alberta also noted that the problematic ballot packages represent a small number of those that have been sent back by voters – only 1.2 per cent of around 250,000.

Albertans are to vote on a series of questions on Oct. 19, including whether to stay in Canada or begin the process to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving Confederation.

Maia Hanrahan at Elections Alberta said in an e-mail Wednesday they’ve contacted those whose packages had problems and are helping voters make the necessary fixes.

“Similar to an in-person voting experience where an election officer would assist the elector in making sure their information was correct and complete, that is what is happening with these special ballots – we are assisting electors in correcting their errors,” Hanrahan wrote.

She said voters are able to provide the required information via e-mail, but if they do not, their special ballots will be rejected.

“Already we have had many people respond and provide the required information.”

stories.title: Big price cut and an under-asking sale for Summerhill townhouse in Toronto
stories.summary: Three-bedroom row home is only 150 metres from a subway station and has rare basement access from the garage
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
2C Tacoma Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $2,175,000 (June, 2026)

Previous asking price: $2,295,000 (May, 2026)

Selling price: $1,998,000 (June, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $979,000 (June, 2004); $725,000 (May, 2002)

Taxes: $12,067 (2025)

Days on the market: 13

Property days on market: 33

Listing agents: Debbie Penzo and Graeme McIntosh, Chestnut Park Real Estate Ltd.

This three-bedroom row home, only 150 metres from Summerhill subway station on Yonge Street, had more than a dozen visitors, not including open house guests, in May, yet none felt a strong inclination to purchase it priced at $2,295,000. The next month, the sellers decided to trim their asking price to $2,175,000. Meanwhile, they caught wind of a similar townhouse, closer to Cottingham Junior Public School, that had cut its asking price and quickly sold for $1,975,000.

“A recent comparable sale set a new benchmark, which gave the sellers confidence in their decision to reprice,” agent Graeme McIntosh said.

“At the new price, within two weeks, we received three offers.”

A bidder at $1,998,000 took the 25-year-old home.

Buyers were attracted by the home’s generous size and built-in, double garage.

“It looked and felt bigger inside than it did from the outside,” Mr. McIntosh said.

“People also liked that you could walk from the garage into the basement. It’s very rare in the area.”

This two-storey home at the end of a row of brick houses has a street level entrance and a west-facing deck at the rear.

The main floor has a 10-foot ceiling, a gas fireplace in the primary entertaining area, and a kitchen between two dining areas.

There are two full bathrooms and a laundry room with a sink by the bedrooms upstairs.

An additional recreation area is in the basement.

“It has an expansive great room with tall ceilings,” Mr. McIntosh said.

“There’s no maintenance, just a small front yard and a back deck.”

stories.title: Oilpatch profits vastly outpacing spending — at least for now: Deloitte
stories.summary: High prices have created a windfall for Canada's oil producers, with that sector the biggest contributor to non-financial industry profits during the second quarter.
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
Canadian oil producers saw a 68 per cent surge in operating profits between the first and second quarters of this year, but capital spending hasn’t kept anywhere near the same pace, says a new report from Deloitte Canada.

The consulting firm notes that crude prices have experienced “considerable volatility” in recent months due to the Middle East war, with the international light benchmark, Brent, fluctuating between US$68 and US$105 per barrel in July and August alone.

High prices have created a windfall for Canada’s oil producers, with that sector the biggest contributor to non-financial industry profits during the second quarter, according to Statistics Canada.

Separate capital expenditure data from StatCan, meanwhile, has shown only modest movement recently, rising about seven per cent to $11 billion in the second quarter versus the first. Citing Baker Hughes rig count data, Deloitte says drilling in Canada was up 17 per cent during the second quarter compared to the same time a year earlier.

“It’s clear that producers are prioritizing drilling programs in plays which offer efficient, short-cycle economics, such as in the Montney, Duvernay and Clearwater, rather than pursue long-cycle, capital-intensive projects,” Deloitte said in the report released Thursday.

“Producers view the current price environment as temporary, or uncertain, rather than rooted in a fundamental supply-demand shift.”

Deloitte is forecasting West Texas Intermediate oil prices — the benchmark for light oil produced from U.S. fields — to average US$76.50 per barrel in 2027, down from a projected 2026 average of US$90.

Andrew Botterill, who leads Deloitte Canada’s oil, gas and chemicals practice, said over the past five to eight years, companies have been under pressure from investors to keep spending and debt in check. The COVID-19 pandemic, and the price collapse that accompanied it, ravaged oilpatch finances when they had barely recovered from the 2014-2015 bust.

But now, Botterill said, there’s a sense of “we could be much more” in the sector. A new million-barrel-per-day export pipeline has been proposed to the British Columbia coast, and Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has made moves to simplify the regulatory process, roll back Trudeau-era environmental policies and expand investment tax perks.

“We could see significant growth coming from Canada,” Botterill said.

“And I think what we are going to see play out over the coming year is companies are going start to look at, ‘Where are we going to make our bets? Where are we going to start to make bigger capital spends for … the medium and long term?'”

Earlier this week, oilsands giant Cenovus Energy Inc. announced an agreement to buy smaller peer Athabasca Oil Corp. for $5.7 billion. Fellow energy heavyweight Suncor Energy Inc., meanwhile, said it reached a deal to sell some of its Atlantic Canada offshore holdings for $1.2 billion as it focuses on its core oilsands business.

Botterill said those transactions are “preparatory steps” for companies looking at growth over a long time horizon.

“Where would we be more likely to play that capital and let’s make sure we get our portfolio in that direction.”

On the natural gas side, the Deloitte report said prices in Alberta have averaged below an anemic C$2 per thousand cubic feet year-to-date, despite increasing exports from the LNG Canada terminal in Kitimat, B.C., which started up in mid-2025.

Output averaged 20 billion cubic feet per day during the second quarter, about five per cent above the same period in 2025. Companies kept growing production as they chased more valuable natural gas liquids, like propane, which come out of the ground along with dry natural gas.

Botterill said in August and September, typically the weakest time of year for Alberta natural gas, prices did not see sharp declines like they usually do, but stayed relatively steady.

“What that shows you is that there is natural gas demand building in Canada. The ability to export off our West Coast is making a difference,” he said.

“We’re much more structurally sound on the natural gas market than we were say, a year ago.”

Deloitte expects Alberta gas prices to average C$1.75 per thousand cubic feet this year, climbing to $2.15 next year and well above $3 post-2029.

The report also touched on artificial intelligence adoption in the oilpatch, which was detailed in another study Deloitte published in February.

It said 72 per cent of energy, resource and industrial companies use “physical” AI — through machines and control systems — to some extent.

However, many struggle to level up from pilot projects to enterprise-wide use, and only 16 per cent of companies reported using AI extensively.

“Oil and gas companies are used to capital intensive investments, with the oilsands as a prime example of making big bets. Simply put: it’s a business that isn’t afraid of risk,” the report said.

“But to compete with capital that is designated to core operations for development, expansion and optimization projects, the value proposition for AI use cases needs to be well developed.”

“And I think what we are going to see play out over the coming year is companies are going start to look at, ‘Where are we going to make our bets? Where are we going to start to make bigger capital spends for … the medium and long term?'”

Earlier this week, oilsands giant Cenovus Energy Inc. announced an agreement to buy smaller peer Athabasca Oil Corp. for $5.7 billion. Fellow energy heavyweight Suncor Energy Inc., meanwhile, said it reached a deal to sell some of its Atlantic Canada offshore holdings for $1.2 billion as it focuses on its core oilsands business.
Botterill said those transactions are “preparatory steps” for companies looking at growth over a long time horizon.
“Where would we be more likely to play that capital and let’s make sure we get our portfolio in that direction.”

On the natural gas side, the Deloitte report said prices in Alberta have averaged below an anemic C$2 per thousand cubic feet year-to-date, despite increasing exports from the LNG Canada terminal in Kitimat, B.C., which started up in mid-2025.

Output averaged 20 billion cubic feet per day during the second quarter, about five per cent above the same period in 2025. Companies kept growing production as they chased more valuable natural gas liquids, like propane, which come out of the ground along with dry natural gas.
Botterill said in August and September, typically the weakest time of year for Alberta natural gas, prices did not see sharp declines like they usually do, but stayed relatively steady.
“What that shows you is that there is natural gas demand building in Canada. The ability to export off our West Coast is making a difference,” he said.
“We’re much more structurally sound on the natural gas market than we were say, a year ago.”
Deloitte expects Alberta gas prices to average C$1.75 per thousand cubic feet this year, climbing to $2.15 next year and well above $3 post-2029.
The report also touched on artificial intelligence adoption in the oilpatch, which was detailed in another study Deloitte published in February.
It said 72 per cent of energy, resource and industrial companies use “physical” AI — through machines and control systems — to some extent.
However, many struggle to level up from pilot projects to enterprise-wide use, and only 16 per cent of companies reported using AI extensively.
“Oil and gas companies are used to capital intensive investments, with the oilsands as a prime example of making big bets. Simply put: it’s a business that isn’t afraid of risk,” the report said.
“But to compete with capital that is designated to core operations for development, expansion and optimization projects, the value proposition for AI use cases needs to be well developed.”

content_blocks.text: Canadian oil producers saw a 68 per cent surge in operating profits between the first and second quarters of this year, but capital spending hasn’t kept anywhere near the same pace, says a new report from Deloitte Canada.

The consulting firm notes that crude prices have experienced “considerable volatility” in recent months due to the Middle East war, with the international light benchmark, Brent, fluctuating between US$68 and US$105 per barrel in July and August alone.
High prices have created a windfall for Canada’s oil producers, with that sector the biggest contributor to non-financial industry profits during the second quarter, according to Statistics Canada.

Separate capital expenditure data from StatCan, meanwhile, has shown only modest movement recently, rising about seven per cent to $11 billion in the second quarter versus the first. Citing Baker Hughes rig count data, Deloitte says drilling in Canada was up 17 per cent during the second quarter compared to the same time a year earlier.

stories.title: Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel literature prize
stories.summary: The 76-year-old, who announced in 2024 that she has Parkinson's disease, has been mentioned as possible Nobel laureate for years.
stories.author: AFP
stories.content:
The Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded on Thursday to Canadian poet Anne Carson, an essayist and classicist who brings a modern twist to mysticism and antiquity in her writings about love, desire and despair.

The 76-year-old — who announced in 2024 that she has Parkinson’s disease — was honoured “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature,” the Swedish Academy said.

The permanent secretary of the Academy, Ingrid Carlberg, said she had briefly spoken to Carson.

“We didn’t have so much time to speak. All she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she’s listening to the wind.”

“She was taken by surprise, but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”

A professor of classics with a background in dead languages, literature, anthropology and history, she was described by The New York Times in 2001 as “one of the great pasticheurs.”

Her unique contemporary poetry earned her several key literary prizes in the 1990s, including the 1996 Lannan Award and the 1997 Pushcart Prize.

A year later, “Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse” — loosely based on the Greek myth of the monster Geryon and Herakles but transformed into a modern tale of a gay love triangle — received widespread praise.

The Academy said almost all of Carson’s literary production “has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning.”

It singled out her poem “Nox”, printed on one continuous sheet of paper in homage to her brother who died in 2000, as “an unforgettable work”.

“Palpable here is a deep sense of loss that works its way up from below. The result is a creation as sculptural as it is literary, an epitaph in the form of a box containing an accordion-fold-out of pictures, letters and other written texts dedicated to her dead brother,” the Academy said.

Carson has been mentioned as a possible Nobel laureate for years.

Women under-represented

Many literary critics had predicted the award would go to a woman this year, given the frequent criticism directed at the Academy over the overrepresentation of Western white men among its picks.

There have been just 19 women laureates out of 122 since the Nobel literature prize was first awarded in 1901.

A 2018 sex assault scandal left the Academy in tatters and more than half of its 18 members were replaced.

Since then, every other literature laureate has been a woman.

Last year, the award went to Hungary’s Laszlo Krasznahorkai, whose works explore themes of postmodern dystopia.

The literature prize is the fourth of the six Nobels to be announced over the course of a week.

The winners of the medicine, physics and chemistry prizes were announced earlier this week in Stockholm, while the peace prize will be announced in Oslo on Friday.

Among those seen as possibilities are the Save the Children charity and Mykola Kuleba, a Ukrainian children’s rights activist campaigning for the return of kids illegally taken to Russia from occupied territories.

Sudan’s Emergency Response Rooms (ERR), a vast network of volunteers risking their lives to help people facing the double threat of war and hunger, could also be a potential laureate.

Yet others mentioned are the UN special rapporteur for the occupied Palestinian territories Francesca Albanese, Pope Leo XIV, press freedoms with an award to the Committee to Protect Journalists, or international justice bodies such as the International Criminal Court (ICC) and the International Court of Justice (ICJ).

The Nobel economics prize will round up the 2026 awards season on Monday.

Each Nobel prize comes with a diploma, a gold medal and a $1.2 million prize sum, to be shared if there is more than one laureate in each discipline.

Carson will receive the award from King Carl XVI Gustaf in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of the 1896 death of scientist and prize creator Alfred Nobel.

stories.title: Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in literature
stories.summary: A poet, essayist, classical scholar and translator, Anne Carson is renowned as a master of esoterica whose body of work constitutes a genre unto itself.
stories.author: Nicole Thompson
stories.content:
Celebrated Canadian poet Anne Carson has won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

The Swedish Academy said the award was in recognition of Carson’s “bold and inventive oeuvre.”

A poet, essayist, classical scholar and translator, Carson is renowned as a master of esoterica whose body of work constitutes a genre unto itself.

With a bibliography of more than 20 books of poetry, essays, plays, libretti and translations of ancient Greek texts, Carson has defied literary conventions with her signature synthesis of the antiquities and the avant-garde.

She’s amassed a devoted readership and a raft of critical accolades, including two Griffin Poetry Prizes, a Governor General’s Literary Award, the T. S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur “genius grant” and a Guggenheim Fellowship.

But as her poetic profile has grown over more than three decades, the particulars of Carson’s personal life have remained notoriously elusive.

Her public reticence is encapsulated by her scant book-jacket biography: “Canadian poet, essayist and translator of Greek mythology.”

A representative for her did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary to the Swedish Academy, said she reached Carson Thursday in Iceland, where she was “listening to the wind.”

Various accounts suggest that Carson was born in Toronto in 1950 and studied classics at the University of Toronto, and has held teaching positions at institutions including McGill University, Michigan University and Princeton University.

Carson made her publishing debut in 1986 with her academic essays on love, “Eros the Bittersweet.”

She gained recognition with a series of genre-bending books in the 1990s establishing her style of culling from the literary canon to explore eternal themes. She invoked influences ranging from the Brontë sisters to the Greek poet Stesichorus in the early sixth century BC.

Carson cemented her reputation with her 1998 novel in verse, “Autobiography on Red,” which recasts the legend of Hercules as a modern-day love triangle.

Carson became the inaugural Canadian winner of the Griffin Poetry Prize for “Men in the Off Hour” in 2001, and was awarded England’s T. S. Eliot Prize for “The Beauty of the Husband” the same year.

In 2014, Carson took the Griffin again for “Red Doc>,” a quasi-sequel to “Autobiography on Red.”

At the time, she told The Canadian Press she was surprised to win, partly because she doesn’t “really like the book” and partly because she’d already won the honour and “thought it wouldn’t be fair” to get it again.

“I don’t mean it’s a bad book,” she said. “I mean, I don’t know if it’s a good book or a bad book. I just have a vision when I start of what a thing is and sometimes it gets there and sometimes it doesn’t.”

She also prevailed in the poetry category at the 2020 Governor General’s Literary Awards for “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy,” which in trademark style blends the story of Helen of Troy with elements from Marilyn Monroe’s life. She was shortlisted again two years later for “H of H Playbook,” a retelling of Euripides’s Greek tragedy, Herakles.

Her more recent works include 2024’s “Wrong Norma,” her first original work since 2016. The collection of “poetic prose pieces” was published alongside her own illustrations.

Carson is the second Canadian woman to be named a Nobel laureate in the literature category, following short story master Alice Munro’s 2013 win. The prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or roughly $1.7 million.

She’s amassed a devoted readership and a raft of critical accolades, including two Griffin Poetry Prizes, a Governor General’s Literary Award, the T. S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur “genius grant” and a Guggenheim Fellowship.
But as her poetic profile has grown over more than three decades, the particulars of Carson’s personal life have remained notoriously elusive.
Her public reticence is encapsulated by her scant book-jacket biography: “Canadian poet, essayist and translator of Greek mythology.”

A representative for her did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary to the Swedish Academy, said she reached Carson Thursday in Iceland, where she was “listening to the wind.”

content_blocks.text: Various accounts suggest that Carson was born in Toronto in 1950 and studied classics at the University of Toronto, and has held teaching positions at institutions including McGill University, Michigan University and Princeton University.
Carson made her publishing debut in 1986 with her academic essays on love, “Eros the Bittersweet.”

She gained recognition with a series of genre-bending books in the 1990s establishing her style of culling from the literary canon to explore eternal themes. She invoked influences ranging from the Brontë sisters to the Greek poet Stesichorus in the early sixth century BC.
Carson cemented her reputation with her 1998 novel in verse, “Autobiography on Red,” which recasts the legend of Hercules as a modern-day love triangle.
Carson became the inaugural Canadian winner of the Griffin Poetry Prize for “Men in the Off Hour” in 2001, and was awarded England’s T. S. Eliot Prize for “The Beauty of the Husband” the same year.
In 2014, Carson took the Griffin again for “Red Doc>,” a quasi-sequel to “Autobiography on Red.”

content_blocks.text: At the time, she told The Canadian Press she was surprised to win, partly because she doesn’t “really like the book” and partly because she’d already won the honour and “thought it wouldn’t be fair” to get it again.

“I don’t mean it’s a bad book,” she said. “I mean, I don’t know if it’s a good book or a bad book. I just have a vision when I start of what a thing is and sometimes it gets there and sometimes it doesn’t.”

content_blocks.text: She also prevailed in the poetry category at the 2020 Governor General’s Literary Awards for “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy,” which in trademark style blends the story of Helen of Troy with elements from Marilyn Monroe’s life. She was shortlisted again two years later for “H of H Playbook,” a retelling of Euripides’s Greek tragedy, Herakles.
Her more recent works include 2024’s “Wrong Norma,” her first original work since 2016. The collection of “poetic prose pieces” was published alongside her own illustrations.

Carson is the second Canadian woman to be named a Nobel laureate in the literature category, following short story master Alice Munro’s 2013 win. The prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or roughly $1.7 million.

stories.title: Updated semi in Toronto’s Seaton Village rakes in 19 offers
stories.summary: Three-bedroom house was one of few properties for sale near Christie Pits Park during the first week of May
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
415 Clinton St., Toronto

Asking price: $1,149,000 (May, 2026)

Selling price: $1,608,000 (May, 2026)

Previous selling prices: $640,000 (June, 2011); $470,000 (October, 2006); $295,000 (June, 2000)

Taxes: $8,023 (2025)

Days on the market: Seven

Listing agents: Sandra Pate and Amy Polson, Sage Real Estate Ltd.

This semi-detached house was one of few properties for sale near Christie Pits Park on Bloor Street during the first week of May. An attractive asking price of $1,149,000 lured nearly 100 visitors, not including open house guests, to examine its charms. Agent Amy Polson sensed that some of those visitors would return with offers, but getting 19 was a welcome surprise.

“There hadn’t been a lot of inventory [in the area] in March or April,” Ms. Polson said.

“We knew it would be busy, but we did not anticipate that number of showings or offers.”

The location and condition of the 126-year-old home were key factors in the final sale price of $1.608-million.

“Most people looking at it were young couples and young families looking for Toronto homes with great access to amenities,” Ms. Polson said.

“It also touched a lot of people emotionally with a combination of original charm and updates.”

This two-storey house has 1,386 square feet of living space, including three bedrooms, three bathrooms and separate living and dining rooms with original hardwood flooring.

The kitchen has granite countertops, an island and stone flooring.

A rear stairwell has access to a recreation area downstairs and a side door to the patio and garage. It faces a laneway behind the 16- by 128-foot lot.

Since 2018, the owners replaced several appliances, including a washing machine, and installed a new roof, windows, air conditioner and water main.

“All of Seaton Village is quite special, but this is in proximity to transit, just north of Bloor Street, and it’s in Palmerston Avenue Jr. Public School district, which is popular,” Ms. Polson said.

“Christie Pits is right there and Karma food co-op is around the corner.”

stories.title: Sun, cloud and gusty winds forecast for London ahead of holiday weekend
stories.summary: Thursday will be slightly cooler across southern Ontario, with a mix of sun and cloud expected in the London area.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Thursday will be slightly cooler across southern Ontario, with a mix of sun and cloud expected in the London area.

CTV meteorologist Julie Atchison says London is expected to reach a high of 18 C, with gusty west winds developing through the afternoon.

Winds will reach 30 km/h, with gusts up to 50 km/h.

Scattered showers are possible north of the city, particularly around Bruce County and areas affected by moisture coming off Lake Huron and Georgian Bay. London is expected to see a fair amount of sunshine through the day.

Friday will be mostly beautiful, with a high of 17 C, while Saturday will bring a mix of sun and cloud.

The holiday weekend could see some changes as moisture from a tropical storm in the Gulf potentially moves into southern Ontario.

Atchison says the exact impact remains unclear, but a 40 per cent chance of showers has been introduced for Sunday, with increased cloud cover expected Monday.

Despite the chance of showers, the weekend is expected to remain warm enough for outdoor activities.

stories.title: Canada’s Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in Literature for ‘her bold and inventive oeuvre’
stories.summary: The 76-year-old modernist poet, translator, classics scholar and Member of the Order of Canada is the third Canadian to be awarded the prize given to a living writer
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Canada’s Anne Carson has won the Nobel Prize in Literature, worth 12-million Swedish crowns (about $1.7-million). The announcement was made Thursday in Stockholm.

The 76-year-old modernist poet, translator, classics scholar and member of the Order of Canada was recognized for “her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”

She is the third Canadian to be awarded the prize, given to a living writer for outstanding career contributions in literature.

“Anne Carson has, throughout her entire career, combined poetry writing with translation work and teaching at various universities. Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning. She has herself identified the etymology of words as the starting point for all her work,” the Swedish Academy said in a statement.

The Toronto-born writer has earned high international recognition before, receiving the Lannan Literary Award for poetry, the T.S. Eliot Prize, a Guggenheim Fellowship, the Princess of Asturias Award for Literature and the PEN/Nabokov Award for Achievement in International Literature.

Upon notification she had won, Carson told the Swedish Academy by phone that she was currently in Iceland “listening to the wind,” and that she was taken by surprise but very happy.

Asked by The Globe and Mail for a response to winning the prestigious prize, she e-mailed back a one-word reaction in all-caps: “Yikes!!”

Among her best-known works is 1998’s Autobiography of Red , both a novel and a poem, both an unconventional re-creation of an ancient Greek myth and a wholly original coming-of-age story set in the present.

In a statement from Carson’s publisher, Penguin Random House Canada, CEO Kristin Cochrane said the poet “continuously dazzles us with her inventiveness and the transformative, revelatory power of her writing.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney offered his congratulations on the social-media platform X. “With wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own, Canadian poet Anne Carson has reimagined the classics,” he wrote. “She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature.”

The daughter of a banker, Carson grew up in a number of small Canadian towns. The future professor at Princeton University, McGill University and other schools twice quit her own studies at St. Michael’s College at the University of Toronto – a compulsory course on Milton was a deal-breaker for her. She eventually completed a bachelor of arts there in 1974.

Carson’s first published poetry, 1984’s Canicula di Anna , resulted in her first international literary prize, the Betty Colladay Award from the Quarterly Review of Literature. Her debut full-length poetry collection was Short Talks , published by Brick Books in 1992.

Her first book of essays, 1986’s Eros the Bittersweet , “stunned the classics community as a work of Greek scholarship,” according to John D’Agata of the Boston Review. (D’Agata also wrote that Carson’s Men in the Off Hours was “trying its darndest to be poetry.”) Eros the Bittersweet was voted onto the 1999 Modern Library Reader’s List for the 100 Best Nonfiction books of the 20th century.

Michael Ondaatje once hailed Carson as “the most exciting poet writing in English today.”

The previous Canadian winners of the Nobel Prize in Literature are short story writer Alice Munro, who won in 2013, and Saul Bellow, who was born in the Montreal suburb of Lachine but moved to the United States as a child. He won in 1976.

Hours after the initial announcement, Carson spoke to the Swedish Academy again. “I’m just eating crackers and drinking tea,” the poet said by phone from her home in Reykjavík . “I noticed the floor needed sweeping, so I leapt up and did that.”

The poet and her husband are currently thinking up ways to spend the prize money. “I have a friend who needs a house,” she said. “We always give a lot to Doctors Without Borders.”

The former classics professor was asked why the classics were relevant. She said they were not: “I don’t think I’m interested in relevance. I’m interested in us being relevant to them.”

The prize has been awarded 119 times to 123 laureates since 1901. Carson is the 19th woman. Among the illustrious laureates are Rudyard Kipling, Pearl Buck, Winston Churchill, Gabriel García Márquez, Jean-Paul Sartre, Toni Morrison, José Saramago, John Steinbeck, Harold Pinter, Ernest Hemingway and, “for having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition,” Bob Dylan.

After receiving the award in 2016, the iconic songwriter waited days before commenting publicly. He ultimately did not attend the Nobel Prize ceremony in Stockholm, choosing instead to meet with the Swedish Academy in a private ceremony there.

Carson is also publicity shy. As noted in a Globe and Mail profile in 2000, she doesn’t like to talk about herself and is so reclusive she wouldn’t permit a photographer for the interview.

Up to that point, despite her international acclaim, Carson had yet to win a major Canadian literary award. (Finally, in 2001, she won the inaugural Griffin Poetry Prize for Men in the Off Hours . She added another Griffin in 2014 and won the Governor General’s Award for English-language poetry in 2020 for Norma Jeane Baker of Troy .)

Asked in 2000 why she didn’t enjoy as enthusiastic a following in her own country as she did in the United States, Carson scoffed: “It’s typical of Canadians. You have to win awards outside this country before they’ll recognize you.”

Griffin Poetry Prize founder Scott Griffin said Carson’s win raises the profile of poetry to its “rightful place as the essence of literature,” and that Carson is the perfect writer to do it.

“Poetry is the craft of using very few words to convey a very big subject. It’s a true art form that is difficult for most people, and even good poets, to do. Anne is the quintessential author of that kind of talent, almost to an extreme point.”

Carson has Parkinson’s disease, which profoundly affects her penmanship and, as a result, hampers her creative process. “Hard to describe or explain the shame of bad handwriting,” she wrote in an essay for the London Review of Books in 2024.

Last year she participated in the album The Great Lakes Suite by the Toronto art-rock band Rheostatics. She read poems from her 1995 book Plainwater for the project.

Established in the will of Swedish dynamite inventor Alfred Nobel, the prizes for achievements in literature, science and peace have been given since 1901.

Hungarian writer Laszlo Krasznahorkai earned last year’s Nobel Prize in Literature for his “compelling and visionary oeuvre that, in the midst of apocalyptic terror, reaffirms the power of art.” He won the Man Booker International Prize in 2015.

The Norwegian Nobel Committee will announce this year’s Nobel Peace Prize winner in Oslo on Friday. Prime Minister Mark Carney is believed to be among the contenders for what is considered the most distinguished award in the world.

stories.title: Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in literature
stories.summary: won the Nobel Prize in literature Thursday “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”
stories.author: The Associated Press
stories.content:
Stockholm -- Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson won the Nobel Prize in literature Thursday “for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”

Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said the author was in Iceland “listening to the wind” when the academy reached her to notify her of the win.

Toronto-born Carson draws on themes and stories from ancient Greek and Roman literature for works that often blend elements of poetry, essay and fiction.

Her books include “Eros the Bittersweet,” a look at the pleasure and pain of desire in ancient Greek literature, verse novel “Autobiography of Red,” “Men in the Off Hours,” a collection of poetry and prose that won Canada’s Griffin Prize for poetry in 2001 and “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy,” which compares Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy.

The prize was announced by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm.

Last year, Hungarian writer Laszlo Krasznahorkai, whose surreal and anarchic novels combine a bleak world view with mordant humor, won the Nobel Prize in literature for work the judges said upholds the power of art in the midst of “apocalyptic terror.”

Three science awards were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognized a scientist’s efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognized two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.

This week ends with Friday’s peace prize. The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about US$1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

Kostya Manenkov and Stefanie Dazio, The Associated Press

Dazio reported from Berlin.
