stories.title: Chinese surveillance cameras are still around, despite ban in government buildings
stories.summary: 'The silence actually to me is the story itself,' said Dennis Molinaro, a former federal national security analyst.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — More than one year after Industry Minister Mélanie Joly ordered the government rip out all Chinese surveillance giant Hikvision gear from its properties, multiple key federal organizations refuse to say if they have done so.

In statements provided over the last two months, the Canadian Space Agency, Employment and Social Development Canada (Esdc), Environment and Climate Change Canada, Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada and Parks Canada all declined to say if they continued to use Hikvision cameras at their offices.

Furthermore, two government agencies — the National Research Council and the Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority — told National Post that they continue to use Hikvision cameras.

That’s despite a clear order from Joly over one-and-a-half years ago that she wanted all those devices out of every single federal government office.

“The silence actually to me is the story itself,” said Dennis Molinaro, a former federal national security analyst and author of Under Assault: Interference and Espionage in China’s Secret War Against Canada.

“The products are ordered out, and refusing to say … whether the cameras are actually removed undercuts the government’s own findings.”

In June 2025, Joly issued a federal ban on Hikvision Canada — a global leader in surveillance camera gear that is partly owned by the Chinese government — due to national security concerns. She gave the company 120 days to pack its bags and shut down its Canadian operation.

According to the minister, the company’s work in Canada created an unacceptable risk of espionage and mass surveillance which raised significant concerns among the federal security and intelligence community.

Hikvision is the most valuable manufacturer of surveillance equipment in the world, but also one of the most controversial. It is partly state-owned by the Chinese government and benefits from PRC subsidies that allow it to sell its equipment cheaper than most competitors.

Ottawa has new powers to ban Chinese telecom companies. It says it's not planning to use them

Huawei ban won't solve the problem of Chinese spying on Canada, experts say

But over the last decade, the company has been linked to multiple major cybersecurity vulnerabilities, allegedly used by the Chinese government for mass surveillance of Uyghurs and other minority groups, and has been blacklisted governments around the world over espionage concerns.

The ban also extended to federal departments, agencies and crown corporations, who were henceforth barred from purchasing or using any Hikvision equipment.

“The Government of Canada is further conducting a review of existing properties to ensure that legacy Hikvision products are not used going forward,” Joly said, all the while “strongly” encouraging Canadians to “take note of this decision and make their own decisions accordingly.”

Hikvision is currently challenging the ban in Federal Court and has dismissed the government’s claims as baseless and unfounded.

“Since entering the Canadian market, we have followed all applicable laws and regulations, and will continue to defend our position that Hikvision products and technology have not endangered the national security of Canada or any other country in which we operate,” Hikvision said in response to the June 2025 order .

In September 2025, a judge refused to temporarily suspend the application of the order pending a final judicial decision, citing the “serious public interest harms” linked to the national security risks posed by Hikvision.

According to a 2024 document tabled in Parliament, over a dozen federal departments and agencies declared using Hikvision gear. Many more said they had previously purchased or used equipment from the company but had since stopped, sometimes citing security concerns.

Contacted by National Post in recent weeks, the majority of the federal bodies who declared Hikvision gear on their properties in 2024 said they had complied with the June 2025 to remove the equipment. That included Justice Canada, Via Rail, Veteran Affairs Canada and the Military Police Complaints Commission.

But a slew of departments and agencies, including some who host troves of sensitive personal data such as Esdc or conduct classified research and work like the Canadian Space Agency, refused to say if they’d complied with the 2025 order.

In all cases, they pointed to Hikvision’s lawsuit against the government to justify their silence. Joly’s office also declined to comment for the same reason.

But more surprisingly to national security specialists is the fact that the National Research Council (NRC) and Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority continue to use such gear, in apparent violation of Joly’s 2025 order.

“The cameras referenced in the 2024 (document) remain in use at Wdba’s community office, which serves as a space for Wdba to share non-confidential information with the public. The cameras will no longer be in service as of November 2026,” said bridge authority spokesperson Heather Grondin.

In a statement, NRC spokesperson Pamela Pilon said the organization removed all Hikvision gear from its security systems in 2025, but continues to use them to monitor “non-sensitive experiments and work areas.”

“None of the Nrc’s remaining Hikvision cameras are connected to the internet or NRC networks,” Pilon said. “The cameras used in research will be eliminated this year.

Neither of those explanations satisfied Molinaro or Andrew Kirsch, a former Csis intelligence officer and founder of risk consultancy Kirsch Group.

“You’d like to think that if the government’s going to implement a ban, at the very least the government can follow it, right?,” Kirsch said.

“If it’s important enough for us to want to look at it, it May be important enough for someone else to want to look at,” Kirsch said.

For Molinaro, the Chinese government’s or hackers’ interests in espionage isn’t just towards classified or sensitive information. Seeing who May be transiting through a federal office, everyday conversations or finding out more about NRC experiments can all be extremely valuable to a foreign intelligence service.

Andrew Elvish, vice-president at Montreal-based security software firm Genetic, said that his company has essentially barred clients from connecting Hikvision hardware to their tech because of the risks.

“If you should wish to make a terrible technology decision, you will have to sign a waiver to hold us harmless when the sh-t hits the fan, as we believe it surely will, and (you) did that against our own financial interests,” Elvish said.

“These cameras, they’re not just cameras,” he continued. “They are computers, and … they are designed intentionally to be insecure computers on a network, so that they can gain a toehold.”

According to Sami Khoury, a recently-retired top government cybersecurity official, it would be “doable” but challenging to use such cameras in a safe way.

“If your networks are not properly segmented, you run the risk of the vulnerability being exploited indirectly,” he explained.

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives back in battleground Surrey on election trail
stories.summary: The B.C. Conservatives will spend their second consecutive day campaigning in Surrey, a critical battleground in the provincial election.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Interim leader of the British Columbia Conservatives Lorne Doerkson has swiftly dumped a candidate in the provincial election over online posts that the NDP called racist.

Doerkson said Thursday that the posts by Victoria-Beacon Hill candidate Joachim Agou cannot be tolerated and if he is elected, he will not be part of the Conservative caucus.

Agou’s ejection from the Conservative election slate was announced about 90 minutes after the man’s posts on social media platform X were highlighted by the NDP.

Although Agou’s account has now been deleted, screenshots shared by the NDP show him saying last year that a car that drove through a pro-Palestine protest “should have reversed” over the demonstrators.

He also shared a meme using an expletive to describe Pakistan.

Agou did not immediately respond to a requests for comment sent to his campaign.

The Conservative website describes Agou as a professional engineer and small-business owner with more than 15 years of experience in engineering research and industry.

His biography says he was born in France, studied in the United States and came to Canada is 2011.

He is also the interim vice-president of the Victoria Conservative Association.

Doerkson said in a statement that there is “no excuse” for the posts.

He told reporters at an event earlier in the day that he hadn’t seen the allegations, but he “of course” would never support the comments.

“Trust me when I say this, I’ll be looking into them the second I leave this podium.” he said about an hour before Agou’s removal was made public.

NDP candidate Amna Shah had shared the screenshots and called on Doerkson to fire Agou immediately for what she called “horrific racism.”

Victoria-Beacon Hill is consistently considered a safe NDP riding, with the party winning the seat in every provincial election since 2005.

A representative for Elections BC said in an email that they have not received notification of a withdrawal by Agou and he remains a candidate on the ballot, noting that the ballots for Victoria-Beacon Hill have already been printed.

Shah, who is running for re-election in Surrey City Centre, told a news conference after Abou was removed that Doerkson’s decision was the “bare minimum” in the circumstance.

She said there are questions about how the Conservatives choose their candidates.

“I think British Columbians are asking some very important questions. Why was this individual allowed to run for the B.C. Conservatives? Why was he not vetted? Why did they allow this individual to have such hateful views to thrive in their party?” she said.

Spencer Chandra Herbert, who is running for re-election for the NDP in Vancouver’s West End, told the news conference that the Conservatives have a double standard and are keeping a candidate who is homophobic.

Conservative candidate Heather Maahs, seeking re-election in Chilliwack was criticized by Chandra Herbert last week for a video where she describes stories of boys in homosexual relationships as “grooming” that desensitizes children.

Doerkson appeared on CTV’s Question Period earlier this month and said he did not share Maahs’ views but that she would remain in caucus.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Traveller costs must stay down in airport privatization plan: industry group
stories.summary: As aviation leaders descend on Ottawa for a conference today, the head of the country’s main airline industry group says any plan for private investment in airports should keep a lid on costs for travellers.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon is promising to keep a lid on fees charged by airports under the government’s partial privatization plan, as airline executives insist the rules must be in place before investors make their bids.

However, it remains unclear if the new approach will include across-the-board caps on landing fees and other charges or whether restrictions will be imposed on a deal-by-deal basis and in a more flexible fashion.

“We will regulate through contract,” MacKinnon told reporters at an aviation conference in Ottawa on Thursday.

“Those concessions will contain price moderation, if I can call it that, or fee moderation.”

Under the plan, private entities from pension funds to First Nations would be bidding on leases to run the full gamut of airport operations, rather than just portions of the airport facility, MacKinnon added.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced last month he wants investors to take over operations at Canada’s four largest airports — in Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver and Calgary — managing them for long-term lease periods while oversight and ownership would remain with the federal government.

However, airlines have warned that privatization in some countries has led to soaring aeronautical charges, costs that are then passed on to customers.

WestJet CEO Alexis von Hoensbroech said he’s seen “the good and the bad” of airport privatization.

“If you just privatize it and then you just let the market play out, it’s a risky game because a private investor will try to maximize the returns and an airport is a local monopoly,” he said in a sit-down interview.

“The temptation just to increase passenger fees would be really high,” he said, pointing to London’s Heathrow Airport as well as some Australian airports “where it has really gone in the wrong direction.”

The chief executive highlighted the “dual till” model in Austria, where he ran the country’s largest carrier before joining WestJet in 2021.

Under that regulatory framework, airport operations are split into two buckets: aeronautical and non-aeronautical.

For the former, which includes landing fees and passenger terminals, any fee hikes are based solely on the costs and capital investments on that side of the business, with a regulator’s approval required before charges can go up.

For non-aeronautical areas — retail, hotels, parking, real estate development — the operators have much freer reign.

“That’s why a European airport looks like a shopping centre and not like a bus station, because they invest a lot in this and that’s where they make all their money,” von Hoensbroech said.

He and other executives at the conference stressed the need for clarity on fee rules before Ottawa solicits any bids.

“The regulation needs to be decided before we do any tenders,” said Porter Airlines president Kevin Jackson.

A rules-first, bid-second sequence is essential to strategic planning for carriers, said Christopher Read, former director of corporate development at Air Canada.

“We need some more colour … You need to be able to effectively plan your business out,” he said.

“The devil is in the details. The devil is in the contract structure.”

MacKinnon acknowledged the government has spoken with potential stakeholders, but said no decision has been made around which of the four airports will transition to a private investment model first.

He did not take issue with a report from the Globe and Mail that the government is in talks with the Musqueam First Nation around privatizing Vancouver International Airport.

“I certainly acknowledge that there have been fulsome discussions, as you can imagine, whether it be major projects, reconciliation writ large, or this initiative,” MacKinnon said. “We’re in constant communication with relevant First Nations.”

Examples abroad offer mixed results, with Australia frequently cited by Ottawa after the country handed control of its airports to private investors between 1997 and 2003.

The move has resulted in billions of dollars in capital investment, yielding faster baggage handling and passenger check-in processes as well as more lounges.

However, Australia’s competition watchdog says the country’s four biggest airports boosted their airline fees by $1.6 billion or 81 per cent in the decade leading up to 2015. Many of those costs would have been passed on to travellers.

Canada already hosts “one of the world’s most expensive aviation markets” due to fees and taxes, said Peter Cerdá, regional vice-president for the Americas at the International Air Transport Association.

“A third of the cost of a domestic ticket never gets seen by the airline,” added Arielle Meloul-Wechsler, Air Canada’s head of human resources.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada is at risk of missing its emission goals, climate report says
stories.summary: Climate policy changes and focus on major infrastructure development could put goals further out of reach, report co-author says
stories.author: Joy SpearChief-Morris
stories.content:
Less-stringent climate policy and a push to develop carbon-intensive major projects could put Canada’s greenhouse gas targets further out of reach, according to a co-author of a new report on the country’s emissions.

Canada emitted around 691 megatonnes of carbon-dioxide equivalent in 2025, about 1 per cent more than 2024 levels, according to the 440 Megatonnes project report conducted by the Canadian Climate Institute, a non-partisan climate change policy research organization.

With climate policy changes at federal and provincial levels and Ottawa’s focus on major infrastructure development to bolster the economy to deal with the U.S. trade war, Canada will need to take more direct action to achieve its goal of net-zero emissions by 2050.

“There’s no question at the federal and the provincial level, governments have backtracked on climate policies, and we expect that to lead to higher emissions. The government has acknowledged that openly,” said Ross Linden-Fraser, acting director of the 440 Megatonnes project at the Climate Institute.

Canada’s 2025 carbon emission levels were about 9.5 per cent below the 2005 baseline levels, and are well short of the goal of a 40 to 45 per cent reduction target for 2030, a gap of about 200 megatonnes, according to the estimates in the early emissions report released on Thursday.

The biggest contributors to the 2025 increase in greenhouse gases were from the building sector, where emissions jumped 6 per cent, and power generation, up 5 per cent compared with 2024.

“Our building sector is still really reliant on natural gas, so when the temperatures drop, and 2025 was a colder year than 2024, our gas use and our emissions go up significantly,” Mr. Linden-Fraser said.

In comparison, oil and gas – Canada’s highest emitters – remained essentially flat, while other sectors made scant progress at cutting carbon dioxide.

The November, 2025, memorandum of understanding announced by Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith envisions Ottawa backing Alberta’s proposal for a one-million-barrel-a-day pipeline to the Pacific Coast in exchange for dozens of provisions to lessen the environmental impact of the province’s energy sector.

Opinion: Not addressing climate change costs the economy more. When will we finally get this?

The subsequent implementation agreement included changes to the industrial carbon pricing system, which is designed to incentivize industries to install electrified technologies. However, the changes did not fix existing issues, such as an oversupply of carbon credits and low demand, Mr. Linden-Fraser said.

“The result is that industries, which particularly in Alberta are the main source of emissions, will not have enough incentive to reduce their emissions,” he said.

Mr. Carney’s most recent policy moves with Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act, would see a reduction in consultation and approval time frames down to one year when fast-tracking major projects. However, Mr. Linden-Fraser said it is too soon to see how Mr. Carney’s climate and economic policies will affect carbon emissions.

He added the institute has done projections suggesting the potential impacts of those policies on Canada’s emission goals “and it’s nowhere near enough to get us on track to net-zero emissions.”

Canada’s best chance of getting back on track, is through clean electrification, the report stated.

But that involves breaking “20 years of history in which we’ve barely electrified at all,” Mr. Linden-Fraser said.

Canada’s electricity generation has only risen 3 per cent since 2005. In the same time period, natural gas use, not for power generation, has risen by 48 per cent.

Growth in non-emitting renewable energy generation has been negatively impacted by climate change with droughts reducing hydro production. Refurbishments to some nuclear power plants have also taken them offline.

As a result, the report found Canada’s electrical production “is less green than it was just five years ago,” down to 80 per cent of the total from 84 per cent in 2024.

Canada has made commitments to double its electrical generation by 2050 and recently announced a $10-billion investment in upgrading Churchill Falls hydroelectrical plant in Labrador to increase clean electrical generation.

“But it’s when we look at the overall picture that we’re not seeing enough progress,” Mr. Linden-Fraser said.

The early emissions data reinforces 440 Megatonnes’ previous study from September , which found the country is 20 years behind its 2030 emissions target goals, part of Canada’s commitment to reach net-zero emissions by 2050 under the Paris Agreement.

stories.title: Operation impact 2026
stories.summary: London, ON (October 8, 2026) – As Canadians prepare to travel over the Thanksgiving long weekend, the London Police Service (LPS) will join services across the country in Operation Impact 2026, a national public awareness and traffic enforcement campaign focused on reducing preventable collisions, injuries and deaths on Canada's roads. Through education and…
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 8, 2026) – As Canadians prepare to travel over the Thanksgiving long weekend, the London Police Service (LPS) will join services across the country in Operation Impact 2026, a national public awareness and traffic enforcement campaign focused on reducing preventable collisions, injuries and deaths on Canada's roads. Through education and enforcement, LPS officers will do their part to help ensure everyone reaches their destination safely.

Taking place from October 9 to 12, 2026, Operation Impact encourages all road users to make safe, responsible choices behind the wheel. This year's campaign theme, "Safety is in Your hands," highlights the important role every driver plays in helping keep Canada's roads safe.

Recent police-reported data demonstrates the continued need for education, awareness and enforcement. In 2025, police services across Canada reported more than 123,000 Criminal Code traffic offences, including nearly 67,400 alcohol- and drug-impaired driving offences, while hundreds of collisions causing bodily harm involved alcohol or drug impairment (Statistics Canada). Dangerous driving contributed to 139 fatal collisions and 556 collisions causing bodily harm .

Whether travelling across the country or just across town, drivers are encouraged to plan ahead, drive sober, avoid distractions, obey posted speed limits, remain alert and well-rested, and ensure everyone in the vehicle is properly buckled up.

“Every serious collision leaves a lasting impact on families and our community. This long weekend, our officers will be watching for the driving behaviours that put people at risk. Slow down, stay focused, drive sober, and buckle up. Your choices can save a life,” said Staff Sgt. Anderson of the London Police Service’s Road Safety Section.

This Thanksgiving, help everyone get home safely. Safety is in Your hands.

stories.title: Toronto trucker says he shipped cocaine for Ryan Wedding to settle $300,000 gambling debts
stories.summary: Rakhim Ibragimov, 49, said he transported cocaine on behalf of Ryan Wedding in a desperate attempt to escape a gambling addiction.
stories.author: Calvi Leon
stories.content:
A Toronto courier says he agreed to travel to the U.S. to transport a large cocaine shipment on behalf of alleged drug kingpin Ryan Wedding in a desperate attempt to settle over $300,000 in gambling debts, a California court heard before his sentencing Wednesday.

In an apologetic plea to a federal judge, 49-year-old Rakhim Ibragimov said he took full responsibility for travelling from Toronto to Los Angeles in April 2024 to help smuggle cocaine into Canada. Before his gambling addiction took over his life, he was a law-abiding citizen who worked hard to take care of his wife and two children, he wrote in a letter.

“I was not perfect, but I worked, supported my family, and tried to provide the best life I could.”

Drowning in debt, he “became desperate … Instead of admitting that I had a problem and asking for help, I tried to fix it myself. That led me to make the worst decision of my life.”

On Wednesday, Sherilyn Peace Garnett of the U.S. District Court in Los Angeles sentenced him to a little more than five and a half years in prison for his role in the high-profile case targeting the former Olympian Wedding and his alleged drug network. Upon his release, Ibragimov will be deported to Canada and subject to three years of supervision with conditions that include participating in counselling.

The Uzbekistan-born Canadian previously pleaded guilty to one federal felony count of conspiracy to distribute cocaine. The remaining counts were dismissed.

His sentencing comes two years after the FBI and RCMP first identified Wedding as the alleged leader of a transnational operation responsible for moving hundreds of millions of dollars of cartel-linked cocaine from the Mexican border through California safe houses and into Canada. Authorities claim the so-called “Wedding Criminal Enterprise” was behind several execution-style murders — four in Ontario. Two of those victims, a middle-aged couple , were mistakenly targeted in November 2023 in retaliation for a stolen drug shipment. The hit men are still at large.

The years-long investigation into the cocaine empire led to two sweeping federal U.S. indictments charging dozens of people and culminated in the arrest of Wedding in Mexico last January.

Prosecutors said a pair of Ontario-based transporters , Hardeep Ratte and Gurpreet Singh , oversaw a transportation network that could deliver cocaine from Southern California to Canada. In Spring of 2024, the men allegedly struck a deal with Wedding’s associates — including a dispatcher turned confidential witness , who was later murdered — to import as much as 1,800 kilos.

U.S. authorities have said the larger cocaine scheme brought in revenues of a billion dollars a year; before his arrest, Wedding amassed luxuries including an ultra-rare $13-million Mercedes supercar and a collection of historic Ducati MotoGP racing motorcycles — the equivalent of Ferrari Formula 1 cars.

Ibragimov, known by the aliases “George” and the “Russian,” was the courier sent to Riverside, California, to pick up the drugs on April 9, 2024, according to an agreed statement of facts.

American authorities said the 62-high end motorcycles that were seized in Mexico this month are believed to be owned by Wedding, who remains at

Just as he and a co-conspirator started transferring boxes containing 375.1 kilograms of cocaine into his car, authorities intercepted the load and handcuffed both men, the statement said. He was released on a promise to appear soon after and returned to Canada.

In October 2024, Ibragimov was apprehended again — this time in Toronto on federal U.S. charges, along with other co-defendants in the case. He consented to the U.S. transfer last year and pleaded guilty to one felony charge in July.

The five-and-a-half-year sentence falls in between the requests by the prosecution and defence. The judge also indicated Ibragimov will receive credit for time spent in Canadian custody.

Prosecutors recommended that he serve eight, pointing to his lack of prior criminal history, his consent to extradition and his personal hardships as mitigating factors.

Defence attorney Humberto Diaz asked for just two and a half years. In court filings, he said Ibragimov was just a drug runner and nothing more, and was enticed to participate by people who took advantage of his financial situation, Diaz argued.

Defence filings and several character letters submitted to court describe Ibragimov as a compassionate, hardworking, gentle and devoted family man.

They say he was born in 1977 in Uzbekistan, and raised in both Russian and Uyghur cultures. Growing up after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, the filings say, his life became extremely difficult and unaffordable, and local gang violence was rampant.

In 1999, Ibragimov came to Canada as a refugee, staying at a Toronto shelter before finding housing in a mostly Russian-speaking neighbourhood. He went on to obtain permanent residency and eventually Canadian citizenship.

The drawing by Rakhim Ibragimov’s daughter.

Ibragimov worked various jobs; first at a factory painting doors, then as a baker at Tim Hortons, and later as a ready-mix concrete truck driver. Confronted with health issues from the role, he became a broker in that industry.

It was the beginning of 2017 when he developed a gambling addiction. His winnings only fuelled it more. At one point, in an attempt to overcome his dependency, he signed up for a voluntary self-exclusion ban at Toronto’s casino. It didn’t last long — his filing says he would instead drive to the casino in Niagara Falls, New York.

While his gambling addiction explains how he was lured by the prospect of making large sums of cash by working for an international drug transportation network, the filings say, “it does not excuse what I did.”

Ibragimov’s kids themselves asked the judge for leniency; his 12-year-old daughter submitted a hand-drawn family portrait as his 16-year-old son shared a personal account of his relationship with his dad.

“My dad is a good person who always took the time out of his day to help others and our family,” he said.

In an apologetic plea to a federal judge, 49-year-old Rakhim Ibragimov said he took full responsibility for travelling from Toronto to Los Angeles in April 2024 to help smuggle cocaine into Canada. Before his gambling addiction took over his life, he was a law-abiding citizen who worked hard to take care of his wife and two children, he wrote in a letter.
“I was not perfect, but I worked, supported my family, and tried to provide the best life I could.”
Drowning in debt, he “became desperate … Instead of admitting that I had a problem and asking for help, I tried to fix it myself. That led me to make the worst decision of my life.”

On Wednesday, Sherilyn Peace Garnett of the U.S. District Court in Los Angeles sentenced him to a little more than five and a half years in prison for his role in the high-profile case targeting the former Olympian Wedding and his alleged drug network. Upon his release, Ibragimov will be deported to Canada and subject to three years of supervision with conditions that include participating in counselling.
The Uzbekistan-born Canadian previously pleaded guilty to one federal felony count of conspiracy to distribute cocaine. The remaining counts were dismissed.

His sentencing comes two years after the FBI and RCMP first identified Wedding as the alleged leader of a transnational operation responsible for moving hundreds of millions of dollars of cartel-linked cocaine from the Mexican border through California safe houses and into Canada. Authorities claim the so-called “Wedding Criminal Enterprise” was behind several execution-style murders — four in Ontario. Two of those victims, a middle-aged couple , were mistakenly targeted in November 2023 in retaliation for a stolen drug shipment. The hit men are still at large.
The years-long investigation into the cocaine empire led to two sweeping federal U.S. indictments charging dozens of people and culminated in the arrest of Wedding in Mexico last January.

Prosecutors said a pair of Ontario-based transporters , Hardeep Ratte and Gurpreet Singh , oversaw a transportation network that could deliver cocaine from Southern California to Canada. In Spring of 2024, the men allegedly struck a deal with Wedding’s associates — including a dispatcher turned confidential witness , who was later murdered — to import as much as 1,800 kilos.

U.S. authorities have said the larger cocaine scheme brought in revenues of a billion dollars a year; before his arrest, Wedding amassed luxuries including an ultra-rare $13-million Mercedes supercar and a collection of historic Ducati MotoGP racing motorcycles — the equivalent of Ferrari Formula 1 cars.

stories.title: Update from the unsanctioned street party task force
stories.summary: London, ON (October 8, 2026) – The London Police Service worked alongside the City of London Emergency Management and community partners throughout the last weekend of September to respond to unsanctioned gatherings in several areas, including Broughdale Avenue, Huron Street, Richmond Street and Mill Street.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 8, 2026) – The London Police Service worked alongside the City of London Emergency Management and community partners throughout the last weekend of September to respond to unsanctioned gatherings in several areas, including Broughdale Avenue, Huron Street, Richmond Street and Mill Street.

An estimated 15,000 people attended the gatherings on Saturday, with approximately 5,000 remaining into the evening. The attendance prompted several traffic measures to support public safety, including the closure of Broughdale Avenue and Huron Street, as well as lane reductions on Richmond Street.

“Most young adults we encountered cooperated with emergency services and partner agencies. Downtown bars reached capacity, and sidewalks remained busy as people enjoyed the warm weather into the evening. At times, people moved from the sidewalks onto roadways, disrupting traffic. Officers responded to maintain public safety,” said Superintendent Bill Berg of the London Police Service.

Enforcement teams from the London Police Service, City of London Municipal Compliance and London Fire Inspectors were deployed before and throughout the weekend. They issued 248 Administrative Monetary Penalties (AMPs) and Provincial Offence Notices (PON) for public nuisance parties, liquor-related offenses, excessive noise and parking violations. Police also made three arrests for public intoxication.

Officers issued multiple verbal warnings while managing the crowds and helping to maintain public safety for attendees, community members, and emergency personnel.

Middlesex-London Paramedic Service reported that their members recorded 23 calls for service and 14 transports related to Saturday’s unsanctioned gatherings.

The London Police Service would like to thank its members and all the task force partners for their assistance throughout the weekend, including City of London staff, City of London Emergency Management, Municipal Compliance and By-law Enforcement officers, City of London Roads, Western University, Middlesex-London Paramedic Service, London Fire Department, London Health Sciences Centre, St. Joseph’s Health Care London, and officers from the Windsor Police Service, Hamilton Police Service and Ontario Provincial Police for their assistance in keeping London Safe.

stories.title: Temporary Richmond Street closure for rail crossing repairs
stories.summary: Cpkc Rail is completing repairs to the railway crossing on Richmond Stree
stories.content:
Cpkc Rail is completing repairs to the railway crossing on Richmond Street. Richmond Street will be closed between Mill Street and Piccadilly Street from Monday, October 12 to Friday, October 16.

This closure will have significant impacts for people travelling through the area. Vehicles, buses, and pedestrians will not be able to cross the railway tracks at Richmond Street during the closure.

Drivers and pedestrians are encouraged to plan ahead and allow extra time when travelling through the area.

A signed detour will direct drivers around the closure. Drivers should follow the posted detour signs and directions.

Trucks must not use the Talbot Street Bridge as an alternate route. The bridge has restrictions that make it unsuitable for truck traffic, so truck drivers must follow the signed detour and posted directions.

At Richmond Street and Oxford Street, southbound traffic will be reduced to one lane.

Businesses in the area will remain accessible. Drivers should follow signs and directions from crews.

The closure will affect London Transit (LTC) Routes 4, 6, 13, 15, 90, 102, 104 and 106, which will be on detour during the closure. Temporary and alternate bus stops will be in place.

For specific detour details, stop locations and updates, visit Ltc’s Richmond Street closure page .

For questions or concerns about the railway crossing work, contact Cpkc Community Connect at communityconnect@cpkcr.com .

stories.title: Colleagues mourn Ontario nurse aboard crashed air ambulance jet: ‘To know her was to love her’
stories.summary: Flight nurse Sarah Paton was one of six people on the Hamilton-based air ambulance jet that crashed early Saturday of the coast of Nantucket, Mass.
stories.author: Elissa Mendes
stories.content:
When she wasn’t on the job as a nurse, Sarah Paton was often cheering on the Buffalo Bills with her partner J.J. and dog Fulton, celebrating loved ones’ birthdays “with gusto” and baking treats for her colleagues and therapy animals.

The death of the registered nurse from Niagara, Ont., missing after a Hamilton-based Latitude Air Ambulance went down in the Atlantic Ocean last weekend , has shaken her colleagues in the Ontario Nurses’ Association.

Paton was the flight nurse aboard the Gulfstream G100 jet, which crashed in the early hours of Saturday during a routine medevac trip from Bermuda to Boston.

Also aboard the jet were three other Canadian crew : captain Philip Childerhose, first officer Thomas Farquhar and respiratory therapist Jolene Weir. A patient with an accompanying family member, both Bermudian nationals, were also aboard.

The pilots were last heard speaking to air traffic controllers shortly after 1 a.m. Saturday, soon after they made a swift descent of around 11,000 feet.

Latitude Air Ambulance captain Philip Childerhose, left, and first officer Thomas Farquhar are among the missing after the jet crashed over the Atlantic Ocean en route to Boston from Bermuda.

In recordings, a controller can be heard repeatedly asking the pilots if they wished to report an emergency, to no apparent response.

The U.S. Coast Guard ended its search of a debris field off the coast of Nantucket, Mass., late Sunday after pieces of the missing plane were spotted a night earlier. The Coast Guard said it had exhausted its efforts with planes, helicopters and boats and help from the U.S. National Guard.

According to the College of Nurses of Ontario, Paton had been a registered nurse since 2016, and she was also registered to work in New York state.

“There are no words to describe the devastation felt upon hearing the news that one of our own was on the flight,” the nurses’ association said in a post on social media .

Sarah Paton was the flight nurse aboard the Hamilton-based Latitude Air Ambulance jet that crashed in the Atlantic Ocean last weekend during a medevac flight from Bermuda to Boston.

Colleagues said Paton, who had worked in the emergency room at Welland Hospital and the Marotta Family Hospital ICU in St. Catharines, is remembered as boisterous and deeply kind.

“To know her was to love her,” colleagues said in the post, especially her nieces, nephews and the children of other ICU nurses who came to their annual camping trip.

“She was truly an amazing nurse, whose advocacy and dedication to helping others led her to medevac transport nursing — a job that she loved.”

The post added, “Her legacy will live on in every act of kindness and her spirit will always remind us to live our lives to the fullest.”

Peter Byl, president of Latitude Air Ambulance, said the missing crew members were “much more than names. They were colleagues, friends and members of our family.

“Each brought something special to our company, to the people they worked beside, and to the patients and families entrusted to their care,” Byl said in a statement earlier this week.

The U.S. Coast Guard searched for the missing Latitude Air Ambulance plane that went missing off the coast of Nantucket. The search has been called off.

The reason for the crash is not yet clear, and as Canada’s Transportation Safety Board (TSB) investigates and attempts to recover the bodies of those aboard, the large search area in international waters could prove challenging.

The Canadian safety board and U.S. National Transportation Safety Board have sent “a small team” of investigators to Massachusetts, TSB spokesperson Liam MacDonald confirmed Friday.

Once searchers find the aircraft, more investigators could be sent in and pieces of the aircraft May be analyzed further in an Ottawa lab, MacDonald said in an email.

“It is difficult to give an exact figure for how long any investigation can take,” MacDonald said, adding “it is not unusual for an investigation on this scale to take up to two years to complete.”

The TSB is hoping to announce preliminary findings within 30 days, he said.

But, he added, if the investigation uncovers any safety concerns, “we will not wait to complete our investigation,” and the TSB would immediately inform stakeholders of any risks.

Latitude said it will co-operate fully with all authorities investigating the flight and with recovery efforts, including the TSB and the United States’ Transportation Safety Board.

stories.title: Bruce Arthur: Elon Musk loves Canadian separatism. He could help further unite our country
stories.summary: What a week for the idea of breaking Canada apart. Quebec doesn’t want a separation referendum at the moment, but had enough of a multi-party electoral logjam that the Parti
stories.author: Bruce Arthur
stories.content:
What a week for the idea of breaking Canada apart. Quebec doesn’t want a separation referendum at the moment, but had enough of a multi-party electoral logjam that the Parti Québécois won a minority government . The Globe and Mail delivered reporting which included motley Albertan separatists offering up the province’s oil and water reserves in meetings with American officials. Yowza.

Even Alberta Premier Danielle Smith didn’t like that idea. Selling out the country is not, as it turns out, a popular position.

And to Canada’s rescue came Elon Musk: the richest man in the world, the man whose destruction of Usaid could potentially lead to as many as 14 million global deaths by 2030 , and a man with a very large microphone. He bought Twitter in 2022 and renamed it X in what seemed like a fit of debauched, over-leveraged pique, and has turned it into a brain-warping engine for right-wing gunk, among other things.

And Wednesday, Musk used his tool to push his agenda. The gambling company Polymarket tweets news without attribution as a means of juicing engagement with the brand, and wrote, “Just IN: Quebec’s new premier declares his dream of Québécois independence ‘will be realized one day.’ ” Musk, who has some 240 million followers, replied, “Good. Quebec should separate.” He added, “They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too.”

“It’s exceptionally important that all elections that are held in Canada and all votes are held are free and fair,” the prime minister said.

Some of the more prominent Alberta separatists replied, along others: organizer David Parker, Twitter influencer Martyupnorth, anti-trans activist Chris Elston. The occasional Quebecois replied, too. Smith did her usual unconvincing federalist dance in response; to his credit, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe simply said, “No.”

Look, it’s easy to make fun of Alberta separatists. Some of them are caught up in potential legal trouble , or mind-boggling alleged financial boondoggles . As the Star’s Richard Warnica chronicled , they are often terrifyingly deluded. And based on all available public polling, they are going to lose.

And Quebec’s new government, meanwhile, has pledged not to hold a sovereignty referendum — which they would almost certainly lose — while U.S. President Donald Trump remains in office. Which is comforting enough, until you remember that they reportedly approached the Trump administration for talks during the campaign. It’s not comforting.

So thank goodness for Musk’s signal, because it both illuminates the stakes and helps influence them. Musk has endorsed both Germany’s far-right AfD and the National Rally in France, both of which have links to Russian money; he pushed the far-right Reform party in the U.K. until they allegedly weren’t quite radical enough for him in relation to Tommy Robinson’s vicious anti-immigrant movement, which has included Canadian Ezra Levant, who runs the far-right website Rebel News. Musk prefers Restore Britain now, and retweeted Levant the other day.

Spain’s far-right party, Vox? Musk likes them. Greece’s neo-Nazi Golden Dawn? Yep. Javier Milei in Argentina? Milei and Musk both brandished chainsaws on stage. Bolsonarism in Brazil? Definitely, both before and after the attempted coup in 2022-23. El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele? Of course.

The rise of the far right is fuelled by a scapegoating of the other, a parallel universe of exaggerated or imagined grievance, and a deep distrust of the state. It is also being encouraged by Trump’s State Department, which has changed its focus from democracy and human rights to far-right causes which encourage the reverse .

This is a war on democracy, using its tools, and Canada’s democratic immune system has worked as intended, so far. As a nation, Canada trusted government advice on vaccines and public safety, writ large; the election of Mark Carney was a clear signal that this moment in history required a certain seriousness of purpose in the face of Trump. It’s an awful lot to entrust to one man, a country. But electing Pierre Poilievre with what was then a rather Trump-friendly Conservative base — that CPC Trump support has eroded, thankfully — would have been a disaster.

Musk, meanwhile, is widely loathed here. An Angus Reid poll last year showed 79 per cent of Canadians viewed him negatively , including a whopping 84 per cent of Quebecers; even among Conservative voters, Musk’s favourability was only 34 per cent. The only person more likely to inflame Canadian patriotism is Trump, who gave Musk the National Medal of Science on Thursday.

We should, however, give a moment to ponder the stakes, and why Canadians have responded the way we have. Trump’s brute imperialism aims for control of oil and the Western Hemisphere, at the minimum, and Alberta has both. Foreign interference abounds . The convoy’s March on Ottawa was the impetus for talk in American right-wing circles about invading Canada in order to save it, in 2023 . Both Trump and Musk are trying to push far-right policies that are cancerous for the human soul. The old world is dying and the new one struggles to be born and now is the time of monsters, and all that.

And somehow, Canada hasn’t been this united since the last great crisis, separatists and all, and Musk should help that along nicely. May it be ever thus.

stories.title: Hanover shooting leaves man injured, suspect charged with attempted murder
stories.summary: Hanover police say a 50-year-old man has been charged with attempted murder after a shooting in the community Tuesday.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Hanover police say a 50-year-old man has been charged with attempted murder after a shooting in the community Tuesday.

Police were called shortly before noon Oct. 6 to a residence in the 300 block of 14th Avenue, where a 37-year-old man had been shot.

The victim was taken to hospital and remains in stable condition while recovering from his injuries.

Police say the victim and the accused, Joel Stephenson, were known to each other and had been involved in a dispute shortly before the shooting.

Stephenson was arrested shortly after the incident and faces one count of attempted murder using a firearm and two counts of possession of a firearm or ammunition contrary to a prohibition order.

He was remanded into custody following a bail hearing Wednesday and is scheduled to appear in Ontario Court of Justice in Walkerton on Oct. 8.

Investigators continue to examine the scene, interview witnesses and collect evidence.

Police say several identified witnesses have yet to speak with investigators and are encouraging them to come forward.

As with all criminal charges, the allegations have not been proven in court.

stories.title: Steven Galloway says his accuser fabricated details of three sexual assault allegations
stories.summary: Novelist and former UBC professor addresses alleged incidents on his sailboat and in his office
stories.author: Mike Hager
stories.content:
Bestselling author Steven Galloway told court Wednesday allegations that he sexually assaulted a former student three times were pure fiction and that he didn’t learn of the details until after he was suspended as head of the creative writing program at the University of British Columbia.

After nearly 11 years, Mr. Galloway testified in open court about the allegations as part of a defamation case he brought against the woman, with whom he had a two-year affair, and three others he accuses of defaming him. He called the allegations “absolutely” false.

“I was shocked to find she was saying that,” he testified.

Mr. Galloway was suspended by UBC in November, 2015 and the university’s public announcement of the “serious allegations” against him was highly publicized. It roiled the Canadian literary community for years and the author maintains it cost him his reputation and his livelihood.

His defamation suit originally included almost two dozen defendants, most of whom settled. The woman who made the allegations, known as A.B. because of a publication ban on her name, is joined as a defendant by three others.

The trial will not hear testimony from A.B. Her lawyer, Arden Beddoes, has told court she withdraws her defences of truth and fair comment, but does not admit to spreading lies about her former romantic partner. Mr. Beddoes has said A.B. has twice tried to kill herself in recent months because of the stress of the lawsuit.

Court heard Wednesday about three instances in which A.B. alleged that she was sexually assaulted.

In the first, she said Mr. Galloway invited her to play a daytime game of cards on his 30-foot sailboat at his False Creek marina in the spring of 2011. She alleged he grabbed her by the throat, kissed her and threw her up against the bed in the bow when she tried to escape. She said she later managed to leave the vessel.

The woman alleged he said to her: “See, that wasn’t so bad.”

Mr. Galloway said this incident was a fabrication.

“That never happened, there was never a day in March of 2011 that we went to that boat,” he testified. “It’s hard to know how to dismantle it because the entire story is just fictional there aren’t facts to dispute.”

He told the court that if he had thrown the woman through the small opening to the berth, he would have injured her badly.

He also testified that later in their affair she asked him to stay on his boat because her husband’s violent relative was coming to stay at their house.

“It’s inconceivable that a person who reported thinking she was going to be murdered and thrown overboard would speak of the boat in subsequent years as a safe space,” he said.

In the second incident, the court heard that A.B. said she got drunk on tequila shots bought by Mr. Galloway at a creative writing program party. He then offered her a ride home but first said he wanted to go to his office to change out of his party clothes.

The court also heard A.B. told Mary Ellen Boyd, the retired judge hired by UBC to look into the matter, that she remembers him straddling over her with his penis exposed and after she objected, he backed off.

Mr. Galloway testified that he didn’t think he offered to drive her home as they lived in opposite directions, but he did recall going back to his office where they had sex “with full consent from both parties.”

In a third incident, A.B. alleged that prior to a scheduled reading on campus by the author Miriam Toews in May, 2011, she found herself naked and hunched on the floor in Mr. Galloway’s office. He had had sex with her and was watching a hockey game on his computer, she told Ms. Boyd.

But Mr. Galloway testified he was not in the room and text messages shown in court indicated that at that time he was watching the game at a campus pub.

Court heard Ms. Boyd found Mr. Galloway had sexually harassed A.B. because of the power differential between the two of them and A.B.’s belief that opportunities in the creative writing program were tied to their sexual relationship.

But Mr. Galloway testified he became program chair after their relationship ended in 2013 and that any power imbalance between them was “extremely minor.”

He said that during his 10-hour interview with Ms. Boyd, only about 10 minutes was spent on the sexual harassment allegation. He said his main focus was refuting the sexual assault allegations.

stories.title: Vancouver airport first candidate for private investment, sources say
stories.summary: YVR earned first spot in line because Ottawa and its advisers expect First Nations to take a minority stake
stories.author: Andrew Willis, James Bradshaw, Bill Curry

Vancouver International Airport is poised to become the first of the country’s large airports privatized by the federal government, as Ottawa’s advisers offer British Columbia Indigenous groups an opportunity to be minority investors, four sources say.

Three weeks after Prime Minister Mark Carney announced plans to open up four of the country’s biggest airports to private investment, the bankers and lawyers advising Ottawa have decided Vancouver’s airport, known in the industry as YVR, should be the first facility where a long-term lease on its ground operations is sold to outside investors, according to the sources, who are involved in the process.

YVR earned first spot in line because the government and its advisers expect to land First Nations investment, the sources said. The Globe and Mail is not naming the sources because they are not permitted to speak for their employers.

Mr. Carney made the privatization pitch during September’s investment summit in downtown Toronto, where he gathered executives with the goal of drawing new capital to Canada and reframing the country’s approach to investment. But the plan has raised concerns about the potential for increased prices for travellers and higher fees for airlines.

Along with YVR, the federal government plans to sell leases to run all or part of Calgary, Toronto and Montreal’s airports. The federal government will retain ownership of the underlying land and assets, a structure that is common in Europe and Australia.

Indigenous investors are expected to take a minority stake of up to 20 per cent in YVR, two of the sources said, with majority control sold to institutional investors experienced in operating these complex facilities. Leading candidates for this role are large domestic pension plans such as the Public Sector Pension Investment Board, known as PSP Investments, which already operates airports in Europe and Puerto Rico.

The federal government and its advisers want Indigenous investment in YVR and other airports as part of a strategy to promote reconciliation and address concerns that privatizing operations will mean handing control to faceless asset managers, or foreign airport operators.

The government’s airport privatization process is in its early stages, and the timing and structure of investments could change, according to the four sources.

Indigenous investors listening to pitches for stakes in YVR include the Musqueam First Nation, two of the sources said. The airport, located in the Vancouver suburb of Richmond, is on the Musqueam’s unceded territory.

Last year, the First Nation struck a revenue-sharing agreement with the federal government on YVR, the country’s second-busiest airport.

On Wednesday, Musqueam chief administrative officer Robyn McVicker said the First Nation wants a role in Yvr’s future.

“Following the Prime Minister’s announcement at the Canada Investment Summit, Musqueam indicated to government that any discussion and plans about the future of YVR must include meaningful participation by Musqueam Indian Band,” said Ms. McVicker in an e-mail. She said: “At this time, it would be premature to discuss any negotiations.”

Ottawa’s advisers have also reached out to MST Development Corp., a Vancouver-based real estate company backed by three First Nations – the Musqueam, Squamish and Tsleil-Waututh – according to one of the sources.

MST owns a $3-billion property portfolio. CEO David Negrin has attended two fundraisers for Mr. Carney over the past two years. MST did not respond to a request for comment.

On Wednesday, Ministry of Transport spokesperson Marie-Justine Torres said the government is working on plans to bring private investment into airports “in partnership with Indigenous groups.”

“There are more important steps ahead, and details will be developed in the coming months working with the airport authorities,” said Ms. Torres.

Canada’s airports are run by non-profit companies that pay rent to the government and fund operations through a host of fees charged to users, including passengers, airlines, restaurants and shops.

YVR spokesperson Stephen Smart said in an e-mail that “YVR will continue to engage with the Government of Canada, as well as with Musqueam, given our unique relationship.”

At the Canada Investment Summit in September, Mr. Carney made signing operational contracts for airports a key part of his pitch to many of the world’s largest asset managers.

“We, as a government, will be able to get tens of billions of dollars of proceeds from this process,” Mr. Carney said at the time.

The Prime Minister also said Canada intends to draw on the experience of other countries throughout the process – and learn from the pension funds and others who already own airports.

After Mr. Carney’s announcement, Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said the government would partially regulate airport fares and fees after privatization. He did not rule out costs rising for travellers.

An executive at the International Air Transport Association told The Globe last month that major airlines oppose the plan , warning it would drive up fees paid by the airlines, which would be forced to pass on the higher costs to travellers.

On Wednesday, a report from the University of Calgary’s economics department said the government needs to set the rules on airport operations before inviting offers from institutional investors.

The country’s four largest airports could fetch between $12-billion and $29-billion, according the report’s author, economist Aidan Hollis. In the report, he said: “That range is not a fact about airports, it is a bet on how they will be regulated.”

Putting passenger-friendly regulations in place “will determine both what users pay and what the airports are worth,” Dr. Hollis said.

Canada’s airport authorities have long pushed for the federal government to reinvest the rent it receives from airports. Since the 1990s, the airports have paid a cumulative total of $8.4-billion in rent to the government, including $556-million in 2025, while spending more than $30-billion in infrastructure and improvements.

stories.title: Sports Notes: London Alliance FC at Nationals, Knights need better starts, PCI wins Wossaa golf in dramatic finish and Panther Day features Western Mustangs
stories.summary: London Alliance FC is looking to bring home a National title to go along with their five consecutive Ontario Cup championships.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
London Alliance FC is looking to bring home a National title to go along with their five consecutive Ontario Cup championships.

The 15U squad represents Ontario in Surrey, BC.

“It’s a group that has been very talented since a young age,” said Luigi Sorbara, head coach of the 2011 born squad.

The girls arrived in Surrey Tuesday after having their early morning flight cancelled, but managed to get a training session in before play started Wednesday afternoon against Halifax.

“It’s a pretty grueling tournament,” added Sorbara.

Chip-in on 2nd playoff hole to win wossaa gold

Preston Gryp knew he had to chip in from off the green to have a chance to win the gold medal.

The Parkside Collegiate student won the Wossaa golf championship at St. Thomas Golf and Country Club in dramatic fashion.

All three of them made bogey on the difficult first hole, so it was off to #18.

Watt made a five to finish third, while Gryp hit his second shot near the front bunker. Bosma nearly holed out from over 100 yards and sat just about six feet for birdie.

Gryp knew he had to make the shot, and chipped in from off the green. Bosma lipped out his putt giving Gryp the individual title.

“I had a wedge in and I was kind of a in between number and I hit it came up just a little short,” said Gryp, one of three players to shoot 76 (+4) on a windy day.

“Jacob threw one in tight and I knew I probably had to chip in for the win. Maybe a little lucky, but I’m happy with the shot I hit.”

“I hit one so close and it just lipped out then just missed for birdie and made the par. It’ll be super fun (Ofsaa) going with everyone.”

London knights need better starts

The London Knights are 4-1 to start the season, good enough for top spot in the Midwest Division of the Ontario Hockey League. They have managed to achieve that record, despite not scoring a single goal in the first period of any of their five matches.

“Even off ice, just making sure you’re showing up to the rink to get all your preparation you need to be ready to go. So just getting the legs into a little earlier and maybe in the gym before if you need to get a little workout in just to get that extra juice and legs for the first period.”

Knights staff have been preaching taking a professional mentality pregame to be ready from the opening faceoff, but attribute some of their slow starts to their style of play.

“We don’t send two-one-twos (formations), we do a one-two-two,” said Dylan Hunter, Knights assistant coach.

“it’s more about getting the puck in deep, getting shots on that when you get them and then trying to get them out of sorts on their system,” said Hunter.

“We’re trying to make a quick play and then making a nice little sauce pass and you know that takes a little bit of timing.”

Panther day celebrates girls hockey in st. Thomas, ont.

The third annual Panther Day in St. Thomas, Ont. was a celebration of community spirit and girls hockey.

A full day of action started with girls games in the morning and continued on both ice pads all the way through the evening and was capped off by an exhibition game between the Western Mustangs and Guelph Gryphons .

“The big difference this year is on and off the ice,” said Panthers coach and spokesperson Jessie Karn.

“We’re taking donations at the door, the rink is entirely pink and as well for our game day fit. All the Panthers have pink t-shirts for their warm up, but then also on the ice they have their jerseys as well.”

The day was in support of breast cancer awareness and the mammography unit of St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital.

“It’s about awareness at a young age and also caring and love,” said Karn.

“At the end of the day, everyone can feel united as one and that’s what the community is all about.”

During the day, the Mustangs players were around the arena taking photos with the young girls before playing their game.

“I love this stuff,” said Emma Campbell, Mustangs captain.

“I talked to a couple of girls and we would have loved having this as kids. Like seeing girls like to look up to, I actually think I really believe if you can see it, you can be it. It sounds cheesy, but it is really true and it really is a community event. There are girls who have their little brothers, and their parents and grandparents out to support them. As someone who’s been playing the game for almost 20 years now, it really reignites the fire and the passion.”

The Mustangs also featured some local ties during the game with head coach Brittany Howard and starting rookie goalkeeper Mya Hepburn from St. Thomas.

“The eight new girls that we have, have been absolutely amazing so far,” said Campbell.

“With Britt (Howard) having a full year under her belt now coming in this year, really like having time to get her bearings and get everything going, we’re so excited. We’ve been learning a lot as a group and we’re super excited to get the season going.”

Rising stars brings mma, boxing and kickboxing under one roof

For the first time in London fighting history, Mixed Martial Arts, Boxing and Kickboxing all came together under one roof at the latest Rising Stars event at 100 Kellogg Lane. The collaboration between Adrenaline MMA and Boomerz Boxing was a massive hit with more than 1,000 people attending the sold out show.

“There were electric fights, and the production spoke for itself,” said promoter Chris Horodecki of Adrenaline MMA.

They also recognized two legendary coaches in the local fighting community.

“We respect the coaches, we honour the coaches and we pay tribute to our fallen leaders,” said Horodecki.

“Shawn Tompkins and Lawrence Boom, we had a moment of silence and a ten-bell salute honouring those who paved the path before us. We’re doing something bigger than just putting on fights, we’re instilling the martial arts in the fighters and instilling the martial arts attitude in our product.”

Rising stars brings mma, boxing and kickboxing under one roof

For the first time in London fighting history, Mixed Martial Arts, Boxing and Kickboxing all came together under one roof at the latest Rising Stars event at 100 Kellogg Lane. The collaboration between Adrenaline MMA and Boomerz Boxing was a massive hit with more than 1,000 people attending the sold out show.
“There were electric fights, and the production spoke for itself,” said promoter Chris Horodecki of Adrenaline MMA.
They also recognized two legendary coaches in the local fighting community.
“We respect the coaches, we honour the coaches and we pay tribute to our fallen leaders,” said Horodecki.

“Shawn Tompkins and Lawrence Boom, we had a moment of silence and a ten-bell salute honouring those who paved the path before us. We’re doing something bigger than just putting on fights, we’re instilling the martial arts in the fighters and instilling the martial arts attitude in our product.”

content_blocks.text: London Alliance FC is looking to bring home a National title to go along with their five consecutive Ontario Cup championships.
The 15U squad represents Ontario in Surrey, BC.
“It’s a group that has been very talented since a young age,” said Luigi Sorbara, head coach of the 2011 born squad.

content_blocks.caption: London Alliance FC 15U team has won five consecutive Ontario Cup titles and is representing Ontario at the Nationals in Surrey, BC (Source: LAFC)

content_blocks.text: The girls arrived in Surrey Tuesday after having their early morning flight cancelled, but managed to get a training session in before play started Wednesday afternoon against Halifax.
“It’s a pretty grueling tournament,” added Sorbara.
Chip-in on 2nd playoff hole to win wossaa gold
Preston Gryp knew he had to chip in from off the green to have a chance to win the gold medal.
The Parkside Collegiate student won the Wossaa golf championship at St. Thomas Golf and Country Club in dramatic fashion.

content_blocks.alt: Preston Gryp
content_blocks.caption: WOSSAA golf champion Preston Gryp hits a shot on the first playoff hole with a big crowd behind him at St. Thomas Golf and Country Club (Source: Brent Lale/CTV London)

content_blocks.text: All three of them made bogey on the difficult first hole, so it was off to #18.
Watt made a five to finish third, while Gryp hit his second shot near the front bunker. Bosma nearly holed out from over 100 yards and sat just about six feet for birdie.
Gryp knew he had to make the shot, and chipped in from off the green. Bosma lipped out his putt giving Gryp the individual title.
“I had a wedge in and I was kind of a in between number and I hit it came up just a little short,” said Gryp, one of three players to shoot 76 (+4) on a windy day.
“Jacob threw one in tight and I knew I probably had to chip in for the win. Maybe a little lucky, but I’m happy with the shot I hit.”

content_blocks.text: “I hit one so close and it just lipped out then just missed for birdie and made the par. It’ll be super fun (Ofsaa) going with everyone.”
London knights need better starts

The London Knights are 4-1 to start the season, good enough for top spot in the Midwest Division of the Ontario Hockey League. They have managed to achieve that record, despite not scoring a single goal in the first period of any of their five matches.

“Even off ice, just making sure you’re showing up to the rink to get all your preparation you need to be ready to go. So just getting the legs into a little earlier and maybe in the gym before if you need to get a little workout in just to get that extra juice and legs for the first period.”
Knights staff have been preaching taking a professional mentality pregame to be ready from the opening faceoff, but attribute some of their slow starts to their style of play.
“We don’t send two-one-twos (formations), we do a one-two-two,” said Dylan Hunter, Knights assistant coach.
“it’s more about getting the puck in deep, getting shots on that when you get them and then trying to get them out of sorts on their system,” said Hunter.
“We’re trying to make a quick play and then making a nice little sauce pass and you know that takes a little bit of timing.”

The third annual Panther Day in St. Thomas, Ont. was a celebration of community spirit and girls hockey.

A full day of action started with girls games in the morning and continued on both ice pads all the way through the evening and was capped off by an exhibition game between the Western Mustangs and Guelph Gryphons .
“The big difference this year is on and off the ice,” said Panthers coach and spokesperson Jessie Karn.

“We’re taking donations at the door, the rink is entirely pink and as well for our game day fit. All the Panthers have pink t-shirts for their warm up, but then also on the ice they have their jerseys as well.”

“It’s about awareness at a young age and also caring and love,” said Karn.
“At the end of the day, everyone can feel united as one and that’s what the community is all about.”
During the day, the Mustangs players were around the arena taking photos with the young girls before playing their game.
“I love this stuff,” said Emma Campbell, Mustangs captain.

stories.title: Canada considers future of foreign homebuyers ban ahead of year-end expiry
stories.summary: The policy that bans foreign purchases of residential real estate in Canada was introduced after home prices surged during the pandemic.
stories.author: Bloomberg News
stories.content:
Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne says the federal government is mulling its options ahead of the expiry of Canada’s foreign homebuyers ban at the end of the year.

“We’re looking at all the options that we have in front of us, considering where the market is going, what has happened over the last few years,” Champagne told reporters in Ottawa on Wednesday. “We want to make sure that we have a higher stock of housing opportunities for Canadians.”

Former prime minister Justin Trudeau’s government banned foreign purchases of residential real estate in Canada in 2023, with exemptions for vacant land intended for development and larger multi-unit buildings. The government renewed the measure in 2024.

The policy was introduced after home prices surged during the pandemic, when interest rates were near zero. But data suggest foreigners owned no more than 5% of properties in any major Canadian market in 2020, while developers have argued the ban cuts off a source of capital that would help fund new housing construction.

The ban is set to expire on Jan. 1, 2027. Housing Minister Gregor Robertson said last year the government would use 2026 to review the policy and examine models that have worked elsewhere, including Australia, where foreigners can purchase newly built homes.

The housing market has also changed dramatically since the pandemic. After the Bank of Canada began hiking interest rates in 2022, demand softened and prices began to fall. The national benchmark price is now roughly 20% below its peak, one of the sharpest corrections on record.

Despite the downturn, many younger Canadians remain priced out of home ownership, making any move to welcome more foreign capital into the housing market politically sensitive for Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government.

Canada's housing crisis is dragging life satisfaction down among young adults

Cmhc warns of a 'very significant barrier' to fixing the housing crisis

Champagne acknowledged that the market is evolving, and said municipalities, provinces and the federal government have all taken steps to improve affordability.

“The market is very different from one region to the other, even one community from the other,” he said. “We’re looking at not only what the federal government has been doing and can be doing, but also what other levels of government have been addressing.”

Benjamin Tal, deputy chief economist at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, has called for the government to let the ban expire.

“It doesn’t make any sense,” he said last week, arguing that Carney has been encouraging foreign investment in other sectors of the economy and that allowing offshore buyers back into the market could help finance new housing projects and boost supply.

stories.title: Ability to fix errors in referendum ballot packages show system works: Alberta premier
stories.summary: Smith and Elections Alberta noted the problematic ballot packages represent a small number of those that have been sent back by voters — only 1.2 per cent of around 250,000.
stories.author: Lisa Johnson
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says the fact the provincial election authority is helping voters correct errors in about 3,000 mail-in ballot packages shows the system is working.

It comes after Elections Alberta announced those referendum ballot packages were returned with either declaration forms missing or with other errors, like missing the required copies of identification.

At an unrelated news conference Wednesday, Smith said the ability for electors to correct the necessary documents in time for their vote to be counted shows Elections Alberta is managing the situation as expected.

“I think that’s a sign the system works,” she said.

Smith and Elections Alberta also noted the problematic ballot packages represent a small number of those that have been sent back by voters — only 1.2 per cent of around 250,000.

Maia Hanrahan at Elections Alberta said in an email Wednesday they’ve contacted those whose packages had problems and are helping voters make the necessary fixes.

“Similar to an in-person voting experience where an election officer would assist the elector in making sure their information was correct and complete, that is what is happening with these special ballots – we are assisting electors in correcting their errors,” Hanrahan wrote.

She said voters are able to provide the required information via email, but if they do not, their special ballots will be rejected.

“Already we have had many people respond and provide the required information.”

Albertans are to vote on a series of questions on Oct. 19, including whether to stay in Canada or begin the process to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving Confederation. The other nine questions pertain to immigration and the Constitution.

stories.title: Accused walks free after pleading guilty to manslaughter in fatal shooting
stories.summary: After spending more than eight years in jail in connection to a brazen daytime shooting death, Zachary McDermott, 26, was released from custody at the London Courthouse and walked out a free man.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
After spending more than eight years in jail in connection to a brazen daytime shooting death, Zachary McDermott, 26, was released from custody at the London Courthouse and walked out a free man.

His second degree murder trial which got underway last week came to an abrupt end on Tuesday after he decided to plead guilty to the lesser charge of manslaughter.

The Crown told the court that new evidence had come to light in regards to threats and possible firearm involving the victim.

On Sept. 12, 2018 after a prior altercation between the victim and the accused, McDermott drove his silver Chevy sedan to a Tim Hortons on Dundas Street East to meet up with 21 year old Christopher Clements-Card.

Once Clements-Card saw McDermott, the victim started running towards the coffee shop and was gunned down at the entrance area. He was rushed to hospital where he later died from two gunshot wounds to the back.

McDermott fled the scene but was arrested nine days later and had been in custody ever since.

Six victim impact statements were read into the court with Clements-Card’s cousin Nicole Barnes saying telling the judge, “Christopher deserved to live. Your Honour Christopher’s life mattered and his death should matter too.”

Another cousin, Kendra Ashe told the court, “Today and for the rest of our lives we will continue to mourn his death.”

Justice Patricia Moore acknowledged those in court by saying, “This has had a devastating impact on the friends and family of Christopher Clements--Card.”

Outside the courthouse, Barnes added, “He (Christopher Clements-Card) is missed by his family every day at every family gathering.”

An earlier ban on publication prevented the media from reporting that McDermott was initially charged with first degree murder in this case.

The media was also banned from stating that in the summer of 2022, McDermott plead guilty to second degree murder but quickly withdrew that plea and a new trial was ordered with different lawyers

This week after the new plea was entered and the jury was dismissed, Justice Moore agreed with both the Crown and the defence that an appropriate sentence is time already served.

McDermott, who was 18 at the time of his arrest, has served more than 8 years in custody with much of it being at the Maplehurst Detention Centre in Milton.

When the courts take the enhancement into consideration, McDermott has served the equivalent of 12 years behind bars.

Before the case wrapped up McDermott addressed the court and said he was remorseful for the pain he has caused saying, “I’m truly sorry, no matter how sorry I am nothing will change and I take full responsibility.”

Clements-Card’s family was not pleased with the final outcome with Barnes saying, “We’ve had to endure eight years of delays and adjournments and Mr. McDermott gets to go free and Christopher doesn’t get to live a life.”

McDermott was ordered to submit his DNA and is also prohibited from carrying a firearm for life.
