stories.title: Writer K.D. Miller crafted stories that glittered like a polished knife edge
stories.summary: Her fiction, which can be blazingly funny or unsettlingly dark, often explores religious themes while marrying pristine linguistic technique with an instinct for drama
stories.author: Steven Beattie
stories.content:
For much of her adult life, author K.D. Miller had a writing ritual. She would rise at 5 a.m., brew a pot of coffee, and head to her desk for two hours before she had to get ready for what she euphemistically referred to as her “day job.”

Fellow writer and good friend Mike Barnes describes Ms. Miller’s writing habit as “monastic,” an appropriate term that hints at the overlap, so central to her identity, between writing and religion. Raised Presbyterian, Ms. Miller was baptized and confirmed in the Anglican Church in 1990, following a period of self-described atheism. On several occasions Ms. Miller, who died in Toronto on Sept. 14 of complications from cancer at the age of 75, described herself as a “default” or “accidental” Christian. It’s the same way her character Robbie describes himself to his friend, the writer Raymond Mayhugh, in the early story A Litany in Time of Plague – a testament to the way Ms. Miller covertly insinuated material from her own life into her fiction.

The title of the story is evidence of Ms. Miller’s preoccupation. On the surface a reference to the poem of the same name by Elizabethan poet Thomas Nashe, the word “litany” carries religious connotations that are unavoidable. And while she eschewed proselytizing about her beliefs – “She was very undogmatic in her approach to spirituality,” Mr. Barnes said – they were an inextricable part of who she was as a person and, importantly, a writer. “Writing stories is the way I pray,” she insisted in her 2001 essay collection Holy Writ , about the confluence between artistic creation and spirituality. One of her later collections, 2014’s All Saints , is a series of linked stories featuring characters associated with the title church.

If religion was one indelible wellspring for Ms. Miller, the other was the theatre. Trained as an actor, she received a BA in drama from the University of Guelph and a master’s in directing from the University of British Columbia, where her thesis was a production analysis of Tennessee Williams’s The Glass Menagerie. In a biographical essay included in the 2003 anthology Writers Talking, she described her mother, the late Isabel Milne Barclay, as “a talented artist and a frustrated actress”; she went on to compare the writing process to Rosalind Russell’s observation that “[g]ood acting is standing up naked and turning around very slowly.”

Writing, for Ms. Miller, involved a similar combination of risk and abandon, something admirers frequently compare to a theatrical performance. “I think it all went back to that early training that she had on stage,” said John Metcalf, who edited her early work. “You had to immerse yourself in [her writing], you had to join the performance. That was what made her so different from many writers in recent years who are firmly outside what they are presenting.”

Novelist Russell Smith also finds aspects of the theatre in Ms. Miller’s work. “She writes these wonderful, humorous but dark monologues. That obviously is the theatrical influence,” he said. It was an influence that was equally apparent in her live readings, which often resembled theatrical performances. This, perhaps, made her the perfect person for that necessary day job: training volunteers at the Cnib in reading books for the blind.

Ms. Miller could be blazingly funny in print: The title story from 2018’s Late Breaking features a pair of competing literary awards – the Biggar Prize and the Olympia Featherstone Award for Fiction – that repeatedly try to one-up each other on the size of their purse. (Somewhat ironically, the book was both a Governor-General’s Literary Award finalist and a Giller Prize nominee.)

But she was also, as Mr. Smith attests, unafraid to present bleak and dark material. In one of her best stories, Magnificat from All Saints , an aged religious spinster witnesses a covert public sex act that crosses the boundary into assault.

“It gets quite gothic and creepy sometimes,” Mr. Smith said about this aspect of Ms. Miller’s fiction. “Who does that remind you of? [Alice] Munro, right away.”

It’s a sentiment with which literary critic Jeet Heer agrees. “There’s the tradition of the Canadian short story where Alice Munro looms very large. K.D. Miller is part of that tradition,” Mr. Heer said. “There’s the idea of the Southern Ontario gothic. I think she was more gothic than most. She did have a sensibility that was partially shaped by things like horror writing.” He points specifically to the 2011 collection The Other Voice as a book that reflects her affinity for writers like Poe and Hawthorne, as well as the uncanny realism of Alex Colville, who served as the inspiration for the stories in Late Breaking. “It’s the idea of realism that’s also a bit unsettling,” Mr. Heer said.

Kathleen Daisy Miller was born on March 6, 1951 in Hamilton, where she lived with her parents and her older brother, Robert Miller. “There was a large family in Hamilton,” says Leah Wallace, Ms. Miller’s sister-in-law. “The Barclays on her mother’s side, the Millers on her father’s side. They actually all lived within walking distance of each other.”

The acting bug bit early. At age 12, Ms. Miller was cast as Annie Sullivan in a school production of The Miracle Worker, and she won the 1967 Hamilton District Collegiate Drama Festival’s award for best actress in Impromptu. She left for Guelph in 1969, graduating with a BA in drama in 1973. She finished her master’s in 1978, “more out of spite than anything else,” she wrote. While in B.C., she met an actor whom she married in 1979; the two divorced in 1986.

Ms. Miller’s first publication was the short story Now, Voyager , which appeared in Flare and won first prize in the magazine’s literary contest. Her first story collection, A Litany in Time of Plague , was published by the Porcupine’s Quill in 1994; the small press in Erin, Ont., also brought out a second collection, Give Me Your Answer (1999), and the essay collection Holy Writ: A Writer Reflects on Creation and Inspiration (2001). A novel, Brown Dwarf, and a story collection, The Other Voice, followed. All Saints was shortlisted for the Rogers Writers’ Trust Award for Fiction, and Late Breaking was a finalist for the Governor-General’s Literary Award, nominated for the Giller, and shortlisted for the Trillium Prize.

An unpublished collection, Alice Walks , is currently under contract with Dundurn Press.

She had three core communities, according to Ms. Wallace: the community of St. Clement’s Anglican Church, in North Toronto, where she served on various committees and attended service every Sunday; the community at Stanley Knowles Housing Co-operative, where she lived; and the literary community. A group of close friends from university that includes Ms. Wallace and goes by the moniker “The Sisterhood” met regularly over the years.

But she also fiercely guarded her privacy and withheld personal aspects of herself from public view, something Mr. Barnes, the writer, believes goes back to an aspect of performing on stage. “She had a real sense of performance; that’s what made her such a dramatic reader,” he said. “But she had a very firm line she drew: A performance was a performance and then off the stage, that’s your private life. At her very best, she was at the pinnacle of writers in this country, combining pristine linguistic technique with a theatre impresario’s instinct for drama. Her painstaking craft – honed morning after morning beginning at 5 o’clock, often before the sun rose – resulted in prose that glittered like a polished knife edge. And like a knife, it could cut deep. That said, Ms. Miller herself was not reticent to admit writerly self-doubt. “I don’t think I’m ‘important as a writer’ yet,” she wrote in 2003, “and have no idea if I ever will be. I do know that I’m happy as a writer.”

One person who is certain Ms. Miller’s writing will endure is her former editor, Mr. Metcalf. “Her stories are acted out vigorously in marvellous dialogue. And very funny, some of them,” he said. “The stories were very vital and quite unusual within the body of Canadian writing. She has a place within the literature that will always be remembered.”

Fellow writer and good friend Mike Barnes describes Ms. Miller’s writing habit as “monastic,” an appropriate term that hints at the overlap, so central to her identity, between writing and religion. Raised Presbyterian, Ms. Miller was baptized and confirmed in the Anglican Church in 1990, following a period of self-described atheism. On several occasions Ms. Miller, who died in Toronto on Sept. 14 of complications from cancer at the age of 75, described herself as a “default” or “accidental” Christian. It’s the same way her character Robbie describes himself to his friend, the writer Raymond Mayhugh, in the early story A Litany in Time of Plague – a testament to the way Ms. Miller covertly insinuated material from her own life into her fiction.

The title of the story is evidence of Ms. Miller’s preoccupation. On the surface a reference to the poem of the same name by Elizabethan poet Thomas Nashe, the word “litany” carries religious connotations that are unavoidable. And while she eschewed proselytizing about her beliefs – “She was very undogmatic in her approach to spirituality,” Mr. Barnes said – they were an inextricable part of who she was as a person and, importantly, a writer. “Writing stories is the way I pray,” she insisted in her 2001 essay collection Holy Writ , about the confluence between artistic creation and spirituality. One of her later collections, 2014’s All Saints , is a series of linked stories featuring characters associated with the title church.

If religion was one indelible wellspring for Ms. Miller, the other was the theatre. Trained as an actor, she received a BA in drama from the University of Guelph and a master’s in directing from the University of British Columbia, where her thesis was a production analysis of Tennessee Williams’s The Glass Menagerie. In a biographical essay included in the 2003 anthology Writers Talking, she described her mother, the late Isabel Milne Barclay, as “a talented artist and a frustrated actress”; she went on to compare the writing process to Rosalind Russell’s observation that “[g]ood acting is standing up naked and turning around very slowly.”

Writing, for Ms. Miller, involved a similar combination of risk and abandon, something admirers frequently compare to a theatrical performance. “I think it all went back to that early training that she had on stage,” said John Metcalf, who edited her early work. “You had to immerse yourself in [her writing], you had to join the performance. That was what made her so different from many writers in recent years who are firmly outside what they are presenting.”

Novelist Russell Smith also finds aspects of the theatre in Ms. Miller’s work. “She writes these wonderful, humorous but dark monologues. That obviously is the theatrical influence,” he said. It was an influence that was equally apparent in her live readings, which often resembled theatrical performances. This, perhaps, made her the perfect person for that necessary day job: training volunteers at the Cnib in reading books for the blind.

Ms. Miller could be blazingly funny in print: The title story from 2018’s Late Breaking features a pair of competing literary awards – the Biggar Prize and the Olympia Featherstone Award for Fiction – that repeatedly try to one-up each other on the size of their purse. (Somewhat ironically, the book was both a Governor-General’s Literary Award finalist and a Giller Prize nominee.)

But she was also, as Mr. Smith attests, unafraid to present bleak and dark material. In one of her best stories, Magnificat from All Saints , an aged religious spinster witnesses a covert public sex act that crosses the boundary into assault.
“It gets quite gothic and creepy sometimes,” Mr. Smith said about this aspect of Ms. Miller’s fiction. “Who does that remind you of? [Alice] Munro, right away.”

It’s a sentiment with which literary critic Jeet Heer agrees. “There’s the tradition of the Canadian short story where Alice Munro looms very large. K.D. Miller is part of that tradition,” Mr. Heer said. “There’s the idea of the Southern Ontario gothic. I think she was more gothic than most. stories.title: Ottawa considering ‘options’ as foreign home buyer ban nears end: minister
stories.summary: The ban was brought in by the Liberals in 2022 to keep foreign investors out of housing markets increasingly out of reach for Canadian buyers.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said the government is “considering the options” on extending a ban on foreign ownership of Canadian residential property.

Champagne appeared non-committal when asked if Ottawa would extend the ban, which banned foreign investors from buying Canadian residential property and was first enacted in 2022.

The ban is scheduled to sunset in January 2027, just months after the expected tabling of the Liberals’ next budget.

“That’s a measure … that has been in place for some time. The market is evolving,” Champagne told reporters on Wednesday.

“We’re looking at all the options that we have in front of us, considering where the market is going, what has happened over the last few years, always keeping in mind that we want to make sure that we have a higher stock of housing opportunities for Canadians.”

The previous iteration of the Liberal government noted in 2024 that foreign investors have been buying up residential real estate, which Ottawa said was “increasing housing affordability concerns in cities across the country, particularly in major urban centres.”

The government at the time extended the ban, which was originally set to expire in January 2025, for an additional two years.

stories.title: Community calls for justice on what would have been Devon Marsman’s 21st birthday
stories.summary: Oct. 7 would have been Devon Marsman's 21st birthday. Community members came together to honour his memory ahead of the trials set to kick off next month.
stories.author: Ella Macdonald
stories.content:
Oct. 7 would have been Devon Marsman’s 21st birthday.

On Sunday, his loved ones gathered at the basketball court on Romans Avenue in Halifax’s west end to celebrate the teen’s life and renew calls for justice in his five-year-old murder case.

For Marsman’s mother, Theresa Gray, it’s hard to believe so much time has passed since she last saw her son.

“He didn’t get to live any of his life whatsoever, he was just stripped of everything,” said Gray.

Marsman was 16 when he went missing after attending a party with his older cousin — Treyton Marsman — and another boy in February 2022.

Gray said she never gave up looking for her son — organizing search parties and marches to keep his face in the public eye.

She always maintained Marsman’s cousin, Treyton, was responsible for her son’s disappearance — a name she said she gave police from the beginning.

On Sept. 17, 2024, police finally announced they had found Marsman’s remains and charged Treyton Marsman with second-degree murder, indignity to human remains and obstruction.

Lisa Fenton is an advocate who has worked closely with Marsman’s family in the pursuit of justice in his name.

“We are still living with the consequences of the violence that took Devon’s life,” said Fenton at Devon’s birthday celebration on Sunday.

“That is why we have to keep talking about it. We have to teach our young people that there is another way.”

In 2024, police charged four more people: Emma Maria Meta Casey, Chelsea Herritt, Mark Douglas Robert Doyle and the other boy who attended the party with Marsman the night he went missing.

The boy was a youth at the time of the alleged crime, and his identity is protected under the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

Casey, Herritt and the youth are facing multiple charges each, including indignity to human remains.

Doyle faces one count of accessory after the fact to murder.

Due to an all-encompassing publication ban, Global News is unable to provide an update on the status of the legal proceedings until the jury is sequestered in the final trial set to begin in March 2027.

For Gray, Marsman’s legacy is reflected in the people who show up for his heavenly birthday celebration, year after year.

“He meant something, he means something,” Gray said. “Hopefully, for everyone that was involved, justice comes sooner than later.”

The basketball court in the Bayers Westwood neighborhood is where Marsman spent countless hours playing with his friends.

On the weekend, it is where family and friends gathered to sing songs, eat birthday cake, and share stories.

Community leaders are currently in the process of getting the space dedicated in Marsman’s memory.

Social justice activist, DeRico Symonds, is taking the lead on the project.

Having grown up in the same community, Symonds said he knows the value of the court and what it represents for the area’s youth.

“I lived at 337 Romans Avenue, and this basketball court was the therapist I could afford,” Symonds said.

Even when things get tough, he told the youth in attendance that violence is never the answer.

Adding, there is a way to transcend your circumstances.

“I did it. Many other people from this community have done it,” Symonds said. “(…) It may be tough, you may be going through all kinds of things, you may be poor, but you can continue to press on and things will get better.”

At the municipality’s regional council meeting held on Sept. 29, Symonds said council moved forward on plans for the dedication.

“Devon’s name along with seven others were all approved without debate, which means that his name is now reserved to be approved and applied to a municipal asset,” Symonds explained.

“Obviously, we want it for the basketball court.”

Once the trials have concluded, Gray said she will continue fighting in Marsman’s name, but with a slightly different goal in mind.

“I’m going to be basically on a mission, to make sure what happened to my son doesn’t happen to any other families with a missing child,” Gray said. “My son was never a runaway.”

stories.title: ‘I think this day is a hurt locker’: London Jewish Community marks Oct. 7 anniversary
stories.summary: A series of commemorations in London’s Jewish community Wednesday to mark the three year anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas attack against Israel.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
A series of commemorations in London’s Jewish community Wednesday to mark the three year anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas attack against Israel. Among the events is an opportunity to hear from the Canadian Regional Director for the Jewish Agency for Israel. “I think this day is a hurt locker. It’s still as painful and raw,” said Ayelet Harris in an interview with CTV News.

Following the events of Oct. 7, Harris spearheaded the frontline response and communication network for 22 dispersed evacuated communities. “And we took care of their bare necessities. Shoes, reissuing documents, canceling mortgage payments. And we organized burial arrangements for hundreds of people across the country.

It was a war zone. They couldn’t be buried at home, they had to be buried elsewhere,” she recalled. Nechamie Silberberg, a member of London’s Jewish community, says she hears from children who have questions about this day. “The after-effects of Oct. 7 on the entire world have seeped into, unfortunately day to day life in Canada as well.

So, they hear about antisemitism. They understand that it’s a very real issue. And they ask why, and how something like this could be prevented,” said Silberberg. The London Police Service says it’s taking extra steps to ensure safety. In a social media post, LPS advises that “you May notice an increased police presence around places of worship and community spaces.”

As for Ayelet Harris, she’s hoping to leave a message of hope with her London audience. “Hope and strength. Community coming together,” she said. Harris will speak at 7 p.m. Wednesday evening at the Memorial Ceremony at the London Jewish Community Centre on Huron Street.

stories.title: Halifax hosting defence firms at record-breaking conference amid protests
stories.summary: International defence companies are gathering in Halifax this week for one of the country's largest security conventions.
stories.author: Mitchell Bailey, Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
International defence companies are gathering in Halifax this week for one of the country’s largest security conventions.

With more than 3,000 attendees at DEFSEC Atlantic 2026, industry representatives and government officials say it reflects a generational wave of defence spending in the province.

“There’s an increased interest from companies around the world about what’s happening here in Nova Scotia,” said Sheldon Gillis, Invest Nova Scotia’s managing defence director.

This year’s conference is the largest on record, according to the province, and is “further evidence” of Nova Scotia’s position as Canada’s defence capital, which supports more than 17,000 jobs provincewide.

The province adds that the defence and aerospace sector contributes $2.7 billion to the province’s GDP.

Earlier this year, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced $3 billion in new infrastructure and defence spending for Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. That included more than $2 billion to modernize infrastructure, expand training and build facilities for new warships and aircraft in Nova Scotia.

“The federal government is reinvesting to modernize and rebuild our Canadian Armed Forces and Nova Scotia is very well positioned to reap some of those benefits,” said Colton LeBlanc, Nova Scotia’s Minister of Growth, Development, and Defence Industries.

LeBlanc says Nova Scotia’s existing military infrastructure and access to the North Atlantic make it easy for companies to set up shop.

2:05 Ottawa spending $4 million on defence industry projects in Atlantic Canada

Dartmouth-based start-up, Omnitech Electronics, was among the companies looking to attract new customers.

“We’re so happy to just kind of meet people as they walk by, whether they be potential folks that we can collaborate with, customers, what not,” said Nicholas Barrett, an engineer with the company.

But not everyone is aligned with the goals of DEFSEC Atlantic.

Protesters outside the three-day event at the Halifax Convention Centre described it as an “arms expo” for companies profiting from conflict.

“The reason we oppose it is because the arms industries is creating havoc and destruction around the world and has been increasing in the amount of resources that it takes up year after year, with the last two years increasingly having been the best years for the arms industry,” said Asaf Rashid, a member of the Halifax Committee Against Imperialist War And Genocide.

In response, LeBlanc says he hears the concerns but his focus is clear.

“My focus here is to support on what’s being displayed here, but certainly respect the voices of those outside,” he said.

stories.title: Cleveland-Cliffs boss dismisses idea of nationalizing Stelco as Ottawa pushes to preserve jobs
stories.summary: Lourenco Goncalves also fired back at a customer critical of his company pulling out of Canada’s galvanized steel market
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CLF-N chief executive Lourenco Goncalves is dismissing the idea of nationalizing Stelco and firing back at what he calls a “walking eagle” Canadian steel customer.

The U.S. steelmaker said last week it was planning to lay off as many as 500 steel workers at Stelco in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., in large part because it can’t compete anymore in galvanized steel as a result of the trade war.

When the federal government approved Cliffs’ $3.4-billion acquisition of Stelco Holdings Inc. in 2024, it imposed a series of legally binding conditions, including maintaining at least the same number of unionized employees in Canada for five years, as well as the vast majority of non-unionized workers.

By announcing hundreds of layoffs in Canada, Ottawa alleges Cliffs is now in violation of that agreement.

On Monday Industry Minister Mélanie Joly issued the Cleveland-based steelmaker an ultimatum to map out a plan within five business days for complying with its employment guarantees under the Investment Canada Act or possibly face legal action .

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Wednesday Stelco's owner Cleveland-Cliffs cannot use the trade war to justify cutting jobs it committed to when it bought the Hamilton, Ont.-based steel plant, particularly when the head of its U.S. parent company has publicly backed steel tariffs.

The Canadian Press

But while Ottawa is pushing Cliffs to preserve those jobs in Canada, some have suggested the government could instead take over Stelco and save them.

Nicolas Lamp, an associate professor in the Faculty of Law at Queen’s University, said in a recent editorial in The Globe and Mail that if Ottawa decides the steel industry is of strategic importance, and Stelco workers have indeed been “ betrayed ” by Cliffs, it could instead “nationalize the company and put Canadian management in charge.”

In an interview Wednesday, Mr. Goncalves poured cold water on the idea, pointing to the example of Venezuelan president Hugo Chávez nationalizing steel company Siderúrgica del Orinoco (Sidor) in 2008. The takeover was widely seen as an economic disaster, with production plummeting in the aftermath.

“Is that what Canada really wants to do?” he said.

When asked if he would entertain an offer from Ottawa to buy Stelco, he replied that “the only thing that makes sense for us as a business” is the Canadian government signing a “Fortress North America” trade deal with the U.S.

Alison Reilander, a spokesperson with Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada, said in an e-mail that the government is focusing on working with the union and the Ontario government to get workers back on the job.

The Cliffs boss on Wednesday also fired back at a Stelco customer who has doubted his rationale for pulling out of the galvanized steel market in Canada. Mr. Goncalves maintains that the 50-per-cent tariff U.S. President Donald Trump imposed on Canada last year has closed off that key market for the company and the Canadian government isn’t doing enough to keep cheap imports out of the country.

Jim Ritchie, the owner of steel distribution company Cascadia Metals Ltd., called that explanation “a joke.” He said the price of coated steel has rocketed higher this year in Canada and “it’s never been a better time to make galvanized steel in Canada.”

Mr. Ritchie said he is a big buyer of galvanized steel from Stelco and with the company no longer producing the product, it has left Cascadia in a jam, forced to import from overseas markets to fill the void.

In response, Mr. Goncalves called Mr. Ritchie a “walking eagle,” meaning a bird that can’t fly because it is full of excrement.

He challenged the notion that Cascadia is a major customer of Stelco, saying it isn’t even among the top 20 and represents less than 1 per cent of its business by revenue.

Mr. Goncalves also said Mr. Ritchie is “part of the problem” because Cascadia imports a considerable amount of steel from overseas, which drives down the price of the product in Canada.

“Clients like Cascadia are the reason I am shutting down,” he said.

Mr. Ritchie said that while he finds the “walking eagle” comment “pretty funny,” he said he wasn’t prepared to engage in “a war of words” with Mr. Goncalves.

He admits that he imports steel from overseas but says he has been doing his best to pivot to Canadian suppliers.

“We were trying to switch from offshore to domestic and we were trying to give them more and more business. We were really ramping up the business we were giving him when they stopped selling to us,” Mr. Ritchie said.

“If we didn’t import, we wouldn’t have a business. That’s because Canadian steel producers can’t supply the entire Western Canadian market. There isn’t enough steel in Canada.”

stories.title: Dyed diesel is now legal on U.S. roads. What are the rules in Canada?
stories.summary: Dyed diesel has now been cleared for general use in the U.S. as gas prices soar, but Canadians could face fines if caught using it on roads and highways.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Dyed diesel has now been cleared for general use in the U.S. as gas prices soar, but Canadians could still face fines if caught using it on roads and highways.

Red-dyed diesel is essentially the same as regular diesel fuel, but is coloured a reddish brown in order to identify it for use off-road, like with farming, construction vehicles and other off-road uses.

U.S. President Donald Trump, on Monday, signed an executive order directing secretaries of the U.S. Treasury as well as the departments of transportation and agriculture to waive the off-road requirement for this tax-free diesel.

The move followed similar changes at the state level, including in Texas , as Americans struggle to pay for diesel and other fuels as a result of soaring prices from the U.S. war on Iran.

The changes mean if someone like a U.S. farmer has red-dyed diesel in bulk, which would have been exclusively used for their farming and other equipment, they can now use the same fuel in their trucks to drive on the roads without facing any penalties or taxes.

Canada’s agriculture industry is heavily reliant on diesel to power its equipment and trucks, and at a time when diesel prices have been soaring, industry leaders say similar changes would be welcomed here.

“Canadian farmers have always had access to dyed diesel on-farm for the equipment that runs on diesel engines, combines, tractors, self-propelled vehicles in general that are used on the farm,” says Keith Currie, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.

“There’s constantly additional surcharge put on because of increased diesel prices, and so if they had an opportunity to run dyed diesel and not have the road tax, that would certainly stabilize some of the pricing of diesel fuel, which has gotten extremely expensive now. “

Is the federal government considering changes?

As it stands, using red-dyed diesel to fuel road and highway vehicles is illegal in Canada, and is enforced mostly at the provincial and territorial level through specific fuel tax legislation.

Although the federal government has waived the excise fuel tax on regular and diesel fuel in Canada, certain road taxes are still applied to diesel cleared for use on roads and highways in some provinces and territories.

“Federal fuel excise tax rules do not include special treatment associated with coloured or dyed diesel fuel,” said the Department of Finance in a statement.

“Provinces and territories may have their own tax rules, restrictions and enforcement requirements governing coloured fuel, including its use in on-road vehicles.”

Global News has sent requests to all provincial and territorial finance ministries to ask if any changes to red-dyed diesel laws are being considered, but none confirmed any changes to the laws were being considered.

Saskatchewan said doing so would mean a significant loss in revenue needed to maintain infrastructure.

“100 per cent of Saskatchewan’s fuel tax revenue is legislated to be used to maintain and improve Saskatchewan’s highways and transportation infrastructure,” said a spokesperson for the Saskatchewan Ministry of Finance in a statement.

“Expanding the Farm Fuel Program to allow all on-road uses of diesel fuel would amount to cutting the highways budget. This would impact the safety of motorists as well as the transportation of the exports that our economy relies on.”

Can you cross the border with red-dyed diesel?

The short answer is yes, but there are important distinctions and requirements that must be followed in order to avoid fines.

Rob Kreklewetz is a lawyer and managing director at Millar Kreklewetz LLP, which specializes in tax customs and trade law.

“The dye is what identifies whether it’s tax paid or tax unpaid. So if it’s red dye, no taxes have been paid on that fuel, and the local ministry of finance officials are going to be hunting for that if used on highway,” says Kreklewetz.

“I’m free to go to the U.S., and load that fuel onto my diesel pickup if I want, and Trump is allowing people in the U.S. to do that. The question is, how do I bring it across the border?”

He explains that it is technically legal to bring most types of fuel from the U.S. into Canada, including red-dyed diesel, but it comes down to declaring it if it is in a container, and if it is being used to fuel a road vehicle.

“You’re bringing in a jerry can of red diesel, it’s just like bringing in the Louis Vuitton purse. Do you want to take the chance of not declaring that Louis Vuitton purse? Well, it could be subject to seizure and then a whole bunch of really bad consequences at the border,” says Kreklewetz.

2:04 Asking locals about gas and diesel spike

Once the red-dyed fuel is placed in the fuel tank of a road vehicle, that’s where things change.

“I am potentially susceptible there to a bit of a problem. Somebody pulls me over, I go through an administrative finance checkpoint, they put a little dipstick into my fuel tank, it comes out red,” says Kreklewetz.

“Technically, they would say, I have contravened the Fuel Tax Act.”

Kreklewetz says it is not necessarily a criminal offence at this point, but if caught, road users could be subject to fines, which differ depending on the jurisdiction.

In Ontario, motorists can be fined between $200-$1000 per offence, according to the Fuel Tax Act.

“Every operator of a motor vehicle to which a number plate is attached as required under the Highway Traffic Act and that is found to contain coloured fuel in a fuel tank of the motor vehicle is guilty of an offence and on conviction is liable to a fine of not less than $200 and not more than $1,000,” the legislation says.

In Saskatchewan, contravening the Fuel Tax and Road Use Charge Act, which describes the regulated use of red-dyed diesel in the province, carries a fine of up to $10,000 for an individual and $50,000 for a corporation.

Although red-dyed diesel fuel may be comparably cheaper than clear diesel used for regular roads, the cost savings may not be worth the risk.

“It could be tempting to save a few bucks on fuel taxes by filling up with that red-fuel in the states and using it in Canada, but it’s a slightly more complicated situation than just your regular gas fuel up,” says Kreklewetz.

“It may not be worth the price that you’re saving in the U.S. to be running with red diesel on the roads in Canada.”

“The dye is what identifies whether it’s tax paid or tax unpaid. So if it’s red dye, no taxes have been paid on that fuel, and the local ministry of finance officials are going to be hunting for that if used on highway,” says Kreklewetz.
“I’m free to go to the U.S., and load that fuel onto my diesel pickup if I want, and Trump is allowing people in the U.S. to do that. The question is, how do I bring it across the border?”

He explains that it is technically legal to bring most types of fuel from the U.S. into Canada, including red-dyed diesel, but it comes down to declaring it if it is in a container, and if it is being used to fuel a road vehicle.

“You’re bringing in a jerry can of red diesel, it’s just like bringing in the Louis Vuitton purse. Do you want to take the chance of not declaring that Louis Vuitton purse? Well, it could be subject to seizure and then a whole bunch of really bad consequences at the border,” says Kreklewetz.

Once the red-dyed fuel is placed in the fuel tank of a road vehicle, that’s where things change.

“I am potentially susceptible there to a bit of a problem. Somebody pulls me over, I go through an administrative finance checkpoint, they put a little dipstick into my fuel tank, it comes out red,” says Kreklewetz.
“Technically, they would say, I have contravened the Fuel Tax Act.”
Kreklewetz says it is not necessarily a criminal offence at this point, but if caught, road users could be subject to fines, which differ depending on the jurisdiction.
In Ontario, motorists can be fined between $200-$1000 per offence, according to the Fuel Tax Act.

“Every operator of a motor vehicle to which a number plate is attached as required under the Highway Traffic Act and that is found to contain coloured fuel in a fuel tank of the motor vehicle is guilty of an offence and on conviction is liable to a fine of not less than $200 and not more than $1,000,” the legislation says.

In Saskatchewan, contravening the Fuel Tax and Road Use Charge Act, which describes the regulated use of red-dyed diesel in the province, carries a fine of up to $10,000 for an individual and $50,000 for a corporation.
Although red-dyed diesel fuel may be comparably cheaper than clear diesel used for regular roads, the cost savings may not be worth the risk.

“It could be tempting to save a few bucks on fuel taxes by filling up with that red-fuel in the states and using it in Canada, but it’s a slightly more complicated situation than just your regular gas fuel up,” says Kreklewetz.
“It may not be worth the price that you’re saving in the U.S. to be running with red diesel on the roads in Canada.”

stories.title: Defence minister delivers pro-Canada message in Alberta, highlights $8B in funding
stories.summary: Federal Defence Minister David McGuinty said Confederation is a national bargain renewed through generations by what Canadians do for one another — particularly in wartime.
stories.author: Lisa Johnson and Jack Farrell
stories.content:
With less than two weeks to go before Albertans vote on whether it’s time to quit Confederation, Canada’s defence minister came to Alberta on Wednesday to highlight the billions of military dollars being spent in the Prairie province.

David McGuinty, with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith standing beside him, reiterated that Ottawa is investing $8 billion in ongoing military projects in the province.

He said when the province joined Confederation in 1905, it was a choice that has been renewed across generations through what Albertans have done for the country.

McGuinty said in an increasingly dangerous and divided world, it’s the current generation’s responsibility to leave Canada stronger than before and Alberta will help lead the way.

“Confederation was not an accident,” McGuinty told the crowd assembled in a training facility at Canadian Forces Base Edmonton.

“It’s a bargain of reciprocity, and that bargain is tested most profoundly when the country is called to defend itself.”

2:02 Army overhaul sees CFB Edmonton take lead on combat readiness, crisis response

Smith said the funding bolsters Alberta’s place at the forefront of defence, but agreed the announcement was also about showing that her province and Ottawa can work together.

“Hopefully these kinds of announcements will give people more and more confidence to vote to remain on Oct. 19.”

On that day, she is putting 10 questions to voters in the referendum. They include proposals on immigration and constitutional reform, but the key question is whether the province should stay in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Smith said her government and Ottawa have been collaborating “for some time” to leverage existing military assets in Alberta in order to help meet Ottawa’s national target of spending five per cent of Canada’s gross domestic product on defence by 2035.

McGuinty said the announcement wasn’t random and there’s an urgency to building up the armed forces.

“This is the execution of a plan that we’ve been devising and working on for some time.”

McGuinty highlighted that Alberta is receiving $8 billion in ongoing spending across multiple projects, including $550 million to establish the western operating base for the Royal Canadian Air Force’s CC-330 Husky fleet.

Nearly $4 billion will go to support fighter capabilities at the Cold Lake base, and over $580 million will be spent over three years for maintenance and repairs across military bases in Alberta.

“We’re not simply rebuilding bases,” he said.

“We’re rebuilding Canadian military power — hard power.”

stories.title: Republican Senate candidate breaks with Trump over trade war with Canada
stories.summary: Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has broken ranks with U.S. President Donald Trump by saying the trade war with Canada needs to end.
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has broken ranks with U.S. President Donald Trump by saying the trade war with Canada needs to end.

In a 30-second campaign ad shared on social media on Wednesday, Rogers said: “Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now. As Michigan senator, I’ll bring both parties together to lower your prices.”

He also made a reference to Canadian brewing company Labatt, saying: “Drinking a Labatt and watching the Red Wings, man, it just doesn’t get any more Michigan than that.”

Though the former congressman doesn’t mention Trump by name, the ad is a clear reference to the 50 per cent tariffs Trump imposed on $28 billion worth of Canadian goods in August, as well as the retaliatory tariffs Canada imposed on U.S. products the following month.

And it’s not the first time Rogers has publicly disagreed with Trump on key issues in recent weeks. Last month, he said the war in Iran needs to “end quickly” in another campaign video focused on bringing down energy costs.

Minneapolis mayor sends message to Canadians boycotting U.S.: 'We don't think of you as the 51st state'

Map shows the U.S. states hit hardest by Trump's trade war with Canada

Trump was asked about Rogers’ latest campaign video during a press conference in the Oval Office on Wednesday. “I viewed him as saying that he thinks Canada should make a deal,” the U.S. president said .

Michigan is one of the states hit hardest by the trade war between the two countries, due to the state’s automakers ​relying on integrated cross-border supply chains. According to the Canadian government , Michigan exports $21.2 billion in goods to Canada annually, and imports $43.5 billion. It adds that 333 Canadian-owned businesses employ 40,300 workers in Michigan.

Rogers is running against Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who has also focused on the trade war with Canada as part of his campaign.

Responding to Rogers’ recent video, El-Sayed wrote on X: “Must have had one too many of those LaBatts, Mike. You cheerled this tariff war from the beginning and you’re flip-flopping now because your poll numbers are in free fall.”

The Democrats need to gain four more seats to win back the Senate majority in the upcoming mid-term elections on Nov. 3.

Canada’s Industry Minister, ⁠Melanie Joly, has previously been open about the fact that Canadian counter-tariffs were in part designed to “target states” and “put political pressure” on the Trump administration.

stories.title: Author Galloway 'floored' by accuser's emails disclosed in his defamation lawsuit
stories.summary: Vancouver - Former University of B.C. professor and author Steven Galloway says he was shocked and "floored" by the contents of emails disclosed in his defamation lawsuit over unproven sexual assault allegations that ended his career.
stories.author: Darryl Greer The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The lawyer for a woman at the heart of a defamation case brought by author and former University of B.C. professor Steven Galloway says her defence no longer includes an assertion that he sexually assaulted her.

Arden Beddoes instead said the former creative writing student referred to as A.B. had amended her defence to say she “reported sexual assaults,” and not that she had been sexually assaulted.

But Beddoes said A.B. was not admitting the assault claims were false.

The exchange between Beddoes and the judge in B.C. Supreme Court on the trial’s third day came as the lawyer unsuccessfully tried to prevent Galloway from testifying about the alleged incidents that he denies occurred.

Beddoes objected, saying Galloway’s testimony about a sexual assault that A.B. previously claimed happened on the author’s boat in 2011, was irrelevant to the alleged defamatory statements, a notion questioned by Justice Neena Sharma.

Galloway told the court such an assault “never happened,” and A.B.‘s “entire story is fictional.”

The author’s lawyer Daniel Burnett said his testimony was relevant to potential damages in the case, due to what he called the “outrageous fabrication” of the sexual assault claim.

Galloway is the award-winning author of “The Cellist of Sarajevo,” whose career was ended by the claims of sexual assault and his subsequent suspension at the university. He now sells yachts for a living.

He is suing A.B. and other defendants over statements published on Twitter, now X, and other forums, including an art show in 2018.

Sharma had asked Beddoes to clarify the defence offered by A.B. who cannot be named under a publication ban.

“Does she still include an assertion of being sexually assaulted by Steven Galloway in her statement of defence?,” Sharma asked.

“No,” Beddoes said.

Sharma said A.B. had asked the court “for the extraordinary remedy of a sealing order and a publication ban on her name indefinitely on the basis that her mental health is in tatters because of what he did.”

Beddoes said his client’s mental health was at issue due to “engagement” with the legal proceedings, and just one basis for seeking the publication ban.

The judge went back and forth with Beddoes about the distinction between a court finding the sexual assault allegation to be false, versus making a “presumption of falsity.”

Sharma said she was “unconvinced … that there’s no difference in a defamation action between the court presuming falsity as a matter of law and making a finding of falsity on the evidence.”

Beddoes said his client had withdrawn the defence that the alleged defamatory statements were true and therefore justified, but she had not admitted they were false.

The judge said withdrawing the defence of justification without admitting the statements were false “doesn’t make falsity irrelevant.”

Galloway’s lawyer said the finding of falsity, rather than a presumption, is relevant to potential damages in the case, and also for his client’s vindication.

Galloway testified earlier on Wednesday that he was “floored” by the contents of emails disclosed in his defamation lawsuit over the unproven sexual assault allegations.

He said he was shocked to learn that an email to the president of UBC from the defendant A.B. — alleging Galloway sexually assaulted her — had been copied to a journalist from the CBC’s Fifth Estate.

Galloway said correspondence between A.B. and others in the university’s creative writing department had been disclosed in an earlier arbitration, and later in relation to the lawsuit he originally filed in 2018.

He said he was “horrified” at emails depicting him as a violent sexual predator, and he never understood why the university publicly announced his suspension in 2015 over what it called “serious allegations.”

Galloway said the public announcement wasn’t standard practice, calling it “verdict first, trial second,” but it made sense in the context of emails from A.B. in which he says she had been “threatening them with a big public thing, at a time when they were extremely concerned with their image.”

Burnett asked Galloway, “did you rape or sexually assault or physically assault” A. B.?

“Absolutely not,” Galloway replied.

Multiple defendants originally named in the lawsuit have settled with Galloway and published apologies to him over the allegations that he denies but which were spread widely on social media.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026

stories.title: McGuinty delivers pro-Canada message in Alberta, highlights $8B in defence spending
stories.summary: Federal Defence Minister David McGuinty is reminding Albertans of billions of dollars in military spending and that a strong Canada includes a strong Alberta.His comments come as Albertans prepare to vote on Confederation in the Oct. 19 referendum.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Edmonton — Canada’s defence minister came to Alberta Wednesday to highlight the billions of military dollars being spent there, with less than two weeks to go before Albertans vote on whether it’s time to quit Confederation.

David McGuinty, with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith standing beside him, reiterated that Ottawa is investing $8 billion in ongoing military projects in the province.

He said when the province joined Confederation in 1905, it was a choice that has been renewed across generations through what Albertans have done for the country. McGuinty said in an increasingly dangerous and divided world, it’s the current generation’s responsibility to leave Canada stronger than before and Alberta will help lead the way.

“Confederation was not an accident,” McGuinty told the crowd assembled in a training facility at Canadian Forces Base Edmonton.

“It’s a bargain of reciprocity, and that bargain is tested most profoundly when the country is called to defend itself. “

Smith said the funding bolsters Alberta’s place at the forefront of defence, but agreed the announcement was also about showing that her province and Ottawa can work together.

“I think it’s both,” she said.

“Hopefully these kinds of announcements will give people more and more confidence to vote to remain on Oct. 19.”

On that day, she is putting 10 questions to voters in the referendum. They include proposals on immigration and constitutional reform, but the key question is whether the province should stay in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Smith said her government and Ottawa have been collaborating “for some time” to leverage existing military assets in Alberta in order to help meet Ottawa’s national target of spending five per cent of Canada’s gross domestic product on defence by 2035.

McGuinty said the announcement wasn’t random and there’s an urgency to building up the armed forces.

“This is the execution of a plan that we’ve been devising and working on for some time.”

McGuinty highlighted that Alberta is receiving $8 billion in ongoing spending across multiple projects, including $550 million to establish the Western operating base for the Royal Canadian Air Force’s CC-330 Husky fleet.

Nearly $4 billion will go to support fighter capabilities at the Cold Lake base, and over $580 million will be spent over three years for maintenance and repairs across military bases in Alberta.

“We’re not simply rebuilding bases,” he said. “We’re rebuilding Canadian military power — hard power.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

Lisa Johnson and Jack Farrell, The Canadian Press

stories.title: An architectural legacy on offer in Toronto’s queer district
stories.summary: Like Russian nesting dolls in reverse, what starts out very, very small turns into big, expressive postmodern architecture
stories.author: Dave LeBlanc
stories.content:
In the heart of the Gay Village at Church Street and Wellesley Street East is Barbara Hall Park. Inside the park is the moving, thoughtful and lovingly curated Toronto Aids Memorial. And, like a Matryoshka nesting doll, within the memorial there is a stone with a plaque dedicated to Dr. Edward Kamski (1947-2006) who was “an early medical leader in the fight against HIV/Aids.”

Dr. Kamski left behind an architectural legacy as well … where there was once only a rose bush.

In the early 1990s, architect Paul Reuber, who had done two renovations for the good doctor, was shown what must have been the smallest scrap of land in Toronto. Standing at the northeast corner of Seaton Street and Shuter Street, Dr. Kamski pointed to a triangular fragment beside No. 63 Seaton no wider than the sidewalk.

“He asked, ‘Can we build something here?’” remembers Mr. Reuber. “I responded, ‘Only if you let me cut down the rose bush!’ Honestly, there hardly looked like there was enough room to plant a second one.”

But, as is often said, a great architect is one that transforms challenge into creativity: Frank Lloyd Wright’s Fallingwater, or Albert Frey’s Frey House II (Palm Springs, Calif.) come to mind. And, says Mr. Reuber, the design flowed from fingertips to drafting board “quickly.” But when Dr. Kamski turned his attention to another property, things were put on hold for “several years.” When work did begin, a vanishing contractor meant the foundations were wrapped up “for a few more years.”

The Architourist: New housing at a former 1940s bombing and gunnery school in Picton, Ont.

By the time “Triangle House” was done, it was a new millennium, and while Mr. Reuber would attend a few of Dr. Kamski’s parties there, by 2003 the house had been sold.

That owner, Catherine Osborne, was once editor-in-chief of the architecture and design magazine Azure. Inviting this writer to have a look at the place she’s called home for 23 years, she wrote: “look for the lime green door!”

Despite the bold colour, it’s an easy door to miss, since, depending on how one approaches No. 61 Seaton, the house itself can look like an addition, or due to the change in grade one can miss the lime green door completely as it sits much lower than the red door of No. 63.

Yet, like Russian nesting dolls in reverse, what starts out very, very small turns into big, expressive postmodern architecture.

Despite a façade not much wider than a door, step inside and one immediately senses an unravelling as the space opens up, visually. That’s due to the view up the stair into the hallway that leads to the kitchen, the view down to the entrance to the separate basement apartment, and, most importantly, the view directly overhead to the second- and third-floor balconies. And the fact that one is in a space filled with photons raining down from massive windows assisted by tiny, square, ‘surprise’ windows.

Walk inside and the surprises multiply. The kitchen, so compact and ship-like yet somehow spacious. The light wood cabinets, typical of 1990s design but rare today. The horizontal window over the sink, the two tiny, operable windows that take advantage of the Shuter façade’s ‘carve-in.’ These, say Mr. Reuber, capture “select street views.”

“But privacy was also important,” he continues. “So sometimes windows are small, sometimes they frame views, other times they are just below the ceiling to accommodate [Dr. Kamski’s] extensive art collection.”

“And when that door is open at the back and this,” adds Ms. Osborne as she cranks one of the tiny windows open, “you just get this nice breeze through; you can hear what’s going on in the street but they can’t see you.”

Walk into the living room, and the eye finds it difficult to choose between Mr. Reuber’s oculus window or the towering bookshelf Ms. Osborne had designed and built by Lebel & Bouliane. Which, in this writer’s opinion, fits right in with the PoMo aesthetic.

“I met Luc [Bouliane] at a party; he was just leaving Teeple Architects and starting his own studio,” remembers Ms. Osborne. “And I said, ‘Well, I’ve got this project.’”

There’s a little window-seat, too, that wasn’t there when Mr. Reuber handed the keys to Dr. Kamski, but many a four-legged friend has appreciated in the years since built.

Speaking of which, Ms. Osborne hasn’t changed little in here: the light parquet floors were stained darker; the foyer and kitchen flooring has been changed; a few Reuber-chosen colours have been painted white (thankfully some remain, including the triangle panels that interrupt staircase pickets); and there is a half-wall in the upstairs guest room. But Mr. Reuber’s exuberant, tiled bathrooms remain, his odd–yet wonderful–celebration of bulkheads is here, and those tiny windows have not been enlarged.

“It’s kind of a house of details,” says Ms. Osborne. “Every room has something that I really love; right now, we’re sitting in the living room and those two windows are my viewpoint. When I’m in my office looking out the moon window, I love that because there’s a tree right there. … Every piece has been taken into consideration.”

Dr. Kamski says Mr. Reuber should be “given credit for his bravery, persistence, complete faith in my abilities and [for] giving me carte blanche.”

And speaking of a clean slate, the next owner of this house should not erase anything. They should, in fact, take this postmodern time capsule and lean into it, hard. Re-lighten the floors; restore Mr. Reuber’s full colour scheme; restore the exterior metal sculpture/canopy near the front door to full neon green; and, if their budget permits, purchase some playful Memphis Group furniture.

Why else buy a legacy?

The house is listed by Iwona Rychalska and Cara Carney, the CR Team, with Royal LePage

stories.title: Carney must hit Iran's Ayatollah with sanctions and legal action, human rights advocates say
stories.summary: The Carney government should directly target Iran's leader and his allies with sanctions and legal action, advocates say.
stories.author: Simon Tuck
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Carney government should directly target Iran’s leader and his allies with sanctions and legal action to close the “impunity gap” and to ensure that this country doesn’t become a safe haven for repression, a coalition of human rights groups and an all-party group of MPs insisted Wednesday.

Speaking on Parliament Hill on the third anniversary of the Hamas-led terrorist attack on Israel that killed an estimated 1,200 people, the human rights advocates warned that more atrocities in Iran are likely if democratic governments don’t do more to limit the Iranian government’s power.

Irwin Cotler, a former Liberal MP and cabinet minister and now an advocate, told reporters that it’s a critical moment in the battle between human rights and the government of Iran. The government killed an estimated 40,000 protesters and critics over two days in January and has since followed with repressive techniques such as controlling mass communications and detentions, disappearances, torture, rape and more executions.

Cotler, who also faced an Iranian assassination plot for his efforts to call out the regime, said the Iranian regime’s repression tactics extend to other countries, including Canada.

Shilan Mirzaee, a democracy advocate and former political prisoner, held up a photo at the press conference of a young couple who were arrested a month ago, just a couple of days before they were to be married. He was then executed while she remains in prison.

Despite the U.S.-led attacks on Iran over the last seven months, that country is still governed by the Islamic Republic of Iran. Canada does not have diplomatic relations with Iran and Ottawa has designated its government a supporter of terrorism.

After tens of thousands of Iranians took to the streets earlier this year to protest soaring prices and a weak economy, government soldiers opened fire after demonstrators called for regime change. A widespread brutal crackdown ensued.

Less than two months later, the United States and Israel began large-scale strikes on Iranian facilities, reportedly out of concern about the advance of Iran’s efforts to build nuclear weapons. The early attacks in February killed the previous supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, 86, the current leader’s father, who had ruled since 1989.

The attacks and the war, which have led to oil supply problems and rising prices, have not ended.

stories.title: Delta Airlines plane collides with Air Canada jet at Los Angeles airport
stories.summary: Aerial footage shows part of the Delta plane’s wing dangling on the Air Canada plane’s rear stabilizer.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
An Air Canada jet was involved in a collision with a jet from Delta Air Lines at Los Angeles International Airport on Tuesday morning.

The pilot of the Air Canada plane can be heard telling an air traffic controller that they “felt a shudder” and asking if everything looked okay, according to audio captured by LiveATC.net. The Delta pilot informed air traffic control that they were stopping due to an “issue with the wing tip.”

The news station obtained aerial footage of the incident via its Sky 5 Telecopter, showing that other planes were operational nearby while ground crews attended to the two aircraft involved. The footage shows part of the Delta plane’s wing dangling on the Air Canada plane’s rear stabilizer, the horizontal fin perpendicular to the tail.

An investigation is ongoing, according to People Magazine . A spokesperson for LAX told People: “We are aware of an incident involving a Delta Air Lines aircraft and an Air Canada aircraft on a taxiway at LAX, not a runway. No injuries have been reported, and flights at LAX continue to operate normally. The FAA and the National Transportation Safety Board (were) notified.”

A Delta spokesperson told People that 275 customers and 15 crew members were on board at the time of the incident. No injuries were reported.

People stated that Air Canada spokesperson Sean Davidson told the publication its aircraft had recently arrived from a Toronto to L.A. flight. He confirmed it was being towed to the gate when “an aircraft operated by another airline made contact with its tail.”

No injuries were reported on the Air Canada plane. The aircraft was taken out of service for inspection and repairs.

stories.title: Ingersoll mayor quits conservation authority transition committee, citing secrecy
stories.summary: The mayor of Ingersoll, Ont., has resigned from the committee overseeing the merger of conservation authorities in southwestern Ontario, saying the process lacks the transparency and accountability the province promised.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
The mayor of Ingersoll, Ont., has resigned from the committee overseeing the merger of conservation authorities in southwestern Ontario, saying the process lacks the transparency and accountability the province promised.

Brian Petrie, chair of the Upper Thames River Conservation Authority (Utrca), quit the Western Lake Erie Regional Conservation Authority Transition Committee on Wednesday, effective immediately.

In a resignation letter shared online , Petrie said the process “lacks the openness required to justify my continued participation or to maintain public trust.”

Petrie told CTV News London he received the committee’s terms of reference, and a sweeping confidentiality agreement, only the Friday before a Monday meeting. He said the requirement was not part of the original appointment process.

“Had it been, I would not have put my name forward,” Petrie said.

He said the board tried to negotiate changes with the Ontario Provincial Conservation Agency, but the revised agreement was not enough.

“One of the reasons this amalgamation is taking place is better transparency and accountability,” Petrie said. “So to have a process, that has so much confidentiality put into it, is kind of a paradox.”

Petrie said the original agreement would have made him and the Utrca’s general manager personally liable if the province considered confidentiality broken, and that the province “didn’t have to prove it.”

The Utrca board later passed a motion to cover appointed members under its insurance, which allowed the general manager to join the committee.

Petrie said he would have agreed to confidentiality on sensitive matters such as legal or personnel issues. He said the terms went further than that.

“They couldn’t give a good answer, as far as I was concerned, about why everything needed to be controlled at that level,” he said.

Petrie said conservation authorities have long been municipally driven, and that the province has said they will remain locally governed and funded.

“One of those things is true. They’ll be municipally funded,” he said.

He said the new authorities will answer to a provincial agency, and that municipalities will continue to pay the bill.

In his letter, he said the closed-door committee “entirely excludes member municipalities from meaningful involvement.”

Petrie said upper-tier municipalities will appoint board members, and that the rules for who can be appointed have not been released. He said earlier rules required at least 70 per cent of members to be elected officials, and that this May change.

“Part of municipal government is open and transparent government,” he said.

Petrie said a motion has been passed to put his replacement on the board’s agenda next month. If the board doesn’t appoint someone, he said, the province can.

Three weeks ago, Petrie told CTV News he was uncomfortable with directions that committee members sign non-disclosure agreements.

The Utrca is set to merge with three other conservation authorities to form the Western Lake Erie Regional Conservation Authority. The consolidation is expected in early 2027.

Petrie stays on as chair of the Utrca. He is also seeking re-election as mayor of Ingersoll in the Oct. 26 municipal election.

“There needs to be a better balance between the voices at the municipal level and the province’s wishes,” Petrie said. “We need to work together better. And right now, that doesn’t seem to be happening. And really, I think it’s our residents who are going to pay the price for that.”

CTV News reached out to the Minister of the Environment, Conservation, and Parks for comment, however, spokesperson Alexandru Cioban sent the same statement that was issued to us three weeks ago.

“As we work to improve a fragmented and inconsistent conservation authority system, transition committees have been established to support a smooth transition and ensure conservation authorities have the tools they need to deliver more consistent services.

Throughout this process, conservation authorities remain municipally governed, and budget decisions continue to be made by conservation authority boards, which consist of representatives appointed by participating municipalities.

Confidentiality expectations are routine and regularly employed by municipalities when individuals have access to sensitive and confidential information, including financial, legal and human resources records.”

stories.title: Ontario COVID-19 vaccine rollout sees ‘delay’ in some regions
stories.summary: Some Ontario public health units say they are working to get doses out to administer to high-risk populations, but there is a delay.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
A central Ontario public health unit says seniors waiting for a COVID-19 vaccine May have to wait a bit longer due to a delay in getting doses to administer.

Lakelands Public Health, which serves areas including the Kawartha Lakes, Peterborough, Haliburton and Hiawatha First Nations, said in an email it received its vaccine supply last week.

“While adults aged 65 and older became eligible beginning the week of September 28, vaccine distribution takes time, and vaccine is continuing to arrive at pharmacies and health care providers in the region,” said Marianne Rock, manager of the vaccine preventable disease program for Lakelands Public Health.

“The current delay reflects the time required to distribute vaccine across the province,” Rock said in the emailed statement.

The vaccines were received by the health unit’s Lindsay, Peterborough and Port Hope offices.

Rock added that pharmacies in the region would begin receiving their supply this week and that there were “no concerns” about seniors not being able to get immunized against COVID-19.

The first vaccine shipments to pharmacies are expected to be delivered between Sept. 29 and Oct. 9 for COVID-19 vaccines, the Ontario Pharmacists Association said in an email. The reordering period then begins Oct. 26, it added.

“Technically it’s possible some pharmacies are still waiting for the COVID vaccine but there is no shortage of vaccine,” said Justin Bates, chief executive officer of the association.

On Sept. 25, the province issued a news release that the initial supply of COVID-19 and flu vaccines would be available for high-risk and priority groups who live, work and study in Ontario starting the week of Sept. 28.

The groups listed as eligible include hospitalized patients, hospital staff, residents and staff in long-term care homes, retirement homes and other congregate settings. Ontarians 65 and older were also included.

An official with the province told Global News on background that eligible high-risk people could start receiving the vaccine the week of Sept. 28, but added initial doses were prioritized to specific high-risk settings, like hospitals and long-term care homes.

2:03 Health Matters: Ontario begins phased roll out for flu, COVID-19 shots

In her statement, Rock added that while eligibility for seniors began on Sept. 28, vaccine supply “was not pre-positioned with local providers.” She said this was why it was taking time for doses to reach pharmacies and health-care providers.

Lakelands Public Health is not the only health unit reporting some delays.

The Northwestern Health Unit, Ottawa Public Health (OPH), the Windsor-Essex County Health Unit (Wechu) and Toronto Public Health each told Global News they have also received their initial vaccines.

Northwestern, OPH and Wechu said they are prioritizing getting the vaccine to high-risk facilities such as hospitals and long-term care homes. Northwestern and OPH said health-care providers and pharmacies in their regions that serve seniors are expected to receive supply throughout October.

Toronto Public Health said seniors in the city can contact their primary care provider or pharmacy to book their shot.

Northwestern also told Global News that seniors can currently book appointments for health unit-run clinics to be held next week.

According to the province, more than 620,000 COVID-19 doses had been distributed to pharmacies and public health units as of the end of Oct. 2.

“Hospitals, long term care homes, and other providers order directly from their public health unit, and public health units and pharmacies order vaccines through a pharmaceutical distributor,” said Lily Barnes, a spokesperson for Health Minister Sylvia Jones.

Barnes added the province had a “large supply” of vaccines available and more doses continue to be distributed as orders are placed.

Ontarians should check with their local pharmacy or public health unit to confirm availability, the province said.

The vaccine will be available to the general public starting Oct. 26.

Of the 620,330 vaccines distributed last week, a government official said on background, 501,940 doses had been delivered to pharmacies. Public health units receiving 118,390.

Lakelands Public Health, which serves areas including the Kawartha Lakes, Peterborough, Haliburton and Hiawatha First Nations, said in an email it received its vaccine supply last week.

“While adults aged 65 and older became eligible beginning the week of September 28, vaccine distribution takes time, and vaccine is continuing to arrive at pharmacies and health care providers in the region,” said Marianne Rock, manager of the vaccine preventable disease program for Lakelands Public Health.
“The current delay reflects the time required to distribute vaccine across the province,” Rock said in the emailed statement.
The vaccines were received by the health unit’s Lindsay, Peterborough and Port Hope offices.
Rock added that pharmacies in the region would begin receiving their supply this week and that there were “no concerns” about seniors not being able to get immunized against COVID-19.

The first vaccine shipments to pharmacies are expected to be delivered between Sept. 29 and Oct. 9 for COVID-19 vaccines, the Ontario Pharmacists Association said in an email. The reordering period then begins Oct. 26, it added.
“Technically it’s possible some pharmacies are still waiting for the COVID vaccine but there is no shortage of vaccine,” said Justin Bates, chief executive officer of the association.

On Sept. 25, the province issued a news release that the initial supply of COVID-19 and flu vaccines would be available for high-risk and priority groups who live, work and study in Ontario starting the week of Sept. 28.

The groups listed as eligible include hospitalized patients, hospital staff, residents and staff in long-term care homes, retirement homes and other congregate settings. Ontarians 65 and older were also included.

An official with the province told Global News on background that eligible high-risk people could start receiving the vaccine the week of Sept. 28, but added initial doses were prioritized to specific high-risk settings, like hospitals and long-term care homes.
2:03 Health Matters: Ontario begins phased roll out for flu, COVID-19 shots

In her statement, Rock added that while eligibility for seniors began on Sept. 28, vaccine supply “was not pre-positioned with local providers.” She said this was why it was taking time for doses to reach pharmacies and health-care providers.
Lakelands Public Health is not the only health unit reporting some delays.
The Northwestern Health Unit, Ottawa Public Health (OPH), the Windsor-Essex County Health Unit (Wechu) and Toronto Public Health each told Global News they have also received their initial vaccines.

Northwestern, OPH and Wechu said they are prioritizing getting the vaccine to high-risk facilities such as hospitals and long-term care homes. Northwestern and OPH said health-care providers and pharmacies in their regions that serve seniors are expected to receive supply throughout October.
Toronto Public Health said seniors in the city can contact their primary care provider or pharmacy to book their shot.
Northwestern also told Global News that seniors can currently book appointments for health unit-run clinics to be held next week.
According to the province, more than 620,000 COVID-19 doses had been distributed to pharmacies and public health units as of the end of Oct. 2.

“Hospitals, long term care homes, and other providers order directly from their public health unit, and public health units and pharmacies order vaccines through a pharmaceutical distributor,” said Lily Barnes, a spokesperson for Health Minister Sylvia Jones.
Barnes added the province had a “large supply” of vaccines available and more doses continue to be distributed as orders are placed.
Ontarians should check with their local pharmacy or public health unit to confirm availability, the province said.
The vaccine will be available to the general public starting Oct. 26.
