stories.title: Canadian portrait of King Charles III is the first of its kind in over 70 years
stories.summary: Painting of King in the Robes of Estate was commissioned by Nova Scotia, painted by Toronto doctor Suan-Seh Foo and will hang in Halifax.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
A Canadian doctor and painter has completed the first official portrait of King Charles III wearing the formal Robe of Estate.

The painting, by Toronto-based physician and artist Suan-Seh Foo , is the first to depict a reigning British monarch wearing those garments since Sir Herbert James Gunn’s portrait of Queen Elizabeth II , which hangs in Windsor Castle in England. It is also the first official portrait of Charles III to include the Orb and Sceptre alongside the Crown Imperial.

The painting was commissioned in 2024 by Arthur Joseph LeBlanc, the Lieutenant Governor of Nova Scotia, ON behalf of that province. Approval was received through the offices of the Canadian Secretary to the King, Canada’s senior operational member of the royal household for the monarch. It’s a position held by Donald Booth since 2019.

“We were just delighted to be given such a great piece of portraiture for a government house,” Christopher McCreery, Private Secretary to the current Lieutenant Governor, Mike Savage, told National Post. “So we were quite happy that it would be shown in London to highlight the connection that Canada and Nova Scotia has with the King and with the U.K.”

The oil-on-canvas portrait measures approximately eight and a half feet by six and a half feet and features a carved gold frame dating to the 18th century.

Charles III is shown wearing the uniform of the Royal Regiment of Canada, whose garrison is at Fort York Armoury in Toronto, and of which the King is Colonel-in-chief. Visible in the background is the top of the Halifax Town Clock, built in 1803 on the orders of Prince Edward, Duke of Kent, father of Queen Victoria and great-great-great-great-grandfather of the King.

Edward, who served as military commander of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and later as commander-in-chief of British forces in the Maritime Provinces of North America, lived in Halifax between 1794 and 1800.

Of the Town Clock in the painting, McCreery said: “Anyone who knows Halifax, the first thing they say is that’s Halifax. The clock tower is so associated with the city, and also with the Royal Family. So there’s these fun little royal connections that are woven throughout the city, and obviously Dr. Foo has woven them into the portrait as well.”

The portrait also depicts the throne of William IV, currently housed in the Throne Room at St James’s Palace. On the left of the portrait is a rudder bearing the insignia of the Royal Canadian Navy. A bouquet of Mayflowers, the official flower of Nova Scotia, can also be seen on the left of the image near the King’s hand.

Foo held a formal consultation with Ede & Ravenscroft robe makers, who provided samples of velvet, lace and gimp from coronation robes, as well as the elaborate cords and tassels used in the King’s robes. He was also briefed on the technicalities of dressing a monarch for such a ceremony. Captain Nicholas A. Lishchynsky, a member of the Royal Regiment of Canada based at the Fort York Armoury, posed in full uniform to help Foo ensure the details were accurate.

Born in Singapore, Foo is a member of the Worshipful Company of Woolmen, a London livery guild dating back to the 12th century, and a Freeman of the City of London . He has previously completed two portraits of Pope Benedict XVI for the Vatican and a 2011 portrait of Queen Elizabeth II that hangs in Rhodes House in Oxford. In addition to his artistic pursuits, he directs a not-for-profit clinic in Toronto treating addiction and mental health.

The Robe of Estate is different from the Robe of State in that the latter is worn by the monarch on arrival at Westminster Abbey for the coronation ceremony, and the former is worn during departure. The Robe of State is crimson or red velvet, while the Robe of Estate is purple silk velvet.

Foo told National Post that his first emotion on completing the painting was “relief.”

“We want to show that we are loyal,” he said of the London showing. “There are Canadians, myself included, who believe in the Crown and believe that this unites the country. We also want to tell the British that this is important, that we matter.”

McCreery said the hope is to have the portrait installed at Government House, the official residence of the Lieutenant Governor, before Christmas, “so that it will be on display for the New Year’s Levy, which is one of the big events that we hold.” He’s expecting upwards of 700 people to attend.

stories.title: Crash involving school bus and gravel truck under investigation near Stratford
stories.summary: Perth County OPP are investigating a crash involving a school bus and gravel truck near Stratford.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
Perth County OPP are investigating a crash involving a school bus and gravel truck near Stratford.

On Wednesday morning around 7:40 a.m., emergency services responded to the incident at the intersection of Line 39 and Road 125.

The bus driver sustained serious injuries, and an adult passenger sustained life-threatening injuries. Police confirmed there were no students on board at the time.

The driver of the gravel truck sustained minor injuries.

Line 39 is closed between Road 130 and Road 122. Road 125 is also closed between Line 42 and Line 36. These closures are expected to stay in place for several hours as the investigation continues. Drivers are asked to avoid the area.

If you witnessed the crash or have video surveillance or dash cam footage of it, you are asked to contact Perth County OPP at 1-888-310-1122. Anonymous tips can also be sent to Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477.

stories.title: Playwright Robert Winslow turned his farm into a theatre that celebrated rural life
stories.summary: On his family homestead in the Ontario countryside, he built 4th Line Theatre, where he crafted plays from local stories and staged them with help from local residents
stories.author: James Cullingham
stories.content:
In 1990, Robert Winslow moved back to Millbrook, Ont., to look after his aging mother on the farm where he was raised, land that had been in his family since the 1880s. At that point he had been working for nearly a decade as a professional actor.

When she died, he inherited the farm, but he knew he didn’t want to be a farmer. He was a playwright, and he wondered if the rolling landscape where his roots ran deep could produce something other than crops.

At the time, Winslow Farm didn’t look like much of a theatre. The grass was overgrown. Rocks and rusted equipment littered the property. Kim Blackwell, then a young artist helping prepare Mr. Winslow’s first production, remembers looking around and thinking, “Nobody’s going to come and see theatre, but this is fun.”

His focus and drive to get the first play onstage were unlike anything she had ever seen.

In the summer of 1992, hay bales became seats and the farm became the setting for The Cavan Blazers , Mr. Winslow’s first full-length play, based on the violent conflict between Protestant and Catholic Irish settlers in the township. It was the beginning of 4th Line Theatre, co-founded by Mr. Winslow and Jerome Ackhurst in Peterborough, Ont.

Before the first Friday performance had opened, the planned six-show run had sold out. It eventually stretched to six weeks. Professional actors performed alongside community volunteers in a play rooted in local history, establishing a standard that 4th Line Theatre would follow for decades.

“He was going to make it happen no matter what,” said Ms. Blackwell, now 4th Line’s artistic director.

The familiar Field of Dreams line, “If you build it, they will come,” has been invoked by many remembering Mr. Winslow, who died on Sept. 12 after playing hockey that morning and finishing a first draft of a play the night before. He was 73.

His legacy is a place where people come together – a stage where artists find their voice and generations of spectators who see themselves reflected in stories about the landscape they call home.

“There are some people who have a kind of an alchemy or a magic that is hard to quantify, and he had that. Robert gathered the stories of the people who lived around him and gave those stories back to his community as theatre,” Ms. Blackwell said. “He celebrated rural Canadian life without romanticizing it, exploring its humour, contradictions, hardships and humanity with an artist’s curiosity and a profound love of place.”

Through his theatre career, spanning more than 45 years, Mr. Winslow was a playwright, actor, director, artistic director, teacher and mentor. His honours included Queen Elizabeth II’s Golden Jubilee Medal, induction into the Peterborough and District Pathway of Fame and the Junior Achievement Peterborough, Lakeland, Muskoka Business Hall of Fame, and an Outstanding Senior Artist Award at the Peterborough Arts Awards.

Yet as a teenager, he couldn’t wait to get out of rural Ontario. After starting his career at the Peterborough Theatre Guild as a prompter in 1978, he went on to study at York University and St. Michael’s College, at the University of Toronto. By 1982, he was based in Edmonton, performing there at the Theatre Network, Northern Light Theatre, Citadel Theatre, Catalyst, Nexus Theatre and the Fringe Festival, and also appeared at the Blyth Festival, in Ontario’s Huron County.

Playwright Leanna Brodie first encountered him around 1983, when she was still in high school. Mr. Winslow was performing with Peterborough’s Magic Circus Theatre and wearing round John Lennon sunglasses and a T-shirt that read “Stop Rocky Five.”

She remembers thinking he was a “fully fledged artist”: cool, self-contained and “very rock and roll.”

“He embedded the arts in that community forever. So when people just think, oh, art is something that happens in downtown Toronto, he proved to generations of people that it literally can happen in the fields and the barnyards where he grew up, that it can be part of your life and part of your soul wherever you are,” Ms. Brodie said.

Mr. Winslow wanted to develop stories not just about the community, but with them. After he decided to transform his family farm into a theatre, his curiosity led him to talk with local Indigenous elders and transcribe their stories.

His choice to return to his rural homestead was unusual in an industry whose most prominent institutions, festivals and artistic leaders tend to be concentrated in cities. Mr. Winslow had worked in that world.

His wife, Janette Froncz, knows what it’s like to move to unexpected places to hone one’s craft. Before meeting Mr. Winslow, she had taught dance in Yellowknife before moving to Peterborough to run a ballet and dance studio. She would act in and choreograph his plays. They got married in 2000.

“This farming community and the surrounding region really became theatregoers, theatre actors. Someone would have been farming all day, and got off the tractor and got on stage,” Ms. Froncz said.

“We needed the farmers. We needed the people who weren’t professionals to help tell stories, and they had stories. You’re told that the only stories that get told are in the States and Hollywood. But we have an endless amount. Then people see that our stories matter and therefore, our lives matter,” she said.

In the 1970s, Mr. Winslow took a summer course in modern theatre at Trent University taught by former Cultural Studies chair and professor emeritus Ian McLachlan. They would become friends and writing partners for decades. Mr. McLachlan recalled that some area residents didn’t agree with Mr. Winslow’s honest approach to storytelling, and were afraid to open up their hometown’s memories.

“No one can escape the past by trying to bury it,” Mr. McLachlan remembers him saying.

Digging up the truth would take commitment. While researching his 2009 play Welcome Death , about the 1873 murder of Millbrook resident Elizabeth Deyell, Mr. Winslow retraced her roughly 35-kilometre journey from Millbrook through Port Hope to Welcome, Ont., ON foot – in February. He later travelled to Ireland while researching the coroner who investigated her death.

In 2005, Mr. McLachlan and Mr. Winslow also created Doctor Barnardo’s Children , part of a series exploring the experiences of British home children sent to Canada.

Child actors as young as seven years old joined the production of Doctor Barnardo’s Children , and they began growing up around the theatre.

Some returned for other plays. Others put themselves through school as apprentices, stage managers or front-of-house workers. Some went on to become actors, but others became doctors, scientists and professors. Ms. Froncz and her husband didn’t have children, but said the ones they got to know over the years became like their own.

Generations of young people found opportunities at 4th Line Theatre. By the company’s 30th anniversary, around 2,000 young people had participated in 4th Line apprenticeships. The establishment of an endowment fund, called “30 to the Future,” will help sustain that work for years to come.

This past summer, Mr. Winslow put on Ms. Brodie’s Schoolhouse , reprising a role he had performed 19 years earlier. On opening night, many of the actors who had played children in the earlier production returned to the farm. At the same time, one of Mr. Winslow’s scene partners was an actor fresh out of the National Theatre School, performing her first professional job.

Ms. Brodie has seen Mr. Winslow’s investment in young artists firsthand. As 4th Line’s first playwright in residence, she had to venture to farm kitchens and verandas all over Cavan Township for research and interviews for her 4th Line plays, Schoolhouse and For Home and Country . There was one problem: She couldn’t drive.

“Rob would generally have to pick me up at the Peterborough Greyhound Bus station and then ferry me around from one cup of tea and plate of cookies to the next. Sometimes I even stayed with him and Janette. We stared at many a sunset together,” Ms. Brodie said.

She knew that initially they were only willing to open up because they trusted Mr. Winslow.

“They knew what it was to stand in those fields, in those barnyards, in those theatres, and have their stories, their parents’ stories, their grandparents’ stories honoured,” Ms. Brodie said.

After handing the position of artistic director to Ms. Blackwell in 2014, Mr. Winslow had more time to focus on what he loved. He taught theatre performance workshops and courses at Trent University until his death. Mr. Winslow wrote or co-wrote 18 original plays, directed 25 and acted in 30 at 4th Line Theatre.

In the final two years of his life, Mr. Winslow interviewed former students for a new play about the former Millbrook High School, carefully recording and transcribing everything himself.

On Friday, Sept. 11, he finished the first draft. That evening, he and Ms. Froncz sat together on the porch while he ran over scenes from the new play with her. She says they were “funny, sweet and entertaining.”

The next morning, Mr. Winslow, a big Montreal Canadiens fan, went to play hockey. He died later that day.

Ms. Froncz will continue to live on the farm, and next summer she will welcome audiences for 4th Line Theatre’s 35th season.

With its open-air stage, 4th Line is just as beholden to the weather as any other farm, Ms. Blackwell says. The weather co mes in from the west, over the Oak Ridges Moraine, a 160-kilometre-long geological landform. As his kin taught him, Mr. Winslow would stand in a field and look west.

Now, hay bales have been replaced by proper seating, and the farm has equipment that measures how far off lightning strikes are. But he taught them how to watch the weather. So at the end of each summer day, Ms. Blackwell still walks into the field and looks west.

“We don’t farm food or animals,” Ms. Blackwell said, “but I have always said we farm plays.”

Mr. Winslow leaves his wife, Ms. Froncz.

stories.title: New Brunswick utility is proposing rate hikes over next three years
stories.summary: New Brunswick's public utility is proposing to raise electricity rates by an average of 5.5 per cent for each of the next three years.
stories.author: Eli Ridder
stories.content:
By Eli Ridder The Canadian Press

Posted October 7, 2026 2:31 pm

New Brunswick’s public utility is proposing to raise electricity rates by an average of 5.5 per cent for each of the next three years.

NB Power says the proposed hike works out to an increase of $13.25 a month for a home using 1,350 kilowatt hours.

The utility says the rate hike is needed to cover the costs of maintaining and modernizing its aging system.

Utility executives say it is proposing three years of rates hikes in its submission — a first for NB Power — to allow households and businesses to plan ahead.

The new rates could come into force next April following a review by New Brunswick’s power regulator.

Last year, NB Power proposed a 4.75 per cent increase and the final number approved by the board was 4.29 per cent for the current fiscal year.

NB Power indicated that its proposal could push local rates higher than some other provinces.

An independent review of NB Power by three experts earlier this year detailed how the utility is struggling to cope with challenges such as its aging infrastructure and a $6-billion debt.

Officials say the new plan slows the increase of its debt, but does not decrease it.

stories.title: Child safety advocate says N.S. changes to car seat rules makes province ‘leader’ in country
stories.summary: Nova Scotia has released the first set of regulations under its new Traffic Safety Act, which includes Canada's first age-based minimums for children's car seats.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Nova Scotia has released the first set of regulations under its new Traffic Safety Act, which includes Canada’s first age-based minimums for children’s car seats.

The act was passed in the fall of 2025 and takes effect Oct. 19. It will replace the existing Motor Vehicle Act, which was first introduced in the 1920s.

The new regulations include modernizing distracted driving rules to include current technology, creating a framework for inclusive cyclist rules and establishing clearer rules for “emerging vehicle types” like electric scooters.

They also include a requirement that children remain in a rear-facing car seat until at least the age of two and remain in a harnessed car seat until the age of four.

According to Child Safety Link, the children’s injury prevention program at IWK Health, Nova Scotia will become the first province or territory in Canada to enshrine these age-based minimums in law.

Katherine Hutka, a health promotion specialist with Child Safety Link, says she’s thrilled the province has taken the steps to entrench the age minimums in law and that “Nova Scotia is the leader on this.”

“We need other provinces to take notice, she said.

“We want kids across Canada to be safe too.”

5:09 Child Passenger Safety Awareness Week: Are you using car seats correctly?

The changes exist alongside the current weight requirements. A child must be 22 lbs in order to use a forward-facing seat and weigh at least 40 lbs to move up to a booster seat.

A study conducted by Dalhousie University in collaboration with Child Safety Link that was released last fall found that eight in 10 car or booster seats for children are improperly used in Nova Scotia.

Among the most common errors were harnesses that were too loose and car seats that weren’t securely attached to the vehicle. As well, people were moving through the phases of seats too quickly.

Child Safety Link says tests have shown that rear-facing car seats better protect a young child’s disproportionately large head and vulnerable neck and spine during frontal crashes.

Aside from the province’s new minimum age laws, Child Safety Link says it continues to recommend that children remain in each stage of car seats for as long as they fit safely within the height and weight limits of the seat.

It points out that many children can actually remain rear-facing beyond age two. It also recommends children continue using a car seat with a five-point harness until they’re developmentally ready to use a booster correctly, which May not be until age five to seven.

“Minimum legal requirements are a starting point, not necessarily the point when a child should move to the next stage,” said Hutka.

stories.title: Hydro pole intentionally cut, causing outage in south London
stories.summary: London police are investigating after they say a hydro pole was intentionally cut down in the city’s south end, causing a power outage for a number of London Hydro customers.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
London police are investigating after they say a hydro pole was intentionally cut down in the city’s south end, causing a power outage for a number of London Hydro customers.

Police said emergency crews responded around 5:45 p.m. Tuesday after a citizen reported hearing a loud noise and seeing smoke and flames near a hydro pole in the area of Exeter Road and Meg Drive.

Officers arrived on scene alongside the London Fire Department and London Hydro, where they found multiple downed power lines and a damaged hydro pole.

According to London Hydro, a chainsaw was used to cut down the pole carrying a three-phase transformer bank. Damage is estimated at approximately $10,000.

As a result of the incident, several London Hydro customers lost power. The utility has since completed repairs and electricity has been restored to all affected customers.

No injuries were reported.

Police have released images of a suspect and a vehicle believed to be connected to the incident in hopes of identifying those involved.

The suspect is described as a white man wearing a ball cap, a black hooded sweatshirt with writing across the chest and grey pants.

The vehicle is described as a grey sport utility vehicle, believed to be a 2019 Honda CR-V or a similar model.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 5:20 p.m. and 6 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 6, who witnessed the incident or has dashcam, residential or business surveillance footage to contact London police.

stories.title: Michigan Republican candidate breaks with Trump over tariffs on Canada
stories.summary: Washington - Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers has broken with U.S. President Donald Trump over his trade war with Canada.
stories.author: Kelly Geraldine Malone The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Washington - Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers has broken with U.S. President Donald Trump over his trade war with Canada as the Republican faces a tight race in a state hit hard by the tariffs.

In a campaign ad posted on social media Wednesday, Rogers said people in Michigan “know that Canada is not our enemy.”

“We need to end this tariff war now,” Rogers said in the ad, which shows the Republican sitting at a bar and holding a Labatt’s beer.

While Rogers doesn’t mention Trump’s name in the ad, it marks a shift in messaging for the former congressman, who previously said tariffs are necessary but not a one-size-fits-all solution.

But the president’s trade war with Canada has become a ballot issue in the close race between Rogers and Democrat candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

Trump rapidly escalated his trade war and rhetoric against Canada after negotiations fell apart in August.

Trump signed an order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America and the United States hit an array of Canadian goods with 50 per cent tariffs. A few weeks later, Ottawa responded with its own retaliatory duties.

Last week, a U.S. import ban on some Canadian liquor, whey products and motorcycles officially took effect.

El-Sayed has been making Canada an election issue in the border state, which is being hit hard by Trump’s tariff regime. Michigan’s economy is deeply integrated with many Canadian communities, particularly in the automobile industry.

In response to Rogers’ Wednesday ad, El-Sayed said the Republican has supported Trump’s tariffs from the beginning.

In a news release, El-Sayed said Trump is the reason for the trade war and the reason Rogers is running. He said his opponent is “not a serious person.”

“Must have had one too many of those Labatts, Mike,” El-Sayed said, adding Rogers supported the tariff war “from the beginning” and is “flip-flopping now” because his poll numbers “are in freefall.”

More Republicans have been distancing their campaigns from the president as multiple polls show Trump’s approval rating is dropping over the war with Iran, higher gas prices, inflation and controversial immigration tactics.

Matthew Lebo, a political-science professor at Western University in London, Ont., said polls are showing a general shift towards Democrats compared to the 2024 election, and that has put many Senate races in play ahead of the midterm elections next month.

Democrats would need to achieve a net gain of four seats to get the Senate majority. The Michigan race in particular could prove critical.

“Michigan is as close to a 50-50 state as there is, having voted since 2008 for Obama, Obama, Trump, Biden and Trump,” Lebo said in a text message.

Rogers is not an incumbent, Lebo added, so it’s harder to link him with all of Trump’s more contentious moves as president.

“He can try to paint himself as an independent-minded Republican who will break with Trump when it’s the right thing for Michiganders,” Lebo said. “That’s a good strategy to get Republicans to the polls even if they are unhappy with Trump.”

Trump praised Rogers during a highly unusual Republican convention in Texas last month. The Michigan Senate candidate also spoke during the event, billed as “Trump-a-Palooza” — he repeatedly criticized his opponent but did not address the trade war with Canada.

When asked about the ad at the White House later Wednesday, Trump said he saw it as Rogers saying Canada should make a deal.

“I viewed him as saying he thinks Canada should make a deal,” Trump said, before repeating his claims about Canada ripping off the United States.

Trump added Canada wants to make a deal but his administration is not satisfied.

stories.title: Drake, Jessie Reyez to be honoured with Socan Awards
stories.summary: Toronto heavyweights among artists celebrated at annual gala for Canadian songwriters, composers and music publishers
stories.author: Alex Nino Gheciu
stories.content:
Jessie Reyez and Drake will be toasted with special achievement honours at the 2026 Socan Awards.

The two Toronto hip-hop and R&B heavyweights are among the artists being celebrated at the annual gala for Canadian songwriters, composers and music publishers.

Reyez will receive the international achievement award for “representing Canada on the global stage” and “influencing music and culture with her talent.” The Canadian-Colombian artist has won several Juno Awards and collaborated with superstars including Eminem and Beyoncé.

Drake will claim his fifth consecutive award for songwriter of the year in the performer category for “his unmatched influence on music worldwide.”

The Toronto rap star made history earlier this year by shattering several Billboard records with his triple-album release, including the longstanding title previously held by Michael Jackson for most No. 1s by a solo male artist.

The Socan Awards will take place Oct. 26 at Rebel nightclub in Toronto, and will be hosted by actor Andrew Phung and TV personality Arisa Cox.

Socan, which stands for the Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada, is a non-profit that manages licensing fees and protects the rights of homegrown songwriters.

Among other honourees this year are Toronto rapper Maestro Fresh Wes and producers Anthony Davis and Peter Davis for their 1989 hit Let Your Backbone Slide .

Socan says the song, which was the first single from a Canadian hip-hop artist to go gold in the country, is a “global success story.”

Quebec singer-songwriter Peter Peter will take home the global impact award for composing the original music for Crave’s hit hockey romance “Heated Rivalry.”

Calgary singer-songwriter-producer Jenna Andrews will receive the songwriter of the year award in the non-performer category for co-writing and co-producing several songs on the soundtrack for Netflix’s hit animated film KPop Demon Hunters .

Toronto’s Nathan Micay will get the breakout composer award for making waves by scoring Hbo’s hit high-finance drama Industry .

Victoria singer-songwriter Jade LeMac will be presented the breakout songwriter award for being “one of the most exciting new voices in Canadian music.”

All winners receive “The Socan,” a trophy that also functions as a musical instrument. Its five custom bronze crotales will be tuned this year to the notes from Let Your Backbone Slide .

Last month, Socan launched a lawsuit against U.S. artificial intelligence company Suno, alleging the AI music generator copied songs in its repertoire without permission or compensation.

stories.title: Artificial intelligence in ways nobody knew before
stories.summary: Artificial intelligence as we know it is rapidly changing everyday. Most people hear the term AI, and what sim...
stories.author: Samantha Luis
stories.content:
Artificial intelligence as we know it is rapidly changing everyday.

Most people hear the term AI, and what simply comes to mind is generative AI. According to Luisa Liboni, a professor at Western University and King’s College, artificial intelligence is really an umbrella term, “the term AI in the AI field is an old one, the term was coined in the 1950s, for systems that could do tasks that normally needed human intelligence.”

It’s hard to miss the current spike in generative AI. Magdalene Thomas, a professor at Fanshawe College says, “every application right now has some kind of AI feature attached to it and it’s become the norm. It’s just become part of our day to day living.”

Photo by: Samantha Luis

In classrooms especially, AI has taken a large hit to students learning process. Thomas says that courses are now changing and adapting so you can no longer just copy and paste from programs like Chat GPT.

“AI especially generative AI has to improve the learning experience, and speed up the learning process, it shouldn’t replace it,” Thomas said.

“Those students have to ask themselves if they are thinking and if they know what they’re doing, if we take AI off the plate,” Liboni said.

This change has had a big impact with students. Fanshawe’s online portal now has the option for professors to choose how much AI is allowed within the classroom.

Thomas says, “it helps in the learning process itself. But at the same time, there are also other courses, which I can’t speak on like journalism for example, you have to write a story on your own and you have to have that creativity within you. You cannot rely on AI completely. It has to aid or it has to be enhancing your creativity rather than replacing it.”

Many people don’t know what AI really is, the biggest assumption online is that AI will be taking over jobs.

“AI is definitely not going to take over jobs, but if you don’t keep up with AI and keep yourself updated and know how to use these AI tools and how to use it for your advantage, You are definitely going to be left behind,” said Thomas

Founder and president of Haggerty Agrobotics, Chuck Baresich says he has lots of concerns for generative AI.

“If we are not using the AI tools for a good purpose, or for a meaningful purpose, well, then all we’re doing is wasting energy. And I think that is harmful,” he said.

Agriculture uses AI in a complete different way from generative AI.

“One of the machines use an AI system to analyze the images that the implement is taking as it’s going across the field. And then once it analyzes those images, we can tell what is a weed and what is a plant,” he said.

He says the use of artificial intelligence in farming can lead to more plant yield and crop growth.

stories.title: Western neuroscientists developing ‘digital brain’ using video games
stories.summary: Western University neuroscientists are studying brain in a way that mimics real life by having people play video games inside an fMRI scanner.
stories.author: Jeff Renaud
stories.content:
For decades, neuroscientists have studied the human brain by asking people to lie very still inside a brain scanner and perform carefully controlled tasks. Those experiments have revealed a remarkable amount about how the brain works. But they also leave out something fundamental.

Real life is not a series of isolated tasks. We are constantly perceiving the world, making predictions, deciding what to do, acting on our surroundings and adjusting our behaviour when those actions produce unexpected results.

Now, Western University neuroscientists Jörn Diedrichsen and Jody Culham are helping lead an international effort to study the brain in a way that more closely mimics this complexity – by putting people inside an fMRI scanner and having them play video games.

The work is part of the Digital Brain Project , a large international research initiative supported by social media giant Meta that aims to create a massive, openly shared dataset of human brain activity. The project brings together researchers from institutions around the world, including Western, to explore how the brain behaves across a much broader range of cognitive states than conventional brain imaging typically captures.

Diedrichsen has spent years developing ways to map brain activity across many different tasks, including the Raynor Cerebellum Project , rather than relying primarily on resting-state scans or one carefully isolated experiment at a time. His lab has developed a battery of more than 60 tasks that can be performed during an fMRI scan, allowing researchers to push one participant’s brain into many different states. “Think of brain activity as an enormous landscape. At any given moment, your brain is somewhere in that landscape, and different experiences, decisions and actions move you to different places,” said Diedrichsen, a computer science professor.

Resting-state fMRI – or functional magnetic resonance imaging, which measures brain activity through changes in blood flow – allows researchers to observe the brain’s spontaneous fluctuations, but gives them little control over where in that landscape the brain goes. Diedrichsen’s multi-task approach deliberately samples a much wider range of brain activity.

Western University neuroscientists Jörn Diedrichsen and Jody Culham, who are working together on the Digital Brain Project. (Christopher Kindratsky/Western Communications)

Diedrichsen and Culham saw a way to bring their strategies together – his work on sampling a broad range of brain activity with her lab’s work on how the brain responds when people actively interact with changing environments. Video games offered a way to put both ideas into the same project.

When someone is playing a game like Pac-Man, they are constantly making predictions. A ghost is approaching, so they change direction. They move the controller, Pac-Man responds, the environment changes and the player immediately updates their plan,” said Culham, Canada Research Chair in Immersive Neuroscience and psychology professor.

It is a continuous loop of prediction, action and feedback, which is fundamentally different from asking someone to look at an image and press a button to indicate what they see.

In previous work, Culham’s lab has compared people playing Pac-Man with people watching the game and with people moving a controller that has no effect on the game. The sensory experience and physical movements can be similar, but the player’s relationship with the environment is completely different.

This experience of making predictions, taking action and getting feedback is called a ‘closed loop’ between the person and the environment. And that loop May be one of the most important things missing from conventional approaches to studying the brain.

Rather than simply asking participants to perform a long list of conventional laboratory tasks, Diedrichsen and Culham are combining carefully designed cognitive tasks with immersive video games, which will be built around rich 3D environments and first-person avatars

A core set of tasks will remain as anchors for data comparison – including activities like kart-racing, action and crafter video games, digital puzzles and go-kart racing, while new tasks and game elements will be introduced throughout the Digital Brain Project.

“By gamifying conventional tasks, our project can provide a bridge between strategies to understand well-established cognitive functions and strategies to provide maximal entertainment and engagement,” said Culham, who like Diedrichsen, is a faculty member in the Western Institute for Neuroscience . “That gives us a way to explore a much broader range of brain states while also capturing the brain as it predicts, acts and adapts.”

The new study is beginning as Western upgrades one of the key pieces of equipment needed to conduct it. Western is investing in an upgraded 7-Tesla MRI scanner, a powerful system housed at the Centre for Functional and Metabolic Mapping capable of producing markedly higher-quality images than conventional MRI systems.

For the Digital Brain Project, the researchers are also developing a new 32-channel head coil designed to improve data collected from deep brain structures, including the cerebellum, thalamus and midbrain. That matters particularly to Diedrichsen, whose research focuses on the cerebellum and its connections with the cerebral cortex.

“We’ve traditionally thought of the cerebellum as being about movement and coordination, but it’s increasingly clear that it’s also involved in prediction and cognition. That makes it a really interesting part of the brain to study when you’re looking at how people interact with a changing environment,” said Diedrichsen.

The upgraded scanner will also provide a much larger visual display, making it possible to create more immersive environments for participants lying inside the scanner. The researchers are working toward 3D displays that could make the participant feel as though they are inside the game world, despite being physically confined to the MRI.

One of the project’s larger ambitions is to move beyond the idea of the “average” human brain. Individual brains can differ considerably, particularly in regions involved in complex actions and cognition, and Diedrichsen wants to collect rich data from individual participants across many different activities.

“If you take a picture of a forest and put all the trees on top of each other, you get a very blurry picture of what a tree actually looks like, brown on the bottom, green on top,” said Diedrichsen. “The same thing happens when we average brains together. We want to understand the individual brain in much more detail.”

That kind of deep individual mapping could eventually help researchers understand why brains are organized differently from one person to another and how that May influence behaviour. For now, however, the goal is to create a large, high-quality dataset researchers around the world can use, with the project’s data openly shared for non-commercial research.

“AI is only as good as the data you give it. If you don’t have good data, you’re starting with garbage. What we’re trying to do is build the kind of rich, high-quality dataset that allows people to ask new questions and apply new methods we haven’t even thought of yet,” said Diedrichsen.

AI will also become part of the experiment itself, with researchers developing artificial systems that can learn cognitive tasks and play simple games. By examining how those systems learn to navigate, predict and make decisions, scientists can explore possible solutions to problems faced by biological brains, using them as what Diedrichsen calls an “intuition pump” for thinking about how complex systems work.

The researchers are not suggesting resting-state fMRI or conventional task-based experiments should disappear. Instead, they see the video-game approach as opening another part of the brain’s functional landscape – one that has been difficult to reach with experiments built around isolated questions and tightly controlled responses.

“We’re trying closely study the brain as it actually works,” said Culham. “Video games give us a way to bring some of that into the scanner and start asking what the brain is doing when it’s engaged in the world.”

stories.title: Loaded handgun, drugs seized in Sarnia raid
stories.summary: A 49-year-old Mississauga man is facing a string of drug and firearms charges after Sarnia police seized cocaine, methamphetamine and a loaded handgun during a search of a property on London Line.
stories.content:
A 49-year-old Mississauga man is facing a string of drug and firearms charges after Sarnia police seized cocaine, methamphetamine and a loaded handgun during a search of a property on London Line.

During the search, officers seized approximately 176 grams of methamphetamine, 54 grams of cocaine, more than $1,100 in cash and a loaded Taurus 9 mm handgun with additional ammunition.

Police estimate the street value of the drugs at about $16,000.

Investigators allege the accused was under a lifetime firearms prohibition at the time of the arrest.

A 49-year-old man from Mississauga has been charged with multiple firearms and drug offences, including possession of a prohibited firearm, possession of a firearm and ammunition while prohibited, carrying a concealed weapon, carrying a weapon for a dangerous purpose, possession of property obtained by crime, and possession for the purpose of trafficking cocaine and methamphetamine.

Investigators noted this is the second handgun seized from an alleged Greater Toronto Area-based drug trafficker operating in Sarnia within the last three months.

stories.title: London man charged after barricade standoff, threats toward police
stories.summary: A London man is facing multiple charges after a police standoff in the city’s southeast end earlier this week.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A London man is facing multiple charges after a police standoff in the city’s southeast end earlier this week.

The London Police Service says officers were called to a home on Frontenac Road at about 6:05 a.m. Monday for a welfare check.

Upon arrival, police learned the man had barricaded himself inside the home. Members of the Emergency Response Unit were called in and nearby roads were closed while officers attempted to negotiate with him.

Police allege the man exited the residence shortly after 7 a.m. and threw an object toward officers. No injuries were reported. Investigators say he then threw another object at the windshield of a London police light armoured vehicle before retreating back inside the home. The vehicle was not damaged.

About 10 minutes later, police say the man emerged from the residence armed with a knife and uttered threats toward officers. Negotiations continued while police maintained containment of the property.

At about 10:05 a.m., the man exited the residence and was taken into custody without injury.

As a result of the investigation, a 20-year-old of London is charged with two counts of assaulting a peace officer with a weapon, failing to comply with a release order, and uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm.

stories.title: Average asking rents fall 4.2% in September, marking two years of declines
stories.summary: Rent prices down 7.3% over that period
stories.author: Daniel Johnson
stories.content:
The average asking price for a rental unit in September was $2,034, down 4.2 per cent compared with a year ago.

A monthly report from Rentals.CA and Urbanation said the figures mark two full years of annual declines, the longest downturn the Canadian rental market has experienced in recent history.

Average asking rent prices in September were down 7.3 per cent over the past two years and 9.2 per cent below the peak of $2,202 in May 2024. The report also highlighted figures from Statistics Canada that show average weekly earnings have risen 19.4 per cent over the past five years, signifying a general improvement in rental affordability.

Rents edged slightly lower on a monthly basis, down by $1 compared with $2,035 in August, a second consecutive monthly decrease. The report said this is part of a typical seasonal pattern where demand rises in the spring and summer and begins to ease in the fall.

Across the provinces, average rents for all property segments were down 4.8 per cent year-over-year in Ontario, 2.9 per cent in B.C., 2.6 per cent in Alberta and 1.7 per cent in Quebec. In contrast, other provinces saw increases, including 1.4 per cent rises in both Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan.

On a square foot basis, average asking rents in Canada’s six largest markets came in at $2.48, falling 1.5 per cent from September 2025.

Asking rents for purpose-built apartments fell 2.7 per cent on an annual basis to an average of $2,036 in September, while asking rents for condominium apartments decreased 7.8 per cent to $2,052. Rental prices for purpose-built apartments saw the smallest annual decline across all property types.

Condo rents saw the steepest declines, led by a 9.6 per cent drop in studio condo rents. Other secondary market units like houses and townhomes fell 7.4 per cent year-over-year to $2,016.

The report said rental markets in Toronto and Vancouver are showing signs of stability though after rents hit their lowest level in five years.

“Our research shows supply has been the main driver of this correction, and in key markets like Toronto and Vancouver, new supply is moving past its peak,” Urbanation president Shaun Hildebrand said in a news release.

“Rents in both cities have trended higher over the past six months, and annual declines have narrowed significantly as renters come off the sidelines. Where Toronto and Vancouver go, the rest of the country follows.”

A few factors support an “upcoming return to positive rent growth” in those cities, the report said. This includes the fact that construction inventory has peaked, data revisions show a modest increase in populations, and both cities are relatively less exposed to tariffs across their respective labour markets.

“In the near term, more affordable rents and move-in incentives are releasing pent-up demand from delayed household formation, as higher rents in previous years led to prospective renters living with parents or roommates for longer,” the report said.

stories.title: Joly threatens ‘full force of the law’ over Cleveland-Cliffs’ Stelco job commitments
stories.summary: Canada's industry minister said Wednesday Stelco Holdings Inc. cannot use the trade war to justify cutting jobs it committed to when it bought the Hamilton, Ont.-based steel plant.
stories.author: Brett Bundale
stories.content:
Canada’s industry minister said Wednesday Stelco Holdings Inc. cannot use the trade war to justify cutting jobs it committed to when it bought the Hamilton, Ont.-based steel plant, particularly when the head of its U.S. parent company has publicly backed steel tariffs.

Mélanie Joly told reporters that the chief executive of US-based Cleveland-Cliffs has supported steel tariffs and therefore cannot characterize the company’s plan to lay off up to 500 workers due to tariffs and market pressures as beyond its control.

“He’s in favor of these US tariffs against steel,” she said, referring to Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves’ public support of American steel tariffs.

“They cannot say that this is now an act of God or force majeure.”

If the company does not respond to the federal government’s demand for a plan outlining how it will meet all of its commitments, including maintaining more than 1,500 jobs, Ottawa will pursue enforcement action, Joly said.

“They need to comply,” she said. “If not, we will use the full force of the law.”

Canada gave US-based Cleveland-Cliffs the green light to purchase Stelco back in 2024 under the Investment Canada Act.

Canada’s approval of that takeover was contingent on the new owner maintaining the number of union jobs and the majority of non-union positions, Joly said.

She sent a letter to Stelco president Paul Simon on Monday demanding a plan outlining how Cleveland-Cliffs intends to comply with all of the undertakings it made to Ottawa when it acquired Stelco, including its jobs commitment.

Ottawa has not yet received a response from Stelco on the letter, Joly said.

Meanwhile, she distinguished Stelco’s planned job cuts from recent layoffs and plant disruptions in the auto sector, saying Cleveland-Cliffs made legally binding employment commitments when it acquired the steelmaker.

“These obligations are binding.”

stories.title: Nova Scotia says new road rules will better protect pedestrians, cyclists and others
stories.summary: Halifax - Nova Scotia is replacing its century-old traffic legislation with new rules that it says will better protect vulnerable road users.
stories.author: Devin Stevens The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - Nova Scotia is replacing its century-old traffic legislation with new rules it says will better protect vulnerable road users.

The new Traffic Safety Act will soon come into force, replacing the old Motor Vehicle Act, which was written in the 1920s and has been modified and amended countless times over the decades.

The new act introduces the concept of vulnerable road users, which include pedestrians, cyclists, drivers of farm vehicles and motorcyclists. The definition, now enshrined in legislation, also includes peace officers, emergency workers and tow-truck drivers working along highways.

“I’m really happy about the addition of the vulnerable road users to this act,” Public Works Minister Fred Tilley told reporters Wednesday. “That will make a huge difference for Nova Scotians and the safety of our highways and roadways.”

Drivers who injure or kill a vulnerable road user could receive double the regular fine for certain infractions, such as careless driving or speeding.

Courts can also consider harm to vulnerable users as an aggravating factor when considering the length of licence suspensions.

The Traffic Safety Act was passed in 2025, but the first batch of regulations needed to describe its specific rules were unveiled on Wednesday. The act and the regulations both go into force on Oct. 19 and the province is rolling out a marketing campaign later this year.

Use of devices such as tablets and global positioning systems will be covered under distracted driving rules that already apply to cellphones.

“Some of the loopholes around driving while distracted have been removed,” said Tilley. “So I think that will make those laws stick better, which will give law enforcement more incentive to actually lay those charges.”

The act clarifies that drivers are now required to clean snow and ice off their vehicles before driving, and it adds a law stating it is an offence for a motorist to open a door into the path of cyclists or other vehicles.

E-bike riders must be 14 or older under the new rules, coming into line with Nova Scotia’s existing age restrictions for e-scooters. The new regulations also give officials the power to impound e-bikes and e-scooters that can travel more than the 32-kilometre-per-hour speed limit for those devices.

Last year in Canada, 57 children riding e-scooters or e-bikes suffered severe injuries that led to prolonged hospital stays, intensive care admissions or death, according to the Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program.

Other organizations have said the number of injuries attributed to the devices have been on the rise in recent years.

Meanwhile, Nova Scotia is adopting national standards for driver fitness and vision, clarifying the ages that child seats must be used and giving municipalities the ability to lower speed limits on municipal roads to less than 50 kilometres per hour.

The changes do not allow for automated traffic cameras to catch speeders. Tilley said the government has more study and consultation to do on the issue.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

Last year in Canada, 57 children riding e-scooters or e-bikes suffered severe injuries that led to prolonged hospital stays, intensive care admissions or death, according to the Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program.
Other organizations have said the number of injuries attributed to the devices have been on the rise in recent years.

Meanwhile, Nova Scotia is adopting national standards for driver fitness and vision, clarifying the ages that child seats must be used and giving municipalities the ability to lower speed limits on municipal roads to less than 50 kilometres per hour.
The changes do not allow for automated traffic cameras to catch speeders. Tilley said the government has more study and consultation to do on the issue.

stories.title: Canned, frozen vegetable merger cancelled after Competition Bureau push
stories.summary: Canada's Competition Bureau says it is 'pleased' a proposed merger, that would have seen two frozen and canned vegetable companies in Canada become one, has been terminated.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Canada’s Competition Bureau says it is “pleased” a proposed merger, which would have seen two frozen and canned vegetable companies in Canada become one, has been terminated.

The merger agreement was announced last year, and if approved, would have seen Nortera, a Canadian-based frozen and canned vegetable processor and marketing company, acquire Green Giant and le Sieur brands in Canada from U.S.-based B&G Foods. Nortera is also the parent company of product brands including Del Monte and Arctic Gardens.

The proposed merger was subject to regulatory approval and the satisfaction of customary closing conditions.

The Competition Bureau’s response to the news of the merger being cancelled was published in a release from Tuesday.

“The Competition Bureau is aware that Nortera and B&G Foods have jointly decided not to proceed with the proposed acquisition by Nortera of B&G Foods Canada’s Green Giant and le Sieur Canadian vegetable business,” the release said.

“We are pleased that a merger, which our investigation found was likely to harm competition, will not move forward.”

This comes after the Competition Bureau, in August, submitted a request to the Competition Tribunal to block the merger because of what it said was a risk to competition in Canada that could lead to higher prices for consumers.

More competition in the marketplace means consumers May have more options for which products to buy, and that can influence companies to lower prices to win over cost-conscious shoppers.

“Nortera is already Canada’s dominant processor of certain canned and frozen vegetables. The transaction would combine it with its only major national brand competitor and harm competition in an already highly concentrated market,” the Competition Bureau said in a release from August.

“Canned and frozen vegetables are staple grocery items that Canadians rely on. Strong competition between suppliers helps keep prices affordable and ensures that consumers have a range of options at the grocery store.”

Rising food prices have been a major issue for Canadians grappling with the heightened cost of living, and canned and frozen vegetable prices have been on the rise in recent months, along with food inflation overall.

For example, data from Statistics Canada shows the average price for 750 grams of frozen mixed vegetables has increased from $4.08 in August 2025 to $4.33 in August of this year. In the same period, a 341 ml can of corn has increased from an average of $1.59 to $1.69.

Food prices have been on the rise because of tariffs, environmental factors, as well geopolitical tensions weighing on supply chains and driving up costs of diesel and other commodities.

The Competition Bureau said its investigation of the proposed merger found, if it were to be approved, would have lead to less competition and even higher prices.

“Throughout our review, the Bureau carefully assessed the transaction’s likely impact on competition and consumers. Our investigation concluded that the acquisition was likely to lead to less competition in the form of higher prices and fewer choices in the wholesale supply of certain canned and frozen vegetables in Canada,” the Competition Bureau said in the release from Tuesday.

“Canned and frozen vegetables are everyday grocery staples that Canadians rely on. Preserving competition in these markets matters because competition leads to lower prices and ensures Canadians continue to have access to a variety of products at the grocery store.”

stories.title: ‘Deeply grateful’: Biscuit the bunny returns home after cash reward posted
stories.summary: Biscuit, an award-winning rabbit that was stolen from the Markham Fair last weekend, has been returned to its family, festival organizers say.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Biscuit, an award-winning rabbit that was stolen from the Markham Fair last weekend, has been returned to its family, festival organizers say.

The Holland Lop rabbit made headlines earlier this week after organizers said it was stolen. Biscuit was entered into a contest by its family and was handed over to the fair last Wednesday.

The McClelland family learned their beloved pet won first place and were going to pick Biscuit up Sunday night. But instead, the family got a call around lunchtime informing them of the disappearance, Victoria McClelland told Global News.

McClelland said the family went to the fair and looked for Biscuit. Eventually, they found out his cage was closed, leading them to believe Biscuit was stolen.

Fair organizers believe the same and said in a statement Biscuit was “taken from its enclosure” at the pet and poultry building on the evening of Oct. 3. The theft was discovered by volunteers and exhibitors, they said.

Devin King, 2026 Markham Fair president, said in a statement Wednesday that Biscuit was returned to the McClellands. The individuals who took the rabbit came forward after a cash reward was posted from a person not connected to the family.

The statement did not indicate whether the reward was paid out, but described the person offering the money as “a stranger to the family who stepped forward simply because she cared.”

“We are absolutely thrilled that Biscuit is home where he belongs,” King said, which gave thanks to all those who were concerned for Biscuit.

“We are deeply grateful to everyone who played a role in bringing Biscuit home.”

King added fair organizers are reviewing security protocols to help prevent similar incidents in the future and is committed to the safety and well-being of all animals at the fair.

stories.title: Kim’s Convenience creator Ins Choi returns to the stage with Son of a Preacherman
stories.summary: Choi reflects on his upbringing in the autobiographical show
stories.author: Ilana Lucas
stories.content:
Title: Son of a Preacherman

Written by: Ins Choi

Director: Kaitlin Williams

Actors: Ins Choi, Belinda Corpuz, Haneul Yi, Yunike Soedarmasto

Company: Pacific Theatre

Venue: Timothy Eaton Memorial Church

City: Toronto

Year: Runs until October 25

There’s an old joke about a man sitting on a rooftop during a flood, waiting to be saved by divine intervention. Confident in his deity’s benevolence, he turns down offers of help from concerned citizens and medical professionals, eventually drowning while still looking to the heavens. When he angrily confronts his saviour-who-wasn’t in the afterlife, the Almighty shows him all the blessings he missed – sent by God in the form of human rescuers.

Also called “the parable of the drowning man,” the story is about embracing your agency to save yourself, rather than waiting for a miracle. It’s a concept familiar to Kim’s Convenience playwright Ins Choi, who literally penned his future; when his prayers went unanswered and he couldn’t find substantive roles for a Korean actor, he created his own.

In his new autobiographical show, Son of a Preacherman , he reflects on his upbringing as a PK (Preacher’s Kid) who was expected to continue on a family tradition in religious service as recompense for the miracle of his birth, a mission that competed with his artistic aspirations to fill the void of Asian representation in North American media. Through 70 minutes of touching family stories, heartfelt songs and irreverent history lessons, he honours his past while allowing himself to break from the path of predestination.

First performed in Vancouver in 2025, the Toronto iteration of the Pacific Theatre production, directed by Kaitlin Williams, takes place in the immersive setting of the chancel of Timothy Eaton Memorial Church. Audience members sit in the choir pews surrounding the playing (and praying) space, which Choi traverses like a rug-covered runway (production designer Jessica Oostergo). Choi’s proximity to the audience and the snug pulpit’s small capacity within a large, ornate sanctuary make the show feel simultaneously intimate and grand, lofty and down to earth.

The stories Choi tells are also at the same time intimately familial and grandly philosophical, and his warm, self-effacing stage presence adds to the tales’ appeal. On the intimate side, Choi wryly recalls being forced to model expectations of good behaviour for other children in the community, along with his secret desire to befriend a martial arts superstar instead of having to chaperone every new kid whose family joined the church. He details his youthful excitement over the paltry few Asian role models he found in media and sports, including a resulting minor obsession with professional wrestling.

Choi shares sweet details about his parents’ relationship, accompanied by projections that contrast their youthful and elderly (but still lively) faces, and offers his late grandmother a deep bow in a moving description of a Korean Lunar New Year ritual.

Grander are his tales about the “curse” that led to his family line’s first clergyman, and the events that caused his family to migrate south in Korea and eventually to Canada. In one of the show’s most engaging scenes, Choi explains the history of the Korean War. He creates a map of Korea, Japan, China and Russia by sectioning off the audience, apologizing for driving political wedges between us. The larger political jockeying feels distant and amusing, until Choi snaps us back to the personal impact this conflict had on his family.

Choi tells his story in nonlinear fashion; we experience his childhood before pulling back into generations of his family history, and we know the conclusion of Choi’s artistic success before he vulnerably unspools the full struggle of how he found his feet. This causes some temporal displacement and loose ends, but adds to the show’s cyclical, generational feeling.

A house band joins Choi on stage, with Belinda Corpuz, Yunike Soedarmasto, and music director Haneul Yi gamely accompanying Choi’s songs and sometimes briefly playing figures in Choi’s life. Starting off with a number that really feels like a gentle Sunday school groove on the subject of whether Jesus would be accepted by the church today, the tunes range from the light and funny, like one where Choi imagines himself safe with Bruce Lee fighting his battles, to the more soul-searching that grapple with his family legacy. Sometimes they feel a little scattered compared to the more cohesive story being told around them, but the specificity of their lyrics keeps them rooted in Choi’s journey.

Though Choi’s family line and father are strong presences in his show, there are actually surprisingly few moments that bring him and his father together to show us their relationship. The ones we get, including a painful scene where Choi reenacts his father’s thunderous disapproval as he excoriates his son for wanting to leave the preaching fold, are vivid and clear. But there’s a certain remoteness in our understanding of the son and the preacherman – perhaps a necessary one that reflects a relationship where God is always the third party in the room.

When that room is his father’s study, though, Choi’s eye for detail comes through, lovingly painting a picture of a passionate man still penning sermons with messy, slanted handwriting in the midst of an untidy, often uprooted world.

Near the end of Son of a Preacherman , Choi delivers his own kind of sermon. As he makes the case for taking the leap of faith to share your ideas with the world, one can see any delineation between artist and preacher collapse.

Choi resolutely chose the path of the playwright, but perhaps there was a little predestination involved, after all.

Written by: Ins Choi
Director: Kaitlin Williams
Actors: Ins Choi, Belinda Corpuz, Haneul Yi, Yunike Soedarmasto
Company: Pacific Theatre
Venue: Timothy Eaton Memorial Church
City: Toronto
Year: Runs until October 25

There’s an old joke about a man sitting on a rooftop during a flood, waiting to be saved by divine intervention. Confident in his deity’s benevolence, he turns down offers of help from concerned citizens and medical professionals, eventually drowning while still looking to the heavens. When he angrily confronts his saviour-who-wasn’t in the afterlife, the Almighty shows him all the blessings he missed – sent by God in the form of human rescuers.

Also called “the parable of the drowning man,” the story is about embracing your agency to save yourself, rather than waiting for a miracle. It’s a concept familiar to Kim’s Convenience playwright Ins Choi, who literally penned his future; when his prayers went unanswered and he couldn’t find substantive roles for a Korean actor, he created his own.

In his new autobiographical show, Son of a Preacherman , he reflects on his upbringing as a PK (Preacher’s Kid) who was expected to continue on a family tradition in religious service as recompense for the miracle of his birth, a mission that competed with his artistic aspirations to fill the void of Asian representation in North American media. Through 70 minutes of touching family stories, heartfelt songs and irreverent history lessons, he honours his past while allowing himself to break from the path of predestination.

First performed in Vancouver in 2025, the Toronto iteration of the Pacific Theatre production, directed by Kaitlin Williams, takes place in the immersive setting of the chancel of Timothy Eaton Memorial Church. Audience members sit in the choir pews surrounding the playing (and praying) space, which Choi traverses like a rug-covered runway (production designer Jessica Oostergo). Choi’s proximity to the audience and the snug pulpit’s small capacity within a large, ornate sanctuary make the show feel simultaneously intimate and grand, lofty and down to earth.

The stories Choi tells are also at the same time intimately familial and grandly philosophical, and his warm, self-effacing stage presence adds to the tales’ appeal. On the intimate side, Choi wryly recalls being forced to model expectations of good behaviour for other children in the community, along with his secret desire to befriend a martial arts superstar instead of having to chaperone every new kid whose family joined the church. He details his youthful excitement over the paltry few Asian role models he found in media and sports, including a resulting minor obsession with professional wrestling.

This causes some temporal displacement and loose ends, but adds to the show’s cyclical, generational feeling.

Sometimes they feel a little scattered compared to the more cohesive story being told around them, but the specificity of their lyrics keeps them rooted in Choi’s journey.

stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vaughan - Police say a hit-and-run victim in Vaughan, Ont., was found dead two days after the crash, as investigators search for the suspect.

York regional police say the live-in caregiver was on her way to work Sunday around 8:30 p.m. when she got off a bus at Major Mackenzie Drive and Pine Valley Drive.

stories.title: Carney says 'more work to do' on behalf of Jewish Canadians on Oct. 7 anniversary
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney said “there is more work to do” to make Jewish Canadians feel safe and thrive in Canada.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa – On the third anniversary of the Oct. 7 Hamas terrorist attacks against Israel, Prime Minister Mark Carney said “there is more work to do” to make Jewish Canadians feel safe and thrive in Canada.

“The government has been taking actions at home to protect the Jewish community, protect all Canadians, but particularly the Jewish community,” said Carney, ON his way into a caucus meeting in Ottawa on Wednesday.

“And it’s above and beyond protection, it’s about the ability to truly thrive, live their lives freely and openly, and thrive as Jewish people in Canada,” he added.

The prime minister outlined measures his government has taken, since the “unspeakable tragedy” three years ago. These measures include anti-hate legislation and $75 million through the Canada Community Security Fund, to protect Jewish community centres, synagogues and day schools.

Carney noted that protection has become necessary, given the recent gunman attack against the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., which was thwarted by Belleville police. One of the police officers, Const. Jeff Smith, is recovering from his injuries and the suspect died from his injuries sustained in the shootout. The attack took place on the holiest day of the Jewish calendar, Yom Kippur.

“There’s more work to do,” said Carney. “This is a job for all Canadians to ensure that all Canadians can live freely and openly in our society.”

Israelis gathered on Wednesday to mark the anniversary of the deadliest attack in its history, which killed 1,200 people and saw 251 people taken hostage by the Hamas terrorist group.

The ensuing Israel-Hamas war in Gaza has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians, with the Israeli military controlling over half of the Gaza strip, following a tentative ceasefire announced last fall.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said the Jewish Canadian community has experienced the consequences of the war here in Canada.

“The hatred that fuelled October 7th did not remain on foreign shores,” said Poilievre. “Right here in Canada, far too many synagogues, Jewish businesses and institutions have been the targets of harassment and hate.”

“This is not, and cannot become, normal,” added Poilievre. “Conservatives will always fight against antisemitism and all forms of hatred: protecting our schools, communities and places of worship so that Canadians of all faiths can live in peace and security.”

According to data from Statistics Canada, police-reported hate crimes against Jewish Canadians jumped from 492 in 2021, to 788 in 2025. The number of incidents were higher in 2023 and 2024, at 959 and 943 incidents respectively.

The Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs (Cija) has noted that despite Jewish Canadians representing just one per cent of the population, they were the target of 71 per cent of religion-motivated hate crimes in 2025.

“Today, Prime Minister Carney unequivocally condemned Hamas and recognized that October 7 was a Canadian tragedy, taking the lives of Canadians and leaving a Jewish community here at home still deeply impacted by the terrorist attacks and the devastating resurgence of antisemitism that followed,” said Cija CEO Noah Shack, in a statement.

“We appreciate the prime minister’s renewed commitment to strengthen public safety and combat hate, with new laws and resources to stop extremism before it takes root,” he added.

stories.title: Liberals announce bill to prohibit Maid for mental illness alone
stories.summary: The federal government intends to permanently bar people with mental illness alone from accessing an assisted death.
stories.author: Christopher Nardi, Sharon Kirkey
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal government intends to permanently bar people with mental illness alone from accessing an assisted death, settling a decade-long controversial debate.

But the Liberal government is moving forward to allow people to make advance requests for Maid if diagnosed with an illness that would threaten their ability to provide final consent, up to the last moments before the lethal injection. They will do so by decriminalizing the act for doctors who administer Maid to patients who made an advance request.

The announcement was made Wednesday by Justice Minister Sean Fraser and Health Minister Marjorie Michel on the same day the House of Commons is set to vote on a Conservative bill on the topic.

The ministers said they intend to table legislation this fall that will maintain the exclusion of medical assistance in dying (Maid) for people seeking it on the sole basis of a psychiatric illness. The exclusion, set to expire next March, will be maintained “on an indeterminate basis,” Fraser announced.

“While there is not a perfect consensus on this issue, we believe this is the correct approach at this particular time,” he said.

On the separate issue of advance requests, Fraser said the legislation will grant access to Maid “to people who have provided consent at a time when they still have capacity but know that they have been diagnosed with an illness that will take that capacity from them subsequently.

“These are not easy decisions. But we believe they are the correct ones,” Fraser said.

The minister did not commit to a date for the legislation beyond the fall. He said the bill was being drafted and promised that the substance would not differ from what he announced Wednesday.

Whether to open up euthanasia to people whose sole underlying medical condition is a mental illness has been one of the most heated issues in the history of legalized assisted death in Canada.

In June, a special parliamentary committee recommended the Liberal government draw a line in the sand and indefinitely exclude people with mental illness alone from eligibility for Maid. Expanding Maid for mental illness, set to take effect March 17, 2027, had already been deferred, twice.

The joint committee of MPs and senators said key issues haven’t been addressed, including whether it’s possible to predict with any certainty whether a person’s mental illness is incurable. Dr. Sonu Gaind, past chief of psychiatry at Toronto’s Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, told the committee that doctors are right less than half the time, comparing the ability to predict long-term prognosis to a coin toss.

Current and former chairs of psychiatry departments at universities across Canada warned the committee that making Maid available to people with depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, substance abuse and other mental illnesses would facilitate avoidable deaths and erode suicide prevention efforts.

The committee said “grave concerns and deep divisions” continue to exist. A recurring theme was the pressing need for better access to mental health services and concerns long waits for care could exacerbate suffering, driving Maid requests. The committee also heard stories of “questionable conduct” by some Maid providers, as well as doctors “with a seemingly cavalier attitude toward ending a life,” committee co-chair Liberal MP Marcus Powlowski wrote in a supplemental opinion.

However, the committee’s decision wasn’t unanimous. Three senators as well as a Bloc Québécois MP, Luc Thériault, wrote dissenting opinions and called on the government to bring the question of expansion to the Supreme Court of Canada.

After Fraser’s announcement, Conservative MPs blasted the move as playing politics as the House of Commons was set to vote on a bill they said did substantially the same thing the government was now promising to do.

They also criticized Fraser’s decision to bundle the issues of Maid for mental illness and allowing for advance requests in the same bill.

“What the minister has announced today is eroding that consensus and introducing division into a very complex subject,” charged Conservative MP Andrew Lawton. “We agree that Maid should not extend to people with only a mental illness.”

Earlier this week, Fraser told reporters he’d heard “a range of different views” since the committee’s report was released in June and that he wanted to take the time “to line things up the appropriate way” in deciding on such a serious issue.

First legalized in 2016 for people whose deaths are “reasonably foreseeable,” Canada’s Maid law was amended in 2021 to remove the “reasonably foreseeable” provision. The amendments under Bill C-7 also included a restriction on mental illness alone as a qualifying condition for Maid, an exclusion that was originally set to expire on March 17, 2023, but was later pushed back to 2024 and then again, to March 2027.

Currently, dementia is an eligible diagnosis for Maid in Canada, provided people have the capacity to make a reasoned request and don’t lose that capacity before they want their lives ended. Dementia is considered a neurological disorder, not a mental illness.

Canadian children’s author Robert Munsch revealed in a New York Times profile last year that, shortly after being diagnosed with dementia in 2021, he applied and was approved for Maid.

Munsch said he would have to pick the moment “when I can still ask for it,” otherwise his wife risks being “stuck with me being a lump.”

Outside Quebec, euthanizing someone in the absence of capacity is a serious offence in the absence of a valid waiver of final consent.

The new bill will amend the Criminal Code to reflect that a doctor who provides Maid to someone who is suffering an incurable illness and who has complied with provincially legislated safeguards “will not be treated as a criminal in Canada going forward,” Fraser said. Provinces would decide whether to permit it. Alberta has already banned advance requests.

Alex Schadenberg, executive director of the Euthanasia Prevention Coalition, said consent can become uncertain under advance request scenarios, because someone else will have to decide when the person is experiencing conditions under which they would have wanted their lives ended.

“It’s really a problematic situation, and then who makes the decision in the end? Some family member, some doctor who says, ‘Oh, I guess this was requested in the end,'” Schadenberg told reporters on Parliament Hill Wednesday.

“To me, it’s almost very eugenic.”

“An advance request is written by someone who cannot know what their future will hold,” said Krista Carr, CEO of Inclusion Canada. “Consent at the time is the most basic protection a person has. Parliament should not take it away.”
