stories.title: B.C. NDP Leader Eby says not everybody shares his concerns about Trump
stories.summary: Victoria - The Ndp's election campaign in British Columbia has moved on from the threat of Donald Trump's tariffs to focus on affordability issues.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The leaders of the two largest political parties in British Columbia were in the election battleground of Surrey on Wednesday pitching plans for businesses and the economy as the campaign reached its halfway point.

New Democrat David Eby promised loans of up to a $1 million for small and medium-size businesses affected by the ongoing trade war with the United States, while B.C. Conservative Lorne Doerkson said he would eliminate the PST on certain machinery, equipment and business software.

Surrey is B.C.‘s second largest municipality after Vancouver and success there in the Oct. 24 election could be a critical factor.

The NDP said its $500-million Small Business Tariff and Wildfire Relief Fund would provide interest-free loans of up to $1 million for up to 72 months for qualifying small and medium-size businesses recovering from the recent wildfires or tariffs.

Eby said there was concern smaller businesses could be “falling through the gap” of federal tariff supports.

“These interest-free loans will provide the support that the small and medium-sized business leaders have come to us and said they need to be able to get through this period,” he said.

The New Democrats would also offer a $5,000 refundable tax credit for small businesses that employ someone aged between 18 and 30.

“Young people right now are definitely worrying about employment. We’ve seen that among young British Columbians, they’re disproportionately affected by the impact of the tariffs on businesses. It means that opportunities for them to work have been reduced,” Eby said.

Elsewhere in Surrey, Doerkson made the Conservatives’ pitch to businesses, which includes exempting more “productive capital” from PST for three years.

“If we want to supercharge British Columbia’s economy, we need to stop penalizing the very companies trying to build it,” he said.

“Right now, when a local business buys the equipment its workers need, the seven per cent PST acts as a direct penalty on that growth.”

The Conservatives have not provided costings for the plan, which also includes promises to cut red tape, appoint a panel to “simplify” the province’s tax system and approve major new capital projects in 120 days or fewer.

Elsewhere on the campaign trail, BC Green Party Leader Emily Lowan laid out more of her plans for the economy, including a tax on extreme wealth, raising an estimated $22.2 billion through a one-time levy on fortunes above $50 million, followed by an annual wealth tax expected to raise about $5.4 billion a year.

They are also promising provincewide commercial rent protections and new tools for municipalities to address long-term commercial vacancies.

“I hear every day on the campaign trail just how difficult it is to start and maintain a small business in British Columbia,” Lowan said in a statement.

“While other parties are focused on fast-tracking projects for foreign resource corporations, the BC Greens are focused on building strong local economies, where wealth stays in the community, local businesses can grow and every region has the power to shape its own future.”

When Eby called the snap election on Sept. 22, he said British Columbia needed a “firebreak” against U.S. President Donald Trump’s economic attacks and Trump-style politics, which he said were threatening to infect the province.

But more recently, he has said he accepts that not everyone shares his anxieties about the U.S. president, even as Trump’s actions make B.C.‘s challenges much worse.

He said on Tuesday that the key matter for voters would be deciding which party can support families during these tough times.

Doerkson said at the start of the campaign that Trump was an “absolute bully,” and that standing up to him required action, not press releases.

Eby said he was trying to express his own sense of anxiety about Trump’s threats, and while not everybody shared his concerns, there was no question Trump’s actions continued to have an impact on British Columbians.

“Whether you believe and accept that Trump is making it much worse, it doesn’t matter because you’re still understanding that the cost of living is significant, that we need a strong public health-care system if you and your family get sick,” he said on Tuesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

stories.title: Anniversary of Gaza war marks 3 years of pain for Canadians with ties to Middle East
stories.summary: Ottawa — Edmonton mother Salomy Abusalim is running out of excuses to give her son when he asks why his dad is still in Gaza.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Edmonton mother Salomy Abusalim is running out of excuses to give her son when he asks why his dad is still in Gaza.

“This is killing me as a mom. I can’t keep going on, lying to him,” said Abusalim, whose husband has been trapped in Gaza due to bureaucratic difficulties.

“My husband was starving, literally starving,” she said. “For three months he didn’t have food at all. Imagine I’m staying here, eating at my table, my son eating my food and my other half — he can’t find a piece of bread just to eat. It was devastating.”

Three years ago, Hamas launched a deadly terrorist attack on Israel which left 1,200 people dead, including Canadians. The victims included some children. Women were sexually assaulted and 251 people were taken hostage in the attack.

Israel responded by launching a war in the Gaza Strip. Local health authorities say 74,243 Palestinians have been killed in the three years since. The United Nations also reports more than a million people displaced in Lebanon and “daily violations by Israel of Lebanese airspace.”

The UN says Israel’s “pervasive impunity” in the West Bank has allowed settlers to attack Palestinians.

Canadians with ties to the region describe three years of horror — of relatives sending them text message updates on an unfolding humanitarian crisis as they grieve for loved ones killed in a conflict far away.

The worst part, she said, is when the internet goes down — when the messages from her husband stop and she grapples with her worst fears, wondering if he has been shot.

“It’s a lot of scenarios in your mind, and it’s not stopping. It’s happening every day,” she said.

Her husband Saed has been caught in bureaucratic limbo since the couple attempted to move to Canada. Abusalim moved to Edmonton in 2018, two years after giving birth to their son, Rashid.

Abusalim and Rashid, who is now 10, both have Canadian citizenship. Saed applied years ago for permanent residency, which Abusalim said was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic.

Saed was set to complete biometrics on Oct. 10, 2023, she said. Three days prior, the Hamas attack ignited a catastrophic war. Technically there’s a ceasefire in place but dozens of Palestinians are still being killed each month.

Abusalim said her husband was on a list of Canadians approved to leave Gaza through Egypt in January 2024, but Egyptian officials refused to let him enter and later demanded hefty bribes.

He still has an active visa application, she said, but Ottawa will not issue the document until he completes biometric screening, which can’t be done in Gaza. Unlike some European countries, Canada appears unable to get citizens or visa applicants out of Gaza through Israel — where biometric checks might be possible.

The issue has come up for hundreds of people in the territory who applied to come to Canada.

The Immigration Department said in a statement that Canada has no control over who is able to leave Gaza and the department is bound by legislation to require biometrics.

“Biometrics can only be completed after people leave Gaza, as Ircc has no presence there,” wrote spokesperson Mary Rose Sabater. She added privacy laws prevent the department from commenting on individual cases.

Abusalim said her son threatened to go on a hunger strike to protest his father being stuck in Gaza. She has now taken that on herself; on Tuesday, Abusalim said she was on her fourth day of consuming nothing but water.

“It’s been eight years since my son held his dad, or smelled him and hugged him,” she said.

“As a mom, I don’t think any mom wants to go through any of this with her son or daughter. I don’t think that keeping up this war is any good for any of us — any side of us, even the Israeli side.”

In Quebec’s Beauce region, Sylvie Labrecque feels acutely the absence of her son, an aid worker killed in an Israeli airstrike in April 2024.

“Every day he’s there in my heart, in my mind, and I do pray and meditate, thinking of him,” she said in a Monday interview.

Jacob Flickinger, a 33-year-old infantry veteran, was on an aid mission with World Central Kitchen, a respected organization that had co-ordinated a convoy with Israel’s military.

“He enjoyed very much to go work for these types of missions, because it meant a lot to him,” Labrecque said.

Israel had drastically restricted the flow of aid to the territory. It also has barred reporters from Gaza and imposed unconventionally tight restrictions on the work of humanitarian organizations.

“It could have been safer, not only for him, but for the whole group, to do their work, even though they were in a war zone,” Labrecque said. “They knew that.”

Israel struck the convoy multiple times, killing Flickinger and six other aid workers. In August, Israel’s military prosecutor decided against a criminal investigation.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand called that finding unacceptable. She argued there were serious failures in the conduct of the strike and vowed to continue pressing for a full account of what happened.

Labrecque said Canada could do much more to raise the cost of killing aid workers. She said she fears the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has no incentive to do better.

paragraphs: Ottawa — Edmonton mother Salomy Abusalim is running out of excuses to give her son when he asks why his dad is still in Gaza.
“This is killing me as a mom. I can’t keep going on, lying to him,” said Abusalim, whose husband has been trapped in Gaza due to bureaucratic difficulties.

“My husband was starving, literally starving,” she said. “For three months he didn’t have food at all. Imagine I’m staying here, eating at my table, my son eating my food and my other half — he can’t find a piece of bread just to eat. It was devastating.”

Three years ago, Hamas launched a deadly terrorist attack on Israel which left 1,200 people dead, including Canadians. The victims included some children. Women were sexually assaulted and 251 people were taken hostage in the attack.

Israel responded by launching a war in the Gaza Strip. Local health authorities say 74,243 Palestinians have been killed in the three years since. The United Nations also reports more than a million people displaced in Lebanon and “daily violations by Israel of Lebanese airspace.”
The UN says Israel’s “pervasive impunity” in the West Bank has allowed settlers to attack Palestinians.

Canadians with ties to the region describe three years of horror — of relatives sending them text message updates on an unfolding humanitarian crisis as they grieve for loved ones killed in a conflict far away.
The worst part, she said, is when the internet goes down — when the messages from her husband stop and she grapples with her worst fears, wondering if he has been shot.
“It’s a lot of scenarios in your mind, and it’s not stopping. It’s happening every day,” she said.
Her husband Saed has been caught in bureaucratic limbo since the couple attempted to move to Canada. Abusalim moved to Edmonton in 2018, two years after giving birth to their son, Rashid.
Abusalim and Rashid, who is now 10, both have Canadian citizenship. Saed applied years ago for permanent residency, which Abusalim said was delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic.

Saed was set to complete biometrics on Oct. 10, 2023, she said. Three days prior, the Hamas attack ignited a catastrophic war. Technically there’s a ceasefire in place but dozens of Palestinians are still being killed each month.
Abusalim said her husband was on a list of Canadians approved to leave Gaza through Egypt in January 2024, but Egyptian officials refused to let him enter and later demanded hefty bribes.

He still has an active visa application, she said, but Ottawa will not issue the document until he completes biometric screening, which can’t be done in Gaza. Unlike some European countries, Canada appears unable to get citizens or visa applicants out of Gaza through Israel — where biometric checks might be possible.
The issue has come up for hundreds of people in the territory who applied to come to Canada.
The Immigration Department said in a statement that Canada has no control over who is able to leave Gaza and the department is bound by legislation to require biometrics.

“Biometrics can only be completed after people leave Gaza, as Ircc has no presence there,” wrote spokesperson Mary Rose Sabater. She added privacy laws prevent the department from commenting on individual cases.

Abusalim said her son threatened to go on a hunger strike to protest his father being stuck in Gaza. She has now taken that on herself; on Tuesday, Abusalim said she was on her fourth day of consuming nothing but water.
“It’s been eight years since my son held his dad, or smelled him and hugged him,” she said.
“As a mom, I don’t think any mom wants to go through any of this with her son or daughter. I don’t think that keeping up this war is any good for any of us — any side of us, even the Israeli side.”
In Quebec’s Beauce region, Sylvie Labrecque feels acutely the absence of her son, an aid worker killed in an Israeli airstrike in April 2024.
“Every day he’s there in my heart, in my mind, and I do pray and meditate, thinking of him,” she said in a Monday interview.
Jacob Flickinger, a 33-year-old infantry veteran, was on an aid mission with World Central Kitchen, a respected organization that had co-ordinated a convoy with Israel’s military.
“He enjoyed very much to go work for these types of missions, because it meant a lot to him,” Labrecque said.
Israel had drastically restricted the flow of aid to the territory. It also has barred reporters from Gaza and imposed unconventionally tight restrictions on the work of humanitarian organizations.
“It could have been safer, not only for him, but for the whole group, to do their work, even though they were in a war zone,” Labrecque said. “They knew that.”
Israel struck the convoy multiple times, killing Flickinger and six other aid workers. In August, Israel’s military prosecutor decided against a criminal investigation.

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand called that finding unacceptable. She argued there were serious failures in the conduct of the strike and vowed to continue pressing for a full account of what happened.
Labrecque said Canada could do much more to raise the cost of killing aid workers. She said she fears the government of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has no incentive to do better.
“They’ve been killing already tens of thousands of people. So to kill a few more is kind of nothing to them,” she said.

The Israeli military said it could not comment in detail as it could not locate a case file for the incident, which occurred during its ongoing operations in Lebanon that Israel says are aimed at routing Hezbollah.
Haidar’s brother Mohamed told reporters the world is letting civilian deaths go unpunished.

stories.title: To get a suitable home, buyers figure out what they'll accept as a trade-off: Re/Max
stories.summary: Toronto - Canadians are willing to make compromises to afford a home that better meets their needs, a new survey from Re/Max finds.
stories.author: Daniel Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Canadians are willing to make compromises to afford a home that better meets their needs, a new survey from Re/Max finds.

The survey, released Wednesday, said 65 per cent of respondents would compromise in at least one way to afford a larger or more suitable place to live. Such compromises might include living further away from city centres or choosing an older home that May need renovations.

“Rather than giving up on home ownership, Canadians are making different choices about how to get there. For some, that means looking outside their current community or reconsidering the type of home they buy,” Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada, said in a news release.

“For others, it means making different financial choices. Buyers are identifying what matters most and where they have room to be flexible.”

The survey found that 63 per cent indicated they would relocate for a home that better fits their needs, including 47 per cent who said they would move up to an hour from the community they currently live in.

Re/Max said the report comes amid a slowdown for the housing market. Data from its own brokers and agents shows home sales saw annual declines in 81 per cent of markets that were analyzed over the first half of the year. During the period, average home prices increased across 56 per cent of markets.

Slower sales and more choice in certain markets could provide more time to compare properties, Re/Max said, allowing buyers to keep focused on their top priorities.

“The market has not become easy for buyers, but in many regions, it is allowing for a more deliberate purchasing process,” said Kottick in the release.

“That matters for people who are already rethinking location, property type or condition to make the numbers work. More time and choice can help buyers compare their options and understand where their budget goes further without feeling like they have to compromise.”

Conditions favourable to buyers are also more common than anticipated heading into the year, Re/Max said, with 32 per cent of markets analyzed currently in buyers’ favour, compared with 15.2 per cent a year earlier.

Canadians were also willing to make trade-offs beyond the property itself in order to afford a home, Re/Max found. Forty-one per cent of respondents said they would reduce discretionary spending, like travel and dining out, while 24 per cent said they would extend their amortization period.

Seventeen per cent would take on a second job or another source of income to afford a home. Another 17 per cent said they would delay retirement or other longer-term savings.

The online survey was conducted by Leger between July 17 and July 19, and responses were taken from 1,532 Canadian adults.

The Canadian Research Insights Council, an industry organization that promotes polling standards, says online surveys cannot be assigned a margin of error because they do not randomly sample the population.

Students who hide their Star of David necklaces for fear of being attacked.

Synagogue services that start with staff pointing out where the emergency exits are.

In the three years since Hamas unleashed a deadly terrorist attack on Israel, and Israel responded with a relentless war it says is aimed at eliminating Hamas in Gaza, life for Jewish Canadians has changed dramatically.

“The society we’re living in is not quite the society we thought,” said Lisa Grushcow, senior rabbi of Temple Emanu-El-Beth Sholom in Montreal. “There’s this feeling of a world that’s really been turned upside down.”

Canadian Jews are facing a spike in antisemitic attacks — firebombings at synagogues like Grushcow’s, shootings at Jewish schools and physical assaults which police have classified as hate crimes.

The Canadian Security Intelligence Service mentioned in its annual report for 2025 a number of disrupted plots targeting Canadian Jewish institutions, and cited the arrest in August 2025 of a Montreal youth who intended to target Jews.

It said religiously motivated violent extremism has “increased significantly since the beginning of the Israel-Hamas conflict,” has driven “violent extremist organization narratives” and “has the potential to inspire a new generation of extremists.”

Since 2023, Jewish communities have been the most frequently targeted group in police-reported hate crimes, despite representing less than one per cent of Canada’s population.

Toronto’s police service said in September it had made 573 arrests and laid 1,398 charges in connection with demonstrations, protests and hate-motivated offences targeting Jewish communities since Oct. 7, 2023.

The Ottawa Police Service Board report issued last week said “Jewish residents have reported fear about wearing a kippah, Star of David or other visible expressions of Jewish identity in public.”

“Community organizations have adopted heightened security measures for religious, cultural and commemorative gatherings — including advance registration, identification requirements, restrictions on attendance and, in some circumstances, limiting public disclosure of event details,” the report said.

Grushcow’s synagogue, which was founded in 1882 and incorporated one year later, represents one of the most progressive branches of Judaism. In June, someone attacked the temple with a firebomb. In February 2025, a swastika was spray-painted on the building’s exterior.

“There’s been a lot that’s become normalized over the past three years that I think is just deeply disturbing — for us as a community, but also for us as a society,” Grushcow said.

She said she encourages non-Jewish Canadians to ask a Jewish friend if they can attend a synagogue. What they would find, she said, is communities grappling with the need to protect themselves without making those attending services feel too afraid to show up.

Jeff Lieberman, president of the Jewish Federation of Winnipeg, said Jews feel displaying menorahs and mezuzahs — a door frame case containing Torah scrolls — makes them targets for hate crimes.

He said Jews in Winnipeg are alarmed by the number of hate messages graffitied around their city.

“It brings back to days of the 1930s when Jews were persecuted. And the feeling of what’s happening now is the lead-up to something like that,” he said.

Lieberman said many Jews are particularly upset that Ottawa has promised to study the drivers of antisemitism when the causes are widely documented. He said the government could be doing more.

“The Canadian government May not support the government in Israel, but that has nothing to do with Jews in Canada. They need to be able to support Jews,” he said.

Lieberman said the fear is compounded by reports of attacks in smaller communities that lead some to wonder if anywhere in Canada is truly safe.

Last month, a gunman shot at a Belleville, Ont., synagogue and a police officer who was guarding the building was shot and critically wounded. Days later, the neighbourhood where the synagogue is located was targeted by someone distributing antisemitic flyers.

Conservative deputy leader Melissa Lantsman said the shooting incident added to the existing climate of fear and shock.

“The next day, our synagogue, as it often does, starts with a security briefing of what to do when things go south, ON where the doors are,” she told reporters on Parliament Hill on Sept. 24.

Grushcow said there are immediate safety concerns for Jewish communities, along with longer-term questions about how to restore civic dialogue.

“I was at the Pride March last summer. Somebody looks at me and sees me with a rainbow Star of David on my shirt and calls me a baby killer. What is that? How has that become our new normal?” she said.

“How is it that any connection or care for Israel — which is the reality for the vast majority of Canadian Jews, for all kinds of historical, religious, spiritual reasons — how does that become something … that becomes perceived as a reason to keep people out of academic and professional and personal relationships?”

At the centre of some of the concern is the wave of anti-Israel protests that erupted after Oct. 7.

Some of the groups behind those protests say they are targeting organizations that actively support the Israeli military — such as a business fundraising for foreigners who serve in the Israeli Defense Force, or a synagogue that appeared to be promoting the sale of land in the occupied West Bank.

Independent Jewish Voices has argued antisemitism is being weaponized to suppress pro-Palestinian advocacy.

But many Canadian Jews feel they’re being targeted for being Jewish, regardless of whether they support the Israeli government.

Grushcow said Canadians need to find a way to balance open dialogue with respect and safety.

She said Canadian society has “become very quick to write people off” over their perceived loyalties and is losing the ability to maintain “dialogue across difference.”

Grushcow is among many Jewish leaders who question whether Iran has played a role in inflaming tensions in Canada. She said it’s hard to imagine who benefits from Jews being threatened and Canadian society losing its civility.

In June, Ruby Sahota, the secretary of state for combating crime, told the House of Commons that people who fired shots recently at synagogues were hired and paid by a “foreign entity.”

Ottawa has boosted funding for security at synagogues and expanded hate-speech laws. Grushcow said Canadians need to do more.

“We have to stop saying this isn’t who we are and recognize that it’s who we’ve become, and then how do we change that,” she said. “That work can’t come entirely from the Jewish community.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

Grushcow’s synagogue, which was founded in 1882 and incorporated one year later, represents one of the most progressive branches of Judaism. In June, someone attacked the temple with a firebomb. In February 2025, a swastika was spray-painted on the building’s exterior.

She said she encourages non-Jewish Canadians to ask a Jewish friend if they can attend a synagogue. What they would find, she said, is communities grappling with the need to protect themselves without making those attending services feel too afraid to show up.

Jeff Lieberman, president of the Jewish Federation of Winnipeg, said Jews feel displaying menorahs and mezuzahs — a door frame case containing Torah scrolls — makes them targets for hate crimes.

He said Jews in Winnipeg are alarmed by the number of hate messages graffitied around their city.

Lieberman said many Jews are particularly upset that Ottawa has promised to study the drivers of antisemitism when the causes are widely documented. He said the government could be doing more.

paragraphs: Ottawa — Security guards searching bags before bar mitzvahs.
Students who hide their Star of David necklaces for fear of being attacked.
Synagogue services that start with staff pointing out where the emergency exits are.

In the three years since Hamas unleashed a deadly terrorist attack on Israel, and Israel responded with a relentless war it says is aimed at eliminating Hamas in Gaza, life for Jewish Canadians has changed dramatically.

“The society we’re living in is not quite the society we thought,” said Lisa Grushcow, senior rabbi of Temple Emanu-El-Beth Sholom in Montreal. “There’s this feeling of a world that’s really been turned upside down.”
Canadian Jews are facing a spike in antisemitic attacks — firebombings at synagogues like Grushcow’s, shootings at Jewish schools and physical assaults which police have classified as hate crimes.

The Canadian Security Intelligence Service mentioned in its annual report for 2025 a number of disrupted plots targeting Canadian Jewish institutions, and cited the arrest in August 2025 of a Montreal youth who intended to target Jews.

It said religiously motivated violent extremism has “increased significantly since the beginning of the Israel-Hamas conflict,” has driven “violent extremist organization narratives” and “has the potential to inspire a new generation of extremists.”
Since 2023, Jewish communities have been the most frequently targeted group in police-reported hate crimes, despite representing less than one per cent of Canada’s population.

Toronto’s police service said in September it had made 573 arrests and laid 1,398 charges in connection with demonstrations, protests and hate-motivated offences targeting Jewish communities since Oct. 7, 2023.
The Ottawa Police Service Board report issued last week said “Jewish residents have reported fear about wearing a kippah, Star of David or other visible expressions of Jewish identity in public.”

“Community organizations have adopted heightened security measures for religious, cultural and commemorative gatherings — including advance registration, identification requirements, restrictions on attendance and, in some circumstances, limiting public disclosure of event details,” the report said.

Grushcow’s synagogue, which was founded in 1882 and incorporated one year later, represents one of the most progressive branches of Judaism. In June, someone attacked the temple with a firebomb. In February 2025, a swastika was spray-painted on the building’s exterior.
“There’s been a lot that’s become normalized over the past three years that I think is just deeply disturbing — for us as a community, but also for us as a society,” Grushcow said.

She said she encourages non-Jewish Canadians to ask a Jewish friend if they can attend a synagogue. What they would find, she said, is communities grappling with the need to protect themselves without making those attending services feel too afraid to show up.
Jeff Lieberman, president of the Jewish Federation of Winnipeg, said Jews feel displaying menorahs and mezuzahs — a door frame case containing Torah scrolls — makes them targets for hate crimes.
He said Jews in Winnipeg are alarmed by the number of hate messages graffitied around their city.
“It brings back to days of the 1930s when Jews were persecuted. And the feeling of what’s happening now is the lead-up to something like that,” he said.
Lieberman said many Jews are particularly upset that Ottawa has promised to study the drivers of antisemitism when the causes are widely documented. He said the government could be doing more.
“The Canadian government May not support the government in Israel, but that has nothing to do with Jews in Canada. They need to be able to support Jews,” he said.
Lieberman said the fear is compounded by reports of attacks in smaller communities that lead some to wonder if anywhere in Canada is truly safe.

Last month, a gunman shot at a Belleville, Ont., synagogue and a police officer who was guarding the building was shot and critically wounded. Days later, the neighbourhood where the synagogue is located was targeted by someone distributing antisemitic flyers.
Conservative deputy leader Melissa Lantsman said the shooting incident added to the existing climate of fear and shock.
“The next day, our synagogue, as it often does, starts with a security briefing of what to do when things go south, ON where the doors are,” she told reporters on Parliament Hill on Sept. 24.
Grushcow said there are immediate safety concerns for Jewish communities, along with longer-term questions about how to restore civic dialogue.

“I was at the Pride March last summer. Somebody looks at me and sees me with a rainbow Star of David on my shirt and calls me a baby killer. What is that? How has that become our new normal?” she said.

“How is it that any connection or care for Israel — which is the reality for the vast majority of Canadian Jews, for all kinds of historical, religious, spiritual reasons — how does that become something … that becomes perceived as a reason to keep people out of academic and professional and personal relationships?”
At the centre of some of the concern is the wave of anti-Israel protests that erupted after Oct. 7.

Some of the groups behind those protests say they are targeting organizations that actively support the Israeli military — such as a business fundraising for foreigners who serve in the Israeli Defense Force, or a synagogue that appeared to be promoting the sale of land in the occupied West Bank.
Independent Jewish Voices has argued antisemitism is being weaponized to suppress pro-Palestinian advocacy.
But many Canadian Jews feel they’re being targeted for being Jewish, regardless of whether they support the Israeli government.
Grushcow said Canadians need to find a way to balance open dialogue with respect and safety.
She said Canadian society has “become very quick to write people off” over their perceived loyalties and is losing the ability to maintain “dialogue across difference.”

Grushcow is among many Jewish leaders who question whether Iran has played a role in inflaming tensions in Canada. She said it’s hard to imagine who benefits from Jews being threatened and Canadian society losing its civility.
In June, Ruby Sahota, the secretary of state for combating crime, told the House of Commons that people who fired shots recently at synagogues were hired and paid by a “foreign entity.”
Ottawa has boosted funding for security at synagogues and expanded hate-speech laws. Grushcow said Canadians need to do more.
“We have to stop saying this isn’t who we are and recognize that it’s who we’ve become, and then how do we change that,” she said. “That work can’t come entirely from the Jewish community.”

stories.title: Liberals to outline plans on assisted dying ahead of mental illness expansion
stories.summary: The Liberal government is expected Wednesday to publicly take a position on whether it believes Canada is ready to allow people with mental illness to access assisted dying.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal government will not allow people suffering solely from a mental illness to access medical assistance in dying, but it does plan to decriminalize advance requests for people who are at risk of losing their capacity to consent.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser said the Liberal government will introduce legislation this fall to make both changes to Canada’s medical assistance in dying regime.

“Today is not based on where we believe the politics is going to land in the House of Commons or in the Senate. It’s based on what we sincerely believe is right,” Fraser said at a press conference on Wednesday.

Fraser cited the recommendation from a joint House and Senate committee, which heard evidence last spring. The committee concluded the government should indefinitely exclude people suffering solely from a mental illness from access to medical assistance in dying, known as Maid.

Following that report’s release, Fraser’s office reviewed the evidence the committee considered and sought additional opinions on the deeply divisive issue.

“When I hear that there is a lack of consensus within the medical community about the irremediable nature of certain mental illnesses, that gives me real cause for concern,” Fraser said.

He said he’s also heard concerns about a lack of access to mental health care and worries that people who aren’t able to get help might turn to Maid instead.

Health Canada has studied the issue of advance requests, which are documents that allow a person who suffers from a degenerative condition, such as dementia or ALS, to ask for an assisted death to be carried out once they no longer have the capacity to consent.

The strict eligibility criteria for Maid requires that qualifying patients be suffering from a grievous and irremediable medical condition and are able to consent at the time of the procedure.

Advocates have argued that requirement means people who know they are going to lose their capacity to consent must choose to end their lives earlier than they would want.

Fraser was emotional on Wednesday when speaking about a friend’s diagnosis with early onset Alzheimer’s disease.

“We need to create space for people to be able to provide consent when they know they’re going to lose capacity, in order to live out their remaining years rather than being put in a position where they fear they have to take that decision prematurely,” he said.

But the justice minister also said the proposed change will only affect the Criminal Code. He said it will be up to the provinces to decide whether to provide advance requests through their health care systems.

That could lead to a regulatory patchwork across the country.

Quebec already allows advance requests; the province passed legislation that instructs provincial Crown prosecutors not to prosecute health-care workers who provide Maid in those cases.

In March, the Alberta government passed legislation that bars advance consent. On Wednesday, the province said it will not change its decision.

The proposed bill will need to pass both the House of Commons and the Senate before March 17, the date on which the law states that people with a mental illness as their sole underlying condition would become eligible for Maid.

The Opposition Conservatives accused Fraser of engaging in cynical politics.

“We have a minister who is, frankly, playing politics with life and death and deliberately sowing division,” said Tory MP Michael Cooper.

The decision to tie the two changes together is drawing criticism from people on both sides of the issue.

Cardus, a Christian think-tank that opposes Maid, and the disability rights group Inclusion Canada both celebrated the fact that the planned expansion for mental illness will not go ahead. They also raised concerns about advance requests.

Both groups called on Parliament to separate the legislation to allow more study of advance requests — something Fraser has said already he does not plan to do.

“Democracy doesn’t demand unanimity,” he said.

Advocacy group Dying With Dignity Canada said it was a “profoundly disappointing day.” While the group has pushed for advance requests for years, its CEO Helen Long decried the decision to allow provinces to create their own rules.

“At best, this will create a patchwork. What’s much more likely is that it will create a situation where many, many people never have access to advance requests in their province or territory,” she said.

Dying With Dignity is leading a court challenge that argues the exclusion of people with mental illness as a sole underlying condition violates their Charter rights.

Fraser acknowledged Wednesday that the courts are going to weigh in, including on that specific case, and said the government will respect decisions from the Supreme Court of Canada.

Fraser said he held the press conference on Wednesday before introducing the legislation because it was the day the House of Commons was scheduled to vote on a Conservative private member’s bill that would exclude people with mental disorders from eligibility for Maid.

The bill was defeated at second reading, with the Bloc Québécois and most Liberals voting against it.

Marilyn Gladu, an Ontario Liberal MP who crossed the floor from the Tories last April, voted with her former caucus along with P.E.I. MP Kent MacDonald. Emmanuella Lambropoulous abstained.

The Ndp’s five MPs voted with the Conservatives.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

Hannah Alberga and Sarah Ritchie, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canadian buoy drifts across Atlantic, washes up on shore of Irish island
stories.summary: Officials in northwestern Ireland say they're working to recover a large Canadian buoy that floated across the Atlantic Ocean and washed up on a coastal island.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Officials in northwestern Ireland say they’re working to recover a large Canadian buoy that floated across the Atlantic Ocean and washed up on a coastal island.

A news release from Mayo County Council says the mariner marker, weighing in at roughly 3.5 tonnes, came ashore on Achill Island, known for its rugged mountains and bright sandy beaches.

stories.title: Three finalists named for inaugural Writers' Trust non-fiction editing prize
stories.summary: Toronto - Award-winning poet katherena vermette is among the three finalists for the Writers' Trust's inaugural prize for non-fiction editing.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Award-winning poet katherena vermette is among the three finalists for the Writers’ Trust’s inaugural prize for non-fiction editing.

The Nancy Flight Writers’ Trust Prize for Nonfiction Editing awards $25,000 to an editor whose work has made an outstanding contribution to a full-length book of literary non-fiction. The organization says the award is the largest of its kind in Canada, with runners-up receiving $2,500 each.

vermette is nominated for editing “Carry Your Heart: Indigenous Helping Wisdom and the Science of Psychological Flexibility” by Cree psychotherapist Louis Busch, who blends Indigenous teaching wisdoms and Western psychology in the self-help title.

The Winnipeg-born vermette previously won the Governor General’s Literary Award for English-language poetry in 2013 for her collection “North End Love Songs.” She also won the Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize for her 2021 novel “The Strangers.”

Also among the finalists is Victoria’s George Galt for Sarah Ellis’ memoir “My Year in Fairyland: Grief, Maid and a Lifetime of Books,” which details the 12 months before her wife’s medically assisted death.

Rounding out the contenders is Vancouver’s Rachel Rose for “Humanitarienne: A Doctor’s Stories from the Conflict Zone” by physician and public health specialist Kirsten Johnson. The memoir explores her career in war-torn and disaster-affected regions.

The Writers’ Trust says the prize will be handed out annually until 2033 as part of a multi-year commitment of $483,000.

A three-person jury selected the finalists. The winner will be announced on Nov. 10 in Toronto.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

stories.title: Move to freeze Osap for all Ontario private career colleges called unfair: 'Can't throw baby out with the bathwater'
stories.summary: Minister Nolan Quinn asks Ontario Provincial Police to investigate “criminal allegations.”
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
Laleh Bighash says she supports the Ontario government’s move to root out student aid fraud in private career colleges. But she says temporarily banning them all from accessing student aid payments unfairly penalizes everyone because of a few bad actors.

Bighash, who left Iran in the late 1980s and later founded Aaps College of Health, Science and Technology for post-graduates after noticing gaps in the system — particularly for newcomers — called Tuesday’s surprise news “disheartening.”

“We have been in operation for 24 years,” said Bighash, who earned an undergraduate degree in pharmacology and toxicology at the University of Toronto and an MBA at York. “We are brick and mortar. We train for the pharmaceutical industry, and we do have a track record.

“At the same time, I do understand that we need to get rid of these actors ... but you can’t just throw the baby out with the bathwater. There are five or seven colleges who are doing fraudulent activities and breaking people’s trust, and they have to be dealt with, and I am supportive of that.”

Ontario students say shifting Osap from grants to loans is forcing them to defer degrees or drop out of school.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced the measures Tuesday afternoon, saying they were a result of “increased complaints related to the growing volume of Osap claims at private career colleges,” and they came after an independent auditor “identified serious concerns about the integrity of the Osap system across private post-secondary institutions that requires further investigation.”

For that reason, the government “paused all Osap payments associated with private post-secondary institutions while the audit proceeds,” notified the auditor general and asked Ontario Provincial Police to investigate “criminal allegations,” including alleged co-ownership of private colleges and immigration firms, and clusters of Osap applications from the same locations.

“I wholly recognize the impact this Osap pause has on hard-working students who attend private institutions,” Quinn said, adding “the government is working on options to provide low-interest third-party loans for students” with banks.

Osap eligibility will be tightened in the coming days, he added, and private institutions will need to reapply. However, online-only schools will be ineligible given the volume of concerns.

“While this May seem like a drastic measure, let me be very clear: It is an entirely necessary one,” he said.

The government’s crackdown is expected to cause a number of schools significant financial hardship — with critics warning some might have to close — and students now left in limbo after starting programs with already approved Osap student loans.

Osap funds can go directly to schools to cover tuition and fees.

The post-secondary ministry had previously banned private career colleges from accessing Osap grants — which are non-repayable — and then in May initially suspended six schools from accessing Osap loans.

The problem of increased Osap usage among some private colleges was identified around 2023 or earlier, and in 2025 Career Colleges Ontario, which represents 280-plus private colleges, also flagged concerns . The federal government has also investigated and found irregularities.

“The Ford government’s failure to properly manage Osap should not fall on the backs of students,” said New Democrat MPP Peggy Sattler, her party’s post-secondary critic, in a written statement.

Liberal MPP Tyler Watt, his party’s colleges and universities critic, said the government knew something was wrong and failed to act quickly .

“The numbers are staggering,” he said in a written statement. “In 2024-25, nearly $1 billion in Ontario grants went to students at private career colleges. Just seven schools received $385 million, as much as all 24 public colleges combined.

“And when Osap grant spending increased by $465 million in a single year, 95 cents of every new dollar went to private career college students.”

(Citing ballooning costs, the government recently reformed the overall Osap student aid system to make it loan-heavy instead of mostly non-repayable grants.)

Bighash estimates about 400 of her college’s 500 students rely on some form of financial aid, and she worried about the impact on the sector.

Career colleges “are part of the puzzle of the training and education system,” she added. “We have 40,000 students (in the province), and we have been part of the Ontario economy for as long as I remember. There are human stories behind us. There are owners, there are students, there are faculty members.”

stories.title: Donald Trump’s trade war is coming for your Thanksgiving dinner — and your pumpkin pie
stories.summary: Rising diesel costs and trade war uncertainty are carving into Canadian grocery budgets this holiday season.
stories.author: Iman Janmohamed
stories.content:
Rising energy and transportation prices — which jumped following oil shortages due to the war on Iran — have helped push the cost of a typical turkey feast up by 10 per cent year over year.

“Diesel is double the price of what it was last year,” said Dalhousie University’s Sylvain Charlebois, whose Agri-Food Lab report studied Thanksgiving dinner pricing over the last three years. “It has impacted harvest this year and it is going to be impacting the entire supply chain.”

The price of a standard turkey dinner for four — potatoes, carrots, dinner rolls, pumpkin pie, cranberries, stuffing, gravy — is expected to rise to nearly $36 from about $32 last year.

Here's why it's easy to have a Canadian-made Thanksgiving. (Oct. 6, 2026)

A similarly priced ham dinner is expected to rise about five per cent, according to the report. And for the wealthy noshing on lamb or lobster — $80 and $88 — the price spike is about three per cent this year, according to Dalhousie.

University of Toronto health studies Prof. Michael Widener says the Canada-U.S. trade war is also pushing up grocery costs — indirectly.

“It creates an environment of uncertainty,” Widener said, “and oftentimes companies will price in that uncertainty even if there’s not a real impact on the price of a particular food item.”

He also points to inflation as a “huge influence” on how people spend their grocery money and can drive people to cheaper, unhealthier options.

“Persistent compromises in diet and the stress of food insecurity are the things that we see linked to issues like chronic disease and poor mental health,” said Widener. “It’s not something that happens overnight, but it’s the sustained exposure.”

Budgeting experts, however, say there are ways to keep your costs down at this year’s feast.

Shopping flyer deals, redeeming loyalty points and buying from independent grocers can help consumers stay within budget, said Barry Choi, a Toronto-based personal finance expert.

“You really got to pay attention to those prices more than anything else,” said Choi. “It can add up.”

To stay on budget while keeping healthy food on the table, Widener recommends people opt for frozen and canned produce in place of fresh, and consider hosting a potluck dinner to share costs.

“It’s easier to have a really nice meal with people that you care about without having to break the bank.”

The key to year-round consumer savings lies in relying on local flyers, whether on paper or through apps, Choi said, adding these flyers won’t just show the best deals but can also be used for price-matching at competing grocers.

“It can be very convenient,” he said. “You don’t necessarily need to go to multiple grocery stores.”

Shopping at local grocers or butchers could also be a cost-cutting measure, Choi said, adding he sometimes opts to visit specialized, international shops that sell products cheaper than big-box grocery stores.

Though Thanksgiving costs have risen, Charlebois said it’s important to put things into perspective.

“It’s been cheaper before, but when you look at other countries around the world, prices tend to be much higher,” said Charlebois. “We need to remind ourselves that, yes, food inflation has been an issue the last several years, but our situation is not as bad as in other places around the world.”

stories.title: The Ford government quietly changed its building code, clearing the way for more triple-bunking in Ontario’s overcrowded jails
stories.summary: Ontario quietly eliminated minimum sleep-area rules for jails, clearing the way for triple-bunking in overcrowded facilities.
stories.author: Brendan Kennedy
stories.content:
The Ontario government has eliminated minimum sleep-area requirements for its overcrowded jails , clearing the way for more inmates to be confined together in single cells.

The change to the provincial building code was quietly made public late Friday evening in a government newsletter for building industry stakeholders.

No explanation was provided in the brief description of the change, which simply removes a requirement for at least 4.7 square metres of sleeping area space, per person, in adult correctional facilities.

Critics fear the province is planning to make triple-bunking — when three inmates share a cell designed for two — a permanent fixture of provincial jails.

Already common in some Ontario jails, the practice of triple-bunking is routinely decried by judges as unduly harsh and inhumane , and has led to reduced sentences as a kind of compensation.

Solicitor General Michael Kerzner, whose ministry oversees provincial jails , and housing minister Rob Flack, who is responsible for the building code, declined to be interviewed about the change. Their offices did not directly answer questions from the Star.

As the premier calls for bail reforms that would see more people locked up while awaiting trial, Ontario’s jails are “in a state of growing crisis.”

In a statement sent via email, a spokesperson for Kerzner said the province is investing $3 billion to increase jail capacity “as part of the government’s plan to strengthen the bail system and keep dangerous offenders behind bars.”

This, the spokesperson wrote, includes changing the building code “to optimize space within existing and new provincial adult correctional facilities to support current and future capacity expansion needs.”

The province did not answer a question about whether it intends to make triple-bunking standard practice going forward in provincial jails, where roughly 80 per cent of inmates are awaiting trial and have not been convicted.

Global News reported earlier this year that documents it obtained from a Freedom of Information request showed the province was planning to permanently add third bunks to 25 cells at the Quinte Detention Centre.

Triple-bunking is already common in some jails due to overcrowding. Data obtained by the Star last year showed the correctional system as a whole was operating at 123-per-cent capacity, with some jails more than 30-per-cent overcrowded.

Currently triple-bunking occurs in makeshift fashion, with one inmate sleeping on a mattress on the floor with their head or feet abutting the toilet.

Shrinking the already limited amount of personal space inmates have will lead to more conflicts and a further deterioration of inmates’ physical and mental health, warned Shakir Rahim, director of the criminal justice program at the Canadian Civil Liberties Association

“It’s going to undermine public safety because if there are no minimum standards — which are so critical for detainees’ health — people are going to come out with more problems than they had going in.”

Rahim pointed to last year’s deadly outbreak of invasive group A streptococcal disease, which killed two inmates at Maplehurst Correctional Complex, the province’s most overcrowded jail at the time, as an example of the kind of events that could become more common if triple-bunking was made permanent.

Violence between inmates and against guards has also increased as jails have become more crowded, according to data obtained by the Star last year.

In May the province announced they are increasing capacity in provincial jails by adding more than 2,500 beds within the next decade, including more than 250 by the end of this year and more than 600 in the “near term.”

Among the methods the province said it planned to employ to increase capacity was “bed optimization,” which it described as “expanding bed capacity by installing permanent beds, along with required ancillary furniture, fixtures and equipment.”

stories.title: It's already going around: Ontario's flu season is getting an early start
stories.summary: The good news is that early signs suggest this year’s vaccine could be a good match for the H1N1 strain now circulating.
stories.author: Kerry Gillespie
stories.content:
Anyone with colleagues calling in sick or kids home with a fever May have suspected it already: Ontario’s flu season is getting an early start.

Influenza tests are coming back positive more often than at this point in recent years, and the rates for children are even higher. It’s too soon to say how severe the season will be, but early signs suggest this year’s vaccine could be a good match for the strain now circulating, Public Health Ontario says.

If trends continue, Ontario will hit the threshold that officially marks flu season within a couple weeks, and typically it takes five to six weeks after that to reach peak flu season, said Dr. Richard Mather, a public health physician with Public Health Ontario.

Positivity captures only people who get tested, and flu isn’t the only virus going around.

High-risk groups are eligible Sept. 28, followed by the general public at pharmacies and doctors on Oct. 26.

Influenza positivity — the portion of lab tests that come back positive — reached three per cent for the week ending Sept. 26, according to the agency’s respiratory virus tracker. Influenza detections were higher among children: a 6.8 per cent positivity rate for children ages five to 11 and 5.3 per cent for kids ages one to four.

Children “are sort of efficient at spreading viruses,” Mather said. “We typically see a higher per cent positivity in kids at the start, and then in other age groups it starts to increase as well.

“It’s important, as we are seeing some increased activity, to get the vaccine as soon as it’s available for you.”

In Ontario, the influenza vaccine is technically already available for those over 65 and under five, health-care workers, residents in long-term care homes and other high-risk populations. But finding a shot depends on the availability of initial supplies.

Last year, there was a lot of concern about a possible mismatch between the flu vaccine and H3N2, a mutated strain of influenza A that was common. But Mather says the latest data from the Sentinel Practitioner Surveillance Network, which analyzes how well the vaccine worked in Canada each year, shows it was better than expected and reduced the risk for that strain by over one-third.

Right now, the most commonly circulating strain is influenza A, H1N1. That was also the strain that was prominent at the end of the flu season in the Southern Hemisphere and a factor in the World Health Organization’s choice of strains for this year’s Northern Hemisphere vaccine, he said.

“It’s somewhat reassuring that the vaccine is anticipated to be a good match,” he said.

Dr. Isaac Bogoch, an infectious diseases specialist at Toronto General Hospital and the University of Toronto, said Canada has weathered two years of challenging flu seasons. He’s hoping this season will be better.

“But hope, of course, is not a strategy,” Bogoch said. “And we need to prepare by getting vaccines and ensuring people remember about staying home if they’re sick.

“It’s not widespread just yet, but it will be, it absolutely will be.”

This early on, it’s impossible to project how severe the respiratory virus season, which includes influenza, COVID-19 and RSV, will be, or just how much protection the flu vaccine will provide, he said.

“People might say, ‘oh, the shot’s not perfect, I might not get it.’ But … influenza, I’m not talking about the sniffles or a cough or a cold, true influenza can knock even a healthy young person on their butts for a few days and they will feel absolutely miserable.”

Dr. Pierre-Philippe Piché-Renaud, a physician in the infectious diseases division at Toronto’s Hospital for Sick Children, said the hospital is seeing what it would expect at this point in the season.

But with Thanksgiving celebrations and long-weekend gatherings coming up, it’s important to keep in mind that influenza is already floating around, Piché-Renaud said.

“It’s an excellent time to think about how to protect children and vulnerable individuals,” he said, “especially in the context of these kind of celebrations. If people do have symptoms, it’s probably best to stay at home and take care of yourself as opposed to spreading these kind of viruses.

“We’ve been repeating that message for some time now. And again, as soon as vaccines become available, to get vaccinated to prevent getting the infection in the first place.”

stories.title: Former defence chief warns Canada must defend its North or risk U.S. intervention
stories.summary: Wayne Eyre says Canada must "ensure that it doesn't receive sovereignty-violating help" with the region.
stories.author: Alex Ballingall
stories.content:
Ottawa — The military’s former top soldier says there is a risk the United States will step in to defend the Canadian Arctic under the pretext Canada isn’t up for the job — one reason that he argues the federal government must maintain increases in military spending, even if it means sacrificing social programs.

In a wide-ranging interview with the Star on Tuesday, retired Gen. Wayne Eyre said Canada must, by showing it is capable of protecting the North, defend against “help” that would violate the country’s sovereignty over the vast region. While multibillion-dollar plans to do that are in the works, including through the construction of new over-the-horizon radar stations, icebreaker ships and military support hubs in the Arctic, “speed of execution” is now key, Eyre said.

ByEdward Keenan Columnist

Good morning. This is the Wednesday, Oct. 7 edition of First Up, the Star’s daily morning digest. Sign up to get it earlier each day, in your inbox.

I was up Tuesday night moderating a mayoral debate. You may have heard how at the last minute it turned from a three-candidate debate into a twosome. (If you haven’t heard, we’ll get to that news in a moment.) Here’s what our team thought the key takeaways from the night were. Lots more Toronto mayoral election news below.

But first up, here are six things to know on Wednesday morning:

The Tumbler Ridge shooter plotted with a U.S. resident who advised her on weapons and even planned to livestream the killings, police allege.

Mississauga mayoral candidate Alvin Tedjo says a volunteer for his campaign was attacked with a knife while putting up election signs.

“Much more than names”: More details on Canadian crew of missing air ambulance as Transportation Safety Board says it will investigate what happened.

Flu season is set to start early. But it looks like this year’s vaccine might be a good match.

Fighting has escalated in Yemen while U.S.-Iran tensions remain high. Here’s a breakdown of what’s going on.

There’s a possible case of pneumonic plague after a lab worker died in Russia. Here’s how the country and the WHO are responding.

Pitter patter, let’s get at ’er.

Just half an hour before early voting opened Tuesday morning, the former immigration minister ended his campaign for mayor of Toronto, saying he lost faith he’d find the path to victory. The announcement leaves Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford as the two main contenders. Quick recap: Alexander failed to garner much support in nearly 10 weeks of campaigning, despite robust policy proposals. At single digits in recent polling, some questioned why he was even running. Alexander missed the deadline to officially withdraw, so his name will remain on the ballot for the Oct. 26 vote.

stories.title: Boler Road construction continues with work progressing through final phase
stories.summary: Boler Road closed between Byron Baseline Road and Norman AvenueFrom October 13 to October 30, Boler Road will
stories.content:
From October 13 to October 30, Boler Road will be fully closed between Byron Baseline Road and just north of Norman Avenue while work continues on the Boler Road Cycling and Watermain Improvements project.

A full closure will allow crews to work in the area more efficiently and complete this section of the project sooner, rather than having several shorter closures.

Crews will work longer hours, with the goal of completing the roadway, bike path, and sidewalks this fall.

A signed detour will be in place, and the Byron Baseline Road intersection will remain open.

Some LTC routes will be impacted. Please check the London Transit Commission website for the most up-to-date information on bus schedules and detours.

The project will replace the aging watermain under Boler Road, which broke 13 times last year and required repairs that caused short-term closures or reduced the road to one lane. Replacing it now will help prevent these repeated disruptions.

The project will also add a two-way bike path, giving people cycling a dedicated route through Byron where there is currently limited cycling infrastructure. It also includes upgraded sidewalks, pedestrian crossings, traffic signals, and repairs to the road, including new pavement, curbs and gutters.

Most of the work is expected to be completed by the end of fall 2026, with some remaining work continuing into spring 2027.

The project is being completed in three phases:

Phase 1: Byron Baseline Road to Griffith Street is complete, including replacement of the watermain and water services.

Phase 2: Griffith Street to Southdale Road is nearing completion, including the new bike path and other road improvements.

Phase 3: Commissioners Road to Byron Baseline Road is underway, including the new bike path, pedestrian crossings, and road improvements.

For information about the Boler road project including construction updates, project timelines, visit the City’s Get Involved webpage.

You can also subscribe to receive project updates by clicking the Follow button at the top of the page.

stories.title: Suspect sought after hydro pole cut down
stories.summary: London, ON (October 7, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) are investigating after a London Hydro pole was cut down in the south end of the city last night.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 7, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) are investigating after a London Hydro pole was cut down in the south end of the city last night.

On Tuesday, October 6, 2026, at approximately 5:45 p.m., a citizen in the area of Exeter Road and Meg Drive heard a loud noise and observed smoke and flames near a hydro pole.

The citizen called 9-1-1, and officers attended with members of the London Fire Department, and London Hydro.

Multiple downed power lines and a hydro pole were located, and it was determined that the base of the pole had been intentionally cut. The damage is estimated at approximately $10,000.

As a result of the incident, a number of London Hydro customers were without power. London Hydro has since completed the repairs, and all power has been restored.

There were no reported injuries.

The investigation has been re-assigned to members of the LPS Patrol Operations Investigative Section.

Images of the suspect and suspect’s vehicle are being released in hopes that someone can identify him.

The suspect is described as a white male wearing a ball cap, a black hoodie with writing across the chest and grey pants.

The suspect vehicle is described as a grey SUV, believed to be a 2019 Honda CR-V or similar model.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area between 5:20 p.m. and 6 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 6, 2026, and witnessed the incident, or who May have dashcam, residential or business surveillance footage, to contact the London Police Service.

Anyone with information in relation to these types of incidents is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Barricaded male
stories.summary: London, ON (October 7, 2026) – A London man is facing charges after an investigation in the south-east end of the city earlier this week.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 7, 2026) – A London man is facing charges after an investigation in the south-east end of the city earlier this week.

On Monday, October 5, 2026, members of the London Police Service responded to a residence on Frontenac Road in relation to checking the welfare of an individual.

At approximately 6:05 a.m., officers attended the area and learned that the suspect male had barricaded himself inside the home. Members of the Emergency Response Unit (ERU) were called to assist, and nearby roads were closed for a period of time while police attempted to negotiate with the suspect male.

Shortly after 7 a.m., the suspect exited the residence and threw an object toward officers. No injuries were reported. The suspect then threw another object at the front windshield of the London Police Service's Light Armoured Vehicle (LAV), before retreating back inside the residence.

The vehicle did not sustain any damage.

At approximately 7:10 a.m., the suspect exited the residence, armed with a knife. He uttered threats toward officers. Negotiations continued while police maintained containment of the residence.

At approximately 10:05 a.m., the suspect exited the residence and was taken into custody without injury.

As a result of the investigation, Ara Husni, 20, of London, has been charged with:

Two counts of assault a peace officer with a weapon;

Fail to comply with release order; and

Uttering threats to cause death or bodily harm.

The accused is expected to appear in London court today in relation to the charges.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-8477. Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: A Toronto cancer patient applied for pricey out-of-country funding. Now Ontario is tightening the rules
stories.summary: Funding will now only be available for drug treatments when “specific conditions” are met, Health Ministry says.
stories.author: Megan Ogilvie
stories.content:
The Ford government has tightened its policy on when it will fund out-of-country treatments, in the wake of a high-profile court fight by a Toronto man with terminal cancer.

The Ministry of Health says amendments to Ontario’s Health Insurance Act mean funding will now only be provided for drug treatments that are already in use and approved for public coverage in the province but are temporarily unavailable.

The regulatory amendments — announced this week — essentially close the door to patients like Alex Shved, a 37-year-old with metastatic melanoma , who has been fighting to have Ontario fund a last-resort therapy in the U.S. He argues that his terminal diagnosis means he can’t wait for the personalized cell treatment to make its way through Canada’s lengthy drug funding process.

Shved called Ontario’s move “a betrayal” and said he’s “incredibly frustrated” the province has blocked access to the out-of-country program for drug treatments that have been given the green light by Health Canada but not approved for public coverage.

Last month, a panel of the Ontario Divisional Court directed the provincial government to reconsider its earlier denial to fund Shved’s treatment in the U.S., citing his immediate need.

The Health Ministry states the new Health Insurance Act amendments were put in place to “protect Ontario patients’ access to affordable, life-saving medication here at home.”

In its Tuesday announcement, the ministry states the province’s out-of-country drug funding program, which has been in place since 2011, will now only fund drugs that have gone through Ontario’s “rigorous, consistent, transparent, evidence-based and expert-led process.”

The ministry said it needed to act to prevent the Ontario Health Insurance Plan from paying out an additional $5.2 billion each year. It also said the policy, as previously written, created “a back door for global pharmaceutical companies to avoid negotiating directly with the province to achieve more competitive pricing.”

Sylvia Jones, deputy premier and minister of health, said in the news release that the government is “protecting Ontario patients and taxpayers from price-gouging and protecting their access to life-saving medications that would otherwise only be available in the United States or overseas.”

“This change supports a consistent, fair and transparent approach to funding decisions, protects the integrity of Ontario’s world-class drug approval process and will help avoid up to $5.2 billion in additional costs to Ontario’s health-care system every year,” Jones said.

The amendments are to Regulation 552 of the Health Insurance Act. The conditions for funding now include that the drug treatment is performed and publicly funded in the province; access to the drug is temporarily unavailable in Ontario; and delay in access “makes it necessary that the insured person travel out of Canada to avoid death or medically significant irreversible tissue damage.”

The province pointed to the need to protect Canada’s ability to negotiate fair drug prices with pharmaceutical companies as a main reason to make the regulatory change. The Health Ministry also said it needed to limit a recent but “significant increase” in out-of-country treatment requests that would otherwise lead to “up to $170 million” in additional annual costs.

Steven J. Hoffman, professor of global health, law, and political science at York University’s Global Strategy Lab, said in an email statement that the regulatory clarification “makes good sense for promoting value-for-money in Ontario’s health-care system and protecting efforts to ensure Canadians pay some of the world’s lowest prices for patented medicines.”

He said the executive officer of the Ontario Public Drug Programs will likely continue to decline Shved’s request for out-of-country drug coverage. Shved confirmed Wednesday the province has again denied his application.

Hoffman said that provinces must be effective stewards of limited health-care resources and noted that how pharmaceutical companies set their prices also deserves scrutiny.

“Companies developing new drugs and charging prices that only multi-millionaires can afford is not helpful,” Hoffman said. He described Shved’s case as “tragic.”

Shved was diagnosed with melanoma in 2020 and is running out of treatment options. Doctors have recommended he undergo tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, or TIL therapy, which uses a patient’s own cells to train their immune system to find and attack cancer.

Produced by an American biotechnology company, the therapy is marketed as lifileucel, also known by its brand name Amtagvi, and is only available at authorized centres in the U.S. Shved said a Florida hospital quoted $1.3 million for the therapy, which requires chemotherapy and time in hospital, in addition to producing the personalized cell treatment.

In its September ruling, the three-justice panel of the Ontario Divisional Court underscored that medical experts had recommended Shved get access to TIL therapy as part of its reasoning for directing the province to reassess its earlier denial.

“The record discloses that he will likely be dead by Christmas if he does not receive the requested treatment within a few weeks,” the panel wrote in its ruling.

The Health Ministry’s news release stated it’s “exploring all available options” for the court ruling, including an appeal “and/or seeking a mutually satisfactory resolution” with Shved.

On Wednesday, Shved said he has yet to receive any settlement details and is unsure what he will do next.

“I don’t know what this (amendment change) means for me, or for all the other people who are in the queue,” he said. “This is a blanket rejection of all applications now and in the future.”

stories.title: An Ontario Trillium Benefit payment is coming soon. Here’s what you need to know to get it
stories.summary: The OTB is comprised of three credits, but you only need to qualify for at least one to receive it.
stories.author: Samm Mohibuddin; Joshua Smith; Jake Ross
stories.content:
For those whose bank balances could use a boost after the back-to-school season and ahead of the holidays, the next Ontario Trillium Benefit payment is going out to eligible Ontarians on Oct. 9 .

The provincial government started issuing the payments in 2012 after including it in the 2011 budget.

Here’s what you should know about the money that could be coming your way.

The Ontario Trillium Benefit (OTB) combines three credits — the Northern Ontario Energy Credit, the Ontario Energy and Tax Credit, and the Ontario Sales Tax Credit — to help offset energy, sales and property tax expenses.

In order to qualify for the benefit, you need to have filed an income tax return and filled out the Ontario Trillium Benefit application form.

The Canada Revenue Agency will determine if you’re eligible to receive the benefit based on the information you provided.

You can receive the benefit if you’re eligible for at least one of the three credits noted in the previous section.

To estimate your amount, use the child and family benefit calculator. Taxpayers entitled to more than $500 could’ve opted for either a monthly payout starting this past June or a lump sum that’ll be issued next June.

If your 2026 OTB annual entitlement is $500 or less, it would’ve been issued in one lump-sum payment in the first payment month, which is usually July.

To apply for the Ontario Trillium Benefit, you have to fill out the ON‑BEN Application for the 2026 Ontario Trillium Benefit and Ontario Senior Homeowners’ Property Tax Grant form.

The CRA will send you a notice if you are deemed eligible for the Ontario Trillium Benefit.

In order to continue receiving the benefit, you have to file income tax annually and reapply by filling out the form each year. If you were previously deemed ineligible for the benefit in a previous year, you can reapply for it.

If you already receive your income tax refund or other benefits or credits by direct deposit, you will also receive your OTB payments by direct deposit. Otherwise, you’ll get your payments by cheque.

The federal government is encouraging people to sign up for direct deposit. Wildfires in Ontario have delayed the delivery of a small number of benefit and credit cheques, the government says .

The first payment is typically received four to eight weeks after applying.

The payments are issued monthly, unless you qualify to receive the aforementioned lump sum.

The funds have been issued on the 10th day of every month this year, except when the 10th falls on a weekend. That’s why the money will arrive on Oct. 9.

Subsequent payments will be sent out on Nov. 10 and Dec. 10.
