stories.title: A timeline of key events in the Regis Korchinski-Paquet case
stories.summary: A coroner’s inquest is scheduled to start Tuesday in the case of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman who fell from a Toronto highrise balcony while police were in her home in 2020.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — A coroner’s inquest is scheduled to start Tuesday in the case of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a 29-year-old Afro-Indigenous woman who fell from a Toronto highrise balcony while police were in her home in 2020.

Here is a timeline of key events in the case:

May 27, 2020: The Special Investigations Unit says it is investigating the death of a woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in the apartment. Korchinski-Paquet’s death sparks questions from her family, local politicians, and on social media about the role of police officers in the incident.

In the days that follow, Korchinski-Paquet’s mother says she called police that day hoping they would take her daughter to the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health but instead the woman ended up dead.

May 30, 2020: Thousands of people take to the streets in Toronto to protest against racism and demand answers in Korchinski-Paquet’s case. Several smaller marches follow over the next few weeks.

June 3, 2020: The SIU urges police to stop speaking on the case after Korchinski-Paquet’s family postpones meeting the watchdog, citing concerns about possible police leaks.

June 8, 2020: Two Toronto city councillors put forward a motion to defund the city’s police force by 10 per cent and use the money for community resources.

June 10, 2020: Korchinski-Paquet’s family says it will talk to the SIU.

June 11, 2020: The family holds a small funeral for her.

June 29, 2020: Toronto city council votes against defunding the police budget but approves numerous reforms to the service, including anti-racism measures and the implementation of body-worn cameras.

July 25, 2020: Family, friends and community members gather for a memorial and walk to honour Korchinski-Paquet.

Aug. 26, 2020: The SIU clears police of wrongdoing in her death, finding the officers tried to de-escalate the situation and “though their efforts were unsuccessful,” none of them broke the law. Korchinski-Paquet’s family rejects the findings.

Feb. 3, 2021: Toronto announces a pilot project to send crisis-support workers instead of police to certain 911 calls in the city. The pilot, set to begin the following year, comes after widespread calls for police reform, including improvements to how police deal with those experiencing mental-health crises.

May 26, 2021: A lawyer for Korchinski-Paquet’s family says they recently filed a complaint with the Office of the Independent Police Review Director because they believe the report by the SIU doesn’t make sense. The Oiprd confirms it is investigating but declines to comment further, citing confidentiality.

June 19, 2021: Korchinski-Paquet’s relatives speak at Juneteenth event in Ottawa aimed at demanding accountability and changes to the justice system. Several Black and Indigenous families whose loved ones were harmed or killed by police also attend the event organized by Black Lives Matter Toronto.

June 2022: Korchinski-Paquet’s family files a $10-million lawsuit against several police officers and the head of Ontario’s police watchdog, as well as Ontario’s attorney general, the City of Toronto and the Toronto Community Housing Corporation.

The lawsuit alleges her relatives suffered severe emotional distress after they were provided with “misleading information” at the time of her death.

April 2, 2026: Coroner Dr. Richard Wells announces that an inquest into Korchinski-Paquet’s death will be held.

May 27, 2026: Korchinski-Paquet’s parents join advocates at the provincial legislature to call for reforms, including that the recommendations issued by coroner’s inquests be binding and implemented in a reasonable time frame.

Sept. 15, 2026: The date of the coroner’s inquest is announced.

Oct. 13, 2026: The coroner’s inquest begins.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Coroner's inquest set to begin examining death of Toronto woman who fell from balcony
stories.summary: A coroner’s inquest is set to begin today to examine the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto — A coroner’s inquest is set to begin today to examine the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.

Korchinski-Paquet, a woman of Ukrainian, Black and Indigenous ancestry, died on May 27, 2020 after police responded to calls about a family dispute at the apartment. She was 29.

Her death came on the heels of the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, spurring further protests amid growing calls to defund the police.

It also cast a spotlight on how police interact with people experiencing mental health crises.

Ontario’s police watchdog investigated the case and eventually cleared Toronto police of wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death.

The Special Investigations Unit found it happened as she was trying to move from her apartment balcony to an adjacent one.

The inquest was announced earlier this year and is slated to last 14 days, with 15 witnesses expected to take the stand.

The inquest jury does not assign criminal responsibility but May make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future. The chief coroner’s office does not have the authority to impose the recommendations, however.

On the anniversary of her death this year, Korchinski-Paquet’s parents joined advocates in calling for the recommendations issued in coroner’s inquests to be binding and implemented within a reasonable timeframe.

Her mother, Claudette Beals, also said there should be a different system in place to investigate allegations of wrongdoing against police officers, adding she has no faith in “police investigating police.”

“My daughter’s been gone for six years and no one’s held responsible for that,” she said in a news conference at the provincial legislature.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

Paola Loriggio, The Canadian Press

News Home

Tuesday, 13 October 2026 07:29

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Share on Facebook

The Braves sit on top of the Doherty Division standings and the Trojans are at the bottom of the Yeck Division standings.

PJHL - It was a mixed weekend for Oxford County's Junior C hockey teams.

The Norwich Merchants suffered a 6-1 loss to the New Hamburg Firebirds on Friday, but they were able to bounce back with a 5-2 victory over the Dorchester Dolphins on Saturday. Liam Nunn scored the lone goal for Norwich on Friday, while Jack Birkbeck, Gavin Balazs, Logan Van Den Akker, Boden Brimmell, and Tyler McDole scored during Saturday's game.

The Tavistock Braves doubled the Dolphins 4-2 on Friday with Jacob Skuta, Tucket Otto, Nolan Miller, and Carter Otto scoring for the home team. The Braves went on to suffer a 7-6 loss to the Firebirds on Saturday with Kaiden Cormier scoring the game winning goal for New Hamburg in overtime.

The Thamesford Trojans only had one game over the long weekend, where they lost to the Aylmer Spitfires 3-2 in overtime on Friday. Yusuf Jomaa scored the first goal of the game from Thamesford, and Rowan Reid scored in the second period for the Trojans.

The Braves sit on top of the Doherty Division standings with 17 points. The Firebirds are tied with the Wellesley Applejacks for second place with 14 points, and the Merchants are in third place with eight points. The Paris Mounties are in fourth place with seven points, while the Dolphins are in fifth place with four points, only one ahead of the last place Hespeler Shamrocks with three points.

The Trojans sit at the bottom of the Yeck Division standings with five points. They're only one point behind the Lucan Irish with six points, while the Port Stanley Sailors sit in fifth place with seven points, and the Petrolia Flyers sit in fourth place with nine points. The Spitfires and tied with the Exeter Hawks for third place with 10 points each, while the North Middlesex Stars sit in second place with 12 points, and the Mount Brydges Bulldogs top the standings with 14 points.

Navy Vets Recap - Oct 9th and Oct 10th The Woodstock Navy Vets suffered two losses over the Thanksgiving long weekend.

Theatre Woodstock Presents - Dracula: A Chamber Musical Theatre Woodstock will debut the first production of its 80th season this Friday.

Assault Charges Laid in Tillsonburg The suspect is facing nine counts of sexual assault, stemming from two investigations.

Upcoming WAG Exhibit Celebrates Peanuts Creator An upcoming exhibit at the Woodstock Art Gallery is going to be all about Charles M. Schulz, the man behind Charlie Brown.

The Woodstock Navy Vets suffered two losses over the Thanksgiving long weekend.

WOODSTOCK/CAMBRIDGE - It was a rough weekend for the Woodstock Navy Vets.

They suffered a 5-4 loss to the Strathroy Rockets at Southwood Arena on Friday. Woodstock had the lead close to the end of the game, by Strathroy scored twice in the final 3.5 minutes to secure the victory. Evan Giannone scored twice for Woodstock, while the other goals were scored by Sebastien Fortin and captain Will McGregor.

The Vets also lost to the Cambridge Redhawks 5-2 on Saturday. Maddyx Chaput and Cole Bonneville scored for the Vets, and Landyn Quirk made 39 saves in the Woodstock net.

The Vets only have one game on the schedule for this coming weekend, with a home game against the London Nationals on Friday.

Woodstock is currently in a three-way tie for sixth place in thre GOHL Western Conference standings. The Vets have eight points, matching the Komoka Kings and the LaSalle Vipers. The Nationals are tied with the Elmira Sugar Kings for fifth place with nine points each, while the Stratford Warriors sit in fourth place with 10 points. The Listowel Cyclones are in third place with 11 points, the Chatham Maroons and the St. Thomas Stars are tied for second place with 16 points each, and the St. Mary's Lincolns sit on top of the standings with 18 points.

The Rockets are one point behind the Vetd with seven points, and the Sarnia Legionnaires sit at the bottom of thes standings with zero points.

stories.title: More damaging AI hacking incidents to come unless changes are made, scientists warn
stories.summary: Reports of rogue AI agents have helped fuel widespread public alarm about AI safety.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Dozens of Canadian academics are among an international group of scientists calling for better containment measures for AI models.

“Multiple organizations have disclosed high-profile security failures: their AI models bypassed insufficiently sandboxed environments to compromise the systems of external organizations,” they say in an open letter.

The letter, released Tuesday, says that unless immediate changes are made to how AI is developed and deployed, “such incidents will continue to occur, and future incidents will be far more damaging to our exposed critical infrastructure.”

They say there is a need for more research on AI safety as well as emphasis on containment technologies and procedures. The scientists also want to see an international body that standardizes best practices.

“In the short term, strong sandboxing mechanisms including airgapping (disconnecting from the internet) should be used to provide high-assurance containment of cyber-capable AI models,” the letter says.

The Canadian signatories to the letter include AI pioneers Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton, as well as Nicolas Papernot and Catherine Régis, who co-lead the research program at the Canadian AI Safety Institute. Johns Hopkins University professor Gillian Hadfield, who was recently named to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s new AI advisory council, is also on the list.

Reports of rogue AI agents have helped fuel widespread public alarm about AI safety. OpenAI disclosed over the summer that its AI agents hacked AI startup Hugging Face without being instructed by any human to do so.

The incident report details “aggressive attempts” to access public data on Canadian and U.S. government web pages.

That was followed by other disclosures. Anthropic said its artificial intelligence models hacked into three other organizations during testing. Meta disclosed that one of its AI models accessed the internet on its own and hacked another company. And Google confirmed its Gemini AI model hacked three companies as part of a test of its cybersecurity capabilities.

A San Francisco-based lab that monitors AI activity said in a report on Sept. 30 that the website for Library and Archives Canada was one of the targets of a failed hacking attempt by an artificial intelligence agent.

Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon said in September he spoke with his international counterparts in the G7 about setting up a “technology stability board” that would evaluate AI models for testing.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Coroner's inquest set to begin examining death of Toronto woman who fell from balcony
stories.summary: Toronto - A coroner's inquest is set to begin today to examine the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - A coroner’s inquest has begun to examine the death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet, a Toronto woman who fell from a highrise balcony while police were in her home more than six years ago.

Korchinski-Paquet, a woman of Ukrainian, Black and Indigenous ancestry, died on May 27, 2020 after police responded to calls about a family dispute at the apartment. She was 29.

Inquest counsel say Korchinski-Paquet had been diagnosed with epilepsy and experienced seizures earlier that day.

Roger Shallow says the inquest’s scope includes how police and first responders are informed about epilepsy and how to ensure safety when a person’s behaviour may be influenced by postictal delirium, a condition that may occur in the period after a seizure.

He says the inquest will not look into general mental health challenges or psychiatric care, however, or the investigations by various police watchdogs into the case.

Shallow says Korchinski-Paquet’s death was “sudden and profoundly tragic” and no matter what the jury concludes, her family has been left to grapple with a loss no one should experience.

Korchinski-Paquet’s death came on the heels of the police killing of George Floyd, a Black man from Minneapolis, spurring further protests amid growing calls to defund the police.

It also cast a spotlight on how police interact with people experiencing mental health crises.

Ontario’s police watchdog investigated the case and eventually cleared Toronto police of wrongdoing in Korchinski-Paquet’s death. The Special Investigations Unit found it happened as she was trying to move from her apartment balcony to an adjacent one.

The inquest was announced earlier this year and is slated to last 14 days, with 13 witnesses expected to take the stand. Korchinski-Paquet’s mother, father and brother have been named as potential witnesses, as have five of the six police officers who attended the scene.

The inquest jury does not assign criminal responsibility but may make recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths in the future. The chief coroner’s office does not have the authority to impose the recommendations, however.

On the anniversary of her death this year, Korchinski-Paquet’s parents joined advocates in calling for the recommendations issued in coroner’s inquests to be binding and implemented within a reasonable timeframe.

Her mother, Claudette Beals, also said there should be a different system in place to investigate allegations of wrongdoing against police officers, adding she has no faith in “police investigating police.”

“My daughter’s been gone for six years and no one’s held responsible for that,” she said in a news conference at the provincial legislature.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Poilievre to campaign for Canadian unity in Alberta next week ahead of referendum
stories.summary: Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says he will be in Alberta next week to deliver a speech on Canadian unity ahead of the province’s referendum on separation. Poilievre told a press conference in Burlington, Ont., today he will be doing “additional campaigning on the ground.” When asked about tech industrialist Elon Musk saying recently that Alberta, […]
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Friday he will be in Alberta just days before the province’s referendum to deliver a speech on Canadian unity.

The House of Commons will be on a break next week after MPs head back to their ridings for the Thanksgiving weekend.

Poilievre is scheduled to deliver his speech during the Canada Strong and Free Network conference in Calgary on Oct. 16. His speech is expected to be followed by an address from Alberta Premier Danielle Smith.

The schedule lists the title of Poilievre’s speech: “The Canadian Drift: Reclaiming Confidence, Abundance and Freedom for Alberta.”

Poilievre told a press conference in Burlington, Ont., on Friday he will be doing “additional campaigning on the ground” in Alberta.

“We encourage all Canadians of all parties to join in uniting all Canadians to make ourselves safe, affordable, and fully independent here at home,” Poilievre said.

When asked about tech industrialist Elon Musk saying recently that Alberta, Saskatchewan and Quebec should separate, Poilievre said “Canadians control their own destiny.”

“Frankly, people can tweet whatever they want, but tweets and memes do not affect Canada. What affects Canada is the decisions made by the Canadian people,” he added.

The premiers of Alberta and Saskatchewan brushed off Musk’s comments, while Quebec’s new premier has said he won’t trigger a separation vote while U.S. President Donald Trump is in office.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said the future of Canada will be decided by Canadians when asked Thursday about Musk’s comments at a press conference in Sherbrooke, Que.

While Musk was born in South Africa, he holds Canadian citizenship because his mother was born in Saskatchewan. He has lived previously in Canada.

Alberta Conservative MP Dane Lloyd has been tasked with leading the federal Conservatives’ unity campaign in the province.

Responding to reports in The Globe and Mail about Alberta separatists allegedly seeking the help of the U.S. government in exchange for potential water rights and oil royalties, Lloyd said Monday “no one has the right to promise away Alberta’s birthright.”

Lloyd stopped short of describing that activity as foreign interference, saying more information needs to be gathered.

Mitch Sylvestre of the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project denied offering oil and water rights to the U.S. in his group’s three conversations with U.S. State Department officials in Washington. He also said he only attended one of those meetings.

Albertans will vote on the prospect of a future separation referendum, along with nine other questions involving constitutional and immigration issues, on Oct. 19.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

— With files from Jack Farrell in Edmonton.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Couche-Tard buying fuel retail sites from Irving Oil in Quebec and Ontario
stories.summary: Laval - Alimentation Couche-Tard Inc. has announced a deal to buy dozens of retail sites from Irving Oil in Quebec and Ontario.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The acquisition includes 50 locations in Quebec already operated by Couche-Tard under an alliance with New Brunswick-based Irving, as well as two in eastern Ontario.

Laval, Que.-based Couche-Tard is also buying 18 cardlock sites serving commercial customers like truckers, 16 of which would be on the same site as retail outlets.

Article continues below

Discover St. Nicholas Street: Toronto's hidden culinary gem

In addition, the deal covers fuel supply to 71 retail sites owned and operated by Couche-Tard in Quebec.

Couche-Tard did not say in a news release how much it is paying for the assets.

It says the deal is subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals, including under the Competition Act.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

stories.title: Top court sets sentencing framework for cases involving Indigenous offenders, victims
stories.summary: Ottawa - The Supreme Court of Canada says in cases where an Indigenous offender commits an offence against an intimate partner who is an Indigenous woman, a judge must apply sentencing principles related to both Indigenous offenders and victims of crime in a harmonious way.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The Supreme Court of Canada says in cases where an Indigenous offender commits an offence against an intimate partner who is an Indigenous woman, a judge must apply sentencing principles related to both Indigenous offenders and victims of crime in a harmonious way.

In a 5-4 judgment Friday, the top court provided guidance and set out a new framework for determining an appropriate sentence in such cases.

The court said Indigenous people are disproportionately and excessively imprisoned, while Indigenous women and girls suffer from unacceptably high levels of violence and abuse.

“Both of these pressing issues have been shaped by the experiences of colonization, and addressing them together is central to the ongoing process of reconciliation,” Justice Michelle O’Bonsawin wrote on behalf of the majority.

Parliament has tried to address both concerns through the criminal sentencing process, the top court noted.

In light of the phenomenon of Indigenous over-incarceration, a Criminal Code provision that took effect in the 1990s directs judges to consider sanctions other than prison that are reasonable in the circumstances. The court pointed out particular attention is to be paid to the circumstances of Indigenous offenders.

The court also underscored the importance of two provisions added to the Criminal Code more recently. One requires a sentencing judge to squarely consider the objectives of denunciation and deterrence when the offence involves the abuse of a person who is vulnerable because, for example, they are an Indigenous woman or girl.

Another section directs a judge sentencing an offender for abuse of their intimate partner to consider the increased vulnerability of women and girls, and to pay particular attention to those who are Indigenous, the court noted.

Sentencing circles may include participants such as the offender, lawyers, the sentencing judge, Elders, the victim or their proxy and community members with knowledge of the offender. The top court said information gleaned from a circle can help the sentencing judge properly apply the principles specific to Indigenous offenders and victims.

The court said although the sentencing provisions invite engagement with distinct Indigenous perspectives on crime and punishment, they do not create a parallel regime for Indigenous offenders, and the consideration of Indigenous perspectives cannot displace a sentencing judge’s authority and responsibility under the Criminal Code.

The court said the sentencing judge must take three specific steps in such cases.

First, the judge must assess the gravity of the offence and the degree of responsibility of the offender in light of the Indigenous backgrounds of the parties.

Second, the judge must sensitively identify the relevant criminal sentencing objectives, emphasizing denunciation and deterrence, while still considering other relevant sentencing objectives.

Third, the judge must select the proportionate and just sentence in light of the Indigenous context, given that Parliament has expressly directed sentencing judges to consider all available sanctions other than imprisonment.

The top court added that the sentencing circle process can be relevant to understanding the availability of alternative sentencing options in the community, as well as the community’s perspective on the sentence that would best achieve the objectives.

The court said the sentencing methodology in such cases is not a mathematical formula but a guide to help judges take into account the circumstances of Indigenous offenders and the vulnerability of Indigenous women and girls to abuse and violence.

“Proportionality requires due attention to the circumstances of the offender and of the victim in light of relevant sentencing objectives,” O’Bonsawin wrote. “The appropriate balancing will inevitably vary depending on the specific circumstances of the offence.”

The ruling comes in the case of Harry Arthur Cope, a Mi’kmaq man with severe mental health challenges who was sentenced to five years in prison after pleading guilty in 2022 to aggravated assault against his partner, a Mi’kmaq woman.

The Nova Scotia Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to three years. The Supreme Court ruled Friday the three-year sentence should stand.

The top court found the sentencing judge did not recognize that the offender’s mental illness contributed to the commission of the aggravated assault and did not consider the effect of that illness on the relevant sentencing objectives.

The sentencing judge would have settled on a shorter prison term had she properly considered the offender’s significant mental health issues, particularly when viewed in light of a sentencing circle’s recommendations in the case, the Supreme Court said.

The four dissenting Supreme Court judges said the Crown’s appeal should be allowed and the original sentence imposed by the sentencing judge restored.

They said the majority’s sentencing framework fails to reflect Parliament’s direction to sentencing judges to prioritize denunciation and deterrence, and to generally impose harsher sentences for the abuse of vulnerable victims, including Indigenous women and girls.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 9, 2026.

Braves will battle the Dolphins tonight while the Merchants visit the Firebirds and the Trojans host the Spitfires.

PJHL - All of Oxford County's Junior C hockey teams will kick off the Thanksgiving long weekend on the ice.

The Norwich Merchants will visit the New Hamburg Firebirds tonight, while the Tavistock Braves host the Dorchester Dolphins and the Thamesford Trojans host the Aylmer Spitfires. The Trojans will be looking for a comeback after suffering a 7-1 loss to the Petrolia Flyers last night.

The Braves and the Merchants will be back in action tomorrow with the Merchants visiting Dorchester and the Braves battling the Firebirds in New Hamburg.

All of the games have 7:30 p.m. start times.

The Braves are on top of the Doherty Division standings with 14 points, followed by the Wellesley Applejacks and the Firebirds with 10 points each. The Paris Mounties are in third place with seven points, only one ahead of the fourth place Merchants with six points. The Dolphins are in fifth place with four points and the Hespeler Shamrocks are at the bottom of the standings with three points.

The Trojans are tied with the Lucan Irish for fourth place in the Yeck Division standings with four points each, only one ahead of the last place Port Stanley Sailors. The Spitfires are tied with the Exeter Hawks for third place with eight points each and the Flyers are in second place with nine points. The North Middlesex Stars and the Mount Brydges Bulldogs are tied at the top of the standings with 12 points each.

The Navy Vets will host the Rockets tonight and visit the Redhawks tomorrow night.

WOODSTOCK/CAMBRIDGE - The Woodstock Navy Vets have two games scheduled for the Thanksgiving long weekend.

They will kick everything off with a home game against the Strathroy Rockets tonight. The puck will drop at 7:45 p.m. at Southwood Arena and it's also Breast Cancer Awareness Night, so fans are encouraged to wear pink to show their support.

The Vets will also be in Cambridge tomorrow to face the Redhawks. That game will get underway at 7:00 p.m. at Galt Arena Gardens.

Woodstock is currently in a five-way tie for fifth place in the Western Conference standings. The Vets have eight points so far and the same goes for the Listowel Cyclones, the Elmira Sugar Kings, the LaSalle Vipers, and the Komoka Kings. The London Nationals are in fourth place with nine points, while the St. Thomas Stars and Chatham Maroons are tied for second place with 14 points each. The St. Marys Lincolns sit on top of the standings with 16 points.

The Sarnia Legionnaires are at the bottom of the standings with zero points, while the Strathroy Rockets have three points and the Stratford Warriors have four points.

stories.summary: Police say a transport truck left the road and went about 40 yards into the ditch.
stories.author: Marcie Culbert
stories.content:
News Home

Friday, 9 October 2026 06:44

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

Police say a transport truck left the road and went about 40 yards into the ditch.

THAMES CENTRE - No one was hurt after a single vehicle crash involving a transport truck in the westbound lanes of Highway 401 in Thames Centre.

Sergeant Ed Sanchuk posted a video about on the OPP West Region X page at around 3:00 p.m. yesterday.

"Just shortly after 1:00 p.m. this afternoon, Middlesex County OPP officers responded a report of a transport truck that left the roadway and went approximately 40 yards into the ditch that you see over here."

He said one lane was closed so heavy tow truck operators could help retreive the transport truck. The other two lanes remained open, but the crash did cause some backups on the highway.

No further details have been released.

Aucun blessé n'est à déplorer. #WROPP ^es — OPP West Region (@OPP_WR) October 8, 2026

stories.title: Montreal mayor says city will offer 3,000 spots in emergency shelters for unhoused
stories.summary: Montreal - Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada says the city is planning to provide 3,000 beds in emergency shelters to address homelessness this winter.
stories.author: Erika Morris The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada said the city is planning to provide about 3,000 spots in emergency shelters to address what she calls the biggest humanitarian crisis the city is facing: homelessness.

“I won’t leave anybody in the street to die from the cold. That’s my promise. So whatever we need to do, we’ll do it,” she said at a news conference Thursday.

The city will set up the 3,000 spots in nine winter warming centres, open 24/7, in seven of its boroughs. Martinez Ferrada says that shelters must be able to provide round-the-clock services, rather than requiring vulnerable individuals to move from one location to another throughout the day.

The mayor said some of the 3,000 spots would be chairs, and was unable to confirm how many would be beds.

She said the city purchased 350 new beds for the new emergency warming centres, which she said were needed since many people who used emergency shelters in recent years had to sleep on chairs.

“Everyone deserves to sleep in a bed,” she said.

The anticipated 3,000 spots are in addition to existing shelters and resources for the unhoused run by community organizations.

The city is not planning to add any new emergency beds in the Hochelaga neighbourhood in the east-end of Montreal, which currently has an encampment with about 200 tents.

It said it wants to ensure resources for those experiencing homelessness are distributed more evenly across the Montreal area.

Last November, the city had about 2,500 spots in emergency shelters and warming centres. Martinez Ferrada had said her administration added 500 added spaces by Christmas, for a total of about 3,000 spots.

“No other city in Quebec has this much capacity,” said the mayor.

The Quebec government estimated there were just over 12,000 people living on the street in the province in 2025, and that about 42 per cent of the province’s unhoused population lives in Montreal.

According to the mayor, Montreal needs about $20 million to put its emergency plans in place.

“I really do hope that this is the last winter that we’ll be waiting for funding, knowing that the winter comes every year. Community organizations need that certainty to retain their teams and workforce and plan ahead,” she said.

She added that she believes the city will get the funding it needs after the premier-designate, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, promised to make homelessness a top priority.

The city’s announcement comes after a woman died in an encampment in the Montréal-Nord borough early Wednesday following a fire.

“It kept me awake two nights in a row to think about what we can do more, and how to do it faster,” the mayor said.

St-Pierre Plamondon reacted to the news of the death on social media Wednesday, saying he is “making the fight against homelessness a personal matter.” He wrote that his government will provide the funding needed for this winter. At a separate news conference on Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he would collaborate with the incoming Parti Québécois government on the issue.

Representatives of community organizations say they welcome the additional resources to tackle a problem they say is becoming increasingly complex. However, they say all levels of government need to commit to building more transitional housing and fund services like addiction treatment centres and mental health support to get people off the street.

The mayor called on the government to increase funding for transitional housing, adding that the city is working on building 2,000 units.

Sam Watts, CEO of the Welcome Hall Mission, told reporters that the city has been efficient at planning ahead but that there is a need for permanent solutions.

“We don’t want anybody to be born in the street or die in the streets, but I also don’t anybody to live in the street,” he said. “You heard the word transition housing over and over again. That is really the solution, to get people … back into permanent housing rather than a whole series of emergency measures, which are very costly.”

Émilie Fortier, director of homelessness services at the Old Brewery Mission, said that rent and housing prices are an additional barrier, with affordable units becoming harder to find.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Stelco begins issuing layoff notices as first job cuts set to take effect Sunday
stories.summary: Hamilton - The union representing workers at Stelco Holdings Inc.'s steel plant in Hamilton, Ont., says the company has started issuing individual layoff notices, with more expected before the end of the week.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Hundreds of southern Ontario steelworkers facing layoffs will be recalled if Canada and the United States reach a trade deal on steel, the head of Stelco’s U.S.-based parent company said Thursday.

Lourenco Goncalves, chairman and chief executive of Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs, said the Canadian market is too small to support galvanized steel production from both Stelco and ArcelorMittal Dofasco, along with imports.

“There’s not enough orders there for us,” he said. “You can’t operate in an efficient and profitable way running at 50 or 55 per cent capacity. That’s what we have been facing with galvanized steel.”

He said he has spent more than a year and a half pushing Ottawa for stronger protections against foreign steel imports, arguing that measures adopted so far have helped the hot-rolled steel market but have not gone far enough to protect galvanized steel producers.

Stelco announced plans last week to lay off up to 500 workers across its Hamilton and Lake Erie facilities, citing the ongoing trade crisis, weak demand and continued import pressure.

Stelco’s Hamilton Works produces cold-rolled and galvanized steel. The company plans to idle both operations.

The company began issuing individual layoff notices in Hamilton on Wednesday, with about 90 workers expected to receive notices this week, said Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers local 1005, which represents unionized workers at the Hamilton plant.

The first layoffs will take effect Sunday, with roughly 330 Hamilton workers expected to be affected over the next three weeks, along with additional cuts at Lake Erie Works and among co-op workers, Wells said.

“It’s a temporary layoff,” Goncalves said. “I do believe that one day we’re going to have a trade deal, I just don’t know when.

“Once this trade deal is reached and we’re back and able to produce and sell galvanized steel, we will bring back these people.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly sent a letter to Stelco president Paul Simon on Monday demanding a plan outlining how Cleveland-Cliffs will honour the legally binding commitments it made when it acquired the steelmaker in 2024.

The commitments include maintaining at least the same number of unionized employees and the vast majority of non-unionized employees for five years.

Joly rejected the suggestion that U.S. tariffs and changing market conditions relieve the company of those obligations, noting that Goncalves has publicly supported the tariffs.

Goncalves called her comments “totally unfair” and “just playing with words.”

While he described U.S. Section 232 tariffs as “the most successful policy implemented on trade in the United States ever,” he also argued that Canada should adopt similar protections for its own steel industry.

Goncalves said he has long advocated for “Fortress North America,” an approach aimed at protecting steelmakers in both countries from foreign imports, while restoring U.S. market access for Canadian galvanized steel.

“What would be the goal?” he said. “To protect the Canadian steel industry the same way we’re protecting the American steel industry, and the consequences are all positive.”

Goncalves said Cleveland-Cliffs will respond to Joly’s letter by Tuesday, within the five-business-day deadline set by the minister.

He said the company is preparing two submissions: one responding to Joly’s demand for a plan to meet its commitments and a second, more detailed document containing commercially sensitive information that he said would be protected under the Investment Canada Act.

He declined to disclose the contents of either submission.

Meanwhile, at Stelco’s Lake Erie Works in Nanticoke, Ont., John McElroy said between 40 and 50 workers could be laid off as early as Oct. 24 as the company reduces operations on its steel pickling lines.

Lake Erie Works produces steel from raw materials, including iron ore, and rolls it into coils that are sold to customers or sent to Hamilton for further processing and coating. Its pickling lines remove surface oxidation from hot-rolled steel.

“There’s no real good paying jobs out here and a lot of my co-workers are the breadwinner of the family,” said McElroy, president of United Steelworkers Local 8782, which represents unionized workers at the plant.

“They’re quite worried.”

McElroy said the union is working with management to reassign affected employees to other jobs normally performed by outside contractors.

Meanwhile, Wells said workers at the Hamilton plant feel betrayed.

“We feel we’re being used as pawns,” he said, referring to the ongoing trade dispute between Canada and the United States. “This is all done for political theatre.”

He added: “This is a manufactured crisis. They’re trying to get our federal government’s attention to get a favourable trade deal.”

Goncalves defended the layoffs as a temporary measure aimed at preserving more than 2,000 other jobs.

“I did not betray anyone,” he said. “I’m temporarily laying off 350 and I’m still hopeful that we’re going to have a trade agreement and I can bring these 350 workers back and continue to grow.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in Literature
stories.summary: Celebrated Canadian poet Anne Carson has won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:

By Nicole Thompson The Canadian Press

Anne Carson, the Toronto-born poet and scholar who’s said to have invented her own genre with work that blends the ancient and the avant-garde, has won the Nobel Prize in Literature.

The famously private Carson became the 123rd Nobel laureate in literature on Thursday, thrusting her somewhat reluctantly into the limelight, according to Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary to the Swedish Academy.

“We didn’t have much time to speak, and all she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland where she’s listening to the wind,” Carlberg said.

“She was taken by surprise, but very happy. I could hear that in her voice.”

Carlberg said the academy rewarded Carson for her “bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney commended Carson on social media, calling her win “a proud moment for Canada.”

“With wit, imagination, and a style entirely her own, Canadian poet Anne Carson has reimagined the classics. She has brought ancient stories to new audiences and transformed the way we think about literature,” Carney wrote on X.

A poet, essayist, classical scholar and translator, Carson is renowned as a master of esoterica. She’s defied literary conventions with a bibliography of more than 20 books of poetry, essays, plays, libretti and translations of ancient Greek texts.

“Almost all her literary production has centred upon the intersection between the philologist’s obsession with words and the poet’s desire for new meaning,” said Anders Olsson, chair of the Nobel committee for literature.

She’s amassed a devoted readership and a raft of critical accolades, including two Griffin Poetry Prizes, a Governor General’s Literary Award, the T.S. Eliot Prize for Poetry, a MacArthur “genius grant” and a Guggenheim Fellowship.

Elizabeth Harvey, a retired English professor at the University of Toronto, described how Carson manages to “invent and reinvent form.”

“She takes things that don’t look like poetry, like a lecture or an essay, and makes it into poetry,” she said, pointing to Carson’s lyric essays.

“They look like prose pieces, but they’re really deeply poetic in their sensibility.”

But as Carson’s profile has grown over four decades, the particulars of her personal life have remained elusive.

Her public reticence is encapsulated by her scant book-jacket biography: “Canadian poet, essayist and translator of Greek mythology.”

Carson was born in Toronto in 1950 and various accounts suggest she studied classics at the University of Toronto, and has held teaching positions at institutions including McGill University, Michigan University and Princeton University.

The Swedish Academy confirmed her year and city of birth, but offered few other details.

Concetta Principe, an assistant professor of English at Trent University who wrote a book on Carson, recalled first reading the writer’s author bio.

“It was like two sentences. That’s unusual,” she said. “In that way, it signified humility — that’s how I saw it initially, and I do still feel that to be the case with her.”

But Principe said she also sees it as a statement about the role of the author.

“We associate what’s on the page with the writer. We think it’s the writer’s life story that we’re reading, and that brings us close to the writer,” she said.

“I think her resistance to sharing is a way of reminding us that even if we think we have found her, even if we had all her biography, we still wouldn’t grasp where she is in the text, (or) what of her life is really there.”

After Carson’s PhD thesis in 1981, she made her publishing debut in 1986 with academic essays on love, “Eros the Bittersweet.”

That book was formative for Louis Ruprecht, director of the Hellenic Studies Institute at Georgia State University.

He said he picked it up when he was a newly minted PhD studying Sappho.

“I was mesmerized and blown away by the book. And when I got back to Atlanta, I wrote her a fan letter,” Ruprecht recalled.

She responded, and they corresponded for a while, he said. They talked mostly about the work — “we had Sappho in common,” he said.

Carson gained recognition with a series of genre-bending books in the 1990s establishing her style of culling from the literary canon to explore eternal themes. She invoked influences ranging from the Brontë sisters to the Greek poet Stesichorus in the early sixth century BC.

Carson cemented her reputation with her 1998 novel in verse, “Autobiography of Red,” which reimagines the 10th labour of Hercules, telling the life story of the monster he slays, Geryon.

Carson became the inaugural Canadian winner of the Griffin Poetry Prize for “Man in the Off Hours” in 2001, and was awarded England’s T.S. Eliot Prize for “The Beauty of the Husband” the same year.

In 2014, Carson took the Griffin again for “Red Doc>,” a quasi-sequel to “Autobiography of Red.” It made her the first two-time winner of the prize.

At the time, she told The Canadian Press she was surprised to win, partly because she doesn’t “really like the book” and partly because she’d already won the honour and “thought it wouldn’t be fair” to get it again.

“I don’t mean it’s a bad book,” she said. “I mean, I don’t know if it’s a good book or a bad book. I just have a vision when I start of what a thing is and sometimes it gets there and sometimes it doesn’t.”

Scott Griffin, the award’s benefactor, said Thursday that Carson’s win is a win for Canada and Canadian poetry.

“Anne Carson has raised the profile of poetry to its rightful place, in my opinion, right to the pinnacle of literature,” he said.

Griffin got to know Carson a little bit when they travelled to Edinburgh together after she won the inaugural prize.

“On stage, she tends to come through — sometimes, for some people — as a little bit severe,” he said. “But she’s very warm and loves to have fun.”

Carson also prevailed in the poetry category at the 2020 Governor General’s Literary Awards for “Norma Jeane Baker of Troy,” which in trademark style blends the story of Helen of Troy with elements from Marilyn Monroe’s life. She was shortlisted again two years later for “H of H Playbook,” a retelling of Euripides’s Greek tragedy, Herakles.

Among her more recent books is 2024’s “Wrong Norma,” her first original work since 2016. The collection of “poetic prose pieces” was published alongside her own illustrations.

Carson is the second Canadian woman to be named a Nobel laureate in the literature category, following short story master Alice Munro’s 2013 win.

The American playwright and novelist Saul Bellow, who was born in Montreal and grew up in Chicago, was awarded the Nobel in 1976.

The prize is worth 12 million Swedish kronor, or roughly $1.7 million.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 8, 2026.

stories.title: Lawyer seeks order forcing Quebec legislature members to swear oath to the King
stories.summary: Montreal - Lawyers are asking Quebec Superior Court to grant an emergency order that would force the new crop of elected members of the provincial legislature to swear an oath of allegiance to the King.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
MONTREAL - Lawyers are asking Quebec Superior Court to grant an emergency order that would force the new crop of elected members of the provincial legislature to swear an oath of allegiance to the King.

Lawrence David and the Consumer Law Group are asking the court to stay the application of a 2022 law that made swearing the oath optional.

The Quebec legislature adopted the law after Parti Québécois members were temporarily barred from taking their seats after they refused to swear allegiance to King Charles.

David argues that politicians who don’t swear the oath won’t be constitutionally entitled to sit in the legislature, and the laws they pass will have no legal effect.

David has already filed a challenge against the law, and believes its application should be suspended to make incoming legislature members take the oath until the case is heard on its merits.

The Parti Québécois won a minority mandate in Monday’s election, and leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has already said he will once again refuse to swear allegiance to the King.

The PQ leader also said he’s seeking legal advice on how to further cut ties with the monarchy, including stripping the lieutenant-governor of her roles and funding.

“There’s something abnormal about a foreign king coming to tell us what to do right at the start of a legislative term, a mandate,” he told reporters Tuesday. “People might say it’s symbolic, but I would reply that it’s still totally abnormal.”

Bill 4, adopted in 2022, amended a section of the 1867 Constitution Act to exempt Quebec from the section that requires the oath.

David argues that the law infringes on Quebecers’ right to vote and right to effective representation, because they’ll be represented by politicians “who are not constitutionally qualified to hold office and whose votes on legislation and other activities in the National Assembly are constitutionally void,” the stay application reads.

He believes the constitutional amendment included in the law requires the consent of the federal government and all Canadian provinces.

David said the hearing date for his stay request hasn’t yet been set, but he will ask for a decision to be delivered before the legislature reconvenes in mid-November.

David is also prepared to file more legal challenges if the Parti Québécois follows up on its plans to break from the monarchy, “including any attempt to unilaterally abolish the office of lieutenant governor,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.
paragraphs: MONTREAL - Lawyers are asking Quebec Superior Court to grant an emergency order that would force the new crop of elected members of the provincial legislature to swear an oath of allegiance to the King.
Lawrence David and the Consumer Law Group are asking the court to stay the application of a 2022 law that made swearing the oath optional.
The Quebec legislature adopted the law after Parti Québécois members were temporarily barred from taking their seats after they refused to swear allegiance to King Charles.
David argues that politicians who don’t swear the oath won’t be constitutionally entitled to sit in the legislature, and the laws they pass will have no legal effect.
David has already filed a challenge against the law, and believes its application should be suspended to make incoming legislature members take the oath until the case is heard on its merits.
The Parti Québécois won a minority mandate in Monday’s election, and leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has already said he will once again refuse to swear allegiance to the King.
The PQ leader also said he’s seeking legal advice on how to further cut ties with the monarchy, including stripping the lieutenant-governor of her roles and funding.

“There’s something abnormal about a foreign king coming to tell us what to do right at the start of a legislative term, a mandate,” he told reporters Tuesday. “People might say it’s symbolic, but I would reply that it’s still totally abnormal.”
Bill 4, adopted in 2022, amended a section of the 1867 Constitution Act to exempt Quebec from the section that requires the oath.

David argues that the law infringes on Quebecers’ right to vote and right to effective representation, because they’ll be represented by politicians “who are not constitutionally qualified to hold office and whose votes on legislation and other activities in the National Assembly are constitutionally void,” the stay application reads.
He believes the constitutional amendment included in the law requires the consent of the federal government and all Canadian provinces.
David said the hearing date for his stay request hasn’t yet been set, but he will ask for a decision to be delivered before the legislature reconvenes in mid-November.

David is also prepared to file more legal challenges if the Parti Québécois follows up on its plans to break from the monarchy, “including any attempt to unilaterally abolish the office of lieutenant governor,” he said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

stories.title: FBI depicts Tumbler Ridge shooter's guns, including 'SKS' once confiscated by RCMP
stories.summary: An FBI complaint against a Washington state suspect accused of conspiring with the Tumbler Ridge mass shooter for months provides extensive new details about the guns that May have been used in the attack, and how the teenage killer May have obtained them.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree says it would be “irresponsible” to disclose what guns were used in the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting after an FBI complaint said the killer intended to use weapons including an SKS rifle, that had previously been confiscated by police.

The complaint against a Washington state suspect accused of conspiring with shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar for months provides extensive new details about the guns that may have been used in the attack in British Columbia, including a photo said to be the killer posing with a rifle on the day of the attack.

Gun expert Frank Grosspietsch, a retired RCMP weapons officer with the national weapons enforcement support team, identified a gun shown in a different set of photos in the complaint as a KRISS Vector, which was banned in Canada in 2024.

The photos were in the complaint setting out allegations against James Bryant, and the FBI said the photos were sent to Bryant by Van Rootselaar in 2025.

The complaint includes chats in which Van Rootselaar allegedly speaks of intending to use an SKS returned by police to carry out her “plan” for a mass killing.

Anandasangaree says an expert panel is reviewing whether to ban semi-automatic SKS weapons, but it’s “absolutely not” a political decision to withhold information about what guns were used in Tumbler Ridge on Feb. 10, when Van Rootselaar killed eight people, including five school students and an educational assistant before killing herself.

Neither the RCMP nor federal authorities have said what guns were used in the killings.

“This is in respect of the people that were tragically killed, the families who themselves were asking many, many questions,” Anandasangaree told reporters on Wednesday.

“And I think it would be irresponsible for me to give you bits and pieces of a very large set of investigations.”

The complaint sworn by an FBI agent in Seattle says Bryant, who is charged with conspiracy to murder in a foreign country, told officers that Van Rootselaar stole firearms and ammunition from her family’s gun safe and hid them in her room “in preparation for a mass shooting.”

It also says in claims not tested in court that 18-year-old Van Rootselaar told Bryant, 30, in online chats that she had convinced another person to purchase ammunition on her behalf.

The RCMP criminal investigation into the shooting is ongoing, despite Van Rootselaar having killed herself at the school.

Assistant RCMP Commissioner Elija Rain, who is acting commanding officer in B.C., said in a statement that “investigators have made substantial progress in the criminal investigation.”

Rain said the RCMP’s release of information about the case has recently been limited “because of the need to ensure our investigative theories and actions were not compromised.”

He attended a news conference in Seattle on Tuesday to discuss Byrant’s case, but he declined to answer questions about the guns, citing a publication ban in Canada.

Grosspietsch, who is a technical adviser to the Association of Firearm and Toolmark Examiners, said in an interview that photos sent by Van Rootselaar to Bryant in August last year show her with a KRISS Vector rifle.

“The firearms industry recognized that if they ‘sexied up,’ and I use that term liberally, firearms to look like military pattern-type firearms or have a bit of a mystique to it, they would sell. KRISS Vector is one of those types of firearms,” he said.

Grosspietsch said the same type of weapon could be seen in a photo of a gun safe shared on social media by Van Rootselaar’s mother, who was killed along with Van Rootselaar’s younger brother before Van Rootselaar headed to Tumbler Ridge Secondary School where the other victims were shot.

The FBI complaint released on Tuesday says Van Rootselaar told Bryant on the Discord platform that she possessed a 3D-printed foregrip, firearm magazines and a “switch” device for an SKS rifle, which the FBI says likely referred to a “machine-gun conversion device.”

Bryant, 30, of Bellingham, Wash., allegedly told the FBI that Van Rootselaar “ended up using some of these same items during the Tumbler Ridge shooting.”

Another photo in the complaint shows a Canuck brand shotgun, decorated with a sticker in the transgender pride colours of blue, pink and white.

Van Rootselaar was trans, and the FBI said Tuesday that Bryant is also trans and identifies as female.

Bryant allegedly tells Van Rootselaar: “Love the stickers … stickers would be so funny to be seen in photos of the incident.”

RCMP say in Canadian legal documents released in August that shotgun shell casings were strewn on the floor of the family home where Van Rootselaar killed her brother and mother and an empty shotgun was found nearby.

A photo in the Bryant complaint depicts a person the FBI says is Van Rootselaar, posing on their knees in a black miniskirt and fishnet stockings, while holding an olive-green rifle with a telescopic sight on the morning of the attack.

On the end of the barrel is what appears to be a suppressor, also decorated in blue, white and pink bands.

The FBI says that in December 2025, Van Rootselaar discussed another gun she said she was planning to use in the attack.

“The police knocked my SKS sights off zero a lil’ bit when they roughly confiscated it, so the gun has been hitting high and to the left,” she allegedly told Bryant.

Adjusting the sights would be “a lot of work and I may end up doing my plan with a gun with sights that are super off,” Van Rootselaar allegedly said, before adding “I’m sure I can still do fine.”

— With files by Chuck Chiang in Vancouver

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 7, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version incorrectly described the KRISS Vector rifle seen in an FBI complaint as a submachine-gun.
